The negative reviews on here and places like Metacritic baffle me.  This is a fantastic follow-up to the New Order (and the Old Blood) that hits nearly every note one could want from a Wolfenstein game--and I trace my Wolfenstein experiences back to a 5.25" floppy on the Commodore 64 through Wolf3D to this.  The majority of low-ratings seem to fall into one of two categories, either people upset with the subject matter or those complaining it's buggy.  Those in the first category couch their reviews by using terms like SJW/liberal/whatever, but at the end of the day it's pretty clear they're upset the game is about killing Nazis.  You can draw your own conclusions there.  For those in the second category, yes, there are some bugs.  It's a new game on PC.  When did PC players become helpless?  If you want a flawless experience that requires zero effort, play on consoles.  Years ago, any game worth its salt would require an hour of tinkering with a config.sys and autoexec.bat and all manners of voodoo to get it half working.  This stuff is easy nowadays and the bugs I saw with this game were easy to address.  I did see some crashes initially when modifying vsync settings, but perusing forums I found two things that fixed everything:  downloading NVidia's newest beta driver created specifically for this game and disabling async computation in video settings.  After that, I've had basically zero issues and they game has run very well.  As for the game itself, it's an example of what a narrative based single-player game should be.  Great writing, an interesting story, characters you actually care about, and plenty of twist-and-turns.  The gunplay is excellent and challenging, the graphics absolutely outstanding and the game even runs well even on mid-tier systems.  The weapons are weighty and satisfying.  I can't remember a better FPS in some time, in fact the last one this good was Doom and that had pretty much no story so for me this is better game.  There are a few little quirks, the extra character traists/skills are not really fleshed out super well via gameplay, stealth only works passably, and the writing is a little heavy handed at times, but on the whole this is a truly fantastic game and some of the most fun I've had in several years on the PC.   Basically, if you like story-driven FPS games like Half-Life or you played and enjoyed the New Order, you'll love this game.   If you want to ensure a wasteland consisting only of games with crappy  microtransactions and focused on multi-player  instead, then this game is not for you.

This game is not an FPS, it is a sci-fi survival horror game.  Survival here means you have resources you need to manage other than health and ammo.  You start out with only 90 minutes of oxygen so you need to keep track of how much you have and try to find a place to recharge before you run out, and sprinting uses 4x the oxygen so you have to be aware of your situation and decide whether it's more important to move fast or breathe longer.
Light is a limited resource that needs managed for survival, but also plays into the horror side of things.  Dark is scary and scary is good, but you can't see items, messages, or enemies in the dark so you need a flashlight to survive.  If you're using a flashlight it's not so dark and not so scary which is bad for horror.  So for middle ground between a scary dark ship and being able to see things and survive you only get 60 minutes of flashlight battery (non-rechargeable).  If you run out completely... good luck with that.
All gamers know with melee enemies and guns that backup+shoot=win.  To disrupt this equation there are boxes all over the ship that are collision enabled.  Here if you try and run backwards shooting you risk running into a box and getting caught by the bad guy if you don't jump over it fast enough.  This is an intentional feature designed to make you watch where you're going and prevent you from playing this like an FPS.  Remember where I said "this is not an FPS" earlier?
Additionally, enemies are very difficult to kill, especially in groups.  It imbues a sense helplessness in the player, and being helpless is scary.  In one variation of the storyline I ended up in a corridor filled with aliens yelling "F*CK YOU DIE DIE DIE! F*CK YOU DIE DIE DIE!" as I poured plasma rifle fire into the oncoming swarm and screamed "NOOOOOOOOO!" as I was overwhelmed and eaten.
Perma-death is listed in the features section and seems self explanatory, but I feel it needs reiterated because some people don't quite get how it works.  The game does save at loading screens so that you can quit and pick up the story later if you need to, but there is no manual saving or loading.  When you die though your last save point dies with you and you have to start a new game.  Having a save point to fall back on makes dying less of an imposition and alleviates the player's fear of dying and doesn't emphasize survival.
The game does lack some polish and is rough in some areas, but if you consider it was made by 1 developer with 0 budget, it is understandable.  He has been continually improving the game over time, releasing updates periodically.  He has also already released 1 free DLC and will be releasing another for Halloween as a token of appreciation to the customers and as an apology for the buggy release.  He's not perfect, but how many developers even bother to try and make things right with their customers?
Even if it is rough in places, the tension in the game is palpable.  I usually play games to relax, and I've got to say that I almost don't like playing this one because it keeps me wound up the whole time.  The biggest part is you don't know what's going to happen next.  The storyline is randomized, enemy spawns are randomized, the only thing you can be sure of from one game to the next is your own name, the location of some weapons/objects, and that you're on a big scary Ghostship.
Even the way you move is tense, difficult, and adds to the atmosphere.  You clunk along slowly in your heavy spacesuit with magnetic boots, and although you can "sprint" (I use that word loosely, its more like a fast jog) it is only for a couple seconds before you have to go back to walking speed.  After all, you are Dr. Jake Abbots from the Colonial Science Division, not a space Marine.
I recommend this game because it achieves its overriding goal, to scare you the entire time, and the randomized storyline is a novel idea that provides tons of hours of re-playability.  I've also posted a few technical considerations in the forums I didn't have room for here.
P.S. I HIGHLY recommend reading the
and watching the getting started video from the developer before playing the first time as you're thrown into the deep end on this game.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is very reminiscent of the legendary Diablo II, an action RPG combining both alot & fast action with character progression. I didn't get really hooked by the storyline, but the action keeps you moving forward. While there is quite some decent game time before you finish the game, the plot seems rather unfinished. Guess we need to wait until the follow-up game arrives.
Bought the game during a Steam sale, which included all three content DLC. The Blue Blood DLC was particularly useful as it improves the usability of Katerina, your ghostly sidekick. Both Thaumaturge and Arcane Mechanic DLC just add two new classes to play with instead of the default Hunter class. I only played the Hunter class as there wasn't much incentive (expect the odd class side quests) to replay the game with another class. Overall, the game is warmly recommended for both new and experienced action RPG fans.

Pro:
+ character progression via skills, auras, perks, capabilities...

+ loot, loot, loot!
Contra:
- character progression doesn't really matter, just stack melee or ranged skills and sweep through the game

- lots of crappy loot
- lack of replayability

An extremely addicting and visually stunning ARPG. Solid graphics and an extremely well designed world with a steampunk-noir feel. If you're a fan of Torchlight, PoE, Diablo (especially if you were left less than satisfied with Diablo 3) then this should be right up your alley.
The character development is pretty unique, in a very good way. Each skill offers various "powerups" which you can use during fights to better suit whatever challenge you face. This makes for a very fun combat system that I would love to see more of in the future. Besides skills, you also have the ability to use XP to purchase auras, tricks, and perks. Your companion, Katarina, has her own attributes as well as unique skills which you can select as she levels with you. This all combines to make for one of the most customizable games I've played in a while.
For this quality and the playtime which it offers this game is well worth the purchase, especially if you factor in the replay value which the DLC's bring with their addictional classes. This game seems to go on sale fairly frequently, so if you can manage to catch it during one of those times you'll be getting more than your moneys worth.

Honestly I preferred the old Gauntlet playstyle, where you had a lot of health, but it decayed over time.
The wizard is naturally the best class 10/10 but the weapons available for him a pretty weak, since in the end the best book is the starter.
I didn't like how most of the promotional stuff is for the warrior, the most button-mashing class in the game.
It's clear you are almost required to play with at least one other person, since the wizard is the only class that can reliably go the distance without taking damage, and he still can easily get overwhelmed.
Honestly, the amount of time it takes to unlock something isn't that bad, it's just that dying loses all your gold, which basically means that the whole point of having played a level gets ruined, other than to progress the story.
I sort of like/dislike death. While he looks cool, and the sounds he makes can be cool at times, his mechanic is bad. Having him instantly kill you, spawn every once and a while only on certain floor types, and chase you rather quickly is very annoying. I feel like the death from the original games was scarier, since it didn't act as a quick way to lose gold or the level, but the entire game itself.
Finally, I really don't like how little damage the characters do. In newer areas, the enemies have more health and are more numerous, meaning tanking as the warrior doesn't work as well, defeating most of the point to playing him.

Gauntlet, a series that instills nostalgia by the very name. I had waited a long time for the next title in the Gauntlet series to come out and wow players again. Granted most of the franchise never really recieved outstanding critical acclaim. However it still managed to captivate my friends and I with the likes of Gauntlet: Legends. Sadly the reboot doesn't quite live up to it's name but still manages to do a decent job of putting a different spin to series and still feeling familiar.
Soundtrack
To start the sound design is pretty much the lowest point of the game for me. The music is uninspired and doesn't try to enhance or go along with anything happening on the screen. None of it stands out. Every sound effect blends and when you have 4 people playing at once good luck figuring out who casted what and when.
Gameplay
In terms of gameplay my biggest gripe is the lack of variation. Despite being a newer Gauntlet I really felt like it succeeded in it's own way but in comparison to it's predessesors it is still weak. This version felt much more formuliac and it really retracted from the entire experience. While the others were similar in that they put you in an area to kill mob spawns, they had environmental variation and power ups that kind of kept things interesting. Better enemy types helped greatly there too. Somtimes simple is better. Moving on I really did not like the shared camera. In Co-Op that may be understandable but online its a dam shame and is annoying. I found the mage to be completely useless and I was dissapointed in the lack of level interactivity as well as character variety. Most secrets are found by blowing up the obvious wall with explosive barrels. A big let down when comparing it to past titles. I really enjoyed the death levels. The Grim Reaper himself chases you in these segments for the whole level and is a constant threat which made for tense and fun filled run throughs.
The game was just a mixed bag. I really feel with a little more thought put into it, it could have been the best in the franchise. But there are too many miss-steps. The bosses are lame. The 1st was interesting and the rest were C grade bosses. If I'm not mistaken there is a total of 3. With a mini-boss or two in some levels. What RPG has 3 bosses? Brutal disservice to the game especially when considering the length of the game. You could definitely reach the end within 4 hours easily. But still despite all this the game is still fun in it's own right and does feel like Gauntlet. It's just lacking the same charm. Even the shopping sucks. The lack of stats is one thing but saving to buy just a single set of weaponry that is good for the rest of the game after 3 levels is so stupid. As Valkyrie I just bought he 3rd weapon choice and was owning the game for the rest of the time. Balance is important. Which brings me to my next point. I flew through this but when I first bought it I guess it hadn't been optimised becasue I couldn't get past the second level. 2 years later I give it ago and I pretty much skip to end where I and 3 others ended up and suddenly we couldn't beat the last boss. It's stupidly more difficult than the rest of the game and comes with the most predictable ending.
Story
The ending was lame. The entire storyline is no different. In fact I didn't even catch a single word of it. I suppose that's not really what this game is about but the fact that there aren't many levels to counteract this is a real kicker.

beautiful.  another wonderful proof-of-concept for videogames as art.  though the game thrusts the player into a confusing universe without handholding directions every few seconds, i found myself immediately driven to understand it- and understand it entirely of my own volition.  too often, i fall into the trap of "i'm lost; time to look up a guide online."  here, however, i feel compelled to learn by DOING.  every switch in the cockpit has a very visceral look and feel; every tiny pixellated detail on the planet exudes a simple beauty.  the game is not about goals so much as it is about the process of exploration.  i may never find the solution to "side b" of my game, and that's ok.  just living in the universe 'mirror moon' sets out for me makes it all worth the time.

Absolutely amazing game, and what I feel is a good example of what happens when love is put into a project. It could've been that it hit all my marks for what I like to see in a game, all in aesthetics, in gameplay, and a great story. Though I feel like, overall, the presentation and the directing of certain scenes/gameplay was the most powerful part (the final battle particularly gave me chills; perfect way to set up a final fight).
Everything from the soundtrack, to the gritty atmosphere, and the constant sound of voices narrating everything you do--all of it only enhanced the experience and helped to create the world around Senua. To show they really paid attention, they made sure to implement psychosis into almost every little part of the game--from the puzzles to even the combat. Every environment in the game had me feeling what the protagonist should be feeling, every scene felt real and moving, and everything fell into place perfectly. The live action cut-ins were a bit strange, but they almost separated Senua's visions from everything else she was seeing, making her the clear focus.
Not to mention how great it felt to have a combat system that actually felt good. If you do it right, you feel like a badass, and if you do it wrong, you have an opportunity to learn from it. With the constant stress of death, but having the ability to stand back up after getting knocked down, only makes you that much more tenacious--something that Senua seems to reflect in the battles, and really, for most of her journey.
Overall amazing, I'm not too picky but I really thought this was an example of a nearly-perfectly done game (personal preferences aside), and for a great price too.

Wolfenstein 2: the new meh
Well, if the title is not a dead giveway, let me put it plainly
its… not that good, the plot is ok and somewhat fun, if frustrating at times (the game actually has a decent ending this time, though one that still leaves a lot to be desired and plenty of sequel hook); though its also a bit on the heavy side at times (as in 90% of this game’s playtime, at the least for me, was cut-scenes or cut-scenes disguised as gameplay); with the game itself being rather short when separated from cutscenes, having about 5-6 ‘areas‘ with diferent stages in them, though the stages mostly look and feel the same baring map layout changes and a few exceptions here and there; with a few extra bonus areas relegated to re-visit side missions… which are a big focus in this game, as outside of its plot missions its entirely built on you re-doing areas for side objectives.
gameplay wise its a confused mess that seems to not be able to decide between being a shooter and a stealth game, the BEST analogy I can think of is that you are an older stealth game protagonist (the kind that basically drops dead the moment they are seen) put on a high action shooter like DOOM… which does not work very well; speaking of DOOM, for more that the two are different games and that wolfenstein builds on the mechanics of the first game… DOOM has kind of became the benchmark I am judging the shooter mechanics by, as a lot of what wolfenstein 1 did, DOOM managed to do better, making the two have similar gameplay styles but DOOM be smoother and more fun to play; wolfenstein 2 DOES polish the first game’s issues a LOT, but it still falls painfully far from being anywhere near what DOOM did (their ridiculous focus on broken, poorly planned stealth does not help).
A lot of gameplay mechanics that would be considered baseline in other games (or even just good additions to the shooter formula) are locked behind the new ‘contraptions‘, of which you pick one at the halfway point of the game, and have to gather the rest on side missions afterwards… except you are not told the upgrades that come with each contraption, only their gimmick (and of the 3, only one has a somewhat useful gimmick… though they kind of ♥♥♥♥ that up too by making it less useful than it seems and finicky as♥♥♥♥♥♥
The weapon wheel is a ♥♥♥♥ing mess to use, specially since you have to manage it individually for each hand and there is NO slowdown while its open (unless you happen to get the right contraption… said contraption otherwise only found on a side mission unlocked right before the final mission of the game, otherwise)
basically, it takes the entire ♥♥♥♥ing game for you to reach baseline Doom marine/slayer levels (and the final level even has a BFG-like gun you can get right before the final ‘boss fight‘… that is actively worthless and useless and using it will just get you killed in seconds.)
ultimately, its an ok game, and has its fun moments, but the annoying and baffling♥♥♥♥♥♥design decisions overwrite a lot of its potential; it is most DEFINITELY not worth its inflated price atm; also, it is NOT recommended for people looking for a DOOM like experience or lacking in patience, you will find yourself wanting to strangle the developers by the 30th time you are all but forced to sneak around.
EDIT: It has been pointed out to me (and I have looked into it myself) that some of my issues with the game MIGHT be due to technical issues, as it has been pointed out, and I noticed myself, that I seem to having been taking more damage than I should have in comparison to gameplay videos.
I will keep looking to see if that is indeed an issue, and if it turns out to be the case I will change my review (though It will remain a negative one, as I still feel the game lacks content to match its inflated price)

My experience with the game so far:
The first hour was essentially just walking down a corridor really slowly, checking some rooms turning on a generator and other minor stuff. Even so it was pretty simple from a game mechanics point of view (i.e. no real puzzles to solve). I actually quite enjoyed this section. It feld authentic walking around that ship, following signs on the wall and getting a sense of the layout, there was no overly gamey stuff to distract you and the whole athmospere was really well done. There was some  jerkiness in the physics, but nothing to problematic in that first section of the game.
After that inital section I got a gun and then I died literally within 10 seconds of encountering the very first tiny enemy creature. Since the game has perma-death that means I have to restart from scratch now, no respawn, reload or anything is available.
Lets just say I consider it a suboptimal game design decision to have such a slow paced game married with quick permadeath. I am not recommending the game to anybody until that permadeath is removed.
Edit: Played a bit more, the permadeath can be "fixed" by manually copying the savegame, which can be found at:
...\SteamApps\common\GSaftermath\Binaries\Win32\gsstorysave0.sav
Just exiting the game and then resuming it before you get killed can also be used to re-roll what monsters appear.
As for the game itself, ammo is extremely rare and most enemies are far to fast to hit with any precision. Thus it's extremly easy and almost unavoidable to run out of ammo. There is no real means to sneak around enemies and enemies kill you extremy quickly. There are also numerous bugs, reloading your weapon will eat up all the ammo in you gun, even if full, and the weapon will get sometimes unequiped, which is hard to notice as you still see you character holding it, only a HUD tells you that it's not equpped.
Essentially whenever the game just lets you explore the ship and enjoy the athmosphere at a slow pace, it's really good. But whenever the monsters pop up, which sadly happens a lot, it's just a broken unplayable mess.
Edit2: Played now some more hours and actually reached the end after some 15 hours. The permdeath is as already mentioned really just completely unacceptable. The game is so full of glitches, bugs and just a general lack of polish so that you will die a lot. I can't imagine anybody having the patience to finish the game with permadeath. Even when the game would actually work and be polished, it's just far to long and far to slow to make permadeath an acceptable solution. This game needs a proper "Restart at Last Checkpoint", which would be trivial to implement and while it wouldn't turn this into a great game, it would at least turn it into a somewhat enjoyable game. Alt-Tab switching and copying savegames around is really not helping the atmosphere.
As for the ammo problem, that solved itself, as the game does respawn ammo every time you reenter a room, so all you have to do is find one of the tiny few location that has ammo and then enter and exit the section a few times to gear up. This feels a little cheap and goes completely against the games goal of feeling realistic and authentic, but at least it makes the game somewhat playable. Health packs respawn as well and the medical bay in general is full of goodies or at least it was on my playthrough.
The way the game handles enemy spawning is also pretty crappy, instead of having the aliens be permanent citizen of the spaceship, they respawn each time you enter a section. Furthermore they only spawn when you walk past specific trigger points, so even if you checked every corner, the game might still spawn an enemy right behind you without giving you any chance to detect it beforehand. In some spots the game will also spawn enemies out of thin air right in front of you.
Enemies themselves are also still far to hard to kill. The slower ones are ok, but all the fast spider creatures require a ton of luck, as while they aren't to hard to kill from a distance, they are completely impossible to kill with any precision when they went close range. You just end up spinning around and shooting at the ground hoping to hit something and more often then not you will simply die instead. The game doesn't have any kind of melee attack to kick enemies away and they can circle you faster then you can turn.
As for mission/task design, it's a bit lacklustre. There are some moments in the game, such as the very beginning, when the tasks that you are giving have an impact on the environment and feel organic. You switch on a generator and that gives you gravity and light and in turn completely transforms not only the look of the location, but also how you navigate it. However those tasks are very sparse throughout the game and most other tasks just feel like rather mundane fetch quests with no visible changes to the environment at all. There are no doors to unlock, no keycards to find, no puzzles that you have to solve or anything like that. It's just lots of going places, pushing buttons, then coming back and pushing more buttons. There is a lot of back and forth through the same location and some of it just feels like unnecessary filler, especially when you just go to a location for the AI to tell you were you have to go next, even so that AI happens to be in radio contact with you all there time and could have told you directly on where to go next instead of having a meaningless side trip.
As for story, there isn't much. As far as I can tell this game doesn't really have much in terms of audio logs or similar stuff to flesh out the background. I found a single log from a doctor and there is supposed to be another one from the captain that I didn't find, but that's about it. The rest of the crew doesn't seem to have left anything behind to read or look at, outside of the random graffiti on the wall, which however are all rather uninformative. All the little task you do over the course of the game, do however result in something in the end, so it's not like there isn't any payoff at all, but a little bit more backstory would have been nice.
The loading times are another problem, even so the game does have airlocks all over it that should make loading seamless, they game still kicks you to a loading screen when the airlock closes, so instead of being able to check your weapons and objectives, you have to stare at a boring loading screen. This hampers the flow of the game quite a bit, as while the loading times aren't very long, they are extremely frequent.
Overall this game isn't terrible, there are a lots of things to like. The atmosphere is great and being able to free roam a space ship is something you don't find in many (any?) other games. The whole exploration can feel a lot like Resident Evil 1 in parts, as you have a lot of freedom and really are left to your own navigation skills without any big arrows pointing the way, although the AI will give you objectives all the time. But the collision detection/physics are incredible buggy and some of the enemies terribly unbalanced, so you need a lot of tolerance for jank to distil some enjoyment out of this game. On top of that you have to deal with the whole permadeath issue, but at least you can work around that.
It looks like this game will receive some further patches and updates, so this is something to keep an eye on, but for the time being it has still a few to many issue to truly recommend it. If you really like the idea of open world space ship exploration, go for it, there are moments in this game were everything clicks together and it feels great, just don't expect those moments to last, as some bug or glitch will surely get in the way.
PS: It's also worth to mention that I so only did a single playthrough, the games story is however randomized, I don't know yet to what degree that will impact things and if some playthroughs are much better or worse then others.

*NOTE NOT A FINAL REVIEW, Since patches are coming to fix up the game. This review is for what it is right now. Devs are patching up and refining the game and are taking notes at the complaints itself. The only reason I thumbed this game down was for those issues that are in the game currently, The reason I thumbed this game up now is because the dev is taking his work seriously, listening to the community and actually making these fixes to make his game better. Which is the best thing a game dev can do.
So after speaking/playing with the dev who is very active with the community and actually playing the game for a good amount of hours I got a better understanding where the devs are getting at in the game. This is a hardcore survival horror that isn't meant to be finished in a single night and also meant to be a really hard game  since the devs goal is to give you the an immersive survival gameplay on a ship with changing enemies, a story that changes up a bit with random events . The game is actually a finished product but has bugs and issues that seriously needs to be ironed out which causes players to not want to progress too far. I am still playing the game as we speak overlooking the bug to see what the game has to offer deeper in. The only reason I didn't progress so far is because of the issues. Going in deeper I see this game has alot to offer.
The game itself is a ported off the rift version and  and was released so that we will get a chance to play it without having to use the rift (devs explained this  to me). The Vr version will be included in what you bought but due to this reason some bugs and problems does exist in this version.
So the game starts off with you entering a ship that was used as an experiment on prisoners when an alien lifeform overtook the ship and infected everyone on board. Your job is to get things operational again and to find out information about the lifeform to counter against it because it will be humanity's greatest threat. Many things are randomized in this game and it is never the same, the events, the branch of the story and the way the enemy are spawned at you.
The gameplay is a first person survival/ horror shooter which starts you off with 59 minutes of battery life, a full tank of oxygen and you'll probabaly be armed with a weapon if you get a certain branch. As you progress you'll find guns and supplies via the clues left by blood and writing on the wall along with hints about enemies  attack. So it has to be found and it is in limited quantity. The laser for the guns recharges slowly and the other weapons is limited by clips so you'll have to be careful on use and also on reload also because you could potentially empty a clip full of bullets from your best gun which will cause you to rely in the laser guns. The guns themselves j
The controls are fixed and feels much better. You can also play this game with a joypad but you cannot change the keybinds in any way. There is also no save function except for checkpoints or where you leave off so be careful
The game main goal is immersion which is very important for these type of games and that is the star here, the enemies jumping out of places, the sound effects is unlike anything you ever heard, the creepy music at times and the environment itself along with the game's roguelike elements where things arent the same makes it immersive and scary because you don't know what will pop out during your second plays after restarting either from death most likely or finishing which will cause you to second guess and panic.
While the strength lies in immersion, its weakness lies in the rest of the places. some of the  enemy's ai is fixed up a bit but can still get stuck in places, they are more effective now. The collision of you towards environments sometimes will cause you to jitter sometimes.
There are 8 guns in the game, each guns handle differently and each gun requires you to find, the guns starts off weaker than you think with the laser guns that are rechargable but takes some time to do so. They can be used to kill off weaker infected while the stronger guns found later will benefit you greatly against the stronger ones. You can shoot enemy in the head to kill them quicker and also the weak  guns has uses such as  using them to strategically light your way in dark areas so that you do not waste your batter power.
The graphics uses unreal engine, has some nice effects and shading at times but unfortunately does look a bit outdated and this is because it came from the rift version, it is supposed to look much better on the rift but looks decent on the non rift version.
Long story short I think this game was rushed just a bit and had some issues and problems that it came with that really needs to be ironed out, as the dev says he is fixing right now and also creating a manual for the community to help them a bit.
Overall I hope the game progress with updates as time goes on to polish it up, so far from just touching the game the game feels MUCH better than what is was previously. Hopefully when everything is done there will be a decent price sale that will gather more players into this great immersive game that is different everytime you play it.
+ Immersion is amazing even without occulus rift you can feel it, scary sounds, music and darkness will scare the crap out of you.
+ Limited supply of battery/oxygen will cause you to panic when things go wrong, thank god you can replenish oxygen but not light so be mindful and use your laser weapon to light your way strategically
+ Lightning and fog is done great well placed in places that will add to the immersion
+ The clues/writing lieing around to help you find what you need is well written to help give you hints
+ The objective is explained very well and its your goal to find the way. The ship is massive and offers places to explore. it is your job to learn how it works and find your way.
+Controls are much better after being fixed!
+- Map is hard to understand and will take time to get use to
+- Decent Ai
- Voice acting is just ok, its corny but fits the game perfectly (lol shaun)
- Needs ability to rebind your own key.
- Some clipping issues at places.
- Graphics looks good but are said to look even better on rift because of the way they are designed
- We can't get a rift yet.
* I really want the rift version to fully enjoy this game immersion, as for the version it is now hopefully the patches will fix up the problems players find unenjoyable at the moment.

I think its about time we get this out of the way off my review list.
Ghostship Aftermath is one of the better indie horror titles of this year. It even took me back a bit with the way the game feels from other games such as system shock 2. Now I understand that many people don't recommend this game due to higher expections or *too much money* or not finished. So really quickly, I wanna get the pro's and con's out of the way before I write a long paragraph.
Pros:
A good horror elemnt, aka The fear of the unknown.
A wide range of weapons.
It is different each playthrough.
A huge open world ship *Though the missions kinda make it hard to roam.*
A good nostalgia factor of both Dead Space and System shock 2.
VERY innovative, which is what helps with the horror.
All the features listen on the store page, are actually in the game, whether or not it's buggy, it's still listed.
Cons:
Poor AI
Unoptimised
Poor voice acting *I know it's one guy but eh, Im greedy.*
Average story.
So heres where the paragraph comes in, lemme start with the pros once more. In this game, while still using Jumpscares*Not loud noises though, so BIG bonus.* it creates the sort of feel of the unknown, especially when you are first trying the game. And while you may get used to the enemy encounter, you never know what to expect with each playthrough. You may have to go though the game without a single important chracter, or some missions are different, or even random encounters with things OUTSIDE the ship. My point is, this guy knows what makes good horror, and thats the fear of the unknown.
So while all that is nice and dandy, there are some flaws that may concern the audience, and that may be its AI. While the gameplay itself is really slow, the ai is VERY basic. Pretty much the ai does nothing but go at you, and once you touch the hitbox, you take damage, and that is it. No pathing, or anything really smart. On the bright side though, you get a wide range of enemies to deal with, whether it be big or small, they still proove to be a challenge to kill, especially in groups.
So I think that pretty much sums up the game in general. I hope this review helps your thinking of the game.

This is a game about exploration in space.  You awaken in a ship adrift in space with no recollection of how you got there or how to fly the ship.  The galaxy is populated with many places to explore and to name after yourself, if you are the first to find it.  Other players are doing the same thing, trtying to figure out what they are trying to do.  Only through exploring and talking on the forums can you eventually start to figure this thing out, and that is exactly what the creator wanted.  This is a very minimalist first-person game with little to guide you other than subtle clues.  This game isn't for everyone yet I think it has a lot to offer those willing to put aside their assumptions and biases and just relax and take in the Mirror Moon EP for what it is.

In the age where narrated tutorials are pretty much mandatory, this game is very refreshing. If you're in the mood for something completely familiar game-mechanics wise, this definitely is not for you.

There are no explanations, you have to just figure everything out (and when you begin to do it, you realise it's not as hard as you thought it is). You're told the basic controls and then you're on your own.
It's a rewarding experience that adds replay value in a much more organic way than "some games these days" do it.

MirrorMoon is probably not a game for everyone, but it provides something that few games do. I had about the same feeling with this game as I did with the later stages of Fez (which might be familiar to more pepole), when the game becomes more meta-gamey and disorienting. In MirrorMoon, you as the player never really know what to do (or even how to do it) but it's this 'enigmatic' quality that in the end kept me looking for the eventual solution (solution for what?).
So, even though the game might be obscure, frustrating and boring at times, it at least never ceases to be beautiful. Most importantly, special discoveries you make have a unique quality to them and the sometimes tedious parts before really let you know that it was you - and only you - that found out about this.

The negative reviews on here and places like Metacritic baffle me.  This is a fantastic follow-up to the New Order (and the Old Blood) that hits nearly every note one could want from a Wolfenstein game--and I trace my Wolfenstein experiences back to a 5.25" floppy on the Commodore 64 through Wolf3D to this.  The majority of low-ratings seem to fall into one of two categories, either people upset with the subject matter or those complaining it's buggy.  Those in the first category couch their reviews by using terms like SJW/liberal/whatever, but at the end of the day it's pretty clear they're upset the game is about killing Nazis.  You can draw your own conclusions there.  For those in the second category, yes, there are some bugs.  It's a new game on PC.  When did PC players become helpless?  If you want a flawless experience that requires zero effort, play on consoles.  Years ago, any game worth its salt would require an hour of tinkering with a config.sys and autoexec.bat and all manners of voodoo to get it half working.  This stuff is easy nowadays and the bugs I saw with this game were easy to address.  I did see some crashes initially when modifying vsync settings, but perusing forums I found two things that fixed everything:  downloading NVidia's newest beta driver created specifically for this game and disabling async computation in video settings.  After that, I've had basically zero issues and they game has run very well.  As for the game itself, it's an example of what a narrative based single-player game should be.  Great writing, an interesting story, characters you actually care about, and plenty of twist-and-turns.  The gunplay is excellent and challenging, the graphics absolutely outstanding and the game even runs well even on mid-tier systems.  The weapons are weighty and satisfying.  I can't remember a better FPS in some time, in fact the last one this good was Doom and that had pretty much no story so for me this is better game.  There are a few little quirks, the extra character traists/skills are not really fleshed out super well via gameplay, stealth only works passably, and the writing is a little heavy handed at times, but on the whole this is a truly fantastic game and some of the most fun I've had in several years on the PC.   Basically, if you like story-driven FPS games like Half-Life or you played and enjoyed the New Order, you'll love this game.   If you want to ensure a wasteland consisting only of games with crappy  microtransactions and focused on multi-player  instead, then this game is not for you.

Wolfenstein 2: the new meh
Well, if the title is not a dead giveway, let me put it plainly
its… not that good, the plot is ok and somewhat fun, if frustrating at times (the game actually has a decent ending this time, though one that still leaves a lot to be desired and plenty of sequel hook); though its also a bit on the heavy side at times (as in 90% of this game’s playtime, at the least for me, was cut-scenes or cut-scenes disguised as gameplay); with the game itself being rather short when separated from cutscenes, having about 5-6 ‘areas‘ with diferent stages in them, though the stages mostly look and feel the same baring map layout changes and a few exceptions here and there; with a few extra bonus areas relegated to re-visit side missions… which are a big focus in this game, as outside of its plot missions its entirely built on you re-doing areas for side objectives.
gameplay wise its a confused mess that seems to not be able to decide between being a shooter and a stealth game, the BEST analogy I can think of is that you are an older stealth game protagonist (the kind that basically drops dead the moment they are seen) put on a high action shooter like DOOM… which does not work very well; speaking of DOOM, for more that the two are different games and that wolfenstein builds on the mechanics of the first game… DOOM has kind of became the benchmark I am judging the shooter mechanics by, as a lot of what wolfenstein 1 did, DOOM managed to do better, making the two have similar gameplay styles but DOOM be smoother and more fun to play; wolfenstein 2 DOES polish the first game’s issues a LOT, but it still falls painfully far from being anywhere near what DOOM did (their ridiculous focus on broken, poorly planned stealth does not help).
A lot of gameplay mechanics that would be considered baseline in other games (or even just good additions to the shooter formula) are locked behind the new ‘contraptions‘, of which you pick one at the halfway point of the game, and have to gather the rest on side missions afterwards… except you are not told the upgrades that come with each contraption, only their gimmick (and of the 3, only one has a somewhat useful gimmick… though they kind of ♥♥♥♥ that up too by making it less useful than it seems and finicky as♥♥♥♥♥♥
The weapon wheel is a ♥♥♥♥ing mess to use, specially since you have to manage it individually for each hand and there is NO slowdown while its open (unless you happen to get the right contraption… said contraption otherwise only found on a side mission unlocked right before the final mission of the game, otherwise)
basically, it takes the entire ♥♥♥♥ing game for you to reach baseline Doom marine/slayer levels (and the final level even has a BFG-like gun you can get right before the final ‘boss fight‘… that is actively worthless and useless and using it will just get you killed in seconds.)
ultimately, its an ok game, and has its fun moments, but the annoying and baffling♥♥♥♥♥♥design decisions overwrite a lot of its potential; it is most DEFINITELY not worth its inflated price atm; also, it is NOT recommended for people looking for a DOOM like experience or lacking in patience, you will find yourself wanting to strangle the developers by the 30th time you are all but forced to sneak around.
EDIT: It has been pointed out to me (and I have looked into it myself) that some of my issues with the game MIGHT be due to technical issues, as it has been pointed out, and I noticed myself, that I seem to having been taking more damage than I should have in comparison to gameplay videos.
I will keep looking to see if that is indeed an issue, and if it turns out to be the case I will change my review (though It will remain a negative one, as I still feel the game lacks content to match its inflated price)

I can't believe this is supposed to come out fully in just a month or so..
I've only played for like 3 hours and have had a horrible experience because of all the bugs.
Characters I've unlocked don't even show up in my character costume menu, only certain parts do, like their heads in the head menu, and then when I try them on they're literally invisible. It just gives my character NO head at all when I try to use the yeti's head, and the yeti won't even show up in my "full costume" menu. My broomstick vehicle also broke when I first unlocked it, and now every time I summon it, it's making a super obnoxious noise on loop the whole time I'm riding it.
Don't even THINK about trying multiplayer, because then your game will be loaded with 400% more bugs. My game was constantly night time and way too dark. My character looked exactly the same as my friend, even though he was in a different costume. Whenever I hit anything it would just disappear instantly, and not drop any money or weapons. Animals and people would literally teleport and disappear all the time. We couldn't interact with any people to unlock them, and unlocking vehicles or objects only worked about 50% of the time. Also, my controls would constantly change WHILE I was playing, making it impossible to pilot any flying vehicles without constantly ascending, and jumping out when I tried to descend. It seemed as though the controls were doubly bound between CTRL and Q to do the same thing, somehow, even though it wasn't like that in single player. When I'd go into key bindings to try and fix it, the game literally only shows the keys, and not what they do/are bound to, so there's no way to know if you're even fixing anything by rebinding stuff, in reality it would probably only make it worse tampering with them. Then to top it all of, the game would just crash every once in a while, and close unexpectedly.
I've verified integrity of game cache in Steam twice now, and it makes no difference. Restarting Steam, or the game itself also makes no difference. Heavily disappointed in this purchase. Even if all the terrible bugs WEREN'T there, it's really just a mediocre feeling game. It's much more of a build sim than a game, IMO, because there's literally no challenge at all whatsoever. The enemies are super easy and don't even attack you unless you're almost touching them. The only game-like aspect is exploring and unlocking new objects, mounts, and Lego characters, and that goes WAY too fast. In my few hours of playtime I've already got a TON of that stuff, and now it's hard to find anymore new stuff when I play. The game shouldn't feel exhausted in three hours.
And before you say "This is an early access game, what do you expect?" well that's not a reasonable excuse in my opinion. I've played plenty of early access games that actually seem finished, and they don't claim to be a month away from a full release. How long has this been in early access? (Very very many months) And with one more month to go, will they REALLY get ALL those bugs fixed in time? I'm banking on this game still being a severely broken heap of trash at launch. Severely disappointed I've played more than two hours, because now I can't return it and get my money back. (And playing the game in an actually finished state is probably years away, if it ever even happens.)

I cautiously recommend this game.  The story is interesting, but unremarkable, in contrast to the graphics which are impressive, but underservered by the very linear levels.  The game has a nice variety of enemies, of varying [imposed] difficulties, that seem to exist more to draw out the limited gameplay, rather than as a real challenge (I'm looking at you Elite Enforcer!).
But it is the controls that will be your greatest foe in this game.  They are, at best, dodgy, and at worst (particularily when trying to target a particular enemy with ranged attacks), unresponsive.  Boss fights will require a peek at a walkthrough to understand what you are supposed to be doing, but it's the mass fights in increasingly confined spaces that will cause you to walk away from the game, thanks to the inaccuracy of the controls.
The idea of remixing memories is interesting, but only occurs a few times in the game, and is as logical as a '90s Sierra game, and will probably come down to trying random combinations, or just looking at a walkthough.
It's not a bad game, but has too many problems to be more than a decent game.   Buy it on a sale if the graphics appeal to you.

This game is really, really good fun. The fluid, graceful chaining of moves and dodging feels very tight. I'm not having any difficulty playing this with mouse and keys, but some may prefer the controller. First boss battle was not overly difficult, but challenging enough to feel a sense of triumph when succeeding.
The environment is stunning. Rich, full of detail and ambiance. The pace of the story is good, I'm only a few hours in as of this writing and I feel drawn in. The first "re-write" of a persons memory...what a great way to handle it. From the mouse input feeling so natural to "scrub" through the memory timeline, to the great visuals...very well done.
Traversing the environment is not anything super-amazing, but it's well done enough and handled decently. Your moves are executed confidently and appear natural and smooth. This is not "Mirror's Edge" so don't expect over-the-top parkour. Your acrobatic moves during combat will make up for it.
Combat may at first appear shallow, but there is some depth to be found for the patient seeker. Finding your pace and timing in combat feels really good when you get into the groove. Evading, flipping over an opponent to continue a chain, rapidly switching targets to maintain control all feel rewarding. Winning a fight against multiple opponents feels like an accomplishment, not just the result of random button mashing.
I always reccomend watching gameplay videos and watching/reading plenty of reviews before making a decision to purchase. Chances are, if you like the dystopian/cyberpunk genre, this game will appeal to you.
It goes without saying, people are different, they like different things. Some will hate this game, some will love it and others will be ambivalent. I can only say that I'm having a lot of fun playing it, and I think it's an experience worth your time and money. Some may disagree, but in my opinion this game is an underrated gem and I'm glad I picked it up.
Thanks for reading, and Good Gaming.

Absolutely amazing game, and what I feel is a good example of what happens when love is put into a project. It could've been that it hit all my marks for what I like to see in a game, all in aesthetics, in gameplay, and a great story. Though I feel like, overall, the presentation and the directing of certain scenes/gameplay was the most powerful part (the final battle particularly gave me chills; perfect way to set up a final fight).
Everything from the soundtrack, to the gritty atmosphere, and the constant sound of voices narrating everything you do--all of it only enhanced the experience and helped to create the world around Senua. To show they really paid attention, they made sure to implement psychosis into almost every little part of the game--from the puzzles to even the combat. Every environment in the game had me feeling what the protagonist should be feeling, every scene felt real and moving, and everything fell into place perfectly. The live action cut-ins were a bit strange, but they almost separated Senua's visions from everything else she was seeing, making her the clear focus.
Not to mention how great it felt to have a combat system that actually felt good. If you do it right, you feel like a badass, and if you do it wrong, you have an opportunity to learn from it. With the constant stress of death, but having the ability to stand back up after getting knocked down, only makes you that much more tenacious--something that Senua seems to reflect in the battles, and really, for most of her journey.
Overall amazing, I'm not too picky but I really thought this was an example of a nearly-perfectly done game (personal preferences aside), and for a great price too.

Love the original Gauntlet?  Me too!  Over 1000 hours playing the original? Check.  Over 1 million points in multiple games? Check.  Played past level 230 multiple times? Check.  Bought multiple computers and consoles with 4 joysticks just to play Gauntlet? Check.  The original Gauntlet is possibly my favourite game of all time, but I hate this new Gauntlet.  It's not Gauntlet!  It's a fantasy version of Smash tv :|  I gave this game a chance and bought an "Xinput compatible controller" just to play it (I already had 3 controllers to play Gauntlet, because I can play it on a PC keyboard).  It's even more awkward to use the controls and all I want to do is just press a fire button to shoot shots!  I'd rather play 3 original Gauntlet characters at the same time (I've done it!) than use the horrible controls this game offers, and it doesn't even allow you to reassign them :(
As for the gameplay...Even after getting to grips with the controls the game is rather repetitive and bland in a way the original Gauntlet never was.  But then I'm not a Smash Tv fan, and I'd even prefer Smash Tv over this game. For those who aren't familiar, the game is a series of "rooms" like Smash Tv, and characters move through doorways to adjacent rooms.  The rooms are rather confined and I feel it takes away a lot from the original.
I'll probably play this game sometime in the future, but I much prefer the original Gauntlet 1+2.  I wouldn't recommend it at anything more than 1/2 it's current price, and there are better games even at that price.  I did get it on sale, but was tremendously disappointed by it.

There's few games where the visuals, animations, music, audio design, voice acting, writing, and gameplay are all great and compliment each other. Flaws you've sort of come to expect in games (and maybe don't even notice anymore) are non-existent in Ori. Things like awkward animation transitions or hiccups, texture seams, the occasional bad line of writing or voice acting. It's clear that an enormous amount of effort went into making Ori as close to perfect as it could be.

The incredible Adventures of Van Helsing ( an all dlc version review )
This game offers you a choice of 3 different classes, each with a very solid selection of skills, first being a hunter which can actually be built in 3 different ways entirely on its own, or hybridized to your hearts content, having melee, ranged ( pistols and rifles ) and occult ( magic ) skills at his disposal.
The second class is the Thaumaturge who is a pure spellcaster with plethora of skills at his disposal both offensive and control/support, all having their specific use, and the final class is a unique Arcane mechanic, having mine and grenade skills at his disposal, as well as gadgets and turrets.
It is a very well done, unique and incredibly refreshing setting that this game is taking place in, there are no dwarves, no elfs, no typical fantasy arpg of which there is 16874 on the market and all look the same in the end.
The game is set in a beautiful gothic noir setting with mythical, as well as mechanical creatures to be fought, and with exciting places to explore.
Speaking about the monsters -
They are designed well and look unique, there is swarms of them, so there is always alot of action, and thus, there is also tons of actually good loot, what more could you wish for, right?
Speaking of loot, the itemization in this game is very well done.
There is very typical item system of normal, magic, rare ( thus far the exact same as diablo II, including colors ) and finally epic and set items, which all have functionality like stat comparison to your equipped item, comparison to your followers equipped items ( more on that in a bit ) etc, a bit of a downside perhaps could be  that later on in the game, you may start getting lost in the constant stat comparations, because in this game it is fairly usual to be swapping items for new ones often.
And what deserves a mention as well is that the devs were not afraid to actually let you drop or be rewarded with the epic items, one of my dislikes about other recent Arpg's is that you basically never get to see any of the highest tier items unless you farm for them for ages or play advanced game modes.
This brings me to quest rewards, and money, since they go hand in hand.
This is another area this game excels at. You get very, very good rewards even for sidequests you'd think were meaningless or not worth to bother with, being used to that from other, maybe even most rpg's.
But in here, you are always rewarded with a rare item, sometimes in fact a unique ( epic ) one, with skill or stat points ( sometimes for you, sometimes for your follower ), and a decent sum of money, which are useful for quite alot of things as well.
The experience reward for quests could I thought be higher, but then again, I reached the max level just playing the game normally, so there was no need for it then.
And regarding money, another often overlooked area in other games, in here, you can then spend them upgrading your weapons, reseting your stat or skill points ( no other limits  for that then your money, awesome! ), gambling for items, and later on even improving the hideout where your character interacts with friendly npc's.
Remember the mention of a follower? You indeed have one, bound to you by the storyline, and when I saw this, I was not happy about that, having experiences from most other games where followers are just constantly dead and useless.
Not so in here, your follower, a ghost woman called Katarina has her own level progression with attribute points and 2 skill trees, one of which improves you by her actions/simply being with you, and the other purely improving her alone.
This leaves incredible versatility and usefulness to her because you are completely free to make her an uberpowerful tank if you need it, and if it so happens she'd die, you can actually enable her to explode on death, usually clearing the whole mob of enemies that was attacking her.
If you are melee, you are in turn completely free to make her your ranged support, or even if you so wish, to leave her out of the battle and just give you a permanent 10% dmg reduction.
Furthermore, you could also tell her which items she would pick up ( if any ) and in which way should she attack your enemies, I wouldnt ask for more.
Along Katarinas level up progression, and yours, which of course also lets you assign the typical attribute and skill points, there is more for your character than that. Much more.
Along the regular skill tree ( or trees, for the Hunter class ), you also get an entire additional passive skill tree, which is in part unique and partially shared to/by all the classes, where you could choose from a number of passive skills two that you want to have active at all times.
Want dmg reduction? Its there, want to heal Katarina with your attacks? Sure, and so much more.
And thats still not all. There is an additional skill tree called "tricks" which you can also invest skill points, which are very useful active abilities like stopping the time, making 2 more katarinas temporarily to help you, or my spellcasters favourite, being able to burn all your mana for a massive explosion around him.
Since the Thaumaturgist's spells are mainly focused on damage over time ( DoT ), this is a great tool to have for burst damage.
Thought thats all? Nope, still not yet, because there are additionally perks too..
You get those for killing big bosses and in general unusual monsters like veterans and champions, and they furthermore permanently improve your character to the point where you can choose to be impossible to be stopped in your tracks, or to not die when killed, and merely become incorporeal for several seconds.
Now thats what I call a character progression, and to my best knowledge, I can honestly say it is unparalleled by any other single player Arpg's out there.
The game as it is at the moment is imo a truly great experience free of any glitches or bugs, after being patched multiple times, which is incredibly impressive for a game studio so small that the final credits only rolled for about 1 single minute, no exaggeration.
The game has very professional voice acting, as well as enjoyable music which deserves a mention, and the game is also full of very funny references to all kinds of things, including other games, of the same genre or otherwise, sometimes fairly hidden, sometimes very obvious.
Some games may try to make jokes which dont fit in it, or some games just go full "funny" all the way, but what is impressive  about this game is that it manages to have an interesting, serious, believable world and atmosphere, and yet, effortlessly manages to include funny references in it that just make you smile..
The games lenght is very solid 18 hours for one playthrough which is great, considering there are scenario mode and a game+ mode available as well, so replayability is great.
Sumarry: An amazing action rpg game that has been a ton of pure fun thanks to its for a single player rpg unrivaled character development options, unique setting, fluent game mechanics that are clear and work exactly as youd expect at all times, and thanks to the constant rewards the game gives you which will never make you leave it for long until youve seen it all.
And that would take at least a while.
Highly recommended to get, the developers really deserve to be rewarded for a game this polished and with this many gameplay features.

Trine is basically GAMEPLAY, GRAPHICS, SOUNDS, and STORY, all touching the Trine and has become one harmonious being…
Honestly, I was late to the party, only now have I started playing Trine, and haven’t even completed it yet. I got it off a sale, and it was on my wishlist in like forever thanks to the recommendation of TekSyndicate.
Anyways, let go on to the review.
Story:
Basically, the 3 main characters: Zoya the Thief, Amadeus the Wizard, and Pontius the Knight, end up touching the artifact known as the Trine, getting their souls becoming one, and are now on a quest to undo the artifact’s doing. Doing so, you travel the land finding a way to undo it.
I won’t go deeper as I haven’t completed it and of course, avoid spoilers…
Graphics:
This is visually stunning! I mean, wow! The colors, the ambient lighting, and a good use of Nvidia’s Physx (albeit, only software acceleration and won’t use hardware acceleration even if you have a Physx capable Nvidia card) for particle physics…
Each level I start I pause just for a moment and enjoy the wonderful graphics and designs each level was crafted on.
It was released way back 2009, and I still say the graphics are beautiful.
Gameplay:
This is 3D side scrolling puzzle platformer; each character has their own unique abilities that can be useful in certain puzzles and have unique ways to ward off adversaries along your journey; you simply switch between characters in order to play as one of them on the fly ala Lost Vikings.
It works perfectly, and if one of your characters does die in a part of a level that his/her ability will make solving a platforming puzzle easier, the other two can still solve it, only a little more challenging; that said, you can solve each puzzle in a number of ways.
You level up by collecting green bottles scattered through each level or hunting down enemies. Getting these green bottles or whatever they are, can be in hard to reach places, so it becomes a puzzle on its own. You can simply ignore it, but for some reason, apart from the XP it grants, the challenge of getting it will no doubt pull you in.
You collect items by opening chests that like the green bottles, are in hard to reach places, but these items can be oh so useful, that you are compelled to reach them either way.
The one aspect I was shocked about the gameplay is that there is absolutely NO IN LEVEL SAVING, it it does save after each level; meaning you can’t save anywhere and quick load where you’d f*cked up. In fact the so called checkpoints don’t do anything but restore your health, mana, and revive a fallen character. If all you die, you start from the beginning of the level. This shocked me as a PC gamer, your used to multiple saves, but this comes to me as a FRESH surprise. It keeps you on your toes and at the edge of your seat, much like the old days of Nintendo, Atari and whatnot.
The euphoria when you reach the end of the level, and you know you deserve a pat in the back and a fist bump because you didn’t f*ck up. And the absolute frustration when you progressed so far in the level, but you had that slight lapse of judgment and you have to repeat from the very beginning. It pumps you up so bad that you want to finish it no matter what.
Perfect.
Sound:
I love the music in this game; it is not over the top, in fact, it is quite soothing, therapeutic. And it certainly has memorable tunes.
Ambient sounds are as what you’d expect. And that is good.
Other sound effects are just as good.
For me, it’s the not so over the top music that stands out.
Another one that stands out the most is the voice overs; I love the voices of the characters and the narrator. In fact, some of their dialogue are funny and entertaining. I love the voice of the Wizard in particular. Great casting.
Replayability:
This for me has a high replay value; especially that each level will tell it has a number of obtainable XP from the green bottles and from foes, as well as chests to open, you’d want to re-explore the levels to get them all if you are a completionist. And even you aren’t you definitely want to try and solve the puzzles in a different way than you initially did just to see how it goes.
In summary:
I was late in getting a copy of this 2009 game and had to endure waiting for a sale; yes I wanted it, but I didn’t feel like shelling out full price for a game released last 2009 no matter how good it may be.
Needless to say, the wait, much like anything else in life is well worth it.
Sure it can get frustrating with no in level saving and you die so far in the level only to restart from the beginning, but that what presses you on to be perfect, to think before you do any action, to know that each step is meaningful and important. The pressure and challenge will pull you in.
This is one beautiful game that you can get lost just looking at it as much as you get lost immersed in the puzzles.
Get this game. Either full price or like me, wait for a sale.
It’s worth it.
Once you install this and pressed the play button, it’s like touching the Trine for real. It will grab your soul. And you’ll love it.
-Chan

Just finished Trine in the free-weekend.
I wanted to play this game for a while, and I took advantage of this opportunity to finally try it out. I am not disappointed, but I'm not fully pleased either.
= Beautiful looking game, impressive degree of immersion for the genre through graphics, sounds and writing. Gameplay mechanics are not terrible, but they are the weakest link in this game. Not a deal breaker though, game is worth a try.
:
:
I know quick-time events are not a necessity for side-scrolling platformers, but when you have a rich 3d environment and heavy physics, they become important. Case in point, the grapling hook from the Thief seems often buggy (often goes through stuff you can jump on, breaks with no clear reason, etc), staying on platform edges or jumping on them can be more tricky than it should, and creating platforms with the wizard can prove difficult if there's the slightest denivalation in the terrain (boxes start to roll, etc). Combat is pretty repetitive and non-interesting, you don't have a lot of moves/attacks, and enemies have an attack animation that doesn't really land with the effect.One more thing; this might be an intended mechanic, or because of time and/or development constraints was not implentend: moving/dropping non-attached stuff with your wizard. It kind of feels like moving an object in editing software; physics are mostly there for the move part, but the drop part is just like dropping from a fixed point with no velocity, no matter what.
This is where the game shines. It looks gorgeus. There's a heavy accent on colours and detail, a beautiful 3d environment with a fixed side-scrolling 2d camera. The style gives every setting the feeling of magic, especially the outdoor forest parts. It's also not extremely demanding, at least in the original version; I was able to run it with an acceptable framerate on an outdated low-end laptop, and it looked great. Enchanted Edition wasn't all that spec friendly :D.
- Not bad. It's sort of like a narrative that you knew as a child, a tale of heroes bound together, who overcome obstacles to reach individual goals, but find that their bond changes their perception, and seemingly work together for the greater good.
- The music in this game is great. It fits perfectly with the story/writing, and with the adequate graphics behind it, it's conveying a sense of immersion. The sound effects and voice acting aren't bad either, but it's the music that truly shines.
- The levels are not too difficult, ergo this game is not too difficult. You may find it troublesome to get some achievements, but all in all it's pretty balanced, at last until the last level, which seems to jump the volume of difficulty to 150% (from 100% obviously...idk, I had no better analogy...). Again, it's not THAT difficult, it's just that the game progresses really smoothly in difficulty, not really increasing or decreasing by much, and at the last one, BOOM, it's like you switched from normal to hard (this game doesn't have a difficulty option, btw).
Well...what can I say, I enjoyed it, even though gameplay mechanics kind of frustrated me. I'll put some of that on my rig though, and considering I'm recommending this game, what I found problematic isn't that much of a problem.

A procedrually generated space themed environmental puzzle game with a focus on exploration and navigation. Puzzles are procedurally generated and run the range of obvious and simple to clever and surprising. And sometimes even after the anamoly is solved there will still be things to do and discover on the planet, revealing easter eggs and other surprises. Once an anomaly is solved you get the right to name the star, as players explore the galaxy and solve anomalies the galaxy fills up with the unique signatures of various astronauts. This is a starkly beautiful game, evocative of the Italian underground indie freeware classic Noctis. The visual themes call back to Kubrick and Tarkovsky's work. This game is all about the journey.

MirrorMoon EP is a game that feels alive, due to the way that it works. You are actually playing with a whole bunch of other people, working together to uncover every last secret in the galaxy. And when the galaxy has been explored, a whole new one is generated and put online.

Man, I really wanted to like this one, but I have to say I'm underwhelmed.
Starting with performance, the game runs pretty well, except for the occasional crash to desktop. At first I thought this might just be my system but it seems others are effected as well.
Gameplay wise, the game is decidely weaker than TNO's. Only one of your weapons, a submachinegun, is entirely new to the series (The rest are slightly tweaked versions of weapons from the previous two games), the new mechanics are gimmicky at best, and the stealth elements are so frustrating that you'll probably just stop bothering with them. The damage and grenade indicators are also extremely easy to miss, so you'll end up dying for what seems like no reason.
The writing is all over the place, with some moments being fun and memorable while others fall completely flat. With TNO, almost every mission was exciting and felt like it was happening for a reason. In the New Colossus however, the missions felt more contrived than anything. The story is almost criminally short for $60, and ends abruptly with a cliffhanger setup for DLC or a sequel. In addition, the game reuses levels several times, both in the main story and in gameplay-padding side missions. As for the characters, the new entries felt mostly one-dimensional or irratating, while favorites from the previous games are fairly underused (this was with Fergus timeline so YMMV)
Overall i'd have to give this one a 7/10, so I'd say the current review score is accurate. I hope machine Games can recapture the energy that hooked me with TNO in future installments.

(Take my review with a very large grain of salt.  I've completed about half the game so far.  If it suddenly becomes terrible by the end, I'll give this review an update.)
First off, while it seems like there's no guarantee of good performance, Wolf II ran brilliantly on my PC with my i5-6600k and GTX 970.  I get a silky smooth framerate on all but the farthest draw distances.  Even then, the fram drops are often small enough to be nearly unnoticeable and don't really take me out of the game much.  The game is graphically beautiful and environments are creatively drawn and engrossing to look at.  On the negative side, the characters (especially Anya :( ) will occasionally turn in to absolute butterfaces up close.  I dunno if it's something with idtech 6's megatextures or something else, but it can look dissapointly jank on human characters.
I'm mostly reviewing this early to try to offset some of the negative reviews.  Wolf II is really a brilliant game, outdoing most of its contemporaries like Bioshock Infinite for immersive storytelling and worldbuilding.  Even setting aside the outstanding voice acting and cutscene direction, if you take the time to search for lore-notes and follow the character sidequests, what you have here is a story that is as genuinely earnest as it is goofy camp.  It's a rare balance for any medium, not just video games.
If you're coming straight from a game like DOOM, be aware that Wolf II does not reward agressive, guns-blazing gameplay.  Despite you having a tanky-looking armor suit, you tend to go down easy when surrounded, and should expect to spend time between gunfights scavenging for armor and secrets to stay alive.  In that sense, Wolf II shares much more in common with Metro 2033 than its id cousin.
I think once some of the irritation over launch issues cools down, the game will firmly cement itself as a worthy sequel.  If you loved The New Order, I don't see any reason why you won't enjoy The New Colossus.

I started with keyboard and mouse (my normal playing method) and kept dying at the first boss. As soon as I switched to controller, I beat him first try. It's just more fluid with a controller. To the Moon takes a story with real-life elements and drives them home with a small sci-fi twist. When I first bought the game, I was pretty skeptical of the concept, even more so as I started to play. The controls are mostly through the mouse, but you can use the keyboard or a gamepad, too. F1 sets up the options, and Alt+Enter toggles the fullscreen. As far as the game goes, it's extremely spartan on interaction, chosing to power itself with story and aesthetic.
In truth, there are few mindless game mechanics, there's even a segment that dispels any notion of the RPG mechanics that typically follow something with this design structure. You go through collecting pieces of the story, and literally put them together into a node, which is further configured through a puzzle. It's very easy to find what you need to advance through the stages, and after a while the block puzzles gain a familiarity that allow you to solve them more quickly. This isn't something you just pick up with the intention of buzzing through.
No, To The Moon reels you in with the story, which, if you're looking to buy a story game, look no further. The setting is a reality with familiar referenes to pop-culture, real people, and honest works of fiction. The characters are all very memorable, and they have a personality that draws one to want to know more about them. There is a firm mix of fun and seriousness that sprinkles inbetween each segment, with one of the protagonists being a consistant source of relief, while the other injects carefully measured drama. Albeit, the overall tone of the narrative is very serious, and there are some segments that can feel very personal once you're exposed to them. The more you advance, the more you seek to know more about what brought along this particular string of events, and soon enough you'll find yourself rollercoasting into the end, seeking to cure what heartache that points of sadness in the story wretch in your heart.
To the Moon has earned a special place in my heart, as few games have, and has driven me to write this spiel, as few games do. You'll probably only get 5 hours out of it at best, but you'll feel more through this trip than you might with any 2 hour production at the cinema.
Additionally, there is bonus content updating periodically, the last one being 2nd Minisode to tack on to the story. It should be in the Local Game Files.
