I first reviewed this game on 12/11/2011 and I had praised it as fun, low cost, and surprisingly active for a much older game. I didn't think much of it at the time other than a generally good game. Boy, I had no idea.
It is now 2016 and the game is almost a decade old. Since then, my opinon of COD4 has actually gone up. Not only is it the oldest game that I still play regularly beating out even newer games I've purchased, but it is still 'surprisingly active'.
Every single multiplayer mode still has at least one or two active servers. More popular modes like FFA and TDM, of course, has tons of active server. I'm still playing FFA/TDM with upwards of 20+ players at all times of the day. A decade old game!
Even better, multiplayer has some mods that people use and my favorite has come to be 'Reign of the Undead' (ROTU) -- a zombie mod which is unbelievably fun and also very active with many servers containing 5+ players regularly (and some as high as 10+). Sounds small compare to the main MP modes, but you really don't want more for ROTU.
Overall, COD4 has turned out to be an incredible value. I wouldn't have regretted this purchase had I paid full $60 price, but instead, I only got it for $20. Frankly, I got a steal for a game that I've been playing for so long and still intend to keep playing.

Let's get some things straight. Yes this game is controversial as hell because of the false advertising or whatever you wanna call it. The developers got carried away with the hype and so did we. I don't think we should judge the game itself based on that alone. I bought it yesterday for the summer sale and stayed up all night playing it. It's fun. Bottom line. I'm not sure if it's worth the full price of $60 yet, but it's fun. That's all that should matter.
Ok, now the actual review. The promise of being able to explore a massive universe full of procedural content was fulfilled. If you want an endless exploration sim that you can just sit back with and take in the ambiance then this game is great. And if you want a more challenging space pioneer experience then the survival mode has you covered. When I finally got my ship up and running it felt amazing. I'm sure there are games out there that do individual aspects of No Man's Sky better, actually I know there are, but it has a lot features that are just entertaining if a little shallow. Dog fighting, trading, base building, first person combat, exploration, resource management, etc. They've all been done better but it's nice to have them all in one package.
I believe it's well worth the sale price and recommend it to anyone who enjoys exploring space and alien planets. Plus there's more free content coming so don't write it off just yet. The last update added a lot. Now excuse me while I log another eleven hours into it...

The game was released almost a year ago. Before I bought the PS4 version I downloaded it as I would not want to fight with SONY for a refund in case I did not like the game so that's what I did. I actually liked it a lot and ended up buying in September the PS version. I just have sold my PS4, I upgraded my graphics card and guess what. I was missing NMS so I bought it a couple of days ago.
There has been endless bad reviews about this game. To be honest, I personally believe the people just like to go with the flow and they are doing so cause everybody and every single youtuber has talked badly about it. I strongly believe 90% of those reviews were influenced by third parties but not their own.
The game:
Is the game boring? The game is not boring. This game has a problem of guidance and it lacks of maps. Leaving the gamer wondering what in the heck they ought to do next. That is a one of the problems. In fact, If I left the game stand still for a week and come back to it later I would have no clue where I was or what I was doing. This is a big time mistake from these guys.
Is the game repetitive? I cannot believe people complain about this. Is RUST or any crafting exploring game not repetitive? Is life not repetitive? Come on! Of course it is. We follow procedures, any game is repetitive and NMS is not left aside. You got to do farming, you got to do A + B so you can get C....
Is the game buggy? Well, it was at the beginning. I had the PS4 version and to be honest, it does run better than PC. I got a MSI geforce 1080ti and my FPS vary all the time so I guess it is missing optimisation still.
Is there multiplayer on the game? Sure it is. I play with my daughter all the time.
Do I recommend it?
Sure I do. Overall when you can get it now at 24 euros. If you like crafting and exploring and getting lost.. This is your game. There is a lot to do but you will need to be very organized or otherwise you will just loose track, get upset and give a negative review.
What is the main problem then with so much negative reviews?
Main problem is that Hello Games should have never got together with Sony. These guys never finished the game and they got so much pressured on the release date that they released an early access instead. An indie company should never get together with a big name when you have got such a "weird" project. Sean Murray took advantage of that marketing injection and started exagerating the product, you can see how much he loved it, he loved it so much that he sold an idea he had in his head but SONY never left him get it finished. There were some places where my screen would go completely black. I don't mean dark, with a hint of light; I mean, completely black, as if my monitor suddenly shut off (even though it didn't). Not being able to see where I was  or where I was going forced me to move my camera around while hoping that bug would go away. Even then sometimes that didn't work, and I would have to wonder around completely blind hoping the bug would go away. Just to be clear: the problem wasn't with my computer, it was a problem with the game itself.
The combat system needs some work.
Quite often if there was 3+ monsters two of them would try to circle around me and sucker punch me. That's okay, I could handle it... usually. There were times where I would dodge one of their attacks by jumping over the monster I'm attacking but the game would instead interpret that as me trying to flip away, which breaks my combo. Other times I would successfully dodge the attack by jumping over the monster, only to get instantly hit by an attack by a monster. I'll give you an example of what I mean. Lets suppose there are three monsters, Joe, Bob, and Sue. Joe and Bob are in line in front of me. Bob is between Joe and myself. Sue is behind me. Sue tries to attack me, so I jump over Bob... only to get hit by Joe the very second I land. I don't even have time to dodge before getting hit. Why? Because, Joe starts his attack the very nanosecond I start to jump over Bob.
I think the combo system is good and bad. It's good because you can mix up your combos. Are you hurting? Go into the combo system lab, swap out a damaging move (aka "pressens") for a healing pressens. Are you full health and want to crank your focus up? Swap out that healing pressens for a bonus damaging pressens. However, I think it's bad that it forces you to have pressens positioned in a certain way in each combo. In your kick combo, if you want a damage pressens in the middle of your combo, you have to chose one of the top three damaging pressens. In other words, it forces you to have certain pressens placed in a certain order. There was no information that it was like this in game. I didn't find this out until AFTER I had bought the pressens. When I did find out I wanted to get a different pressens, but the only way for me to do that was to redo the entire episode.
There is a problem with the s-pressens UI. I can't hold down any movement keys when I press the s-pressens button, otherwise it won't let me select the s-pressens I want, assuming it will let me select any. However, if someone is about to land an attack on me right as I activate a s-pressens, I like how it will make me avoid the damage, as if the attack never happened.
The UI is not very good. This is especially true with the combo lab system UI. It's like some keys are bound to perform more then one function when they aren't supposed to. A good example of this is when you get a new s-pressens. You're supposed to hold down the s-pressens wheel button to bring it up, select the new pressens, and then using the same button, select the new power, while at the same time, NOT releasing that button. In other words, you're supposed to NOT be holding down the button while at the same holding it down. Finally, you can use the mouse to navigate the menus... but it's not worth the trouble. It's a lot easier and less finicky to use the keyboard then the mouse.
The (cinamatic) cutscenes were awesome and unique. The only time I've seen gameplay like this was briefly while playing batman: arkham asylum. However, there needs to be a way to skip the cutscenes. There were times where I would do something stupid and die, come back, try to jump a platform, but only die again... all because the person talking wouldn't shut up and let me make the jump.
The path you travel from point a to point d is completely linear. You are unable to take any detours while traveling from point a to point d. Despite this you are rewarded for exploring and deviating from the path, as you can sometimes find upgrades. When an opportunity to find an upgrade a screen appears along your path, giving you a clue as to where the upgrade is. Sometimes the upgrade is nearby, sometimes you have to travel a ways to get it. The problem is sometimes while looking for an upgrade you can accidentally go past the path to it, then something will happen that will prevent you from getting to the path while the game at the same time saves your game. This forces you to either skip the upgrade, or redo the ENTIRE episode all over again to get it. Considering it takes 30+ minutes per episode, that can be a lot of wasted time.

I cannot recommend this game.
But let's start with a love letter. I love the work of Ninja Theory. They ♥♥♥♥ing care about their job. They ♥♥♥♥ing care about their games. DmC was an awesome take on the Devil May Cry license, extremely well narrated, with a spot-on gameplay feeling and an outstanding harmony in visuals, music, sounds and action. I couldn't wait for their next beat'em all and was very glad when Hellblade was announced.
Well first of all, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice hardly delivers on the beat'em all part. I admit I may have been expecting too much fighting without really reading about the game beforehand, but that's not the problem here. Combats are tight, interesting, demanding, and YET, the game's not delivering. Why ? Because though there are only few combats in the game they mostly happen NOT when you would expect them to happen. Combat seems like an excuse for the game being a narrative experience in Hellblade. It feels like they were afraid the game'd get boring so they threw in a couple of fight here and there to wake us up. But it never felt, up to when I stopped playing it, that any of the combats I fought were legit.
When I say "legit", I mean that this game talks about the heroin's fight against psychosis, and NONE of the fights felt like I was fighting myself, or some illusion, or anything unreal. None of these fight actually fit in the groove.
So... ok. Too bad they've failed at making these combats a strong part of the game experience, but that's OK. This game is not about sword fighting really. They could have just not coded them and most of what makes this game awesome would still stand.
'Cause despite not being able to recommend this game, I can still realize how awesome it is. The art direction is very strong, researched and coherent. Game's mood is handled with finesse. Sound design is a whole masterpiece of its own. And Melina Juergens, OMG, what have you done to yourself?! They've turned their video editor into a bleeding and screaming drama actress! WTF is wrong with you guys?! It's awesome!
All of this is great, but I can't recommend the game, and that's pretty much it for me: I can't recommend the GAME itself.
Movements in the environment are taxing. Slooow, even when running. With "walking simulators" I tend to try and enjoy the landscape, the experience. I tried to do the same here and it was fine, but only up to the point where it started not being so surprising anymore. Then I started to run but then it downed on me how sloooow the game really was. You take a looooong time to do anything in the game. Most puzzles are quite fast to solve in your head, but the actual execution is damn too slow.
Also, the camera placement is only partially controlled with the mouse. You can look nearly anywhere around you... but NOT when moving around. It's the first time I ever get sick while playing a third person videogame because the game keeps on leveling my viewpoint each time I start walking. I still can rotate and look around, but only on the horizon, which is a BIG perception dissonance between what I see and what I do with my hand.
Note : for scale purpose, I NEVER get sick in VR, but this game's camera actually managed to make me sick.
But worst of all, and that is, again, the biggest mistake a "walking simulator" can make : they never really explain anything to you, the player. They forgot they were making a game, and that there would be players. It took me five fights to realize that Focus had a STRONG role in combats. It took me eight fights to realize that I could kick opponents to try and stun them. How come?! Why do we STILL believe we can afford the false luxury of NOT explaining players how to play? Why do we keep on believing that writing text on screen is ugly and dirty?
Also, because combats and explorations are so different, you fail at guessing when you're in danger and when you're not. The game lets you know that if you fail too much times, darkness will engulf you and scrap your save files (which is, by the way, told to you in plain text and this is GREAT, because I now know that rule! see? that wasn't that painful...). This explanation happens just after you lose your first combat. One can only conclude that you shouldn't die in combat, right ? Wrong. Sometimes you have to not wait too long standing. Sometimes fancy visual FX are your enemy. Sometimes you stepped on water, but not the right kind, whatever that means, and you're dead.
So, OK, they just forgot how to make good games. It wouldn't be that big of a problem if you could at the very least expect to learn the dangers at your own pace. It doesn't bother me that some FX actually warns you about an upcoming danger...
But remember : if you fail too much, you WILL start the game from the beginning. And that is unacceptable. I can only accept such a feature if the game puts all the responsibility of losing in my sole hands.
If I have 100% game information in mind, take my time, wonders, then act, and still repeatedly make the wrong choices, I can totally accept that the game will scrap my saves. It puts pressure on me, of the good kind.
If I don't even know how to play the game, if new forms of danger jump on you without even giving you time to learn how they look like and how to somewhat avoid them, and then if I am promised that "failing too much" like that will end up scrapping my saves, well guess what? I'm not thrilled by it!
And then it would still be kind of OK with me... if the game wasn't so damn SLOOW. I now know that if I die a couple of times more in the situation I'm in, it won't cost me 2 minutes like each time I lose, it'll soon cost me 4.3 hours. And even then, I would still don't know HOW to STOP dying all the time! So I don't even have the guarantee that when I come back to the point I was, I will prevail. Why would I even bother spending the time to try again?
But you might say that starting a new game might be the opportunity to enjoy another round of awesome visuals and nice acting. This would be true, but the story never proved to me that it wasn't absolutely linear. Starting a new game doesn't feel like it would be anything close to rewarding.
So here you are : if these problems don't concern you, if you fancy slow, long, exploration, and if you don't mind losing 4-5 hours of your time each time the game won't tell you how to play, just go for it.
Otherwise, wait for their next game. They've proven they can do much better than that, so let's give them another chance later.

Outstanding game, the binaural sound is very immersive if you are using headphones. The soundtrack is great, and can make you feel invincible one minute and helpless the next.
Some words of caution though, the game is primarily a story driven psychological journey with puzzle solving and illusions and a fighting game second. That being said, the combat is quite intense, and the fact that there is a perma-death mechanic after too many failures adds to tension of each fight. You must use all your skills in combat when surrounded, timed parries, evasion, and a bullet-time mechanic called focus.
There is no proper tutorial to introduce you to the various combat moves, perhaps this was a design choice to enchance immersion. A quick look at the control settings can tell you, and there is a counter-attack opportunity for well timed parries that you can execute with a heavy or light attack. You can also charge and leap with heavy or light attacks when combined with sprint, and there is a stab attack that can be done tapping sprint and light attack. These are things that I discovered while playing and aren't listed.
The game is not long, I found most of the optional lore stones that tell excerpts of norse folklore stories and completed the game in 8 hours. But it was a wild ride for sure, and I loved every minute of it!

BROWNIE LAYER:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter
1 1/2 cups bittersweet chocolate chips
1 cup granulated white sugar
1/2 cup packed light brown sugar
4 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup all-purpose flour
COOKIE DOUGH:
3/4 cup (1 1/2 sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature or almost melted
3/4 cup granulated white sugar
3/4 cup packed light brown sugar
1/4 teaspoon salt
2 tablespoons milk or cream
1 1/2 teaspoons vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 cup miniature chocolate chips
additional miniature chocolate chips, if desired (to garnish the top)
Directions:
Prepare the brownie layer-
1. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Spray a 9x9-inch pan with nonstick spray, then line with a strip of parchment paper so that it covers the bottom and comes up two sides of the pan. Spray the parchment with nonstick spray too.
2. In a microwave safe bowl (or in the top of a double boiler or pan set on top of a pan of simmering water), microwave in 30 second bursts to melt butter and chocolate chips together until all is melted and smooth. Whisk in the sugars, then whisk in the eggs, vanilla and salt. Sift flour into the bowl and stir that in too. Scrape the brownie batter into the prepared pan. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, or until the brownie layer is cooked through (toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean). Place the pan of brownies in the refrigerator to speed up the cooling process (or cool at room temperature and add the cookie dough layer later).
Prepare the cookie dough layer:
3. In a large bowl, use an electric mixer to combine the butter, sugars and salt until soft and creamy (1 to 2 minutes). Mix in the milk and vanilla. Sprinkle in the flour and mix in until combined. Stir in the 1 cup of chocolate chips. Scoop the cookie dough onto the top of the brownies and spread onto the brownie layer. I find that it's easiest to do this if the brownie layer is chilled and firm. Wet your hands or spray them with nonstick spray and pat the cookie dough on top in a even layer. Sprinkle additional chocolate chips on top to create a nicer, visual appearance. For easy, clean cutting, chill the brownies (wrap the brownies with plastic wrap and chill until firm- 1 to 2 hours or up to 2 days).
4. Cut the brownies: Run a knife along the sides of the brownie pan and then use the parchment paper to lift the brownies from the pan and onto a cutting board. Slice the brownies with a sharp knife, wiping the knife with a paper towel between cuts. If you'd like all of your slices of brownies to look clean-cut without edges, use the knife to cut the sides of the brownies off before cutting pieces. Keep brownies slices covered and chilled until ready to serve.

From the beautiful art and awesome colours to the intuitive gameplay and story, Ori is an experience. It's not a grindy sandbox you need to play or replay for a total of 100+ hours in order to feel done, it's a linear experience which is definitely something you can and should use if you want to be a "games are art comparable with movies and literature" advocate.
It's challenging but not too much so, anybody can play it and enjoy it. Probably something people might have a hard time seeing as "one of a kind" right away, but the immersive soundtrack, fun metroidvania gameplay and clear, pure and colourful art design will, in time, make you reconsider.
I'm not going to write a long essay like I've done in my "reviews" of other games, I'm just going to press the recommend button and go play it / experience it some more.
If someone reading this wants a good, concrete example of why Ori is a smooth and graphically amazing game, go look up the Ginso Tree sequence on YouTube.

A beautifully made platformer, from the art style, to the moving orchestral soundtrack, everything about this games look and feel fit together seemlessly.
I'd heard this game described as Super Meatboy-esc, but I wouldn't agree. While the controls and platforming, the movement and "puzzle solving" are tight and impressively done, I don't believe the game requires quite the white knuckled precision that Meatboy demands. The jumping feels extremely responsive, each ability that you unlock lets you traverse the terrain in a new and smart way, and make any amount of backtracking a breeze. The combat is also seemly, and while not very complex, adds enough to the game in terms of enemy tactics that you have to stay aware of your movements around them.
The story is heartfelt and really uses the art style to its advantage, though I will say, there is a moment towards the middle to end that is supposed to explain the main antagonists motives, and it leaves a lot to be desired, but I feel that the ending wraps up well enough.
The negatives for me were fairly minor. Some of the setpiece moments in the game, usually requiring you to race away from some impending insta-death, while they were good in the initial runs, giving you that thrill and pushing you along at breakneck pace, that was ruined by a couple deaths and having to rerun the same path multiple times. I didn't have too much of an issue with this but I can image some people running into a lot of trouble with these events and having the immersion and impact of the events lost to frustration.
Along with that I'd say the game wasn't exactly difficult. While there are plenty of later game areas that required precise movements and use of your abilities, and one screwup could mean death, the freedom of setting your own save points really took away a lot of what was supposed to make the game difficult. Run up against a tough spot? You could have your save right before it and just ram your head into it until you make it through, though even still most of these spots weren't too difficult and didn't require too many attempts at least for me.
Conclusion, its a really great, short game and I'd really recommend it to anyone who enjoys platformers of this type and want to see a beautiful game in motion.

Seemed like they were aiming for Lego Minecraft - we'll give you tools, blocks, unlockables, and you make your own stories...  Sure, they give you all that, but it still feels lacking in several areas - the biggest one is incentive however.  There simply is no incentive to do anything after the initial bit of running around aimlessly.  After you run around for a bit, you'll realize that that is all there is - run around and collect things.  There is no incentive to actually build a base, there is no real incentive to explore beyond collecting cosmetic things, there is no real incentive to do much of anything.
Minecraft works not because of The End, but because you get so many tools and options that go beyond simply cosmetic use - circuits, traps, survival gear, etc.  You also have an environment (several actually) that is fraught with danger - filled with creatures that come after you.  In Minecraft your incentive is to build to stay alive, to explore and discover the tools you'll need to build to survive, and if you want, there is The End for an end game incentive.  This doesn't even take into account the other things such as farming, bosses, building games within the game, mods, etc.
I actually didn't want to compare this to Minecraft as there aren't a lot of actual similarities beyond building, but it is the very lack of overall structure that they tried to "copy" from Minecraft that causes this to be a lesser game - there simply is no point to any of it - no reason to do anything because there is nothing to motivate you to do so.

I don't review games often on Steam, but New Colossus ticked a few boxes (wrongly) that compelled me to jump on and give it a review.
First up: Functionality.
Look, it's 2017. The days of PC being the 'third wheel' are gone and every game released for PC (outside of direct ports) are expected to have a certain level of function to cater to PC players. Not only does New Colossus fail to include much of that functionality, the functionality it does have is either broken or works poorly. Make no mistake, New Colossus is not a graphical powerhouse, and at no point in time will you be marvelling at the wonder of modern technology as you play it; you will, however, be constantly cursing at the failings of modern development as your game freezes for the ninetieth time before you could get to a new checkpoint.  (Note, I've heard that Adaptive Vsync can possibly be the cause of this issue. This doesn't absolve the developers, but does give you an option for getting past their failures).
Beyond the technical issues, we come to the tech itself. Look, Wolfenstein isn't the Crysis of 2017, it's graphics are average, it's animation is average, and it's sounds is average/below average. There's nothing spectacular here, but also nothing to draw a big negative against the game.  For every wonderfully lit hallway, you get the bizarrely incongruent open field where Nazi soldiers blend in like camoflauged stealth action figures
Gameplay:
If you played Wolfenstein, you probably really enjoyed the punch and power you felt, rampaging (or maybe stealthing) through levels, knocking the Nazi war machine down a peg with your superior grit and determination. Well screw that noise, now (spoiler alert!!!!) you're a Master Chief lookalike war machine, sustained by technology and constantly complaining about how you're going to die and can't go on (as you finish your three hundredth close range melee kill). Gunplay has been toned down to a point where it makes you wonder if the devs thought they were working on a different game. Melee is bizarrely overpowered, especially on non-heavy enemies, and your guns are oddly underpowered against those same enemies, which leads you to feel like chopping off limbs is how the creators intended you to play most of the game. Add in your ability to run like Usain Bolt with rocket shoes, and closing gaps to stick an axe in a Nazi's back is usually far more expedient than wisely lining up shots and picking off your enemies. Stealth, which the game really tells you is a way to play (as fas I can tell, without intended irony) is almost hilarious in its implementation. Yes, on rare occasion the game will set you up with a nice room to use a silenced pistol in (don't ask why they let you silence your submachine gun, which can kill literally no one before an alarm is raised), but even those rooms are obviously still designed for you to run and gun through, with stealth being the optional 'other way'. The rest of the rooms in the game don't even pretend like you should get through without being seen: enemies facing each other, psychic commanders that immediately know you're there when you breathe just a little too hard on the opposite side of the stadium, and patrols that are obviously intended for enemies to find those silently killed bodies you dropped: it's all setup to make stealth a pointless endeavor.
This would all be forgiveable if the gunplay was more fun, but it's not. Filling a Nazi commander with a hundred submachine gun bullets feels like an excercise in tedium. There's no reaction to the majority of your shots, besides the occasional falling over or, with a lucky shot,  holding of the groin you just shot by accident (because you wouldn't really do that to a guy, would you?). When I started the game I figured 'Oh, well that's just the submachine gun. They didn't want it to be too op. The rest of the weapons will really bring the kick', but by the time I got the shotgun I was already relegating myself to 90% melee kills, because those kills were both easier and more satisfying. Similarly, the enemy shooting you  is so poorly done that half the time you'll die without even realizing you were being shot.
This isn't to say that the gameplay is all bad. There are still plenty of times where that good old Nazi-killing Wolfenstein tradition shines through, and you get to remember the glory days of BJ, when he was chewing chicken dinners and taking names. The problem with New Colossus is that the devs seem to almost intentionally break up these sections with sections intended to force you into a different style of gameplay that is foreign to the series. As for other minor gameplay things, like jumping (which is just... I mean... I can run 60 mph but can't jump a foot off the ground?) or collectibles, there's not much to say. I will add that the collectibles have not compelled me at all, given how little interest they inspire once found; but there are plenty to find if you're a hunter of that breed and looking for a good distraction.
Last I'll briefly talk about story:
I'm sure by now you've either read a bunch of reviews by 'professional' gaming sites declaring  New Colussus an amazing game, or a bunch of reviews by average players decrying SJW infestation. I think the latter is a bit overdone (though not without warrant, for sure), but the former is... well... let's just say that the 'professionals' are doing nothing to retain credibility by heaping praise on this story. Spoilers Ahead!!!
You start off as a broke, busted BJ (picking up right after the first game), which seems initially to be a great opportunity to show your unbreakable spirit and turn New Colossus into a comeback tale for the ages. We even start the game in epic fashion, so absolutely unwilling to die that we pull ourselves into a wheelchair and snag a weapon to bring down the Nazi's from the ground. However, to reach this epic beginning, we first have to sit through a bizarre opening sequence that seems utterly unconnected to the game (though it does give you a bit of insight into how unconnected political diatrebes are going to be forced on you throughout the game). Then, after finally reaching a point where we feel like we're going to hit that 'overcoming' story line, we are instead turned into the Tin Man 12.0, and the human element of the game is almost entirely undone. The devs try, and fail, to bring back that human element by turning BJ into a whining sack of a man (no, seriously, at one point I was wishing for an option to turn BJ's dialogue off, it's so annoying). From there we meet a host of cartoon like characters that seem pulled from bad exploitation movies in the 70s-80s, not real life or any sembelance of it. Add in the constant political dialogue that seems to have no relation to the game world, and you won't really be surprised when BJ starts calling out the White man, even as you cringe. It's not the existence of these things per se that hurt the story, but the fact that they are obviously interjected and not a natural part of the story. The dialogue comes off as more a bad college essay than real story with real people, and the story itself, for reasons unknown, starts to take a backseat to this nonsense. You have a nuke, you're going to use it to blow up Nazi command, so shouldn't that be the focus? Why are we talking about how happy we are to be blowing them up because they're white? The story hamstrings itself by focusing on things that have no real relation to the story, but seem rather to have been interjected by writers wanting to pat themselves on the back. That said, if you can ignore all this, there is still a basic, if underwhelming story to enjoy.
All in all, New Colossus is a mediocre game riding the success of its predecessor, and unwarranted praise given by the 'pros'. If you want to try it, I recommend waiting for a steep sale down the line, as the game, even when enjoyed, is not worth 60$ in its current state.

With Wolfenstein 2, i feel like it is a bad case of the first one being so smooth, so fun, and so satisfying, that it basically set its sequal up for failure. Overlooking the problems with the game restarting PC's and all the other graphical issues (which isn't acceptable by any means, just feel like its been touched on enough.) and all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about political standpoints being pushed on anyone, I wanted to touch on why i think this game doesn't work gameplay wise at times. First off, im gonna get this off my chest, whoever thought it was a good idea to have you only have 50 health through half the game really needs to take a look back at what kinda game Wolfenstein is. It is a run and gun shoot em up for the most part, and it is so satisfying in these types of games to crank them up to the hardest difficulty and get to it. With this game, I can't tell you how MANY times i saw those two general signal detections pop up at the top of the screen and immediatley became frustrated and began to beg for the mission to end. For the first half of the game, i was begging missions to end because 50 health simply just isn't enough in this game, since the commanders either are blind as a bat or has they eyes of a hawk that just visined his eyes. With the amount of guys that get thrown at you if you're caught, the hardest difficulty seems, and i know im going to get thrashed for this, but it seems just too hard sometimes. The first Wolfenstein had the difficulty measured just right where it was so much fun to play on the more difficult settings, but then this one comes along and just lets you have it full force. I know this game has a community that usually go's by the code of "WE'RE REAL OG GAMERS WHO LOVE EM HARD AND ROUGH!!! I LOVE DYING 100'S OF TIMES!!!" Look, I like difficulty too, but there definitley is a point where the line gets crossed. After you get your 100 health back tho the game returns to somewhat familiar grounds, with smart movement, cover, and overcharging at the right times, most levels can be beaten with no deaths. I also feel that there are a few too many moments that signals are detected and you're encouraged to go stealth mode. I felt that the first game had more freedom for decision in this aspect. There is still a choice no doubt, but here it feels much more forced.I have 24 hours in the first game and around 5 on the old blood, and thats because i wanted to go through again on a higher setting. I think im already done with this game because after trying to get through the first half of the game on a higher difficulty was just flat out frustrating, so i turned it down to the medium setting so i could at least enjoy the game. The massive amount of head bobbing is awful, and graphically i feel like the game could have more to offer. The cutxcenes were fun to wathc and i feel like the cahracters were written fantastically. I enjoyed the story for the most part once i stopped getting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me wit a ribbon. I like the game a lot, but it definitley is not as good as the first. I'd say get this, but if you can grab the first game and the Old Blood, do that until this game gets patched and fixed a few times. I want to recommend it so bad, but the issues rn are too much to warrant a good review. Im going to play through it again once some patches get rolled out and then ill edit this review.

Right. Here I go:
The game was released almost a year ago. Before I bought the PS4 version I downloaded it as I would not want to fight with SONY for a refund in case I did not like the game so that's what I did. I actually liked it a lot and ended up buying in September the PS version. I just have sold my PS4, I upgraded my graphics card and guess what. I was missing NMS so I bought it a couple of days ago.
There has been endless bad reviews about this game. To be honest, I personally believe the people just like to go with the flow and they are doing so cause everybody and every single youtuber has talked badly about it. I strongly believe 90% of those reviews were influenced by third parties but not their own.
The game:
Is the game boring? The game is not boring. This game has a problem of guidance and it lacks of maps. Leaving the gamer wondering what in the heck they ought to do next. That is a one of the problems. In fact, If I left the game stand still for a week and come back to it later I would have no clue where I was or what I was doing. This is a big time mistake from these guys.
Is the game repetitive? I cannot believe people complain about this. Is RUST or any crafting exploring game not repetitive? Is life not repetitive? Come on! Of course it is. We follow procedures, any game is repetitive and NMS is not left aside. You got to do farming, you got to do A + B so you can get C....
Is the game buggy? Well, it was at the beginning. I had the PS4 version and to be honest, it does run better than PC. I got a MSI geforce 1080ti and my FPS vary all the time so I guess it is missing optimisation still.
Is there multiplayer on the game? Sure it is. I play with my daughter all the time.
Do I recommend it?
Sure I do. Overall when you can get it now at 24 euros. If you like crafting and exploring and getting lost.. This is your game. There is a lot to do but you will need to be very organized or otherwise you will just loose track, get upset and give a negative review.
What is the main problem then with so much negative reviews?
Main problem is that Hello Games should have never got together with Sony. These guys never finished the game and they got so much pressured on the release date that they released an early access instead. An indie company should never get together with a big name when you have got such a "weird" project. Sean Murray took advantage of that marketing injection and started exagerating the product, you can see how much he loved it, he loved it so much that he sold an idea he had in his head but SONY never left him get it finished. As simple as that.
I personally believe in the project and I think it is a fun WEIRD game to play which has a big future. If they could make the multiplayer to work they will beat any other game around...

Remember Me promises a lot more than it can ultimately deliver, but it's still a solid third-person brawler with some fantastic production values (easily one of the best game soundtracks of 2013) and a story that touches on a lot of themes and emotions most games don't bother with. The fighting is fast and fluid, and there's some scope for customising how you want to play - as a heavy hitter or constantly using heals and specials, say. It's just a shame much of the game is so easy by default you never have to do any of this. The platforming and exploration takes you through some phenomenal environments - visuals like few if any other videogames out there - but it's annoying that they're so linear you're rarely given much time to properly take anything in. And the puzzles, the "memory remixes", are a neat idea and presented well, but they're really just a case of slow trial and error to get the right boxes ticked or left unticked. A lot of Remember Me feels "good enough", then, rather than great, or makes you wish it gave you more freedom, or challenged you more, or spent more time fleshing out its story. At the same time it frequently looks and sounds phenomenal, it is still fun to play, and its story does manage some very moving, thought-provoking moments even if it's not as brave or as smart as it seems to think. Definitely pick it up on a sale if you like third-person brawlers with some smarts - just be aware it's not really as deep or as meaningful as the developers originally seemed to be implying it would be.

If you like minesweeper/puzzles/challenging-fry-my-brain-this-is-hard games, I highly recommend this game. I can't stop playing this game and it's one where my brain is being seriously worked and so I don't feel so guilty about playing it when I should be "productive" ;)
What I love about this game:
-Super challenging, but possible and therefore really rewarding
-No annoying tutorial where the game practically tells you what to do. No, this one drops hints at the beginning, either through some text below the puzzle or through the title, but it never tells you how to solve it, just helps you be aware of things to use as helps (symbol telling whether the number references corners or not, etc.)
-I have to reuse strategies but with each new puzzle am adding another new one to my toolbelt. With each new "aha" moment I'm more motivated and excited about this game.
-You never have to guess. You can play through every puzzle perfectly, but it's not easy. (Understatement) There are times where I feel completely stuck and swear that I've looked at everything but eventually find the nugget I missed and it's super satisfying. Now, this aspect annoys a lot of people so take it with a grain of salt. Personally, I LOVE it. Because I know that to solve something I don't have to guess, I will be determined to find what I'm missing. The creator does a marevelous job of making these hidden and really hard to find as one gets further in the game and I think it's genius.
As I've talked with others who've played this game, I've found that this game is most enjoyed by people who really like hard puzzle games that take time and effort to crack their secrets. Some don't quite like how frustrating this game can be, so if that sounds like you, then this game probably isn't for you. If you're willing/wanting to stare at a puzzle, stuck, for up to 30 mins then I present to you, Tametsi. A game with marevelously designed puzzles that works all of your brain that I can't stop playing. XD
Extra: When you first hit play and the small launcher comes up, there's some different options for gameplay that I think was genuis to add. I prefer to have tile and column numbers count down (as opposed to normal minesweeper where the numbers indicating how many bombs there are don't change). In addition, I prefer night-mode (or nighttime, I can't remember) so that on upon finishing a puzzle, the screen changes to a gentle dark color instead of the harsh bright that kinda hurts my eyes. The latter is the default so I encourage you to change that setting if that's something that bothers you. Don't let that turn you off from this amazing game ;)

This game is very very fun. If you enjoy puzzles, I highly recommend checking it out. Everyone has drawn comparisons to minesweeper, and rightly so. But making that comparison entirely discounts the incredible difficulty and level diversity this game has. Certain concepts can be re-used and help you get through levels faster after you get familiar with the basics, but no level can be solved entirely with simple deductions, requiring more and more advanced logic. The first 10 or so level are fairly easy, but introduce these concepts you can use to solve the rest of the game. And then after that, every single level requires intense concentration to get past.
After 10 hours, I've only beaten about half of the levels, and I fully intend to get all the way through this game, which could easily take me another 20. This is a crazy amount of entertainment for 3$. Really, my only complaint is that there is no background music, but I suppose that means you can pick your own.
If you enjoy puzzle games and logic, this game is a must-have.

Puzzle game. Minesweeper with a twist or two.
The best game I know using the minesweeper principle is Hexcells, and Tametsi is almost as good. It's using irregular grids, row clues, and different tile counts for different colors to mix it up a bit, and that is quite fun.
Options are handled on the pre-game settings screen, tab to the options. I recommend "darken finished tiles", the second "flag style for colored tiles", and "treat grey like other colors"; of course these affect only the options, not the puzzles themselves.
If you like Hexcells (or Minesweeper), you won't go wrong with this. Recommended.

If you like minesweeper (and especially if you're bored from the standard variant) this is for you.
It adds twist with tile shapes and colors. And most importantly all levels are made to be able to figure out without a single guess.  It takes a fair work to prove something to be mine or openable, so you can feel some accomplishment completing a level.

Surprisingly long puzzle game in the style of Hexcells and similar, if you enjoyed those you'll love this. This is significantly more difficult than the majority of Hexcells content, with 100 levels and various tile setups. Traditional Minesweeper style (squares with diagonals) is most common, but you also have quadrilaterals without diagonals, hexagons, and tesselations of hexagons/triangles and octagons/squares. Very clever and creative puzzle designs, all well designed with logical solutions which force you to learn as you go. I'm not quite done yet after 30 hours, extreme value for money here regarding both quality and quantity.

The Dark Souls of Minesweeper.
The puzzles are all fairly hard and cleverly crafted, with a pretty good variety of layouts and themes, so the levels don't feel as repetitive as they may in other games.

Tametsi is an incredibly tough thinking puzzle, reminiscent of minesweeper. Each level brings a new challenge to the table, forcing the player to think in different ways. The constant reminder that the player does not have to guess in order to complete a level encourages a very tangible sense of possibility: that the player can overcome each difficulty by thought. Enjoyable to play, Tametsi is guarenteed to work your mind as you logic your way through every tile.
The levels are challenging from the very start, yet not impossible. Sound too hard? Fear not! You are not penalized within the game for guessing—only perhaps the satisfaction resultant suffers.
The sound effects complement the minimalistic graphic design quite well, providing a perfect framewrok geared towards solving the puzzle. The level design is unique, with no level solving exactly like another. The tiles themselves are also varied within levels, of different sizes and shapes. To say that this game is an extension of minesweeper hardly does justice for the extreme diversity found in Tametsi.
Overall, Tametsi is a game worth playing. Level completion is the primary objective, rewarding players who think their way through. If you enjoyed minesweeper or sodoku and wanted an extra challenge, Tametsi is the perfect game for you,

Tense and challenging, Depth is probably my favorite game in the shooter vs creatures branch of FPS. It's main mode is 4 divers vs 2 sharks and each side is a unique experience. The sharks come in 6 different species (7th is coming soon) and each has a unique ability and playstyle, such as the tiger shark being able to camuflage, the hammerhead dealing extra damage while "hammering" a diver  to the wall, or the thresher dealing AoE damage with its tail. There are a few quirks that people have had and I'll focus on them:
Permadeath - Going into the game I didn't realize this was a part of this game.  I think it was very qood to enforce it early on so you realize there are consequences to not learning quickly.  I think it really pushed me to play fights conseritvely to learn my enemy so I didn't simply "hack and slash". It really made me focus and stressed out during larger fights with multiple oppenents.
Boring start... While I fully understand what some folks have written with only 2 hours of play time.  The game really begins to shine after that.  The puzzles at the begining did tend to be a  boring but they are training you how to think for the later part of the game where you'll apply what you learned.
Allot of walking... yes in the first two hours of the game this is very time consuming.  There is also allot of backtracking which irritatied me but this downtime was needed to build up the story.  You'll know what I mean when playing it and reflecting on it.  I hope they also address this with more content at some point via DLC as I'm sure this is where allot of people will drop off.  With Steams refund policy that will be the kicker.

Outstanding game, the binaural sound is very immersive if you are using headphones. The soundtrack is great, and can make you feel invincible one minute and helpless the next.
Some words of caution though, the game is primarily a story driven psychological journey with puzzle solving and illusions and a fighting game second. That being said, the combat is quite intense, and the fact that there is a perma-death mechanic after too many failures adds to tension of each fight. You must use all your skills in combat when surrounded, timed parries, evasion, and a bullet-time mechanic called focus.
There is no proper tutorial to introduce you to the various combat moves, perhaps this was a design choice to enchance immersion. A quick look at the control settings can tell you, and there is a counter-attack opportunity for well timed parries that you can execute with a heavy or light attack. You can also charge and leap with heavy or light attacks when combined with sprint, and there is a stab attack that can be done tapping sprint and light attack. These are things that I discovered while playing and aren't listed.
The game is not long, I found most of the optional lore stones that tell excerpts of norse folklore stories and completed the game in 8 hours. But it was a wild ride for sure, and I loved every minute of it!

Well this game has been rattling around my library for quite some time now, I finally clicked "play". Then I didn't get out of my chair for the next 3 hours.
To the Moon is a great story, the whole game plays out like a nice movie. A few 4th wall breaking references here or there, some comic relief, and of course TONS of sappiness. I really wasn't sure what to expect going into this, but with so many positive reviews and such a neat pricetag I remained fairly optimistic, and honestly any expectations I might've had were blown out of the water by what this game really delivered. I didn't think such a story could be told in this format, I didn't know that so few pixels could make me experience so many feels..
I can't make a pros/cons list for this game really. It wouldn't really make sense. If you want to sit back and casually navigate your way through a captivating story then this game might be for you! If you're looking for a more interactive experience - or maybe want to blow some♥♥♥♥♥♥up - I wouldn't recommend this for you.
Honestly even if this isn't the type of game you think you'd enjoy I would still recommend waiting for a sale and giving it a shot, I spent 2$ and then one day I was in the mood for something different, and now here I am adding another thumbs up to the mountain of positive reviews this game has :)

A heartbreaking and beautiful story, and an absolute must play in my mind.  This should be made into an film...
As for the gameplay itself... The controls aren't the best ( it is worth noting that it's clearly made for mouse play, so don't fret it when your gamepad doesn't work ) and at the start the gameplay isn't fully clear with the links and mementos (which again.. it becomes pretty intuitive), but none of this should stop you from playing this game.  It is absolutely worth playing despite any minor flaws.
As a side note.. there is only one achievement, and it is granted simply for completing the game.  This is actually quite perfect, because the only thing that is important about this game IS the story.  Enjoy it.  Don't expect a lot of gaming as this is just the chosen vehicle for the narrative.  Don't stress about missing anything.. you won't.  Just enjoy the story.
Also.. the music is great.
Bonus points for all the nerdy pop-culture references.

- MINOR SPOILERS -
Compared to "new order" the game had some improvements under certain aspects and setbacks on others, it overall doesn't deserve the high scores and praises most of critics gave them.
To put it really simply the game received the Doom treatment, the movement in particular is almost an exact copy of the most recent doom game, it works extremely well since one of my issue with new order was the slow movement speed, an other thing it inherited was the music, here i'm not sure it was for the best, i loved the Doom soundtrack but while the low "demonic" tones had a meaning there, here they somewhat feel out of place in my opinion, great inspiration but somewhat of a more original take to it would have been more appreciated.
Gameplay is where the game excels, from the sound of the guns, to the animations, to the particle effects, everything help to give a feel of badassery that surpasses even what we saw in doom 2016, there's not a huge variety of weapons but everyone feels unique and the enemy ai is good expecially compared to the low standards we saw in recent years. My only minor issue is that  weapons are too big, if you play with high fov they cover almost half of the screen and it becomes really annoying after a while.
The game wants to be an engaging and immersive single player story and here is where it falls flat. While it has some interesting characters the plot is way too much segmented, it really lacks linearity and continuity, it's not a long journey like in hl2 or metro games, it's a set of missions that don't have too much to do with each other (blow up something, talk to the resistance, get secret documents, kill general ... ). It also ends in a really incomplete way, while in the recent Doom you did what you had to do (stop demonic invasion) and it ended with a cliffhanger, here you don't defeat the nazis, everything you were working on just stops in the last mission, similar to Deus Ex Mankind Divided.
The way they decided to implement really long cutscenes in such a frenetic game is really questionable, they really drop the pasing of the overall experience, it's fun for a while but when it ends up being 5 minutes of cutscenes every 10/15 of gameplay it starts becoming an issue; furthermore they don't help building up an interesting plot, they focus on building up only the characters.
An area where the doom treatment doesn't work is the overabundance of collectables, firstly they are mostly useless, and secondly they don't fit with the approach the game takes : everything in the game tells you to go fast, to just kill and move ahead, from the movement speed, to the narration, to the draining overcharge health but at the same time the game seems to want you to slow down, explore and find secrets; i was once in a room after a gunfight where i had a guy screaming at me to move and just jump to the helicopter to finish the mission while at the same time there were collectables scattered all over that room.
While not a bad game per se, it underwhelmed the high expectations.

So I've just beat the game on the Do or Die difficulty and have experimented with some of the side missions, and I have to say that the game is everything I wanted it to be. (I am aware that the game doesn't work for some people due to some faulty programming, but I am reviewing the game based off of my personal experience with it as it worked fine with me.)
So let's start with the pros:
1. Stellar gunplay (very similar to The New Order and DOOM 2016)
2. New skills (won't spoil how you get them but they are pretty cool)
3. Amazing voice acting and characterization.
4. Pretty good story. (Not the best, but it's more than good enough to give you good reasons as to why you are killing Nazis and tie the experience together as well)
5. Mick Gordon's soundtrack. Seriously, I essentially am influenced very positively into buying a game if Mick Gordon handles the soundtrack. I loved his work in DOOM last year, I loved what he did with Prey this year and I also love the soundtrack he expertly crafted for The New Colossus.
6. More content is coming in the future in the form of The Freedom Chronicles! I'm personally very excited for this additional content as it gives me more reason to play The New Colossus once they are released. (And even then, I am still playing it to kill Ubercommanders and I hope to kill them all).
7. Depending on the difficulty you play on, it will kick you in the♥♥♥♥♥and be a good challenge which is a good thing as I played on one of the harder difficulties to enhance my Nazi killing spree.
Cons:
1. This doesn't happen too often, but I sometimes get caught in the geometry of the map and I can't move. Occasionally, I'll be walking through a door and I'll collide with some faulty geometry and I have to fidget to get through. Doesn't happen all the time, but it was something that I noticed.
2. As cool as the story is, I found that the ending was a little tame compared to the ending of The New Order. This might be because they are setting up for a DLC pack, but I'm not sure we'll be seeing more content centered around the main cast until the next Wolfenstein game as the DLCs are going to center around different characters with new skills and such.
3. Technical issues, likely due to either faulty programming or a rapidly approaching deadline. Although the game ran great for me (specs below) many other people are having issues which is something to consider if you are wanting to play The New Colossus.
Overall, it's an amazing game and I recommend that anyone who is a fan of first person shooters tries this game. (I'd also wait for some hot fixes or patches to address the technical issues that others are dealing with) and is my 2nd favorite game of the year only behind NieR: Automata. I commend MachineGames for carefully crafting a beautiful and brutal new installment of the Wolfenstein franchise and I hope that they are able to take this feedback and improve either the DLC packs or the next game. (Or both, for that matter!)

I've always been a fan of ARPG's, since the very start of the first Diablo, so began my journey of endless clicking and replacing one pair of apparel with another due to a minor stat change! If you've played several ARPG's already, you'll know how they basically all share the same concept and pretty much are one in the same, perhaps the only difference would be the actual story, and even then it can become quite monotonous and you don't actually end up following it.
Surprisingly, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is nothing like that! Sure it may be a hack 'n slash clickfest, but within its core lies a beautiful system unlike any other! The fast paced combat, the synergy with abilities and auras/tricks as well as the ability to craft (transmute) and enhance your items by adding and combining "essences" combined with a rather interesting story that one cannot help but follow (as there isn't many side quests to get lost on) makes for one hell of a good time in the beautiful world of Borgovia!
I can however say from experience having played several ARPG's that this is by far the more challenging of the lot I've actually come across, and I mean that in a really good way. Though I did play on Hard it felt more like Hell of Diablo II right from the get go, and loot certainly wasn't overpowering (I was playing the newly released Thaumaturge class and it seems there isn't much unique loot as compared to the original Hunter class which every second unique I got was for it).
The gameplay is really well polished, and so too are the graphics, which is surprising for an Indie release! I honestly cannot find any faults with the game itself, perhaps only that it was rather short (30 odd hours exploring EVERYTHING) but it strikes the perfect balance and somehow doesn't take you on a grindfest to actually progress and unlock everything you need or want! So all in all this is definitely a game I would recommend to any ARPG fans who loved Diablo or Torchlight!

It is astounding that this game has been reviewed so poorly. Simply put, this game is fantastic. Neo-Paris as a location is excellently crafted and includes some fantastic looking scifi landscapes and locations. Story is great and action mostly satisfying. And even when the actual game takes place on Neo-Paris where most citizens live in a life of luxury and wellfare, most of the world is in complete chaos. Hunreds of millions people live in destituon and are suffering greatly, when few lucky ones are living in a nation that has survived the last war that ravaged the Earth. There are nice tidbits of information here and there if the player finds a time to look for them.
Still, this game has it's issues: sometimes when you are climbing it feels like player interaction is at its minimum. On the other hand at least you are not getting any frustrating mis-jumps because the game failed to interped where the player wanted to jump. Also playable areas are very restricted and the game is VERY linear. I have no issues with linear games, in fact many of the best games ever are linear, but I cannot shake the feeling how awesome it would have been to be able to freely explore Neo-Paris. It just is so fantastic looking place that explorable open world would have been even better. Also, English voice acting is not very good. It is not bad either, but if you compare it to the French voice acting, the French one is far superior. That is why I wholeheartedly recommend that you play this game with the French voice overs and use subtitles.
Rarely I get to see such an excellent scifi game that also has very unigue twist to it, memory manipulation. I cannot recommend this game enough. If you still wonder if the game is worth its asking price, then wait for a sale and grab it. You won't be dissappointed if you do not mind linear games. Also, play this on the hardest difficulty setting if you want to have challenging combat.

Remember Me is an odd duck of a game. It's a mix of ideas all thrown into a pot, some of which don't pan out and others that turn out really, really good.
First and foremost: don't buy this game at full price. It's entertaining, but it is by no means worth the $50 base they are still trying to charge. However, it is one of those games that does get exponentially better the lower it gets, and I found it to be a very solid $10-$12 mid-range title. It doesn't go on sale very often, either, so get it when it gets down to that range.
The actual gameplay itself is a bit of trial-and-error. The combat follows the now-standard Batman and Sleeping Dogs formula with the twist of being able to create your own combo systems. It's not as fleshed out as I would like, and the controls are not as tight as others with the system. However, being able to reset timers or heal yourself via punching is a nice addition.
Some of the cooler segments involve rearranging memories, in which you are placed into a scene and must make small changes to it that greatly affect the outcome (i.e. make a doctor kill a patient instead of curing him by messing with the hospital room, etc). The only downside is that the system is used very infrequently, with only two or so such scenes in the first several episodes. Again, a lot of cool ideas but none of them fleshed out much.
What really makes the game, though, is the story and atmosphere. The game is absolutely gorgeous, and in the absence of good Cyberpunk games, it really does stand out. Nilin is a great character, and the city is breathaking on systems playing the High settings. I found myself actively trying to find the little Journal Mnesists things so that I could learn about the world you play through. They did a great job of building a futuristic Paris. I wish it was not such a linear game (especially for one that promotes the exploration aspects of it), but what paths we are set on really demand a lot of admiration.
It's not a perfect game, by any means, and the half-hearted attempts at some of the gameplay gimmicks keep it from being a true AAA title. That said, however, it really is a very unique and mostly fun game that will likely leave you entertained, if for no other reason than the story, visuals, and grand locations. It's a game with a ton of ambition behind it that fell just short of being fantastic, and it could warrant a sequel to tweak or expand what it does right. Well worth a steep sale price, but avoid at retail.

This game is a fine remake of the original, although it may be a little overpriced for the content provided. The game is a simple top down beat 'em up, and each character has a lot of customization. Unfortunately, very few people play the game online, so you'll probably have to play alone or with friends. The campagin isn't all that fun, which is why $20 is a bit much for this game. You'll probably want to buy it on sale. Also, I would recommend playing this with a controller. I've used both an XBox and Steam controller, and they both work. However, I would say that the XBox controller works a little better.
In terms of customization, each character can use different weapons, relics, ways to use the potions, and appearances. The weapons can change the two main attacks and the special attack for each character. Relics are separate powers, such as a speed boost or another monster that fights at your side. Each character has a few ways of using potions they find in battle. Appearances just change the look of your character.
The only real drawbacks in this game is the lack of players online (mitigated by just playing with friends, which is more fun anyways), and the DLC character which costs $5. I think it's overpriced for just one character, and that character is probably overpowered due to its price (although this doesn't matter that much in a co-op game).

Ninja Theory has titled Hellblade as a AAA indie, and it shows from the beginning to the end of this game. The graphics and atmosphere are stellar, even superior to more recent AAA games. Without any spoiling, the story is very engaging and interesting, and it is constantly developing through the many chattering voices in Senua's head. The puzzles in this game are mostly simple and can be solved fairly easily, but the real center of attention for me here is the combat. I don't review games often on Steam, but New Colossus ticked a few boxes (wrongly) that compelled me to jump on and give it a review.
First up: Functionality.
Look, it's 2017. The days of PC being the 'third wheel' are gone and every game released for PC (outside of direct ports) are expected to have a certain level of function to cater to PC players. Not only does New Colossus fail to include much of that functionality, the functionality it does have is either broken or works poorly. Make no mistake, New Colossus is not a graphical powerhouse, and at no point in time will you be marvelling at the wonder of modern technology as you play it; you will, however, be constantly cursing at the failings of modern development as your game freezes for the ninetieth time before you could get to a new checkpoint.  (Note, I've heard that Adaptive Vsync can possibly be the cause of this issue. This doesn't absolve the developers, but does give you an option for getting past their failures).
Beyond the technical issues, we come to the tech itself. Look, Wolfenstein isn't the Crysis of 2017, it's graphics are average, it's animation is average, and it's sounds is average/below average. There's nothing spectacular here, but also nothing to draw a big negative against the game.  For every wonderfully lit hallway, you get the bizarrely incongruent open field where Nazi soldiers blend in like camoflauged stealth action figures
Gameplay:
If you played Wolfenstein, you probably really enjoyed the punch and power you felt, rampaging (or maybe stealthing) through levels, knocking the Nazi war machine down a peg with your superior grit and determination. Well screw that noise, now (spoiler alert!!!!) you're a Master Chief lookalike war machine, sustained by technology and constantly complaining about how you're going to die and can't go on (as you finish your three hundredth close range melee kill). Gunplay has been toned down to a point where it makes you wonder if the devs thought they were working on a different game. Melee is bizarrely overpowered, especially on non-heavy enemies, and your guns are oddly underpowered against those same enemies, which leads you to feel like chopping off limbs is how the creators intended you to play most of the game. Add in your ability to run like Usain Bolt with rocket shoes, and closing gaps to stick an axe in a Nazi's back is usually far more expedient than wisely lining up shots and picking off your enemies. Stealth, which the game really tells you is a way to play (as fas I can tell, without intended irony) is almost hilarious in its implementation. Yes, on rare occasion the game will set you up with a nice room to use a silenced pistol in (don't ask why they let you silence your submachine gun, which can kill literally no one before an alarm is raised), but even those rooms are obviously still designed for you to run and gun through, with stealth being the optional 'other way'. The rest of the rooms in the game don't even pretend like you should get through without being seen: enemies facing each other, psychic commanders that immediately know you're there when you breathe just a little too hard on the opposite side of the stadium, and patrols that are obviously intended for enemies to find those silently killed bodies you dropped: it's all setup to make stealth a pointless endeavor.
This would all be forgiveable if the gunplay was more fun, but it's not. Filling a Nazi commander with a hundred submachine gun bullets feels like an excercise in tedium. There's no reaction to the majority of your shots, besides the occasional falling over or, with a lucky shot,  holding of the groin you just shot by accident (because you wouldn't really do that to a guy, would you?). When I started the game I figured 'Oh, well that's just the submachine gun. They didn't want it to be too op. The rest of the weapons will really bring the kick', but by the time I got the shotgun I was already relegating myself to 90% melee kills, because those kills were both easier and more satisfying. Similarly, the enemy shooting you  is so poorly done that half the time you'll die without even realizing you were being shot.
This isn't to say that the gameplay is all bad. There are still plenty of times where that good old Nazi-killing Wolfenstein tradition shines through, and you get to remember the glory days of BJ, when he was chewing chicken dinners and taking names. The problem with New Colossus is that the devs seem to almost intentionally break up these sections with sections intended to force you into a different style of gameplay that is foreign to the series. As for other minor gameplay things, like jumping (which is just... I mean... I can run 60 mph but can't jump a foot off the ground?) or collectibles, there's not much to say. I will add that the collectibles have not compelled me at all, given how little interest they inspire once found; but there are plenty to find if you're a hunter of that breed and looking for a good distraction.
Last I'll briefly talk about story:
I'm sure by now you've either read a bunch of reviews by 'professional' gaming sites declaring  New Colussus an amazing game, or a bunch of reviews by average players decrying SJW infestation. I think the latter is a bit overdone (though not without warrant, for sure), but the former is... well... let's just say that the 'professionals' are doing nothing to retain credibility by heaping praise on this story. Spoilers Ahead!!!
You start off as a broke, busted BJ (picking up right after the first game), which seems initially to be a great opportunity to show your unbreakable spirit and turn New Colossus into a comeback tale for the ages. We even start the game in epic fashion, so absolutely unwilling to die that we pull ourselves into a wheelchair and snag a weapon to bring down the Nazi's from the ground. However, to reach this epic beginning, we first have to sit through a bizarre opening sequence that seems utterly unconnected to the game (though it does give you a bit of insight into how unconnected political diatrebes are going to be forced on you throughout the game). Then, after finally reaching a point where we feel like we're going to hit that 'overcoming' story line, we are instead turned into the Tin Man 12.0, and the human element of the game is almost entirely undone. The devs try, and fail, to bring back that human element by turning BJ into a whining sack of a man (no, seriously, at one point I was wishing for an option to turn BJ's dialogue off, it's so annoying). From there we meet a host of cartoon like characters that seem pulled from bad exploitation movies in the 70s-80s, not real life or any sembelance of it. Add in the constant political dialogue that seems to have no relation to the game world, and you won't really be surprised when BJ starts calling out the White man, even as you cringe. It's not the existence of these things per se that hurt the story, but the fact that they are obviously interjected and not a natural part of the story. The dialogue comes off as more a bad college essay than real story with real people, and the story itself, for reasons unknown, starts to take a backseat to this nonsense. You have a nuke, you're going to use it to blow up Nazi command, so shouldn't that be the focus? Why are we talking about how happy we are to be blowing them up because they're white? The story hamstrings itself by focusing on things that have no real relation to the story, but seem rather to have been interjected by writers wanting to pat themselves on the back. That said, if you can ignore all this, there is still a basic, if underwhelming story to enjoy.
All in all, New Colossus is a mediocre game riding the success of its predecessor, and unwarranted praise given by the 'pros'. If you want to try it, I recommend waiting for a steep sale down the line, as the game, even when enjoyed, is not worth 60$ in its current state.

- MINOR SPOILERS -
Compared to "new order" the game had some improvements under certain aspects and setbacks on others, it overall doesn't deserve the high scores and praises most of critics gave them.
To put it really simply the game received the Doom treatment, the movement in particular is almost an exact copy of the most recent doom game, it works extremely well since one of my issue with new order was the slow movement speed, an other thing it inherited was the music, here i'm not sure it was for the best, i loved the Doom soundtrack but while the low "demonic" tones had a meaning there, here they somewhat feel out of place in my opinion, great inspiration but somewhat of a more original take to it would have been more appreciated.
Gameplay is where the game excels, from the sound of the guns, to the animations, to the particle effects, everything help to give a feel of badassery that surpasses even what we saw in doom 2016, there's not a huge variety of weapons but everyone feels unique and the enemy ai is good expecially compared to the low standards we saw in recent years. My only minor issue is that  weapons are too big, if you play with high fov they cover almost half of the screen and it becomes really annoying after a while.
The game wants to be an engaging and immersive single player story and here is where it falls flat. While it has some interesting characters the plot is way too much segmented, it really lacks linearity and continuity, it's not a long journey like in hl2 or metro games, it's a set of missions that don't have too much to do with each other (blow up something, talk to the resistance, get secret documents, kill general ... ). It also ends in a really incomplete way, while in the recent Doom you did what you had to do (stop demonic invasion) and it ended with a cliffhanger, here you don't defeat the nazis, everything you were working on just stops in the last mission, similar to Deus Ex Mankind Divided.
The way they decided to implement really long cutscenes in such a frenetic game is really questionable, they really drop the pasing of the overall experience, it's fun for a while but when it ends up being 5 minutes of cutscenes every 10/15 of gameplay it starts becoming an issue; furthermore they don't help building up an interesting plot, they focus on building up only the characters.
An area where the doom treatment doesn't work is the overabundance of collectables, firstly they are mostly useless, and secondly they don't fit with the approach the game takes : everything in the game tells you to go fast, to just kill and move ahead, from the movement speed, to the narration, to the draining overcharge health but at the same time the game seems to want you to slow down, explore and find secrets; i was once in a room after a gunfight where i had a guy screaming at me to move and just jump to the helicopter to finish the mission while at the same time there were collectables scattered all over that room.
While not a bad game per se, it underwhelmed the high expectations.
