No Man's Sky is a single player experience game by Hello Games.  There is no object of the game nor is there an end of the game.  The game is about exploration and survival in a procedureally generated universe.
There is no multiplayer.
There have been two major updates since the game was released in August 2016.
First came the Foundation Update which gave the game three different modes, Normal (the original game), Creative (same as Normal but but without worrying about resoures or player health; a sandbox mode if you like) and Survival (same as Normal but with more difficult conditions to be encountetred).
Next came the Pathfinder Update which added Permadeath (same as Survival but when you die, your progress is erased, gone forever).  It also added base building and three vehicles to aid in your exploration.  And a whole host of other graphical enhancements.  Also included in this update for PC players is the ability to share your base via Steam Workshop.  Another addition in Pathfinder is Photo Mode which helps the player take screenshots by giving the ability to 'move the sun', different filters, add or remove effects such as fog or cloud layers.
Though there has been no offical word, it appears that a third major update is in the works, possibly involving portals.
There is a passionate community around this game and also a passionate crowd of detractors.  I would not reccomend No Man's Sky to everyone but if you into chill games with no objective, I'd reccomend it.

Okay, Remember Me is a good game. It is absolutely stunning even on lower graphics settings, with a gorgeous cyberpunk setting and beautiful (if very, very linear) environment, and has an interesting story and compelling main character that made me want to play it all the way through. It also has a terrific soundtrack.
All of that said, the gameplay gets difficult and tedious quite early on. Combat simply takes too long and is too predictable for it to be really fun, especially during boss fights where missing a single quick-time event (which flash up extremely quickly) will force you to get that last bit of health down again (and again). I feel like a simple counter button would have helped speed things along a lot, given that the only way to avoid attacks without it is dodging (pretty much always breaking your combo).
Other minor complaints I have would be the fiddly, fiddly controls during the remix sequences (otherwise a very neat and interesting addition), and some of the dialogue writing - it often sounds very false and purple-prose-ish, particularly whenever Edge is on the line. I don't find that it detracts overly from the story, it's just a little jarring at times.
Like I said, Remember Me is still a good game, and I would recommend it if you're looking for a interesting story and a great main character (how many non-white female protagonists do we get in video games at the moment?). I definitely also recommend, however, waiting for a good sale, and preparing for a few rage quit moments along the way.

It's not perfect and there are games that do a better job implementing similar mechanics with much more polish but Remember Me is a game with a lot going for it; the story is compelling and in Nilin it has a strong, interesting lead character whose ability to remix or steal memories makes the game a distinctive and enduring experience. Remember Me sets out to explore the relationship between our memories and our identities and what might happen if we were able to really take control of our narrative identity and remove the parts of our pasts that don't fit the story we tell ourselves or others. The dialogue sometimes isn't great and the game doesn't make use of it's unique features nearly enough, but despite its flaws Remember Me is one of the standout games of 2013.

First off: As an Intel/Nvidia user I experienced no performance issues whatsoever, using max settings and WQHD resolution.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice carries you off to a journey into the mind of a troubled young woman. The voices and memories in her head are a constant companion along the way. Sometimes they help you, sometimes they confuse you, sometimes they try to scare you, sometimes they mock you, and sometimes they are plainly getting on your nerves. 3D audio creates the feeling that these voices come from every direction. Near, far - it's almost as if someone sits on your shoulder whispering in your ear. I mention that, because it's almost the first thing you notice, when starting the game and it's done very well - technically as well as in terms of voice acting. The music in this game is coherent and tasteful. It fits every situation, never feels out of place or time.
Graphically the game looks amazing. There are some people who claim world textures look bad. I don't share their opinion. The environment looks convincing to me. Taking a look at Senua, the main protagonist, should eradicate any left over doubts. There is so much visual detail on this character, I found myself several minutes in sum just studying them. Sometimes Senua encounters what seem to be ghosts. Graphically they are real live captures of some actors, blurred a bit, to make them look ghostly. This can feel a bit out of place and weird, but in the end, for what they are, you can accept them.
Gameplay: You're confronted with mainly visual riddles. Find matching patterns, travelling through alternative versions of a map to find a way around obstacles, blurred visions where you have to focus on details to find the right direction. Sometimes you have stealth segments, or segments where you get important imput from the vibration of your gamepad. These riddles and tasks are not particularly hard to master, but from time to time you will  have to think and look closely. It's not a stressfull experience, but it's also not painfully obvious. All in all I think it's a good mix of tasks, aimed toward casual players. Which is fine for me. I liked it.
The fights: Fights are visually well presented. When Senua fights it's pleasing to look at, because her fighting style is akin to a dance. The controls are fluent and fun. It just feels right and even when there is no tutorial, you somehow figure it out without big efforts. The whole game lacks any hud, but you will always see what is happening, and you will always know when a situation is critical. It's so well done, you almost can feel Senua's pain yourself. Difficulty within the fights is rather steered by quantity, than by quality. If you're carefull and attentive you will master each enemy in a short period of time. However, sometimes many enemies will sorround you and that's when things get a bit more exciting. You then will have to position yourself tactically and/or prove some quick reaction capacities. Otherwise you will simply be pummeled into the ground. Boss fights mix it a bit up. Sometimes you have the chance to slow down speed for the enemies, which gives you an advantage in certain situations, but this effect will drain and vanish. You cannot rely on it forever. Again it's certainly not the most challenging experience, especially not when you're accustomed to fights like in Salt and Sanctuary or Darksouls, but if you're good and like to mess around a bit, just to make your character look cool, you will have some enjoyable moments for sure. After all, this game's emphasis doesn't lie on combat. It's story driven.
And Hellblade does drive the story pretty well. A plus point: If you are interested in north mythology you definitely get your money's worth. It's presented very well and as far as I can tell very faithfully. It's hidden in the world and searching for it can be fun in it's own rights. The lore snippets have just enough good cliffhangers to keep you invested in finding more.
All in all. For this price I am surprised. The quality of the game is great. Even though it's 'only' 8-10 hours long, it just feels round and complete. I think it's enough. You don't have to drag something out. When it's done, it's done. It just has to be done right. And I think Hellblade is just that - done right. I don't have something big to complain about. Maybe some rare camera quirks? Nothing game breaking however. If you are an AMD user though I'd suggest you wait for a patch. As of now (mid August 17) there seem to be some performance issues for you. Nevertheless I recommend this game. It's worth the story and psychological experience. Very enjoyable.

This game is a cross between Dear Esther and Dark Souls.
Through melancholic and often disturbing storytelling Ninja Theory unveils the story of Senua, a celtic warrior who seeks to avenge the death of her lover Dillian, who was slain at the hands of viking invaders. She travels through the various areas of Helheim, defeating increasingly monstrous enemies on her quest.
The first thing that I noticed when playing Hellblade is its beauty. Both landscape and character design as fantastic and in particular the facial animation of Senua is strikingly impressive, knocking AAA games like Andromeda out of the park (granted, that's not hard).
The gameplay can be split fairly evenly into three parts: combat, puzzles, and exploration, and while the pacing does at times feel a little off (having a tense, long boss fight followed by a less high-stakes fight instead of downtime), for the most part the experience flows, pulling you back and forth between suspense, intrigue, and action.
For this alone the game recieves 9/10, but Ninja Theory takes a risk in including a focus on psychosis; Senua suffers from delusions and hallucinations and the source and effect of these are revealed steadily throughout the game. Rather than trivialise the conditions, Senua's struggle is a thoughtful, evocative look at how early middle-age Picts treated mental disorders. The risk pays off, adding layers to the story's depth.
If you enjoy story-driven, cinematic interactive works of art, buy this game. It is not an RPG with items and customisation. Niether is it a hack-and-slash with fighting around every corner. It's a thought-provoking masterpiece - 9.5/10

I've never really written a review before about a game, But I must say this game is one of the best I have ever played in my entire 25 years of being on this earth. The visuals are stunning the motion capture is amazing and the whole genre and setting is just a complete emotional rollercoater throughout your playtime.
The whole basis of the psychosis and dealing with it is just tremendous, I have never experienced mental issues but this game really shows you what its like to live with such a terrible illness, *HEADPHONES MUST BE WORN* don't even play if you dont have any the experience and the 3D surround of the "voices" is an experience that can only be truly felt through the comfort of your headphones. The fact that this game is the first AA title I cant really see any other Dev producing something even half as good, The story was just the right length I literally played from start to finish because I felt like I could'nt leave the game I just had to play more and more, For a game to do this to me is very special and should be well rewarded.

Thank you Ninja Theory you make me proud to be British and I would of gladly paid full price for this game.

So after first hearing about this title about a year ago I have followed its development rather keenly and now that its finally out, I get to have a little bit of a say about it after about 6 hours or so of play (At the time of me writing this)
In a world where so many games have been made, so may ideas turned into fantastic tittles its hard to put forward unique ideas. Ninja Theory however, have certainly done a number with Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice.

Of course one of the biggest attractions to this game isn't even in your control at all. Its not some super cool looking takedown, its not cool acrobatics or the ability to throw bolts of lightning infinatly to stun lock Invaders (I am looking at you Dank Souls) but its the use of the binural audio to simulate the mental illness that Senua suffers from.
Senua who suffers from Phychosis hears voices, whispers, sometimes helpfull, sometimes mocking and some times even just being downright anoying, especially if you get stuck at a puzzle. But this adds a different fell to the game, its nothing I have seen implemented in any game before this and it makes you fell, somewhat more connected to the character.
(IF YOU DONT PLAY THIS GAME WITH HEADPHONES, THE WHOLE EXPERIANCE OF THE FEATURE ABOVE WILL BE LOST ON YOU AND I FEEL ITS A RATHER IMPORTANT ASPECT TO THE GAME)

The ammount of effort put into this game is astounding. The combat although it starts rather slow really shines especially when you go into a boss fight. You cant just left and right click to win here. You really gotta watch and learn attack patterns, learn what needs to be dodged, what can be parried and general dodge direction. Its fun but not the main focus of the game

Ninja Theory are no strangers to the TrippleA market, Pushing out popular games such as DMC Devil May Cry and Heavinly Sword. But they describ this as am "Indie TrippleA" game. The quality of something you would see released from a major developer but not quite as long (10 hour playthrough Ninja Theory say) so they have set the price acordingly and at only $30 its well worth your time. There's a great story in here but it needs a professional writer to edit and redraft it. As it is, the dialogue is very clumsy, very painful, very awkward, very unnatural - the inappropriately shoehorned jokes range from unfunny to baffling. Half the story deals with people middle-aged to elderly but the characters all speak consistently like teenagers or young adults. I hate to be that kind of snob but - maybe the overwhelmingly positive rating comes from a mostly younger audience who don't notice the bad dialogue as much? Like how Stephanie Meyer's books are so successful?
It's a shame, the core ideas - mostly Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind with chunks of Elfen Lied - are solid and at times I came tantalisingly close to feeling something.
Art and animation and music were all polished, can't fault them. Found the controls to be clunky, seemed a bit haphazard as to whether I could click on a thing or not, and invisible walls everywhere. There's no real gameplay, there's objects or places in the map that when clicked on will help progress the story, same as a lot of walking simulators, which I don't mind if the story's worth it.
This is a completely un-cynical game written with passion and some talent, about a quasi sci-fi future where a dying man's memories of his sometimes troubled marriage to his childhood sweetheart, who lived with asperger's, are relived in a bid to grant his deathbed wish of going to the moon. That's such an awesome setup, and how many video games are we going to get with that kind of thoughtful and creative elevator pitch? And I hate, hate, hate this game for wasting it on what's basically a particularly surreal and lengthy Big Bang Theory episode. Bazoonga! or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ that guy says.

Bethesda realising the golden turd that they hold is actually worth more than standard retail release decided to add an extra paywall for The New Colossus in the form of a much needed brand new £200 graphics card. (Good luck trying to play this unoptimised mess, screamed MachineGames dev team). Bethesda's genius finance team then realised that a player will be forced to spend over 2 to 12 hours installing new hardware and possibly longer if ordering a GPU worldwide. Thus, ensuring any effort worth dedicating this much time to will not be refunded after. Confusingly enough after upgrading their PC's players will still find themselves unable to play the game, twice I found myself laughing maniacally after suffering a BSoD (Bethesda really know how to tug at your emotions).
With the knowledge that Bethesda had invented a new market for dlc in the form willing self-inflicted pain a player will find an elated sense of depression unmatched by other games with strong narratives. It's an odd sort of 'out the box' approach that Bethesda are wanting to take with The New Colossus, but it is in this reviewer’s humble opinion gamers from young to old will all find something to cherish.
To summarise I would give the new colossus an 8/10 for its brave 'face facts life is♥♥♥♥♥♥ theme, though there are a few rough corners (Maybe add dlc, were you get past the first menu?).

A compelling experience, not without its flaws.
An intriguing sci-fi concept, some pretty great art direction and a unique and challenging (if perhaps for the wrong reasons) combat system.
Well and truly worth your time (and the soundtrack is *incredible*).

When I play a game I want to like it, and there is plenty to like in Remember me. There are of wonderful elements to appreciate in this game from the amazing soundtrack, to the incredible visuals, to the fun and intriguing cyber punk story, and a unique take on a free flow melee combat system.
The game is far from perfect of course. A few mechanics don't quite always work and it seemed like there were a few hit detection issues, sometimes enemies seemed to have an unfair reach, and at times they seemed to have a near precognitive ability to know right where I would dodge so that they were waiting to get another cheap hit in as soon as I landed. Some of the cheap shots and other issues seemed to be alleviated as you found the best rhythm in each fight. Quick combos to regain health then dodge dodge, quick cooldown combo and etc. The combo system, combined with your various special abilities, do give combat a very strategic feel and there is a nice array of enemy types to always test you. Overall it can be very rewarding when you manage to pull out a win against all odds, or bring your health back up from the brink of death, but on the flip side it can be terribly frustrating. Not often but in some of the bigger battles certainly.
However, I would still highly recommend this game. I was surprised how much I liked the story and it certainly went certain places and explored certain themes I had not expected. This is a game and setting with so much potential. Sadly, I feel they didn't get to explore the full potential in this game. But then that's all the more reason to support original IPs like this. Its entertaining and it felt incredibly unique, which is often hard to do these days.
So pick this one up and give it a try.

I got
which included this game as well as
for $5. What a deal! This game alone is worth more than $5. In a nutshell,
is a fantasy-themed platformer with physics-based puzzles.
The player controls a knight, a thief, and a wizard on a quest to rid the land of a growing evil after they all become bound to a mysterious artifact called the Trine. Each character has his or her own attacks  and abilities. The knight has a sword and shield, the thief has a bow and a grappling hook, and the wizard can conjure objects and levitate them. It's fun to use the abilities of each character to figure out how to traverse wide spaces, open gates, and navigate to hard-to-reach areas. Because of the physics in the game, you can interact with the environment in all kinds of interesting ways. For example, when I first started playing, I thought the wizard was the weakest of the three characters to play. He seemed like a utility class since he can conjure up boxes to use to activate pressure plates or planks to traverse dangerous gaps. A running joke in the game is that he can't even cast a fireball. But even with no direct offensive capabilities he could, using the objects he conjures, crush enemies or push them off of dangerous ledges.
You aren't stuck playing just one of the three characters, but you can hot swap to any one of them during the game when you find that the abilities of one are better suited to your present situation. You can play solo or with one or two friends in local or online co-op mode. I have done both and the game is fun to play either way. It feels very balanced no matter how you play.
This game is a really polished product. The graphics are quite beautiful, with use of colors and lighting that really show off the artwork that makes up the environments that you traverse. The voice acting is also quite good and the narrator especially does a good job of unfolding the story as if he is reading a fairy tale. I also give high praise to the music and sounds effects which exhibit the same quality that the rest of the product has. The controls also feel very solid. I have played with a keyboard and mouse or, my preferred, way, with a game controller. I like how the knight, for example, can be running away while aiming his shield behind him. It's also neat how you use mouse gestures for the wizard to conjure up objects of varying sizes.
To sum it up, if you haven't tried out this game, you should. I think you'll find a lot to like about it.

Trine is an enchanting old-school platformer with three unique main characters and excellent level design. It suffers from some difficulty issues, especially in the end, yet those can be easily forgiven when you get yourself lost in the immersive visuals.
Indie platformers on PC are far from being rare, but seldom do we see a gem like Trine. The largest selling point of the game is the breathtaking visual style and carefully constructed, detail-rich levels. The backgrounds are just teeming with and movement, making you feel you are playing in a living 3D environment, even though the gameplay itself is limited to 2D.
The game itself is a very traditional platformer, where the levels require agility and a bit of resilience to get through. You also get three characters with distinctive abilities, but they all seem to lack personality. Although the original design suggests that all three are needed to clear the levels, in reality most stages are beatable by using mostly, or only the Thief. Despite this shortcoming, the level design is fun, and gathering all the (optional) experience can be a challenging, but not impossible task.
The only part where the game falls short– like most platformers– is the story, which really boils down to: “Evil wizard is evil, go kill.” Still, the narration is pleasant and the banter among the three reluctant heroes is entertaining enough to keep you interested in the simple plot line.
You can also switch to the Enchanted edition in the Betas tab, where the engine is replaced by the sequel’s, but even though I can run Trine 2 with no problems, the Enchanted edition suffered massive frame drops for me, so I can’t judge the upgrade.

First off I'm really late to the party even though I've been aware of Skullgirls (SG) for a minute but why is that?
I love fighting games and been playing them for years but what put me off SG was the "Marvel"-type of gameplay when you got a ton of characters on the screen at the same time just throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥out for the sake of it. I like my fighter a bit more clean. That and all the negative things I've heard about the game (mind you this was when they game was brand new).
But recently I decided to give this game a try, mainly because I really like MikeZ and wanted to support him, and I'm really glad I did. This game is great!
You can tell that MikeZ has put a lot of thought into this game and if you play other figthers you wish that some features that SG has was the standard.  Like what's key for a good fighter nowadays? Good N E T C O D E, period.
Too many developers overlook this or simply doesn't care because they know that their game will sell anyway (NRS etc) and that's just sad. I haven't played Killer Instinc online (heard great things about that netcode) but the GGPO rollback netcode for this game is by far the best netcode I've come across. Thank you based MikeZ!
Everything else about the game is just fantastic! Great visuals has it's own style which gives this game it's own identity and it also has excellent music to accompany that. But the thing I like the most about this game is the character designs and their respective playstyle. They're so cool and fun to play and for the most part really easy to pick up and play. I don't care if some ideas are borrowed elsewhere because I think it's cool as long as you build and further exploring the possibilities of that borrowed idea. And clearly this is the case here.
The only thing I don't like is that there are too many clone characters in the game (sure they play very differently but they're still clones) and I'm also aware that some of them are in there as a joke but that doesn't change the fact they're clones, jokes on you I'm afraid.
I do like fighters with small character lineups but not when many of them are clones.
I'd love to see MikeZ add a few original characters to the DLC lineup. But he's done with this game, right? :'( :'(
Anyways I give this 8.5/10 I highly recommend this game.
And thanks MikeZ and Cowboy for the PS4 drivers <3, you guys are godlike!

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is a mixed bag on several fronts.  It attempts to continue in the spirit of the last game as a story based shooter, but the story falls short of delivering on that promise.  New characters aren't fleshed out nearly enough, older characters are ignored almost entirely, and the game doesn't give itself time to do any better: I finished the main story in around 12 hours on normal difficulty, and I'm a very slow player.  For a first person shooter with no multiplayer, that's simply unacceptable.  I'd be able to forgive it for that if it didn't end at an illogical closure point: the only thing that clues you into the fact that the game is almost over is the difficulty of the final boss fight/gauntlet.  It ends in what feels like its second act: the best contemporary example I can think of to compare this to is The Force Unleashed 2: ending early in what feels like an obvious setup for another sequel or DLC.
The combat is more or less the same old fun, with some small segments thrown in that change the paradigm that make it a little more interesting.  One sequence, which was shown off in the trailer, has BJ riding a Panzerhund through New Orleans, which is undoubtedly one of the most fun levels in the game.  Different sections require you to adapt your playstyle according to your enemies: sometimes, running and gunning will quickly get you killed, and other times staying in cover and taking pot shots will do the same.  The result is a combat experience that involves a great deal of trial and error.  The biggest complaint that I have is that the Commander mechanic from the previous game has made a return, but I never felt like stealth was a viable option.  The positioning of the Commanders in various levels make it almost impossible to eliminate them without being discovered first, which defeats the purpose of the game allowing you to try: all you do is get yourself killed.
That aside, what it does well it does very well.  There's a strong focus on the relationship between BJ and Anya, and numerous flashbacks to BJ's childhood, and BJ's pensieve asides and reflections work very well at making the story personal.  The combat is as much fun as in TNO.
Some people have reported glaring technical issues, but I didn't have that issue.  Playing on a PG348Q 3440x1440 monitor, the only issues I had are a glitch with G-Sync that prevents it from working (this is supposed to be addressed in a driver patch from NVIDIA) which introduces a lot of screen tearing, and no SLI support.
All told, I think it's a little too short to gain a recommendation from me.  If the incoming DLC adds a significant playtime to the game, maybe pick it up in a complete edition or if it's on sale.  But $60 is too much for 12-15 hours.  Even South Park: The Fractured But Whole gave me more playtime in a single playthrough.

The gunplay as much as it seems ok at first and some guns are very cool there's no real impact to both how they feel vs the enemies and how they sound. That makes the shooting feel like you need to shoot the enemies 20 times when they wiggle like christmas pudding. At times i did enjoy the combat, but i've noticed that it was only when it was in tight corridors and you could just mown down everyone in front of you.
Other element is the melee combat - it's ok, but it's pretty much useless in-fight because the animation is so slow and long (like he has to jab the guy 3 times...), if you're playing on hard and try to use "glory kill" you end up getting shot in the back by other enemies. Again: i get it, you don't need to use it, but than why actually having super  fun melee kills if you want people to only use it in stealth sections - this is not (primary) a stealth game! Before someone says they are not "glory kills" and should not be used in combat: they are glory kills and the whole game is designed around you moving. It reminds me how much Id Software talked about the "glory kills" taking time to get right in Doom 2016 because they wanted to make sure they never make you feel like you're compromising combat and fluidity. Apparently MachineGames didn't feel they need to polish it.
Pretty much all these issues are super polished in Doom 2016, combat was fast, crazy and anything you did always felt like you are in control of what's next. This is the opposite of Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus.
Like i get it, it's not a bad game, but it feels very unpolished - including terrible pc version that crashes very often and has crazy (often funny) bugs. Honestly, I'm really enjoying Wolfenstein II.
It's been really fun so far, with tons and tons of creative Nazi killing goodness. I'm also really enjoying the story, it's great that it picks up where the last game left off.
1. Performance: Excellent
- Consistent 120+ fps @ 2k (1440p) using "Mein leben" w\ all possible Uber settings enabled.
- Absurdly fast load times, like dirty fast.
- Zero crashes.
- Zero bugs encountered.
- M + KB used. (Using a controller for a game like this on PC is ridiculous)
2. Gameplay:
- As you'd expect, lots of fun Nazi killing goodness.
- Story picks up from where it left off, and so far is interesting and engaging.
- Dual wielding can now mix and match guns, allowing for some pretty devastating combos.
- Lots of cool guns, many new, with multiple attachments for each.
- Levels are well designed, allowing for a variety of ways to deal with enemies/encounters.
- Lots of collectibles and challenges.
- Quite a few difficulty choices, catering to all gamer preferences/skill levels.
3. Graphics:
- Overall pretty solid graphics, the game looks really great.
- Lots of graphics choices, to cater to a wide variety of hardware/preferences.
- Excellent in-game atmosphere, really captures the time period well (even with the crazy tech).
NOTE: There is the odd low quality texture here and there, but it's really nothing to cry about and doesn't take away from the game at all. I think this issue is being really blown out of proportion by some reviewers. (Overall texture quality may be tied to GPU performance for some, due to id Tech 6.)
TL;DR - All in all, a pretty solid game which is really fun to play, has overall great graphics/atmosphere, and runs flawlessly on my PC.

I love everything about this game. It's got a great visual appeal and style, very reminiscent of works from Hayao Miyazaki. It's soundtrack is gorgeous and has decent sound work in regards to the ambient and player avatar noises. It's platforming is decent, not stellar however not bad to say the least.
So what really drove the first nail in the coffin with this game for me was the running segment from the first dungeon, where the dungeon is rapidly filling with water. The design "Blue Shells" itself with the Water rubberbanding, which basically means "the better you are; the faster the water rises". It  kills any real feeling of accomplishment of being good platforming or knowing the path to take. I understand that the segment is supposed to build tension and a sense of imminent danger, but it's annoying when player skill is negatively returned. Still, I got through that segment of the game around my fifth or so try (Death Counter: 20) and made it through all the way to the second dungeon.
The second dungeon drove the second nail in the coffin. The segments where you have to carry an orb around and be affected by the direction of gravity is going is really finicky. Sometimes it's difficult to jump off of an inverted platform on to another, just because the game rigidly sticks you to a platform, due to the orbs weight. Giving the player the use of the already obtained double jump in this section would of helped, but it's disabled for reasons. Not to mention there are some serious blind jumps in this section, which makes it even more annoying as there's instant death pits everywhere. So it's a ton of trial and error along with clunky mechanics.
The final nail was the save system, it works in some respects but it's really counter-intuitive in others. I understand the backups and all that for those aiming for a "No Death Run" which is nice for those people. However, sometimes the game just decides to not backup a save for some unknown reason. Maybe there's something hidden I don't know about, but it really annoyed me in the second dungeon where I was using a back-up save at the beginning of the dungeon due to my primary save being bugged (No Orb on load) and not being overwritten properly. As soon as I saved again, it wouldn't overwrite my previous primary save and wouldn't back-up my current save due to some arbitrary limitations. I basically quit after this point (Death counter: 20), deleted my save and put the game down.
To wrap this up, Ori is a wonderful experience for what I had with it, but poor design decisions and some really wonky systems really made it a chore to play effectively. I might give it another go in a year or so, but currently it has left me miffed and unwilling to give it a second chance.

On the surface this game appeared like it was nothing more than a cheap game made to cash in on an older more famous license, but after playing it I can say that in my opinion it's a very high quality product, and a genuinely fun game.
By setting your match to Public it's easy enough to get grouped up with some people, you may not always be doing the exact mission you want if you don't host, but playing with people is what makes this game fun and it hasn't been difficult to do so.
The missions themselves seem to vary a lot in length and difficulty, without much sense of a precise progression...but the game is fun and rewarding enough to simply hop into a session and grind some levels out for gold or to help someone with their progression.
My biggest complaint is that even after you accrue gold it just never feels like there is a ton of upgrades to buy for your character. You never really get the sense of being that much more strong or powerful by the end of the game, and your left slot is essentially useless because of how sparingly the tokens are given out for using that power. As far as I can tell after you've bought a couple upgrades the only thing to spend your money on is gear, but it wouldn't appear to enhance you in any way and seems to be purely cosmetic.
So on the positive side, lots of fun coop action, and the gameplay/presentation all feel high quality and well made. The downside is just not a lot of depth to the progression.
Would recommend, even if you don't have friends who play you can surely find some random people online to join you.

Even though at the very beginning I was put off by the old styled, low-resolution graphics and without any previous knowledge about this game, it very quickly grew on me soon after I started it.
The dialogues, sadly all just in written form, are both funny and extremely touching.
Seriously, how can such a "simple" point & click puzzle adventure move me to tears?
Answer: The story! The characters!
Even though they're just plain pixels, you feel a deep connection to these characters, from the two buddy scientists to the tragic couple with a very complex backstory which unfolds chapter after chapter, memory after memory.
Gameplaywise you won't be overwhelmed, though sometimes still a bit challenged, especially when you can't find all the necessary clues at first or have to figure out the minigames.
But with some time you'll get the groove of it.
Also there's always some good humour interjected into the experience.
Nevertheless, when you finally have reached the ending, and you've both laughed and used enough tissues to wipe away your tears (
), there's just one thing to say: WOW!
A big bravo to the people who wrote this story and developed the characters.
This would actually make an excellent mini series (for a feature film it might be a bit too long)!

Sci-fi Punch-em-Up
I decided to have a "female game protagonist experience" and bought Remember Me along with Tomb Raider. On the whole, Remember Me is an interesting game let down by its short length and slightly repetitive combat.
Gameplay: Remember Me is essentially a beat-em-up with some platforming/puzzles. The problem is that it emphasizes on the former much more than the latter. The combat system, at first glace, seems extremely confusing with all the Pressens and S-Pressens and so forth. However it's actually quite simple and effective, making multiple combos with only 2 attack buttons. The combat is made interesting by its focus on combo tactics, rather than outright skill. Unfortunately, while it was interesting at first, by mid-game I had established full combo-chains for each of the 3 main attributes (power, health regeneration, and cooldown reduction) and just methodically finished enemies off. Further unlocks did little to affect how I played, and the combat boiled down to a game of picking which combo to execute. I'm talking a lot on the combat because the platforming is fairly simple. The puzzles are mostly for getting unlockables, which despite being a bit frustrating to find, are completely worth it as they unlock pages of a Mneist (encyclopedia) which provides some fascinating backstory. Oh and I almost forgot about the Memory-Remixes! Easily the most interesting part of the game, but unfortunately far too few, and not deep enough. The possibilities are so endless for this mini-game that I would advocate that Remember Me's sequel be a game based around Memory-Remixing. I thoroughly enjoyed it and spent much longer messing around with Memory-Remixing than I had to, simply because its fun and interesting.
Graphics: The game has an amazing sci-fi feel to it, and environments look completely out of this world. Graphics and details are great. However the actual animations are a bit average, particularly Nilin's mouth during dialogue.
Sound: I don't have any complaints here.
Story: Remember Me tells the story of Nilin, a woman who unwittingly is the key to a human revolution. It is set far in the future, where humans have embraced Sensen technology, a sort of memory interface which means that our memories are no longer recorded by brain, but instead stored as digital data. And like all digital data, it can be accessed, stolen, leveraged or interfered with as a means to an end. This is an utterly fascinating concept which is well explored in Remember Me. The story itself is also very interesting, and takes some truly interesting turns near its conclusion. However, while Nilin and the world's backstories are well executed, those of the supporting characters leaves a bit to be desired, and I just wish I knew more about the various inhabitants of Neo-Paris that Nilin encounters on her journey.
Verdict: Remember Me really scores on the story. If you love science-fiction and exploring the issues of our increasing reliance on technology, this game will please you to no end. Unfortunately it is let down by its slightly repetitive combat and extremely short length. I finished the game in about 14 hours.
+ fascinating story, cool setting, novel combat system, great memory remixing
- too short, repetitive combat, NOT ENOUGH MEMORY REMIXING!!!

Barring a few bugs here and there, this game is absolutely exceptional and so damn refreshing!
It's such a shame we only seem to get one truly great SP game a year. Doom last year, Wolfy this year. Instead, the market get's flooded with the same multiplayer, P2W nonsense.
The storyline, gunplay, graphics, and replayability are all excellent. The campaign isn't overly long, but even after the game has finished there are plenty of other side-missions to complete, collectibles to find, and general exploration to be had.
The engine isn't quite as optimised as it was for Doom, but i expect that a couple of patches down the line, it will run as smooth as butter. Using my Fury X / 1600 combo I was maintaining over 50fps @1440p at Ultra so the game certainly still runs well. I just think i've been spoilt by how well Doom looks and plays. There is another setting above Ultra, 'Mein Leiben' which i would imagine bumps the AA upto extreme levels. This led to my rates tanking to the 20's, but there is no noticeable difference in fidelty so Ultra is still more than acceptable.
Some of the minor character textures could be a little more defined. BJ's mother, for example, looks a little drab in comparison to your comrades throughout the rest of the game.
Oh, but you can kill Hitler if you so choose!
All in all, the game is fantastic and I highly recommend it. Get in on the action so that Bethesda's bank account justifies another sequel!

Let’s start very briefly and clearly, if you know barely nothing about Occurrence at JCR Outpost and screenshots looks interesting to you, don’t read any reviews and go for it. This way you can enjoy it.
You’ve become an admin. Finally! Well ... The Antarctic research station admin. In a secluded area of permafrost you command tough guys who gather and analyse samples from under the ice. It’s not an easy job, you suffer from isolation, monotonous work and desire to make a breakthrough in research. And suddenly it comes, an ice crack was identified. Your job as manager is to drive to the cracks, blow it up using dynamite and figure out what’s in it and what new it brings. Simple task. But your command is not exactly an example of discipline. Guys can do almost whatever they want, and one of them unauthorised took the key from the garage with dynamite. First you have to find out who took it, and then continue on your mission.
Occurrence at first looks like a retro adventure with the flair of movie The Thing and Lucasfilm’s adventure games from the ‘90s with the midi music and the sounds you probably don’t even need a sound card for. In fact, it is rather a mini puzzle adventure game, because pure adventure game elements are only few and your goal is to perform a series of correctly chosen text options that lead to the goal. In the game you are moving only by selecting the right options and all you need is one finger on keyboard. You can move to the rooms, hold only one item at the same time, talk to a team member or just wait a while doing nothing. That’s because the whole game is acting as if it takes place in real time. When you take an action, others do too, so to track down the owner of the keys you need to survey crew rooster and map to find out where he is and meet him. To make it more difficult, the game also features "survival elements" where you need to eat, relax or go to the toilet / take a shower. It slows you down and away from searching for the right people.
The main part of the game begins after completing the first task. From the crack under the ice "IT" appeared, and it goes after the crew and of course after you. In that moment, you have to perform tasks with great caution, because "IT" gradually kills crew members, you can hold only one item (a weapon, if possible) and get somewhere safe. The game is really pleasantly chilling with oppressive atmosphere at these moments and you feel like you’re just a one step from death. And you’re tired, hungry and you’ve discovered another crack in a service shaft...
The problem of the game, however, is its brevity. During the first play you’ll find out options, controls and strategy, and during the second play you no longer have a bigger problem. You’ll find that "survival" features are not so important, because when you pass out nothing really happens and you just appear in another room. Crew members have nothing to say and to find the needed keys is just a matter of few keys presses. And "IT"? You can get defensive items in a few places and you are always one step ahead, so you can decide which way to escape. Everything is resolved within an hour of playing and for a set price that’s very little for such a nice concept.

J.C.R. stands for James Clark Ross. He was a British naval officer in the 1800's. He is remembered for his exploration of the Arctic with his uncle, Sir John Ross, and Sir William Parry. Furthermore, he is also known for his own expedition to Antarctica. You play the role of the new administrator of the outpost which is located in the Antarctic. Your aim is to gather scientific samples from under the ice. However, it quickly becomes obvious that things are not as they seem. This is because there is an ancient monster in the midst with the intention of killing you. Therefore, you will quickly discover that the game is one of cat and mouse.
Due to the subject matter of the game older science fiction readers and viewers will immediately recall John Carpenter's, The Thing. It is also clear that the developer has drawn further inspiration from classic adventure games such as Maniac Mansion, Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders and many more. As I am an older gamer and was raised on these types of games I was immediately interested in finding out whether Brizzi's writing and game design skills could rekindle some of those memories.
The welcome to the game was not a pleasing one for me. Windows 10 advised me that the game was not at my optimal settings. This was a little distressing as it is the first game to do that. As a result my first visit was to the settings screen. Thankfully I was able to change the game's settings to a full 1920 x 1080. The second thing that I noticed was the old midi style computer sounds.  However, given the style in which the game is firmly established - retro - it is somewhat unsurprising that these choices have been made. This is especially relevant when considering the marking of the game in both the graphics and sound department.
The quality of the graphics and the sound both leave a little to be desired. However, the emphasis on the game is in neither department so you theoretically could listen to a podcast and ignore the graphics for the most part. In fact, I would almost argue that the game may be better played with neither. Unfortunately, this may decrease the already niche audience for this game.
The player does not move their character throughout the course of play. Instead, you are given a number of options in each room and you must choose one of them to advance the game. Therefore, the game is played almost entirely through the text related offerings. It almost feels that the graphics themselves are irrelevant. This, in some way, is a reminder to how games used to be like long ago. This further puts the game into the niche category. Because of this older gamers - or those who have played the classics - are much more likely to gain a positive experience from the game than younger whipper snappers who have not played this type of game before.
When you finally get to the stage where you release the monster it will hunt you down. It will also attack the other members of your crew. When it has successfully killed them it will shapeshift into them. You will only discover that the monster has shape shifted into one of your crew members when you are alone with that particular member. Once this occurs it shapeshifts back into its natural form and will attempt to devour you. This will be successful if you have nothing to defend yourself with. Therefore it is always important to find a weapon and to have one with you at all times. Thankfully unless you're being lazy this shouldn't be too much of a problem as there are a variety of weapons scattered throughout the game.
Once you come to grips with the gameplay and learn what is expected of you individual gameplays are about an hour long on average. The game has been designed to support multiple playthroughs. However, unless you are a perfect game achievement hunter, I do not believe that your gaming hunger will be satiated by playing this game multiple times. Therefore at the cost of $9.99 for a little over an hour's worth of entertainment the cost per hour ratio is sadly very high.
Unfortunately, the game has some very annoying components to it.
First, let's look at the rest, eat and bath component of the game. You are forced to do each act on an in-game hourly basis. I don't know about you but I certainly do not need to do each of them every hour. Because of this I argue that the game includes this feature to artificially increase both the difficulty of the game and the amount of time that it takes to complete a playthrough. Consequently, this is not a system that I support and wish that it was stripped from the game.
Secondly, and perhaps even more aggravating than this is the way in which the game coded the AI. If an NPC is standing where a door is the game removes the option of going through that door. No "excuse me dude, get out of my way I need to go through that door" option exists. When this happens you have to choose another option one of which is to do nothing but wait. I would argue that this feature is either bad coding or another example of the developer wanting to unnaturally increase the amount of time it takes to complete the game.
Partially. There are no trading cards but there are a set of 12 Steam achievements.
Some retro gamers may get a kick out of the style of the game. However, I find the gameplay in Occurrence at J.C.R. Outpost to be limited and the playthroughs short. There isn't enough of a lure for me to persist with the game through the first playthrough. Consequently, the $9.99 asking price is inflated when considered from a value perspective. The likelihood is that you will pick this up in a bundle at some point and unless trading cards are added to it it will remained unplayed. This is a shame as I really wanted to like this one.

Note: This game was reviewed with a code provided by the developer this doesn't change my opinion about the game.
Occurrence at JCR Outpost is an adventure game inspired by John Carpenters The Thing and classic adventure games like Maniac Mansion. It's not as scary as The Thing, but it's pretty fun.
The story is you are a scientist in an outpost who is there to open a ice hole, but after opening it you find out that you let out a monster who can shape shift into your crew, so you have to figure out how to contain it.
The gameplay is not a point and click adventure game, but more of a choose an action and see how it pans out. You also have to take care of yourself, like sleep, eat, and bathe so you don't black out and have to backtrack to some place. You're given a bar which tells you how much time you have left until you black out and before every action you have a nifty time counter which tells you how time you will use up doing a certain action.
The puzzles are fairly simple. It revolves around exploration and using certain items in certain places. There's only one difficult puzzle, but after that it's a fairly simple ride.
Now let's talk about the monster itself. The monster is a lot like the monster in The Thing. As soon as you let it out, it moves around the map and hunts down your crew. The monster will kill them and will then shape shift into them. The only way to know which crew member is the monster is you being alone in the room with it. It will then shape shift into this crab creature and will kill you if you don't have anything to defend yourself with, but don't worry there are multiple weapons scattered around the map so you have plenty of chances to save yourself.
Atmosphere is also really good. Since the map is small and very claustrophobic, it helps build tension when you're among the final people alive.
The pixel art style is alright for the most part. It's nothing too special and I didn't mind it that much, but the soundtrack is a whole different story.
The soundtrack is beyond horrible. I liked the intro song, but the song that play's during the game is terrible. It was annoying and it wasn't that good.
The game has a few negatives as well.
The game has one big problem and that's the crew  AI. When you do certain actions, your crew members will also do something and this sometimes happens to be blocking doors. When you want to go somewhere and they're standing in front of the door, it's impossible to go through it. The monster is also sometimes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to deal with. I had a run of the game where I was stuck in a room with the monster and I had no weapons, which forced me to restart the game from the start.
The game also has this strange bug where you can access the final area of the game without even solving the puzzle. Just by inspecting the door you can get through it, but the puzzle within the door isn't solvable. This issue has now been fixed.
The game lasted me 40 minutes to finish and for the current price I really cannot recommend it. It's way too short and I think if it was 5 euros that would be a better deal, but the game is definitely worth the time.
Overall I liked my time with Occurrence at JCR Outpost, it's a fun game inspired, by an awesome movie. If the issues are fixed and the prices is a bit lower this is a decent game that's worth your time.

I stil believed it would be great...some day.
And thus far, the crew at Hello Games have done a magnificent job of righting the wheel on NMS. I've spent full, real-life days exploring the universe, and feel that I got my money's worth a few times over.

Sure, this game is YADC - yet another Diablo clone: you walk around, meet hordes of interesting monsters, and slay them. They drop loot and gold, you pick it up, and either wear it or sell it. A tried-and-true recipe with little to improve on.
And yet... they managed. The ghost companion provides for rather amusing dialogue and banter, though her shopping spree quips do get old after a while. The setting is a classic, and well done, at that; the monsters are quite appropriate, and the Eastern-Slavic NPC's got at least a chuckle from me.
Maps are pretty much static; while loot drops are mostly random, the only thing that changes are the shrines - not their position, but only their conferred bonuses. It might not be a big deal, but a touch of variety wouldn't hurt.
Without the DLC's you only get a third of the game: one character out of three. And you still get loot drops for the characters you're missing. So if you're buying, take that into account: whatever the game price, add in the price of all the DLC's.
This is not how DLC's should work, much as they often do.

The game To the Moon is a story driven game where the player takes control of two scientists who are sent to an old mans' home to work in his memories to send him to the moon. It has many moments to make you smile, and many moments to make you cry, as well as some to bring about both reactions at one time.
While this game may seem boring, it can get emotionally attaching, especially for those in a relationship or very close with another person. I repeatedly kept looking at my own life and thinking, "Yeah, that sounds familiar!" While other times I looked at my own life going "OH NO, WHY IS THIS SO FAMILIAR!" And proceeded to cry for the next couple minutes, trying to play the game still. This is definitely a game to make you feel happy, sad, and even maybe a bit mad, but not a game for mindless joy.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I played this game completely open to myself, my life, and people around me. I tried to find parallels, or think to the future in order to connect to what was happening. I am certainly no old man, so it helped to think about how it would be to be taking my final breaths. I could do this safely, I have what I would classify as a strong mind. However, I know some people very close to me that tried that and got highly anxious, some even breaking down completely. If this may be you, please, do not feel pressured to play this way, and don't try to. Besides that, try to play the game by putting yourself inthese situations. Try to put yourself in the shoes of an old man wanting to go to the moon,
Finally, be prepared to cry. This story is so tragic, it isnt even the love story. In one scene, the big twist,
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Anyway, this game is so touching and amazing, with some funny moments, sad moments, and joyful moments.

I was at first very interested by this game because it has positive reviews and recommendations everywhere so I bought it on purpose (not part of a bundle). So I went deep into the story with great expectations. As a result, I finished with a rather bias and negative overview of the game.
First, the gameplay is definitely not a strong point, it has no real depth, repetitive, bad controls consisting of point&click and arrows keys that I barely used, Slow movements and dialogue that are frustrating. The fixed resolution of 640x480 is also a pain with the mouse. But this wasn't the reasons that makes the game that positive anyway.
As for the graphics, I didn't dislike them. The pixel art genre with old style is alright and depends on budget and choices. Although, there were time when you couldn't tell what was the ground to the limits of the map so you just had to click everywhere around to find the right way. A genre is fine as long as it doesn't impact the gameplay.
Now, the strong points were the soundtrack and story. I have no negative opinion for the soundtrack, I thought it was beautiful, also because I like piano and sentimental music.
The story, however, was surprisingly normal, not as amazing as I expected. I have to admit there were great moments that were emotional, but it lacked interest and was boring at other times. The second half started to become weird and random. The game tried to make an impact through the story but it didn't reach the real goal intended in my opinion.
Overall, it was well executed for the genre, however I'm against the general consensus to consider it a masterpiece. I was looking forward to have my heart torn apart and played with great emotions, but that never happened.

Trine is an action/puzzle platformer with 3 types of heroes, 2 types of bosses and 1 type of level.
The graphics are pretty gorgeous, but unfortunately for the gameplay it's not great. There is quite a mess on screen and it's sometimes hard to tell a bonus pickup from an enemy attack.
The controls - which should be the most important thing for a platformers - don't allow for enough precision and feel sloppy, which will often trigger misses. Not that it matters because the game is too easy anyway.
All the levels feel exactly the same, beyond level 1 there is hardly any new mechanics, from there it's just grinding your way through.
The fixed camera placement is annoying. You know objects are there but the camera won't budge or allow you to place objects outside the current field of vision.
There are just 2 bosses, they're not epic, just merely a slightly tougher foe, and they come back several times in later levels.
Not much variety in enemies either, it's just the same skeletons from the beginning to the end.
All in all, this is just like playing the same level 15 times over again, with a different backdrop.
I can appreciate some may be drawn by the medieval fantasy storytelling or by the luxurious backdrops. The graphics got overhauled recently with the enchanted edition and it's quite superb. One can wish the gameplay had got improved instead!

I recommend this game to anyone who want some  adrenaline spike. It's simply genious

On the whole, an underrated game that deserves more love than it's gotten.

This is absolutely worth playing if you're into sci-fi at all, especially the kind of near-future sci-fi that deals with new technologies that reveal something about the human condition, a la Deus Ex: HR. This is unfortunately not nearly as well-written or engaging as Deus Ex, but it does present a similar sort of experience (and with much better graphics. Worse music though). Remember Me runs really well too, and plays great-- the fighting is actually really fun despite the terrible lack of enemy variety, and the ability to nimbly leap over enemies as you're comboing them really makes you feel like you're controlling a skilled fighter (serioulsy, the nimbleness is off the hook here, and a nice departure from the usual cover-based face-shooting of Every Other Action Game Ever). The main character Nilin is another reason to play-- the character model is really a nice design, and i love the way she gets all out of breath after running a lot and the way she kind of looks around while  she's walking-- these are great details that really add to you caring about her. Hell, play it just because you get to play as a cool biracial French woman with a sweet haircut instead of the usual Generic Beefcake White Dude-- an extremely refreshing departure on this count as well (and if it bothers you that everyone is speaking English in a game set in freaking Paris, there's actually the option to switch the audio to French with English subtitles, so if you're a great big hipster like me and want it to seem more authentic then you're in luck).
Short version: very nice looking and never frustratingly difficult, and although the story is basically a Luc Besson movie stretched over ten hours, it does at least broach on an interesting subject and also makes you care about the character and what happens to her. Definitely a solid purchase if you're into Sci-Fi, though if you're not you can probably skip it unless, again, you want the rare experience of playing a game where the character isn't like the character in every other game out there.

This game is good, but has some serious flaws that (for me at least) threaten to undermine the experience.
The graphics and music are very pretty and well-executed, although the optimisation on PC is appalling; I've noticed slowdowns on my PC that I don't see with The Witcher III on maximum settings, so something's clearly not right somewhere under the hood.
The platforming is good and inventive, but the biggest problems with this game are the difficulty curve and the punishing nature of certain sections.  The gameplay is built around a "save anywhere" approach as the game fully expects players to die frequently and to have to re-attempt sections multiple times.  This is acceptable but can still be frustrating, especially early on in the game when you have a more limited amount og energy orbs (which facilitate your ability to create a save point).  This issue is alleviated somewhat later in the game as you acquire more orbs, but is then offset by the prevalence of enemies with instant-kill attacks and instant-kill scenery elements, so the repetition persists and mis-timing or mis-placing a jump is still punished just as harshly as in the early game.
The biggest annoyance, which really makes this game frustrating and repetitive to the point of tedium, are several prolonged "chase" sections.  In these you are being chased by encroaching instant-kill environmental hazards and/or an enemy.  This requires you to perfectly execute a number of precise jumps and manoeuvres to escape unharmed.  These sections have no save points or checkpoints and also employ the hideous tactic of "rubber-banding", i.e. the hazard will always be one step behind you, regardless of how quickly you proceed through the section.  This makes it impossible to build up any kind of room for error, requiring precision from start to finish.
I appreciate that this is meant to be a difficult game, but the game offers no workaround for these sections - you cannot change the difficulty setting, you cannot opt to skip them and you have no way to progress past through them piecemeal.  Even a single half-way save point would make these sections substantially less obnoxious.  None of these things would have been difficult to implement and would have made the game more accessible.  After attempting to escape a rising surge of water for the 40th time, I realised that my goodwill towards the game had almost completely evaporated.  The beautiful music was something to ignore and had become repetitive and the artwork flashed by in a blur as I tried to get past this section.
I am by no means an incompetent game player, but this made me feel pretty hopeless.
That being said, the game is fun outside of these sections and there is some good, clever puzzle-solving required.  The emotional heft of the story is probably being overstated in other reviews, I found it a little sad in places but not heart-breaking.
It's also extremely frustrating to find that once you have completed the story, your save file is "locked" and you cannot return to the world to find any of the missing collectibles or explore parts of the map that you'd not found yet.  Whilst it does say that entering Mt. Horu is a point-of-no-return, I was disappointed that it was implemented in this fashion.  I would recommend that players striving for 100% completion make a copy of their savegame file before they enter Mt. Horu if they want to be able to go back again afterwards.
In conclusion, it's a good game but I'd hestitate to call it a great one - its silly flaws really do spoil the product and the port to PC hasn't been handled with as much care and attention as it should have.

The game play is phenomenally fun to blast through, tearing nazis apart limb from limb, and the acting and cutscenes are masterfully executed.
I have a few issues with how much content there was throughout just in comparison to the first game, but I figured that could have come down to publisher deadlines, and we will see more via downloadable incoming.
I sunk about 14 hours in across 2 sessions and finished, but there’s still a bit more to explore and finish up, but almost feels pointless now.
As for gameplay, the weapon wheel felt a bit weird to use for some reason, just not that fluid and the stealth felt a little under loved, they introduced these traps in the very beginning and never re used them.
And on the subject of that, there was even things from the end of the last game that never carried through.
There was also a lot of stuff left unanswered and a few story points between characters that didn’t fully feel resolved, as well as some major moments that didn’t carry the same impact that they did in the first game.
Although a lot of this will be addressed in the next instalment, it would have been nice to see a bit more character padding here and there.
Otherwise 9/10, excellent game, can’t wait to see what they do in the next chapter.

Senua is the titular protagonist of
, a Celtic warrior. She’s a young woman who suffers from severe psychosis which causes her thoughts and fears to become a reality. Her mind is overrun with thoughts and emotions that often paralyze her in fear and doubt. Voices plague her every waking moment and she’s bombarded with visions that are dark and twisted. Sometimes you'll find some clues in those voices. While to the outside world none of it exists, it is potent enough to kill her because she believes so strongly. A large focus of this section of the game is Focus. It is tragedy that sets the ball in motion and places players into the dark, twisted world of the game.
is quite possibly the most complex game I have ever played. The game draws you into Senua's mind, instantly facing you with questions about Senua and her story. She’s a great warrior, and while the voices in her head might warn her when an enemy is about to stab her from behind, arguably a manifestation of her own fighter’s instinct, they’re not going to whisper some nonsense about pressing LCTRL to block. Making fights even more tense is the game’s threat to delete your progress if you die too many times, a blunt but effective way to make players fear failure and the darkness that grows inside Senua as much as she does. The game gradually progresses further and further into Senua's mind, learning more about her 'illness' and making you ask more and more questions. The storyline is addictive and I couldn't take a break. It's beautifully told and the crisp sound the voices make sends chills down your spine as it keeps gaining momentum and intensity. Stunning visuals and aesthetics coupled with some remarkable motion capture, Melina Juergens' performance as Senua, strong and responsive combat, the sound design is marvelous, interesting puzzles with a few neat twists, and the over lap of Senua's story with the Nordic myths was lovely. Best played with headphones as some of the sound is binaural (3D).
- this is an experience that is more powerful the less you know about it in advance.On last word though, If you like games that put a heavy focus on story, atmosphere and dialogue, but go rather light on game mechanics, this game will be perfect for you, I still cant believe it was only $30. When I previously decided to write this review, my patience was worn a bit thin by repeated instantaneous kicks from public games. As it turns out, the host only gets to change any of the settings after choosing the game mode and difficulty, while already in the lobby.

Regardless of that I won't change my opinion. For a game of this type a server browser seems like the only reasonable choice. I don't want to repeatedly try my luck with a "Quick Join" button that brings me to a random and entirely anonymous server.
Gameplay feels floaty and never seems rewarding. I wouldn't say this lightly since my perception of video games is usually not blurred by nostalgia, but even the original arcade version from the 80s was more exciting and felt a lot more mysterious and immersive. This new version is a very generic representation of the concept

This review is not going to be a fair one. I'm not sure the game deserves any more fairness than it offered me, though.
As you can see, I've barely even played the game. From what little I have seen, the gameplay appears to be fine, although certainly not very complex.
The feature that bothers me to no end, is the direly misdesigned multiplayer interface, or more specifically the lack of reasonable options for hosting or searching an online game. When starting a game and you want to join a running multiplayer session, you're given exactly one option: Quick join. The game then searches for a random session and drops you right in the middle of the action. If the host didn't expect you, chances are you'll be kicked, as soon as he/she finds an opportunity that won't get him/her killed.
Apparently, someone who starts a game alone automatically hosts it as a multiplayer session. Thus there is an abundance of running games where the host doesn't expect other people to join. So, if you click "Quick join" be prepared to be kicked out - a lot.
I do not comprehend why someone would design a multiplayer interface of such a rotten quality, but I very much believe that such a person shouldn't earn a single dime from it, regardless of how many other games also use this braindead multiplayer system.

LEGO Worlds is by no means a perfect game. It lacks any real story but instead focuses on the concepts of exploration and construction. Both of these fall short of what the potentially could be but due to the game being in Early Access there is still room for much improvement.
It would be normal to assume that a construction game involving LEGO would seem like the most logical step for the brick building toy. Unfortunatelly the controls make it rather hard to make anything worthwhile. The asiest solution around this is to build in an external program like LEGO Digital Designer and import the file into the game. This process does have the potential to be troublesome of course as LEGO Worlds lacks the brick library which LDD posesses. Hopefully, as updates quickly come, the "brick gap" can be made closer. Construction is also limited to static objects, the ability to build vehicles is not yet available and I am unsure if it will ever be implemented.
Exploring offers an array of totally different biomes to find. The major motive to explore is to find new objects, minifigures, and vehicles. Although effective at forcing the player to explore, the game becomes repetitive from the constant travelling. It is sometimes more effiecient to merely keep generating a new world until you discover new biomes at spawn. Exploration could be improved through having more structures to find. There are already a few but they do end up repeating after a few hours playtime.
In retrospect, the only real reason to buy this game is the ability to experience LEGO in a totally new scale. Being able walk around a LEGO house as a minifigure is a totally unique experience which this game offers. For that this game is worth being if you so happen to be a fan of LEGO or it's games.

Throughout this game I was astounded by just how beautiful this game is. Gameplay wise the game was phenomenal, having a good level of difficulty that created intense boss battles. The platformer and puzzle elements of this game were brilliant, with creative puzzles and abilities. The music that accompanied the game was magnificent as well, really bringing the world to life. Many games struggle with getting the player to care about their characters, however just five minutes into the game I was completely in love with all of the characters.
As with any game there are some downsides, luckily with Ori and the Blind Forest there are only a few. Most notably is the inability to rebind controls. I played the game using a keyboard and mouse and had to spend the first couple hours getting used to having my jump button as Space instead of Shift as I prefer. The second drawback of this game is that you cannot go back and continue playing after you beat the game. So make sure you create a copy of your game file before fighting the final boss.
Overall this game was a great purchase, and although it was rather short, I am happy I bought this game. The developers did an amazing job with this, and I hope to see more games from them in the future. And for anyone who is contemplating buying this game, do it.

One of the most moving experiences I have ever had in a game. I applaud Ninja Theory for tackling such a difficult subject as mental illness, one that has historically been handled very poorly in many mediums - especially games, and crafting a compelling experience around it. Immediately after playing this I was compelled to look up more information about the conditions presented in this game, so as a work that in some way is trying to raise empathy and understanding through immersing yourself as someone else - this game is a huge success.
It is not for everyone though. Touchy subjects aside, there is something to be desired in the gameplay - combat especially. I felt like you could pretty much button mash most of the encounters, only dodging or tapping block when the voices called out to you. There is one particular fight that requires the use of audio, which I thought was well done, I just wish the actual mechanics behind fighting was tighter and required more commitment, gave more control, etc.
Some people have critiqued some of the puzzles in the game, and while there is a bit repetition I feel after playing the game and watching the accompanying feature describing Ninja Theory's consultation with mental health specialists and patients - I think they succeeded in listening to the feedback they were getting and provided (what seems to me) as an authentic representation of what one with psychosis may be dealing with.
Even with my criticisms - this is one of the best experiences I have ever had.
