Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus (Abbreviated as TNC from here on) is not a game I can recommend. Performance wise the game ran well and as for length it took approximately twenty hours to beat. Why I cannot recommend it is based on its gameplay. It’s just not fun to play on the higher difficulty’s like its predecessors in the series.  The story I will not be covering, as you can find that information has been readily covered by others.
The mechanics that are present in TNC are by and large the exact same as the previous Wolfenstein games from this developer. What that entails is a modern mish mash of older style shooting with modern design philosophy, including action packed shooting and stealth segments, with exploration being optional if desired for weapon upgrade kits, readables and collectables for 100% completion.
However, there are key points in the main gameplay loop and quality of life systems for shooting Nazis and sneaking around that are lacking when compared to the previous titles.
The user interface went through a redesign coming from TNO, offering a sleeker look. Its nice to look at. One complaint is that for collectible collection, there is no dedicated key to open the map. Pressing J by default opens the journal, and this menu opts to default to any number of random tabs found within. This is frustrating to go through repeatedly just to look at the map, more so when collecting items, the ones you missed only show up when you are confidently far enough away from the room you were just in to make backtracking a pure chore. Easily fixed in a patch.
The music in this game is great. Done by the now legendary Mick Gordan, the soundtrack is phenomenal whenever it plays, even if its totally out of place with the setting of the game. It also tends to ramp up with no one around, or only a single Nazi looking around for you, so it can be a bit jarring at times. What I have issue with is general sound effects. Guns when shot have a decent crunch to them, are sub par when compared to TNO, and when used against the player they are quite and distant, to the point where if shot far enough away the only tell is your imitate death screen. Its almost as if the game totally lacks any impact sounds for rounds hitting surfaces, I cant really put my finger on in. This only adds on to the lack of information feedback when playing, leading to increaseing frustrations as you go further in.
For comparisons sake, The New Order was a balanced, fair game that while on the easy side at times, presented a challenge in a fair manner with encounters staying away from being cheap. Deaths in that game where deserved, and felt fair. In TNC, this is no longer the case.
Damage is straight up stupid on Death Incarnate, especially when considering that enemy accuracy rivals Aim bots used in competitive shooters.  Death at a full life pool comes in roughly three shots, and said pool is heavily gimped for around half the games length. Receiving damage lacks proper feedback, leading to moments where health just seems to evaporate at random, plus gunshot sounds not being balanced correctly or having audio for getting shot at leads to random feeling deaths. More deaths then I am willing to count came from foes behind particle effects that I could not see past, and down long hallways or open rooms where you just get picked off in seconds.
Due to this, this leads the player to adapt a save scum strategy, employing trial and error to pass through engagements and abusing corners and walls to pick foes off. This is fine and all, but there is no real challenge to massing F5 after every single kill. Anyone and their mother can save scum through fights, and its encuraged here!  It comes off as untested and lacks polish, almost as if the quick save system is only in place to combat that, and is not fun to go through. It was no exaggeration that on mandatory combat segments I dreaded continuing and wanted to end it as fast as possible.
This in turn makes the player want to stealth through as much of the game as possible.
The available arsenal in TNC is standard and comes straight from TNO and TOB, with three upgrades for each weapon. Gone is the ability to carry a heavy weapon around through perk upgrades, however they are now found commonly enough that if you wanted one chances are there is one laying around, not that I would recommend using any of them unless you like dying more than me. The upgrades range from game breaking for the shotguns to purely useless like the SMG and grenade pistol. Nothing new or exciting to be found here.
Guard AI appears to be the same as TNO. In combat, however humanoid enemies hunker down in cover and rush you, or just stand perfectly still at a distance and either attempt to pick you off at range with their far superior accuracy, or just look at your general direction depending. Anything past that tends to simply rush at you into melee range, or just walk around slowly tanking damage while dishing out huge amounts. Standard fair here.
Stealth is thankfully preserved and improved on from TNO, with the addition of several tools and mechanics that are introduced later that I cannot get into without spoilers. What I can say is that these new mechanics do make for an easier stealth experience.  However there where several segments with commanders that where straight up impossible to go through without triggering the alarm, and I don’t know if that was due to AI roaming patterns not favoring me at the time or hand placed guards just to prevent the player from progressing too easily. This then goes back into my point on combat.
With all the above stated, there where segments that where mandatory that where simply infuriating with massive difficulty spikes that reeked of poor design. Prime examples being the courthouse and the "Cowboy" segment. Courthouse for being purely save scum to get through, and the "Cowboy" for removing cover and having the longest sight lines found in the game and including kill rooms. Only here does strafing moderately work, yet here is also where the damage is highlighted the most. Few guys with ARs do so little, then go a bit further and the same gun can strip your armor pool in seconds, and they are placed in spots that are by design there to score cheap kills out of you and rapidly drain your armor pool. It was a chore to grind through those spots, and left a bitter taste in my mouth after completing them.
All that builds up to a point where the end game gives you the ability to get all possible "contraptions" and its here the game actually feels fun to go though and combat isnt annoying, for the half hour or so that is left once you get at that point. If the entire game was like that last half hour with all the tools and contraption perks at your disposal, my feelings on the game would have been much different.
It feels half baked, and poorly tested for people who wanted a challenge out of it. Not in a million years would I attempt Meine lieben difficulty in its current state, not because it was too difficult, but how it presented that difficulty. I have no urge to go back and finish the sidequests or attempt to replay it by mashing F5 all day like a teenagers dirty sock, thats not good design if you feel forced to do so.
Could I have dropped the difficulty? Oh yeah for sure, but I wanted that stupid achivement.

I'm not sure why so many people didn't like this game; while not the greatest ever, it is a really enjoyable game with a unique story and features.  Sure, its very linear; but not every game has to be open-world.  Games with a strong narrative, such as Remember Me, would not work very well as an open-world game (the devs would have to impose annoying restrictions on where you go in the open-world anyway to enforce any kind of narrative).  So, if you're looking for GTA or something, this isn't for you.
That said, the story is very compelling: you are a memory hunter whose memories have been stolen in a future-parisian city where memories can be traded, bought, and sold.  The gameplay reminds me of something like Uncharted or Tomb Raider where you have to climb around, jumping and hanging from ledges.  The fighting, which can get a little repetitive is like a not-as-good version of the fighting from the Batman: Arkham Asylum games with some sci-fi elements thrown in.  However, the memory remix sequences were some of my favorite parts and something truly unique to Remember Me.  Basically, you can scroll through someone's memory and make tiny alterations to change how they remember what happened; for example, you can turn the safety off on their gun and move a stool slightly, causing them to trip on the stool and the gun to accidentally fire, shooting someone else.  The soundtrack is also really amazing; I sometimes listen to it while working.  Graphically, the game is pretty impressive, especially the remix sequences and other memory areas, which are very stylized; especially when you use 3x1 Eyefinity :)
My only complaint with the game is that the fighting can get a little repetitive.

"Remember me" takes you on a journey to a decadent future where peoples memories can be recorded, shared and sold...
The year is 2084, the place Neo Paris a futuristic version of Paris. Here the population is oppressed by an agressive and ruthless corporation named Memorize.
Memorize created a tecnology that makes possible the recording of personal memories from any person. These memories are then sold to the public in ATM like machines, downloaded to your brain through an implant in the back of you neck called sense, that everyone as it seems, and then voila enjoy the ride. This process causes addiction and it's like the new legal drug on the streets.
"Remember Me" is an action game play on a third person perspective with a focus on combat. An editor called "Combo Lab" let's you costumize your attacks in to combos. These combos can heal, do damage, reduce habilities cool downs, amplifie effects or a mix of some or all of those as you see fit. Besides these combos there are special powers that you unlock through the game like becoming invisible or doing extra damage for a few seconds.
After a while combats can become a bit repetitive mainly because you will stick to 2 or 3 combos and use them again and again until the jobs done. The exception to this are boss fights. Those are demanding and require a more strategic aproach requiring you to rethink combos to adapt to the situation.
I found the story to be interesting specialy the memory hunting part where you have the chance to change peoples memories by altering little details in it to create a new memory that suits your goals. Also the scenario is awesome, they really put a lot of effort in creating Neo-Paris. It's a shame that the game is so linear because a world like this deserved to be explored more.
The Good:
- The story is interesting;
- Future Paris is an awesome scenario to experience;
- Memory manipulation is fun.
The Bad:
- Camara angles are bad in some parts of the game, mainly on insides and tight places;
- The game is linear, theres no room for exploration or side questing.

I'm a big fan of the origional knytt series and was interested to see what the author could do on a grander scale. I really loved playing through this game.
It does well to recreate the same sense of wonder, scale and adventure. There is a huge map to explore and gorgeous zones and landscapes with different almost tangible atmosphere.
The world created is beautiful, mellow, mostly silent and in places very dark and meditative. Seeing well crafted siluetted scenes of foleage swaying in the breeze is just stunning and very peaceful.
In terms of gameplay its an open world with items to collect, quests to do and well made jumping platformer type puzzles. It also has a lot of secret passages and areas. I always found it immensly rewarding when my meticulous exploration or jamping and timing skills gave me a bit more story, a puzzle and/or item to work out and collect.
It was frustrating at times and I did wonder if I would ever get the satisfaction of seeing an ending but got there with some perseverance.
To compare it to other 2d open world exploration games its like Ori and the Blind forest, VVVVVV, Fez, Cave story+, but it has its own unique character upgrades and game dynamics as well as art style and atmosphere.
Some things I didnt like as much: The player and NPC artwork didnt really gel with the overall mood for me it was a bit too cartoony against the siluetes and real life digitised background artwork.
I also thought the writing was pretty bad and 9 times out of 10 the attempts at humour fell flat for me. The whole story felt a little half baked if im honest. I loved the allusions to some apocolyptic disaster in the distant past sort of like the game Hyperlight Drifter and the items and coversations revolved around it. However while I found the game immensly satisfying for its stunning atmosphere and well thought out and executed challenges, I thought the ending was a bit of a cop-out and it ended too abruptly.
Overall this game is a beautiful addition to the knytt series and one for those who love exploring a huge map with lots to discover. I'd also recommend if you like jumping puzzles that require practice and repetition to master but feel satisfying when you get it right.

The story is just as contrasting and contradictory as the world. It is a carefully crafted exploration of Communication and Belief, and all of the challenges that this brings with it. Everything about the story is mellow, sometimes dark (even exceedingly so), often thought-provoking. And for all the questions that are asked, none are answered in any satisfactory way.
Overal, Knytt Underground is a strange game. It is one of the most relaxing games I have ever played, but challenging in both its gameplay and its themes.

LEGO Worlds is by no means a perfect game. It lacks any real story but instead focuses on the concepts of exploration and construction. Both of these fall short of what the potentially could be but due to the game being in Early Access there is still room for much improvement.
It would be normal to assume that a construction game involving LEGO would seem like the most logical step for the brick building toy. Unfortunatelly the controls make it rather hard to make anything worthwhile. The asiest solution around this is to build in an external program like LEGO Digital Designer and import the file into the game. This process does have the potential to be troublesome of course as LEGO Worlds lacks the brick library which LDD posesses. Hopefully, as updates quickly come, the "brick gap" can be made closer. Construction is also limited to static objects, the ability to build vehicles is not yet available and I am unsure if it will ever be implemented.
Exploring offers an array of totally different biomes to find. The major motive to explore is to find new objects, minifigures, and vehicles. Although effective at forcing the player to explore, the game becomes repetitive from the constant travelling. It is sometimes more effiecient to merely keep generating a new world until you discover new biomes at spawn. Exploration could be improved through having more structures to find. There are already a few but they do end up repeating after a few hours playtime.
In retrospect, the only real reason to buy this game is the ability to experience LEGO in a totally new scale. Being able walk around a LEGO house as a minifigure is a totally unique experience which this game offers. For that this game is worth being if you so happen to be a fan of LEGO or it's games.

Trine Enchanted Edition is a 2D fantasy adventure RPG, where you can choose between three different characters whom all have different play styles. You can get through most of the levels and puzzles simply by playing as one character, or make it easier on yourself and switch characters.

I don't want to give away too much about the story, because the story is what makes this game so great. Whenever I play this game I feel like I'm listening to a bed time story being red to me by my grandfather. It has a magical attraction too it, many times it's very over-the-top just like real fairy tales, but it's that approach that just makes a game like Trine, shine (rhyme intended).
You play as Zoya the thief, Amadeus the wizard, and Pontius the stout errr knight; each one has a unique game play style, but I'll explain more about that later, these three hero's are joined together by the trine, and must save the kingdom!
As has been hinted above, you play as three characters: Zoya, Amadeus, and Pontious. Firstly, Zoya (thief) is the most agile character, you shoot arrows, grapple hook and swing your way around the game. Amadeus (wizard), being a wizard can conjure up boxes that can be dropped on enemies, or used to help get to high hard-to-reach-locations. Lastly, Pontius (knight) has always been used as my "meat shield", he has his own unique qualities but those don't reflect my play style very well. He uses a sword and shield and a hammer; while he doesn't help for puzzle solving very much, he is very useful for bashing enemies!
Seeing as how the game is 2D, it controls very simply, but I've always felt that the more simple the controls the more tight and enjoyable the game. You move right left and jump. You use the mouse buttons to shoot, attack, etc. When you start the game the game explains to you how to play it.
An additional note is that thanks to the latest update the games graphics have been revamped! It now looks and feels like playing Trine2 on trine1, if you miss the old graphics or are curious about how the original trine looked like, just change the launcher to the classic trine and you can play the original game again)
Another quick note about the enchanted edition: you can now play the game in multiplayer, which makes the game a whole lot more fun. I played with only one friend, but you can have 2 friends playing with you at once.

I have earned all the achievements in trine. After trying to get past hardcore mode on hard difficulty on trine2 I never thought I would get all the achievements on Trine, not for a long time anyway. after getting all the achievements aside from hardcore, I literally speed ran my way through hard mode and beat the game in one day.
What that says to me, is that for those of you who want a really tough game experience, you might want pass on this game, for others who just casually play the game you're not going to get much out of it aside from a simple play through, for achievers this is a great game to increase your "perfect games" count +1.
"What other types of achievements are there, oh derailed one?" I'm glad you asked! Trine (and trine 2) have very straight forward achievement categories: Beat the game, Collect all the things on all the levels, do this with this character (different character challenges), and beat the game on the hardest difficulty.
Trine the Enchanted Edition is currently $14.99 I spent 13 hours playing the game, that's almost a dollar an hour, which according to my value system; is very good. I really liked that the graphics were updated, I don't grade a game based on their graphics I was enjoying the classic trine just as much as the enchanted edition, but the updated graphics really helps.

I rarely have very negative things to say about games that I play, I tend to enjoy games more then find them annoying. To quickly recap: I have always loved the Story in Trine. The gameplay is always smooth and enjoyable. The achievements were usually easy but enjoyable. the price was fair.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fantasy games, platformers, or 2D games.

I will not recommend this game based on the following two factors:
- It is NOT worth $60 to me
- The practices of the developers were/are unnacceptable
With its current amount of content after two updates, I feel the game is worth about $20-$25 (which conincidentally it is now, with the Steam sale), but there simply isn't enough content and well-developed game systems to make this comparable to games asking $60.
The exploration is repatative and often lackluster. Planet and creature generation is not unique enough. Interaction with the 3 alien races feels trivial. The ending is still a complete joke (it's literally nothing).
Hello Games have added in tools for exploration and settlement, but there still isn't enough drive and interest to actually use them. The structures generated are bland (and again, repatative) and are overly common (generation has been reduced, but not enough, they still don't feel unique at all).
The game sort of feels frozen in time because planet rotation and orbit isn't a thing, making settlement somewhat shallow (would be amazing to see planets move by in the sky from your base).
There is a supposedly large update coming in the next month or two which may fix these issues and I will update this review if it does. But the issues of "saltiness" over the way Hello Games treated the release is still very present. It's simply unnacceptable for the company to go radio silent to the waves of criticism and questions about all the missing stuff. Whether or not they "lied" to us is up for debate. They absolutely mislead prospective players and their flip-flop marketing didn't help. I don't really expect an appology because that has legal remifications and such. They had a window of opportunity to communicate with players around release and they ignored it. The excuse of using "actions not words" doesn't fly for me. They could have done both like most major games developers. Instead they lost the vast majority of their playerbase because of the silence.
I have hopes for this game, but it is not up to par yet. More ammends and updates need to be made/roll out. Eventually we might have the game we were advertised.

depth is AWESOME!! underwater isolation and sharks are two of my biggest fears, and I was interested to see if I would get a good thrill! verdict: still, every time i play.
depth gives you the option to play as a diver or a shark. as a shark, you're just trying to hunt the divers and STEVE before they finish their spelunking. the divers are trying to collect as much treasure as possible for items and weapon upgrades, defend STEVE, and make it out alive. there's different game modes-meg. hunt, which is basically all players v. giant shark, and hide and seek. i've played so many games and never gotten to play hide and seek. with matchmaking you can choose meg. hunt or blood and gold(regular mode), but not h&s! a huge bummer for me as i feel like it'd be amazing. there's so much customization and different shark types which is really awesome-if they did different diver types...like different skills/attributes, i think the game would be absolutely stellar.
while a lot of players say the community is good for the most part, i both agree/disagree. other folks are generally nice but there's a real team purpose to being a diver and i haven't been in that many games where people actually care about working together! it's a definite advantage to play with friends. i would suggest waiting for a sale and find some buddies, it's a lot better with people you know and can work with!
overall, it's a game you can really get sucked into. i still get a good scare when a shark strikes out of the pitch black dark, and the heartbeat effect really helps with the atmosphere! imo there could be some really good improvements, maybe other game modes, but the game is actually updated a decent amount and it's a LOT of fun. sometimes the matches are really unbalanced as in you'll find yourself with people on your team with a 15+ level difference, but. if you're willing to just try your best and have a good, thrilling time, there's a good chance you'll love it! i'd say my top advice for new players is try out a bunch of different weapons and items and really get to know them all, so you can find out what you like when maybe it wasn't originally something you would have tried!
good luck, have fin!

There weren't too many chances of me not liking this game. Dark, bleak fantasy? Check. Dark Souls-esque combat mechanics? Check. Horrific monsters? Check. What pushes this game beyond others, in my opinion, is its use of mental illness.
To make a long story short, I'm not fazed by normal horror tropes anymore, like gore or jump scares. Mental illness, however, scare me deeply. Our minds are the only thing we really have, and being reminded of how fragile they are creeps me out to no end. I was a bit nervous at first because most entertainment doesn't really present mental illness correctly. Luckily, Hellblade manages to use it really well while still presenting it all in a very meaningful and relatable way. You really feel for poor Senua and you want to help her make it through.
Like most things, the game is not perfect. It has a few glitches here and there, and it even crashed on me once. The combat could have used some more polish, but it doesn't detract from the enjoyment. I really don't have much else to critizise.

This is a tough game to recommend.
At first, the setting and story really pulled me in. The sound design is also pretty incredible and did a lot to sell the experience. It was almost enough to make me forget how lousy the combat is...
... but I never forgot, and the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor combat only gets worse towards the end of the game when they throw enemy after enemy after enemy at you. It got to the point where I just sighed out loud anytime I saw Senua pull her sword out.
There were some really agonizingly slow sections towards the end where you also had to use that focus thing to see past illusions. I used a 2x speedhack from Cheat Engine just to make my character run faster.
The combat and puzzles are fine when the game limits them to short spurts. But by the end of the game, the combat hasn't changed 1 single bit so I was just on autopilot when I saw enemies. I wanted to fast forward it all so I could just see the end of the story (which didn't really come as a surprise to me).
I think they could have trimmed an hour or two from the playtime and the whole experience would have felt a lot tighter. Would have ended right when I felt best about the game. But man... when it felt like a slog, it really soured the experience for me and I had to push myself to load the game up to finish it.
That said, I do think it's a game worth experiencing and some people may be able to tolerate the combat more than I could. Hell, people liked Ryse so they SHOULD like this even more.

As with any game there are some downsides, luckily with Ori and the Blind Forest there are only a few. Most notably is the inability to rebind controls. Overall this game was a great purchase, and although it was rather short, I am happy I bought this game. The developers did an amazing job with this, and I hope to see more games from them in the future. And for anyone who is contemplating buying this game, do it.

Remember Me is a very fun game in my opinion.
First of all the positives:
1. One of the biggest positives of the game is it's graphics. From the very start right to the end your treated with breathtaking views, wonderful scenery and some great detail. it's not perfect but it's certanly a lot better then most games I've played.
2. Sound and music is another big positive. The music soundtrack is absolutly brillant and the way the music reacts to what is going on in combat is a nice feature. The sound effects are quite well done as well but the ambient background noise along with the great scenery work really well together to create a relistic enviroment that makes you want to explore.
3.  It has a great story line and the game does well to help keep track on whats going on. The story has many plot twists and does a good job of making you think "what's going to happen next?" or "who's the real enemy, Edge or Memorize?"
4. Gameplay. Some people have complained about the combat system in this game but personally I like it, it involves timing your punches and kicks and remembering different combinations to pull off the biggest combos. On top of that you can customize the types of attacks you throw in those combos for example you might start with some regen pressons to heal yourself at the start then put some power pressons at the end to do big damage dealing attacks at the end of the combo.
Another type of gameplay this game brings is a feature called memory remixing. At certain points in this game you have to remix someones memory and this involves going backwards and forwards in the memory to alter certain things at certain times to meet the required objective. It's a very nice feature that is fun and gets your brain thinking but it looses its charm slightly once you know how to succeed in them. Also they could of done with having more of them in the game.
Sadly although it does have it's good bits, it does have bad bits as well.
1. Controls. The biggest con is definetly the controls. They are very fiddly and Niln isn't exactly the best when it comes to turning and sometimes it can take a second for the controls to work which is a nightmare in this one perticular point where you have 1/2 second to react to things otherwise you die. The control problem can also be seen when your climbing around on walls as the camera sometimes confuses the game on where you want to go for example instead of going left it might send you down.
2. Bugs. This game has quite a few and I've defiently come across a few game breaking bugs that have caused me to die or get stuck. Even the tutorial in the 1st memory remix can cause a bug as it stops you from altering the memory unless you do exactly what it says but it's very easy to stray slightly away from that and it has hit me twice already. Another bug that has happened was myself hopping out of a window (which your meant to do) but then I accidently climbed back in but the game treated it strangly and instead of putting me back in the room it glitched me through a wall and giving me the abillity to walk in the air which caused me to reload the last checkpoint.
Overall if you look past the bugs and the fiddly controls it is a very nice and entertaining game and I certainly love playing it. Different people have had different reactions to this game but this is my overall opinion.

Wildly popular, this COD marked the turning point and a new direction for the franchise. A much needed break from WW2, this pushed the modern shooter further with some fresh ideas and additions. However, it also marked a shift in the target audience towards appealing to the masses with some questionable design decisions.
Technically it was excellent (and still is, years after release), It struck the perfect balance of shiny new graphics that leave the responsiveness smooth.
The addition of levelling and perks made the game more addictive and hooked in more new/casual players. However it also added a lot of "noise" and randomness to the game. Killstreaks, martyrdom, triple frag grenades, grenade launchers, airstrikes, aimbot heli = giant clusterf***. The game was designed so anyone can join a public TDM server and get a few kills without much skill.
After removing the noise (promod + SND mode), this game is very competition friendly due to its fantastic handling.

Fun little game, with lovely (albeit limited) physical shooting mechanism and great looks, but I can't recommend it at the moment. Mainly because there's no "real" online multiplayer, you can only play with people locally or online with those in your friends list - no lobby and no self-hosted games.
If you have 3 friends who want to play often, it could be fun, but for me I am too busy due to life/work, so I just want to jump into a match sometimes.
Therefore I could just play a match against bots, which felt unsatisfying.
Other problems imo:
- controls feel a bit clunky sometimes, but are generally fine.
- Not enough power ups & difference in weapons.
- The automatic zoom is annoying and broken, manual zoom would be much better. Some user reported that he get's killed because the camera zoomed in and therefore he was out of the match area (which kills you after 3 sec).
- No ability to rebind keys, set mouse-sensitivity etc.
- Game menu controls are clunky.
- No timer for your weapons, this is okay with the normal shot but when flying you want to know when you can shoot the carpet bomb to time your shot, which is important because of the gravity.
- Only three maps, not enough variety in them. Could use more different scenery and interactive environmentals (like a black hole, nebula, shooting stars, ..?)
- The sun mechanism is really cool, but feels unsatisfying graphic whise. It should look more fire like and less like a vector graphic.
Other than that I have no complains, and I think if all this gets adressed, then this game could be a cool little multiplayer gem.
Plus the team behind it seems to be very active in the discussion, which is a good sign.
Edit: The developer said they are thinking about adding matchmaking. So keep an eye out for it and definitely check back later. Or buy it if you want to support the developers.

I've never written a review on steam before, but I simply had to for this game. I bought it 4 years or so ago, and completed it once back then, and once more now after finding all the secrets. This is an absolutely incredible game.
What makes it incredible? It utilises the full potential inherent in the platforming genre, with lots of cool movement sections, some interesting movement-altering abilities you pick up, and just overall tight controls and a well-designed world. The soundtrack is so good you'll be listening to it long after finishing the game (I certainly still do). As a nice bonus, if you enjoy speedrunning you'll find this game is perfect for it, which a built-in maze-like shortcut system called The Disorder which makes the any% category really wild.
Your character, Mi, can both walk around normally AND transform into a ball, which gives completely different movement possibilities. Travelling through the (enormous) map is never dull in Knytt Underground.
The map itself is a masterpiece. There are two sections before the main game, both of which are small sections of the main map (which you revisit in the main game). The trailer does a decent job of showcasing how atmospheric this game is but it doesn't show even a fraction of the epic-ness you feel traversing the all the little tunnels, both obvious and secret, while listening to relaxing and ambient soundtrack. If you get lost, there is a an actual 'map map' which shows you where you've been, where you need to go (to ring the bells for the main story) as well as where any save points are. As you play through it you feel like an explorer in a vast cave system, and that's what makes Knytt Underground so fun to play and play again - there's always something new.
Secrets are the core of what this game is. This is a game about exploration and surprise and it's got plenty. There are secrets WITHIN secrets and none of them are too hard to find. If you do the exploring, you WILL find them, but you'll probably never expect to find them where you do. Even when I began deliberately searching for any leftover secrets as I did this year, I still found myself laughing out loud at just where Nifflas had managed to hide them all.
TL/DR: If you love secrets and you love exploring, you WILL love this game. It has the best atmosphere of any game I've ever played in my entire life, and yes I DO mean that literally. If, however, you prefer games where everything is laid out clearly, or you particularly dislike secrets that have no clues attached to them, then this game is probably not for you. If you're at all unsure, then just buy it anyway. In GBP it's 4.99 and for the amount of time you could spend on this game, that's a steal

Another pleasant feature is the depth of the world, there's loads of little side missions you can do that you discover during your travels, they don't affect the main plot but they add so much flavour to the world.
The game does have its downsides however, it can vary greatly in difficulty in places, varying from very, very easy to punishingly difficult, this isn't too much of a problem though and can be easily overlooked. Pros and Cons at the end. Getting recked by divers has set a good example and made me a more fearless diver, and as such that side of this game has been more fun. Might be Dual Toxic Pistoles OP for the gold cost. That said, I still prefer to be a shark.
If you can't get some early kills on the diver's you're going to have a bad time, but if you're diving team is dumb, which they often are, it can be a real drag when you aren't dying and your team is making poor choices and dying often. When I play I play as the Great White, the only communication I need is at the begining of the match when i say "Let me go in first, you follow through on the chaos." By treating myself like the right hook, and my team mate like the surprise left, we are usually pretty successful, at least at having fun XD
The sharks introduce an interesting gameplay mechanic that is pretty unique to Depth in that you need to plan you're exit as much as possible. The most successful sharks are the ones that push or drag a diver out of LoS of their team, because this game is defined by your ability to survive to kill again. I think not understanding this is why a lot of people prefer to play as diver, it plays more into what people are used to (typical FPS with gear mechanics similar to CS), where as if you have trouble thinking like a mutated shark, I can see why you may think that the sharks are either too slow, or are too weak/dont have enough HP.
Pros:
* Unique 2v4 PvP  (the game Evolved wishes it was)
* Great and CHEAP skins on the community market. (7 cents US to make my Tiger shark skinned like a Whale Shark? Yes Plz!)
*Both Teams actually fun, (Pro Tip: Move as fast as you can in the beginning, an early lead can turn into a steep win for either team)
*Quest system for free loot boxes for free skins, and regular events where we all vote for the next cool thing by picking a side and earning points towards it by playing, oh and even more free loot boxes. Oh, and randomly doled out free skins too.
*Great White Shark evolved for speed with the evolution to instantly refresh it's fully upgraded tank ability, isn't possible every game, but by Poseidon's beard, it is ruinous.
Cons:
* I struggle to find any issues that don't stem from dumbass divers saying dumbass things
*My friend is really good at the thresher and I suck at the thresher :(((((
*Toxic Dual P 11's may be OP for how fast you can earn them, haven't decided.
tl;dr: This is a fun game if you can make smart, calm decisions. If yer gonna panic and do dumb things, yer gone have a bad time.

There were some really agonizingly slow sections towards the end where you also had to use that focus thing to see past illusions. I used a 2x speedhack from Cheat Engine just to make my character run faster.
The combat and puzzles are fine when the game limits them to short spurts. But by the end of the game, the combat hasn't changed 1 single bit so I was just on autopilot when I saw enemies. I wanted to fast forward it all so I could just see the end of the story (which didn't really come as a surprise to me).
I think they could have trimmed an hour or two from the playtime and the whole experience would have felt a lot tighter. Would have ended right when I felt best about the game. But man... when it felt like a slog, it really soured the experience for me and I had to push myself to load the game up to finish it.
That said, I do think it's a game worth experiencing and some people may be able to tolerate the combat more than I could. Hell, people liked Ryse so they SHOULD like this even more.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a charming, very beautiful game that gives you warm and fuzzy feelings throughout. The combination of storytelling, a rapidly changing environment, and challanging puzzles makes this game an interesting and worthy purchase for any fan of platforming titles.
The game stars Ori, a spirit tasked to bring life back to the forest which he and his family call home. Ori must face hostile life, dangeous environments, and the incredibly ticked off antagonist as he wants to save the forest and restore order to the world. The few characters that make an appearence are all lovable and interesting characters, despite the lack of any dialouge present. The only source of story telling is through a main narrator and Sein, the equivalent of Navi but without the annoying interruptions. The game flawlessly jumps between action and narration as Ori travels even deeper into the dying landscapes. By the end of the 10 hour story you come out of it satisfied and given a immense sense of accomplishment.
That being said, their are some minor problems that I find somewhat annoying. The game, despite the first few minutes implying it being a simple puzzle game, can get insanely hard at certain points, especially before major events take place. These points often require you use a skill you may have just recently attained and basically force you to learn to use the full ability to full effect almost instantly. This results in a Dark Souls esque "♥♥♥♥ you" level in an otherwise soft and easy going game when traveling between these areas. They even added a kill counter to tell you how many times you die (I clocked in exactly 600 times the cute little Ori got pummeled, burned, or drowned). The developers seemed to want to make the game more challanging to extend the lifespan of the main story, when in reality it can be almost rage inducing to suddenly have such spikes in difficulty appear out of no where.
Overall I would rate this a 8.5/10. It is a fantastic game but I dislike how the developers had seemingly no plan to increase the difficulty and add steep learning curves into the game. Overall, however, the good parts vastly overshadow the bad, and Ori and the Bling Forest left me satisfied while at the same time wanting more.

Everything about this game is impressive - (primarily is it's) soundtrack, graphics, story and (usually) gameplay but theres one thing that ruins the whole experience for me... game design. It turns out after the initial tutorial section, the game shows its true colours. Under all its flashiness, it's just another one of those "trial-and-error" games.
Huge sections of the game force you into a constant rinse-and-repeat cycle. You get punished for not knowing how to advance until you fail and die (and you will) therefore experiencing it. To make matters more frustrating, the save system plays on this fact, asking the player to save manually but only when the game decides its okay for you to do so. I'm sorry but my free time is sparse and I don't want to be wasting it replaying the same sections until I "perfect" it. It's a shame that a huge chunk of the game the developers spent sweating over will now be left unseen due this bad decision.
The game will gradually give you abilities as the game progresses asking you to revisit parts of the map you have not yet fully explored. This in itself is a fine but for some reason the developers chose to block off certain areas of the game mid-way though the story without notice. Why do this if you're asking the player to revisit parts the map with their new abilities? So another bad design choice has stopped me enjoying the game and hunting down my 100%. Suppose this is to re-enforce the "rinse and repeat" mechanic they've stuck by?
It's ok to pay homage a game from the early 90's but at least take the best parts and learn from what they did wrong. I honestly thought we were past this annoying gameplay trope. If you like these type of games where you like being repeatily frustrated by bad design choices then go for it. Me, I have far too many other games I could be getting on with having actual fun. Another disappointment :(

If you're at all into platformers (and I do not consider myself to actually be one of these people) chances are you have already played and loved Ori and the Blind Forest.
If you aren't, like me, I would heavily suggest you give Ori and the Blind Forest a try anyway. There are already plenty said on the subject, but here's the succinct version of it:
1) The visuals and music of this game are distinctive and beautiful. They create a great atmosphere for the game. Throughout the -entire- game. No Zelda-dungeon cramped and looped backtracking dreadfulness, thank you.
2) The game is not "easy". I am one of those girls that like to run through my RPGs in 'normal' or 'easy'. Ori doesn't have these settings, it is based completely on your own logic and dexterity. There's multiple ways that different people can go about solving the puzzles set in the dungeons or maps. It makes the game incredibly satisfying to play (and frustrating, ahaha, so much swearing on my part.)
3) I've never played a genre like this before (what others have called Metrovania?) but the expansive map allows for a great level of exploration, and the restrictions placed feel very natural, limited only by your abilities (granted in-story and by your own personal skill-tree growth.) I enjoyed the puzzles of the map (in and out of dungeons) greatly. And the game never forces you to go through most of them, although I enjoyed to do so anyway.
That is to say: it's a game you can try to rush through (ahaha, reach the 3 hours completion achievement, I dare you) or savour.
Anyway, go and play it.

This is a tough one to review. I love the Wolfenstein series, and overall I'll say this is a relatively solid addition -- and whether it's a positive or negative experience for you will really depend on what matters to you, so I've added a few pros and cons below:
Pros:
Same consistent run'n'gun / stealth that you're used to with previous games
Fun perk / upgrade system
Great storytelling
Fun Assassintation mode where you can revisit past levels with modifications
Cons:
No New Game Plus mode (this is a big deal to me)
Some crashes. I had 4 over 17 hours and 3 of them were related to picking up collectibles.
No formal chapter select, but they do let you revisit levels through the assassination mode you unlock later in-game.
As an additional note, and minor spoiler (so don't read ahead if you don't want any spoilers), I just wanted to add for informational purposes (and not necessarily as a pro or con for me personally) but there is no end-game boss fight. You have a fight at the end of the game that's meant to be difficult but it's just an "intense mob" vs an actual proper boss fight. Personally I hate boss fights a lot of the time, but they do give you a feeling of accomplishment afterwards that mobs just don't give you.
Overall I'll say this, not having a New Game Plus mode is a HUGE detractor for me, but I recognize not everyone cares about that, and even despite that I still had a lot of fun playing the game. Story-wise this game is very much a continutation of the previous game and works as a set-up for the next game, so don't expect all loose-ends to be tied up by the end of this game.

From time to time you will maybe encounter smaller problems with camera placement and the climbing passages are far too easy, thanks to an automatic system which shows you where you can hang on to or jump to.
The combat system is combination based similar to the actual Batman game series, but with the unique twist of giving you the ability to design your own combos with different effects for different demands. The sound is pretty fitting and the music is also adaptive, which means that, for example, if you make a successful combo the music boosts up.

-- Skullgirls 2nd Encore Review --
// Summary //
This is my favorite fighter available on Steam at present.  All of the graphics are hand-drawn, beautiful art; all of the fighters are fine-tuned and sexy.  The developers have supported this game long after its release:  The 2nd Encore Version is a free upgrade which represents the second major free-DLC pack for the game.   Three new characters are given to the player free of charge.   Fukua, a clone of Filia, Beowulf, an unfogettable epic, and R. Fortune....a robotic Ms. Fortune.  There are also three pay-for DLC characters available.  Squigly, a host to Leviathan, Big Band, a cyborg cop with an instrument for every situation, and Eliza, ancient and divine host of Sehkmet, the Egyptian Goddess of BLOOD!  Whether you pay for the three or not, you will see them in the story, and fight them in Arcade mode.  The free-LC also comes with a slew of new stages.
// Gameplay //
Solid Marvel vs. Capcom style mayhem!  You get to choose your team in arcade and vs. mode, you can choose one super-strong hero, two strong heroes, or three normal heroes.   The game's fighting mechanics are MUCH deeper than I initially believed, and they are completely covered in the game's Training - Tutorial mode.  Are you alone against three heroes and they're switching in and out to regenerate their health?  Perform an 'Out-take' (a move that knocks the current fighter off stage and forces a new one in) and you will remove all that fighter's red health, and restore your own!
Back up against the wall while you get pounded?  Block low, and prepare to do a technical counter.  They call it something else, I forget.  Essentially, you hit two punch buttons while you block at the moment of impact and you force the opponent back, it bounces him away.  Another reviewer has complained about hit-stun recovery times being too long, allowing one hit to win the match if the fighter follows up with a good enough combo.  This is pretty untrue.  A perfect, top notch combo ended in a 'Blockbuster move' (Think Hyper, or Ultra combo) will take a third to a half of health off of you, if you're both single fighters and not teams.  Every move in this game has an adequate defense or counter.  The hit-stuns and recovery times are well calculated, and are explained in the Tutorial.  In fact, it explains that only certain moves can be cancelled into other moves before the opponent recovers.  Meaning, you can't just button mash after your poke lands.  You have to know what combos work and which ones don't.
My very favorite element so far, is that combos (called chains) are adaptable.  A combo that goes, LP, MP, MK, HP can just as easily go LP, MP, HP.  You can remove one or more moves from a chain and it still works as a chain.  Further, Standing LP, crouching MP, standing MK, crouching HP will also be a chain, if the original was true.   The combos are adaptable.  Once you know the 'rhythm' of the chain, you can adapt it to jumping, standing, or crouching.  You can edit it for when you need a shorter chain, for example; the medium kick may not be in range, and if you attempt it, and miss, the opponent may have enough time to recover from hit-stun, so you leave it out and proceed directly to the Heavy Punch.
This is a game of pokes, like a lot of fighters.  You poke until you land a hit, then you build a combo off of the poke that lands.  You don't just rush in with your heavy moves, you'll get eviscerated by an opponent that is defending waiting for you to do a move that has x frames of recovery, so that he can poke you safely, and then take off with his combo.
// Style //
No fighting game I've played has more style than this game.  I've been playing fighters since Super Street Fighter II was new.  From the music, to the announcer(s) [4 available options], the theme of showbiz, the stylized art (all of which is available in the in-game Art Gallery, plus guest art), the zany characters, the whole package.   It's never boring, and it doesn't disappoint.
Finally, it has story.  It's not like it's a novel you'll be unravelling for years, but it has a story that is compelling.  Much more compelling, in my humble opinion, than Soul Caliber or Street Fighter.  Mortal Kombat and Skullgirls are among my favorite for stories.   At least they're epic.  Save the world or change it's fate, and all that.
Fighting Shadaloo just isn't as...rewarding as taking over the world as a giant Goddess of Destruction named Sehkmet...
// Synopsis //
I imagine it will be a very long time before I get bored of Skullgirls.  Of course, I still play Marvel vs. Capcom.  This game is similar to that fighting style.

I feel conflicted about this game - I wish there was a "neutral" feedback option.
I certainly enjoyed many aspects of the game, such as most of the design elements, as well as the soundtrack.
However, I feel that there are also some issues that need to be pointed out here.
First, the game is too long for what it is. While I do appreciate the designer’s efforts to create the large and diverse map, the gameplay does not really benefit from it. By the time I was about 75% through the game, I was already bored with it, to the extent that I almost didn't even have the motivation to finish the game.
Second, the ball physics are rather frustrating. The ball is difficult to control with any degree of accuracy, and in many tasks that involve using the ball you basically have to rely on a serious dose of luck in order to get through.
Which brings me to the third, and most important point. In many of game's puzzles, the solution can be fairly obvious. However, you then have to spend a significant amount of time repeating the same action numerous times, until you get everything lined up to the millimetre and the timing to the second, exactly as the developer intended - or else it won’t work, and you'd have to try again. This type of challenges is just not particularly interesting to me, as they are in no way intellectually stimulating. In fact, they are not fun or entertaining, but rather frustrating and annoying.
Also worth mentioning is that in some areas of the map the soundtrack is bugged by various crackling and popping noises - I guess some of the soundtrack files might be corrupted.
The ending is also kind of a letdown, to the extent that the developer himself admits it. Personally I expected that there might be another puzzle after the last bell, possibly involving the giant clock in the area right above it. But no - the ending is kind of abrupt, and basically  it leaves you with the sensation that something is missing - some kind of definitive conclusion, one way or the other. It is obvious that the dev left it that way on purpose, but what can I say - philosophy and entertainment don't mix particularly well.
Anyway, the game is not perfect, but despite its flaws it would be difficult not to recommend it. Most of the artwork in the game is beautiful, and creates a special atmosphere that is worth experiencing. Chances are, you will enjoy it, at least up to a point. Pick it up when on sale, and you won't regret it.

I have been a fan of Nicklas's games since I first played "Within A Deep Forest" so many years ago. While most of his games tend to have a similar gameplay style, they are always enjoyable and have an amazing aesthetic.
Knytt Underground is one part "Within A Deep Forest", one part "Saira", and one part "Knytt". The simple platforming and exploration gameplay of Knytt is merged with the harder, physics-based platforming from WADF and is then set in a world using surreal photo-realistic environments akin to Saira.
This all produces a massive, metroid-vania-like, ambient, exploration platformer that is easy to get lost in. It is not afraid to crank up the difficulty in a few areas to keep you on your toes, but the whole map is incredibly non-linear so you are rarely forced to go through a section when you first come to it. This game is essentially one huge scavenger hunt, but it never feels like a chore, even when you are backtracking through areas you have already been to. There are quite a lot of secrets as well, many of which provide the hardest sections of the game and are completely optional.
I honestly cannot remember much from the plot apart from having to ring 4 bells, but this game left a lasting impression in the memories of simply exploring the beautiful and serene world along to the ambient, relaxing soundtrack. To me, this is the mark of a good game, and I eagerly look forward to all of Nicklas's future games.

Maybe it's that one second, I'm swealtering through a barren wasteland with only two inhabitants, and the next I'm on a water-world filled with massive fish and flying whales.

Hello and welcome to this review of Moonshot! A game where you pilot tanks in space, attempting to repeatedly kill your opponents with missiles and bombs. Moonshot has a simple concept and simple gameplay, with some added elements and great execution to make it really shine, so let's talk about how it plays.
There are several gamemodes planned for Moonshot, and a few already present with Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and Last Man Standing. With two other potential gamemodes I know of in the works, Online/Lan functionality, and AI matches, you'll have tons of options for how and who you want to play with.
In terms of actual gameplay, once you get the controls down, you have a flying tank that can fly in the direction you point it, drop 3 aerial bombs once you have been flying long enough to transform, shoot targeted missiles while on the ground, and siege mode while on the ground. Siege mode allows you to charge missiles faster, allowing them straight and fast flight, and a recharging shield that can take 3 hits before going down.
So to reiterate you can fire charged missiles straight and true, arc less charged missiles, bomb in the opposite direction you are facing, artillery strike in siege mode, or perhaps try to quickly fly to an opponent, land, and hit  them with a missile. If this sounds to you like there's a lot of options for taking your opponents out, and like there will be many missiles flying everywhere, you're right!
The result is a beautiful frenetic chaos full of explosives and death, and I've never had so many laughs just playing with one other person before, and I'm sure you can imagine, looking at the trailers, how crazy a 4 player match is. Network mode is newly arrived, and improving to feature parity quickly. There are some extra features in gameplay like solar flares, item/powerup drops, gravity of the sun, planets, and asteroids all thwarting to send your tank into the sun or asteroids to blow it up, etc. If your tank gets blown up, it isn't the end! (Unless you flew into the sun.) You will now become a pilot, and have a chance to evade your opponent's attacks to reland, giving you a renewed tank, albeit at the cost of your opponent getting some points. (If they are the reason your tank blew up.)
Keep in mind that when you are flying, you have a limited amount of fuel, so if you get going too fast and use too much at the same time, you will likely find yourself dying off the edge of the screen.
So this is what Moonshot boils down to: Blow up your friends, laugh at unexpected things constantly, feel like a badass when you pull off awesome kills. The presentation is great, and while the gameplay is simple to execute, the resulting chaos and skill ceiling introduced from the different forms of interaction will keep you on your toes, laughing, and challenged.
On an ending note, the controls are a bit strange when using WASD, because you only use A/D to control movement of your tank, W and S to fly/brake. With a control, you get a better feel, since left analog acts more like a universal "go where I tell you" movement option, however, it will be much harder to quickly aim missiles. I haven't found a good remedy to both of these issues, but it isn't too hard to adjust the m/kb controls, I just find it worth mentioning a controller may be more comfortable if you aren't playing super competitively.
To sum it up breifly the graphics in Moonshot are simple, very stylized, and very beautiful. The UI is a wonderful treat, beautiful and thematic, and elegantly proportioned ... if just a touch clumsy to navigate currently due to the controls.
The sounds are fairly distinct, and do not lack for the feel of impact or satisfaction, but I do still find myself feeling like something is somehow missing, but I can't put my finger on it. Maybe it's just that I want my tank to sound like a fully fledged spaceship when hurtling through the air, but either way the music and audio in general is very serviceable, and you won't even notice it much anyway over the voice of your screaming and laughing friends.
Moonshot is worth your time, especially if you like party games, or can only play with your friends online. Both are very rewarding experiences. If you have friendships you need to repair (or break) I recommend Moonshot at:
It actually feels fairly generously priced at its current total of $8.00.

A multiplayer game where you control a tank in space and try to annihilate your friends?  On paper it sounds excellent and gladly in practise, it’s superb fun!
Your objective is to kill the guy inside your opponent’s tanks.  This is done by first destroying the tank and then trying to shoot the ejected pilot before he can land back on a planet and respawn a new tank.  There's a variety of ways to die which keeps things fresh e.g. tank fire, bombs, being rammed by a fast flying tank, being off screen too long, impact to a planet/sun, etc.
There are a number of weapons at your disposal with more planned and it sounds like there may be possible load out choices in the future.
Main things to consider currently is that the full early-access version is local multiplayer only, but the steam beta version which is easily accessible is online multiplayer.  This seems to be coming along really well and I've been playing games with friends with no problems at all.  I can't imagine it will be very long until online play is implemented into the full version.
I had a previous concern about some of the weapons balancing and the developer has promptly addressed this issue.  Previously the siege mode a tank could turtle into was a bit overpowered meaning the game favoured the defensive player.  The developer has reduced some of the power of this mode and the game seems to now reward risk-taking again.  Great stuff!
The game plays great with a controller and I believe they have designed the controls so that whether you play KB&M or controller there should be no distinct advantage.  So they've tried to balance things here too and apparently done a good job.

Upon acquiring Moonshot, I was hoping for a tank wars replica. What I got was an interesting concept that has the potential to be extremely fun if properly done.
Moonshot is a game in which you are a tank and your primary mission is to defeat all other opposing players by force. You are stationed in space and are able to circumnavigate any planet your own. Moonshots uniqueness let's you move about and even thrust off to other planets. So instead of being stuck to one place, you are able to move about freely in a sense in space. The thrust controls take a bit of practice to properly familiarize oneself. Once you get this down, moving from planet to planet while shooting becomes feasible. It can also make for some competitive game play as shooting a moving target is not easy.
The shooting scheme itself is not that bad. The gravity of the planets can effect your shot depending on weak the power is. Obviously, the more power means less gravitational influence on the shot. Adding more power isn't always necessarily what you want. The advantage is to use the gravity and try to psych out players with shots that are difficult to dodge. If you want to unleash some mayhem, you are able to transform your tank into what's called "siege mode". Siege mode fixates your tank to one position but makes firing a heck of a lot more effective. Pressing both triggers at once will initiate a shield to generate to protect your tank. It's pretty hard at first to remember this feature when you start out as you'll want to bounce everywhere but this can play a very vital role in tactics when used properly. There are power ups that drop in throughout the game. These power ups have some pretty nice visuals and have some crazy damage effects.
What I like about the game is it's fluidity. When being shot, you're not completely eliminated from the game entirely. Once your tank is blown up, there is a good chance a space man will start floating around. You have some control of the space man but are extremely vulnerable to enemy fire. He will get back into his tank as soon as you are able to land safely on another moon. The moon's themselves can be chipped away at (which is a great feature) and other "sun" moons (that are on fire) can use their gravity to pull you into your death. The game is quite good at it's function and it's inception. Issue now is taking it to a whole new level. I believe a lot more game modes need to be added with more interactive space debris. I like landing on moons and sometimes asteroids, but what else can you think of? Maybe a space station that rotates or has a death trap on one side? Modes are definitely something worth a look as changing the rules of a game is what can make a game go from good to great.
The
are quite suitable to the game and it's atmosphere. It resembles the game Planets Under Attack. I think some animations could be fine tuned a bit better for smoothness but overall it's appealing. The
are good (a little loud at first) but would like to hear variation in shots. The player will be shooting a lot, why not have fun with it even? Maybe have some shots make a duck sound or steam notification sound in different frequencies? Sound diversity can really fine tune a game in the best ways possible and provide for an even immersive experience.
Overall the game is decent at this point. There is a lot of potential but it's going to take some creative thinking to take this game to an immersive level. The price tag is quite stiff and would only recommend buying it if it REALLY appeals to you. Otherwise, it's probably best to wait for a good reasonable sale price.

Did you love the New order? If the answer is yes then do not buy this game.
TL;DR The New Colossus is a watered down version of The New Order which is ironically lacking the Colossus bossfight.
It is everything a sequel shouldn't be(Ironic since the Old blood was actually good.)
Let's start with the storytelling, it is bland. The first two games were quirky and over the top alternate universes. This is like the TV show continuation of a good movie. The universe is still there but the quirk is gone. Other reviews have already told you how hamfisted the writing is, they're right, I have nothing to add there.
Now onto my biggest gripe with this game: THE MONOTAMY
You run from one dieselpunk infused street to another dieselpunk infused street, blasting the same 4 enemies in the face with the same gun you've been using for the past hour because they're all either decent at everything or total trash(kampfpistole I'm looking at you.) Where the previous game had a nice variety of weapons with new unlocks actually making sense(remember picking up that laser rifle for the first time?) The New Colossus just gives you new guns without any ceremony.
All the guns lack feedback and Oomph when shooting. The pistol has a silent and loud mode, the loud mode might as well be the silent mode for how wimpy it sounds. Alternate fire modes are a total bore, no more mini rocketpod under your assault rifle, just a flip up scope and single fire mode. The biggest change is the shotgun going from full auto slow fire to 3 shot burst at super fast rpm(essentially turning it into what is usually the double barrel, but with none of the satisfaction of flipping the action shut.) Meanwhile weird teleporting nazi robots tease you with their cool plasma blaster arm things.
I'd like to touch on the heavy weapons too: They're great, so great that you might as well never use a normal weapon, the laser beam rips through armies of nazi scum like there's no tomorrow. I had more fun the first time I picked one up than I did for the rest of the game.
The enemies are like I said a total bore. There's the basic soldiers with SMGs/ARs, heavier dudes with shotguns, teleporting robots like things, heavy super soldiers, and ♥♥♥♥ing dogs. The dogs come in 3 different sizes and for some stupid reason the smallest are the most dangerous: tackling you to the ground and forcing you to drop whatever heavy weapon you're holding while the nearest shotgunner empties his mag at you. The supersoldaten are total pushovers that die to a good volley from any gun. After which you can replenish your heavy weapon ammo from the two they drop.
There's these huge mech robots in a few different parts of the game that you might as well skip for how uninspiring they are. No real strategy required, just dump 3 dual wielded AR mags into their face and that's it.
There's no real unique bossfights like the previous games, just these skippable mechs.(I'm not kidding, you can just run past them.)
Now onto my final point: In a last ditch attempt to add hours to their otherwise incredibly short game they added nazi commander hunting missions......where you go through previous levels and a few small new areas to hunt for higher ranking commanders to kill. No real reason to do them.
I beat the game in about 6 hours, which is sadly 4 past the Steam return policy.
I wish I could say that the scene with Hitler is a saving grace but all you can do is kick him once.

As a life-long fan of the Wolfenstein series, and having put 25 hours into The New Order, all I can say is this:
This is the best two acts of a movie packaged into a 7/10 game I have ever seen.
You are better suited watching the cutscenes on youtube, as the majority of the actual plot development only happens inside those. (The final boss fight is a one button QTE which transitions immediately into one of the most underwhelming end cutscenes I have ever seen. Genuinely, I am AMAZED anyone signed off on this ending, as it just left me mad that I paid £30 to play 2/3 of a game).
The level design is the major flaw in this. In an attempt to try accomodate three play styles (stealth, guns blazing, or 'tactical'), they've managed to create a gunplay system that WILL instantly kill you multiple times with no room for adapting. The stealth system is incredibly flawed, with random enemies able to instantly detect you across maps. And as for 'tactical'; it has no unique features, and will instead make you wish that you picked the other two paths.
I did 1 year of games design at a UK college, but even I learnt in that time that you shouldn't put main objective in the shadows with no visual indicator that you should go there, other than a GOD AWFUL 'press G for a hint' system that clearly never went through an extensive QA period, as 90% of the time you will press it and literally not be able to see any hints whatsoever.
If you're from a bygone era where janky gameplay is considered 'a challenge' instead of just lazy design, this will be right up your alley. For anyone else, I'd suggest waiting until Bethesda inevitably slash the price in a couple months.

Very nice visually, good animations, good gameplay, and above average story.
I am someone that mostly plays for the gameplay, and despite loving plateform-action games, I usually have much trouble actually mastering them.
The only points that were actually frustrating were the end section of each dungeon (an "escape" section), that are fairly long and require you to be precise with your actions, and make you start again from the start of the section if you miss at any point.
While the powers and actions are relatively limited (you don't have 20+ actions to remember), most of them are designed in such ways that they remain useful through the game.
It is complemented with puzzles that actually allow for multiple approaches when you back track, making it actually fun to try other ways with your newly acquired powers.
Speaking about puzzles, most of them are actually different enough that it doesn't repeat too much, and there are not too many areas with instant death.
The "saving anywhere" costs the blue balls of energy (you find things to replenish it, but not that frequently), so you can save regularly, making "death" not as painful, as you spawn back nearly instantly after you died.
There are also a lot of small hidden areas to find, encouraging you to revisit earlier areas with each new power.
The story is not award winning, but it's does fit the game well and doesn't force you through hours of insipit dialogues, most of it actually coming from playing.
Length wise, it took me around 8-9 hours to complete it, and this include trying to find most of the secret areas, but I enjoyed most of it, with very little filler except when you personally choose it (baktracking and such).
As for the visuals, the images on the store page already show quite a few areas, but each area is different, some feel opressive, others are just nice to watch, but it's always full of details and colours.
Overall, a fairly short game, especially if you have godlike skills, but I am definitely happy with my purchase of it.

An utterly superb visual feast. The visual design, aestetic, characters and scenes are superb. Unfortuntly that's it. It's one good thing. Otherwise the gameplay is distinctly below par, starting with jarring slow dialogs, overly verbose tutorials to forced input scenes which slow down the flow of the game.
The combat system is confusing and will take time. It's a departure from things like Devil May Cry, button-mash-fest, to a more rythmic setup where maintaing combos means being able to press buttons with good timing in the right order, whilst excessivly using the dodge button at the same time.
The boss fights are long drawn out affairs which take a good 5 minutes or so to work out before you are even given any pointers. They all revolve around special abilities which must be recharged using combat, so be prepared to have to fight, dodge and generally run around wasting time waiting for your special abilities to recharge. After all that running around, you're finally greeted with a QTE, as if things weren't bad enough already! If you happen to fail the QTE you face another 2-3 minutes of running around waiting for the your special ability to recharge again to get another shot at the QTE.
The story is okay and the setting good, but the visuals are the real winner here. I wouldn't spend any more than £5 on it as you'll be disapointed with the gameplay. If you can stand it for the visuals perhaps you'd stretch to £10, but it's just simply not worth more than that.

There are so many talking points about Hellblade and it is the most refreshing experience I've had. The graphics, audio, scenary, and story all combine to make an incredibly atmospheric and engrosing game. Senua's story will grip you and I'm incredibly thankful to have stumbled across this masterpiece.

One of the most powerful experiences I’ve had regardless of media type. When telling a gritty story of a hero overcoming the greatest odds to achieve their quest, this is the story they would love to tell but shy away from. It is unlike any other game and shows what can be done in the medium. I experienced the story with a sense of engagement that I rarely feel when playing games. I could feel Senua’s desperation and uncertainty. The story and character development exceed many books and movies. The visuals are breathtaking and creative. It's dark, terrifying, and only lets up enough to keep you together. The game trying to accomplish a singular quest while constantly on the brink of failure.  Don’t go in expecting complex combat or inventory management. It can be frustrating at time, but in a way, it fits the theme. Instead, put headphones on, play by yourself, and take your time.
Beyond the incredible story, the game engages the topic of mental illness in most accurate way to date. It demonstrates what individuals with psychosis experience with a backdrop that allows you to leave your preconception behind. They don’t beat you over the head with lessons or morals about psychosis and schizophrenia or keep the subject matter at arm’s length. They bring you into Senua's mind and don't pull the punches. Their ability to walk this razor’s edge is masterclass, which makes it one of the most important games of the year.

I'm so glad i didn't missed out on this one.
It's a pretty good game, though i can't deny it has it's flaws (but imho it's just minor ones).
First things first: You play as Nilin, a Memory-Hunter in Neo-Paris (Year is 2050something).
People can actually alter memories, share them and remove unwanted ones.
You've lost your memory and escape a facility to search for the truth and your own identity.
Gameplay is very similar to the Batman-Arkham Games. You'll fight your way through enemies, using combo-attacks. There are predetermined combos mixing punches and kicks, while you can decide which special ability should be triggered, as you can have an attack either be powerful, giving a bit of health back to you or shortening the cooldown-time of your more powerful skills.
It's an interesting concept and i found myself playing around with it, trying different playstyles.
The graphic is very good and has a great artstyle.
The story is also quite good, and keeps you interested (at least it did for me).
One of the more unique features, to actually alter memories to give it a different outcome (plays a bit like watching a videotape, fast forwarding, rewinding plus the ability to change different predetermined things), is used rarely, which is a shame as this was pretty much fun.
About the flaws:
The camera is annoying from time to time and using mouse + keyboard feels a bit inaccurate.
It is VERY linear, though i didn't found that a negative thing as it was supporting the story, people might dislike the lack of freedom.
The Story itself also feels a bit like a mix of Inception, Assassins Creed, Johnny Mnemonic and other Movies and/or Games, but it still felt pretty unique.
All in all, if you like 3rd person games like Batman Arkham Asylum/City or Assassins Creed, then you should keep an eye on this one.

I have been a big fan of Nifflas' games since Knytt Stories, and that game inspired me to play through Knytt and Within a Deep Forest. This game is essentially a mash-up of those two games, and it does very well.

A great exploration game. The OST is fantastic, the best ambient soundtrack for a game I can think of. The map is huge and waiting to be explored, but not to the point of being impossible or overwhelming. The scenic visuals are beautiful silhouettes with colored backgrounds.
The characters leave a lot to be desired. Their artstyles are very unflattering, and the dialogue in the game feels very low quality. If it wasn't for them, this game would be perfect.
The game combines the Knytt series with Within a Deep Forest, while at the same time changing the upgrade-based gameplay of each. Instead, it begins as linear, having you learn both forms of basic gameplay, then combines them into one for the bulk of the game. The only powerups are area-specific, which is both good and bad.
So, so much to see and do in the last chapter. Reminds me of some of the gigantic levels for pure exploration in Knytt Stories, only with more bouncing. And Cilia.
A very large platformer filled with secrets.  The checkpoint system is very forgiving, which is good since the platforming can be difficult.
