The story in this game is enough to pull you in and make you laugh, cry, and angry, and then happy. It's been an awfully long time since a video game story was able to keep me entraced to play it through all in one go. Very simple game play, but the game itself was well worth the time in my book.

So this review is long overdue, but no matter.
After having gone through the game several times over, it is about time. So here we go.
To The Moon review: short version. (for all the tl;dr people out there, let's get right into the good stuff).

*The story in this game is very gripping.
*The overall design is well done.
*The mood is just right.
To The Moon takes you on a journey that will make you laugh & cry. The story is well written, the art is surprisingly well done. As is the scripting.
The game isn't super long, but the story contents is well worth it, in all honesty. After having gone through the game to check for bugs & other options during gameplay, I can honestly say that I find nothing truly wrong with the game itself. All I found was one -tiny- glitch point that didn't really change anything. All it did was allow me to take one more step in that direction.
One of the best parts of this game is that the story isn't spoon-fed to the player. You are put to the task of exploring even the smallest of possibilities, learning more as you go. A puzzle here & there, talking. And the more you find out, the more you want to keep searching to find the truth.
I'll be honest. Once I started playing, I couldn't stop. In the end, I literally could NOT stop myself from shedding tears.
If you want a good story-driven RPG that is light enough in size & you can just relax with, then this is the game for you.
So if you haven't tried it yet, I highly suggest checking it out. It is money well spent for such a beautiful game.
So out of a possible 5 on my Demanding Gamer scoring system, I rate this game 4.9/5

To the Moon is clearly one of the best games I've played.
I must admit that it was hard for me to get past the 16bit graphics, but after half an hour I totally forgot about it. Don't let the graphics make you think twice before purchasing this game (as it happened to me). Everything is so good about it, that the graphics don't count.
The great story and the excellent original music make the atmosphere of this game one hard to forget.

So, To the Moon. What should I say? It's a brilliant story, I'll say that. As you play, everything comes together, like pieces in a puzzle. It's definitely worth playing, and the ending is, vague spoilers,
, something that isn't seen in an awful lot of story-based video games. There are no downsides to it. There's not much to break down about it, but I'll try to summarise the following.
First of all, I have a 16:9 screen and this game seems to be designed for 4:3 screens. Which is disappointing since in this day and age, all games should be optimised for 16:9 screens, but at least don't make things stretch hideously in order to fit my resolution. But, apart from that, the graphics are of a consistent, retro, pixel style, which, in my opinion, suited the game perfectly. I don't think that it would have been the same had the graphics been more realistic or of any other style for that matter.
The soundtrack is brilliant. It sets the mood for each scene and I love the incorporation of soundtracks into the plot, adding meaning behind what was coming out of your headphones as well as emotion.
Simplistic though it was, the plot was moving and unravelled in a well-formatted sequence. It's not often that a story is told from end to beginning, but I think that this was structured perfectly. It worked for me and kept me engaged and, I admit, my eyes did water at the end, and that's a first in the realm of video games and a second in the realm of fiction in its entirety.
Now, is this everyone's cup of tea? No, I would definitely say that it's suited to a specific genre of gamers. If you like story-driven games which aren't, admittedly,
deep and meaningful but still give you a luxorious quantity of the feels? This is for you. Prefer action? There's absolutely none in this game. Want something with metaphorical value? Probably not for you, but hey, still might hit you in the feels. Want a long game? Well, I just played this for four hours straight and finished it, so probably not for you. But, is it a good game? Subjectively, absolutely. Just perhaps not to every single gamer's likeability.
Worth the money, in my opinion. Not much else to comment on in terms of pricing.
I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes plot-driven games or puzzle solving, even if it doesn't quite sound to your liking. Great if you want a quick dose of the feels.

I took a chance on this game and I'm pretty satisfied that I did.
Set in Neo-Paris in 2084, Remember Me drops you into a world where our current social media obsession has evolved into the Sensation Engine (Sensen) - a technology that allows someone to upload and share their personal memories, experiences, and emotions with the always-online world or even go so far as to erase bad memories or live someone else's.
The player takes the role of Nillin - an amnesiac who finds herself locked up and about to be lobatamized but escapes with the help of the mysterious Edge. Edge claims he and Nillin are vital members of the resistance fighting to take down the company who created the Sensen and as a result have indirectly achieved incredible power and influence.
The gameplay balances 3rd person melee combat with fairly straight forward platforming sections. While the combat is no God of War or Devil May Cry, its simplicity doesn't actually hurt the game and presents a challenge in its own right as the player encounters numerous enemy types with differing strengths and weaknesses - forcing you to adopt different strategies, use different abilities, and create your own combos. Platforming on the other hand is more akin to the Uncharted series rather than the open world type found in Assassin's Creed.
Overall the game is quite well polished, it looks fantastic, the voice work and animation is great, and the soundtrack is superb. The only real downsides to the game is that some experienced gamers may find it too easy even on the hardest difficulty as well as the fact that the game might only be six or seven hours in length.
The most important thing to know before buying this game is that it's a linear story/character driven experience. If you were a fan of Ninja Theory's Heavenly Sword and Enslaved Odyssey to the West you'll enjoy Remember Me. If not then you're taking your chances with it.

A visit to Neo-Paris 2084 itself is worth playing this game. It has good action and puzzles, great storytelling, and an absolutely amazing setting. The environment and the methods that require use of the remixer glove to navigate make me think that this is what Hydrophobia Prophecy, a different game from a defunct indie developer, should have been.
'Remember Me' takes place in a beautiful futuristic city, with a little cyberpunk slum thrown into the mix. You play as Nilin, a wicked-awesome memory hunter that starts off with her memory being wiped, and goes on an adventure to get her memories back and take down a corrupt system. To help along theway, she has a glove that does everything from opening doors and moving objects (similar to Kate's keytool in Hydrophobia), to taking down enemies like a cannon, and ultimately steal/remix memories.
The climbing and navigating challenges were fun, and there's also a very unique puzzle system, which exists in this game here; remixing memories at major points in the game were pieces of art themselves! However, these were used rarely (only on key characters), but I suppose the writers wanted to emphasize that this was a power not to be abused by the heroine. Still, I wouldn't have minded if they added one or two more events along the way.
The story is interesting and tight, avoiding inconsequential side-quests that don't contribute to anything, and instead opt to let you see the amazing sights around you while pursuing your objectives.
There are several QTEs, which I found a little annoying, but the combo system they have is entertaining and allows for interesting combat. I would really like to see whatever improvements DONTNOD might have planned if we're ever fortunate enough to see Neo-Paris again.
Meanwhile, go and play this game!

If you've ever played or enjoyed any of Nifflas's other games, you will probably both enjoy and feel familiar in this one. (And if you haven't, Within A Deep Forest and Knytt Stories are both freeware, so go play them). And I don't just say that because your characters control like the two from those games. However, this is not just "more of the same", and does see him treading new ground.
Gameplay is exploration heavy and very atmospheric. Many areas have puzzles or hazards like enemies and lava, and in some cases (mostly in secret levels) those can be quite difficult. However, those are not the focus of the game, and many other areas there's only platforming or even no obstacles at all. You don't gain permanent powerups, but areas may have objects that give you temporary abilities. Emphasis is on the scenary and atmosphere instead, and on the story.
Yes, the story. And that's the new ground: The story here is very good. You spend most of the game with two companions with layered personalities and backstories, and can choose which one of them will talk for you with most NPCs. As you explore you'll uncover more of their backstory along with the mute protagonist's. The story defies a lot of genre conventions; quests don't always end in a way the characters find satisfying (though they usually do), people are occasionally unable or unwilling to compensate you, and ultimately a lot of doubt is cast on the claim that your quest to "save the world" is actually doing anything. Combined with the unusual backstories and themes, it is a pretty unique experience.
The game becomes extremely nonlinear once you beat the introductory chapters. You can explore in any direction as far as you want, and the world is huge, but if you want you can "beat" the game before seeing huge portions of it. There's also tons of secret rooms and levels, both within the game world and accessible from exploring the menu/hub world.
Overall, I'd highly recommend trying this game. Just don't expect any aspect of it to be fast paced.

Physics-based action games have been around for as long as I remember. Some of my favorite games that I first played on PC over twenty years ago were physics based games. This was headlined by Scorched Earth, a shareware artillery game that was written and developed by Wendell Hicken. It’s really nice to see that modern developers can draw on the inspiration of classics such as Hicken’s in creating and developing new games for modern audiences. Such is the case with Pump Action Games’s exciting new early access game Moonshot.
Moonshot will be released either late in the first quarter or in the second quarter of this year after some fine tuning and the addition of more weapons, maps and modes to play. At this stage of the title’s development everything is in a very playable state and the presentation is already very good. It’s difficult to pinpoint anything abjectly negative about the game in its current state. Some may argue that there isn’t enough variety in game play but that argument is soundly defeated when one factors in the fact that the developers are working hard on adding more content than you can poke a stick at and that the three modes already in the game – deathmatch, team deathmatch and last man standing – have different enough objectives to offer distinctly different modes.  It can be argued that the game needs to be played via multiplayer in order to bring the best out of the game even though the computer AI is intelligent but this has long been a point of difference with this genre. Multiplayer adds longevity and keeps things fresh whereas one can become bored even with the most intelligent of AI systems. Some slight tweaking here and there will perfect them. The power ups can really change the outcome of the game and make those who acquire them unstoppable which can turn games into a race to get the power ups. I anticipate that this will change come the final version of the game. I’d also like to see multiplayer extended to online multiplayer to provide the game extra longevity.
The physics are, as one would hope, pretty spot on. The presentation is outstanding. I’m a big fan of the futuristic beat music though some may find it becoming repetitive. I also find the graphics featured to be rather charming. They are easy on the eye though at times it can become a little busy. The menu system is easy to understand with the right amount of clarity.  Game play in both multiplayer mode and single player mode is very enjoyable. There is much to like here and not a lot to pick apart. It is what one would hope to find in a physics based game.
Given the time and effort that Pump Action games continue to put into Moonshot I have no doubt that come full release that the title will be among the best of its kind on Steam. At this point in time we recommend the game for those who have friends to play with locally and those who simply enjoy physics based games.

It's time to grab a spacetank and start hurling explosives through the gravity wells of the solar system with the aim of blasting your opponents into moondust - or at the very least, vaporising the planetary floor from under their treads! It's nice to see an early access multiplayer game with such fully-formed and enjoyable game mechanics. However, there is a bit of a problem, in that multiplayer has yet to be implemented.
I always try to base my reviews on the singleplayer elements alone, but this sort of crazy arcade action game is in dire need of a human element in order to keep the gameplay fresh. The developers have promised that this element is of top priority and will be implemented ASAP (so I'll update my review accordingly), but until then, all the player has to fight are bots. Dumb, slow, suicidal bots.
At first, I thought the easy setting was just there to introduce new players to the gameplay, but after just a few minutes of play, I was winning flawless deathmatch victories against 3 Hardcore bots. Once the player gets hold of certain powerups like the laser or homing missile, they are pretty much unstoppable. These should either be nerfed, or made harder to get a hold of, perhaps by splitting up the components over a match, which the player needs to collect by traversing from planet to planet, or blowing up opponents that have collected a weapon component they need.
I've pointed out a lot of problems with Moonshot, but only because I want to see it improve. I'm also giving it a positive recommendation because I want to see more of my friends playing it ... so I can crush them 'neath my armoured tread.

This game will appeal to a certain sort of a person. That sort of person is not me. Let's start with the positives:
1. The graphics are nice.
Now the negatives:
1. The game plays extremely slowly. Senua's "run" is more like a mild jog.
2. This is important because the game has perma death in it. So slogging back through all the other sections will be tedious.
3. You cannot skip dialogue sections explaining what is going on. So every time you play, you have to listen to it again.
4. The combat is frustrating. Your character moves like a log. You have no health bar to show you how you're doing. Enemies will sometimes surround you, but you cannot turn to face them, nor can you move away easily.
5. There are constantly whispering voices that gets old very quickly.
6. The slow pace of the game feels like it is used to make a small game bigger.
7. The screen shot function is broken. When you try to take a shot, it blurs everything (I'm sure this will be fixed later.)
8. Sound levels seem messed up.  If you place this, turn on subtitles, because you will miss monologues and dialogues to ambient noises if you don't. (And this game is supposed to be story rich, so that's a bit of a problem.)
Neutral:
1. There is a warning for this game about psychosis. They hired a mental health professional to review this, but you should heed the warning if this sort of thing may trouble you.
Overall, this is going to be the first Steam game I've ever asked for a refund for. After 78 minutes, I realized I was just frustrated. Its slow, a chore to play, and will have no replay value. I suggest picking it up on sale.

Van Helsing is a Diablo like action RPG developed by the Hungarian studio NeoCore Games known for their King Arthur series. Van Helsing combines a lot of the quality-of-life tweaks developers have been adding onto the genre ever since Diablo 2 became bigger than sliced bread. Some of these include the companion and pet system, the ability to respec your character without ever having to be afraid of gimping them, and the ability to disenchant and unsocket weapons without destroying either weapon or gem. However, the game is plagued by tons of bugs and performance issues and its multiplayer component should not even be considered playable.
Issues in co-op:
- The questline is not saved unless you are the host. Either play through the game entirely with a party or play it solo.
- The tower defense portion and all the Secret Lair upgrades are inaccessible to anyone who is not the host.
- Constant crashing when transitioning between areas.
If you're opting for a single player only experience, then you'll get an average game that never takes off or goes anywhere. Remember, this is part 1 of an unfinished trilogy. Van Helsing lacks replay value as well. The level cap is 30 and there is no real endgame content. While the combat is genuinely fun despite adding nothing new to the genre, the customization options are very weak due to limited skill trees.
NeoCore have rushed out an average game then proceeded to sell extra content for it without fixing longstanding issues. Both extra character classes, and the 2nd skill tree for Katarina, were sold for real money which is absolutely deplorable for an action RPG. Let’s not forget that people who pre-ordered this game got an exclusive permanent boost to their magic find. If you plan on buying the 2nd game, you can probably expect the same treatment. Buy a buggy game for $15, then pay $10 for additional content. These 3 games and all their content combined will end up costing you more money than a new game in the long run.
Unless you've experienced every action RPG on the market right and starving for more, then there is no way I can recommend this title.

This game I picked up on a whim, and it turned out to be one of my, if not my absolute, favorite dungeon crawlers ever! The combat is visceral and has loads of impact and tons of play styles. Creature designs are interesting and varied. The loot system rains equipment upon you as frequently as the gore of your fallen foes.
Graphically, for a 3/4 view dungeon crawler, this game looks fantastic! Character models are noticeably detailed and the environments look great. I'd say they are on par, and in some places, better than Diablo 3. Sound design is fantastic as well. The voice acting, while sometimes almost purposely cheesy, is very well done. The music, while not memorable, is not BAD. It just often gets drowned out by screaming and explosions. Story is decent as well. Not the games strong point, but no one plays dungeon crawlers for the story. However, I will say the story is significantly better than most I've played.
Has several multi-player modes, but I haven't had the opportunity to play them, so I can't say how they are.
The game has 2 glaring down sides, neither of them deal breaking:
1 - I don't know if the game is optimized poorly, or what, but when you start the game, there is a very long pause, almost as if the game has frozen. There is no indication that anything is loading. After the first time it isn't an issue, but initially, it's jarring.
2 - A similar problem happens with the loading screens. It takes quite a while for the loading "bar" to start to fill and the whole screen just reeks of "frozen game". I've nearly Alt+F4 many times because I assumed it had frozen.
Only other bad thing I can think of is the game is pretty short. A max level cap of 30 and a 10 hour campaign feel prematurely ended. I wanted more of this game very badly, but for $15, I can't complain to much. I will definitely keep an eye out for Neocore games in the future

A solid fps, with smooth animations and fluid combat. The weapons are a blast to use, although I found stealth to be pretty flat. I recommend just running in like a maniac, that's when I had the most fun. Difficulty is a little bit rough but once you learn how to break line of sight mid combat, causing enemies to lose track of you - it gets alot easier.
Each session was long and kept me hooked for hours at a time. The worldbuilding is well done and overall the game has alot of personality and style. Environments on the main path are lovingly set dressed and background npc interactions are surprisingly detailed, adding a lot of character to the world.
However the biggest issue is it just ends too soon... and too abruptly. The whole third act just felt... unfinished. Just as soon as I was getting good at the game and learning how to most effectively use my new powerups - the game was over. There are side missions but they can be hit and miss, some of the encounters are good while others use too many of the same enemy type and kinda fall flat. I would love something like DOOM's arcade mode to replay the main path missions with all my new gadgets and gear.
It hasn't really "stayed with me" like The New Order did. Still recommended if you're a fan of machine game's wolfenstein universe, and if you're looking for a fast paced FPS similar to The New Order. If not, then maybe wait for a sale. I was disappointed with how abruptly it ended but I think the gunplay made up for it.

Before you look at my rating and go "hurr durr hello games are liars hurr durr". I would like to point out what I find good about this game, and also what can still be done to make it better.
With the new updates adding home bases, vehicles and freighters, the player's possibilities have ben drastically expanded. Now, this does not imply that the current content is sufficent, both in regards to this being an AAA game, and also because it is sold as a full game which it in no way is. Luckily we are seeing a development model similar to what Mojang are doing with Minecraft, meaning continuous free updates bringing more content to the game, keeping it fresh.
Now, what can be done to make this game better? First off, I want to point out a major bug that has rendered me unable to play the game properly. It has to do with teleportation from space stations, back to your home base. Personally, I would advise you to not buy the game until this is adressed, unless you want to make new bases whenever you travel to a new star system.
Another quirk has to do with the space battles. Sometimes when you enter a new star system, you can encounter a space battle where pirates are attacking a freighter. You can either side with the pirates and attach the freigher stealing their cargo, or you could help out the freighter and receive a reward from its captain. If you decide to side with the freighter, a single stray shot, hitting it or any of its allies, will turn it hostile, even though you are in the process of killing the pirates. Kind of like accidentally killing a chicken in Skyrim while saving the entire village from a dragon. A solution to this problem could be to turn the freighter and its allies invulnerable whenever you decide to side with them.
My final opinion of this game is, despite it's bugs and broken promises, positive. With their new development model adding fresh new content, I am sure this can turn into something great. I would, however, advise you to wait until some of the major bugs (like the teleportation one) are fixed before buying it, unless you want to end up as frustrated as I am.

The memory remixing sections are clever and better show off that Nilin is hardly the flawless hero, as well as how much memories can affect your entire personality.

The story premise is very interesting and yet it goes nowhere; you're made to believe you are heading for some dark guilt-heavy narrative but it doesn't turn out to be like that at all. Nilin is interesting as a character but (due to them jettisoning the abovementioned plot thread) comes across as a fairly conventional goody-good herione, while the rest of the characters are just embarressing stereotypes without a hint of depth. The gameplay: I liked the fighting mechanism, combos and all.. but on the other hand the platforming sections are completely linear to the point it's an insult to even call it platforming. They (un)helpfully point out the next ledge you can jump to and you can only jump there and nowhere else, for example.The world of Neo-Paris they've created is gorgeous, but as with everything else, this positive is saddled with the fact that you can explore exactly zero portions of it outside the intended path. Memory rewind is an interesting gameplay mechanism which gives you the choice of altering outcomes of events by screwing with people's memories of them.. but as I'd guessed it before the game's release, they are scripted to occur only at predefined points, which makes no sense since Nilin the character is an expert in doing such things, she should be able to do it anywhere? There's a guard standing - why no make him go home and leave his post, for example. These rewinds were what I was looking forward in this game the most and by not making them occur dynamically they sucked the fun out of it.
In a nutshell, I did like the game but damn if there weren't so many areas where it could have been better. If only had they adopted a little more of the open-world design philosophy, game game could have benefitted immensely. And given that it's published by Square Enix and the reception hasn't been exactly stellar, the chances of a sequel with corrected mistakes are rather bleak. Which is a shame because the core of a good game is here, it's just riddled with missteps.

in many ways, for me, a therapeutic, spiritual - i think the word "zenlike" is used in the description and it's apt. gorgeous, soothing visuals and soundtrack; tight controls; puzzle platforming ranging from easily doable to devastatingly brutal, but always cleverly and fairly designed; a story that's partly just a bunch of tropes and jokes but sneakily filled with subtle moments of heart and bittersweet character development. the open world is massive (beyond the first two chapters, which function as tutorials) and a pleasure to explore, full of small side quests, collectibles, and secrets beyond the main quest, all of which you can finish at your leisure and as quickly or methodically as you like. very little content is gated once you enter the true game in the third chapter; you're free to take off in any direction you see fit and are really only held back by how well you understand the game's physics and control of your character.

If you've never played a Knytt game before, stop reading right now,
, and play Knytt and/or Knytt Stories for free. These games, created by a lone developer called Nifflas (also of NightSky and Saira fame), are some of the finest exploration-based platformers I've ever had the pleasure of playing. Knytt Underground is the most recent in the series, and while it might be the most ambitious, it makes some unexpected departures from the previous games.
You know you're in for something special when the game loads straight to a tutorial that turns out to be the main menu. There are three chapters in Knytt Underground, though the first two are essentially introductions to the massive third. You play both as Mi Sprocket, a mute little sprite, and Bob, a sentient bouncing ball from another early Nifflas game, Within a Deep Forest. Together they embark on a grand journey through the underground of a post-apocalyptic Earth far more mysterious and colorful than anything you've seen in Fallout. The surfaces you traverse are all shown in silhouette but the backgrounds are vibrant, animated collages of Photoshopped worlds. Every alien landscape you can imagine is represented here, with enormous gardens, crystal caves, blasted deserts, crumbling temples, ominous graveyards, and sinister machinery among them.
While you have a massive, massive map to explore, don't confuse this with a metroidvania. Mi and Bob never gain new abilities to navigate with, though their own basic skills provide a wealth of options. Mi can climb walls and Bob can bounce, and switching freely between the two allow you to pull of some surprising maneuvers. There are also colored seeds that grant Mi a one-time power like flying in a straight line, and robots that Bob can tether to. Creative use of these resources can indeed get you anywhere you need to go, no matter how impossible the passage seems. The result is almost like a puzzle game, where you'll find rooms that look like they need special powers to traverse, but eventually you'll have that eureka moment and puzzle it out yourself.
You'll have tons of items to find as well, and the denizens of the underground give quests that'll reward you with what you need or point you in the right direction. These items are used to pass the gates barring your ultimate objective, but there's some welcome flexibility to the collecting. One gate might require 5 items out of a possible set of 8, and if you find some of the game's well-hidden coins you can substitute them as well. This means you'll never get stuck on a particular puzzle for a single item, and exploration will always reward you with something you can use.
Previous Knytt games had stark pixel graphics and a distinct sense of isolation to them. Nifflas often populates his strange and alien worlds with little harmless critters but not sentient creatures, usually leaving you alone to explore the vast spaces in solitude. Knytt Underground is a sharp departure here, adding not only loads of characters to talk and deal with, but also giving them incredibly unexpected personalities. Everyone speaks with modern sensibilities, almost like irreverent sitcom characters. They'll call out their own foibles and contrivances, and denigrate a lot of your quests as pointless busywork. One of your two pixie companions is also as foul-mouthed as you can imagine, frequently telling people to go ♥♥♥♥ themselves and eat glass and such. It's such a weird departure in tone from the previous games, even moreso in how their hideous, blobby portraits clash with the clean lines of the rest of the game.
The NPCs are the only major knock against an otherwise atmospheric experience, and to be fair, seeing their character arcs through redeems the worst offenders. Even on top of the 10+ hours of exploration the game offers, there are a host of secrets to find. Some are tied up in the game's unique and challenging fast travel system which I won't spoil, but be aware there's no easy teleporting around the enormous map until you master it. Just like the rest of the game, though, it's worth putting the time into to experience. Knytt Underground is a marvelous journey from start to finish, one that's easy to immerse in and immensely rewarding to play.

I'm in love with this game, when I first got it I knew that I was going to love it. The sounds, the music, the backgrounds, the art, the gameplay, the characters, everything! It just feels so thought out like a giant complete puzzle. As such, I'll be going into detail about things that make this game great, and also replying to the most Popular Negative Reviews here on Steam.
Gameplay -- The most important thing in any game is of course how it plays. And Knytt Underground plays execellently. It's an entirely physics based platformer with neat power-ups that don't make you stronger, but instead allows you to navigate in different ways to get past obstacles. There's also a transformation that turns Mii Sprocket (The muted character you play as) to become a bouncey ball, where you can bounce up to high places. This transformation is entirely physics based, and it's damn accurate! It's very addictive.
Exploration -- Chapter 1 and 2 of the game are basically Introductions to the World, Tutorials, and the primary characters. Chapter 3 is where the training wheels are removed and you're allowed to freely explore an underground world of massive size with varying environments and hundreds, thousands of secrets to discover. There's even secrets in the main menu!
Themes -- Probably the second most important thing in games, at least in my opinion. Here in Knytt Underground you have some pretty serious themes that you have to stop and think about, they also reflect the Modern World in a way or too. Religion, Atheism, Emotional trauma and finding happiness in the little things play a major key in the story and even gameplay in the form of quests. "Hey! You're that Sprocket Explorer kid, right? I don't suppose you could help me by going up into some dangerous caves to fetch me my dead Brother's skull? I need to complete his grave. He blew up, you see. In a nasty dangerous awful accident-- blah blah blah blah~" Dialogue is usually like that, except that you can reply, in an interesting way...
Artistic Themes -- The literal themes of the game are very pretty, sometimes dark, and othertimes just bizarre. There's some characters who look like a Child drew them, othertimes there's characters who look batshote crazy, but each is charming in their own way. I love how there's basically zero limitations to the amount of characters you'll find. A weird monkey creature and can speak fluent English? Yup. A 6-inch high Ninja Warrior who wishes to kill you? Yup. A literal blob that's just chillin' around toxins? You bet'cha!
Dialogue -- There's hundreds of different and unique characters in Knytt with who you can interact with and even alter their futures, past sometimes as well! However, being the Mute Video-Game-Protagonist, you can't talk, you can certainly think, but never talk except for dreams. Instead you have to find two Fairies, a Moon Fairy called Cillia and a Sun Fairy called Dora. Their elements reflect their personalities. Cillia is dark, sarcastic, and down-to-earth, emotionally limited on the outside. Dora is the opposite, a bright optimist who's willing to give everyone a chance, but has a very dark past, and most likely a dark future. The dialogue for every character is usually really well written and is light-hearted at times, and dead-serious at other times. There's a secret where you find a Dead Body and you have to learn about the Dead Body's past, pretty grim stuff.
Interactivity -- To interact with this world's characters, you must send out two of your fairies; Cilia and Dora. Black and White. Moon and Sun. Negative and Positive. So you're limited between being Negative and Positive with your response, very black and white. There's no middle line, no silver lining, no inbetween that you can pick. Instead the characters of the world which you interact with are the Grey between these two choices. There's no perfect person in the world of Knytt Underground, they are realistic with the fact that they have problems and personality traits unique to them. So it's up to you to decide how to deal with them. Your choice will affect other outcomes and Cilia and Dora themselves. Pick Dora too much and Cilia will feel like she's a third-wheel. Pick Cilia too much, and Dora won't think that you're too good of a person. Not even Cilia and Dora are perfect at what they represent, Dora can be mean, while Cilia can sometimes be nice. Very realistic and solid.
Sound Design and Design in general -- I'll start off with Design in general. There's no Main Menu, instead you play through the menu and enter different path ways, it can take up a little too much time, but it's very pretty to look at and is always a good way to prepare you for your saved game. Sound Design is brilliant! It's super crisp quality that's authentc from the sounds of waterfalls, to mechanical robots, to the sounds of magical chimes.
Story -- I won't give away any spoilers, but you're an Explorer called Mi Sprocket of the Sprocket Family. You have been chosen to save the world by serving a Religion called Myriadism, where they believe in a God and have no respect for technology that was left over by Humans. Also forgot to mention that it's set after Humanity has killed itself, so the surface is a no-go, thus Knytt UNDERGROUND. Then there's the Internet, where they believe that the Human's technology is God-Like in design and activation, they value technology, but don't care too much about life of others. The Story is often interrupted and recapped to you by Nicklas, the developer and creator of the Knytt Series where he breaks the fourth-wall quite often. He's a really chill and cool guy in real life, and his personality and wall-breaking comments don't ruin the flow of the game.
Music -- The Musical Musicsky Musics of Knytt Underground are really relaxed and really fit well. There's a few songs which I dislike, but they did fit their environment. Some of the secret musical pieces are pretty repetitive since in their context they were just 10-second loops and entirely optional and don't impact the game in any big way.
Difficulty -- Chapter's 1 and 2 are very easy as they're tutorials. But some of the puzzles and platforming in Chapter 3 are really frocking tough, and sometimes will take at least an hour to nail down. But being such a large world, you can usually always skip through the platforming and puzzles via a secret path or completing certain quests.
Replayability -- I've never really heard of a replayable 2D Platformer before, except for maybe Mario Maker, but that's not really a game. But I've replayed Knytt Underground a few times now. A typical playthrough, focusing just on story takes roughly 5 hours. Filling up the map of each chapter, roughly 15 hours. 100 percenting that playthrough takes around 50 hours.
Modability and Community -- Since Knytt Underground is such an underrated and hidden gem in Steam, the community is small and inactive, likewise is the modding community. Infact, there's little to no mods, nothing major at least.

The stories were so spread out and so jumbled over the many hours of play, it was difficult to necessarily remember characters from time to time as they came up.  Even with the three protagonists, this was a problem, as I couldn't always recall what details were true of which one.
The second thing that didn't work out was the warp zones.  The entries to them were so spread out, and the exits not marked on the map at all.  So it always seemed better not to use them and walk straight to where I was going, rather than possibly walk the same distance and break a crystal.
What is great is the feeling that you are exploring a real space.  This isn't an over map and castles, everywhere is connected to everywhere else, there are no barriers.
There are also some quite surprisingly beautiful set pieces, with music that wonderfully accompanies them.
And as in Knytt, the pitter patter of the running and jumping is very satisfying.
Finally, I have not idea why this game is M-rated.  Because one of the characters is a lesbian?  I find making a game M-rated simply because lesbians exist extremely offensive.

I went in expecting a few hours of just another neat-looking puzzle platformer and wound up starting one of the most memorable video game journeys I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing.
You mostly have complete freedom in Knytt Underground's world, comprised of about 50 x 30 rooms, and you can tell the developer put a lot of passion into every single one of them. While the main storyline may not be exactly brilliant, I found myself so fascinated with the world, the characters and the puzzles that I kept wanting to return, eager to see where my next adventure would take me.
This is much more of an exploration game than a puzzle one: it is not the destination that matters here but the journey itself, and there are dozens and dozens of secrets scattered around just waiting to be found, the characters are also surprisingly fun and well-written, and some puzzles very cleverly crafted.
My only complaint is that due to its open-worldy nature and the sometimes overwhelming freedom that you're given, the pacing will often feel a bit off.

Moonshot has that "retro hotseat" feel in spades. Do you remember when you and your buddies would crowd around the computer for some quick arcade battle action? This brings you right back to that feeling.
It's kind of a Asteroids meets Scorched Earth, with some clever arenas (solar systems, complete with gravity) to mix it up. It's not turn-based; it's decidely real-time arcade. The game is about shooting, thrusting, and dodging, while hopefully using gravity in your favor. There aren't weapon shops that provide a dizzying array of arms, but there are occasional powerups that appear for an enterprising explorer. Just be carefuly while going after those powerups that you don't get sucked into the sun! (Though I have to say is a pretty awesome effect when it does happen.)
This game has some amazing moments. The first time you shoot an incoming rocket out of the sky, you will cheer. Nailing an unprotected astronaut flying through space after his tank gets blown up is beyond fulfilling. And forcing an enemy into the sun made me cackle with glee.
There are multiple modes: deathmatch (timed), team deathmatch (timed), and last player standing. Beyond that, the mechanic is the same. From that sense, the game is spartan. But if the multiplayer battle aspect (with real people or with bots) is what you enjoy, you will love this game.
(This review was written against the Early Access version.)

If you want to rush through the game, not care much about the main story, "lorestones" that narrates Nordic stories, you can finish it in 10 hours. If you take some time to cover the above, it increases up to 12-13 hours worth of gameplay.
About the surviving part, the game has permadeath system if your character died too many times. Each time she dies, a "rot" spreads in her arm, starting from the wrist. If the rot climbs up till her head, her journey ends, and so does your progress. All progress is lost and you have to start over.
I personally think this system is good, as it makes you more aware of the enemies surrounding you during a fight and you make every guy count. Please play the game with headphones, they will help A LOT!

The 9 hours long story is strong, it certainly made me think about the morality of manipulating memories if this technology existed in real life. Before you look at my rating and go "hurr durr hello games are liars hurr durr". I would like to point out what I find good about this game, and also what can still be done to make it better.
With the new updates adding home bases, vehicles and freighters, the player's possibilities have ben drastically expanded. Now, this does not imply that the current content is sufficent, both in regards to this being an AAA game, and also because it is sold as a full game which it in no way is. Luckily we are seeing a development model similar to what Mojang are doing with Minecraft, meaning continuous free updates bringing more content to the game, keeping it fresh.
Now, what can be done to make this game better? First off, I want to point out a major bug that has rendered me unable to play the game properly. It has to do with teleportation from space stations, back to your home base. Personally, I would advise you to not buy the game until this is adressed, unless you want to make new bases whenever you travel to a new star system.
Another quirk has to do with the space battles. Sometimes when you enter a new star system, you can encounter a space battle where pirates are attacking a freighter. You can either side with the pirates and attach the freigher stealing their cargo, or you could help out the freighter and receive a reward from its captain. If you decide to side with the freighter, a single stray shot, hitting it or any of its allies, will turn it hostile, even though you are in the process of killing the pirates. Kind of like accidentally killing a chicken in Skyrim while saving the entire village from a dragon. A solution to this problem could be to turn the freighter and its allies invulnerable whenever you decide to side with them.
My final opinion of this game is, despite it's bugs and broken promises, positive. With their new development model adding fresh new content, I am sure this can turn into something great. I would, however, advise you to wait until some of the major bugs (like the teleportation one) are fixed before buying it, unless you want to end up as frustrated as I am.

In the midts of all the negativity of this game, I had decided to take a diffrent approach than everyone else.
The biggest problem people have with this game is not the game itself per say, its the developers. They hold them responsible for the promises they made and never delivered on. But lets take a step back fpr a moment.
When I first bought this game, I had herd NOTHING about it execpt what I saw Markiplier and Jacksepticeye play on it. Yes, the $60 price tag was steep for me, but that was the price of nearly every big name game at the time, so I held it at the same level as the other games.
When I first started playing, I was enthralled. I was loving the whole concept of the game. The multiple lange system that you had to learn each and every word for, the barter system, the space combat (albeit kind of lacking in enemy diversity),  and the ever changing planet terrain and weather.
After about 35 hours (Which is longer than the ENTIRE GAMEPLAY of MOST games coming out on the market today), I started to feel a sense of repetitiveness. So I looked up reviews on the game, and thats when I got swept away in the torrent of negativity. I critasized every little flaw could find and beratted the game because it was not what it was supposed to be.
But now, I have taken a step back and I realized something. I bought a game. I payed this price for something that came from someones mind. An Idea that sprang up and was turned into digital data. I have attempted to make games before before, and let me tell you, the complicated algoritms to even make 10% of a game like this function correctly is a level that I will never understand. Its a game, and for all its negativity, its well made. I found very little glitches. Its a fully explorable, 100% Free Roam environment space exploration game. Which is actually pretty cool. Its fully 3D, and in VR, this would really be something special, and its GIGIANTIC. It took me 41 hours to explore 3 galaxies. and only FULLY explore 1 of those. And that alone, is worthy of my time. Sure, a lot of the Textures are a little blocky and flat, but no game is perfect. and maybe thats just the idea behind it.
I can argue all day with people about this, but this is my review. I give this game a positive rating because its a Well Put Together idea. I have no play issues. Everything flows smoothly. The game holds my attention and for all its bad hype, its a GAME. I have seen people pay a LOT more for a LOT less. I have seen people pay $70 for games full of bugs and compleatly incomplete. So I say, play it with an open mind and be honest to yourself. Its a game. I dont care what the developer diod or said. what I care about is the GAME and thats what I am reviewing. Plus, at least the developers are taking the critasism to heart and trying to make the game better. The newest release added a lot of new things to the game, so I say check it out if you want to. Anyway, thats just my opinion. take it as you will.

Hello Games, with the release of
, you have vandalized countless hours of patient discovery, rendered thousands of units of stored products obsolete, damaged my base, ravaged my home planet, and killed my dog.*
But, before I go all John Wick on you, I suppose I can put in a few hours of play to see if this new version of No Man's Sky has anything to recommend it --- at least I will after you stop patching it so that I can update my mods properly....
I'm still wrestling with the mods, but never mind, I'll play unmodded for a while.
I didn't start over from scratch, but I did play through the official
quest line.  It's not bad.  Without spoiling it, I can say you will learn a lot about the back story of the three sapient lifeforms, and your own story as well.  It will also introduce the new mission system and some new factions.
As I mentioned in my opening rant, the new update resets a lot of what came before.  The planet generator has been revamped, and in the process all previous planets were regenerated.  That beautiful, lush paradise that was your favorite hang-out?  Gone -- replaced by a newly generated world.  It might still be nice, or it might be a wasteland.  That is particularly annoying on the world where you have your base.  And, if you built parts of your base outside the defined boundary, those parts will be gone, too.
The worlds you discovered and named still exist -- sort of.  You discovered them, they're in your list, and yet you must re-discover them again.  When you scan for creatures, the old ones you found before are still listed, but they are around anymore, and there are new ones.  It's really odd.
I'm not sure why the discovered worlds couldn't have been preserved.  Resetting them has no impact on new players, but it's upsetting to the veterans who've spent the most time playing, and the most time supporting this game.  It seems short-sighted.
I was so depressed about the changes to my home planet that I decided to move away.  Far, far away.  After completing the
quest, I traveled all the way out to the 10th galaxy, which is named
.  The
reports that it seems to have a larger number of lush planets that other galaxies, which I thought sounded nice.  I found a pretty place to build a new base, and I'm settling in quite well.
By the way, the games still breaks all your stuff when you jump to a new galaxy.  I don't put up with that crap.  I just open the save game file, search for
, and replace it with
.  Problem solved.
The new planet generator supposedly produces more rational planets.  I don't know about that, they seem pretty much like the old planets.  There are some nice new things:
- These have some very different types of things in place of the more conventional flora and fauna, such as shards of metal, bubbles, glowing cones, and weird cog-like things.  It's pretty cool.
- There are crashed freighters on some planets, which you might be able to loot.  It will at least make for some dramatic screen shots.
- Speaking of freighters, you can now use your freighter to jump between systems with you and your ships inside.  If you are playing without mods, the freighter, when maxed out, is capable of jumps that are about 20% farther than your ship.  To actually jump, go to the place where your freighter's captain stands, and approach the glowing spherical map thing.
- On of the better new things, these are extra inventory pages in your exosuit, starship, and freighter.  All three gain an extra page for "Technology", where you can install technology upgrades without consuming general inventory slots.  It sounds great -- but there's a big catch.
Certain technology items are "core" units, which can't be dismantled or moved (at least not without mods).  Those units must remain on the General inventory page.  Since you need to add technology upgrades in slots adjacent to their main unit to get the synergy bonuses, all of those upgrades will have to stay on the General page too.  Also, you will want to keep rechargeable technology on the General page, because it's much faster to open that page for a refill.  All of that leaves a limited range of technologies that you will want to place on the Technology page.  It's not useless, by any means, but it's a lot less helpful than it could have been.
Your exosuit also gets a third inventory page, named "Cargo".  This is the most useful one.  The slots have a high capacity, like your ship slots, for substances or products.  Once you have built up a supply of stuff, you can operate independently of the resources in your ship.  Technology can be recharged, and products and base elements can be crafted directly out of the Cargo inventory.
However, moving inventory between the General and Cargo pages in your exosuit is absurdly clumsy.  There should be a simple left-and-right layout like when you are swapping ships -- but no, you must laboriously move each item by switching from page to page.  Worse yet, there appears to be no way to access the Cargo inventory while trading goods.  Really?
- You still have the old main missions, like "Atlas Path", but now you can have a  whole list of secondary missions.  This includes familiar ones like the base technician missions, but also faction-based missions for the three sapient lifeforms and the new Guild factions:  Merchants, Mercenaries, and Explorers.
- You still have your basic standing with the three sapient lifeforms, but there are now multiple factors that contribute to that standing, and new standing ratings for the new Guild factions.
- I never understood all the hype about the portals before, but anyway, they are now a thing that work, if you know the glyphs.  There is some major lore around portals.
- Interesting idea, but it's a crude first attempt.  This needs a lot of work by the developers to become useful.
- Finally!  A built in guide to how stuff works in the game.  The original game was needlessly obscure and confusing.  The new guide finally explains things you should know, given that you are out in the universe, flying around in starship and so forth.  Why were you so ignorant of everything before anyway?
- I haven't seen this.  Going by the samples, it looks a bit silly, but it does mean that there is now infrastructure in place to begin supporting multi-player.  I'm not sure if folks really understand how challenging real-time multi-player interaction is.  It requires a big investment in hardware and software infrastructure to connect, move, and coordinate the required data.  Multi-player was the big promise that was broken by the developers, of course, so I guess they feel compelled to make it happen.  Personally, I don't care all that much.
I was really disappointed that things that I had built got trashed.  From here on I will assume that it will happen again, and act accordingly.  But with a nice new storyline, new stuff to do, weird new planets to visit, and all the old features still there, I will definitely enjoy the game more.
For new buyers, it's still overpriced.  With the current feature set, I'd call it about a $35 (USD) value, maybe $40 max.  Adding some actual player interaction would change that quite a bit.

Awesome party game!  Trash talk your friends as your bullet weaves between asteroids toward them - only to have them reflect your own bullet right back at you at twice the speed!
This game is like a real-time action version of Worms, but with multiple planets, solar flares, killer asteroid belts and bullets that slingshot around planets for crazy trick shots.  Switch on the fly between three tank modes:  Cruise the planet's surface in driving mode while reflecting bullets with your directional shield.  Anchor into siege mode for a heavy bubble shield and fire high velocity shots.  Or take off in flight mode to drop 3-round bomb barrages underneath you, then pick up speed and slam into a grounded target to detonate them or send them hurtling off-planet -- and yes, that is as awesome as it sounds!
This game offers casual, crazy fun.  But at the same time, a skilled player can pull off crazy trick shots, shoot down incoming bullets, reflect bullets straight back to sender, or cause solar flares to wipe out enemies on the opposite side of the star.  So far I've played with three of my nephews, my brother, and my girfriend, and we had blast at all ages and skill levels.

Have you ever dreamed of zooming through space while shooting missiles and lasers at your friends while driving a rocket powered tank? If you answered yes to this question, then this game is for you. If you answered no to this question, then this game is still for you. Moonshot is pure awesomeness and should be picked up by anyone looking for a hysterically awesome time.
Pros:
+ Sound effects and music are great
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Rocket powered tanks
+ Good physics
+ Continuously moving planets and asteroids to navigate
+ Local multiplayer is a lot of fun
+ 4-player controller support
+ 3 different levels of AI difficulty that ensure the right match for every skill level
Negatives:
- Using a controller can a little hard at first but is easy to pick up quickly
Possible Additions:
~ Tank color customization
~ Editing of game mode settings such as round length
~ Online multiplayer could be a good addition
Summary:
Moonshot is an incredibly awesome game that any casual or pro gamer should add to their collection. From the gameplay to the physics that make you feel like you are really in space, this game is done right. Strongly recommend getting Moonshot!

What if the old Scorched Earth tank game was reborn as a fast action physics-y party game?
Moonshot is a non-stop action game about tanks battling it out on small planetoids orbiting the sun. You can start up a match for up to 4 players locally (or AI) in Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch or Last Man Standing modes and let the carnage begin. Each player starts on a different planet and the goal is simply to destroy your opponents, but how you do that is up to you. These tanks have three different modes that you can change on the fly:
Rover mode - this is the default mode when on the surface of a planet. You can drive around the planet freely, fire the cannon, and activate a reflector shield to send those pesky bullets back where they came from.
Flight mode - use the tanks thrusters to take off and transform into flight mode. Fly around freely and carpet bomb your enemies. Get going fast enough and a shield activates that can be used to block bullets, dislodge a target from a planet, or destroy them outright by crashing down on their head. Which is awesome.
Siege mode - activate this mode while on the surface of a planet to hunker down in a defensive bubble and blast away with more powerful shots.
Each mode is a ton of fun and gives you the opportunity to play how you want. At the time of this writing, there are also 2 powerups that can drop from destroyed tanks or planets: Homing missiles and lasers. Homing missiles are currently pretty overpowered, but the laser is fun too.
The game perfectly encapsulates the old adage "easy to learn, hard to master" because it is so easy to pick up and play, but with lots of room for skilled players to shine. I was just having a raucous good couple of hours with my nephews, who were able to pick it up pretty quickly.
Keep in mind, though, this is primarily a party game. Tons of fun with 2 - 4 local players, but not a lot for one. However, the devs are planning to add more of everything in future updates including maps, powerups, a wave-based survival mode, and possibly online multiplayer. Get it now to show your support and let the devs know what you want to see more of.
With that in mind, I heartily recommend Moonshot in it's current state, and it can only get better. It's a must have for any group game night.

Knytt Underground is an atmospheric exploration platformer with a huge world, great soundtrack and fun mechanics. However its story and characters come with some unexpected surprises which you'll probably find off-putting, while late-game can get tedious with lengthy backtracking.
This game has left me with very mixed feelings, but my overall enjoyment still outweighs the frustrations and disappointments. For the measely $5 there's plenty of quality content even if you ignore the main story.

Barring the fact that this game cemented the style that Nifflas apparently refuses to stop using, I was pretty enamored with Knytt Underground. With past experience playing both Knytt and NightSky, you could be forgiven for saying that KU is something of a midway point between the two, with the sprite design of the former and background and atmosphere of the latter.
The controls take a bit of getting used to, but are eventually smooth and fluid and make for a lot of moments that make the player feel like a badass. There is a bit of flab in the plot, and I eventually defaulted to skipping the majority of the dialogue, but there's something innately satisfying about exploring, pulling off jumping puzzles, and finding all the little nooks and crannies in the map that would otherwise go unexplored. The tone isn't too light-hearted but also(thankfully) doesn't feel the need to take itself seriously, and the background design has this amazing, almost Pikmin-esque quality to it that looks incredible.
EDIT: I wrote this review right as I was beginning to explore the full map that's revealed to the player a fair bit into the game. I will say that the map is kind of ridiculously huge, and the fetchquests get way, way too numerous to care about or keep track of. Also, something I failed to mention in the beginning is that the sprites look pretty odd, and it doesn't seem to be a stylistic choice. In-game character sprites all have this very weird look to them that makes it hard to take any serious moments seriously.
HOWEVER. Everything I already said still stays true. Satisfying mechanics, beautiful backgrounds and atmosphere. Buy it anyway despite its occasional flabbiness.

+ Beautiful atmospherical graphics. Just look at those screenshots.
+ Nice music as well. No wait, the music is awesome, and so is the sound design.
+ Very simple but fun, tight mechanics.
~ Don't expect any kind of deep emotional storyline. It's cute and funny at times and there is some (actually quite some) intruiging lore to try to make sense of, but the way it's conveyed didn't work quite enough for me, personally. I would have loved a bit more of immersive style of writing, the wit of the dialogues pull me out of it too much. Or rather they fail to draw me in.
- Unfortunately the fixed resolution is kinda low, especially on a 27" monitor. I have played this before on the PS Vita (one of my favorite games on that platform) and there it looks pretty clean and sharp. Not as much now, although it's still pretty enough to get fully immersed in. So arguably the PC is not the best way to play this game, maybe. Maybe.
Having said that I would nevertheless heartily recommend this game for anyone fond of 2D platforming world exploration kind of games. It's very satisfting discovering new areas while jumping around like the most agile spelunker in history. Get this game, especially when it's on sale.!

When you do get to the end, you're probably going to want to come back to the beginning - or at least the beginning of third chapter. Knytt Underground is a more conspicuously narrative-driven sequel to Knytt Stories and Within A Deep Forest, and puts the platforming mechanics of each (climbing and bouncing, respectively) to good use. Those two mechanics are most of what you'll be doing in this game - besides gawking, since the art and soundtrack are absolutely lovely - and honestly it's a lot of fun just to get around. The game world's vast, once you get into it, and if you want to take it all in, you can easily spend upwards of twenty hours just exploring its labyrinthine and visually stunning caves, tunnels, and underwater labs. It's paced a bit slow for a metroidvania adventure - Knytt Underground is about exploration, with very few enemies and a lot of map. But it's the world design, not the enemies, that make this game what it is, and the environments will make you work out how to get from A to B in some very clever ways. There are caverns and side challenges that require you to string together perfectly timed mid-air button presses, secret rooms (over 500 of them in addition to the 1,440 that appear on the map) and a huge variety to the places you'll visit that makes discovering a new area feel exciting. What a game! Knytt Underground brings together the knuckle-biting platforming challenges with an endearing and memorable landscape, introspective dialogue, really genuinely fantastic sound design, and over three and a half hours of gorgeous background music. Don't miss the music, it's really great.

Knytt Underground absorbs you into a beautiful world. The music is atmospheric and changes according to your location. There's striking and interesting scenery wherever you go, and the intricate maze of platforming puzzles fits naturally in these mysterious and serene environments.

exploration puzzle platformer with only a nod to story.
I'd recommend a gamepad. Some parts expect quick reactions and precise timing where activating abilities mid-air is vital. There are a few puzzles involving the somewhat erratic bouncing physics which are frustrating, but when your character dies, you just restart at the last safe spot you were standing, so there's not much tedious repetition.

Now that Robo-Fortune is up and game is starting to get finished for real, might as well throw a review. Cautious not-recommend. The online of this game is pretty much dead in Europe, so you need friends of your own to have fun with this game. As for gameplay, it has its problems. All characters have unique movesets and really creative animation to it (which was what got me interested in the game in the first place since I'm animator myself) but the core meta of the game itself is rather lacking.
The main problem is the length of combos. 10 second combos are a norm in the game, even when you know what to do and can break away from one without getting baited into yet another one. 50% of the time you spend in this game is waiting for another persons combo to end, then you doing your own combos. The back & forth is almost nonexistant even in higher level play. The player engagement isnt there because the game takes away the controller from your hand for lengthy periods of time. It is truly a sad state of affairs when other highly competitive genres like MOBAs have faster games than Skullgirls, or at least games that FEEL faster because you cant go and get a beer from your fridge while youre playing them. It shouldnt be this way. I shouldnt be able to feel the game is more fastpaced with games like SMITE, or RTSses. Those games shouldnt have more player involvement than a traditional fighting game.
Combos become double the problem when lot of the cool character mechanics get completely ignored in the meta. Why bother doing mindgames and zoning with Sguigly and her cool stances when you can just do the same 15-20 second combos like everyone else? Why bother using the crowd-raising mechanics of Beowulf and do some fun custom wrestling throws when you can just do combos that are way less risky to do and yield more results?
Compare to other fighters like Killer Instinct which is all about combos, combo length there is 5-6 seconds at most. Or Guilty Gear where devastating combos are also a reality but only take 3-5 seconds of real-time at most. The problem isnt the fact theres combos in the game, but the fact they take way too long. Getting wrecked by a combo is fine, but it shouldnt take so long as for the receiving player having enough time to start thinking about things other than the game itself. Either making the combos do way more damage, just making matches shorter, or otherwise promoting more back & forth/risk-reward gameplay would fix the issue.
Alas the community of the game does not want it to be fixed, and want this game to remain a long-combo galore where versus matches turn into turn-based single-player modes where the referee takes the controller away from one player at a time for lengthy periods. That is why you wont find any newer players or intermediates online, you have to rely on your friends also liking the game and playing with you. I used to have one, until he got fed up by the combo lengths as well. Theres random spikes whenever a new character is up or free weekends are a thing but otherwise the pool of players remains the 100-200 or so players for the reasons stated above. The game didnt even get a place in EVO this year which is extremely sad.
Skullgirls is a game you really wish would be better. The animation and visual aspect is great, theres some real good ideas thrown in there especially in the ways some of the characters play, but the core gameplay itself is deeply flawed, goes against the "easy to learn-hard to master"-rule that makes so many other fighters good, and ultimately is a barren desert where you will face only those same 100-200 or so die-hard proplayers who still keep playing this. If you like doing lengthy combos, this game is for you. If you want an exciting, fast-paced fighter you can easily train your friends to play with? Avoid this one.
Heres hoping theres going to be Skullgirls 2, and its going to be more like Guilty Gear or Vampire Savior in gameplay, and less like a long combo bore-fest "fighter" where you can read a book on your lap while playing.

A very positive experience. Remember Me is a French sci-fi action adventure set in "Neo-Paris." Europe has descended into a corporate future where human memories are a commodity. There is no fascist regime but the people have become memory consumers out of choice. In one street scene there is a man buying a memory of a first kiss and many others want painful memories removed from their minds altogether.
The lead, Nilin, is a strong character who overcomes doubts and anxieties to accomplish something larger than herself. She is capable but not a demigod and is not sexualized in any way. She has an unique skill of re-writing people's memories so their personalities and goals change. The process is, of course, incredibly immoral and Nilin is painfully aware of this.
While the setting and other characters besides Nilin are what makes Remember Me so special, the gameplay is good too. There is practically no exploration involved but the platforming looks and plays great. Close combat follows the general Arkham Asylum - pattern as practically all post - Arkham games tend to do, but it is entertaining with some original twists. Graphics and sounds are stylish, with a cool temperature.
I was surprised and disappointed at the lukewarm reception Remember Me recieved, but I enjoyed the 10-hour adventure very much, and would definitely try any DLCs or sequels.

Knytt Underground is, by and large, one of the best 2D platformers available on the PC.
The game has beautiful environments, an excellent soundtrack and level ambience that can put sites like
to shame. Simply put, it's therapeutic to the nth degree. The platforming is simply top notch with (

miss secrets on your first playthrough, guaranteed.
However, KU is not without its faults. One
con - no native controller support. It's very easy to work around this, (try
for Windows,
for OSX, or
for Linux) but you'd think for a PC platformer it would come with partial support at the very least. There is also a surprising amount of dialogue for such a game, but you're really not missing much if you skip through all of it. If you're capable of reading a minimap, you can skip through all the dialogue you want.

Moonshot is a game about being in a tank on a small planet whilst shooting at other tanks who are in the same position on different planets. It brings for an amazing amount of local multiplayer fun or fun against the bots. The main objective is to get the most points through gaining the most kills, vehicle destroys or lasting the longest depending on game modes.
Positives:
+ Audio and Graphics are really good
+ Local multiplayer is a lot of fun
+ Controller support
+ AI's are real fun to play against too
Negatives:
- Not much content yet
- Online multiplayer would’ve been a great addition
- Lack of customisation (i.e changing color, tank)
- Lack of game mode settings (Cannot change round length for example)
If you love small party games or games where you  get to play locally against friends this is the game for you. I really enjoyed playing the game although it lacked much content and without no real life friends  it limited my experience and time playing the game a lot. I did eventually manage to get a few friends over to play the game and it was a blast.
I would love to see customisation added and much more content and then the game will be a real solid title. Again it’s only in early access so this is expected.
I would definitely recommend a purchase.

Decided to play the game with  my character, spawned into the Vault, and grew up.  I watched the place fall apart, fled, and found myself in a vast wasteland. Tried to take a gun that was laying around, not realizing that "red" meant "stealing."  The junkie started punching me, but she was so weak that I was able to shoot her to death with her own gun before she killed me.  Decided then that I was not a good person, killed and stole anything and everything in the wasteland...  until the slavers.  I found honest to god human slavery in the wasteland, was offered caps by the slavers to track down runaway slaves because of my hardass reputation.  I heard the slaves, humans in cages, pleading. It sunk in.   It took nearly every chemical and every bullet I had on me, but I killed every slaver in that settlement and freed every slave that wasn't too scared to run once the shackles were loosed.  Discovering you're willing to shoot/beat a junkie to death to survive is not a quest, nor is destroying a hub of human slavery, but when you wander around the wasteland, you find our own quests woven between the person you were and the person you are becoming.

[SINGLEPLAYER REVIEW]

Call of Duty 4 was a turning point for shooters, and to some fans, the last 'true' Call of Duty game. Gone were the days of gunning down Wehrmacht soldiers and in came the faceless terrorists and faceless russian wannabes. But this wasn't all bad. On the contrary, Call of Duty 4 innovated a lot by having its campaign take place in a contemporary setting. What now seems overdone and saturated felt hugely creative back in 2007. The presentation of the game is indisputably fantastic throughout every level. The graphics hold up to this day and the soundtrack was fitting if not memorable. The game now included setpieces, cutscene-like pauses for story-telling or scripted events to take place, which helped to break the pace of the loud and bombastic firefights with exceptional voice acting and mostly 'alright' writing. The campaign also never drags on, which helps to keep the game feeling fresh.
In the game, you play as an American marine and a British SAS operative, the perspective shifting every couple of levels. The arsenal of the game is broad but doesn't quite feel as unique (aside from an aesthetical point of view) as it possibly should have felt thanks to average sound design for the weapons.  Nevertheless, the gunplay is extremely responsive, sharp and more often than not, satisfying. All levels feel special, and yet they don't feel disconnected. The game has a few of the best Call of Duty missions ever, including the AC-130 gunship bombing, the Pripyat exclusion zone assassination, and more. My biggest complaint comes with the enemies that seem to be spammed across some sections of the levels to create an illusion of difficulty, all that does is hurt the pacing of the game with frequent cover-taking to replenish lost health due to the relentless waves of thrown grenades and assault rifle fire.
A great game back in the day, still a game worth playing nowadays, if not for the story, for the innovations in the gaming medium as well as for its cinematic and frenetic gunplay and pulsating action setpieces.

If you like thought-provoking science-fiction this game is for you. With a great story and breathtaking world design – Neo-Paris looks spectacular! – Remember Me is a very memorable experience. Especially because of the four memory remix sequences scattered throughout the game, where you must change the memories of certain people in the story. While four does not sound much, the sequences gives one very much food for thought – I think even more so because of this low number.
This memorable experience is coupled with an interesting combat mechanic, somewhat reminiscent of Arkham Asylum/City, where you can and in some situations must mix the effects of your combos in mid-combat. Furthermore, Remember Me has an atypical and very striking musical score, which supports the game’s themes very well.
The only thing somewhat lacking in this game is its very limited platform sections, due to its level design, which almost entirely does not give any room for any exploration deviating from the main path. However, this problem with the weak platforming sections is somewhat alleviated by the beautiful and atmospheric world design, and the combat sections throughout the game.
If you want to support an original IP, with a great and thought provoking sci-fi story, excellent world design, outstanding musical score and superb gameplay (thanks to its combat and memory remix sequences) only marred by a weak platforming mechanic, then Remember Me is for you.
Info: I played Remember Me with a controller, with French audio/English subtitles language settings, and on the highest difficulty.

Anything you could find to nit-pick about a game, I love in Remember Me!
That being said, it's really hard for me to nit-pick at anything. Sure, the linearity of the game can be scrutinized but that's only because this world is so gorgeous and inviting that I want to explore more! Or perhaps the repetitive combat? The combo lab can add so much more! Everything about this game screams that it needs a sequel. The chance to give you everything missing from this game. And that's what the reviews of this game gripe on, everything that's missing, instead of enjoying everything that's already in it and what it offers.
That's the sad part. The mass of gamers will probably glance over this game based on it's review ratings. I encourage you to look past the ratings and to buy this game. It will introduce you to a world that you want to see more of and that you want to explore more in. Hopefully the success will warrant a sequel and we all can continue to enjoy this creative, original game.
Remember you soon.
