One of the best art direction I've seen in a video game. When I say art direction, I include graphics, sound and writing.
- graphics: Neo Paris is stunning. Backgrounds are full of details. Architectural styles merge in both an organic and a fantastic way. Character models are not the main appeal of the game, but they're at least original.
- sound: Music always feel adequate, and enhance the experience. It seems more like sound design than melody : it reacts to what your character is doing, action has its own music. Besides, environmental sounds are well thought and full of details (ie. you hear flies buzzing around)
- writing: The world is coherent and overall well thought despite the quite unoriginal evil megacorp. Characters are well documented, they have their own agenda and believable motivations. As for the story elements, well, they managed to avoid many clichés. The plot isn't needlessly ambitious and ties the fate of the main character to the overall plot. It ends up more as a personnal journey than anything else and somehow managed to move me at times.
As for Gameplay, well, it sure could be better, but it has many merits. The game tries to be many things: an innovative beat'em up, a beautiful exploration game and a classical adventure one. Despite some new and original ideas, Remember Me never excel in any of this style of gameplay. But the whole is better than the sum of its parts. In conclusion, I'd recommend this game either to aesthetes looking for an original setting or to open-minded gamers looking for a fresh twist in a classical gameplay.

Also being able to heal from landing a combo is great - even if a fight is going badly, you are never completey out because you can be careful and land some healing combos to make a comeback.
The setting is captivating and the voice acting and characterisation are good. I really identified with Nilin and I liked the moral uncertainties the game presents to you. Also, having been to Paris, it was fun seeing places I recognised transformed into a cyberpunk future. This game is very evocative and if the premise sounds interesting to you, you should definitely try it out!

"Remember Me" exemplifies everything I love about video games. The depth of the storyline pulls you in, makes you care about the world and the characters, and leaves you determined to change what has gone awry. I even got a lil emotional at certain points of the game... T.T
And like, the gameplay... got awesome all over my face.
The ability to craft combos was neato, and the fluidity of the fighting mechanics was really enjoyable. The jumping around/traversing heights was a nice touch. Even with the indicators lighting your way, there was still a need to find a safe path inherent. The creators even threw in a few riddles to solve.
*GASP* The game actually makes you think? The horror.
Which brings me to the memory remixing... super fun! Some of the remixes weren't really easy to determine a progression of events that would shape the desired outcome. This led to a fumbly bit of trial and error that, initially, left a bad taste in my mouth. However, as the game moved on, the memories you resculpted offered a series of choices that began to highlight a specific pattern to uncover.
Yes, more thinking. D:
Also, the game is realllllly pretty.
This game has everything. I will be replaying it veryveryvery soon. <3

This is a really fun installment in the Wolfenstein franchise. While The New Order may be the overall more solid and polished (while admittedly safer) title, the highs of New Colossus far exceed those of New Order.
Pros:
- Looks brillaint. Graphics are top notch, a huge improvement over TNO.
- Enemies come apart brutally when shot and during stealth takedowns.
- Guns are meaty as hell, every bullet has alot of punch behind it.
- Characters are very well written and acted, making each one feel real, and adding stakes to events throughout the campaign.
- We get to know BJ alot more in this game, and come to understand why he is the way he is.
- More player choice which adds further replayability.
Cons:
- Dual weilding is needlessly fiddly this time around.
- You die incredibly quckly, we're talking going from full health to dead within a couple seconds of fire from a grunt... Many times I've died and had no idea what killed me. I'm fine with difficult games, but this at times just felt cheap.
- Laserkraftwerk feels less unique in this game. Its now just rail gun, as opposed to the multi-use tool in TNO allowing you to modify specific areas of cover to an extent.
Overall, recommended.

Overall, I ♥♥♥♥ing loved this game. The gameplay is the equivalent of a summer blockbuster - it's heart-pounding, head-banging,♥♥♥♥♥kicking action, again and again, through every level. Unlike last year's DOOM, a shooter with a similar focus on being as badass as possible, the gameplay never gets boring. In addition to the adrenaline-pumping action sequences, you've got a wonderfully well-implemented stealth mechanic: in certain areas, a Nazi general will raise the alarm if you're detected, and reinforcements will keep coming. So either sneak through the area and silently assassinate the general, or sprint in with shotguns in both hands and eviscerate him before he can say "Mein leben!"
The story is an absolute show-stopper. You'd expect it to be a goofy pretense for balls-to-the-wall macho action, but it's not. It's a haunting story of people trying to eke out a living in a seemingly never-ending rebellion against the Nazi war machine. Even when you're kicking Nazi♥♥♥♥♥left and right, the protagonist comes across as sympathetic and vulnerable. Every character is so perfectly human, and every line is so wonderfully written, and every moment is perfectly evocative of the emotion it wants you to feel - whether that be joy or (as it often is) sadness.
But here's the rub: remember when I said the gameplay never gets boring? I think the developers were scared of that happening, so when the credits roll after about 8 hours of story missions, I couldn't help but feel a little crestfallen. You could extend the game for yourself by doing a handful of side missions every time you're back at base, but the opportunity for side missions only opens up a few times before the post-game "finish up anything you haven't done yet" section, and the game is very bad at telling you what missions will be quick and what missions will lock you into a few hours of action. It's possible that this just my preference for ultra-long 100-hour RPGs and such, but still, $60 for such a quick game is a little bit much (even if it is polished to hell and back).
Also, the story ends on a "to be continued!" note, and it feels a little bit like the next few episodes of the Wolfenstein story rather than a full-on sequel. I hope we see things like DLC or expansion packs on this engine that support cheaper continuations of the story, but that's not gonna happen, and that's a little disappointing.
Despite this, it's a wonderful game, and well worth your time.

Depth has got to be my favorite recent purchase, and clearly the most enjoyable asymetrical multiplayer game I've ever played. The mechanics will feel familiar to anyone that has played a FPS, while still providing a refreshing new side to the formula that marks the game as a unique experience.
Pros:
-Well balanced asymetrical multiplayer.
-Fast paced combat that puts an emphasis on teamwork, while allowing the remarkable player to shine by himself
-Incredibly atmospheric!
-Fair leveling and progression system that emphasises letting low level players be viable, and introducing them to new equipment early on. Later the in-game rewards that incentivize playing are all skins.
-Absolutely no pay2win, once you've bought the game you've got every advantage a player can have.
-Active development with frequent events that will give you a reason to keep coming back!
-Easy to pick up, fun to play. With friends or just through solo play.
Cons:
-Modest player base that will result in some uneven matchups.
-Relatively small selection of gear or customization. You will have build-options and several viable ways to play, but for this kind of game the selection is "adequate" at best.
-Ties into the above point, but every diver is mechanically the same while every shark starts out with too few evolution points to begin any 'build' at the start of a game.
If you enjoy asymetrical multiplayer games you owe yourself to buy this game. Frequent sales and immense play value sets the game apart with remarkable bang for your buck, and will most likely allow your friends to get a copy during a sale even if they are low on money. Events and content updates makes the game a delight to follow, and there's always enough of a dedicated community to quickly get into games. I could not reccomend this game fondly enough!

This is my first review on steam. I'll try to make it simple.
Knytt Underground is a platformer with puzzle mechanic. Most of the time these puzzles are simple.  switch between 2 forms (human for climbing, and ball for bouncing) and  use "right one-use-power" at the right time to get to hard to reach places.

The thing is some solutions are not so simple and not very obvious on first sight so you might end up trying to go around some areas ... often leaving you in this "what the fudge" state. That made me use a uncovered map i found on google :P.  And made me revisit most of the areas and try to "re-reach" areas if there was some hidden passage. And belive me there are lots of them. But there are also areas only accessible if you uncover lore about characters. Just do every quest you find(or events marked as "?"), so dont get frustrated if you cant reach something now.
First two chapters are more of a tutorial short and simple. Real challange is chapter 3 wich is HUGE, map covers WHOLE SCREEN. played almost 20 hours of it to reach to the end (i started to use uncovered map after having about half of the map reveald and it had lots of uncovered holes).
There is this teleporting mechanic wich lets you teleport across the map but i havent use it ... cause i didnt know how so i ignored it.
In overal the game is challenging. ESPECIALLY if you plan to unlock all steam achevements. so if you are aiming for that i suggest reading steam community walkthroughs cause there is one achevement you get for "not paying bell guards for entrence" wich i did unfortunately.
Other reviews state that dialogues are bad ... well maybe because this world is confusing, maybe that was the aim for the creators to make strange relations between races while engaging in some dificult topics about main characters. Depends on personal tastes . I didnt find them that bad. Some funny more or less. (there is even one adult joke but i wont spoil it :P)
Background pictures are amazing. Music is calm and pleasing. For adventurer LOTS of secrets to uncover.
In overall its a average game, good choice if you have nothing to play, Would be nice addicion for a mobile game.(there would be problem with implementing chapter 3 world map).

What is beauty?
When you boil it down to a core meaning, it’s the subjective interest of a person in a certain style or sense. It’s something that’s different for every person, yet there are certain things which are always considered beautiful.
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of them. No matter how your taste may differ, we all can agree that this is one of the most beautiful games out there. But is aesthetics alone a reason for me to suggest this game? No.
Outside of the artstyle Ori and the Blind Forest offers metrovania 2D plattformer with solid controls, no matter whether you play with controller or keyboard. It plays very smoothly and after a few minutes with a new ability the usage of it becomes natural and integrates into your playstyle. A big gripe, I have with other metrovania like games, is the problem of having too many different abilities with which you hardly interact. Just like any game of that genre Ori starts out easy and slowly becomes something that is quite challenging at the end. Especially the climax which is one of my favorite and hardest platforming experiences to date.
Binding these two together is a soundtrack which just keeps you wanting to play more. While it is a static loop of music for each area, dungeon and boss fight it never conflicts with the situation, no matter how action heavy or relaxed it is. Something that I occasionally bugs me with games like Transistor, Kingdom, Not a Hero or even Undertale, games with amazing soundtracks of their own, but not soundtracks I couldn’t listen to forever while playing. Ori and the Blind Forest’s soundtrack is so well crafted that it just blends into the game so well they just become one. The last game I remember doing this was Super Mario Galaxy.
As for story it is the only aspect of Ori where it doesn’t stand out to me. Maybe because I am very well read and therefore this doesn’t stick out unlike previously mentioned games like Undertale and Transistor, but nonetheless it is a good and solid story which utilize the gamespan of about 5-8ish hours (6 hours in my case at the time of writing) to constantly pushes forward without forcing the player to do something. The story has many fun twists and turns which end up in a beautiful climax. Note how I never say ending but climax and that for the second time in this review. Unlike endings, a climax is the point of most tension in the story and the way Ori and the Blind Forest is written and presented takes the rather normal story and turns it into something fun and engaging.
So overall what is Ori and the Blind Forest?
It’s a game where all individual parts form something bigger than a collective of mechanics and music and art. They become something new and even more fascinating and fun. For that alone I can suggest this game to anyone.

I played with an Xbox One controller and the experience was fantastic. Two thumbs up.

By this point you're perhaps already aware that Trine is a very visually stunning game, with some great artwork & lighting yet behind all of that lies a really challenging and fun platform puzzle game.
The level designs are fairly basic to begin with an help introduce you to the 3 characters and their abilities without over complicating things. You have a Wizard (who can build blocks and platforms), a Thief who can swing and climb and a Warrior who can fight.
You can only use one character at a time, but the game lets you switch between them easily enough so it's not hard to link abilities together. So, for example you could build a platform with the Wizard to setup an easy jump and climb with The Thief. It's that level of combination and thinking that makes Trine a fun game to play. It also helps that the designers have done a good job of scaling the difficulty at just about the right pace to keep the game challenging, but never boring or frustrating.
The native 360 Controller support is a welcome feature too, and makes gameplay slightly more friendly.
Further more the developers have kindly updated Trine with the engine from Trine 2, which is why it's now referred to as the 'Enchanted Edition'. The real bonus here is if you already owned Trine, it was updated free of charge.
The only real negative could be the slightly wonky fighting mechanics, but that's none issue as the game isn't about the fighting or enemies.
In short, Trine is a fun, well presented Platform Puzzle game that offers a good combination of problem solving, exploring and physic manipulation. Well worth a play.

I bought the retail version of the game when it came out, admittedly taken by its visuals and its concept but unsure if it would be worth the money I paid.  I am not too keen on using controllers when I play games so unfortunately I played Remember Me a little bit then shelved it. Recently playing another Capcom game with a similar concept led me to dust Remember Me off and replay it. So here is my belated thoughts of the game:
I'm going to start with its combat because there is so little to be said about it. If you have played games such as the Batman Arkham series and do not mind the combo building style of combat and platforming, then Remember Me will not disappoint you, however if combat like this is not your cup of tea and you are not fan of hanging from high buildings, then you will be very frustrated while playing Remember Me (especially on the hardest difficulty).
On the other hand, if you are not too fussed about the combat and are more interested in a very well told story, amazing art work coming to life with perfectly executed graphical design, as well as interesting characters and enemies, then this is a must-play for you. Not to mention, the soundtrack is quite good and the voice-over acting is flawless. It was also nice to play a female protoganist that was desinged very well with a realistic attitude and body posture, and not running around in bikinis.
The setting is in 2084 Neo-Paris. The details in the environment, characters, and enemies are amazing. I recommend you try and find all the collectibles (as some of them are very well hidden and will take you to every nook and cranny). The audio is flawless, from the music and the enviornmental sound to the voice acting, especially the voice acting which is very professionally done - it definately puts the player in the right mood.
Despite of the unfortunate events the protoganist goes through, her desperation is just, without sounding needy. The rest of the voice acting is also perfect, as it gives you the correct emotions towards the other characters, (such as liking or disliking them, getting annoyed by them or feeling sympathy for them). The physique of the character in my opinion stands out - recently the protogonists in video games have been on the extreme side of appearances (especially females with unrealistic body shapes that in the real world would make it impossible to do the things they do in games). However in this one, the protognist (Nilin) is designed perfectly to play the role of the fast, agile and lean heroine without going over the board and shadowing her feminity.
The most important thing that captured me about this game was the main concept of the game, playing with people's memories. I found it quite unique and I don't think I came across anything like this before in a game. It was very refreshing.
(TL;DR Version) I highly recommend this game to players who are looking for story-rich, beautifully designed game with Batman Arkham series style of gameplay, set in Neo-Paris with a unique concept.

If you liked TNO, you'll probably like this one as well. It's a bit on the short side, but consistently fun from beginning to end. One thing that really sticks out to me is the perk system, which never made me feel like I had to go out of my way to unlock the ones I wanted. If you like to sneak around and go for headshots like me, you'll get perks that make you better at stealth. If you like to dual-wield and run in with guns blazing, you'll get perks to help you with that, too. The switch from static to incremental bonuses is a big part of this, and it feels great.
As far as technical issues are concerned, I didn't run into any aside from not being able to use the Steam overlay, which was annoying but not the end of the world. Not much else to say here. It's a fun game while it lasts, and I'll definitely play through it a second time at some point.

New Colossus is New Order with a lot more cutscenes, a bigger home base, districts you can revisit, side missions, more collectibles and a return of the dual Fergus/Wyatt timeline. Gunplay is awesome, guns all sound amazing, you can update your weapons, dual wield, perk up and so on, same as in New Order. Current technical issues include permanent freezing and occasional screen tearing, though I haven't fiddled much with the options. There are hotfixes and beta patches available for the more curious or unfortunate. I wouldn't rush to spend €60 on this until they've released a patch or two.
I can't fault MachineGames for not making another HL2, but ever since HL2, I want single player FPS games to be more like HL2, especially since Valve no longer makes single player games. Yes, I should get over myself, but I also know what I want. Granted, I don't want all FPS franchises to turn into formulaic open world games like Far Cry, even though I enjoy those games, but I do wish they were more open and would let you experience its story in-game. I don't understand why developers shy away from environmental storytelling. Excessive use of cutscenes is time spent away from actually playing your game. When you take the time to craft a world, let us be in it. I still have hundreds of films I want to see before I die, I don't need that same experience from my games as well.
I would've liked a mission set in a pine forest, where dozens of trees are blown to smithereens, harking back to the nightmares of WW2, or rather, a scene in Band of Brothers. There are open levels in New Colossus with multiple routes just like in New Order, but you spend a surprising amount of time in confined spaces, in giant vehicles both under water, under ground, in the air and two of the locations are used twice, mind you. There's also a level that's a conceptual copy of one in New Order.
When New Order took me roughly 20 hours to complete and 3 hours of that were cutscenes, I'm fine with that, but when 4 hours from a total of 15 hours are cutscenes, that I have a problem with. Some of these cutscenes are quite funny and intense though, both well directed and well acted, but there are also some that could've been cut entirely or written much shorter. The direction of NC is a commitment and they saw it through, but it's easier to cut scenes before you animate and render them than redoing entire areas to fit an in-game approach. What we have here is Doom meets The Man in the High Castle and it's weird when so much game is lost in the process. Thankfully NC's use of cutscenes isn't so intrusive to end up as Max Payne 3, which was an incredibly misguided attempt for a video game. That said, some of them are so long that your display will go to sleep, sometimes twice during the same scene, provided your sleep mode is set to 5 minutes.
New Colossus goes deep into the reasons why BJ became the man he is, but I'm not sure that's the level of depth I'm craving for, especially when there's a tonal shift halfway through the game that mostly abandons the first half for more tongue-in-cheek entertainment. I thought the BJ of New Order was often more morose than Max Payne, which is quite an achievement, so in a way it's good that those reasons are explored here, but tonally it's a mixed bag.
Cutscenes are so intertwined in NC's campaign that I had three occasions where I was thrown into a battle I wasn't ready for and yes, you're not always supposed to be ready, but watching a long cutscene set in a room you haven't had a chance to explore and then being ambushed in that same room isn't my idea of fun. Especially when I have to replay that part 10 times. In that same room I was then being shouted at for not jumping on a helicopter, when I simply wanted to restock and look for the collectibles.
The highlights for me were time spent in different parts of the US before I entered another compound or high security area. The nuclear wastelands or cities in ruins reminded me of the parts that mattered in RAGE, despite being a setting used in so many franchises. New Order had better variety, while New Colossus reuses some old ideas and in some case has you replaying locations. There are many heavy weapons this time, with their respective charging stations, which makes the game feel a bit ridiculous on Bring 'Em On, but will come more in handy in higher difficulty levels. Those weapons slow you down, but they make a quick end of big enemies who wield them. There are more surprises and upgrades, but I'll leave it at that. It's a good addition to the franchise, but after my first playthrough I prefer New Order.

Perhaps the most fun Gauntlet game since Dark Legacy (you remember--the finished version of Legends, which Midway tried to charge people money for despite being unfinished).
The benefits over Dark Legacy: Drop-in, drop-out online play. Each character has a unique playstyle. None of that unprofessional Midway "charm" regarding bugginess, a lack of optimization for the system it was on (how did they get it to lag on a Gamecube?), and their general ambiance of a wannabe-metalhead-roadie's high school dropout career.
Dark Legacy did have a stronger sense of advancement overall. Slayer does improve by streamlining experience and currency into one unit, but DL allows the player to unlock interesting advanced classes to give players a more solid sense of progression. The other downsides to Slayer are the lack of fulfillment at slaying enemies--typically the best this accomplishes for you is unlocking the next room in such a case. There's also very little variability in game areas compared to DL.
Five bucks is kind of a lot just for a new character.
The bottom line though is that none of this is relevant. None of this works. Gauntlet is traditionally a multiplayer game, but if nobody ever plays together, it's worthless. This game can also be completed in four hours. That's more than a dollar per hour.

(NOTE: This game was reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher)
Video Review
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
For $3 it really is fun. Reminds me of Combat for my old Atari 2600. 3/5, controls can be an issue.
The "Meat & Potatoes" Review:
Great throwback! Are there limitations, yes. There are. So, I'll cover those first. Controls are an issue and you will be resetting these between levels IF you do the missions one at a time, during the "Challenge" mode this is not a problem (except setting them initially for each run). The interface is a tad clunky, but you get used to it really quickly. The music is also good, but after hearing the same track between each round it can get hold. This is not a reflection of it's quality at all though, I actually liked it. It simply got repetitive. That is it though, for the limitations. The actual positives in this game were far more numerous than I originally expected. It allows for some nice customization (difficulty, hitbox size, etc) that can increase/decrease difficulty as desired. There are three game modes, one of which allows you to essentially practice on any level you choose. The Online Leaderboards make this one to run and stack High Scores up with your friends. All in all, for $3 this is actually a nice little gem. A great little casual game to pass the time and as you get hooked, there are aspects to keep you playing. Fans of Speed Runs or achieving High Scores are going to want to be all over this one. No achievements or cards, so steer clear if that's all you want. Good fun to be had here on the cheap.
3/5 and would definitely recommend at this price!

Hit Tank PRO reminds of an old game, whose name I can't remember, where you're a tank pitched against others. You have the same core mechanics here. And thanks to Bechstein, I found the name: Battle City.
You're directing a tank through different levels and your goal is to destroy every enemy present. Some of them are stationary and slow to fire, while others are moving and sending many rockets towards you. You get hit? You're trying the level again with all enemies spawning again. Depending on the difficulty, you will have less lives to do.
8 minutes is short to write a review. However, when you've played some levels, you know already how the game will be. The graphics are correct and the soundtrack is just a jingle and tanks sounds.
The game is itself a nice little one when you want to take a little break. However, my main problem is the menu in the Missions mode. Indeed, while it's great to have included the three different types of moving (arrows, WASD and ZQSD), while it's great to choose for each level your difficulty, some options, your speed or the hit box, the problem is that when you're pointing your cursor on the keys options, speed or hitbox, you can change the options you have set. And when you're think that ZQSD is chosen and that in reality, you have the arrows.... I mean, it would be great that at least, the choice of ZQSD, WASD or arrows is on another menu and not on the one where you're setting your preferences for the level. Also, when you finish a level, instead of advancing to the next one, you're sent back to the menu (which is normal if you want to change the difficulty or anything else) and if you don't click yourself on "Next", you're going to play the level you've beaten again.
However, the Mode Pro/Challenge is changing that way: you set your configuration, your number of life (Pro), level and difficulty and you'll be passing from a level to another without being sent to the menu.
Because of the menu in Missions, I'm not quite satisfied - it should have a description of each mode - I would have gone directly to the Mode Pro instead of Missions. Hit Tank PRO is a challenge mode based action strategy game, releasing on December 2nd 2015, by a single developer Bacq Stellan.
Gameplay in Hit Tank PRO is set in a birds eye view of a small simple map, where you are in control of a single tank, and you have to destroy varying numbers of enemy tanks. Each of the maps are set out differently, some come with mazes, some have destructible objects,  whilst others have a fog of war mechanic, leaving you in the lurch as to what you can see.  Whilst the gameplay is very simple, it comes with a very addictive nature to it, and the higher levels can get really fast paced and hectic as the levels progressively get harder and more enemies that you have to deal with. I would really liked to have seen some sort of levelling process for your tank, or some sort of customizability, maybe to upgrade weapons or your armour, but the only sort of customizing you get, is changing the speed of your tank at the start of the game. You can obviously make your tank the fastest, but this will in turn give your score a handicap compared to if you didn’t make your tank faster. There are 60 levels in this game too, so quite a stack of levels to go at.
Graphics are very basic, the top down view helps it a little here, but honestly the graphics are nothing to shout about. I was a little let down by the sprites of the tanks and the overall aesthetic of the game, it would have been nice to get some better looking maps to fight in. The sound effects are OK, however the music is weird…it sounds a bit like Wild West music, but in tanks? I don’t quite know how to explain it, something just didn’t sound right about the music in Hit Tank PRO.
There are a varying amount of difficulties here, there are four difficulty settings, Easy, Normal, Medium (aren’t they the same?) and hard.  Onto of these difficulty settings, you can also make the game harder or easier by changing the bullet speed, your hitbox size, and of course, your tank’s speed. This adds another layer of difficulty settings, allowing you to tweak how hard (or easy) the game is for you.
I have been playing on Normal difficulty for about half an hour now, and I have managed to clear all sixty levels, that to me show that whilst there are a lot of levels, there isn’t anything really challenging unless you ramp up the difficulty settings to a higher level. You could probably get three or four hours of more content out of the game with varying levels of difficulty, but that’s about it.
I sadly had a few annoying technical issues, one is that the game doesn’t use any direct x engine, so I was unable to capture any footage using Fraps. Secondly (and the most annoying) is the game doesn’t lock your cursor in its window, this is only really an issue for anyone with more than one screen – you’ll often find your cursor has wandered across to your other screens, you’ll click and the game minimizes, this is an infuriating bug which almost always results in you dying. The third and probably the biggest big, is a game breaking one unfortunately. Some levels you’ll end up clearing all of the tanks you can see, and the game will insist that there is one tank left alive, when there quite clearly isn’t. This is even more prominent on the levels past stage 50. You can’t even kill yourself by shooting a rocket into yourself, the game just breaks, you actually have to quit the game in order for it to work again, and obviously this loses your scores.
To sum up, I really like the premise behind the gameplay of this game, but sadly in its current state it isn’t going to be recommended. I am not going to lie; I did actually have fun in the game, when it worked. I think the game can improve a lot on the graphical front, and include some customizability in to make completing the levels feel more like an accomplishment. I personally think that this game would really benefit from a local or online multiplayer mode as I can see that being a ton of fun too. Most of all, the bugs and glitches need to be cleaned up ASAP.  The game is priced at £1, 99 when not on sale, and there is also a demo to try out too if you are still interested in trying it out.

I was someone who was only casually interested in 2D fighting games before, but Skullgirls's in-depth tutorials not only acclimate you to the game itself, but fighting games in general. With easy-to-understand lessons about cancelling, executing and defending against mix-ups, as well as specific tutorials for each character in the game, Skullgirls is both an easy game to pick up and play, as well as a well-made gateway into the world of 2D fighters.
As for the merits of the game on its own, Skullgirls boasts a small but extremely varied cast of playable characters, ranging the gamut of every fighting game character archetype. As I delve deeper into fighting games, I come back to Skullgirls and find I understand and appreciate more and more of the special features Skullgirls boasts to improve its experience, learning where other games in the genre have been lacking.
Skullgirls is well worth the price, and I expect to be playing it for years to come.

My original review was positive of the sound, visuals and environments, but very critical of the actual gameplay. Either my own temporary ineptitude as well as a bug prevented me from being able to continue, which made me give this a negative review for the difficulty, as I was unable to proceed without getting stress and frustrated.
So, it turns out the “Auto” difficulty level is not the smartest, and not the best thing to put in a game revolving around story. Combat in games is generally accepted to be consistent in order for players to learn and adapt to. I can understand why the developers did it however, due to the nature of the games overbearing darkness
.
And that’s what this game is all about. It’s a journey into darkness, a story about a Celtic woman going to rescue her lover from the Nordic version of hell. A journey to face her own demons of the mind.
The atmosphere sound effects and music are utterly on point. 10/10.

The voice acting is a mixed bag. The main character is A+, but the “voices” that follow you throughout the game suffer from less appealing voice acting. It’s clear they are there to add to the concept of psychosis and create a further feeling of unease, but it begins to grate on you after a while as their quality is sub-par compared to the rest of the game, and prevent you from hearing other things.
The puzzles are slow, easy, and nothing more than time consuming breaks between the segments of combat. Depending on the type of games you enjoy, this may be considered a welcome break or a dull slow slog through the well-constructed environments.
The combat at first glance is bare bones, but taking the time to look at the key-bindings is definitely a requirement. Once you learn the controls from the menu and put them to test in a few fights combat becomes significantly more fluid and bearable. Even if you still get hit sometimes, even when you evade. I highly suggest switching the combat to medium at the start of the game, rather than Auto, and adjust it accordingly from there.
The plot itself is not terrible, but not amazing. It’s the acting and sheer overwhelming detail of the main character Senua that makes the story exceptional. You’re there with her though every harrowing experience, every high and low. It’s a story of emotion and psychosis, wrapped in Norse mythology. She is the most human character I have seen in any game so far.
This is a game that contains very few mechanics and very little actual gameplay, but I didn’t care, and you shouldn’t either.

Btw, performance tip: if you use the enchanted version with an NVidia GPU, make sure to add the trine1_32bit.exe file to the NVidia control panel under Manage 3D Settings, otherwise even though it uses the same engine as Trine 2, you will get a lot worse performance. The enchanted executable is in a subdirectory of the main Trine game folder. Doing this with the free downloadable nvidiaInspector and adding to the predefined Trine 2 profile is probably the best way to take advantage of the optimizations for the updated engine.

I love this game.  It is the sort of thing that you can play for ten or fifteen minutes and feel like you accomplished something, or intend to play for an hour and find yourself still playing after four.
The ball mechanics are as close to perfect as you can find in a game.  Importantly, there is some ability for course correction mid-air, so you are not bound to just ricocheting around based only on your bounce.  And the transformation mechanic lets you move in ways that neither the sprite nor the ball could alone.
The core of the game is exploration.  Puzzles are usually “how do I get there from here?” and typically aren’t more than four or six rooms.  They are spread about often enough to be interesting, yet sparse enough that at no time does it feel like you just completed a difficult challenge only to be rewarded with a harder one, and in fact almost always do reward you.  The rewards vary from inventory items (which may be quest related) to story exposition, and sometimes earthquakes that open up new paths elsewhere.
Death is mostly non-punishing, typically at most it resets you to the last safe position you were in, which is usually in the room you are currently in.  If you collected an item just before dying, it does not reset the item.  That said, you do have to then make it to a save point to keep the progress after leaving the game.
Mi, the character, is mute.  When you have a conversation with an NPC, you can choose if you want your friends Dora or Cilla to answer for you.  Dora is generally going to give an optimistic or positive answer, while Cilla tends to be cynical if not mean.  But they can and will also surprise you.
While I very much enjoyed this game, the experience was certainly heightened by having played the developer’s previous games, which are not currently available on Steam.  I think it stands alone well, however there are many references to several other games (including ones for both Knytts and the Ball) that were very cool for those in the know.
As much as a third of the game’s rooms are hidden off-map.  Some are short or long challenges or even just “easter eggs” accessible from secret paths accessible from the chapter select area - hidden in secret tunnels.
Also please note the rating!  Cila in particular can be quite vulgar, and both of the fairies have histories that might be surprising and a bit colorful.
I do recomend this game!

An exploration platformer where you can switch between the tight wall-climbing controls of Knytt and the fast bouncy-ball controls of Within a Deep Forest.

The control-switching feature makes for interesting challenges and feels well-suited to smooth, efficient movement when exploring (although you might prefer to slow down and admire the backgrounds). Furthermore, the game is overflowing with secrets, to the point of having secrets nested within secrets.
The game stars a mute sprite named "Mi" and later a pair of fairies that speak for her - your interactions with other NPCs serve to characterize the trio. The game is sometimes silly, but it also sometimes touches on weighty issues. The world's inhabitants, despite being mythical creatures, are relatable and act very human.
An excellent game, well worth your time.

The Knytt franchise at this point has gained a good bit of history.  Underground's predecessors might even be older than some of the folks reading this review.  Fortunately, they are all available on the developer's website, free of charge.  Since 2006, I've played them many times; seriously, they're some of the most charming games out there.  If you're on the fence about this title, look up Nifflas and give Knytt Stories a test drive - you won't regret it.
Knytt Underground is a game of simple two-dimensional platforming and exploration, broken up into three chapters.  The first two chapters are short mini-stories introducing your characters - one, a humanoid who can scramble up walls, and the other, a strange ball with elastic properties.  The third chapter is the main draw, and has the two main characters join forces to accomplish a great quest.  The quest itself is basically a series of mini-fetch-quests, but that hardly matters.  The fun comes from exploring the enormous, intricate map.  Level design seems relatively minimalist, but the gradual change from region to region, and the charming, easter-egg like decorations on every screen are the real reward.  Expect a lot of soft, ambient lights, soothing sounds and music, and a satisfying, effortless grace to your navigation.  There's no frustration here, and navigation is pure joy.
If you're coming for hardcore gaming, I'd stay away; this is not that game.  Also, don't expect much in terms of story; Underground has inexplicably included a couple of fairies to join you on your grand adventure; neither of them are very interesting, none of the dialogue is well-written, and one of them has a penchant for dropping F-bombs, detracting from the family-frendliness of the game.  It's kept to a minimum, though, so it's not enough to detract from such a joyful exploration experience.  Give the original Knytt games a go, and if you love them as much as I do, go ahead and get this, too.  Support this developer.  This is every bit as good as I was hoping, and I would love to keep revisiting this series for a long time to come.

I'm just getting my review out there now—I'm also one of those typical players who hasn't even made any progress since I [left the Vault and became a wanderererere going all over the place]
I also decided I would review this game, as I've selected it for the 2016 Steam Awards; in the 'Game within a Game' category. Though, looking past what you might be thinking—the text-based game inside of Hubris Comics—this is obviously a game about harsh survival; in an even harsher, post-apocalyptic world with an amazing backstory to it [I can assume, as I've forementioned that I haven't made any progress with the game's story]
It's a personal story for me, the idea of a 'Lone Wanderer'—a hero among the world that's left. It's amazing, and just so facinating to me. And the Karma aspect of the game really enhances the experience for us gamers, and there are way too many games out there nowadays that restrict you into playing a set character profile and stuff [looking at you, Fallout 4]. Sure, there aren't that many options in this game where you can customize your character, but, with the kind of game this is, you don't need to be a loud-mouth, drunk-off-your♥♥♥♥♥kind of guy/girl, or whatever. You can either be a hero or a villain; silent, at that.
Anyway, the 'Game within a Game' comes from nowing how to survive out there. Yes, I know it's a game, and you can just reoad your last save if you screw up, but I'm one of te few who NEVER do that, because, as with real life, you can't just turn back time and forget about a bullet lodged in your shoulder, or a sledgehammer right to your skull. I love challenging myself like this: it makes the experience all the more real and authentic. In a war-torn land, you must do absolutely everything you can just to make it past a group of bandits. There are also too many recent games that rob the player of this particular experience—the true survival apect of a game. You might look at Fallout 3 and instantly compare it to something totally outlandish like Call of Duty 'Zombies' being the definition of hardcore, or Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode in Borderlands 2 [which actually is VERY challenging and rewarding], but for a game that has rightly earned a 'Game of the Year' tag, you need to try Fallout 3. It's one of the most authentic games from the last generation. ^w^

My original review was positive of the sound, visuals and environments, but very critical of the actual gameplay. Either my own temporary ineptitude as well as a bug prevented me from being able to continue, which made me give this a negative review for the difficulty, as I was unable to proceed without getting stress and frustrated.
So, it turns out the “Auto” difficulty level is not the smartest, and not the best thing to put in a game revolving around story. Combat in games is generally accepted to be consistent in order for players to learn and adapt to. I can understand why the developers did it however, due to the nature of the games overbearing darkness
.
And that’s what this game is all about. It’s a journey into darkness, a story about a Celtic woman going to rescue her lover from the Nordic version of hell. A journey to face her own demons of the mind.
The atmosphere sound effects and music are utterly on point. 10/10.

The voice acting is a mixed bag. The main character is A+, but the “voices” that follow you throughout the game suffer from less appealing voice acting. It’s clear they are there to add to the concept of psychosis and create a further feeling of unease, but it begins to grate on you after a while as their quality is sub-par compared to the rest of the game, and prevent you from hearing other things.
The puzzles are slow, easy, and nothing more than time consuming breaks between the segments of combat. Depending on the type of games you enjoy, this may be considered a welcome break or a dull slow slog through the well-constructed environments.
The combat at first glance is bare bones, but taking the time to look at the key-bindings is definitely a requirement. Once you learn the controls from the menu and put them to test in a few fights combat becomes significantly more fluid and bearable. Even if you still get hit sometimes, even when you evade. I highly suggest switching the combat to medium at the start of the game, rather than Auto, and adjust it accordingly from there.
The plot itself is not terrible, but not amazing. It’s the acting and sheer overwhelming detail of the main character Senua that makes the story exceptional. You’re there with her though every harrowing experience, every high and low. It’s a story of emotion and psychosis, wrapped in Norse mythology. She is the most human character I have seen in any game so far.
This is a game that contains very few mechanics and very little actual gameplay, but I didn’t care, and you shouldn’t either.

It feels more engaging than your typical isometric arpg, especially playing at higher difficulties. They made most of the abilities have combinations, so you're constantly doing things. Unless you're playing the game on an easier difficulty, it shouldn't be a matter of spamming a single ability over and over (which is nice compared to a majority of these style games).
The leveling system feels nice. It's usually exciting to get a new level. There's also a reputation system, where you get to choose a new strong buff after gaining enough reputation. The reputation system felt a bit slow, though. I'm nearly at the end of the game and I've gotten around 6 levels in reputation. The loot system felt on-par with other games in this genre. I got the feeling that there weren't many "set" items, but that actually was a positive thing given the length of the game and it's focus on a single player experience. I was able to complete 2 sets in my playthrough. I usually don't like forced companions in these types of games, but I enjoyed the companion in this one. She had a lot of dialog, and actually felt helpful. She also buffs you as you level her up. There are side quests that give you unique items for the main Hunter class, but you can equip them on your companion if you're not a hunter.
Overall, I had a ton of fun with this game, and I highly recommend it if it's on a sale or even if it's not. Just keep in mind isometric arpgs are not everyone's cup of tea.

I have been on Steam for a good many years and own a fair number of games. I have played them quite a bit, some more than others (I'm looking at you Skyrim and Fallout).
This is the first game I have made a review for.
This game is absolutely amazing. At the risk of sounding like any number of other reviewers, the stunning visuals, the well-spun story, the haunting soundtrack, the fast and fun gameplay are well worth whatever you pay for it. I loved every minute of this playthrough.
The story is well planned out and is never forced. Ori is cleverly narrated and interspersed with beautiful cutscenes to help you unravel the story.
The beauty of the world is captivating. For a 2D platformer, it jumps off the screen with mulitple layers of fully animated, vibrant level art. I kept ignoring the speed run achievement, and will continue to do so, because I loved just running around and exploring, trying to see everything.
When I wasn't trying to see everything, I was trying to listen to the music. Simple, haunting melodies that drift out of your speakers like mist. I will be acquiring the soundtrack as soon as I can.
To top this, it is by no means an easy game to beat. There were many deaths on my part because of my lack of skill, but the game never bogs you down with annoying "You died because you suck" screens. It keeps track, but it throws you back in to get lost in the world of Ori once more.
10/10 Would DEFINITELY buy again.

Knytt Underground is one of my favourite games that I have played this year, totally unexpectedly. I came into this thinking I'd mess around on it for half an hour but what I found is one of the most deep and immensely enjoyable puzzle exploration 'complete the map' games I have ever played. I can't really explain it, but I found the mechanics really fun and easy to get the hang of yet difficult to master and the game has an unexplainable charm to it that I haven't found in many other games this year. Initially in the first two chapters the game seems small and limited, but this is simply a tutorial or prologue if you will to the massive chapter 3 which is when the whole game's map opens up. It's addictive to try and discover and explore each of the grids in the game's map system and to discover the secret and story behind each area. Many areas involve puzzles which make use of enemies and hazards and the game's climbing and jumping mechanics to solve, and the ability to *SPOILER* transform into a ball and use momentum to bounce and reach previously unreachable areas *SPOILER* which is fun in itself.
It's one of the games that looks simple and low-budget and to an extent it is, but it also has this deceptively deep story and an incredible atmosphere and soundtrack which to me at least is one of the hardest but most important elements of a game to get right.
To say go play this game and see for yourself isn't very helpful I know, but it really is something that you need to play to understand the points I'm making. If you're feeling hesitant, buy it on sale, but keep it on your wishlist because this is a game that you need to play.

Knytt Underground follows the sprite Mi on a mission to ward off the apocalypse. At least, that's what she's doing if you listen to the angel on her shoulder; her shoulder devil is of another mind.
It's also about life after us. The little buggers who built their civilization on whatever garbage we left behind seem to be doing just fine, impending doom notwithstanding. Vexing, but hardly surprising.
But, at its heart, what Knytt Underground is really about is an impossibly large map.
Man, that thing is big. There's about 1,500 screens in the main world, and there is even a little extra hidden beyond the boundaries.
This is not quite a metroidvania -- your "verbs" are limited to jumping, bouncing and the occasional single-use power-up used for the trickier platforming puzzles (firing one shot, double jump, limited flight ability). A lot of the Nifflas experience is going through vast areas with no real challenges, taking the scenery in. All the same, it's not just a stroll in the park: there are also tricky jumps, shortcuts and hidden passages galore. While your palette of actions is limited, the controls are tight enough that this is all doable on a keyboard.
The backgrounds in this game are pretty, even if they're mostly saturated pictures of nature. Character portraits are kind of goofy. As for the writing, it can be grating in an indie games kind of way, but it's just self-aware enough to land on the "charmingly quirky" end of the spectrum.
But again, this is a game about a map. A huge map. It beckons.
It's calling out to you.
"... Heeeeey", it says. "Do you like exploring?"

In February 2015, I decided to start a new Fallout 3 play through. My goal was clear: Doing Everything!
That means talking to all the NPCs, visiting all the landmarks, every little shed, cave, settlement and unmarked point of interest; doing every quest, obtaining every unique weapon, collecting most of the pre-war books and sugar bombs, and acquiring so many bottle caps that I could safely say that I could start my own soda manufacturing company!
The apocalyptic open world of Fallout 3 offers the player a great atmosphere. The music is well suited in terms of capturing the essence of this devastated world, where everything is reduced to mere antiquated forms of junk and scrap. I am always amazed by how great the mapmakers at Bethesda recreated the ruins of D.C. There is even a whole metro system underneath the city, waiting for someone to explore it. The map is pretty cool, you can’t argue with that. So take your time and explore every square inch of it – you won’t regret it.
Since I knew this was going to be my last playthrough for the next couple of years, I meant to do it in style! So I went ahead and spent countless hours of tweaking and installing mods to shape the game to my liking. The outcome was rather impressive, especially since I am not easy to please!
I had a blast! It took me 200 hours (18 months of playing) to finish the game (including expansions). I could go on and on and explain what kind of character I played (he was neither good or bad by the way) and what decisions I made, but this is a review after all, right? So let’s get to it.
The apocalyptic open world of Fallout 3 offers the player a great atmosphere. The music is well suited in terms of capturing the essence of this devastated world, where everything is reduced to mere antiquated forms of junk and scrap. I am always amazed by how great the mapmakers at Bethesda recreated the ruins of D.C. There is even a whole metro system underneath the city, waiting for someone to explore it. The map is pretty cool, you can’t argue with that. So take your time and explore every square inch of it – you won’t regret it.
What is not so great, on the other hand, are the graphics. They were outdated even back in 2008, when the game was released. Bad textures, bad lighting and this green filter that was put over everything – Gross! Luckily, there are tons of mods that aim to fix what Bethesda missed, and if done right, the game can look absolutely stunning.

I would also like to make an observation on the combat system: While I don’t think it’s bad, it offers much space for improvement.
BUT: Fallout 3 is not primarily a shooter, but a RPG with shooter elements - and it does a pretty good job at this. In my case, it was easy to stay in character throughout the whole game (unlike in Skyrim (in my personal opinion)). And I am not talking about the way I killed people, rather, it refers more to about how I approached situations, and how I resolved them. In many cases, the game offers the player a wide spectrum of possibilities - Some of them are hidden (that’s why I had the Wiki close to me). Fallout New Vegas did this whole RPG thing even better.

Remember when companies still sold expansions or add-ons instead of just DLCs? (I am looking at you, horse armor). Fallout 3 got some really good expansions, though they are not all great.

is the worst of those add-ons in my opinion - You are basically trapped on an alien ship with only few characters to interact with, no interesting loot and no story or other assets. Also, you seem to simply be walking from room to room, through endless corridors, hoping for it to end after the one before.
The best thing you can get in this add-on (referenced above), is the pretty cool (and not so lore friendly!) Samurai armor you can obtain by killing one of the few NPCs you meet on the ship. *Sigh*

(another add-on) is almost as bad as Mothership Zeta, but you get some pretty good loot at the end (nice for stealthy characters). It also offers a little bit more depth by putting you in the role of a soldiers of the U.S. Army during the 2070s. So lore-wise, this add-on is not a complete waste.
is pretty good, since it simply expands the quite vanilla Fallout 3 story in a good way.
and
are pretty amazing. Both add a new map for you to explore, with a main quest, side quests, new weapons, enemies, loot and characters. My personal favorite though is The Pitt, because of the dark atmosphere and the possibilities for the more, shall we say, evil characters.

I could say so much more about this game, but I am lazy - so I will just say that I love this game and recommend it to anyone who is looking for a decent RPG with a great atmosphere; And if that’s not enough you can always enhance your experience (and you should do that, because the Vanilla version of Fallout 3 is rather, well, “meh”) with many awesome mods.
Thank you for reading my humble review, and, if you need help with identifying the mods from my screenshots you can contact me via Steam. Comment on this review and I will add you as soon as possible.

If you liked TNO, you'll probably like this one as well. It's a bit on the short side, but consistently fun from beginning to end. Pretty much everything that was good about TNO is just as good (if not better) here. One thing that really sticks out to me is the perk system, which never made me feel like I had to go out of my way to unlock the ones I wanted. If you like to sneak around and go for headshots like me, you'll get perks that make you better at stealth. If you like to dual-wield and run in with guns blazing, you'll get perks to help you with that, too. The switch from static to incremental bonuses is a big part of this, and it feels great.
As far as technical issues are concerned, I didn't run into any aside from not being able to use the Steam overlay, which was annoying but not the end of the world. I also made sure my video card drivers were up to date before starting the game for the first time, which probably helped. I have an overclocked Ryzen 5 1600 and a GTX 1060 6GB, and the game was silky smooth at 1080p on the "high" preset.
Not much else to say here. It's a fun game while it lasts, and I'll definitely play through it a second time at some point.

Basic pancakes recipe
A delicious and easy pancake recipe that is fast to get on the table and better tasting than any convenience pre- packaged mix.
Serving Size:
8
Category:
Basic recipes, Breakfast, Budget, Cakes & Baking, Dessert, Easy recipes, Kids cooking, Kids food, Lunch box, Pancake recipes, Snacks
Prep Time:
5 mins
Cook Time:
10 mins
Ingredients:
1 cup (150g) self-raising flour
1 tbsp sugar
1 egg, lightly beaten
3/4 cup (180ml) milk
50g butter, melted
Method:
In a bowl mix flour and sugar.
Beat in the egg and then milk at little at a time until batter is smooth and lump-free.
In a hot pan or flat grill, brush butter over cooking surface and pour 1/4 cup measures for each pancake.
When large bubbles form on the surface, flip over and cook until lightly golden on the other side.

I have to say I really enjoyed my first play  through of this little gem of an ARPG. Honestly my only gripe was the somewhat forced linear progression of some areas and a lack of mob respawning mechanics or procedurally generated side quests dungeons to create a deeper more replayable experience for even a single character. This combined with a fairly short playthrough time left me feeling honestly abit annoyed considering Torchlight 2 when onsale as it so frequently goes and its huge workshop mod community makes it such a modern titant among ARPGs that should be considered by others developing in the genre.
The fact you have to pay for various classes as DLC vs again TR2s active modder community and free classes to explore need to be kept in mind by would be rivals. Still I honestly didnt mind grabbing the DLC for this game as it did show enough potential I wanted to try and show all the support I could.
The vibes this game gives off are honestly the best of the ARPGs Ive seen for a while. The voice acting, banter from your ghostly lady companion, the story over all has a fun factor I have to admit captured my steam punkish goth nature very solidly.
To me the real hidden treasure is the eventual base you get to set up and the handful of defense events you get to enjoy. IMO these needed to be more frequent or something, the system though alot of fun to watch the creatures die in the traps  and think it would of been great to see there be a way to have endless invasion options at the end to add to extending the life of a given play through.
Over all if you enjoy the various related genres, the ARPG genre, and enjoy a shorter playthrough game to see the end I totally encourage this game for a easy dif with hardcore on one and done play approach for each class currently out.

A beautiful blend of action, platforming, and puzzling Trine manages to offer lots of fun and even some challenge. There are also some RPG elements through level ups, skills, and hidden equipment. I will admit, the story wasn't very gripping and my friends and I would often just skip it, but the gameplay is top notch.
Armed with a bow, the thief is the most agile of the three and you can use her grappling hook to traverse the environment. The knight is the traditional melee character and comes with a shield, sword, and a hammer. Probably the best character though, is the wizard. He can create boxes, planks and floating platforms, and he can also move them around. If that doesn't sound exciting, wait until your slinging boxes at all your enemies or throwing planks on your friends to make them fall into pits.
When you aren't busy knocking each other off of cliffs or into fire or spikes, you will find that Trine is an extremely well made co-op game. Everyone character and player really has to work together to get through the game, and everyone fills a role. The thief's grappling hook is perfect for those hard to reach places and she is often the one retrieving experience potions, though she can hardly do it alone and the wizards platforms help immensely. The wizard is arguably the leader of the team because he is able to carry everyone on platforms, disable traps by obstructing them, and he can handles enemies fairly well with his objects. Admittedly, the knight seems to have the short end of the deal as he really only shines in combat; he can throw boxes and break walls, but there are very few cases outside of combat where he is absolutely necessary.
Trine was the only local co-op game me and my friends would play for quite a while, it was just too good to put down. Now with the automatic update to Enchanted Edition, this game just got better. This game goes on sale often, and I buy it for friends whenever I can because this is a well made game and this is great developer. They worked tirelessly to completely update a 5 year old game that probably didn't rake in as much other less deserving games, and when they finished they just included it for every owner for free.
You might find find a better action platformer, or a better puzzle platformer, but you probably won't find a game that blends the two together well and offers a terrific co-op experience.

Ori is a superb game, with a very, very emotional story behind it.  Within the first few minutes of playing, you are subjected to some of the most impressive video game I've ever heard.  The game mechanics are reasonably balanced, and the controls are intuitive enough to be enjoyable with just a few minutes of initially starting the game up and learning how to jump.
The game is artistically beautiful, and feels like you are regularly walking through massive segments of a fairy tale. The creator's put an impressive amount of time into the foregrounds and backgrounds.
-- Seriously, don't open it up unless you don't care about the storyline. (If you don't care about storyline, I do not recommend this game for you. There's really very little else to play it for.)
The game is exceptionally emotional throughout the story. I played this game after finishing
. The graphics are significantly better than Dust, but the effects don't compare. I digress.

The game does not have much, if any, replay value to speak of. Once you've finished the story, that's pretty much it. Basically, for $20, its got 20 hours worth of gameplay. $1 an hour to be entertained is worthwhile.  It does not offer multiple levels of difficulty, so you can't make the game more challenging after beating it the first time. Its just the game, play it, love or hate, its exactly as it is.
The first challenge dungeon that Sein takes you to in order to restore the Element of Waters, high atop the Ginso Tree, is fun. It is challenging. After that, you gain the ability to double jump and 80% of the additional Health and Power orbs become availability. It rapidly scales Ori's power beyond that of the enemies, thereby making survivability significantly easier.
Even with a maxed out Defensive skill tree, you take an exceptionally high amount of damage from "spikes" which prove to be more of a threat than the monster. This game should not be considered a Hack and Slash game, or even be taken into consideration for people who prefer the "battle system". The enemies provide very little to no challenge whatsoever, while the environment significantly deadlier than any foe.
Personally, I powered up the defensive tree before the middle support or far left Attack tree. I wanted Triple Jump and Underwater Breathing more than any of the battle abilities. As soon as you get the "Bash" skill, enemies are even more laughable. Their risk factor drops to nothing because you can charge in, grab them, kick them into the floor, and then blast them repeatedly. If they don't die, grab them instantly again -- rinse and repeat!
The game has no "quick travel" trait. Considering it sends you
back and forth across the map numerous times it starts to get annoying walking through the same areas over and over again. Don't need to teleport, but the only reason the game lasted me 20 hours is because I couldn't just use the "Spirit Wells" to teleport around the map to save time. Taking that into account, the game is probably only about 6-8 hours of gameplay and 12 hours of walking.
The three most exciting parts of the game are the "escape scenarios", which demand you focus intensely upon where to leap, Bash, and double jump to next. It is fun, and exciting, but due to all three of these being filled with nothing but instant-death mechanics it can get redundant going through the same things over and over again.
Even with my complaints, just for the story and the music, I would've paid $25 for this game hands down. Compare this game to a movie ticket to waste 2 hours, to see sub-par acting and listen to an easily anticipated and underwhelming script... or you have this game for $20 that will easily delight your senses and keep you on edge during the intense moments of the story. This game is beautiful, emotional, and very well made. I give it a 10/10, and if they made a sequel, I would gladly buy it and play again.

I have no idea how Metacritic gave this game a 66. It is absolutely incredible. Mix one part bioware intense storyline, with one part mirror's edge parkour, stir in some intense combat scenes and you have Remember me.
From the moment the game begins you're immersed into a world of incredible 3D models and beautifully detailed environments. The storyline is fascinating, along with the core concept of the game - Memory Hunting
In this futuristic world everything is controlled by a person's memories; which have been digitized through something called a Sensen chip. One company, Memorize, has the monopoly on digital memories. You play as Nilin, a former "Memory Hunter" who has the special ability to "remix memories" - you can rewind through a person's memories and utilize "glitches" to change the memory and manipulate the person (How they think about you, how they feel, their alliances etc.etc). Somehow you've lost your memories and all you have is a mysterious voice named Edge and a few friends/fans willing to help you.
The gameplay is fairly simple, if you've played games like Mirror's Edge you'll catch on quickly on how to move throughout the environment. The gameplay is very linear, however, leaving you little room/time to explore the environments -which is disappointing for those who want to experience the art as well as those who like treasure hunting.
The biggest downside to the game is that combat controls, while interesting, are not well explained. There will be a period of trial and error while you figure out how to win fights, all the while they'll be throwing new abilities at you.
This game is a ton of fun and definitely worth picking up.

You play as a Celtic woman named Senua, who's on a mission to save her lover, Dillion. Dillion was captured by Northmen (Vikings for you people who slept through history class). Senua is gripped by psychosis.
The game communicates her disturbed mental state through whispers in the background, graphical oddities, and sudden visual distortions. It's very well done, and you can feel Senua's suffering and anxiety. These cues also serve gameplay purposes. In combat a whisper or hiss might say, "look out behind you." It means you should probably block because there's some dude about to smack your backside with a huge ♥♥♥♥ing sword.
The gameplay and especially combat is visceral. It's a solid melee system. It's not overly complicated like Dark Souls. You get a sword. You have a heavy attack, a light attack, a block key, and a dodge key. Success in combat is determined by reflexes and timing. As the number of enemies increases, your positioning also becomes important. Gameplay consists of this combat and what boiles down to a walking simulator. But a really good walking simulator. The Nordic atmosphere is always tense, and while there are gorgeous vistas here and there, the overall environment evokes claustrophobia. Like any good walking simulator you also have puzzles, but these are all visual puzzles resolved by finding a location and standing there. You don't have any kind of inventory -- there is no item management at all, and I for one am ♥♥♥♥ing joyous.
The game does have shortcomings. It's an indie title after all, but I can tell that the studio didn't ♥♥♥♥ about. The graphics range from amazing to okay. The game uses Unreal Engine 4, and I'm starting to think UE4 is really bad at rendering distant scenery. Anyways, Senua's model itself is amazing, nearly photorealistic. They gave her dreadlocks though, which is utter nonsense as Celtic women only braided their hair, however it probably saved a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of rendering resources (just see Rise of the Tomb Raider), and isn't that distracting. How do I know this? BECAUSE I'M AN EXPERT ON LADIES' HAIR. From highlights to flat irons to blowouts, I know terminology that'd blow your mind.
Overall, I found the game to be a refreshing and highly original experience. You could even call it a postmodernist art piece that's actually art instead of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Although the story appears simple at first, it quickly develops in unexpected ways. The setting is also steeped in Norse mythology, and for any Viking buffs this title is a must. Highly recommended.

This might be one of the most interesting games I've played. The actual mechanics aren't extremely original but its how it incorporates those mechanics in a way that humanizes mental illness and suffering to tell a story of loss.

I don’t know about you, but I sure love it when the game tricks me into believing that it’s something else. Knytt Underground looks like a small and cute trifle with nothing but a cool photo-collage backgrounds paired with primitive art-style and rather abstract jokes. And it ends with explosions, quite literally. Well, at least the author inserts himself into the game to tell you this in person. First two short chapters (out of three, mind you) don’t look like much. The player is introduced to the base mechanics, of which there aren't really a lot of: you can jump, climb any vertical wall, transform yourself into a big rubber ball (this particular one can be seen only in demo-level, which is included along first two chapters and has its complete separate level) and gain access to higher jumps. Occasionally you can collect a one-time-use-power-up which looks like glowing flower bud; and most of the time this “special ability” is nothing more than some fancy high jump or short free-fly-mode for getting where you couldn’t just climb up, because the wall isn’t completely even.
So I was ready to write it off with I a notion “I certainly understand why it’s so highly praised on indie scene, but…”. But then the third chapter happened. Forty minutes later, when I was realising in panic that I haven’t seen even 10% of the map and found a single save point, I realised I got into the rabbit hole; what I didn’t know is, that it would turn out to be a truly amazing adventure. The seem-to-be-obvious primary purpose of “just following the story” is being crushed by the enormous world size. You don’t really know the right path, there’s a lot of obstacles and, finally, the path to the story points is blocked by some treasure-hungry NPCs; so you have to wander off. And that’s where it becomes firstly mysterious, then great, and finally, near the end, obvious. You didn’t come here to just play it through. You’ve come here as a discoverer of sorts. The one that boldly steps into the unknown and makes a map of the journey; all this quite literally: the world is divided into a familiar grid of separate screens and there’s no telling what will you see in the next one for most of the time. The game also acknowledges this fact without a single doubt: formal purpose is what it is — formality, cause for an adventure.
So what did I discover here? I found a whole surrealistic underground world inhabited by sprites and fairies, who barely remember the history of this world, but call themselves strange names, like “The Internet”. They remember though the catastrophic events of war waged by humans, that ended with the world being reduced to these scattered survivors, living in ruins, holding mystic beliefs and treating leftover household items from pre-war times as magical powerful artefacts. And yet these folks have enough in them to give you a good reason for watching them in natural habitat, exploring their lives and getting from them pieces of history. It will never, though, become clear what really happened. You didn’t really expect that from a game, which literally is dedicated to uncertainty and meaning of seeming obscure final goal? Yep, that’s it, fourth wall is a regular punchbag here.
Aside from the cryptic story and chilling ambience of the scenery, there’s more too. The gameplay makes a sudden skyrocketing, shifting from “mindless jumping” to “carefully solving puzzles with jumps”; and not only with jumps. Rubber ball form now becomes useful not only for jumping higher, but for doing all kinds of tricks. Those simple power-ups now require planning before their usage. One wrong move — and at best you’ll have to try again, sometimes dying from contact with molten lava or not-so-friendly-robot laser beam. And that’s not worst that could happen, sometime you’ll fail so bad, you’ll fall to the other screen; getting back up isn’t an easy task for most of the time. But with enough focus and thinking you’ll get all those coins, and flowers, and keyboard keys, and maybe even some secret symbols. Even if you don’t it won’t change much; a game that is filled with secrets won’t hide that much if you won’t find all of them. After all, that was the message of it. If the goal isn’t clear, or doesn’t really make sense, it will be the false one.
