There is no saving grace to this game in which I can even recommend this to anyone. If you really… absolutely must have more then please continue.
Gameplay: The game boils down to opening a few menus comparing a few numbers to find the “true” highest value, select, go to the ship out screen make sure you’re gonna make it in time and have enough fuel. Select your destination then press go. That’s it… that’s 95% of the game, sure you’ll go through a few other menus to buy ships but that’s about it.
The mini game that you play to dock and undock your ships is played a total of 10 times, and then you’ll only do it for the achievements. Especially once it gets later into the game you’ll just pay the fee because the time it takes you could make many more millions instead of saving a few hundred thousand. Its ok at best, boring most probably.
Ships: So this is like any basic game you could believe, the ships constantly get better… all the way up to the end. Suddenly the final ship just isn’t as good as the one you get before it. Not being able to navigate the Panama Canal is suddenly a big deal, even when you don’t think it will be. I wanted to love it, but it just didn't quite work.
It's a nice little game, but only a brief diversion with little replayability.  Its general mechanic of buying ships and sending them out, optimizing routes, cargoes, and fuel use to make a profit, is fun.  But it has some flaws that kill the experience.
Every time you dock, you have a choice - pay a high tug fee, or dock manually. The docking mini-game is a waste of 2-3 minutes, with terrible frame rate for its looks, and people who want to play the shipping strategy don't want to play ship simulator every 30 seconds. So you generally just eat the tug costs once you can afford them.
Customizing ships for certain cargoes - refrigeration for food and medicine, for instance - means almost nothing. There's no penalty for not doing it except if you get caught by customs, and that's a super rare event.
There's little difficulty.  It's very, very hard, if not impossible, to lose at the game. I never even had to take out loans and contracts were super easy to complete.
There's little replayability.  Once you unlock the largest ships, all you're doing is running the same routes over and over, just watching your account balance spiraling into the multiple billions.  There's nothing to achieve, and it quickly gets boring.
This could be a fun game with a little more depth, a little more difficulty, and either no mini-game, or more and better ones - sort of a Sid Meier's Pirates! with cargo vessels.  As it is... it's not terrible, just a little lacklustre.

O3DX, how shall I compare thee? To a summer's day? Uh, no, think again buddy!
...Ok, let's start positively...
- First of all, we can see this game is very acceptable graphics-wise, and is perfectly acceptable for what it is.
- Sounds: Can't say they're amazing, but I didn't find them annoying either, so we'll call that a positive as well.
...So now we'll talk Negatives...
1. NO resolution options - this might only affect the Mac version (which shouldn't be an excuse), but it's a little annoying because the way this game is setup (due to the camera, mentioned in my gameplay issues below), you really need to run it in a smaller window.
2. Although a minor gripe, it's still something that should be better implemented, and that is, I found it hard to navigate all the menus with the keyboard, and had to use mouse to get around half the time.
3. Lastly, and this is probably the most serious of issues - the actual gameplay. Seriously, this is perhaps the most important thing to get right, and it bombed badly. This issue is so important to address let's have subsections:
a. The first gameplay issue is the camera zoom/pan/angles - because the camera is zoomed in so much most of the time, you can not see far enough ahead in the track to adjust your speed or angle of the vehicle. This single point alone made most of my gametime frustrating, restarting levels because I stuffed up due to not seeing the obstacles in time.
b. Second gameplay issue I came across was the sudden drop in speed of the vehicle when going up a hill or when you land even slightly unevenly - this caused me to have to restart levels due to not having enough speed to get over an obstacle, or not getting big enough jumps.
c. Third gameplay issue that I'll mention is the unexpected vehicle crashes that occur - I might be driving over an obstacle, and all of a sudden the vehicle will crash, or, on one occasion, the vehicle randomly jumped in the air and crashed into nothing before landing in a mess on the road.
I can forgive everything else, but I gave up playing after 1 1/2 hrs due to the gameplay issues alone. The random vehicle crashes, the vehicle speed issues, and bad camera make this more of a game of luck than skill. I actually played this briefly quite a few months ago before it came onto Steam, and it really doesn't seem to me like it has changed much at all since then. Due to this, I am not putting much hope into the gameplay issues being sorted before release, but let's hope the devs do.

Lets go with the graphics, at first glance it looks alright on the screenshot right? Well not really because take a look at this
those line effects you see? Not dynamic, they are baked in which means that in the situation like you see in the image in which I am going at 1 km/h it still appears giving a silly illusion of speed which is not there. The textures are muddy and bland plus the props are overused.
Sound
The only saving grace this game has is the powerful BGM meanwhile the SFX is terribly inconsistent. E.g the sound of the engine is simply a few second of sound noticeably looped ad infinitum while the sound of tyre crunching against the dirt sounds like someone took a plastic dustpan and ran it over a gravel road over and over again whilst Simultaneously drowning out any other sound the game might have had. Also that gravel sound also plays even if you are driving on the snow. Meanwhile other sound effect sounded like they came out of the SNES era, not powerful and actually felt pretty awesome, for a child that is.
Gameplay is hanging corpse for this kind of genre, to get addicted to this sort of game it must provides plenty of physic puzzles, great illusion of speed, and a compelling enviroment all which this game does not have. The car [a ♥♥♥♥in.g humvee] cannot even get its sorry buttock over the a little hill and it will find any reason it can to lose its goddam.n speed. Go over that bump? Lose speed. Tight corner? Lose speed. Best part is when you manage to conjure enough speed and go over a ramp only to find out you triggered a bulletime mode [that is only specific to that one spot] you will inexplicably lose all of your speed. Physic puzzle? More like pray to whatever god you have that the model of physic they are using does not screw you over, I restarted a level 3 times and it behaves differently for all of those 3 times not to mention that so called obstacle will screw you over because they are placed just outside your camera view and other obstacles are just floating rings given no reason as to why they are so and will blow your car up because fuel tanks are convenietly placed all over it and will explode at the touch of a feather.
So would I recommend this game? Hell no. If this game was my student and I am its teacher I would give it a B+ for effort but a deserved D- for execution. Avoid it if you can and just get the other game that does it even better than this.
Oh I forgot to mention, in order to give off a feeling of dynamic to the track the camera will randomly move around a preset path to show you highlights and so on which does not work of course and instead gave me a goddamn migraine instead. Plus I can clearly see the car is going 10 km/h you are not fooling anyone.
In short, a sloppy game done wrong in a genre where explosion, speed, and a sense of visceral is of the utmost importance.

Hi all, nukes here.
Gauntlet is a top down, dungeon crawler, which will have you hacking and slashing your way through hordes of enemies. Which sold it for me, who doesn't love running through dark dungeons slaughtering everything you are faced with.
Based off of the original 1985 Gauntlet, this version captures its magic beautifully.
Still offering four player co-operative locally and online as well. Gauntlet offers a story mode, Endless mode and a Coliseum. Each can be played with friends or on your own.
I love this game, as it is easy to pick up and play, playing with friends made my experience even more fun. Although the community is not massive people still do play this online.
Before you jump into raid the dungeons in search of glorious riches. You are able to choose from four playable characters,
Each with very different abilities and play styles.
Warrior, Valkyrie, Elf, Wizard and
Personally my two favourite are the Valkyrie for mirror shield and clone combo, and the Wizard for his awesome spell combinations. Don't get me wrong though all the classes are brilliant.
Personally Barbarian felt a little dumb and clumsy to me, Elf well his accent was just to annoying which really put me off his character.
The difficulty of this game comes in three flavours.
With each increase in difficulty monsters have more hit points and run faster. Although more gold for all you looters.
Easy - Says it all.
Normal - Pretty much default.
Hard -Well I am sure you get the point by now.
Keep in mind the Colosseum mode the difficulty is fixed.
Endless mode gradually increases as you make your way through the levels.
The controls are simple and easy to pick up, on original release the campaign had a tutorial,
With Slayer edition release this has been removed. It is now in the form of a
page on the main menu, which has controls laid out for each class.
This game can be played with keyboard and mouse or a controller making sure you activate the controller before starting the game.
Personally I found this game is more suited for controller use, especially with the wizard class.
This game has achievements, some of them a fairly straight forward but even now I still haven't got to wave 50 on Endless or killed 15000 Orks.... Hurray for me.
Unfortunately some of them are a grind.
The campaign is based on going deeper through a series dungeons to challenge yourself, looting as you go. To find three pieces of sword for a sketchy wizard, on this Gauntlet journey you will encounter many deaths.
Once you have completed a map
you are able to freely navigate to old and new missions plus bonus ones.
The combat is fairly straight forward, swing here swing there, heads fall off
Least from a Barbarian or Valkyrie's point of view or for Wizard and Elf you use the right analogue to fire your bow or burn, zap and freeze.
This game can be fast paced and chaotic at times, keep yourself moving or knowing your choke points will keep you alive. It is easy to lose your character in the commotion.
Since Slayer edition release the skills and abilities have changed, now equipment you buy will determine what moves and skills you have.
Personally why they decided to change it is beyond me, I loved that the items were more cosmetic based.
They also removed the perk system for masteries, which again is beyond me completely. As masteries, other than boasting rights are pretty much useless now.
Sounds decent and fitting for dungeon scene. Although very loud on start up so remove your headset or be deafened.
Some of the voice acting can be a bit much.
The graphics settings are straight forward, this game is not to demanding although later levels on Endless mode could cause issues for lower spec'd machines.
Gore can be turned off for the younger audiences.
Definitely a love hate relationship with the voice acting on this game, although humorous to a degree I cannot stand the Elf's strong accent.
This multiplayer on this game works well, as mentioned before can be done locally on a decent sized screen
Or can be done online with friends or strangers.
I have never had problems finding a Story or Endless mode game, although keep in mind if you are joining someone else's game you may not have choice of your favourite character.
Multiplayer is stable and I have never had connection issues unless host is in a distant country. If you are unsure just host your own.
Story mode progress is saved whether you do it multi or single player.
I don't think I came across any game breaking bugs. Only annoyance is I mentioned before, is about starting the game after you turn on or connect your controller as sometimes Gauntlet may not pick it up.
Overall I found this game very fun to play, par some of the changes to Slayer Edition
I still play to get last achievements to this day, but I have had many hours of dying to hordes of enemies with friends and strangers.
I personally hope they make another Gauntlet down the line sometime with even more content.
I felt this game did do the originals games justice and I hope you will feel the same way.
Hope I helped.

This is quite a good game, still very playable in 2014 considering its age (it was first released in 2009). It's not a classic sidescroller-platformer, more like an 2.5D platform game with moderately difficult puzzels incorporating jumping and some nice, quite modern feeling physics.
You play as one of three members of a party (a Wizard, a Knight and a Thief), and the nice touch is that you can switch between these three at any given time. This is often necessary to solve a puzzle or to make further progresss in the game, which means that once a party member is killed, chances are there you have to go back to the last savepoint. Thankfully, these are plenty enough to keep things agreeable - mind you, not quick save in this one. A bit surprisingly, difficulty seems to diminish once the game gets going - after level 5 or so (from the 15). Since by then you have far more abilities and more powelfull weapons, it gets easier to bruise through the levels. That's not a real problem, since each new level presents an different set of colours and atmosphere, but it is somehow surprising.
The department where Trine really shines, is its visuals. Not that there are really fancifull effects, it's just that the atmosphere of the different levels is captured to perfection. There is something fairytale-like about Trine, which is really enthralling and keeps one playing for a while.And since the
was relased, visuals have even been improved by more than a notch. Alas, the story really is not so entertaining, so after a bunch of levels you could lose intesest. Physics are great and enhanch the puzzels to a considerable effect, since you often have to resort to them.
Still: recommended for those who love a game with real atmosphere and good albeit rather simple game mechanics.

If you're waiting for rescuing hostages, taking down terrorists or simply sniping scarecrows, you will be served with Reload! And watch your step, make sure not to be hit by... paint bullets. Because in Reload, you're shooting at wooden/metal/paper targets. And it's like that at every scenario in your carrier.
Anyway, the goal is to score points and to earn medals. Platinum medals are the highest one. By doing the campaign, you'll unlock glasses that will make random targets appear for extra points.  And the more the glasses are upgraded, the highest are the points.
You have also some rail shooting actions - these are my favorite.
Yet, there are some problems: the shotgun scenario named Quick Target is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you want to avoid any civilian casualty. But as I discovered, it's possible to earn the platinum medal with some of them being shot down. The sniping sequences are probably the hardest: given the fact that you're breathing, your crosshair is going crazy, like in Sniper Elite. But you can't zoom more. And when you're reloading, the game is messing the spot you were monitoring: I have my zoom on the grass most of the time. Thanks god, you can let some targets "alive" and still score a platinum medal.
The graphics are correct, though not so extraordinary, the soundtrack is good, so is the replayability.
Why? Because you can play unlocked levels outside the campaign and improve your score. The bonus levels are also a good idea: shooting fruits and vegetables or cans is a nice change of scenery.
However, I largerly prefer the Heavy Fire games, for the scenario and for the action.
Anyway, I'm perhaps mixed about the game but I'll recommand it for people that prefer a little more arcade than action and that prefer to shoot on objects than on humans.

Reload is an on rails shooter where you train to use firearms, but will you want to play it ?
Reload is simple, all you do is go through different objectives ranging from clay shooting, to terrorist takedown operations and target practice.
The game is simple and you use only four  buttons. Right and left mouse buttons to shoot and reload, space to hold your breath and shift to use iron sights for sniper rifles. It's all really simple.

The game also is really easy. Apart from the missions where you can fail, you can do literally nothing and you will win.  Out of curiosity , I decided to not shoot anyone and to my surprise I still finished the level.
The game took me 2 hours to finish every level, but there's still a lot to do, like challenges and Multiplayer ( not sure if that works though).
The game ran really smoothly from start to finish, but the only problem is the horrific resolutions and to my knowledge there's no way to fix it.

Boss combat is what finally led me to say something though. It's incredibly console oriented. It includes scripted cycles to the boss fights followed up by quick time event finishers. The combos and abilities don't really seem to play into it a lot. The memory diving was kind of interesting to play with the first couple of times, but actually became annoying as things progressed. Also I wouldn't even attempt to try playing this with a mouse and keyboard. It was definitely made for a xbox controller. The way the camera functions makes that clear from the start.

Depth is truly a diamond among coal. I started playing depth years ago, but I didn't convince friends to get it until it went on sale for $5. They now love it and we play it a lot. After having this game for a while, here are my Pros and Cons!
Pros:
1. Almost completely balanced
2. Good community for the most part
3. Unique experience from your average shooter. The weird angles and floating mechanics can add some interesting moments and makes the gameplay very dynamic.
4. Updated Frequently (not like every week, but more often than not)
Cons:
1. Certain levels are imbalanced towards divers, who already have it easier than the sharks.
2. Small community can make it hard to find matches occasionally. (This has only been at strange hours in the morning and other rare occasions. Normally I don't wait more than a minute or two)
3. Team composition can be a challenge with stubborn players, just like any other game
4. For the sharks to win, you either both have to be really good, have one shark that is GOD-TIER, or have communication via VOIP, which is rare for the randos in the game.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OVERALL: I LOVE LOVE LOVE this game! It is very fun and I highly reccomend it. I would wait for a sale, because personally, this game is worth $10, not $20. But if it goes to $10 or below, grab it! Make sure you can convince some friends too, and if you find me in game, friend me! I'm always down to play some depth! -- Cowbarn

The length of the game is perfect, it allows enough time to tell the story, without becoming boring.

Many 15 year old spoiled 'merican brats hate this game because their own ignorance led them to believe that it would be Mass Effect, a means to be cool, a cure for acne, and a bag of chips.
For those of us who are actually aware of the survival genre and expect this game, which is part of that genre, to reflect that fact, No Man's Sky is absolutely awesome.
Pros:
+great graphics
+runs smoothly with little load time
+the universe you have access to in this game is beyond massive
+tons of unique environments yielding various resources
+compelling progression goals focused on utility and advancement as well as travel and discovery
+huge amount of awesome looking ships any of which can be obtained in game for your use
+in addition to owning several smaller starships, the player can own their own gigantic space freighter complete with a hanger for all your other ships as well as base building real estate
+meaningful, fun, and cool looking base building
+the new exocraft land vehicles are really useful and feel great to use, especially the Roamer
+compelling milestone in-game achievements
+enjoyable dog-fighting while in space complete with the choice to defend freighters against bandits or attack the freighters for their cargo
+fun combat vs sentinel droids that you get steadily more effective at as you upgrade your exosuit and multitool
+your base, ships, freighter, and planets you discover can all be renamed as much as you like
Cons:
-a little buggy sometimes (I've had about 3 crashes over the course of just under 100 hours and sometimes when I dismount my exocraft after farming for a while it flings me several yards away)
-minor graphic errors in a couple spots (nothing major though)
-learning curve can seem a bit much at first (during my first run I thought about starting over and doing things more effectively but stuck with it). After almost 100 hours I'm still learning things about this game and how to manage my base, ships, and resources better. I personally like this but some might not.
-if you accidentally attack sentinel drones in space their response is a little too strong (they jam your hyper drive so you can't jump away and then continue to attack you until they take you out).
-navigating both on planets and in space can be tricky until you get the hang of it.
If you like the survival genre, I can say with confidence that you will probably have a blast with No Man's Sky for many many hours. However if you're a hater then let's be honest- a million dollars and a new Ferrari probably won't please you, so a video game probably won't either. A lot of people jumped on the hate train for this game like it was a fad or something but I'm having a great time and although I say it about few games- this one feels like a great deal of love was put into it. As a long time gamer, I truly appreciate that, regardless of the rocky start this game had.
Just some context for those who don't know: Some of the features I mention here as pros were recently added in a new and very large (free) content patch (base building for instance is new) and people who have played the game post-patch seem to feel it's a welcome update.
Sorry for being pissy about the haters but I really love this game and I want to support it :P

Think of it as a low grade interactive comic spinoff from the TV show "The wire".
A sort of choose-your-own-adventure graphic novel. Split across 3 chapters you get to play as several different characters as their stories intertwine at different points. The presentation is pretty well done for the budget and while the game does involve a fair amount of reading, the writing overall is high enough to keep your interest. At times you will groan with some of the generic bad guy lines that are used, but it's not a deal breaker. There's no voice overs but that's probably a good thing considering the game has plenty of different ethnic characters and it most likely would have sounded corny.
All the characters are somewhat flawed to make them a bit easier to relate to and how their actions play out. While you do get to control the characters at certain points (e.g checking out a crime scene, finding clues and working out what happened) you are led down a fairly narrow path on how you can alter the underlying nature of the story. You'll only notice this issue if you replay the game several times though. For example at the very beginning you are are choosing how 2 police officers enter an apartment to investigate/catch a suspect. While there are 3 odd choices in how to tackle it, with another quick time event (pass/fail makes no difference) and a further 5-10 choices amongst it all, either way you'll end up cuffing the suspect (regardless if you choose the most reckless path and he gets the jump on you). However I will note as you proceed further through chapter 2 and 3 there are a few different scenarios and endings that can play out based on your actions. There is plenty of grey area moral choices throughout the game and while most are an illusion it still feels like you have entire control on how everything plays out.
If you play through the entire story in one go you'll enjoy the trip. There are some minor bugs (characters walking with wrong animation or missing textures) these are very few and far between and overall do not damage the experience. I didn't experience any game crashes and all the achievments popped.
Total game time (depending on how quick you read and how much you examine all the environments) would probably be in the 3-5 hr timeframe (to complete all 3 chapters). To 100% the game achievements you'll need a bit longer on top of that to basically go through every different choice and ending the game has to offer. You'll also probably get a bit annoyed with how slowly the characters walk when you want them to move from spot to spot. It can be painful when you forgot something and need to wander back to other locations.
On sale definitely worth a look if you enjoy this genre.

Skullgirls borrows mechanics from some of the most well known fighting games out there (King of Fighters, Marvel, Guilty Gear, Street Fighter, etc) and fuses them into a very solid and accessible little package.
I cannot emphazise it enough, the game is very, very accessible. The control scheme is a 6 button layout, something with which almost everybody should be familiar with by now. However, for the execution of supers, you will be hard pressed to find moves that uses anything other than quarter circle motions (exception being the obligatory charge characters and DP motions).
Blockbusters (flashy meter-dependent moves) even use the same motions, only requiring the press of two punches/kicks at the same time, reminding me of good old Darkstalkers.
Every character has something to offer for people who are already used to certain archetypes, but puts a small spin on them.
Wanna play as the usual Ryu clone? We have one, sans projectiles! Kind of...
Wanna play the rushdown character who is fast as the wind? We have one! And she can throw her head at you...
Wanna play a hit-hard but slow character? We have a Juggernaut/Iron Tager fusion!
The game is also full to the brim with Tutorials, which range from "How do I walk?" to character specific moves and the many many many mechanics of the game (pushblocking, infintes prevention, overheads, all that jazz). These tutorials are very clear and easy to understand, and only a few mechanics might get you stuck for a few minutes.
However, when I say this game is accessible, I don't mean this game can't have high level play. Quite the opposite.
Every character has some kinks here and there that makes them viable in more ways than one, and you won't see 2 people play the same character the same way. The combo system is rather flexible, after all. Even if the tutorials teach you usual Bread n Butters and strategies for everyone, you can always think a bit and come up with something of your own.
The other aspects of the game are also top notch. The music and animation are really great, and the story modes for each character range from "that was pretty cool" to "OH GOG DID THAT JUST HAPPEN".
The only gripes people might have with this game might be the disappointing final boss (just a projectile factory at first, tho not as bad as Magaki) and the amount of DLC characters (which go rather cheap, and even cheaper during sales, so no biggie).
The online play also has a few hiccups here and there, but if you stick to playing with people from your same continent you should be fine.

It's been years since I first played this game, back on Xbox 360. Back then, I loved it, and I enjoyed coming back to the DC wasteland and find new locations to explore. More importantly, it's the game that introduced me to what is now one of my favorite franchises, and I have a healthy dose of nostalgia for it.
But holy hell, the passage of time hasn't been kind to Fallout 3. I would not recommend playing it today unless you are ready to sit down and mod it for a few hours just to get it to
Graphically, I think it actually kind of holds up, and the capital wasteland still has a certain beauty and charm that the Mojave desert and the Commonwealth didn't quite manage to capture. Characters look like potatoes but don't completely distract from the experience. Musically, it's quite good. The new direction for the ambient music is great, if not as dark and chilling as the Fallout1 and 2 soundtracks. The radio's a brilliant element and GNR and Enclave Radio both have a solid, if unsubtle ("Do you get it this game is about the APOCALYPSE ?!") choice of themes.
Technically, it's a mess. Glitchy as hell, difficult to run on modern hardware and operating systems, yet surprisingly stable once you actually get it to run. This is why I said the years haven't been kind to Fallout 3. In terms of gameplay, it's the second most shallow entry in the series behind Fallout 4, and the gunplay and gun selection is downright terrible by modern standards. Heck, even back then, the lack of ironsights made it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to play and the spread of some weapons is unfrigginbelievable, even with a gun skill of 100. You'll spend most of your time shooting things and the combat is terrible, so...yeah.
But the cherry on top of the cake is the absolutely atrocious writing of the main quest and most sidequests. Thanks Emil. Back when I first played the game, I kind of tuned out the story because it was so boring, with a lot of rude and uninteresting characters who make stupid decisions all the time. Oh, and of course there's next to no choice in this game, because that's absolutely not something Fallout is known for, right ?
And yet, despite all my criticisms, I still bought the game and played through the whole story again. Is it nostalgia ? Is it the dumb fun of exploring the ruins of a blasted wasteland ? Probably both. Regardless, Fallout 3 is still worth playing through at least once, for shitz and giggles if nothing else.

I really tried to like this game.I mean, I really did. The game seems to be inspired on the original Airline Tycoon - at least the ship / cargo parts - but it sadly can't be enjoyed. After the first few minutes the game shows how it really is: a boring, repetitive task of 1) refull / repair 2) accept contract 3) select contract 4) sail. And you repeat this a lot. And I mean, A LOT.
For every time your ship gets into a port, there is this repetitive, mindless, 15 clicks you will have to do, with no challenge, no fun or changes. You can't make fix routes, or define ships by cargo or anything basically. You are struck with those 15 clicks for everytime your boat arrives at a destination.
And what is even more dissappointing besides the fact you can't "automatize" anything to make the game more enjoyable is that, the game actually becomes even worse the better yoiu get at it. Because the more ships you have the more time you will be clicking 15 times for each boat. Taking ages just to even a month gets by because of the amount of times you have to repeat that task that can't be dealt with any other way.
Sadly, even though the idea is interesting, and that mini-game added of manually taking your ship to and off the port - which then it's impossible, since, for example, I automated that process over 800 times in my few hours, I can't even think of doing it manually - the game feels like a chor.
Unless you are really, and I mean REALLY into the idea of having a fleet of trading ships, I would skip this game. Even then, I would still reconsider getting it if you see some gameplay of it since you will notice the issue of the "repetititve 15 clicks" I'm talking about.
Ps.: Just look for another Tycoon game instead.

So, imagine Trine gameplay with Life is Strange/Last of Us feels. That's basically what this game is. Hits straight for the emotions within 15 minutes of the game starting. Just prepare yourself.
In terms of gameplay, it plays like any other platformer with a bit of parkour involved. Abilities gained through experience don't feel too overpowered and the puzzles make use of the abilities very well. Like any other platformer, the game is going to tease you by showing you some item or ability that you can't get without further advancing into the story.
This brings us to the story, told by an unknown entity (a light-being?) in a foreign, non-terrestrial language as games of fantasy usually do. But, it's not tacky or humorous like Trine. Instead, the story-telling is atmospheric and ties in extremely well to the theme and graphics of the game.
This brings us to the graphics and the game is absolutely gorgeous. Trine looked a bit cartoonish and more 3D-ish than this game which suited well with its themes and story-telling. This game is much more 2D but boasts multiple layers of foregrounds and backgrounds inside and outside of cutscenes.
Unlike Trine, which is a traditional platformer, this game is more parkour oriented with more parkour abilities being offered as you progress through the story or buying them using your experience.
I haven't finished the game yet so I can't fully tell you guys how well the game was made or what improvements could be made so I'll keep updating this review as I complete it. But the overwhelming positive reviews on Steam should speak for themselves. If you enjoyed Trine and enjoy a bit of 2D parkour, this is your game.
EDIT: Just a follow up after finishing the game.
This game is ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant. Absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing top notch. For the price I paid, this was worth twenty times some of the AAA titles that I've played. The "bash" skill isn't a bash at all. OVERVIEW
Reload is just what it claims to be: a MIL/LE simulation-style rail/range FPS, only, instead of shooting live baddies, you're shooting target representations of them in varying circumstances. In addition, some less combat-oriented levels are included. It accomplishes this premise in a mostly enjoyable fashion, with some flaws.
GAMEPLAY
The levels are pretty well-designed and nicely explained, and it's not that difficult to get a handle on how things work, while also not being so easy that you're bored. The eyewear and camouflage unlockables are great touches that make obtaining platinum on levels feasible, while also adding a sense of accomplishment. There's enough variety in the types of levels to give the game good replay value. Enemies that shoot back in some levels are quite nice. Really dig the move-and-shoot factor on some stages. Controls are good.
On the negative, the tutorial thingies are quite excessive. You should be able to turn them off. The F key is definitely your friend once you get the hang of the game. Also, in the first skeet shooting level, at least, when it says you have less ammo this go around, it's...meaningless, because you've still got hundreds and hundreds of rounds you won't need even if you're a terrible shot. Quite odd. Also, it's irritating that the game zooms in every single time you get a pumpkin or a small target in the sniper levels. The first times, fine; every time, no thanks. The grenade levels are poorly designed, as it's unclear as to what you have left to shoot. The most irritating factor of all is how poorly the reflexive fire rifle level is. Its platinum (and even gold) rating is absurdly difficult, not to mention that the two pop-up targets in the very back are nigh impossible (if not impossible?) to shoot (the shotgun level with hostages had a similar issues). The dot can be right on them and firing does nothing. Really bad hitboxes. In fact, that entire level is broken - you don't get any bonuses from one of the rounds, no matter how you do, which is probably exactly why platinum is borderline impossible.
GRAPHICS
Quite decent, once you change them to the highest resolution - why the default is so low, I'm not sure. There are some slight glitches, but overall it's quite nice.
AUDIO
Sound is pretty good, from the instructor's voice to the gun effects. Music is OK and it fits well with the game.
STORY
You're some random dude who's learning some mad skills. That's about it. I did, however, use these skills to save the girl I love and the world (plus every other world out there), so I guess the idea is to just create your own story in real life, like I did. Thanks, Reload!
CONTENT
Nothing to say here. It's a clean, classy game in which you're preparing to toast bad guys 4 realz by toasting them in their simulated forms. Zero profanity, sexual content, worldview issues, or anything else.
INTERFACE
I'm assuming the word "Interface" works for this...Anyway, I'm talking about stuff like options and such. It's pretty basic but solid, with some problems, such as the aforementioned tutorial pop-ups, and the fact that, when you start a new career, it ditches all of the unlocked levels, too. That's...quite annoying. I assumed it would just delete campaign progress and that was it, letting you play all the scenarios straight through, but it doesn't. One other minor negative is that start-up is just a tad slow - staring at "Copyright 2014" (paraphrasing) gets old fast. Some other minor issues are, for instance, the lack of proper grammar in, "Exit to windows?", and it saying you unlocked two of...the same thing, or using "Unlocked" in reference to locked things (I can kinda understand the last one, but it's a bit weird. It would also be nice if it told you what some of the changes actually did (almost all are obvious). On El Presidente, it says to watch out for hostages...But there aren't any. Also, sometimes the game says, "Better luck next time", for...seemingly no reason. The "All Weapons Drills" don't work for me yet (I can't select anything), but it doesn't say why. In the mounted machine gun levels, reloading is still there even though it's irrelevant.
(Note, of course, that a lot of these are quite minor, "polish" issues - I'm just trying to list everything I can, positive and negative.)
CONCLUSION
The more I played this, the more I liked it, which one other reviewer alluded to (more skill, more fun). For five bucks, it's not bad. Its simplicity is rather attractive.
Overall, I think I'd give it about 6/10, maybe a 7. If you'd like a casual, at least remotely realistic FPS sim, then I'd recommend giving Reload a try.
I hope you found my review helpful. Thanks for reading, and Godspeed.

Depth is a first person shooter set underwater with one team playing as divers looking to protect the robot STEVE for the other team, the sharks.
As humans you can buy equipment such as guns, mines, flares, etc and upgrade said equipment with different bullets, scopes and so on. All the weapons work well, fire rate and ammo capacity is reasonable, damage is fair and the upgrades are very useful. As a human there are two ways to win: 1) Kill all the sharks, 2) Get STEVE back to the boat safely, this makes for nice gameplay as most divers will protect STEVE but some may go on a shark hunt if thats more your thing.
As a shark you can eat divers and evolve with better fins, sharper teeth, etc. The sharks also have 2 ways to win: 1) Kill all divers, 2) Destroy STEVE. In my experience all sharks are balanced except maybe the Hammerhead if on the map Galeon.
Maps: Good, bar galeon and Temple which are just aweful as a diver
Overall a very fun game, lacking in gamemodes as "Blood and Gold" is the only one anyone plays but still a good game, made better by having friends to play with

This game is great, it's an assymetrical battle with small teams and some really unique concepts and execution. Every functionally unique weapon/upgrade/etc can be unlocked in 12-20 hours depending on skill, so everybody is on the same playing field.
Divers are easy to play and have really tight controls, as well as a wide set of very different feeling guns and tools. Whether you like harpoon pistols, full-auto bullet-based rifles, or a shotgun that shoots a ring of spears, every weapon handles a little differently. Utility and support items aren't underpowered or unfun either, you can look in the shop menu and none of the items are too situational or underpowered.
Sharks are harder to play, or at least to get used to, being that they are larger and don't have the ability to swim backwards. Sharks play from the third person, and they control with their bodies following where the nose goes, it's a little difficult to explain. There are currently six shark species with two more on the horizon and possibly more in the future. Sharks all have different stats based on species, as well as each having a unique special ability. Other universal upgrades can be bought, with very meaningful alterations in gameplay, such as the ability to change your direction while lunging (a long range dash), or serrated teeth to force divers you don't manage to kill to seek out healthpacks or bleed out. Shark upgrades are more limited, meaning the decision is more meaningful than choosing a gun, as the wrong upgrade can result in you not having enough power to fight effectively against the divers in the late game. As such, some upgrades are simply more universal than another, though this is more because there are so many counter-play upgrades for shark, should they be faced against divers utilizing net guns or tranquilizing bullets or whatever else.
The only problems with the game are minor things like balance tweaking and a slightly undersized playerbase, it can also feel a tad monotonous because of the limited gamemodes. The game is very stable, and with wide graphical options I can get thirty frames even on a five year old prebuilt.

Now, i feel it worth stating, that, while i might come off as trying to be edgy or the like during this review, that's not the intention. I'm just someone who immensely enjoys toying with and ripping prey to pieces.
In my opinion, after having played 100+ hours almost exclusively as a shark, Depth is an immensely fun and interesting game that breaks the mold a lot of other similar games fall into. While it can be extremely unforgiving for new players, especially due to the comparatively limited playerbase over other games making a matchmaking system based on skill impractical for que times, once you get past the learning curve, Depth becomes an extremely well balanced asymetrical multiplayer game, with neither side having a particular advantage as long as the divers even remotely coordinate and work together.
Now, of course, there're some players out there who will absolutely destroy you, (myself included) no matter how good you think you are until you reach the peak in skill, but that's par for the course with any game, and shouldn't be taken as the norm. It's also worth noting that the community is, for the mostpart, extremely welcoming even if we don't appear that way, and willing to work with people to improve. I myself almost always offer the divers a choice of difficulty, for example, and play accordingly to make it fairer, and even give a tutorial style game to those who've just started playing.
The only other thing i can really think to say at this point about depth is that if a player answers get good in regards to a question about how to deal with a particular problem, it's a legitimate serious answer in depth's case. that learning curve is vicisious, and we were all at the bottom of it at one point.

Strongly recommended if you're a fan of the wire or the shield or any other cop drama.  It's a point and click adventure delivered through a comic book style, interspersed with some Walking Dead style level of minimal scene investigation by your character around some fairly static scenes where you interact with objects and talk to other NPCs.  You play from the perspectives of various characters including a policewoman, a detective, and an informant.
The graphics are a mixed bag.  The comic book style cutscenes are good, but some of the character models are a bit ropey.  Particularly when they're in movement, they look a touch unnatural.
Sound is pretty minimal.  And though voice acting would have been a boon had it been done right I'm aware this is a fairly indie game, and it's better to have none at all if you can't afford the quality stuff.
It's also got it's fair share of bugs.  With disappearing hotspots, unclickable hotspots, conversations coming out nonsensically if you do them in the "wrong order", and I definitely noticed my after-episode summary incorrectly identified my actions on more than one occasion.
But where this game really shines and is the key point for my recommendation, is the story, and the end has a great pay off.  The pacing is good, the dialogue in general is pretty good.  I did feel at times that a lot of my decisions didn't alter the story that much, and that there was a fair bit of the game chaperoning me through the scenes, and couldn't really take a step wrong without the game getting me through the scene anyway, but then again that's a criticism you could level at L.A. Noire.

Within each of these, you can choose to either use violence, or try and talk your way into and out of situations.  I'm not sure that the episodes end differently either way, but the Steam achievements vary.  The police-procedural runs on a successful formula that has spawned nearly 20 years of Law&Order, CSI, NCIS, Criminal Minds, etc.  There's nothing really new here, but it's all put together pretty well for a noirish point/click experience.  Maybe wait for a sale, because I finished both episodes 1 and 2 in a total of about 3 hours.

Many 15 year old spoiled 'merican brats hate this game because their own ignorance led them to believe that it would be Mass Effect, a means to be cool, a cure for acne, and a bag of chips.
For those of us who are actually aware of the survival genre and expect this game, which is part of that genre, to reflect that fact, No Man's Sky is absolutely awesome.
Pros:
+great graphics
+runs smoothly with little load time
+the universe you have access to in this game is beyond massive
+tons of unique environments yielding various resources
+compelling progression goals focused on utility and advancement as well as travel and discovery
+huge amount of awesome looking ships any of which can be obtained in game for your use
+in addition to owning several smaller starships, the player can own their own gigantic space freighter complete with a hanger for all your other ships as well as base building real estate
+meaningful, fun, and cool looking base building
+the new exocraft land vehicles are really useful and feel great to use, especially the Roamer
+compelling milestone in-game achievements
+enjoyable dog-fighting while in space complete with the choice to defend freighters against bandits or attack the freighters for their cargo
+fun combat vs sentinel droids that you get steadily more effective at as you upgrade your exosuit and multitool
+your base, ships, freighter, and planets you discover can all be renamed as much as you like
Cons:
-a little buggy sometimes (I've had about 3 crashes over the course of just under 100 hours and sometimes when I dismount my exocraft after farming for a while it flings me several yards away)
-minor graphic errors in a couple spots (nothing major though)
-learning curve can seem a bit much at first (during my first run I thought about starting over and doing things more effectively but stuck with it). After almost 100 hours I'm still learning things about this game and how to manage my base, ships, and resources better. I personally like this but some might not.
-if you accidentally attack sentinel drones in space their response is a little too strong (they jam your hyper drive so you can't jump away and then continue to attack you until they take you out).
-navigating both on planets and in space can be tricky until you get the hang of it.
If you like the survival genre, I can say with confidence that you will probably have a blast with No Man's Sky for many many hours. However if you're a hater then let's be honest- a million dollars and a new Ferrari probably won't please you, so a video game probably won't either. A lot of people jumped on the hate train for this game like it was a fad or something but I'm having a great time and although I say it about few games- this one feels like a great deal of love was put into it. As a long time gamer, I truly appreciate that, regardless of the rocky start this game had.
Just some context for those who don't know: Some of the features I mention here as pros were recently added in a new and very large (free) content patch (base building for instance is new) and people who have played the game post-patch seem to feel it's a welcome update.
Sorry for being pissy about the haters but I really love this game and I want to support it :P

It's been years since I first played this game, back on Xbox 360. Back then, I loved it, and I enjoyed coming back to the DC wasteland and find new locations to explore. More importantly, it's the game that introduced me to what is now one of my favorite franchises, and I have a healthy dose of nostalgia for it.
But holy hell, the passage of time hasn't been kind to Fallout 3. I would not recommend playing it today unless you are ready to sit down and mod it for a few hours just to get it to
Graphically, I think it actually kind of holds up, and the capital wasteland still has a certain beauty and charm that the Mojave desert and the Commonwealth didn't quite manage to capture. Characters look like potatoes but don't completely distract from the experience. Musically, it's quite good. The new direction for the ambient music is great, if not as dark and chilling as the Fallout1 and 2 soundtracks. The radio's a brilliant element and GNR and Enclave Radio both have a solid, if unsubtle ("Do you get it this game is about the APOCALYPSE ?!") choice of themes.
Technically, it's a mess. Glitchy as hell, difficult to run on modern hardware and operating systems, yet surprisingly stable once you actually get it to run. This is why I said the years haven't been kind to Fallout 3. In terms of gameplay, it's the second most shallow entry in the series behind Fallout 4, and the gunplay and gun selection is downright terrible by modern standards. Heck, even back then, the lack of ironsights made it a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥to play and the spread of some weapons is unfrigginbelievable, even with a gun skill of 100. You'll spend most of your time shooting things and the combat is terrible, so...yeah.
But the cherry on top of the cake is the absolutely atrocious writing of the main quest and most sidequests. Thanks Emil. Back when I first played the game, I kind of tuned out the story because it was so boring, with a lot of rude and uninteresting characters who make stupid decisions all the time. Oh, and of course there's next to no choice in this game, because that's absolutely not something Fallout is known for, right ?
And yet, despite all my criticisms, I still bought the game and played through the whole story again. Is it nostalgia ? Is it the dumb fun of exploring the ruins of a blasted wasteland ? Probably both. Regardless, Fallout 3 is still worth playing through at least once, for shitz and giggles if nothing else.

Honestly, it's not like it's -completely- terrible, but it completely missed the mark on what made the Gauntlet games fun, regardless of whether you're referring to the classic arcade games or the 3D ones of the Playstation 1/2 era,
Rather than build on what the previous Gauntlet games had been like they decided to take more inspiration from the old arcade/nes games and it really just feels like a giant step backward. Gauntlet Legends had the players climbing an active volcanoe, exploring a disease-ridden town, and fighting through a huge, corrupt cathedral, among other locations. This just has you exploring dark cave corridors ending in square rooms, over and over and over. Sometimes instead of cave corridors it's generic, grey, uninspired dungeon corridors that still end in square rooms. Sometimes the caves have spiders, or maybe even a single demon, who are some of the only enemies who break the monotony of killing hundreds of generic dead-in-one-hit mooks.
That in mind, the idea of blasting hundreds of minions is pretty standard for gauntlet games, but this game seemed to miss everything that made them fun. The original Gauntlet/Gauntlet 2 had you moving at practically a breakneck speed as you stormed through the dungeon killing minions and spawners, hoping to find your next food before your health bar ticked away. In this game, a single spawner will easily take 15-30 seconds of just sitting there wailing on it until it finally dies, spawning wave after wave of enemies the whole time which makes it just take even longer, and it's downright boring whenever you have to fight through a room with more than one spawner in it.
Even the bosses manage to be completely and utterly bland. To again use it as an example, Gauntlet Legends bosses all had somewhere around 4-5 attacks, if not more, and it sported 6 boss fights, with even more added in the Playstation 2 remake. This game only has 3 bosses, two of which only seemed to have a single attack (the other only had two), and one of them is basically just fighting wave after wave of regular enemies and then the boss using his -only- attack in-between waves when he was vulnerable.
Even though it has barely 8 hours of content(for all I know even less, a chunk of that time was probably the game idling for trading cards) you feel like you've experienced 90% of the game after the 2-hour mark, everything past that is just tedius, and there's plenty of far better twin-stick shooters out there for the same price or cheaper.

★OVERALL★
Let me start by saying I'm
a fan of platformers. Out of the 264 games I own only 7 of them are platformers. Generally speaking, I find them boring, too difficult, or lacking in story development. I wasn't a Mario Bros kid, I was a Sonic the Hedgehog kid.
Ori and the Blind Forest takes all the great mechanics from Metroid, Castlevania, Sonic, and other 2D platformers from the classic console era and puts them into their game with expert precision. Then wraps the gameplay in one of the most emotionally driven and deeply touching stories since Bamby or the Lion King. And if that wasn't enough to get your Feels O' Meter hitting 9000, they finish you off with an amazing soundtrack choreographed by a real chamber orchestra that could easily compete with the big boys at Blizzard and Disney.
Despite all this praise I must err on the side of caution to tell you that this is
an easy game! There are times when exact precision and retention of muscle memory is required to complete dexterous maneuvers, especially during "escape" runs. Trial and error by death is the only way to get past a lot of the obstacles and objectives. However, if you can push past these difficulties you'll be rewarded with a story that will touch your heart, thrill you when completing challenges, and become an instant favorite among your game library.
★STORY★
You play as Ori, a cat-like spirit that resides within the a great tree at the center of the forest. When Ori becomes separated from the Spirit Tree during the great storm, Naru, a "forest mother," discovers the young spirit and raises it as her own child. The two quickly bond and, for a time, find peace. But the forest of Nibel is dying, food is running out, and Naru must protect her new family as long as hope holds out. But hope alone cannot sustain them, and Naru sacrifices herself so that Ori may live. An orphan once again, Ori sets out into a dark, decaying forest full of enemies to solve the mystery that plagues his home, find a way to revive the Spirit Tree, and (hopefully) revive the creature Naru whom he's come to know as mother.
Moon Studio wasn't exaggerating when they said that Ori and the Blind Forest explores a deeply emotional story about love and sacrifice, and the hope that exists in us all. This story will make you believe in love again.
★GAMEPLAY★
This is one of those games that starts off incredibly difficult to the point of hair pulling frustration. Your health is low, the Energy you use for save points is minimal and rare to find, and you have no special abilities with which to overcome most of the obstacles you see. But with time comes power. More and more health to the point of almost invincibility. Ludicrous amounts of Energy allows you to save as often as you want. And once all your Abilities are unlocked, you'll be able to navigate the entire map and reach any objective you desire.
But that doesn't mean things will be easy. There's still plenty of challenge to go around. And even at max HP, you'll still die occasionally. This is emphasized during "escape" runs, sometimes appropriately called "gauntlets." Trial and error, success and failure are the only means to surpass these events. You'll have to remember the pattern of traps, pitfalls, and execute maneuvers with expert precision. Gameplay can run between 7 and 15 hours depending on how much you complete and/or if you speed run through the game. So put the dog outside, turn off your phone, and tell work you're pulling a sickie, because the forest of Nibel needs you, and Ori is their only hope!
★SOUND & MUSIC★
With a beautiful soundtrack choreographed by a chamber orchestra that resonates through your heart, the music of Ori and the Blind Forest perfectly sets the mood of the story as it unfolds through animated cutscenes that were hand painted. Sound effects are spot on, adding to the whimsical ambience of a spiritual forest full of creatures both light and dark in nature. Everything feels appropriate and natural.
★BUGS & BOTHERS★
I'm pretty critical of games. Coming from a 90's kid, I remember when video games had to ship out perfect and bug free, because there was no way to update the game once it reached the hands of gamers. Sure, you could re-release it later with a special edition to fix bugs and add new content, but since most people either had no internet or 56k modems, pushing big updates through the internet wasn't an option. Unfortunately, with the easy access and huge bandwidths of our modern era also comes lazy developers, bulky code, and bugs galore. A general attitude of, "Just fix it later" has become the norm. Pressure to ship new games each yearly quarter has filled the pockets of big corporate developers, but it's emptied the expectations of us, the gamers.
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of those extremely rare games where I experienced absolutely
bugs. NO BUGS! The game mechanics worked perfectly every time and deaths were the sole responsibility of my own mistakes. Since I can't speak of any bugs, I guess the only bother I'd give this game is that it might be too difficult for some people. It is frustrating sometimes and that might deter a few gamers from completing the whole thing.

This game is all about immersion. A few of the most striking features include its wonderfully designed setting and a unique soundtrack which blends the traditional adventure sound of the orchestra with the exhileration of electronic modulation. The scenery of Neoparis is a stunning and enveloping display of the vast abilities of the design teams, and many of the futuristic concepts, such as ever-present drones, weirdly yet creatively designed robots, and the center of the game's technology: the sensen, are all innovative and pioneering ideas. I also enjoy what most of the major gaming companies identified as its biggest mistake: having a female protagonist. Nihlin is strong, smart, and has nicely rounded character development throughout the story. I wish some of the things in the game would've been further explained, such as the existance of Leapers, the history of sensen technology (rather than limiting it to simple text entries), and how it has affected the world as a whole, rather than focusing singularly on Neoparis. The combo lab is another really interesting feature that I feel could've been a bit more in-depth than it was designed to be. Still, that's what future games are for, which I hope is something that this developer will utilize. I believe that Remember Me is all-in-all a fantastic game, but to me, it's only a beta test of sorts for the real talent and potential that the game team can present, and I sincerely hope that they get the chance to show us what they can do.

Think of it as an extended tutorial section taken from some kind of FPS game. You get to shoot different targets with variety of weapons, such as pistol, shotgun, sniper rifle or AK-47. You don't move your character - you only aim, shoot, and reload (sometimes you use scope as well). In most missions your time is very limited, so you have to work fast and try not to waste ammo. The game is not too hard though - if you just want to finish it there are only 2-3 missions that can be really challenging. Getting platinum medals in all missions is a different story and a real challenge. Game contains no violence - you only shoot objects such as wooden figures, pumpkins or cans, so kids are safe to play it.
Cons? Graphics are a bit dated (but acceptable in this price range) and the game itself is very short - you can easily play through all the levels in under two hours. There are achievements and medals, however, that will keep you occupied for a longer period of time. If you're looking for something casual or need a break from "serious" games - Reload should do the trick.

For the majority of the time the game is ridiculously easy, the only time I ever got frustrated, is when I "lost" (using that word very loosely) at the aka-47 level, I got splated 10 times (due the aka-47 being the most annoying to use in the game) and I exspected to do the level all over again. To my surprise, the game kept my score and I got the platinum medal. Almost as if I did not lose at all. So if you are achievement hunting, those platinum medals are far more easy to get than you thought. You want you're game to have some form of punishment for loseing, naturally you don't want to punish you're players to badly to the point where they don't want to play anymore, yet at the same time you don't want to make the game so easy, that their is barely little to no punishment for losing.
Multiplayer, at this point as far as I know, is just a hot seat. Meaning you and you're friends "localy" take turns to see who can get the highest score. I can honestly say for a game like this, it might be the best thing the devs can up with.

^ Although the graphics are relatively polished for a story game, the rather hideous character models and uninspired environment really let it down - how are things this unpleasent to look at outside of the 90's?  It's well shaded and most objects look like they belong (although there's a girl on couch in the first ep that doesn't actually look like she's lying on the sofa - more like she's propped up at a 45 degree incline, despite the absence of anything supporting her -  this almost levitation looks really off and breaks the rather dark undertones of the girls situation).
^ The basic facial models are just way too bland and not differientiated enough to hide the cookie cutter template underneath - how much inbreeding is going on in this rather unpopulated city?
^ The women's facial models are even worse - they look kinda dumpy and the NPC's are all in grey and static indicating that you cannot interact with them, I get what they were going for but it's just plain ugly imo (e.g. why not show that if you roll your cursor over them but leave them fully fleshed out in the environment otherwise?).
^ Basically, the comic book and noir style has been done better in older games so this really should look gorgeous by comparison but when you compare this to say the 20 year-old classic noir Bladerunner game you'll see why I'm complaining; there is very little imagination going on here and so much more could have been done to fill out the world atmosphere.  If you compare this to the far more recent and substantial in content, The wolf among us, it just pales in comparison and never hanbles the mature subject matter in an impactful way like Life is strange managed to do.  Of course these are far larger games by much larger studios.
* Puzzles offer zero challenge  (calling them puzzles is a stretch tbh).
* No voice acting, this game is done in a comic book style but I think it would have helped the imersion and also help break up the constant drone of depressing music.  If they had invested the money and time in more graphical assets, refining the environments and storyline I'd understand but I find the graphics pretty unapealing.
* Cannot really skip when forced to replay (bugs - I lost count of how many times I replayed episodes)
* Music is heavy handed - yes we get its supposed to be a representation of our burnout protagonist but its wears quickly and it never seems to stop.
* No sound effects whatsoever
* The twist is meh and I'm sure its supposed to make the climax of the game tense but its all so predictable and I have no investment in any of these ugly♥♥♥♥♥chacters
* Dialogue is as cliched as the rest of this "game"
Bugs
* When this game first came out, every update whether a patch or actual new episodes would completely delete your save games, so I had to play the first 2 episodes at least 3 times and it really highlighted how godamn bored I was.  There is no replay value here - the first episode tends to have more impactful choices but it really doesn't change the narrative to any significant degree and far too much happens off screen.
* Random crashes - which again forced me to replay sections - over and over again, if you look at my playtime you'll see its way higher than other reviewers', when each epside only lasts a few hours knocking up 30+ hours of game play really illustrates how many frigging times I had to slog through this crap.
Verdict
Maybe I'm being harsh but I love detective games and noir and this didn't really satify either itch.  Go buy some silly putty or plastersine and make some ugly character models of your choice whilst watching an old episode of columbo - believe me it will be far more satisfying.
Go for it if you like the telltale game series. This is more of an interactive story than a game. A very mature detective story with some hard moral choices.

I was very late getting to this game, and the reviews and praise had been out for several years before I got to play.  So I was expecting great things, I was expecting to be crushed by the end of the game, I was expecting an amazing soundtrack.  I was expecting-- something fun, at least-- out of the gameplay.  None of those things were delivered.
Why make a game out of this?  Is this the best medium to tell your story?  Is your story even worth telling?  The premise is that an old man full of regrets effectively wants to cancel his entire life on his deathbed through memory manipulation.  He dies with false memories.  Would you rather die knowing the truth, or die in a lie, ignorantly blissful?  Now thats an interesting question, but it was completely ignored by the game creator who unequivocally sides with the lie.
Its cool that games want to be art.  There are not many games that strive to be.  But you can't just praise a game because its one of few that tries to be something greater.  If this was a book or a movie, if the soundtrack was a standalone CD, if the game was simply a 2D puzzle game without any art, it would be completely criticised in EVERY aspect.
Ultimately this game is a waste of time unless you just want to see where the indie game industry is trying to go.  If you're looking for a thoughtful story, beautiful art and music, all wrapped up in an interactive video game, you might be disappointed.

Short form: This game offers massive potential, but lacks key features to compete with other games in the genre. Recommended to wait until dedicated servers and custom vehicles are released.
Long form: Minecraft's inception defined a brand new genre that many others are taking advantage of, like Terraria, Starbound, Robocraft to an extent, and From the Depths. It was only natural the the LEGO company tried their hand at the genre, because that's what LEGO is, right?
So, what does the current Update 6 of LEGO Worlds offer?
Not much to be honest. You get a procedurally generated LEGO world that you can explore and do some fetch quests. I attempted to build a home from scratch, however, it was clear the controls are suited to gamepads and controllers - building anything decent with a mouse and keyboard is a nightmare. The potential is there however - as it is a voxel based game (and the voxels themselves are quite small), having enough patience with the building system allows you to build literally whatever you want, from the city of Manhattan to a giant dragon, even a 1:1 replica of the Bismark...
Unfortunately, the fun ends there. You can't really do much with your finished builds except look at them, maybe take a screenshot and show off to your friends. You can't animate your dragon and have it fly around and you can't attract people to your Manhattan and build an empire... Worse yet, you can't take that Bismark you built out to sea, locate the nearest player-built costal village, and then transform it into a LEGO crater with your 15 inch guns while fending off attacks from those players trying so desprately to protect it.
For what LEGO Worlds is at the moment, there is a distinct lack of real cooperative and competitive multiplayer elements that make the other sandbox games what they are. There's no dedicated servers (which Minecraft has), only 4-player splitscreen like a console game. There's no ability to truly enter space and perhaps jump into another persons world arbitrarily, like in Starbound. Lastly, there's no mad scientists in the community building precisely engineered war machines to take LEGO Worlds on by storm like what From the Depths has.
In the end, LEGO Worlds has the potential to be a truly great game (it IS LEGO), but they have stiff competition to stand out from the giant that is Minecraft, to the endless possibilities of Starbound, and to the savage genius of From The Depths.
Keep the game on your watch list, but don't buy into it just yet.

O3DX is a game I find hard to recommend. In my short time playing the game I had a bit of fun with it, but there were also a lot of frustrations and parts that just made me want to rip my hair out.
The game plays a lot like a Trials type game. The only issue is that the vehicles in this game have physics that are constantly changing each time I play the level. It took me a good while to beat the first level just because the car would sometimes not go fast enough to get over a rock.
The game is also very unforgiving. There are no checkpoints at all, and if you make one mistake you are stuck and have to go back to the beginning. I just found this rather annoying. I would go too slow and get stuck. I would go too fast and hit explosive barrels that blow up my vehicle.
Another issue I had was the controls. This is more so due to how the camera is worked in this game. With a static camera that stays in one position the controls make sense. With it constantly rotating it makes it hard to figure out which button will rotate me forward and which will rotate me backwards.
The only other thing I found wrong with the game is my timer always seemed to be bugged. Instead of going up at a constant rate it was very jumpy and updating at random intervels. A sort of meh thing but it still bothered me to look at.
Not all of the game is bad though. It looks really nice and and the music, though it does drone, is also well done.
Overall I'd say my experience was rather lackluster, but it is in early access (according to the store page as I'm writing this) so maybe some of this will change in the future? I don't know. I enjoy the concept of the game and love games like this but it's just hard to recommend this one in particular.

O3DX is fun. That's the first thing you should remember. I'm saying it at the beginning, because this game is early access, and this review is going to mention a lot of things that still need to be improved. But the game is fun, and challenging, and I really enjoy playing it.
What the creators of this game say, is that with O3DX they have tried to create a new game genre. Something different for gamers to experience. Have they accomplished it? Well...
Lets start with first impressions. First impressions are not that great. The first few levels of O3DX are extremely easy, and honestly left me somewhat confused to what the point of the game is. If you've ever heard of Trials Fusion, then you will know what I mean. O3DX is like Trials Fusion, but with cars. If you don't know what Trials Fusion is, it's like a side scroller, but in a 3D environment. Your vehicles is somewhat "glued" to a set path, and all you can do is choose when to accelerate.
The steering is extremely simple, you can accelerate, reverse, break, and lean your vehicle forwards and backwards. Which is where some of my initial confusion came from - in the first levels all I needed to do was hold the up arrow button. You can imagine my reaction, what's the point of game where you just hold one button to complete a level?
However, I looked at some of the reviews, so positive, all mentioning, you should at least get through 6-8 levels before you judge. So I did, and then I got to the good stuff.
What the first levels did was getting me used to how the vehicles react. They also showed off the truly lovely graphics of the various environments that you drive through. (This game is definitely lense flare central, and I love it, I'm a sucker for a good lense flare.) Getting used to the dynamic, cinematic camera angles is another thing. They look great, but they also add some difficulty as very often they won't allow you to see the path ahead. You have to quickly learn to memorize the paths. The first levels also allowed me to enjoy the badassery of the short but very rock'n'roll soundtrack. On a side note, some levels also offer a sudden unexpected slow motion moment, when the car is doing a particularly epic jump. Not gonna lie, it's entertaining.
The developers also mention extremely realistic physics in the game, and I would be willing to agree the cars reactions are usually very much on point. With the occasional sillines, when for example my car instantly flipped onto its hood when it literally touched a wooden plank on the road.
Once you get through the first few levels, and you think you got the hang of this simple game... it gets unbelievably more difficult. The further you get into it the more obstacles the levels introduce. Some of them explosive, some of them mobile, some of them just really really difficult to get through. Having a good feel of the acceleration rate and timing in this game is everything, and it's very unforgiving. When a game is challenging I start really having fun. If I am willing to retry the same level 20 times in a row, that's a sign of a great game.
In the end I do have to remind everyone that this is early access, and early access always comes with a baggage. In the short time I played it, the game crashed on me twice.
