Never written a Steam review I don't think so here goes.
I really enjoyed The New Order (even if it did drag on a bit towards the end) and had high hopes for The New Colossus (especially after watching gameplay videos before release - maybe they captured those from the console versions). I love the whole alternate history idea where the Nazis won WW2 and took over the world.
The game starts off OK and the story seems good (picks up after New Order) but, after about three hours, it's just too glitchy and buggy to continue (for example, missing textures in the New York City sections). I thought I'd push through this (maybe just one of those rare cases?) but then I encountered hanging loading screens, and then the game wouldn't load a save file until after multiple restarts (of the game itself) and a files integrity check through Steam (which came back OK).
When you eventually get into the game it can be quite fun. The gameplay is good (brutal like the first one) with stealth and run-and-gun sections; the guns and melee take-downs are cool and the enemies are quite interesting. The environments didn't pull me in as much as New Order's (just not as interesting - things like posters, newspaper clippings, buildings etc) - same for the characters (there's a little bit of a background of events given at the start of the game if you haven't played New Order).
Unfortunately, I can't get a refund as I'm past the cut-off mark. I've uninstalled the game but hopefully (HOPEFULLY) it will be patched and brought up to a better quality - until then, I probably won't reinstall it. I know there are a myriad of PC setups, and it's hard to account for all of them, but I think this version should've been delayed (perhaps a couple of months) to further work on it and refine it (I certainly don't remember encountering anywhere near the same level of issues as with New Order). If you have a PlayStation/Xbox, perhaps you'd be better off getting the game for them (if they're less buggy/glitchy).
Overall, like many others here, I'm quite disappointed and even kinda feel like I've wasted my money but I hoped the game would be as good as its prequel (if not better). At the moment, I can't recommend it - perhaps I can if they fix the issues and/or the game drops in price.

5th Nov. update:
I ploughed on and completed the story/campaign. Fortunately, the number of bugs and crashes seemed to die down as I progressed further (nVidia released an updated driver recently so perhaps that's why). I got about 10 hours or so out of the campaign and that was me taking my time through the environments, having a 'nosey' around, looking at posters, the landscapes, and making sure I saw everything (or most things) in an area before moving on.
I think the story was good but still not as interesting as New Order's. Some may like it and some may hate it. I'm not sure if it's strictly a political commentary on past or even current events in America (and elsewhere) but my personal opinion is that, at times, it felt a bit "preachy" (even from the "good guys'" point of view).

I'll not spoil the ending. While I think it wasn't quite a cliffhanger, it did feel a bit underwhelming compared to The New Order's (including the level that precedes it).
The levels themselves are good, though sometimes they felt repetitive (a lot of corridors, stairs and confined spaces - not much variety). Areas can be quite similar to each other, maybe TOO similar at times - frequently, I had to check the map to see if I had gone round on myself.
Saying that, I did like when (spoiler?) I got to ride the Panzerhund - basically, a big mechnical dog with a flamethrower in its mouth - even though the ride was quite short, it felt like one of the few moments when the game offered something new/different in terms of gameplay (the other being a "contraption" of your choosing later on in the game which gives you another ability. I chose the Battle Walkers, mechanical legs which allow you to reach higher places - stilts, essentially).
You can upgrade your weapons in the game though I didn't really feel like the upgrades actually made the guns, or gameplay, much different.
There's no multiplayer on offer but that doesn't bother me. I even like that they focused solely on the singleplayer.
Having finished the story/campaign, would I recommend Wolfenstein 2? Yes and no. (unfortunately, Steam doesn't offer a middle ground!)
Yes, because the game is fun - the shooting is great, the characters are quite interesting, the cutscenes are good, and even the audio and music are good (especially if you're into Metal/Rock during action scenes). You might even like it if you enjoyed last year's Doom. And, for such a violent game, the story can be surprisingly heartfelt.
No, because while the game is fun, I don't feel like it radically improves upon New Order. It can be quite "samey" in terms of its enemies and environments.
Overall, I personally would still wait until the game drops in price. It's not bad by any means but, in my opinion, I don't think it's an essential purchase.

I was introduced to this game by my brother, who bought and played this on his Xbox One. We are both long time fans of Nintendo and Metroid, and he said to me, "This is the best 'Metroid' game we've had in years.". He told me I had to play it. I said I'd get to it when it went on sale on Steam. It did. I bought it, but I didn't play. One night, he thrust the Xbox controller in my hands and demanded, "Play." I did. And then I finally played it, and I was overwhelmed by nostalgia, beauty, and mirth, for I died many times to silly things. After that, I picked up the game here on Steam, replayed through the first half of the game, and went on to beat it. The 'hype' for this game is real. It is worth every minute you put into it, even if you're just jumping around as little Ori for the sake of playing and enjoying the atmosphere.
Some have called this game rage-inducing, too hard, or punishing on the player. These are perhaps true, at least to a degree. Rage-inducing? Sure, I was pretty frustrated escaping the Ginso Tree. Too hard? There sure were parts that ramped up the difficulty, especially around the final third of the game. Punishing on the player? What game -isn't-? If you don't die a few times and learn from your mistakes, where is the challenge of a game?
The fact is, this game is not for everyone. If you're a casual gamer and don't like trying different methods to get through a section, by all means, pass up playing--BUT WATCH A LET'S PLAY for the experience. But, most other players should be able to get through this just fine. Yeah, you might die a thousand times (not even joking there), but the heart-warming message of the story is worth every minute of game play. The fact is, this game didn't need to happen (you'll understand if you've experienced the story). And that's the beauty of it.
Please do yourself a favor and give this game a chance. If you're on the fence, watch someone else play it. Just experience this game. It'll kick you in the feels.

A great management company simulation, hindered by some design and depth issues.
At it's core, you manage a fleet of ships for a budding company and an insane investor (maybe they're like this in real life too).

For example, there's no way to tell what port your ships originally bought goods from in-game (write it down), you can't "assign" ships to a mission, you manually tell em where to go each time and what goods to buy (rename your ships each time for 100k LOL, or write it down), and contraband is illegal and smacks you for like 20-60% of your net worth, but you won't find out till you get caught (random, almost never worth it after a while).
On sale, for a bit of fun, yes, I would recommend this or just grabbing Factorio lol.

Ok, let's get this straight out of the way: if you're looking for a standard hack and slash action game in which you can just skip all dialogue and mash your controller all the way to victory, just walk away. This game is not for you. It does have epic, very difficult battles, against enemies of all sorts, but those are actually kind of sporadic, especially in the early game. They are never the main focus of the plot. So, if you want to play Call of Duty, just go play freaking Call of Duty and look up the word "plot". I'll judge you, but that doesn't mean anything.
What I found in Hellblade was something I hadn't felt in a long time, and missed dearly. It allowed me not merely to control a bunch of pixels on my screen, but to feel so immersed in the game that it felt like I WAS the main character, who is not only amazingly interesting, but the owner of a very peculiar mind. As someone who has some history with mental illness and the way it pushes you away from others and deeper and deeper into your own issues, I was touched by Ninja Theory's bold decision to portray that ugly aspect of an ill human mind and make it the center of their story.
Thank you for that, and congratulations on a job done so amazingly I have actually been defeated by Senua's illness, and not the enemies around me, more than once in fight scenes. The way the voices address you can be quite disturbing and uncomfortable. Not the case for me, thankfully, and I'm glad I could enjoy the game so thoroughly, squeezing more than 24 hours out of it in a single playthrough. And we're talking about a game with no collectibles, so it's not like I you need to frequently check for supplies in suspicious containers. IIRC, you can go through the entire game picking up merely 5 objects (maybe less!), and using your eyes to take in the beauty of Senua's world, instead of scouting for medkits.
I have enjoyed the game greatly, with its unusual narrative techniques, great research work and a character that actually feels relatable. I was also happy to see a female character in a lead role, especially one that directly involves physical skill and fitness, fine tuned reflexes, and an overall ability to simply kick everyone's butts. It is the sort of game I would gladly play with my daughter, just to break the unstoppable "you're supposed to be pretty and delicate" doctrine we so frequently see, even amongst our own generation.
Anyhow, just wanted to let you know that you have created an absolutely amazing work, and definitely got yourselves a fan. For me, a solid 10/10. Keep up the good work! ;)

Just finished the first two episodes and I have to say, I'm very impressed.
I read my fair share of graphic novels so I took to the art style straight away. Exceptionally well done and lovely to look at. The game also feels like a graphic novel as it's choice and dialogue focused; there's no inventory in this game. So you have to think about what your character is going to do and how he's going to respond to each person.
I liked the interface: just hover your mouse cursor over something then use right-click to select between the various options to interact with that thing. Quick, easy and efficient.

Although I currently don't recommend buying this game, read on to find out why:
The Detail is an indie crime-thriller adventure game using a motion comic aesthetic. It's very nice. The story and characters might come off as a little cliche, but the amount of detail that's gone into the police investigation side of things makes the experience fairly immersive. I played through Episode 1 twice in order to see just how much player choice mattered. There are many gameplay similarities to the Telltale adventure games, though choice in Telltale is nearly nonexistent (it's an illusion). It's hard to make that conclusion with The Detail from a single Episode, but choosing much different approaches certainly led to different situations coming up. Not drastically, but the narrative wobbled about in different ways before re-converging to the main plot thread. From a technical stand point, the game ran without issues on my computer.
Having said all of this mostly positive stuff, why do I not recommend the game? Basically, game length, and bang for buck. There just isn't much here. With my play time above, I was able to do Episode 1 from start to finish twice, and I wasn't even rushing things. The police investigation pickings were detailed, yes, but it had barely gotten started. I still felt like we were in the character introduction stage and the Episode ended. To put a number on it, you can beat Episode 1 in about 40 minutes, which quite a bit shorter than, say, the Telltale games (which are also quite short, but usually on the order of 2 hours).
As of the writing of this review, there is an Episode 1 and an Episode 2. I KNOW for a fact there's no chance the story can resolve itself, or get particularly deep, with one more episode of the same length as Episode 1. Also, $7 for 40 minutes is a little on the steep end. For my part, I'm going to wait until more episodes are released so I can experience the entire story.
There's something good here, and the developers have done a good job with what there is, but there needs to be... more. More... Detail.

The Detail
Pros:
- Fast paced gameplay
- Fast paced narrative
- Casual pick up and enjoy game, great for busy lives in need of quick escapism
- Replay value for achievements and gameplay decision options
- Fantastic art style
- Perfect mood setting musical score
- The stereotypical characters are developed well to become interesting in the round
Cons:
- The raw gameplay derives more from dialogue or action options rather than traditional point and click puzzles
- Lack of traditional systems like verb icons or inventory mean the gameplay lacks depth (but this does not mean the narrative lacks depth)
- The lack of episodes is the real problem
Overall:
- The hybrid visual novel/point and click hybrid allows the narrative to take centre stage. There is no turning back due to the comic book style narrative.
- This also means there is no room for endless backtracking talking to NPCs over and over and no fidgetting with inventory items wondering what to do next. Thats a good thing though. The endless backtracking and fidgetting really only works in comedy point and click games with humorous exchanges rather than in serious toned games where you just become frustrated if you can't progress
- I did find that the game only let the player do the raw policework but did not let the player "solve" any of the clues or policework. The characters often solved it for you or automatically explained what a clue meant etc.
- The biggest downside is that so much is put into the narrative that it works almost too well. Episode 1 really does feel like a pilot episode of a really engaging crime noir series. Then you realise only two episodes are available!

Fossil Echo is a challenging, story driven platformer that often requires quick reflexes, and good timing.
You play as a boy on a quest to climb a massive tower. The story is short, but I was immediately interested in finding out what happened right after the first cutscene. After reaching the end of the story though, I did wish there was more. While the ending makes sense, it felt like I didn’t quite get the full closure that I was hoping for.
You can take your time on some of the levels, but others are highly dependent on speed and precision. You have no way to kill enemies face-to-face, but you can jump from a high enough distance to knock them out by landing on them. You can often avoid enemies completely if you time it well, but you can also get them to kill each other if you position yourself right.
I played through the game three times in around 5 hours. After my first playthrough, I realized I missed all the optional levels, so I wanted to go back and play it again. Then I went back to play it a third time to see if I could find more secrets. I was able to find some secrets, but there were still so many secrets that I missed, so there’s definitely replay value if you want to search for secrets, or speedrun the levels. I also recommend playing the optional levels, as they are the most challenging levels, and will really put your platforming skills to the test. I died a lot on those levels, but once I finally beat them all, if certainly felt like an accomplishment.
If you’re only interested in experiencing the story, it is a good one, but it is short, so I’d suggest waiting for a sale price. However, if you’re a fan of searching for secrets, and trying to speedrun challenging platformer levels, then Fossil Echo may be right up your alley.

My review is from single player only. I work for a container shipping company, so this game caught my eye a while ago. I expected something like the classic Railroad Tycoon series, but with ships. What I got was something different, but in a bad way. The game itself isn't horrid, but more something that is vastly inefficient. The mini-game of docking the ships manually when they call ports is tedious and just isn't worth it at almost any point in the game. The whole thing is pointless.
The business element is very lacking, and I was disappointed that the one of only ways they could think to make the game challenging was to vary the same starting scenario. The only thing that changes is the insane interest rate the player is required to pay to the angel investor, along with her ability to sign annoying shipping contracts with huge penalties without your consent. Starting capital should be something the player is in conrol of, or at least given some options. I haven't beaten the game yet, but so far the only risk is getting caught without proper liscense to carry goods and varying interest rates. All of the systematic risks associated with shipping, storms, fire, whatever are all completely random and don't even affect other ships on the same rotues. There is no political risk, market risk, exchange rate risk, or purchasing power risk. The game is supposed to be global, but has nothing global about the simulated economy nor is it dynamic in supply/demand.
Last, and probably the biggest deal breaker, I don't enjoy the micro management required in this game. Having to approve every single ship when you call port is annoying, and it seems almost impossible to set up a static voyage using supply and demand or contracts. Every port you have to pick new goods based on what is available and then decide where the ship is to go next, and because goods cant be transferred at ports for a hub and spoke strategy, the only way to play is by having direct routes for every ship. In late game, you have so many shipts they are calling ports every 4 seconds so the gameplay never feels like it is going anywhere. Youre costantly being inturruped by having to agree to pay the docking fee, load more goods, and then choose the next port. The only way to keep ships in specific areas is to basically micromanage contracts, and have them sit in port waiting for a contract that keeps them from having to go from the EU to Asia, or float them completely empty to another port, which is again heavy micromanagement when you consider how many ships you have to track in late game, and not realistic at all.
These business simulators still have things to learn, and it makes you truely appreciate games which are very well done like the Railroad Tycoon seres. They are still amazing. The next installment of Transcean is out this summer, I hope it is a little better.

This game has an excellent foundation, but totally whiffs on the foundation of the diablo genre. It's fun to become crazy awesome over time. If you make a game where I have limited resources and can never overpower the enemies, then it becomes a strategy game with diablo playstyle. And since it's basically a strategy game, you have to have creative enemies and encounters. It doesn't. It has repetitive waves of monsters that you fight through. So in that essence it's a bad strategy game.
In short, you'll have a fun time starting out. As the game progresses though, it turns into a horrible strategy game. I give it 8/10 to start, and finishes around 4/10. I'll average that out for overall score.

**Contains game details to make points, so beware spoilers.**
Game was interesting and had a lot of good bits, but was too shallow overall. There's no real company progress, just meet a few requirements and you unlock the next bigger ship; rinse and repeat. They did a job creating an investor that you'll grow a seething hatred for as she continues to leech your funds ever quarter whilst creating contracts that you can't complete without breaking the law [get product X from city Y; this city only allows the tiniest ships to dock at it, and you need an upgrade to lawfully carry product X - an upgrade that the tiniest ship cannot get]. The end game requires building up a very large amount of spare cash to free yourself from the investor; the amount is 2x the company's late-game value, so if you're punished if you like to have some spare cash on hand. Building a large fleet - which is required to buy out the company - generates a ton of busywork, as there's no sort of automation available. I really enjoy sim-management games, but this one punishes you unless you grind towards great profits; mainly, trying to keep your head above water as Ms. BS gouges you for 10% of your value every quarter [her name is Ms. Blythe-Smith, but maybe the initials were chosen intentionally]. I think I would have enjoyed TransOcean much more if it focused on managing the company rather than managing the minutia.
The ability to manually dock and cast off is fun, but it gets tedious considering how many shipping runs you must make; I think if you did every maneuver manually it'd about triple the amount of time played, and eventually feels a bit like busy work [the game forces you to do some maneuvers later game in order to progress, which may help some discover this bit they've been missing out on, but it also feels forced for those that want to focus on the management aspect].
It looks like a TO2 is in progress, and I'll probably check it out based on how it looks and the price. TO isn't a bad game, and I was on the fence about giving a 'No' recommendation. I'd probably give it a 7/10 overall - there are just many better games in genre to spend time on, especially ones that have better replay value.

I don't have any issues with the technical side of the game, it seems to run smoothly on maxed settings. It mostly looks good aside from some dodgy facial animations at points, not unlike Mass Effect: Andromeda. Most of the segments where you fight the Nazis are pretty good, aside from possibly a slightly underwhelming final battle, which just feels like a grind through hordes of tough to kill enemies in a small area, followed by a pretty unrewarding ending.
However, the U-boat segments and the resistance crew get old really fast. It ranges from so-and-so, to tiresome, to cringy. I'm not sure if they're trying to be satirical and mocking various groups, or just failing to present them in a positive light, it's this kind of weird middle-ground where it isn't well-written enough to add depth to the universe or particularly humorous. These segments make up a significant portion of the game and detract from the experience as a whole.
It is a shame, because a lot of the shooter gameplay is fun, and I wish there was more of it. Wolfenstein is known for being "out there" and over-the-top, and while The New Colossus has a lot of good and unique segments (the wheelchair warrior and panzerhund ride especially spring to mind) it gets bogged down in tedium and bizarre "fetch quests" in the resistance U-boat. A lot of these are thankfully optional, but some are not.
It isn't a terrible, awful or even necessarily bad game. I just wish there was more game, and less filler... because the filler was kind of bad in the previous installment, and it has only gotten worse in The New Colossus.

Cool turn-based strategy game that's quite similar to Valkyria Chronicles. Instead of being tile-based like most turn-based strategy games, you can freely move characters around within a certain movement range and then fire at enemies within range, with all other allies nearby following up with assist attacks.
Each character has their own unique skill tree which allows them to learn special attacks and passive abilities they can use in battles, and you can make all sorts of crazy combinations between characters to further improve the effects of these.
The main gimmick of the game is a randomized system where in each of the game's levels, one of the characters in your squad will randomly turn out to be a traitor. You have to correctly identify them and execute them or there will be repercussions later on in the story.
It's a fun game overall and doesn't outstay its welcome, especially if you liked Valkyria Chronicles, but it does have some critical flaws.
Primarily, the traitor system is a neat concept but in reality it's entirely up to luck who becomes a traitor and you might lose one of your favourite or most useful characters. The skills of dead characters can be "passed on" to one of the remaining characters, but if they died before you got a chance to invest a lot of points in their skill tree you'll never get the chance to see the full potential of their abilities.
In addition, the game is specifically written to use only very generic wording and phrasing when discussing the deceased. Other characters will only vaguely talk about the person who just died using words like "they" instead of "him/her" or a name and as soon as you notice this it removes most of the impact.
Another disappointment is that despite the skill trees being very deep if you want them to be, there's really no need to ever use them to their full extent. The game's difficulty ramps up very slowly and if you simply keep buying the stronger new weapons available for your main damage dealers on every level you shouldn't ever run into any issues. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but some challenge would've been nice. There's a few easily accessible skills that completely break the game, for example one that boosts all stats for every squad member other than the user's, and one that lets you skip an entire enemy turn and move all your characters twice in a row.
Finally, seeing the game's true ending requires you to play through the whole thing twice, which is a huge pain considering it's almost exactly the same up until the very end. New Game+ won't carry over any equipment or skill tree progress, you'll simply get a free batch of skill points to distribute right at the beginning. This means you have to slowly level up all your characters and earn money to buy weapons again if you want to see the true ending.
I still enjoyed the game a lot overall, but it might be better to pick it up in a sale.
One last note, the soundtrack is surprisingly good, which kinda took me off guard. It's pretty interesting too because it's impossible to find any info about who composed the music anywhere, they're not even listed in the credits.

Trine is a fun 2D platformer with puzzle elements. The only problem I have with it, is that it is way too easy. There is no penalty for dying besides going back to a checkpoint and even then, enemies don't respawn. I do like this better than the sequel though. There is more gameplay and less story than Trine 2, which I prefer. If you want to play a fun game that does not take itself seriously, I would recommend it. Not a amazing game, but still good.

Even on its own, Trine is a visual puzzle-platform delight, containing 15 levels (plus 1 bonus level) for you to journey through. If you remember the old console game "The Lost Vikings", then know that this is a slightly faster-paced version with more emphasis on combat, as well as beautiful backdrops to the various levels.
The game has you play as 3 characters (wizard, thief, and knight) fused into one existence; during play, you can freely call in one of the three to handle fights or puzzles, while the other two hover in a mental limbo. Depending on your tastes, you may relish the idea that the game's puzzles are generally flexible, and let a player choose one of many ways to solve a puzzle. You can conjure planks as a wizard to reach a ledge, or simply grapple to the top as a thief. Even combat is up to you, fight head-on as a knight, at range as a thief, or use a wizard to conjure blocks that crush.
Though the game has its downsides. The enemies are bland, with only a majority of skeletons and two other generic creatures. After a while, combat with them becomes a chore to check-off inbetween puzzles. The story is nice, but has little involvement with the gameplay, as the plot comes in verbal chunks during 3 sections: the loading screen; the level beginning; and the level end. The game itself is quite linear and straight-forward, with only small branches that lead to secret collectibles, that in turn upgrade the three heroes' abilities.
However, note that this game has a Local Co-op option that I did not try.
Overall, this game is more like an appetizer instead of a main course; it lets you get used to how the game mechanics work and tells you the backstory of Trine 2, and you could finish this in less than a day. If you strip away the distractions of plot and combat, Trine is purely a quick (though not without some thought) mildly-challenging puzzle game. Still, I heartily recommend this game as it is a brisk body-swapping romp through a scenic fantasy world. If you want this game, get it purely for its pretty puzzles.
NOTE: Trine is packaged with Trine 2 in the packages "Trine Complete" and "Frozenbyte Collection" which may make your purchase more worthwhile, particularly during a Steam Sale.

Lost Dimension is another PS Vita game that got unnoticed (also released for PS3 too), and ported onto Steam. Needless to say, I've heard about the game since last year thanks to it's catchy final boss theme, but because it was on the Vita, I could never get itplay . But since it's on Steam I finally have the chance to play it.
Pros:
- Interesting mysteries in the story, and a great reveal for them
- The areas are really cool to look at, same with the models of allies and enemies
- The portraits have hair physics and look sweet
- The music is catchy and memorable (time of joy is overused though)
- Opening gets bonus points for being in the game (and you can even put in your own song if you mess with the file, for better or for worse)
- Levels can be tough, but there's never a need to grind thanks to side missions (and beserk)
- Sanity meter adds a good limit to how you use gift abilities
- The traitor mechanic, where any unit can be the traitor besides Sho, is really well done and easily the most unique part of the game
- Each unit feels unique and useful
- Very replayable thanks to the traitor mechanic and gift abilities transferring to other characters thanks to Fate Materia
- Always satisfying to beat levels
Neutral:
- Voice Acting is only in English, and a lot of them don't do a good job, they lack emotion
- Characters are iffy, some are really interesting, others just didn't connect (George and Zenji come to mind)
Cons:
- This port is filled with tecnical problems (audio cutting out during battle, random crashes at the end of missions, AI don't move around their own allies letting you negate an attack, etc.)
- The sections where you influence who gets voted off after each mission gets repetitive after awhile, especially when you know who the traitor is
- The ending is kind of anti-climatic
Overall, a 9 of out 10. I really enjoyed Lost Dimension, and for $20 (I got it 40% off, also in Canadian dollars) I got more than my money's worth. I'm currently on my third playthrough of the game, and I'm still not sick of it yet.

There's a lot of negative reviews for this game that point out very real and important problems that this game has. I recommend this game
like I do. This review was also written just after Update 6 Patch 2, and I haven't been playing the beta versions so broken things I mention may be fixed in the current version of the game when you read this.
I'll start with the worst so it doesn't ruin my review at the end. LEGO Worlds has serious problems with its camera and controls. Now I've been playing this game since it came out, and I can attest that the devs have made significant improvements in these areas. Despite this many controls are still very hard to use (trying to precisely place a copied model is nearly impossible at times) to the point where I prefer to simply avoid those features when possible. This is bad. However, I have been watching the devs slowly fix and add things that the players have asked for, and I think that somewhere on their monumental list of things to do is fix the camera and controls. But we'll have to wait and see.
The other major negative is that you can only build static bricks. The game has tons of vehicles but you can't make any of your own. Many parts such as hinges are only available pre-built into destructible models; you cannot build with them. Also, you cannot build your own destructible models. As fun as building with the static bricks is, there is a frequent longing to build things that come to life. I have no idea if the devs plan on adding these features, but if they can add those models themselves then I'm pretty sure they can let us do it too.
I would have complained about the lack of multiplayer here - a HUGELY important feature - but very recently they have added a multiplayer beta to the game! Multiplayer is here/coming, like we've asked for since the day LEGO Worlds was released!
LEGO Worlds is not for you if you're looking for combat, scoring, preset goals, storyline, etc. By some definitions LEGO Worlds isn't actually a game, but more of a toy. It's LEGO on your computer. There is stuff to explore but exploration can become tedious as you hunt for item chests or elusive minifigs. I've seen several negative reviews here that came in part or full from people expecting to play a normal game instead of building with LEGO bricks.
Now, for the good stuff! I will deal here with the obvious comparison is to Minecraft. LEGO Worlds is more unlike Minecraft than, say, Terraria is. It's not at all about survival. This game is quite entirely about building creatively with LEGO bricks. You have much more creative freedom than in Minecraft for a few reasons. The most important one is the smaller scale of the bricks, allowing for more detail in your builds. LEGO Worlds also has a nice set of terraforming tools which let you sculpt the terrain, as well as the ability to save your models and paste them around wherever you want. The creative experience is certainly the main draw to this game. Minecraft is better if you want to bulid with a purpose; LEGO Worlds is better if you want to set your creativity free. It's also lots of fun to climb around your builds Assassin's Creed style after you finish them, or to blow them up with dragonfire. I know this doesn't sound like much, but I have greatly enjoyed bulding in this game, much more than I have in Minecraft, and I expect the experience to keep getting better as the devs fix and add things.
TL;DR: This game is, as of this writing, super early access, with many major problems and missing features. Despite this, it's given me a better creative experience than any other building game I've played (notably Minecraft and Terraria). It's not really a game; it's endless LEGOs on your computer.

Pros -
Easy to understand gameplay mechanics and controls
Charming graphics
Cons -
Very little content, even compared to other LEGO titles
Simplistic mechanics that leave no interest for replay
Tiny part list to build from when making custom creations
No moving parts or vehicles to build
Worlds are mostly empty terrain
Overall -
I was really hopeful - as a fan of Minecraft and other sandbox games, combining that concept with the LEGO brand seemed like a great idea.  However, there's very little heart here.  Prepare to be dropped into an empty, sparsely populated world with limited options to create within it.  This doesn't feel like LEGO - it feels like a poorly realized Minecraft clone.  I kept waiting for more content to come in patches, and it just hasn't happened (and may not ever happen).  I don't need any game I play to be constant stimulation, but in every sandbox game I've liked I've come across something that took my breath away; some beautiful vista, an interesting creature, a really cool premade structure ripe for customization.  In a game that pretends to be about creativity, seeing so much empty space and so little to fill it with just left me cold.
I love LEGO - my husband and I still collect as adults - and I understand that games like this are meant for children.  However, I don't know of any child older than six who would be willing to put up with so much emptiness and boredom in a creativity-based game.

As having played many Lego games in the past, I was really, really excited for this one when I found it. And I have to say that at its current state, I'm overall pretty satisfied! I know I haven't played this game for long, but it's a great substitute for Minecraft (I used to play it until it just stopped working on my computer-) for me. Sure, it may be in development, but it's very fun to watch a game grow, even if you aren't playing it now. I think the whole "open world lego game where you can use legos in any way" is pretty neat to me (even if it does give me a little bit of Minecraft vibes, but not a lot as this game has its differences-), as I've been playing/building with legos for over half my life. I do agree with some other people on here that the game can be laggy at times, and there's not much to do at this point, but you have to remember that it's only in early access- as of posting this- (and it probably will be for much longer).
I love the "touching new items gives you more items to build with" concept, as well as the "find an item and give that to a specific character roaming the maps to unlock them" concept. I really do like how you can customize your character, too, and in any way (you don't have to use the models in the game; you could make an astronaut with caveman apparel, an archaeologist with diver gear, etc.) on top of that. I'm super excited for multiplayer, as I've been hoping to play this game with friends! ^^
If you're wondering whether or not to buy this game, well, here's a few things:
1. It's still in development, so you should expect to see bugs with the game.
2. There aren't many things to do at the moment, but there's enough to keep you occupied.
3. The game is still being updated (as of posting this it last updated about a week ago), so it's not dead.
4. There's a wide variety of characters, animals, mounts, vehicles, pre-made sets (like houses or trees, you get the idea), plants, and other environmental pieces that you can collect (yes, I said collect) as you go on with the game, but some are given to you at the start.
*Just a side note, but the driving controls are a little wonky for me. For instance, I have no idea how to stay going forward or backwards because for some reason they're either reversed or unresponsive. It's either a bug, or I just have no idea how to use them, haha. Putting this in here just to let you guys have a heads-up!*
Overall, I think this game is pretty great where it's at right now, but as time goes on, I could definitely see major improvements to make it even better (I've also got hopes for more Ninjago things (I already am highly appreciative of Cole's Earth Driller ((thank you guys so much for that one)), but I'd love to see characters and other sets if it's possible! ^^)), but one can only dream at this point...)! As a good fan of the Lego franchise, I once again am fairly happy with this game. It's a wonderful time-killer and I recommend it if you are okay with minor/moderate lag issues (that don't last very long) and enjoy games that Lego-styled and are (somewhat) like Minecraft. c:

4 stars out of 5. A fascinating, smart film noir comic-book game that's more visually interesting, and makes better use of framing, than anything I've seen in a long time.
As noted by others, "The Detail" may in theory be closer to an interactive graphic novel, but damned if it doesn't feel like a game when you're playing it. The game smartly restricts you from doing too much, which means you don't get frustrated or stuck very often trying to figure out what to do next. The writing tries to ape film noir, and mostly succeeds (it falls into cliche at times).
The moment when you shift from one POV character to another is a wonderfully unexpected shock.
Worth it for the visuals alone. If someone figures out how to take this new format and make the next "Stanley Parable" or "Little Inferno' with it, it'll be astonishing.

The benefit of buying the EUIII collection over EUIV, simply said, is that you are purchasing a complete, self-contained experience. If you are anything like me, you've shared the frustrations of booting up EUIV only to realize your save files have been corrupted with a new update or expansion. If you're anything like me, you've shared the frustration of being left behind as new expansions are released, and you lack the incentive to purchase immediately or at all. The graphics, by comparison to EUIV, are clunky; likewise, the interface may seem so as well. However, when not in comparison, the graphics, interface, gameplay, replayability, etc. are commendable. The game, in short, holds up. Truthfully, I would prefer grappling with the minor gripes throughout the game than to spend another hour on EUIV. The price is well worth the security, knowing I won't be left behind with expansions, knowing the fundamental game mechanics will not change with every additional game I begin. EU III is a simulation of intricate detail, and will repay its cost in time spent playing.
In summation, EU III is a deep simulation at heart that will keep giving to you as you play. EU IV is but a platform at heart that you must keep giving to continue to play. Just pick this up.

If you went to high school in the times of the current computer age, you have probably attended mandatory IT classes, in which one of the tasks may have been engaging with a program in order to learn how to type faster. Well, these programs provide certain tips how to achieve that but are pretty dull - if they introduced this game instead, the students may actually enjoy improving themselves.
+ Practicing useful typing skills in a game? HELL YEAH!
+ Extra value added thanks to some cool puzzles
+ Nice artstyle with the world unfolding infront of you
+ Quite interesting story that makes you wonder what is this about and then comes the twist
+ Thanks to being a typing simulator, it has quite some replayability potential (arena ftw) - especially if you want to get all the achievements
- Some of the achivements are just an unnecessary grind (looking at you Insect's bane aka Keyboard's bane)
- No other real negatives but while playing I came up with some minor QoL changes that could be easily made:
a) when playing arena the music stops after a the first death and never comes back until restart (not when retrying the level from the next screen, not when going from the menu);
b) it feels a bit annoying that after switching or creating profiles you are thrown right into the story mode - it would seem much better to put the player in the menu instead
VERDICT: Worth a try even for those who think typing random words does not seem like a lot of fun since the story, the puzzles and the artsy unfolding of the world will prevent you from getting bored.

The art, narrative, and atmosphere in Epistory are absolutely amazing; Epistory is easily one of the most memorable games in these aspects that I've experienced from any genre, and I've played a lot of games over the years. The music and sound effects flowed well to keep the intended atmosphere intact.
The difficulty scaling of the typing was excellent. Most typing games are a bit too easy for me; I loved that I could play and still have some challenge, while a friend (with a slower typing speed) played through the game and was challenged as well, but not with a difficulty level so high to make it unmanagable.
The actual gameplay mechanics mixing typing with RPG elements was a wonderful mix, and kept things interesting and added a level of strategy I very much appreciated.
The quantity of content could be a bit higher, but I admit I say that because I would have loved to have been able to keep playing: I thoroughly enjoyed playing through Epistory. The story did progress and end in a logical and timely fashion.
The only thing that I might consider a negative was the puzzle difficulty. I love puzzles in games, and would normally prefer puzzles require a bit more logical breakdown (I'm a big fan of puzzles -The Talos Principle was amazing!). Epistory is, however, a typing game, and I'm torn on the subject because I think that increasing puzzle focus and difficulty could easily have the effect of breaking the immersion and the typing focus. (Not something I would remotely desire!)

When you hear about a game that has been described as a beautifully drawn and scored Metroidvania then the possibility of it being "bad" just doesn't even cross your mind.

✔ I mean, yeah, the game is wonderfully beautiful. The art, the music, the story, all of it
✔ It's an interesting, unique world. Very few established tropes are used here
✔ Everything has a nice weight and "oomph" to it, especially combat. It just feels right
✘ Overall terrible level and encounter design. Too often based on trial & error, and the game-flow is constantly interrupted
✘ Uncompelling abilities. It's a Metroidvania, but none of the abilities are very interesting and I felt no urge to explore
✘ Insta-kills are poorly telegraphed to the player. Mundane-looking enemies and environmental hazards can kill you without warning
✘ No fast travel or teleporting.The levels are bland enough the first time through, how could anyone want to go through them multiple times?
✘ Poor execution of a potentially innovative save system. It's manual and uses an in-game ability, but it's easy to forget about and very limiting. It's is devestating to lose levels worth of progress due to an insta-kill.

I've told my friends that this is possibly the best game I have played in over a decade. I absolutely loved this game, and it fast became my game of the year. The game was built for surround sound headphones, so if you have them, make sure to use them.
The game strongly relies on the voices in Senua's head, most of which are fantastically acted, but 2 voices were really jarring, and sounded too much like a Severus Snape impersonator and his demonic cousin
The combat is personal and intense, though once you get used to it, can be pretty easy, even on Hard difficulty. I only died once in the game to an attack from a boss that didnt have a clear telegraph (an insta-kill AOE attack)
The game features an apparent Permadeath mechanic, if you die too many times, your save is deleted - Note the "apparent" part of that. No one has triggered it yet, it could all be a bluff. A fear tactic, or a way to increase anxiety. It's also something you don't need to worry about, like I mentioned, on Hard difficulty, first playthrough, I died once in combat. I also never died in puzzles.
All I can say of the story is that it is just great. You are given a task - Save Dillion's soul from Hel, and that is pretty much everything the game focuses on. All other narrative elements tie to Senua and Dillion, and further their involvement with the world.
Only experienced 3 bugs, Senua tried to balance on a narrow platform instead of shimmying a ledge, so she clipped through the wall, and after ducking below a beam, Senua moved too far and clipped me onto a rock, trapping me there, and the game froze after I died to the boss mentioned above.
FINAL BOSS SPOILERS:
Story: 10/10 (Ninja Theory show off a mastery of narrative direction and focus)
Music: 9/10 (it's great, there just doesnt seem to be enough)
Sound Design/ Voices: 9.5/10 (only loses points from the Severus Snape impersonator)
Level Design: 9/10 (the game forces you to backtrack a lot - helps you find the collectibles and gives you time to listen to the voices in Senua's head)
Graphics: 8.5/10 (character model graphics are near perfect- Senua's hair has a mind of it's own. There are a lot of low quality textures in the world)
Gameplay: 8.5/10 (loses points from the unclear telegraphing of that particular boss and a few bugs)

I've been a big fan of ninja theory after their DMC remake.
But this game, oh Lord, it's something. The soundtrack, the voices in Senua's head (they are all so amazing) give me the chills in a good way. The combination of puzzle solving and combat is done pretty interestingly. Graphics are top notch that's for sure.
And Senua herself is just so adorable. You pity her for all the suffering she had to go through during her flashbacks. You dont think of her as a freak who suffers from psychosis. Why? Because you are Senua. You are here to fight for the only person that truly loved you, the only person who knew you were not the source of darkness. You are ready to travel to Hell, descend into darkness and madness within you and defeat not only the guards of this wretched place but the monsters inside you.
The setting is just breathtaking (my favorite part was by the big tree). I really love the weather that always changes depending on the presence of darkness. Also the whole story based on viking legends is just a masterpiece. You dont want to miss any lorestone on your journey. And the whole wisdom of the Senua's story that teaches you that there's no light without darkness. And all our life we fight even though we know that we will lose at the end (because there's only death waiting for us) but we have to keep fighting because there's so much beauty in every little moment of our short lives. I thank you so much for this beautiful game Ninja Theory. There's no game as weird as scary and as dark and beautiful at the same time as Hellblade. I really hope you read these reviews. A rock solid Action RPG which borrows the right elements from its competitors and mixes it into something unique.
The fighting switches fluently from ranged to close combat complete with different skill sets with the press of a button and can be quite taxing at times - even on normal - with hordes of canon fodder, champions and unique monster all with different and often synergizing abilities. To easen it up a little we have a battling companion at our side who doubles as a packmule (best known from Torchlight).
Character development is fairly shallow with a handful of active and passive skills in the melee and ranged trees, some spells and some auras to choose from. While each skill has a couple of passive and activated power-ups, it's still nothing too dazzling and hard hitting combinations are obvious. Our ghost companion meanwhile just provides a couple of passive buffs like higher damage or resistance.
The world is handmade and thoughtfully designed, offering beatifuly scenaries packed with interactions and secrets which invite you to explore the world off the main path and rewards you for it. The downside is, that it has very little replay value and infact after you're done with the story, you can either play a couple of challenges to find new loot and get some passive boni upon completion or start a New Game+ with your character against leveling monsters whereas you're left at the level cap.
There are a few things to be wary of, though:
Multiplayer seems still broken, some people experience plot stopping bugs (which thankfully are addressed very quickly and can be fixed ingame) and the game is badly optimized. Even with the recommended speccs, you'll experience input lag and frame rate drops which will ruin the experience at times.

There's a lot of negative reviews for this game that point out very real and important problems that this game has. I recommend this game
like I do. This review was also written just after Update 6 Patch 2, and I haven't been playing the beta versions so broken things I mention may be fixed in the current version of the game when you read this.
I'll start with the worst so it doesn't ruin my review at the end. LEGO Worlds has serious problems with its camera and controls. Now I've been playing this game since it came out, and I can attest that the devs have made significant improvements in these areas. Despite this many controls are still very hard to use (trying to precisely place a copied model is nearly impossible at times) to the point where I prefer to simply avoid those features when possible. This is bad. However, I have been watching the devs slowly fix and add things that the players have asked for, and I think that somewhere on their monumental list of things to do is fix the camera and controls. But we'll have to wait and see.
The other major negative is that you can only build static bricks. The game has tons of vehicles but you can't make any of your own. Many parts such as hinges are only available pre-built into destructible models; you cannot build with them. Also, you cannot build your own destructible models. As fun as building with the static bricks is, there is a frequent longing to build things that come to life. I have no idea if the devs plan on adding these features, but if they can add those models themselves then I'm pretty sure they can let us do it too.
I would have complained about the lack of multiplayer here - a HUGELY important feature - but very recently they have added a multiplayer beta to the game! Multiplayer is here/coming, like we've asked for since the day LEGO Worlds was released!
LEGO Worlds is not for you if you're looking for combat, scoring, preset goals, storyline, etc. By some definitions LEGO Worlds isn't actually a game, but more of a toy. It's LEGO on your computer. There is stuff to explore but exploration can become tedious as you hunt for item chests or elusive minifigs. I've seen several negative reviews here that came in part or full from people expecting to play a normal game instead of building with LEGO bricks.
Now, for the good stuff! I will deal here with the obvious comparison is to Minecraft. LEGO Worlds is more unlike Minecraft than, say, Terraria is. It's not at all about survival. This game is quite entirely about building creatively with LEGO bricks. You have much more creative freedom than in Minecraft for a few reasons. The most important one is the smaller scale of the bricks, allowing for more detail in your builds. LEGO Worlds also has a nice set of terraforming tools which let you sculpt the terrain, as well as the ability to save your models and paste them around wherever you want. The creative experience is certainly the main draw to this game. Minecraft is better if you want to bulid with a purpose; LEGO Worlds is better if you want to set your creativity free. It's also lots of fun to climb around your builds Assassin's Creed style after you finish them, or to blow them up with dragonfire. I know this doesn't sound like much, but I have greatly enjoyed bulding in this game, much more than I have in Minecraft, and I expect the experience to keep getting better as the devs fix and add things.
TL;DR: This game is, as of this writing, super early access, with many major problems and missing features. Despite this, it's given me a better creative experience than any other building game I've played (notably Minecraft and Terraria). It's not really a game; it's endless LEGOs on your computer.

Pros -
Easy to understand gameplay mechanics and controls
Charming graphics
Cons -
Very little content, even compared to other LEGO titles
Simplistic mechanics that leave no interest for replay
Tiny part list to build from when making custom creations
No moving parts or vehicles to build
Worlds are mostly empty terrain
Overall -
I was really hopeful - as a fan of Minecraft and other sandbox games, combining that concept with the LEGO brand seemed like a great idea.  However, there's very little heart here.  Prepare to be dropped into an empty, sparsely populated world with limited options to create within it.  This doesn't feel like LEGO - it feels like a poorly realized Minecraft clone.  I kept waiting for more content to come in patches, and it just hasn't happened (and may not ever happen).  I don't need any game I play to be constant stimulation, but in every sandbox game I've liked I've come across something that took my breath away; some beautiful vista, an interesting creature, a really cool premade structure ripe for customization.  In a game that pretends to be about creativity, seeing so much empty space and so little to fill it with just left me cold.
I love LEGO - my husband and I still collect as adults - and I understand that games like this are meant for children.  However, I don't know of any child older than six who would be willing to put up with so much emptiness and boredom in a creativity-based game.

As having played many Lego games in the past, I was really, really excited for this one when I found it. And I have to say that at its current state, I'm overall pretty satisfied! I know I haven't played this game for long, but it's a great substitute for Minecraft (I used to play it until it just stopped working on my computer-) for me. Sure, it may be in development, but it's very fun to watch a game grow, even if you aren't playing it now. I think the whole "open world lego game where you can use legos in any way" is pretty neat to me (even if it does give me a little bit of Minecraft vibes, but not a lot as this game has its differences-), as I've been playing/building with legos for over half my life. I do agree with some other people on here that the game can be laggy at times, and there's not much to do at this point, but you have to remember that it's only in early access- as of posting this- (and it probably will be for much longer).
I love the "touching new items gives you more items to build with" concept, as well as the "find an item and give that to a specific character roaming the maps to unlock them" concept. I really do like how you can customize your character, too, and in any way (you don't have to use the models in the game; you could make an astronaut with caveman apparel, an archaeologist with diver gear, etc.) on top of that. I'm super excited for multiplayer, as I've been hoping to play this game with friends! ^^
If you're wondering whether or not to buy this game, well, here's a few things:
1. It's still in development, so you should expect to see bugs with the game.
2. There aren't many things to do at the moment, but there's enough to keep you occupied.
3. The game is still being updated (as of posting this it last updated about a week ago), so it's not dead.
4. There's a wide variety of characters, animals, mounts, vehicles, pre-made sets (like houses or trees, you get the idea), plants, and other environmental pieces that you can collect (yes, I said collect) as you go on with the game, but some are given to you at the start.
*Just a side note, but the driving controls are a little wonky for me. For instance, I have no idea how to stay going forward or backwards because for some reason they're either reversed or unresponsive. It's either a bug, or I just have no idea how to use them, haha. Putting this in here just to let you guys have a heads-up!*
Overall, I think this game is pretty great where it's at right now, but as time goes on, I could definitely see major improvements to make it even better (I've also got hopes for more Ninjago things (I already am highly appreciative of Cole's Earth Driller ((thank you guys so much for that one)), but I'd love to see characters and other sets if it's possible! ^^)), but one can only dream at this point...)! As a good fan of the Lego franchise, I once again am fairly happy with this game. It's a wonderful time-killer and I recommend it if you are okay with minor/moderate lag issues (that don't last very long) and enjoy games that Lego-styled and are (somewhat) like Minecraft. c:

If you come to this game for a griping and emotinal story. You are very much in the wrong place. A common complaint of trafitional jRPGs these days is that they tell a good story but they don't have the gameplay to back it up. Lost Dimension has the opposite problem. If jRPG stories where on a soectrum from games like Chrono Trigger & Persona at a 5 and garbage as a 1 then Lost Dimension would be a 2. Not the worst story ever in that you understand character motivations and what is happening at all times on the screen but past that... I found myself at the end the game frustrated with the characters for their stupidity in their motivations for their actions and by characters I mean character. The main boss of this game is dumb and should go sit himself in the corner with his edgy name and think about how stupid he is. And we should all point & laugh at him.
But the gameplay. Oh mama. The best way to describe it would be Valkyria Chronicles but your soldiers all have super powers. "Quests" as they called him in the game or missions does most humans know them go by lightning quick and by the end of you're playthrough you can beat the final boss in one turn with your six remaining heroes.
That reminds me, a main mechanic of this game is the traitor system where in at each floor (of which there are five) one of your party members will be secretly working as a spy and you have to find out who and send them to their deaths. And that's not an exaggeration they will straight up die once you and your other party members have voted them off the island. But this brings up perhaps Lost Dimensions most fun game mechanic, once your party member has been killed you can take their superpowers. This leads to fun combinations of powers that can be used in distinct ways.
The one thing I find the most disappointing about this game is the potential that it seems to miss. If someone told me that there is a game that combined elements of Dangan ronpa & Valkyria Chronicles I would do anything to play that game. And I Felix that potential which lost dimension could reach if given a sequel.
TL;DR The gameplay extremely fun in the vain of Valkyria Chronicles but the story is at best mediocre that I have to warn those who only really care about story in the game to stay away. Overall I feel a 7.5 out of 10 is appropriate. Nothing groundbreaking but a fun title none the less. Make something out of the traitor system (like Ace Attorney or Danganronpa) and keep the gameplay for a sequel and we're looking at a masterpiece.

The game itself is simple enough for anyone to pick-up but the platforming and puzzles later on can be very challenging but the feeling of satisfaction you get from finishing those puzzle-platforming sections is just bliss.
The way the game is presented is very much like a story-book with the narrator, the cutscenes and those amazing setpieces. You can seriously take a screenshot of any section of this game and it'd look like a painting worth being framed and hung on someone's lounge room!
In single player, you can play as one character, either as the mage, the thief or the knight; each with their own strengths and weaknesses and you are allowed to switch as whichever character you want in order to get through a particular puzzle or platforming section. For example, the mage can conjure boxes and platforms to help you with puzzles and getting to places but is pretty useless when it comes to battle while the knight can lift heavy objects and is the main fighting force when it comes to battles. This interesting mechanic has been implemented extremely well within each level as you will be encouraged to play as all of the different classes in order to get through it and that makes for an already enjoyable game all the more enjoyable!
All in all, Trine is an amazing-looking game with fantastic gameplay to boot and if it ever goes on sale again, don't hesitate and dive right in!

Frozenbyte creates an epic story with the brilliant game Trine. Trine offers a side-scroller hack ‘n slash platformer game that combines puzzles with action packed adventures.
In a magical far away land the world is slowly falling apart as corruption spreads through the kingdom. Yet who will save the kingdom, but three mismatched fools who found themselves drawn to an artifact of power. A lustful wizard Amadeus, a greedy thief Zoya, and a gluttonous knight Pontius all become bound by the Trine. The Trine takes the heroes essences and combines them into one individual. In order to free themselves from the Trines bindings they must complete the quest and bring peace back to the land.
The campaign offers a great tutorial which starts off as you playing each of the characters as they find their way to the Trine. After you have got each character to the Trine the campaign truly begins. There are fifteen levels: Astral Academy, Academy Hallways, Wolvecote Catacombs, Dragon Graveyard, Crystal Caverns, Crypt of the Damned, Forsaken Dungeons, Throne of the Lost King, Fangle Forest, Shadowthorn Thicket, Ruins of the Perished, Heartland Mines, Branblestoke Village, Iron Forge, and Tower of Sarek. Each level includes puzzles, secrets, and numerous enemies. Some of the levels are incredibly long, although all the of levels have checkpoints spread throughout so even if you die you will only be set back a small bit. The campaign offers a lot of amazing features, but the best part is that how you complete the puzzles is up to you.
The Trine allows you to play as three characters, but you can only operate one of them at a time; the Trine operates as a way to switch your characters. Amadeus, the Wizard, uses spells to conjure platforms and boxes which you can use to build structures, as weapons, or even as a shield. Zoya, the Thief, has a bow and a grappling hook giving her the benefit of range and agility. Pontius, the Knight, has a shield and sword which makes him a formidable tank. The levels are filled with puzzles and mysteries, but unlike most other puzzle games Trine allows you to choose how you complete the puzzle. Use Amadeus to activate switches, or maybe stand on it with Zoya and grappling hook before the door shuts. How you solve the puzzles and defeat the many foes ahead is up to you. I played the game and essentially never used Pontius, not that he is bad, but I preferred to play as Zoya and Amadeus.
If you love hack ‘n slash puzzle games then this is the adventure you have been awaiting. Trine is a fantastic game at an incredibly reasonable price. If you can get Trine on sale, even if the sale is only 10% off, you are getting one incredible deal. Trine offers character variation, brilliant dialogue, a wonderful ambience, a fantastic story, and gameplay that is almost impossible to find elsewhere. By combining Hack ‘n Slash, Plat former, Puzzle, and RPG Trine offers something that everyone would love. I would entirely recommend Trine and every second you don’t have it is just another second you will regret once you’ve got it.

The New Colossus had some big shoes to fill with the previous title for Wolfenstein, The New Order. It fills the shoes quite nicely. While The New Colossus manages to bring something new with each level, in terms of overall gunplay, it's more of the same; which isn't a bad thing in this case. Weapons pack that familiar punch and response The New Order showed off while carefully balancing that fine scale of weapon variety without having too many weapons and this is a big plus in my book. As for level design, it manages to stay pretty fresh section to section. A fine range between situations caught in spaces almost too tight for words, the invasive destroyed cities of New York and New Orleans which only add to the chaos and tension; but most of all pacing. Well. Overall pacing at least.
The story is pretty straight forward from the previous game, wrapping up some questions you may have had involving the almost ambiguous ending and quickly wheels you into combat in a wheelchair. This right here is something that helps make Wolfenstein 2 here special. For a good chunk of the game, spoilers aside, you are forced to deal with your enemies while missing half of your health. Now granted, you can have double the usual armor. This formula is changed later on in the game, but I feel it adds an extra layer of tension and gives combat a very different flow for a good while, really keeping you thinking on the fly while soaking up every bullet in sight as you violently trudge your way through hordes of Nazis. But as said, the pacing for this game is overall very well thought out.
The graphics aren't anything jaw dropping, but do provide a good atmosphere and substantial detail to the varied levels. Though some do come across as borderline generic, the more almost comical or absurd set pieces break this up like a good plunger taking care of a heaping pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥your neighbor left in the john. But this game runs smooth as can be. Even in the most frantic of situations, explosions and bullets flying about, I don't think I saw the fps counter drop below 60 once on the highest settings, ranging from 720, 900 and 1080 monitors and a television. This was with a GeForce GTX1060 6GB. I did go ahead and plug in another computer with very similar specs, but with a GTX 960 4GB. I had to tone things down a bit, but that hardly compromised the game and still looked great.
As for the story, it's nothing amazing but its gripping enough with political satire, comically absurd setpieces with a suprising tone of realism and some pretty damn wild fights that may leave you sweating. As for this games almost coincidental development and release during some events here in America, it's left plenty room open between trolls or the truly insane of our society to come out of the wood work and stir the pot. Let's just step back and look at what Wolfenstein is. An FPS based around an alternate reality where the Nazis were technologically superior and dabbled in the occult. Simple as that.
One thing I will note, is The New Colossus pulls a similar manuever as before with having to different timelines involving either Wyatt or Fergus, two major characters who only exist in either one timeline or the other based on a player choice early on. Wolfenstein 2 manages to quickly take care of this in the opening moments in a pretty simple way. I'm sure it's not for everyone, but it does add another layer of little differences in the gameplay. However I suspect The New Colossus may have just a tad bit more than a difference in the minigame in how you unlock things. But that's up to speculation from me for now.
In the end, it's a fun game that really keeps you going for more. It is clear that this is not the last in the current Wolfenstein story, spoilers aside and all I can say is Bethesda and Machine Games made a success here and I'm sure a third installment will probably be on it's way sometime in 2020 or later. Now. Is the game worth $60? That's a difficult tell at the moment. If you really want to get it and feel you can spare the cash, go for it. For to the more frugal or those who simply don't have an immense amount of time on their hands, I suggest holding out for a bit. It's not a bad game, far from it, but between what amounts to roughly a ten hour campaign with a post game bit, it may not be in everyones favor to pick it while it's fresh out. I thoroughly enjoyed New Colossus.
This is one of those games that prods at the line between games and storytelling. The narrative-- helping to spur a demoralized American Resistance-- is a high-tension bit of drama. The characters range from bitter and jaded to angry and powerless. A common theme of frustration is the helplessness of the people versus the unstoppable might of the Nazi war machine.
The voice acting really blows the cutscenes out of the water. It's raw and unapologetic, and the voice actors do a great job with their lines. The hate, anger, and desperation is just tantalizing.
For people who didn't have graphics issues, gameplay is fluid, fast, and pretty. It's not the most gorgeous game ever, but a GTX 1080ti makes short work of it at high FPS in QHD resolution. The cutscenes are expertly rendered. The gameplay itself feels a lot like the recent Doom, with fast, frenetic movements and firefights that demand a lot of strategy and twitchy reflexes at higher levels. There are a wide variety of enemies and multiple locations rendered with fantastic detail.
The stealth mechanic is simple but fun and ably executed, allowing you to clear areas with shadowy ambush, full-frontal assault, or huge gains in mobility at higher levels. The Perks system works similarly to the previous game; weapon mods are found by exploring areas and upgrading your arsenal.
The main campaign was, if anything, too short. There was room to tell a longer story. But there were some incredibly powerful and evocative images told in both cutscene and in gameplay. There's a real sense of raging helplessness that makes this game not just fun, but a great experience.
It's a game that challenges. There are moments that are hard to get through. But it aspires to tell a story, and in that regard, it succeeds roundly.

The satisfaction of taking down the Nazi regime comes to life again, as you blast, saw, detonate, and axe murder your way from a wheelchair to the surface of Venus.
There are technical issues, but Bethesda has already said that they are working on fixes to them and that they will be deployed ASAP.
All together, I'd give this a high-eight to nine out of ten, the story is very interesting, the gameplay is outstanding, the weapons, characters, scenarios and the like are, in some cases quite literally, out of this world.
This game is a must play for fans of the series, and even if you've only picked up with The New Order, you'll still love the game!

Simply put its a great game, if you are interested in a game that is all about managing a network of ships, ensuring you can afford the ships, fuel, repairs and any fines you incure all the while needing to keep enough money in the bank to pay your greedy investor then this may be the game for you.
The graphics are exactly what you would expect from a game that is essentialy a map and a bunch of finance screens, simple clean and easy to understand. The docking part of the game is quite fun but when you have 10+ ships can become very tedious to dock every ship. The advantage of actually docking yourself is you save the moring fee's and when it come to the most expensive ship in the game thats a lot of money especialy if you dock the ship and leave the port. So it comes in handy throughout the game and while you dont need to use it ever it can be useful (especialy if your ships is empty and you need to move to a different port and want to save some money), its also quite fun and challenging as some of the docks are very oddly shapped and possitioned. The graphics for the docking are nice clean and I expect will stand the test of time nicely.
Every aspect of the game is fun, if a bit repetative, however with the docking mini game you can vary it up and keep the fun alive. It does become very repetative nearing the end of the game as you are simply trying to buy out your investor and the money you need is huge and can take a little too long to reach, which is the only real downside to this entire game. I wold have liked to have seen a few other elements like competiton with other companies and the such but alas not in this game. If the game starts to feel repetative try taking on a contract that is restrictive or try and get a chain of contracts, there are many ways to keep your interest, you just need to look for them.
The tutorial is very good and is perfectly integrated into the main game so no need to stop and start. You follow the instructions and you start making money. My personal recomendayion is to always but the ship with the highest top speed and bigest hold, the distance it can travel is imaterial, especialy when you reach level 3 and 4 ships.
Pro's
Graphics are simple and clean and will not feel dated in the years to come
A number of different challenges throughout the game.
Piloting the ships are fun and challenging, the latter ships with thrusters, makes piloting a dream.
Finding the best routes to make money is a lot of fun.
Con's
Can be repetative, especialy later on.
You will hate how much the investor takes from you and can be annoying when you simply want to finish the game.
Becomes a little to easy in the late game.
When you have 15 + ships it still takes forever to buy out the investor
Conclusion, this is a fun game that will keep you occupied for many hours, however its not for everyone and you need to be a tycoon fan to get the most out of this game, and even then trying to end the game will annoy you.

PROS: Great atmosphere, amazing narrative
CONS:
The hints you're given to work through the puzzles can very quickly become extremely misleading. This is a huge problem because these hints are often akin to "hot vs. cold" and you can very easily start having those 'helpful hints' lead you in exactly the opposite direction, completely tearing you out of the epic narrative and into a pit of frustration as the game makes death come quickly and bear a heavy consequence. (You die too much, all your progress is lost).
Many segments of the game did leave me saying "this is absolutely the future of immensive RPGs," but I was equally left with moments where I would solve a puzzle I had died to once or twice, figure it out, and say "Are you ♥♥♥♥ing serious?" What caused me to die personally was rarely from a failure to properly analyze the situation, but more a failure to not get snagged on an awkward protrusion while something was chasing me or see a passageway that could only have been seen through the perpetually suffocating darkness of some levels had you leaned up exactly against the wall where it is and looked right at it. By the way, you often can't, because you spend a lot of time running for fear of death.
Combat encounters offer decent action combat you'll recognize from games like Dark Souls, or perhaps a more apt comparison in this case would be the Witcher 3. Most of the combat is just a nice change of activity to carry you through the experience, but some encounters can become pretty busted and get you killed instantly much in the same way you'd die in Dark Souls 1 if you leashed certain enemies in such a way they backed you into a wall and spammed you to death. The difference here is the permadeath mechanic, or illusion thereof. Dark Souls is a game in which you adapt from repetitive failure, Hellblade is a game in which you MUST. NOT. FAIL.
I'd also like to share a moment in the game where I was fighting a certain beast, died, and repawned with my blade stowed and completely unable to draw my blade. (Seems good?)
The TL;DR of it is that Hellblade is a really genuinely good story to play through which often fails to deliver on its mechanics properly enough to keep emotions like anger and frustration out of an experience that depends so heavily on its emotional queues of fear, relief, and adoration for its characters. I would recommend this game, but I would also like to post a thumbs-down steam review so that some vote is taken into account here that this game is immensely flawed mechanically and not entirely what you might hope for after you've spent your $30.
