In quick summation, stop reading this review and play Hellblade with headphones on.  You may skip the rest.
If that is insufficient, Hellblade is, in all seriousness, probably the most artistic game I've ever played.  The Citizen Kane of games, if you will, which elevates the capability of storytelling in games.  It draws the player in deep and keeps them immersed without button prompts, healthbars, waypoints, or any other game mainstays.  Whispering auditory hallucinations act as prompts and guides and preempt the need for most forms of communication and set the tone and largely tell the story--Senua does a lot of crying but rarely speaks.
The story is excellent and both the best character study of psychosis in any medium as well as an interesting introduction to Viking mythology, even for those already aware of it.  The heroine is strong but troubled and she serves as the most unreliable of narrators but peices together an even more troubled history leading to her dark quest.
Sound design is epic.  Headphones are required--open-backed, if you got em.  Several dark areas ask you to navigate by sound, and it works well due to excellent binaural design.
Visuals are mostly excellent--the only downside is textures that are visibly low-res for 4K or 1440p displays.  Give that a pass and the lighting and materials quality really shine when you aren't looking too closely.  Visual design is also excellent.  Enemies are sick and later areas are seriously twisted.
The action is intense--scaling difficulty is interesting.  That said, most of the time is spent walking slowly while the plot sinks in, or the voices simply hound you.  This is necessary to build atmosphere but it does mean the first third of the game, before the plot starts really taking off, feels rather monotonous and very slow.  The speed never ramps up but the areas and puzzles start to feel a little less stale.  There aren't that great a variety of enemies and you will probably tire of the same guys after a bit.
That said for low points, for high points, the visual and audio tricks and general tone of the game resulted in both the most anxiety-causing rush I've had in a game as well as the most thrilling boss encounter I've experienced--both as a result of the way the story is told rather than the mechanics, which are solid for combat, but limited.
End result, if you view Hellblade as a game divorced from its content, it's slow, repetitive, and just has decent combat and puzzle ideas.  But if you take it as the immersive auditory and visual experience that it is, it is the most important game you'll play for a while.

With the plethora of options available to the modern ARPG connoisseur, Van Helsing finds itself an average product on a shelf packed with fantastic games at extremely reasonable prices. It's unfortunate, because I'm sure this game would've been considered great in 2004-2008. With Torchlight 2, Diablo 3, and Path of Exile easily available - all superior options, and all unique from each other - the generic and mediocre Van Helsing cannot be recommended in good conscience.

This is a great hack n slash adventure. If you like games like torchlight and diablo then you'll love this one. The voice acting can be weak at time, but the lush and detailed environments more than make up for it.
My one gripe is the last boss is near impossible to defeat and then you are rewarded with a quick cut scene that makes absolutely no sense and the game abruptly ends. Way to give your players the middle finger on that one.
WHat Diablo 3 should have been

For the genre of ARPG this game stands out among those like Path of Exile and Torchlight as the spiritual successors to Diablo 2.   What makes this game more unique is its story, and its skill system.   It takes the story of Van Helsing and throws you into the very midst of a gothic era where monsters rule the landscape.    With only the basic class to choose from unless you get DLC there isn't much variety in the terms of classes, but in my opinion the DLC is worth the price because it gives you two other, very unique classes to play that give a very distinct flavor to the game with each class you play.  With a full fledged multiplayer system, friends make this game even more enjoyable as you go on a monster hunting romp through a forest with your buddies.

Played the game on hard mode.
The previous reviews pretty much summarized the good sides of this game:
- Well designed world.
- Some really nice background music (definitely getting game OST if there is one).
- Attractive graphics.
- Highly customizable settings (could play this game on my laptop).
- Some interesting references to pop culture (really liked Baggins dude!).
- Good voice acting.
- Decent storyline.
But all in all I would advise you to avoid this game. Here is why:
- If you do not buy DLCs then there is only one character class you can 'choose' from. The character can do both melee and range attacks, however, due to horrible difficulty balance I had to specialize only on one attack type. The result is there is not a lot of variation in the action.
- Except very rare short conversations, the sidekick ghost lady is useless. She dies really fast and eats up all the health potions. I have ended up keeping her in a ghost form all the time. The result is the game would not change much if she was removed completely.
- The game gives you impression of customization, but it actuallly punishes you for doint it. After mid point of the game, customization becomes really expensive and you can end up spending all the gold and still not getting what you want.
- The essense system (aka gems and gem slots) is useless. Items where you can put gems are rare. If one is found then usually it does not have enough essense capacity to put useful essense. You can use an essense to increase the capacity but during my 27 hours of gameplay I had collected only 3 capacity increasing essense. Finally, there is not a lot of variation in essense types. I had collected only 20 or so different essense types during the entire game!
- The fighting becomes really repetitive quite fast. There are many enemies that look different, but really just a skin deep difference. All off them can be categorized into melee enemies that charge in mass, melee enemies with hooks and ranged enemies. There is no interesting behavior from AI. More challenging enemies have simply 1) more HP and higher defense points, 2) just attack in bigger numbers, or 3) have more HP and defense and attack in higher numbers. It is not possible to use interesting tactics. Most of my gameplay consisted of repeating two things: have a short skirmish and then running away to use potion before having another short skirmish. Bullet spongy enemies just killed all the fun for me in this game. Most annoying are the enemies with hooks. It is not possible to predict or avoid hooks using your skills. The hook animation is instantaneous. The problem is, at least on higher difficulty, if you get hooked then you are basically dead.
- Horrible camera angles. It is not possible to control the camera. Did I tell you about enemies with hooks? Well many times I was hooked by enemies I could not even see. I am not even talking about number of times I was shot at by enemies outside of the screen.
- Bad character controls. There is no keyboard-based movement control. Mouse is used to click on a place where you want to move your character. Sounds good enough right? Well not. Combined with horrible camera angles and enemies swarming everywhere you will end up in many situation where you cannot find a free space to click on and move your character. I ended up more than dozen times dead because my character refused to move. The complexity of the surrounding world makes the situation even worse because it is not immediately obvious where you can and cannot click.
If you are looking for a good ARPG then go for Path of Exile. PoE is superior to this game in everyway. Plus, PoE is free, and there is no DLC nonsense.

All I can say is WOW! This is the first "typing" game that I have ever played. Didn't know what to expect, and was blown away. The presentation of this game is outstanding. The story is told with a book motif from words (100% voice over) being typed directly on the world to new areas being opened up on pages of a book and poping up like the pop-up books. The art style is a paper origami style. The presentation of the game is top shelf.
For the game, you play as a girl riding a fox trying to understand the world around her. The entire game is played with the keyboard, of course. As you explore, you may find items in your path. Press the space bar - if words appear above the obstacle type the word to destroy it. Combat is handled in the same way. Monsters will hone in on your character. Some will move faster. Some will have simple words. Others longer words. Most will have banks of words and all words will need to be typed before the monster is destroyed. Each successfully typed word will award you with experience points and a timer. Chain together successes to rake in the experience points.
As you progress you will gain access to four types of magic: fire, ice, electricity, and wind. Each one of these does something different. Fire magic will burn the next word in the bug's word bank. Ice magic freezes enemies. Using the spark magic will zap words from adjacent bugs' word bank. And wind magic will blow monsters back.
If you are not much of a typist there is what is called adaptive learning. The game will change the difficulty based on several factors. From what I read, there is a scale from -80 to 100 that is given as you play. Typing words without error will increase the score. Dying will decrease the score. The entire score is then multiplied by your WPM value to give an overall difficulty. In this manner, if you are not a fast touch typist, you can still enjoy the game.
Epistory isn’t without a few issues. Right out of the box, the movement controls are awkward. You can use the E and F keys on your left hand and the J and I keys on your right hand. But, for me this was not intuitive. You can also use W, A, S, and D for movement. However, then your hand is out of place when you want to type. There is a mod you can download that allows you to use the E, S, D, F keys in place of the W, A, S, D keys for movement. This is a great solution and one that should have been thought of by the developers. Second, this is a typing game. When there are a lot of insects on the screen sometimes all the words get jumbled up and it can be difficult to determine which are the most critical words to type. One touch by a monster and you are dead. Thankfully, deaths don’t cost much. The last item is more of a nitpick, but I am not sure how the words per minute are calculated on the stats page. I have gotten over 40 WPM but not much more. I also found a couple of words are not possible to type if you have certain magic enables. One I remember is FIZZ. Since typing FIRE changes to fire magic, if you type F-I the game registers this as the FI for FIRE and won’t let you complete FIZZ. So, you can only type FIZZ if you have fire magic enabled. Not something you are thinking about in the middle of a battle.
The issues are definitely not a show stopper. More of an annoyance I hope the developer addresses in any future games of this type they may create. This is an extremely well developed game. The story is interesting with 100% voice over. But it is the presentation that steals the show. The graphics are amazing and the presentation and world-building are phenomenal. I didn’t know what to expect with a typing game, but Epistory is an excellent game.

I'm sure this is going to get downvoted by diehard fanboys of this series, but really. The graphics are nice, yes. The music's decent. There's a good premise for a game here. So why is it /so bloody boring/? There's very little variation in the levels here, aside from one or two notable exceptions most every level plays the same. Even then the only notable departure is the last level, which is instead just flat-out flawed. The game focuses far too much on its combat system and too little on platforming or creative puzzle design. There's about three different types of enemies throughout the entire game, and they're all over the place in each level. So fighting them gets... really boring, really fast. Though the bats never stop being annoying. Ever. The puzzle design is mostly physics-based and can also be entirely broken, basically defeating the point. I have plenty of fun playing as the thief and doing neat platformery stuff, but that's fairly limited throughout the game... I kind of wish the game was based more around that mechanic than the combat or physics puzzles, really. But as it stands the game just felt like it dragged on forever to me despite not even having that massive of a play time to it overall. Not going to say it's outright terrible but it's not particularly impressive either.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one hell of a game, no pun intended. Seldomly I felt myself drawn into a story so easily and so very deeply. The voice acting is incredible, as are the visuals.
But Senua's Sacrifice is not an everyone's game.
The main theme, mental illness, and how it affects the protagonist and her struggling to achieve her final goal, that is what makes this game an exceptional experience. It's not about solving riddles and heavy-handed swordfights in a surreal setting filled with norse mythology. It's about the storytelling, the creepy and foreboding atmosphere; the voices, the visuals, the bizarre hallucinations.
I strongly suggest to play without reading about the storyline first. I was diving right into it after downloading, and that created a suspenseful atmosphere right from the very start while my decision to buy Senua's Sacrifice was solely based on the positive reviews.
But one needs patience to allow the story to develop and unfold and also the willingness to immerse fully with what happens on the screen -  to be able to empathize as much as possible with Senua and what she's going through.
I cannot tell if this game has any replay value after finishing it, but that's not important to me anyway. I rather play an unusal and rather unique game only once instead of watering it down by beating it over and over again. Because Senua's Sacrifice deserves so much more than that. Especially because it's not so much a game as it is an experience.
Buy it....  just buy it

With a seemingly never-ending flock of "retro" platformers hitting the Steam store these days,
takes the opposite route: a story-driven adventure with stunning visuals, a bewitching atmosphere and some pretty mad feels.
The first thing that will captivate you is the sheer beauty of the game. The art, the characters and their animations, the lighting and the splendid instrumental music score will instantaneously create a deep feeling of immersion. The storytelling, most of which occurs in-game, will also be supported by small doses of narration and beautiful cutscenes, just enough to give you a sense of purpose and accomplishment.
The gameplay is everything you could possibly wish for: tight and responsive, with top-notch level design and an increasing number of mechanisms to master as you progress, in pure Metroidvania fashion. The overall difficulty achieves a fine balance, making
both accessible to players who just want to enjoy the story and atmosphere, and challenging enough at times to keep veteran players on their toes. Exploration is rewarded with power-ups that give you more leeway to fill the simple-yet-efficient skill tree, which nicely complements the other abilities that you unlock as you advance through the game.
A casual playthrough will last you a good 10 hours, and that alone would be well worth themoney. But
also nudges the more hardcore players into giving it another go with an online speed run leaderboard and some pretty tight achievements like completing the game without dying. All in all, a very fair amount of content for its price tag with refined quality on top of that. The standard for an up-to-date adventure platformer and a definite recommendation for me.

This is my first review.  I'm thinking about doing more.  I'm not one for a number system, it always feels arbitrary and/or contrived.  Constructive feedback is welcome.
TLDR: Buy it already.  Seriously.
Intro:
I stumbled across Ori and the Blind Forest while I was randomly searching through games on Steam.  The picture I saw for this game seemed pretty cute so I decided to check it out.  As I was doing so I was reminded a lot of the Rayman series, particularly the 2D games, all of which which I thoroughly enjoyed.  I found the artwork and the videos on the store page for Ori to be quite beautiful.  Out of reminiscence for Rayman, the beauty of what I was seeing, and the Overwhelmingly Positive reviews, I decided to get it.  I was not disappointed.  After completing the game, I don't think a comparison to Rayman is inappropriate, but it may not be the most appropriate.
During the course of this review I will try to give enough information about the game but not spoil anything.
Review:
Graphics:
Simply gorgeous.  The screenshots and videos do not lie.  The game is beautiful.  I did suffer some lag though, but nothing game-breaking.  My specs are listed further down.
Sound:
The music is pretty, and added to the feel and mood of the game.  The sounds are nice enough, I can't recall anything that made my ears ache.  I don't know what else to say on this point.
There is no discernible language in this game even though there is speaking, sort of.  It's a made up language, but it's presented in a likeable manner.  There's also very little of it.  Only a few lines here and there.  Dialog is shown on screen in English (or presumably in one of the other supported languages) and the game is paused during this.  Nothing is taken away from the game through this technique.
Gameplay and Controls:
I used keyboard and mouse with no issue at all.  I found the controls are very accessible and intuitive.  The store page says "Full Controller Support" which I can't speak of, I generally don't use controllers.
It's a 2D platformer.  For the most part I found the game easy enough, but there were times when the difficulty was "punch-the-monitor" difficult.  There are some "run-for-your-life" sequences that were quite difficult.  Depending on your skill level, those sequences can take maybe 20 or so tries (each), like for me, or, as I've read on the forums for this game, potentially dozens of tries.
I had roughly 360 deaths by the time I beat the game.  Most of those, probably 2/3, were my own fault, just running along merrily and then misjumping into deadly terrain, or running into an enemy I didn't see, or forgetting how to play and I just stand there taking damage until dead (because I do that kind of thing), or running into a laser and forgetting to jump, or because food.  So, I would say probably about 120 of those deaths were related to difficulty, and 60-80 of the 120 were from the "run-for-your-life" sequences.  Given that, I don't think it detracted from the game at all, it just got extremely frustrating at times, like during the "run-for-your-life" sequences.
You can gain health, power, and ability upgrades along the way.  Many of them are in secret areas.  You can also acquire ability points through the combat system.  You can learn skills through the use of ability points, and you can gain certain skills through story advancement.  I didn't find any of the story skills to be arbitrary or useless, and I had a hard time deciding in what order to purchase skills because they all seemed useful though some more than others.  There is an achievement for beating the game without purchasing skills, but I believe that to be for advanced players.
Story:
It's a beautiful story about the power of love and how we should treat each other with kindness.  I was quite moved by it, despite its overall simplicity.
Achievements:
There are plenty of them.  I'm pretty sure some will go unachieved for most people, such as the one for not dying.  I also think a few of them are bugged, I'm pretty sure I got a few to show on screen but do not show properly on my achievement list.  I could be wrong, but I don't think so.  There may be a solution to this but I have not looked into it, I'm not an achievement hunter so I'm not concerned about it.  Still, would be nice to have the credit I deserve.
DLC: I do not own any DLC for this game as of writing this review and cannot provide an opinion for any.
My Specs (at the time of review):
Vista Home Premium SP 2 64 bit
GeForce GTX 750 TI
AMD Phenom 9550 Quad-Core 2.2 GHz
6 Gigs system ram
DirectX 11
Conclusion:
Regardless of your personal skill level, it's worth giving this game a shot.  I bought it on sale for $11.99 but I think it's worth the full price of $19.99.  I am definitely looking forward to another Ori game.  I highly recommend this wonderful piece of art.

I...really tried and yearned to love this game, as I do with every indie project that shows some semblance of original thought.
I ended up...liking, if at times only TOLERATING, a lot of things about Van Helsing.
Why do I say such a thing? because it got pretty bad at parts, but I also don't shy away from games totally unafraid to make me feel like a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥like they did 15 years ago. This game succeeds on that front unquestionably.
Ideally for 2-4 players, I actually just finished the entire game solo. Be forewarned, if you're not an ARPG guy, you're even in for a rough time on easy difficulty, which I all but mandate in your first playthrough. This game will swarm your♥♥♥♥♥like Starship troopers with things that do not, I repeat NOT, die in 1, 2, even 5 hits. It's rough, and it works for the setting and the game.
Now at this point the average Joe has some idea of what they're in for, so maybe you ARPG die hards are now asking: "What's in it for me?" Well I'll tell you!
Great music: I had to talk about this here. It's a standard we all have with games of substance, especially a good APRG. This game delivers EXCESSIVELY. The entire score features soft harps and pianos, things you would expect to hear in this alternative dark fantasy Transylvanian tale. Hit up youtube and hear some of it for yourself. This is one of few games that I actually left on while I wrote the review because of how great an atmosphere the menu theme provided.
Story: One thing I found funny about a game as goofy as Torchlight 2 is that it took its Story as seriously as Diablo did. This flip flops- very believable, gritty, down to earth graphics, sounds, and atmopshere, totally slapstick everything else. The characters engage in light heartened banter while picking up quests, interacting with objects, and more.♥♥♥♥♥♥ there's even a message board in town at the beginning that is for nothing beyond "click for great pop culture reference." It's a true joy to experience.
Gameplay: Not much not already said here, You are in for a challenge, no way around that. A fun challenge with friends, but a challenge. Bring your A game, this game's "easy" is NOT TL2's.
Fresh and new ideas: Ever think how badass it'd be to properly have your own hideout/camp, or even gather resources and build♥♥♥♥♥♥in a game like an ARPG? well VH almost delivers. I can't say there's any proper crafting, but midway your township where your vendors reside can actually get attacked, and you play a metagame of tower defense to protect it. Very innovative IMHO, and successful.
Overall, if forcibly shoehorned into rating it on a 1-10 scale, which I like to refrain from, I would call this game a 7 without question. Flawed, buggy still, but the devs care about the latter and are working on it, it's an all out riot most of the time, and most important of all- it's fricken $10 until the 2nd. Consider snagging it if you're a fan of the genre, or even a new guy looking for a semi hardcore trial by fire.

Steam doesn't keep track of my hours since I had to stop launching it through Steam in order to get it to run properly on Windows 7 (it's possible to do a work-around and get it to run through Steam but I haven't bothered with it), but I have easily logged over 1,000+ hours into this game, with about 150 on xbox 360 and 900+ on PC.

For $15, this is one game you can't skimp out, even if you suck at fighting games like me.
As a standalone title, Skullgirls (Encore) is simply one of the most complete titles in the Steam library, and while a sequel/expansion (Skullgirls Second Encore, AKA Skullgirls Endless Beta) is on the way, this current edition is still quite worth picking up.
Artistically speaking, the game looks gorgeous with its steady frame rate and reportedly hand-drawn characters that are both smooth in frame transition and movement. The backgrounds and the character designs all bring in a very early 20th century look that I wholesomely appreciate. Furthermore, character designs also have plenty of references built into them, such as the most widely advertised character of Filia sporting the Japanese "Futakuchi Onna".
Gameplay is also very solid. The game responds very well to button inputs, and the slight lag experienced during online matches are excusable as a common problem. However, the control really requires a joystick or some sort of analog equivalent. Moves like Beowulf's "Wulfamania" just love having the player a joystick 270 degrees, a move that is very difficult to replicate on a keyboard. Other than that, the game works great.
The game does have some drawbacks though. At an initial of only 8 characters, its a very small roster to start off with. The presence DLC is also slightly irritating, as 3 more characters are restricted to DLC, such as Squigly, Big Band, and Eliza. PC users get Beowulf and Fukua right off the bat, but its still rather weak for a competitive roster. Online play doesn't help either, as Lobby matches require a HUGE amount of wait time and quick-matches are paired without any consideration to the skill levels of the players. Finally, the tutorial works as a great teaching tool for fighting game beginners, but some of the instructions are a bit vague, especially when it comes to pulling off expected combos and reacting to the CPU's blocks.
While the game has its downsides, the overall value greatly justifies the game. I do not regret picking the game up whatsoever I sincerely hope that more will come out for this sprouting franchise. Maybe figurines?

Disclosure: I was a beta tester for Lost Dimension
Lost Dimension is a port from the Playstation 3/Vita and as you can tell is a JRPG. I just wanted to give a quick bullet point review of my thoughts on the game.
• Story: The overall story is pretty generic, big bad wants to destroy the world because of reasons and high school kids with magic powers go in to stop him. The hook here is that there are traitors among your group (randomized each playthrough) and it's up to you to figure out who the traitor in the group is each floor in the tower you're exploring.
• Graphics: As this is a last generation game, the graphics are about what you'd expect for a Playstation 3 JRPG but with the added clarity and 60fps 4K options added. I'm a personal fan of the "anime" aesthetic and love how the game looks. Interactions with characters use a Persona style character portraits to get a good look at who you're talking to.
• Gameplay: Combat is slow, but takes careful planning each turn as the tides can turn at any moment. The game lets you control characters within a field and you need to move to oppenents or get within range of them (varies with close-quarters and long-range attacks) in order to do damage. Having characters nearby is best as linking attacks is possible and really determine if you're going to be able to take down a tough opponent or not.
Overall the game looks great for a port, has challenging gameplay and the story, while generic, is interesting with the added traitor mechanic. I'd highly recommend this game to fans of JRPG's and want to thank Ghostlight for bringing this gem over to Steam.

Lost Dimension tricked me in a way few games have done before.
At its surface is a bog standard tactics RPG, turn based, move your dudes, attack the enemy, use spells, return to lobby, gear up, start next mission from the mission list. It is a simple loop, quick to get you playing. There are a few tricks. Namely, one of your team is a traitor.
You would think that is important, but it actually is not. The game is not about what is essentially a secret agent/superhero team going up against a madman with a traitor among them. The traitor is one of your party members, and he or she does not move against you in any way. You control the traitor's every move in battle and he will never act poorly or try to stop you. You suss out the traitor with a simple mind reading metagame that is only tough if you still do not understand it fully, and you must do so before proceeding at the end of each chapter as at least one person must die each chapter. So I won't spoil it by explaining the rules, just saying if you figure out what the rules are, you will never let a traitor go by.
Yes, a traitor. There are multiple. In fact, beyond one scripted traitor, it is random each chapter who becomes a traitor next, and each NG+ run is all random. Weird, huh? Like I said, the game isn't about the traitors. It could not be with this level of plot muckery. This is a game about the mechanics. I will come back to this later and talk more about the mechanics.
Lancarse has experience with Etrian Odyssey. If you have not had the pleasure, EO essentially has some of the best RPG combat on the market. Varied classes, deep skill trees with a lot of options, a lot of challenge, and yet no needless complexity or lame arithmetic. Every skill, buff, debuff, ailment, it's all meaningful, even on bosses, and yet with immense variety between the classes. You have much of the same stuff here: Each of your twelve characters has a massive skill tree with three major branches focusing on different gimmicks. You have a healer, a tank, a warrior, a fire mage... but you also have a linker who can copy the stats and movesets of any other character in range, a teleporter who can control the spacing of the battlefield; you have more skill trees and classes than you can shake a stick at. While the expertise of EO is not fully realized here, the variety on offer is incredible.
Now, wouldn't suck to randomly lose one of these because he was a traitor? That's the trick: You don't. When the time comes to execute a traitor, what gets left behind is his materia... essentially, his skill tree. You can then equip his skills to one of your living characters. You can no longer level them up, but suddenly you can give your healer the buffer's skills, or your fire mage the psi mage's skills. Some of these materia combinations can even unlock ultra moves in certain characters that can be real game changers.
THIS is Lost Dimension. Everything else is in service to this mechanic. Your team is whittled down from a dozen rotating team members to a lean half dozen hybrid classes where everyone is holding so many skills you do not quite know what to do with them all. This is where it tricked me; it took me two full plays to realize this is what they intended with this game.
This is also why the game insists on a NG+ run for the true end: Lost Dimension wants you to replay it again, each time building up a new team, culled at random, to build a new series of hybrid warriors. In fact, you barely get to enjoy this system until NG+ where you get bonus skill points to really enjoy it (You start again at level 1 with no gear, but with extra skill points. Be careful not to overspend and make your mana costs too high before you have enough mana to support it!), and extra missions to really cut your teeth on.
Does Lost Dimension succeed at making an endlessly replayable game? I do not think it does it perfectly. The skills aren't all equally viable. The balancing isn't at EO level; some characters are just much better. The assist shot system, where enemies and allies near to an attacker can join in on the attack, overrides almost all that skill tree strategy and makes the positioning and "defer" system, essentially a baton pass to pass your turn to another character after you have moved but not acted, mean a lot more than clever skills. The game is also a little long to encourage repeated play, about 12-15 ish a run.
To get into the spirit of the game, I recommend you keep separate endgame saves of every team just so you can compare what your teams end up looking like from run to run.
As far as the actual plot goes, you figure out pretty quick that The End is doing all this for some grand reason, and the first ending isn't a disappointment like Nier Automata was, but you have to get to the NG+ true end for the full gist of it so between start and the various endings is a lot of faffing about and social link type stories. The writing is on and off; your comrades all have serious issues, stuff that is too weird to take seriously and not goofy enough to be successful comedy. Your protagonist is at least written as a forceful personality, eager to slap down or call out these dopes, but it is not enough to save the conversations from feeling kinda stilted and autistic.
But beyond all that, what Lost Dimension offers is a very clever turn based strategy with a lot of interesting ideas. It's easy to play: just pick a mission and roll, then check your math and see if you are closer to figuring out the traitor. Just... don't get too attached to your waifu. You might only get to keep her in the next run.

When I first laid eyes on Lost Dimension I wasn’t really sure what to make of it. I have never seen a game where your own party has traitors hiding within it, let alone you having to discover them and eliminate them. When I learned it had an interesting turn-based combat system, I was completely stoked to check this title out. Did it live up to my expectations?
The world only has 13 days left. A mysterious man called The End has perched himself of top of the “Pillar,” a tower that phases between dimensions. The only way to save the world is to climb the “Pillar” and defeat The End. An elite team of gifted individuals called SEALED must scale the tower to defeat this mysterious individual. They will need to use their special psychic powers against the various enemies that lay in wait for them. However, there is another threat they must overcome — their group is filled with traitors. You will need to sniff out these traitors and erase them in order to ascend each floor and reach The End.
While the graphics aren’t the strongest asset, they look decent. The character models are fairly detailed, and the animations look smooth. The environments are all well represented, from the ruined city streets to ancient ruins. The soundtrack only adds to overall experience. While there are not a lot of tracks here, these techno / industrial songs will get you ready for some serious combat or set the mood for the mystery that surrounds
I am having a blast with Lost Dimension. The combat is fun, the story is great, the characters are interesting and it has some great replay value. The playthrough will take around 20-40 hours, and you will need to do at least two or three to discover everything this title has to offer. Despite its drawbacks, for the price tag, you’re getting one of the most interesting and unique games that has been ported over to the pc. 8/10

This game intrigued me with its typing elements, but what surprised me the most was how much fun I actually had playing this game. I loved unveiling the world through exploration.
The combat is surprisingly intense. Sure, typing is easy enough, but the game adds different elements to combat – quite literally! There are fire, water, lightning (spark), and wind elements. If a word has those elements, you have to type the respective magic and defeat the words that way.
I’d like to say I’m fairly decent and accurate at typing, yet some of the battles were really challenging to overcome. The enemies/words get tougher the farther into a fight you go (honestly, the dev must love the word pupivorous and antiestablishmentarianism  because I got those ones a lot). There are ways you can get around harder words, such as using a lightning element word on an easier word to chain a lightning attack to harder words. It’s interesting what kind of combinations you can do in battle!
The artwork is absolutely beautiful and I loved the landscape. The music was also very beautiful. My one complaint is that after a music track was done, it was complete silence until you triggered another area/scene with music. I would have loved either a loop in music or more background music while I played!
The game is also sadly not very long. I found myself wanting more and was surprised I completed the entire game in one day (I completed the entire story in 6.3 hours).
Overall, this game surprised me in how much I came to love it. Definitely try out the demo!

Didn't I already type enough in this game? Do I really need to type more for a review? >_<
So Epistory is quite an interesting game. I think the last time I played games about typing was when I was a kid and they were very basic educational games. But this game drew my attention anyway.
Epistory adds in some mechanics to make the adventure more interesting even if the gameplay mechanic might not seem exciting. There's an interesting narration going along as you explore the world, giving you some information about the character, and it is painting an image of the areas you go into. Note that the ending of the game seemed pretty obvious early on, at least for me, and wasn't exactly surprising. Funnily enough, though, if you
You get to walk around and slowly explore as the world opens up in an origami art style, unfolding from paper tiles. There is a main hub world and a handful of dungeon-like areas you enter throughout the game. When you explore, you encounter obstacles in your path and enemies that will fight you. In order to destroy obstacles or enemies, you must enter the "Typing Mode" and literally type the words above the obstacle or enemy.
At first, that starts out pretty simply. But as you go through the dungeons, you start to earn elements that you can use, like Fire or Ice. Then, the game starts giving you enemies that can only be destroyed by a particular element, so you have to switch modes during combat quickly. Even further, you might encounter battles where using a particular element is better than the rest, because they each have a special power. For instance, Ice can temporarily stop enemies from moving, and might be useful in earlier fights where many enemies spawn. In that situation, you might be able to write the first word per enemy, rotating in a circle around the screen. That would slow each enemy one by one, and you could keep repeating that rotation to slow them again and continue damaging them. Sometimes, that might not work and you might need to use Fire or another element, depending upon enemy speed, the size of words, the quantity of enemies, and so on.
Besides the above gameplay, the dungeons and some parts of the hub world contain puzzles, but most of them are not extremely difficult. The majority of them simply involve moving to specific items really quickly, or following paths in a specific way in order to toggle multiple switches altogether.
The last comment I have is on the difficulty of the game. I feel like it's actually awkward to review, considering the difficulty will vary per user's typing skills in ways. Note that the game has an "Adaptive Mode" where the game will learn based on your performance whether to increase or decrease difficulty. I used this mode for the entirety of the game because I am a pretty good typist, and the game definitely increased difficulty over time. Even so, I was usually alright in most places and only lost fights if I had to use a particular element that I wasn't noticing would be beneficial.
However, there is also a way to disable the "Adaptive Mode" and choose basic difficulties of Easy, etc. I am not sure how these work as you progress throughout the game, so other players might be more helpful. Or there is even a demo for the game, for you to try it out if you want.
Needless to say, I enjoyed the game more than I expected, because the art, music, narration, and even the usage of the elements for combat formed something of a unique output for Epistory, which is unlike other typing-based games that I have seen in the past.

To great heights, some lows, and lukewarm destinations.
RPGMaker, we meet again. As a foreword, I have a personal distaste for RPGMaker games, as a lot of the games developed with the engine tend to reuse a lot of stock assets, and To the Moon is no different in that regard. To its credit, it does use a lot of unique assets, but the overall vibe I get from the game is that it would be much better if it was developed on a different platform.
The premise of To the Moon is a simple one. You are tasked with overseeing two doctors with a simple mission - to make a dying man's dream come true. Tragedy, romance, it's all there as you journey back through his memories to make his wish come true. The doctors are the facilitator of this, and they're more like dream technicians. And to be fair, they are the weakest part of the story. The two of them can be typecast as the straight (wo)man and the fool, which is my biggest complaint. Too often they interject their discourse into an intimate moment with no tact or subtlety whatsoever, which often ruins the mood. The rest of the game is incredibly well-written EXCEPT for the people you play as. The dying man's memories are way more interesting than listening to a neurotic's caffeine addiction or his complaints. I'm guessing it's written like so because it's "another hohum job" for them to do and that it's a simulation, but they come off as tactless. Outside of those two knuckleheads, the plot and story as a whole still manages to stay strong. There are also a couple of mini-episodes included with the game, but they're more fluff than anything, designed to give more of an insight to the background technology of the main story.
As much as the visual medium of the game requires it, the RPGMaker graphics are servicable. There are some unique art pieces here and there, but it's acceptable for what it is. But once you've seen those trees and ground textures in one game, you'll see it everywhere else.
Where the game really shines, however, is the soundtrack. The piano-heavy ballads and melodies have that right amount of melancholy and nostalgia to stick with you and make the scenes feel more impactful. When music is absent, the mood turns coarse and heavy. Where the graphics fail, the sound design helps to ease over the lackluster presentation into something more palpable.
With all of those points in mind, the story is rather short and concise as most people can finish it through one sitting. As much as I was looking forward to playing this, I can't help but feel underwhelmed, and not of any fault to anything else but the mystique around it. The game is not perfect, far from it. It has its flaws and moments of heavy-handed writing. Even so, it's not a bad game. It tugs at the heartstrings at the right times and even made me well up at times.
Ultimately, your mileage will vary. Some will cherish it far more than others, who might leave it as a cute story. For the price point it's at, you honestly can't go wrong.

Gauntlet is an action adventure game from Arrowhead Game Studios and WB Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I don’t think I’ve ever played the original Gauntlet game, but I played the living hell out of the one on the Playstation. I’m pretty sure it was Gauntlet Legends. Anywho, this Gauntlet is still just as fun as the previous installments.
Now, bearing in mind that I haven’t played a Gauntlet game since the days of the PS1, this Gauntlet let’s you change your character’s armor, helmet, and weapon. What’s more, you’re not just throwing your weapon at the enemies in an endless stream anymore. No, you’re actually attacking them with that giant warhammer you’ve got. Warrior class, I’m looking at you. But, in all seriousness, actually being able to hit someone with a battleaxe, instead of throwing one at them repeatedly (as awesome as that may sound) is so much more rewarding.
While the game itself is shiny and improved, it still maintains that classic Gauntlet feel. You and your friends (or, in my case, just me) against teeming hordes of monsters and it’s up to you to reduce them all into greasy gore piles, snag the gold, and get out with your lives.
The levels are pretty large for what they are. It’ll take you a good ten minutes or more per level, depending on how much of a completionist/explorer you are as a gamer. That being said, there are a ton of levels to play through. And, if you finish them all, there is also an arena mode where you can slaughter monsters to your heart’s content.
The Bad
Maybe it was intended to be so, but the dialog is laughably bad. It doesn’t really detract from the experience, but you’ll wonder how some of it got past quality control.
The Meh
The game is a bit of a grind and, if you’re not playing with friends, it might start to get monotonous after a while. You’ve been warned.
Verdict: Yea
At full price, I probably wouldn’t recommend getting this one. But, if you can get it on sale, I’d recommend adding it to your collection. If you can convince a friend or two to get it and play it as a team, even better.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one hell of a game, no pun intended. Seldomly I felt myself drawn into a story so easily and so very deeply. The voice acting is incredible, as are the visuals.
But Senua's Sacrifice is not an everyone's game.
The main theme, mental illness, and how it affects the protagonist and her struggling to achieve her final goal, that is what makes this game an exceptional experience. It's not about solving riddles and heavy-handed swordfights in a surreal setting filled with norse mythology. It's about the storytelling, the creepy and foreboding atmosphere; the voices, the visuals, the bizarre hallucinations.
I strongly suggest to play without reading about the storyline first. I was diving right into it after downloading, and that created a suspenseful atmosphere right from the very start while my decision to buy Senua's Sacrifice was solely based on the positive reviews.
But one needs patience to allow the story to develop and unfold and also the willingness to immerse fully with what happens on the screen -  to be able to empathize as much as possible with Senua and what she's going through.
I cannot tell if this game has any replay value after finishing it, but that's not important to me anyway. I rather play an unusal and rather unique game only once instead of watering it down by beating it over and over again. Because Senua's Sacrifice deserves so much more than that. Especially because it's not so much a game as it is an experience.

When the game was released, it wasn't half-bad. Now, though, there's far better options for the same price.
PROS:
+The first Fallout to take a FPS perspective. Many dislike the "Oblivion with Guns" gamestyle Fallout took with this game, but I personally like being able to shoot rats five feet in front of me.
+A number of locations which make welcome additions to the Fallout Universe (Rivet City, Vault 112, and the National Mall)
+Some new weapons and enemies which feel setting-appropriate.
+You can wipe a city off the map with a nuclear bomb for money. While stupid, it's so audacious you can't help but to admire it.
+LIBERTY PRIME IS ONLINE!
+Liam Neeson!
+Mods!
+Shoulder-based Nuclear Bomb Launchers!
CONS:
-Talking the Enclave out of their evil plan isn't a matter of working to show the flaws in their logic (like in Fallout 1 and NV). Instead, it's a simple speech check and telling them "Don't! It's bad!"
-Aiming MUST be done through VATS. Trying to iron sight it results in missing your target, frustration, and frustratedly missing your target.
-Setting has potential to be something special. Instead, it's a typical good-vs-evil setting grossly dissimilar from every other Fallout ever released (except maybe 4, and 4 was far more in-depth about its what's right vs what's wrong approach)
-Brotherhood and Enclave are simplified from technophobes and unirradiated-human-supremacists to generic good guys and bad guys, losing all character they once had.
-References to previous games feel out-of-place when the game messes up on so many other levels to be a spiritual Fallout. It feels like seeing Chewbacca in Episode III.
-Grossly reduced roleplay elements compared to the other games in the franchise (except 4).
It's not a complete waste, but it's a mediocre roleplaying game, a bad Fallout game, and a frustrating shooter. If you're looking for a better example of what Fallout is all about, a better sequel to Fallout 2, or a similar game done right, get Fallout: New Vegas.

This was by far one of the greatest gaming experiences I have ever taken part in. This is an expertly crafted game, created through the tireless and constant work of Bethesda studios that culminated to form the greatest gaming experience of the century.
This is apparent from your first few minutes with Fallout 3, where you are shown the life of your character from childhood. This is am excellent tutorial, as it not only introduces you to the new Fallout mechanics, it intertwines it with the story and character development. I have never cared so much for a game's tutorial.
The game play is just as exciting. Fallout 3 strikes that perfect balance between Action and RPG, making it well deserving of its GOTY title. Even with no FPS skill, you can Excell at the game by using VATS, a call back to the Fallout RPGs of the past. The different stats and skills you put your points into completely change how you play the game. You can go in guns blazing like any other action game by investing in weapons skills, strength, endueance, ect. You can invest in Lockpicking, stealth, and perception to become a silent killing machine. You can even invest in things like Intelligence, Medicine, Barter, Science, and Charisma to Excell in unorthodox areas. The game gives you so many options, I can barely keep track, adding to it fun and replayability.
The presentation is excellent as well. Some might not be fans of the graphics, but I love the rugged and abandoned feel they give the game. And the atmospheric soundtrack always thrills me to listen to it. This game is a great experience in the audio and visual sense as well.
In conclusion, Fallout 3 is one of the greatest games ever made. It can be complex or simple, slow or fast paced, thrilling or emotional, all depending on how you want to play. Fallout 3 is am excellent game that puts the player first, and I love it for that.

I bought this game very soon after it was made available, and not even for the panties and boobies.  "What are you, gay?"  the average internet-goer may inquire, and sir / madame / wolf / otherkin, that is not a question even I can answer, as I identify as a genderfluid planet.
For the fightin' game vets, Skullgirls is a 6-button fighter that feels like the perfect middle ground between the tactics of Street Fighter and the combo chaos of Marvel VS Capcom.  The mechanics are varied and unique between the small-yet-growing cast of characters (the only "Ken" literally started out as an april fool's joke, and even then it's hardly the same character).  Variable team sizes of 1 to 3 is a huge part of your pre-game choice and playstyle as it directly and dramatically affects the power and health of your individuals and how many assists you get.  The combos chain fluidly, the action stays fast, and wins feel earned.
For the newcomers, this is a fantastic introduction to fighting games, or a great one to play casually.  There are step-by-step tutorials, ranging from the basic buttons and mechanics to how each character's unique moves work together.  I had no experience with the infamous insane difficulty leaps between difficulty settings, and there's neat storylines for each character explaining why they're all clawing each other's eyes out in the first place.  The frantic pace makes even button mashing exciting, and all of the aesthetics look friggin' sweet.  Which brings me to my next point...
The atmosphere is inviting and flashy, the music is snazzy and classy, and the animations are as smooth and beautiful as the characters.  This is quite literally art in motion, and it all comes together nearly flawlessly.  I don't think I have anything bad to say about this game other than some of the paid DLC (which are offered for free in the first while they are released) but eh, that shouldn't detract from the rest of it.  A steal of an experience for the 3 dollars or so it's on sale for at the time of writing.
Oh, and there's a Zone-Tan skin for one of the girls, Squigly.  There is also a Zone-Tan background sprite in the game.  Steam wouldn't allow me to tell me who that is if you don't know.  Among that, there's plenty of other sneaky references and nods to things in places like background characters, voice lines, the moves themselves, and the fighter's color palettes.

One of the very few fighting games that has held my attention for an extended period of time. Amazing hand drawn graphics, interesting stories, very satisfying to play, great music, every character feels unique to each other. The online also works very well, rarely game breaking lag from my experience (Though expect to be wrecked if you don't know what you're doing.) The only thing I'd complain about is how few modes there are, but I don't think it's a big deal because what's there is great and the game is pretty cheap, especially during steam's frequent sales obviously.

I cannot recommend buying this game due to Paradox Interactive increasing prices just before the Steam Summer Sale. Many of their games were increased by approximately 20-30%. In the case of Stellaris, the discount was upped from 40% to 50%, but because of the base price increase there was only a $0.40 cent drop rather than a $4.40 drop. On many other games the discount percentage was not increased, meaning the sale price was more expensive than usual. This is absolutely a shady tactic to increase sales due to a perception of getting a better deal than you are actually getting. I would much rather the discount be kept at 40% off the original base price, yes I would be a little disappointed if I was looking to buy, but I wouldn't be angry at being manipulated.
I only ever expect price increases to occur when a game exits Early Access and during Early Access itself. Perhaps even if it was a massive update to a finished game, increasing the price would be reasonable. But this was a clean sweep across most of their catalog, without reason.

If you read between the lines you will notice that this is not an automatic refund, and you only get 1 key regardless of how many games you bought. This is my favourite game of all time!

That said, here are a few facts you might need to know in case you're uncertain if this game is for you:
Lost Dimonesion has tactical, turn-based combat system and some very minor VN/Dating-Sim elements, means between the fights you get to rest and have the opportunity to get to know your team mates better. It's not that much reading though, so no worries on that point.
You build relationships with them (no romance or anything like this), but mutal trust is important when it comes to another of the games uniqe features: voting and eleminating traitors among your group. Team mates who trust you will more likely vote the ones you want to get rid of.

There is a decent amount of customisation in the game, so you have the chance to play in your own style, but keep in mind you never know which of your comrades might be a traitor. I won't say much about the story, this is personal taste anyways, but I loved it, and I will play this game over and over again. And again and again and again.
I suggest to give this game a shot while it's on sale.

- Mysterious, reserved thief who uses a grappling hook to pull and swing herself around. Kills enemies with bow.
- Overweight knight and wannabe hero who likes food and drinking. Uses shield to avoid damage. Kills enemies with sword.

OK, this review is primarily for the campaign game as I still am in the progress of completing it.
THE GOOD:
If you remember Ports Of Call, this game has a very familiar feel to it.  So much so that I would consider it the spiritual successor to that fine game.  The ship docking is nearly identical, smaller feeder ships are more difficult to dock than the larger post panamax & larger ships that have side streamer jets that will allow much better maneuverability than the tiny ships.
Many varied ports are available worldwide to sail into and each port has very unique feel to it.  Hamburg & Santos are especially technical and can be quite challenging and fun to sail into at full speed.  They have an option to pay a tug to skip the manual docking for a fee based on your ship size.  The fee can be quite a hit to the profitability of the runs... Which leads me to the Bad...
THE BAD:
Profitability:  I have noticed that the smaller ships, while they carry much less cargo, and in some cases are significantly slower, are FAR more profitable than the larger ships.  Cargoes are 3 to 5 times more profitable per container than the larger ships.  THIS IS A COLOSSAL FLAW IMO, and a huge reason that my fleet of over 200 post panamax ships is starting to bog down my computer.  I refuse to make runs where the cargo value for my huge UCLV ship is equal to a post panamax ship 3 size classes smaller.
I have found that there are ways to crock the game model by leaving feeder ships in the company contract ports to generate hordes of tiny highly profitable contracts meant for feeder ships, but this exploit should not be needed.  The value of the cargo should remain similar through all the ship classes to motivate players to want to get the giant ships (which are a blast to drive) because they are big money as well as big fun.  Instead I am forced to slog through thousands of port tug fees to remain profitable.  Which leads me to the UGLY...
THE UGLY:  The worst part of the campaign is the outright thievery of the investor.  The first several status upgrades come along at reasonable intervals and have logical milestones to nudge the player to create a shipping empire.  Once the player hits the Magnate level though, the game bogs down into mindnumbing repetition.  The game becomes a treadmill of completing company contract after company contract.  The fun "quests" of filling a whole slew of varied contracts to a specific city are no more.  The "driving quests" where you are tasked with parking several of each ship are gone.
Tycoon level is the worst though.  Your only goal is to gather enough money to buy out this thief, who wants roughly triple the value of your empire when you hit Tycoon.  That wouldn't be so bad if I hadn't spent the entirety of the game building up a world spanning empire.
The main problem is that the thief/investor comes in every 3 months and steals 25% of your cash!  This game mechanic alone is almost enough to stop even the most diehard players in their tracks.  I have found that after a point, it becomes nigh impossible to break through this crock of a game mechanic and actually succeed and "win" the game.
All in all I would give a thumbs up to the game as a whole, but not the campaign.  While the campaign starts out great, it ends like the Hindenburg explosion...  OH THE HUMANITY of repetition!
I have read the previews for Transocean 2, and multiplayer mode sounds like great fun. For now though, I have to agree with may other reviewers.  Grab the game on sale, and enjoy it.  Very likely it will be cheaper per hour of entertainment  than a movie, and when you create your own conditions for victory, the non-campaign could be quite enjoyable indeed.

To great heights, some lows, and lukewarm destinations.
RPGMaker, we meet again. As a foreword, I have a personal distaste for RPGMaker games, as a lot of the games developed with the engine tend to reuse a lot of stock assets, and To the Moon is no different in that regard. To its credit, it does use a lot of unique assets, but the overall vibe I get from the game is that it would be much better if it was developed on a different platform.
The premise of To the Moon is a simple one. You are tasked with overseeing two doctors with a simple mission - to make a dying man's dream come true. Tragedy, romance, it's all there as you journey back through his memories to make his wish come true. The doctors are the facilitator of this, and they're more like dream technicians. And to be fair, they are the weakest part of the story. The two of them can be typecast as the straight (wo)man and the fool, which is my biggest complaint. Too often they interject their discourse into an intimate moment with no tact or subtlety whatsoever, which often ruins the mood. The rest of the game is incredibly well-written EXCEPT for the people you play as. The dying man's memories are way more interesting than listening to a neurotic's caffeine addiction or his complaints. I'm guessing it's written like so because it's "another hohum job" for them to do and that it's a simulation, but they come off as tactless. Outside of those two knuckleheads, the plot and story as a whole still manages to stay strong. There are also a couple of mini-episodes included with the game, but they're more fluff than anything, designed to give more of an insight to the background technology of the main story.
As much as the visual medium of the game requires it, the RPGMaker graphics are servicable. There are some unique art pieces here and there, but it's acceptable for what it is. But once you've seen those trees and ground textures in one game, you'll see it everywhere else.
Where the game really shines, however, is the soundtrack. The piano-heavy ballads and melodies have that right amount of melancholy and nostalgia to stick with you and make the scenes feel more impactful. When music is absent, the mood turns coarse and heavy. Where the graphics fail, the sound design helps to ease over the lackluster presentation into something more palpable.
With all of those points in mind, the story is rather short and concise as most people can finish it through one sitting. As much as I was looking forward to playing this, I can't help but feel underwhelmed, and not of any fault to anything else but the mystique around it. The game is not perfect, far from it. It has its flaws and moments of heavy-handed writing. Even so, it's not a bad game. It tugs at the heartstrings at the right times and even made me well up at times.
Ultimately, your mileage will vary. Some will cherish it far more than others, who might leave it as a cute story. For the price point it's at, you honestly can't go wrong.

While I personally want as many people to play this as possible, it's not an easy recommendation. That might sound like I'm condemning the game, but the fact of the matter is that it simply isn't for everyone. For me however, it certainly was. It is a fascinating and thoughtful dive into subject matter that hasn't really been explored much in this space. Since my experience in psychosis and mental illness is limited, I can't exactly comment on the accuracy and authenticity, but after finishing the game I do find myself wanting to acquire a better understanding. What it does do is equal parts unsettling, emotional and completely engaging.
As for the "game" part, I've been reading a lot of feedback that I find myself disagreeing with. Yes, there is a lot of walking, but it's hardly as simple as that. There's rarely a moment of quiet time as you're constantly bombarded with external stimuli, which is serving a very specific purpose in this case. When you do engage with the world, it's primarily in the form of puzzles, and combat. Puzzles are for the most part straightforward, and you're often led to the solution. There are a few instances of clever design that momentarily gave me pause, but there probably could have been more. They also tie in to the overall narrative theme.
Combat is where I disagree most with the negative reviews. No, this is not a PlatinumGames brawler, and indeed lacks that level of depth. To dismiss it as "simplistic" however is misrepresenting what depth it does have. More importantly however, is the execution. Combat in this game has a "feel" to it that's difficult to put into words. Every swing and hit has a weight to it that translates into such intensity that puts me on the edge of my seat in every encounter. It's the combination of the music, the voices in your ears, the enemy design, and extreme fidelity in visuals and animation that make it so incredibly engaging. As I said before this game isn't for everyone, but that's ok. I'm glad games like this exist, and I hope they continue to do so.

Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is an unimaginable pain of self-preservation, as you try to not get consumed by the darkness…literally. If you’re a fan of a good story with a powerful message, that has adventure, fighting, and beautiful eyes gazing graphics-this is the game for you. After finishing the game last night, I want to play it all over again.
Before the game starts it is advertised that it is best played with Headphones. The heavy dreaded atmosphere along with the great sound design, and the voices in Senua’s head makes the thrill and the psychotic experience a great game changer in the industry, as well as a Public Service Announcement about people with mental health issues. This story is about a girl who suffers uncontrollable from mental illness. Her mission is to journey to hell to free the soul of someone she loves, so they won’t be tortured by the darkness…her darkness.
Through this journey they’re puzzles that she must solve, and demons she must fight. The voices in her head help her at most times, but if there’s a chance she might be in danger, they either tell her to flee, or help her fight in combat. So many times, while I was fighting monster the voices would say “BEHIND YOU!” and I would duck out the way as the demons from my back try to slash me open.
30 minutes into the game you have your first fight, and it is made clear that if you keep dying, the darkness will spread closer and closer to your brain, and if it does, you will fail. All your progress will be lost. With that, the game keeps you on your toes, and makes you feel like you actually have something to lose. That’s a rarity in games, because in others you can just hop back onto one of your saves and do it again. Not This Game. I had the combat difficulty set to Hard so I can get the most intense experience from it. Luckily till the end I had only died/failed twice, I’m guessing it takes a lot more for you to start over from scratch.
The combat system is not at all hard to learn, when you’re surrounded by 5-10 demons however it can get challenging and you’re concerned for your life. Even in some puzzles you can die, especially if you’re walking on a plank to the other side, and at the bottom you’re high above the air and one wrong step will cost you all the hours you spent. The sad thing about Senua’s journey, is that the darkness spreads regardless whether you die or not. Every win you get the darkness spreads, every challenge you fail the darkness spreads. It is unfair and that is the message Hellblade expresses so justly. People with mental health issues, who try to escape their darkness but can’t, is an unfair battle.
If you’re going to buy this game, let me leave you with this: Even through all the hellish things you’ll experience in this dark twisted game, there is still hope to find the light. When playing as Senua you’ll notice that you too want to help her on her quest, and you’ll also discover that you too…might be one of the many voices in her head…the light in the darkness that tries to keep her alive.

You are cursed.
How many times would you need to hear it before you believed it? How much dissention before you questioned it?
Senua believes things that are not real, and so will you.
Hellblade gets better and better the more you play it and the torturous narritive and mind-twisting puzzles never let up. There are things here I've never experienced in a game before. Most of the audio in this game has been recorded with Binaural microphones so play with headphones for the best experience.

I bought this game very soon after it was made available, and not even for the panties and boobies.  "What are you, gay?"  the average internet-goer may inquire, and sir / madame / wolf / otherkin, that is not a question even I can answer, as I identify as a genderfluid planet.
For the fightin' game vets, Skullgirls is a 6-button fighter that feels like the perfect middle ground between the tactics of Street Fighter and the combo chaos of Marvel VS Capcom.  The mechanics are varied and unique between the small-yet-growing cast of characters (the only "Ken" literally started out as an april fool's joke, and even then it's hardly the same character).  Variable team sizes of 1 to 3 is a huge part of your pre-game choice and playstyle as it directly and dramatically affects the power and health of your individuals and how many assists you get.  The combos chain fluidly, the action stays fast, and wins feel earned.
For the newcomers, this is a fantastic introduction to fighting games, or a great one to play casually.  There are step-by-step tutorials, ranging from the basic buttons and mechanics to how each character's unique moves work together.  I had no experience with the infamous insane difficulty leaps between difficulty settings, and there's neat storylines for each character explaining why they're all clawing each other's eyes out in the first place.  The frantic pace makes even button mashing exciting, and all of the aesthetics look friggin' sweet.  Which brings me to my next point...
The atmosphere is inviting and flashy, the music is snazzy and classy, and the animations are as smooth and beautiful as the characters.  This is quite literally art in motion, and it all comes together nearly flawlessly.  I don't think I have anything bad to say about this game other than some of the paid DLC (which are offered for free in the first while they are released) but eh, that shouldn't detract from the rest of it.  A steal of an experience for the 3 dollars or so it's on sale for at the time of writing.
Oh, and there's a Zone-Tan skin for one of the girls, Squigly.  There is also a Zone-Tan background sprite in the game.  Steam wouldn't allow me to tell me who that is if you don't know.  Among that, there's plenty of other sneaky references and nods to things in places like background characters, voice lines, the moves themselves, and the fighter's color palettes.

For example, a circle appears under the monster showing how long until the move triggers, this combined with a slight slowed time effect creates great tension. Will you get the move off before your opponent, did you tell your monster to move/block in time?
Battles are already fun. Not alot of people to battle at the moment. But theres plenty of AI to hone your skills.

The game needs a lot of work still, but at the same time has a LOT of potential. I had to make some minor adjustments to the graphic/video settings but after doing so the game play was smooth with no issues. For anyone leaving negative feedback regarding lagging or glitches, I suggest you first make sure that the computer you have can properly run the software. They also give you a strong notice of it being a BETA version which may have bugs, glitches or lags, so leaving negative feedback in regards to this is a little unfair.
With that being said....
< Controls >
I really don't care to much for the controls. It was a little weird at first, but I adapted. I will be using my XBox controller rather than the mouse and keyboard.
< Camera Movement >
I don't like how the camera moves once the character starts motion. If I rotate the camera to a fixed position it should stay in that position until I move it.
< Quests & Achievements >
I like how you must interact with other characters and objects to unlock them. I'm sure Tt and Lego will develop achievements and quests along the way. I also agree with other users that more random events should happen.

Building isn't bad, but could be a lot better. Lego should really unlock this games full potential by providing every block Lego has (or the option to purchase additional Lego block sets as DLCs). Lego City, Lego Pirates, Etc......

By making users purchase each item, each time, would give it more of a challenge. Market? An online Marketplace for users to trade, buy or sell their bricks and/or creations is also an excellent ideas.
< Overview >
I'm sure we can all suggest a million and one ideas when it comes to this game. I like it. I think they have a good thing going and can't wait to see the game as it continues to develop. Dear god, this is possibly the best $5 I've ever spent.  I was really disappointed with what I saw today when I went to check out the first day of Steam's summer sale, but this looked interesting enough, and I have a mild obsession with sharks, so I figured, "Eh, for $5, why not?"  What a damn gem I found.
Depth is an asymmetrical multiplayer game where one team of four plays as divers, equipped with various kinds of harpoon guns, and a team of two plays as sharks.  The divers have to protect their little treasure finding robot called S.T.E.V.E. (I don't remember what it stands for; I didn't care) from vicious sharks while it goes to search for treasure.  The sharks, meanwhile, have to eat the divers and damage the S.T.E.V.E. to get those pesky fleshsacks out of their home.  The scoring system is a bit like Battlefield in that each side starts the game with 30 respawn tickets, and once one team's tickets are exhausted and their last member is killed, the team loses.
If you're playing as a shark, rather than choosing weapons, you choose your species, and each species has different abilities.  For example, Great Whites are slow but immensely powerful; makos are a little weaker but wicked fast; threshers are the weakest but the fastest, most agile, and smallest (meaning they're harder to shoot); hammerheads do extra damage to weak walls in the environment, etc.  You can also either buy or unlock through earning treasure (similar to how Overwatch's loot boxes work) new skins for your sharks, although these are purely cosmetic.  They add new playable species over time, and from what I can tell, they take community feedback into account when deciding what species to add by way of contests not unlike the contests Splatoon did (Cats vs. Dogs, Mustard vs. Ketchup, etc).
While there's no career mode, story, or campaign so to speak, you can play solo offline with bots filling in for the other five player spots.  For most people, this won't matter, but as one who thinks about whether or not a game will be playable when the multiplayer servers are offline, this is a big deal to me.  That's what irks me off about Destiny, Overwatch, and The Division and why I swore off buying anymore "online only" games like that; it will literally be unplayable in the future.  It's not a big deal to most people, but the fact that I could play solo with bots is actually what tipped me over the edge and convinced me to buy it.
Depth is a simple yet wildly addicting and entertaining game.  The concept is interesting, and the way they balanced the teams - having the diver team have twice as many members as the shark team - is a great way to keep things fair while also keeping it from being everyone against one guy.  While I wish there were some kind of career mode or progression or something with the single player, the fact that you can play solo against AI bots at all is a huge plus in my book, although this is one game I have absolutely no problem playing online despite the fact that I'm terrible at it.  It's currently on sale for $5 in Steam's 2017 summer sale from a normal price of $20, but if you're one who enjoys online multiplayer and are interested in a unique asymmetrical game, I'd say that even with the full sticker price, it's worth it.

Right off the bat: everything about this game is phenomenal and I would recommend it wholeheartedly to anyone.
The art and animation in this game are by far some of the most beautiful of any game I have ever played; every environment feels so lovingly crafted that sometimes I just had to sit there and admire it before getting on with the game! As far as the actual gameplay, I'm not usually a big fan of platformers but the controls in Ori felt intuitive and seamless most of the time. Even though I died more times than I would ever admit to anybody and got super frustrated in some spots, my interest in the rest of the game drove me to keep trying (and trying...and trying...) until I finally got to the next section. I'm not the most strategic or careful person, though, so it might just be me...
One of this game's biggest strengths that makes it stand out to me is its storytelling. There's not a ton of dialogue, as Ori does not speak, yet there were many powerful and moving moments in this game that made me more emotional than I ever anticipated I would be over a game with a tiny forest cat sprite! The other huge strength that goes hand in hand with the storytelling, for me, is the soundtrack. I'm biased towards any soundtrack that uses a live orchestra, but the music for this game is truly breathtaking and I still get those same emotional moments when listening to the soundtrack all on its own. That intense connection between the plot elements and the music playing at those moments means somebody did their job awesomely, and that truly changes the experience of a game for me.
In short: I'm not sure I can find anything to dislike about this game! Art, controls, plot, and music are all fantastic. Even after dying [redacted] times in my first playthrough I still ain't even mad.
