One of the best games that I've ever played, I would honestly give it a 9.5 out of 10 because of it's wonderful backstory, graphics, art, and overall game function. The plotline of the story transitions smoothly between each section or "chapter" that Ori encounters on her journey to help rekindle the essence of the Spirit Tree and bring light to the darkness that has developed in the world. Playing through the game, I was constantly enthralled with the graphics and mechanics of the game, because with a few keystrokes, you can either perform a fluid and acrobatic movement, or bring yourself to certain demise and restart at the nearest checkpoint. This constant revival checkpoint system may be seen to some as stereotypical, but actually develops into the players best friend (As long as you're not an achievement hunter). Although the game also starts off quite slow, with low damaging attacks and less mechanical skill because of how everything progresses based off of your experience that you gain and put into three different skill trees, it can become a playstyle oriented to the player's wish. Putting points into each skill section (Top - More map and support based, Middle - More Utility and skill based, and Bottom - More offensively based) allows for a different playthrough experience until a person has spent many an hour experiencing the great fun and story line that comes with the game. With all these different oppurtunities, achievement hunters such as myself are left with both frustration and excitement. As some challenges become impossible to near difficult (like finishing the game in a certain amount of time, or finishing the game without dying or investing into the skill tree. Each oppurtunity is different, and provides a meaningful and full experience to the player. But hey, this is just my opinion and experiences in the game. In the hours that I've obtained, I've always been so enchanted with the game that I wouldn't stop playing until I was absolutely forced to get up by moral obligations, and I'm sure to put many more hours into the game in the future. Making your own decisions on the game is up to you, but its definently something that I would recommend to any player ****Who can support it on their computer****.

I really tried to like this game; I had heard nothing but praise towards this for years so finally this sale I decided it was time to get it but I really just did not like it at all. So here is why:
First lets start with the surface level reasons, the stuff that hurts enjoyment but could be looked over by those who enjoy it:
Controls: The controls are just plain bad, if you use the keyboard the map is designed in a grid (as in 1 press up goes one block) however the actual design of the area does not make this clear, causing keyboard controls to feel floaty, as if when you let go of the button the character will continue moving until they reach the next grid block. The mouse controls a little better with characters auto moving to where you click, but when switching surfaces or rooms they will randomly stop despite having more to move towards; overall it just controls poorly.
Art Style: I know this one is just an opinion and I'm sure many will disagree but I just really don't like the art style; I can't really put a finger on why but it just rubs me the wrong way.
So now for the more pressing reasons why I don't like this:
Dialogue: This game isn't funny; the character's say cutesy jokes and puns so so often (especially Dr. Watts) but they just arent funny, I cringed through so much of it. Overtime these characters progress and make jokes less often but it just feels like a blatantly obvious way of showing chracter progression, take a bland character and make them say jokes then stop saying jokes and it will make it feel like they differed greatly.
Emotion: All of the big emotional moments felt pointlessly manipulative; often having important bits of information or character motivation hidden simply for a twist later.
Theme: I also disagree with the point the game tries to push about manipulating the past to be happy but I wont go into detail because spoilers.
Ludonarrative Dissonance: The primary gameplay mechanic is finding these glowing orbs to go deeper into memories, but how does wandering around looking for glowing orbs relate to the themes of manipulating the past or memories what so ever? These things are completely arbitrary, if there aren't enough inspectable objects in the room to attach orbs to the game will literally just give you them for walking around.
Overall I really disliked this game, I really wanted to like it, and I have heard nothing but positive regard from others but I just cannot see why. And it isn't just a matter of me not usually playing this sort of game, all of my favorite games are the artsy slow type that your 'average gamer' would hate (Her Story, Gone Home, Pathologic, etc) but this just did not click with me.
A short game but with a beautiful story that you should definitely play!

Sometimes all a narrative game needs is a good story and you can forgive the faults. However, To The Moon has everything going against it despite having a very unique and interesting story.
The dialogue is quite bad. At some times cringeworthy, and other times just missing the mark on a joke/reference. It feels as if the author knew the destination for their story, but didn't put enough effort into how the characters would get there.
The music does all the heavy lifting. Due to the terrible dialogue, the game relies on the amazing soundtrack to carry you through the story beats. This is the biggest strength of this game because the music completely nails every setpiece. I'm confident if they removed every line of dialogue from this game, used only emotes and sprite work, this would be a knockout.
The controls are frustrating. Since you are really just walking around in this game, easily moving your character around should be a top priority. However, your character advances too many steps in a button press, leaving you to run into many walls because you overshot.
A very unique story dragged down from the sum of its faults.

is a point and click RPG which has a fantastic story and great music. There is no battle system in the game and your entire playthrough (6 hrs average) will be story driven.
The following are my views and feelings about the game after a single playthrough. I will not be discussing the story to avoid giving spoilers but will say that the story, nay, entire playing experience was absolutely wonderful.
- The story gets really interesting early on and the experience goes only uphill from there.
- The characters and their dialouges are very well written and unique.
- The game has great flow and pacing.
- The "Time travelling" mechanic, especially solving memento puzzles was fun and added to the story.
- The Music is the strongest point of the game imo. 10/10 if I would rate it.
- The humor is great and jokes are plenty. I mostly had a grin on my face.
- I like how the game was not very difficult which at least made my playthrough enjoyable.
- The game also makes one feel a mix of emotions including feeling weird at times, which was good.
- There were several neat refrences like animorphs books etc.
- The graphics are standard RPG style and the controls are simple/easy.
- I could not play the game on my gaming laptop as it would not run even after following instructions by the developers. I do know that many players have had the same problems which started during the steam summer sale (2016). I played the game on my brother's laptop and it ran most of the time.
- I changed the DEP settings on my laptop but I kept getting "Script is hanging" error and critical errors afterwards.
To the Moon is an excellent RPG with a great story and an even greater soundtrack. I had a blast playing the game. I would recommend this game just for the soundtrack alone but luckily it has a touching story and well written characters which makes it a must have if you like RPGs.

I'm very impressed with this game. If you've ever wanted a step up from Mario Teaches Typing and want a pseudo interesting story to take you away for just a couple of hours, then this game is for you.

In short Epistory is a novel take on the age-old genre of typing games, here combined with RPG elements and exploration. It does come with several flaws and limitations, but the core gameplay is rather solid. If you are proficient in touch typing and enjoy it, you might want to take a look at this game. While I do recommend it, I don't think it is worth full price.
In long the game certainly has
and consistency. I mostly liked the visuals and even on the lowest settings the game looked decent. Early on you will encounter a flood cutscene where to me the papercraft aesthetic really came together. Also, from the very first moment you are greeted by beautiful lush ambient soundscapes. Unfortunately their volume is tied to the game sounds, which means if you want combat feedback you'll have to suffer through oppressively loud winds howling, water rushing, circadas chirping, etc. A little better mixing or separate controls would have gone a long way.
The experience is also somewhat tarnished by the unusual
. It's a typing game, so obviously you want to keep your fingers on home row. But since this is not an auto-scroller (like Typing of the Dead) inbetween you still have to navigate your character. They came up with a novel control scheme using both hands and RFJI. It took me hours to get used to and while it does work, it never felt intuitive. To their credit, I don't know of a better solution. And during exploration it's not a big deal, but the problem is compounded by the inclusion of tightly-timed movement puzzles (checkpoint races). At one point I switched over to WASD because I just couldn't handle it and was so frustrated. There are also issues where the geometry looks like you could pass, but the character still gets hung up on something.
Thankfully the core
gamplay is pretty solid in comparison. Monsters approach you and you have to ward them off by typing the words above their heads. This turned out to be surprisingly fun and with some of the optional fights also pretty damn challenging. I really liked the range from calm open-world exploration to a panicked flurry of typing during epic fights. There is supposed to be "adaptive difficulty" but whenever I had to retry fights, they were equally difficult. I thoroughly enjoyed the combo system, encouraging stringing together kills for more XP. The upgrade system was good, with the caveat that I maxed out my level before unlocking the final abilities, so the game kept prompting me to upgrade while none were available. The first three were great, but the last elemental ability was also a bit of a let down as you already had knockback and it was just more of it. Speaking of knockback, this is related to the only truly frustrating aspect of combat: The text only appears once the monsters are well into the screen (presumably so it fits centered above them). But if you then hit the monsters with knockback, you can still see them, but the words disappear and are not accepted by the game anymore. I can see the monster, I know the word, my focus is there right now - why the hell doesn't the game allow me to kill them? This kept happening every once in a while and was very frustrating to deal with, tripping up my flow.
There is a rambling narrator commenting on everything (Bastion-style) which is fine. There is a very thin over-arching meta
, but it's pretty weak and ended about as clichéd as one could possibly imagine. I would have liked it more if the story was confined to the world and had some goal or purpose within, because right now the in-game story of the girl riding a fox doesn't go anywhere.
I took my time and explored everything. In about 8 hours I had thoroughly exhausted the main game. It was a good experience and I can see
, since all the words are chosen randomly from a dictionary anyway. The endless arena mode feels aimless and boring to me and honestly, after 8 hours across 3 sittings I had enough of typing random words for now.
I've never had
problems with the game and it ran well on my terrible system. It does offer tons of different languages and keyboard layouts, which is great for a typing game. It took me a while to clue into how it works, but you can navigate all the menus by simply typing the words, which struck me as very cool and nifty to make sure you never have to lift your fingers from the keyboard.
The concept of the game is neat and the implementation is mostly competent. There are some brilliant ideas and design choices here and there, but also some striking flaws in other places. I'm glad this game exists and it provided an enjoyable short experience entirely different from most games on the market. Still, it feels like a brushed-up novelty one-trick-pony and personally I wouldn't pay full price for it. Whether it is improved puzzles or a captivating story - it needs some other quality besides typing combat to justify the price in my opinion. If you like typing and are already somewhat proficient, do pick it up on sale though.

Seriously, you can't establish liners services or anything; you're picking up one or two cargoes at best and essentially tramping. It's really not very complex, and the campaign is just a grind. The price of tug service doesn't make sense (It's about 50 to 1000 more than they cost in real life, seriously), and neither do the ship improvements - I have to stop a ship for two days to get a license to carry dangerous goods? Not only is firefighting gear an option, it's only available on the largest ships?
If you're looking for a remotely realistic simulation of the shipping business, give it a pass.
The ship simulation aspect is similarly basic... No transverse thrust on the propeller, only the larger ships have bow and stern thrusters, there's no wind or current and the ships don't have inertia. Give it a pass, and be very careful when considering the new version.

Fallout 3 or Fallout New Vegas?
I see a lot of people asking about if they should play Fallout 3 first, or Fallout: New Vegas. I went through this dillemma myself. I chose to buy Fallout: New Vegas.
Let me first give you a brief summary about the two games:
Fallout 3: You are a vault dweller. Your father has left the vault for an unknown reason. You go after him and enter the Capital Wasteland. You're main goal is to find your father again.
Fallout: New Vegas: You are a courier who had to deliver a package, but in the middle of your journey you were shot in the head by a member of the Chairmen (one of the families of the Strip). You wake up after being healed by an old man and you track him down. There is also a war going on in the Mojave Wasteland between the NCR, the New California Republic which is a faction that works with laws and such as they did before the bombs fell, and Caesers Legion, a faction based upon the old Romian Empire which is build upon slaves.
There are two major differences in the two games.
Fallout 3 is build upon the idea that you are fresh out of the vault. In the game, everything is new to you ánd your character.
Fallout: New Vegas is not really build upon this idea. You were shot in the head and you start your journey from a little farmers town.
Fallout 3 has an interesting storyline which I really enjoyed. It feels more personal then in New Vegas.

Please not that this review is by no means a reflection of the game in general, but more for an overlying issue: the fact that it is not optimized for any Windows OS newer than Vista.
Unlike New Vegas, which basically uses the same engine, older BGS games like Oblivion and Morrowind, or even Interplay's Fallout games of 1, 2 and Tactics, Fallout 3 generally will not run correctly, if at all, on Windows 7, 8/8.1, and 10.  While select few have been able to make the game run just through Compatiblity mode, the overall majority of users require numerous steps to go over and hoops to jump through.  And even then, if you are in the minority of those like myself, you can still find yourself unable to play even after jumping through the hoops.
While the avid modder for Bethesda games might find it normal and only slightly more frustrating, the average user might just find it to be one massive headache.  And again, they might just find it a waste of time if, like myself, can't seem to get it to actually start up a new game even with things like FOSE (Fallout Script Extender), G4WL Disabler (Games For Windows Live Disabler), a 4GB Patch, and the Unofficial FO3 Patch.
If you are one of those users who actually wants to put in the effort and see about getting it working, then there is a guide located here:
The Guide itself is simple to understand, easy to follow, and contains links to nessecary additions to help get the game running.
However, it by no means ensures the game will work.  While you could find success in the early steps, you could just find yourself stuck with nothing solving it.
If you are truely desperate in playing Fallout 3 again, but don't want to deal with the hastle of the steps in the guide, or are in the minority of users that, like myself, can't get it to run even with the steps in the guide, then you have one of two options.  If you are and avid PC player and might even want to mod it, then find a good quality PC that is running Windows Vista.  Or, if you don't care about mods, how it looks, or even what platform you play it on, then go down to your local Gamestop/EB Games, or whatever the store is called for you and purchase a PS3 or Xbox 360/Xbox One (as it is a backwards compatible title) and Fallout 3 Game of the Year edition, as the console versions still work fine.

Dear god, this is possibly the best $5 I've ever spent.  I was really disappointed with what I saw today when I went to check out the first day of Steam's summer sale, but this looked interesting enough, and I have a mild obsession with sharks, so I figured, "Eh, for $5, why not?"  What a damn gem I found.
Depth is an asymmetrical multiplayer game where one team of four plays as divers, equipped with various kinds of harpoon guns, and a team of two plays as sharks.  The divers have to protect their little treasure finding robot called S.T.E.V.E. (I don't remember what it stands for; I didn't care) from vicious sharks while it goes to search for treasure.  The sharks, meanwhile, have to eat the divers and damage the S.T.E.V.E. to get those pesky fleshsacks out of their home.  The scoring system is a bit like Battlefield in that each side starts the game with 30 respawn tickets, and once one team's tickets are exhausted and their last member is killed, the team loses.
If you're playing as a shark, rather than choosing weapons, you choose your species, and each species has different abilities.  For example, Great Whites are slow but immensely powerful; makos are a little weaker but wicked fast; threshers are the weakest but the fastest, most agile, and smallest (meaning they're harder to shoot); hammerheads do extra damage to weak walls in the environment, etc.  You can also either buy or unlock through earning treasure (similar to how Overwatch's loot boxes work) new skins for your sharks, although these are purely cosmetic.  They add new playable species over time, and from what I can tell, they take community feedback into account when deciding what species to add by way of contests not unlike the contests Splatoon did (Cats vs. Dogs, Mustard vs. Ketchup, etc).
While there's no career mode, story, or campaign so to speak, you can play solo offline with bots filling in for the other five player spots.  For most people, this won't matter, but as one who thinks about whether or not a game will be playable when the multiplayer servers are offline, this is a big deal to me.  That's what irks me off about Destiny, Overwatch, and The Division and why I swore off buying anymore "online only" games like that; it will literally be unplayable in the future.  It's not a big deal to most people, but the fact that I could play solo with bots is actually what tipped me over the edge and convinced me to buy it.
Depth is a simple yet wildly addicting and entertaining game.  The concept is interesting, and the way they balanced the teams - having the diver team have twice as many members as the shark team - is a great way to keep things fair while also keeping it from being everyone against one guy.  While I wish there were some kind of career mode or progression or something with the single player, the fact that you can play solo against AI bots at all is a huge plus in my book, although this is one game I have absolutely no problem playing online despite the fact that I'm terrible at it.  It's currently on sale for $5 in Steam's 2017 summer sale from a normal price of $20, but if you're one who enjoys online multiplayer and are interested in a unique asymmetrical game, I'd say that even with the full sticker price, it's worth it.

I really tried to like this game; I had heard nothing but praise towards this for years so finally this sale I decided it was time to get it but I really just did not like it at all. So here is why:
First lets start with the surface level reasons, the stuff that hurts enjoyment but could be looked over by those who enjoy it:
Controls: The controls are just plain bad, if you use the keyboard the map is designed in a grid (as in 1 press up goes one block) however the actual design of the area does not make this clear, causing keyboard controls to feel floaty, as if when you let go of the button the character will continue moving until they reach the next grid block. The mouse controls a little better with characters auto moving to where you click, but when switching surfaces or rooms they will randomly stop despite having more to move towards; overall it just controls poorly.
Art Style: I know this one is just an opinion and I'm sure many will disagree but I just really don't like the art style; I can't really put a finger on why but it just rubs me the wrong way.
So now for the more pressing reasons why I don't like this:
Dialogue: This game isn't funny; the character's say cutesy jokes and puns so so often (especially Dr. Watts) but they just arent funny, I cringed through so much of it. Overtime these characters progress and make jokes less often but it just feels like a blatantly obvious way of showing chracter progression, take a bland character and make them say jokes then stop saying jokes and it will make it feel like they differed greatly.
Emotion: All of the big emotional moments felt pointlessly manipulative; often having important bits of information or character motivation hidden simply for a twist later.
Theme: I also disagree with the point the game tries to push about manipulating the past to be happy but I wont go into detail because spoilers.
Ludonarrative Dissonance: The primary gameplay mechanic is finding these glowing orbs to go deeper into memories, but how does wandering around looking for glowing orbs relate to the themes of manipulating the past or memories what so ever? These things are completely arbitrary, if there aren't enough inspectable objects in the room to attach orbs to the game will literally just give you them for walking around.
Overall I really disliked this game, I really wanted to like it, and I have heard nothing but positive regard from others but I just cannot see why. And it isn't just a matter of me not usually playing this sort of game, all of my favorite games are the artsy slow type that your 'average gamer' would hate (Her Story, Gone Home, Pathologic, etc) but this just did not click with me.

The dialogue is quite bad. At some times cringeworthy, and other times just missing the mark on a joke/reference. It feels as if the author knew the destination for their story, but didn't put enough effort into how the characters would get there.
The music does all the heavy lifting. Due to the terrible dialogue, the game relies on the amazing soundtrack to carry you through the story beats. This is the biggest strength of this game because the music completely nails every setpiece. I'm confident if they removed every line of dialogue from this game, used only emotes and sprite work, this would be a knockout.
The controls are frustrating. Since you are really just walking around in this game, easily moving your character around should be a top priority. However, your character advances too many steps in a button press, leaving you to run into many walls because you overshot.
A very unique story dragged down from the sum of its faults.

If you have not played ‘Wolfenstein: The New Order’ then go play that before touching this game as this game picks up seconds after the end of the original. This game runs like blood through your system. My settings were a custom high as I seen this was a Ryzen/vega optimised game from the opening splash screen... That and the only API was Vulkan. FOV 120, Anisotropic 2x and AA 1x. I managed to maintain roughly 120fps at any given time with dips just north of 90 in some regions and 1 part of a mission filled with fire, explosions and literally infinite Nazis had me hovering about 80fps when I attacked.
I did have some teething issues when I first tried to launch the game and it kept crashing – to fix this I had to disable my iGPU according to the developers on the Steam Forums. This however worked well and I only ever crashed twice whilst playing. Once was a hard crash and the other from Alt+Tab-ing too much. I experienced no other issues, however I have seen that others have had a different experience from myself.
What a story! Rife with Betrayal, Nazis, Plot Twists, Mick Gordons Soundtrack and excellent character development for B.J. From the first 10 minutes of gameplay we see a young B.J and hear of his past through his own eyes.
The plot picks up seconds from where the first game leaves us and gives us a look into B.Js past before skipping 5 months to B.J being rudely woken from a coma to his stolen U-Boat being raided by Nazis. As such B.J –after having extensive surgery to save his life- wastes no time in picking up an SMG to slaughter the Nazi invaders. Soon after he hears of a resistance cell not unlike his own in Manhattan and so he and his team head to New York to team up and take back America from the Nazis by trying to spark a resistance. Some scenes in this game are just superb and must be seen to convey the true emotion of the scene.
This game has some of the most perplexing systems I have ever ran into: You acquire the SMG before the Pistol - essentially Downgrading the progression of weapons. Perks are a series of Actions with tiers that unlock extraneous (Things that cannot be controlled by B.J) buffs. The game Pushes the SMG on you with U-boat loads of Ammo, even though the SMG is by far the worst gun in the game even when fully upgraded.
This however should not detract from the gameplay – The gunplay is fun and opens up a world of possibilities with the modifications you acquire that can turn an automatic rifle into a semi-auto DMR with rifle scope, or a 9mm pistol into a .44 Magnum.
Levels can be attacked in a full on brutal Nazi killing war machine or as a stealthier KKK butchering assassin. Every fight can leave you gasping for health and armour pickups if you are not careful and the game puts a real limit on you for the first half of the game by only giving you 50% heath with 150% overheal.
The game always finds a way to keep things fresh and entertaining in each level and some of the cutscenes alone will leave you crying in laughter.
Overall I highly praise and recommend this game for anyone who wishes to kill roughly 6-10 hours of their life slaughtering mecha-nazis all over the USA and Space. The storyline is impactful, memorable and serious yet funny at the same time. For me this game ran like a dream however your experience my differ and for that: I am sorry.

A great little tycoon style game.
TransOcean is not a simulator; it doesn't go into much detail. The game basically just consists of loading crates on your ships and sending them from A to B. There is also a "minigame" where you can sail your own ships as they dock or leave the port.
The sailing minigame will not keep you entertained for hours, but it is fun to play now and again when you buy a new ship, and it will save you some in-game money when you play it, as well as grant you some achievements.
There are 5 classes of ships, all of which can have various upgrades installed, like better engines, water canons to fight back pirate attacks, or a license which allows you to transport juicy nuclear waste.
The rest of the game just consists of carefully choosing contracts of what merchandise to transport where, and it's up to you to find the route planning that will be the most lucrative. You can also transport drugs or contraband for extra cash, but risk losing all if inspected by coast guards.
There are also company contracts, which grant you substantial bonuses if you guarantee you will transport X amount of merchandise on a designated route in X amount of months. Fail to fulfil it and you will have to pay a big penalty.
One of the most fun I have found in this game is deliberately accepting a ludicrous amount of company contracts and then having fun struggling to complete everything in time!
In addition, as you level up, your antipathetic investor will throw some ridiculous contracts at you that you cannot refuse. These moments are the big highlights of the campaign.
Once you have fully leveled up, there is not much end-game, so TransOcean won't keep you entertained for ever, but all in all the campaign has a good 25 hours in it.
Technically it's well built, the interface is designed okay and I encountered very few bugs. The game comes with a set of elevator music tracks which I recommend you switch off from the beginnnig; then it just plays relaxing seaside sounds
Definitely one of the best tycoon style games out there.

This review is a toss-up between recommend or not.  It's not a great game, but it isn't awful either.  This is simply a mediocre twin stick shooter that does nothing to set itself apart from other games in the genre.  There is no story, no intrigue, and hardly any funny humor (there's plenty of bad humor).  You merely walk through level after level, killing whatever enemies you encounter along the way.  Sometimes you don't even have to kill the enemies and can merely run past them.  The game is fun for a few hours with friends, and that is why I chose the Thumbs Up instead of Thumbs Down review.
Here are my main points of discontent:
The characters attack too slowly, making it easy to get swarmed on all sides and unable to move or do anything, causing you to die.  There is not nearly enough gold available so you can't upgrade enough of your equipment.  The game forces you to g rind for hours in endless mode just to get enough gold to upgrade a single character to the best equipment.  Hopefully you never ever want to try out one of the other characters, else you'll have to start the grind all over again.
There are hardly any useful items for you to purchase, and most of the upgrades you can get are just for appearance.  None of the choices for the combat equipment (weapon, potion power, and relic power) really provide any meaningful help for you fight better.  Oh, they are certainly necessary and you'll want them upgraded fully, but they cost ridiculous sums of gold for the most minor of benefits.  I honestly found that most of my character's default equipment was better than any of the items I purchased, and that's just dumb.
The game also has a silly mechanic that allows you to accidentally (or intentionally) destroy food, taking away the ability for you to heal. This is supposed to be funny, but in practice it's just annoying, especially on the levels that are so dark you can't even see where anything is.  Food is also often placed behind objects you have to destroy, making it likely you'll accidentally destroy your meal instead of eating it for the health you desperately need.
The final boss is nearly impossible on Normal difficulty yet ridiculously easy on Easy difficulty.  I made no less than 40 attempts on Normal with various friends.  We could get to the final wave of enemies before killing the boss, but we always ended up dying.  I hate when games make the final boss stupidly difficult just to increase play time.  It's a dumb practice that just makes players resent the game.

Overall this game is great and does the Gauntlet series justice. The combat is responsive and satisfying and is a ton of fun on its own. Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses along with a handful of items that allow different types of attacks for each. Both endless mode and the campaign become progressively more difficult and punishing. Each change of scenery brings new enemy types and forces the player to adapt and react to the overwhelming waves of foes. The cast of characters offers a play stile ranging from the straightforward hammer slams of Thor the Warrior to the more complex button combination induced spell switching of Merlin the Wizard.
Co-op is a great deal of fun as well, from mindless hack and slash through the early game of endless to the hectic coordination required to take down bosses in campaign. This game is satisfying as it is through playing solo, but once more players are added into the mix the onscreen onslaught only becomes more enjoyable.
This game doesn't have a ton of depth in terms of long-term upgrade paths and out of game mechanics, but due to the satisfying combat it is fun to grind gold and upgrade characters' weapons to have a better chance against that room filled with summoning stones or that new boss. The main sense of progression is reliant on player skill and being able to react to enemies and wiggle out of tough spots, which is great.
The soundtrack isn't groundbreaking, but does add to the intensity. In terms of audio, though, the best part is the remarks made by both the narrator and the characters. Thor boasts about his godlike strength and perfect execution and the narrator's voice mocks players for destroying food unintentionally and praises them for overcoming difficult rooms.
This game is a great time through and through for anyone that likes hack and slash and is interested in how this arcade classic plays out in a modern light.

I skimmed through some other reviews here and I get the impression some people come into the game with the wrong thing in mind. That's not their fault, everything has it's demographic. This is quite similar to a choose your own adventure, but with fantastic art and interactivity that makes it much more satisfying. The story is good enough that it sticks with you. Like a decent short novel or something. It's not an action game, or even a puzzle game. It's a story, an experience.
The first episode has a great climax and ending, and left me wanting more immediately. The ending of the second was quite sudden to me, and I was a little bit disappointed.
The art in the second isn't as nice in my view. I'm not an artist, but I feel like some of the art used was a draft that ended up as the final piece due to deadlines. There was also some mismatch in the characters depictions in different areas of the game. Character X in a scene sometimes looked different once they were in a conversation and at the forefront of the screen. One officer was wearing a different outfit. I think one persons skin colour changed. Mostly it seemed to be different interpretations of the same character. It's a shame, because the first episode had art that really impressed me, that I could stare at for ages. Staring at the art of the second mainly brought inconsistencies to mind.
There were also several glitches I experienced with episode 2. My save game wasn't used initially and sometimes the characters in scenes would walk in areas they wern't meant to (like the roof), and I see others had more issues too. The developers have released several updates addressing all the known issues, provided steps to remedy problems, and are generally active in the steam discussions.
Overall I think episode 1 is AMAZING and episode 2 was rushed, but good nonetheless. Realise small dev teams don't have the luxury of being able to extend development time indefinitely. Bills have to be paid.
I absolutely recommend both episodes if my first paragraph describes something you could enjoy (story game, not action game, etc). Reward good developers.
It's worth nothing that the game is short. My 4 hour playtime was me taking my time, though I havn't replayed with different choices as some people do. I was satisfied with what I got from this and clearly the length of the game is limited by what is feasible with the type of the game (art HEAVY), and the manpower of the developers.
With context, some leniency for circumstances and such, 8.5/10?
Compared to a perfect game, 7.5/10?

Please not that this review is by no means a reflection of the game in general, but more for an overlying issue: the fact that it is not optimized for any Windows OS newer than Vista.
Unlike New Vegas, which basically uses the same engine, older BGS games like Oblivion and Morrowind, or even Interplay's Fallout games of 1, 2 and Tactics, Fallout 3 generally will not run correctly, if at all, on Windows 7, 8/8.1, and 10.  While select few have been able to make the game run just through Compatiblity mode, the overall majority of users require numerous steps to go over and hoops to jump through.  And even then, if you are in the minority of those like myself, you can still find yourself unable to play even after jumping through the hoops.
While the avid modder for Bethesda games might find it normal and only slightly more frustrating, the average user might just find it to be one massive headache.  And again, they might just find it a waste of time if, like myself, can't seem to get it to actually start up a new game even with things like FOSE (Fallout Script Extender), G4WL Disabler (Games For Windows Live Disabler), a 4GB Patch, and the Unofficial FO3 Patch.
If you are one of those users who actually wants to put in the effort and see about getting it working, then there is a guide located here:
The Guide itself is simple to understand, easy to follow, and contains links to nessecary additions to help get the game running.
However, it by no means ensures the game will work.  While you could find success in the early steps, you could just find yourself stuck with nothing solving it.
If you are truely desperate in playing Fallout 3 again, but don't want to deal with the hastle of the steps in the guide, or are in the minority of users that, like myself, can't get it to run even with the steps in the guide, then you have one of two options.  If you are and avid PC player and might even want to mod it, then find a good quality PC that is running Windows Vista.  Or, if you don't care about mods, how it looks, or even what platform you play it on, then go down to your local Gamestop/EB Games, or whatever the store is called for you and purchase a PS3 or Xbox 360/Xbox One (as it is a backwards compatible title) and Fallout 3 Game of the Year edition, as the console versions still work fine.

Despite being (at times) horribly flawed, REVERSE SIDE's "Demo" is an expedition into a beautiful technical experience, in a living, atmospheric, and musically gifted world.
REVERSE SIDE invites you to take a moment to ponder the bright, exploding starlight as it streams into your character's eyes, thanks to the new Unreal 4 engine. The meditative qualities of the game's world are apparent from the get-go: as soon as the game finishes the initial loading screens, the player is sure to pause, held by the stunning beauty of both the main menu's visuals and its stirring soundtrack. Composer Nikita Sevalnev shows his mettle by producing and writing one of the finest space operas in game history (or, it will be, if the music is as fleshed out and thought-provoking as it is in the demo).
Glitches such as clipping through walls, nonexistent control tutorials (hint: "E" is your go-to button, besides the standard WASD movement system), and a lack of advanced video options plague the game, but the latter two end not so much in being problems so much as things that the player will enjoy having to deal with.
For example, nonexistent control tutorials assist the player in feeling as though they are truly alone in the game, and the lack of advanced video options sets the game (for me, at least) at a comfortably cinematic 24 frames per second while playing at "maximum" video settings.
Users complain that there is no sense of direction for the demo, but user TigraWantabe has posted the athorotative and thorough (and only) guide that is easily accessible through the Shift+Tab menu.
In other words, the REVERSE SIDE demo is certainly a work in progress, but therefore is in that way a labor of love, both for developer and player alike.
10/10, and after seeing the trailer, I can't wait the painful last eight days until the game's and soundtrack's release.
I absolutely reccomend this game.

I've been big fan of this franchise since the original Europa Universalis came out years and years ago but I've always known that the game isn't for everyone. Though it will never have the mass appeal of games like Civilization it certainly fills a niche and feeds those gamers who are looking for a deep and involved historical strategy experience. With that in mind, Paradox has milked the franchise for years now, using it as the basis for a variety of other games that are little more than reskins of the original.
This sequel finally shakes things up by exploring some new gameplay concepts and including some interesting new presentation elements. The new interface is definitely welcome and it gives the player access to a bit more information while also reducing the clutter of popups and notifications that seemed to accumulate in the other games. The new gameplay ideas aren't revolutionary but they manage to add more realism and a wider range of options to the basic historically-themed gameplay.
It doesn't have the same impact that the original did so many years ago but the improvements definitely add a lot to the experience and make it more convenient for gamers who sometimes grew frustrated with the limitations of the earlier versions.

(Caution: may be a spoiler or two here....) If you like Torchlight II, Diablo (or any mouse-driven dungeon crawler RPG with great loot) then you'll love this game. Though it also has full controller support for those who don't want to play with the mouse. Makes it great for Big Picture. And there's a free demo which I always appreciate.
Bugs & Playability: Some people seem to experience a couple of bugs here and there (I did) but there are easy fixes in the forum & fabulous support from devs. The game is so interesting that I've been happily playing 3 characters despite the little glitches. I'd buy it again in a heartbeat. Wish there were more games out there like this!
DLC & Gear: The DLC for two other character classes (Arcane Mechanic & Thaumaturge) make for a nice change as well. (And they are not quite as strong in the damage department as the original 'Hunter' character, so it makes for a nice challenge on subsequent playthroughs.) You can save gear for your other characters. Epic items (akin to the Legendary items in Torchlight) are easier to find, but full sets seem much harder to come by. (Though admitedly I've only played single player and I'm sure you could trade for set pieces in multiplayer... Another difference, your 'pet' is not a pet but sidekick, the ghost Katrina, whom you can equip with armor, weaponry and jewelery. That adds an interesting level to the dialogue & gameplay that I liked a great deal.
Builds & Enchantments etc: As with Torchlight, you can allocate your own upgrades when you powerup and use enchantments and the like, so there's room for unique builds. If you have the money, you can enchant & disenchant repeatedly to get what you want. (In general, I found the skills, the gear, and the enchantments in this game even more interesting than Torchlight 2... and enchantments were more affordable which was nice.) I also thought the sequence with the tower defense was interesting even though that's not usually my bag.
All in all, a lot of fun & a very solid buy -- especially if you're watching the sales!

I HAVE, though, run into smaller, more annoying bugs.  For instance, the lack of the steam overlay.  This makes it impossible to take screenshots, and makes it so I have to tab out of the game to use the chat.  The game is well-optimized in most parts, but drops down to 5-10 fps in a couple areas on higher-end hardware (i7-4790k, gtx 980) and medium settings @ 1080p. Recommended overall if on sale, with some caveats.
I liked this game a great deal overall, despite the criticism I'm about to give it. It's been good value and good fun for me. Read on to see if it's for you.
This is a Tycoon game, not at all an accurate ship simulator. It's really more logistics oriented, and the financial aspects are weak. The simplistic mini-game of docking ships helps break the tedium, especially early on, but itself becomes tedious, particularly due to the lengthy loading times. I had no difficulties with the mini-game and I am decidedly not a twitch fast reflexes gamer. That said, casual or older gamers might not like the ship docking mini-game; fortunately it can mostly be skipped at the cost of some revenue. As the game progresses you'll likely be skipping it more and more.
I'd like to say it accurately depicts running a shipping company, but it really doesn't. The financial side of the game is incredibly weak and simplistic, with poor tools (no concept of a balance sheet or even a proper income statement, and some very strange criteria for a successful quarter. (e.g. there's an effort to calculate return on investment, but little concept of the passage of time, so back-loaded heavy ship purchases make your quarter 'unsuccessful' and you lose reputation.)
That said, the logistics (while simplistic compared to a genuine shipping company) are a nice thing, and piecing together company contracts and profitable semi-sustainable routes can be enjoyable for those who like that kind of thing.
Random events can be pretty irritating with wildly disproportionate penalties. More frequent cargo inspections with lower penalties would make more sense from a gaming perspective; as it is, the user is just tempted to reload when a potentially company-destroying penalty is applied randomly every couple of hours.
A couple of major downsides: some have reported major bugs, particularly in late game. While I've not yet encountered game-destroying bugs, I have encountered extreme slowdowns in the interface later in the game, especially with several ships in port. These lead me to suspect the coding to handle shipping consignments is at best weak and poorly optimized.
The final negative point is this, and why I cannot recommend paying full price. It's a quite good game for the first little bit, but the endgame feels very rough and unfinished. Red Johnson's Chronicles is a point-and-click adventure that has a certain attitude, with decent graphics and some quick time events (i.e. press button X before time runs out, and then some other button, and then some other mouse move...) to pass the "challenges", and the usual puzzles. While the writing is somewhat fresh, the puzzles are forced and derivative, QTE's are boring and out of place, and the weird interface really turns you off. This game was clearly NOT written for the PC, and it shows.
RJC has you playing the titular character, Red Johnson, who's a private investigator and he's been tasked by Officer Johnson of the metro police to help check out a murder... someone got whacked on the bridge... unfortunately, no body (may have fell into the water). You have to solve a couple puzzles to get access to clues, find more, and solve a couple QTE sequences on the way.
The graphics has a sense of those "noir" detective novels / graphics novels, with brown and gray being the primary colors. The transition between scenes are often animated and the cutscenes are quite nice with good if a bit cliched voice acting.
There are three major problems to this game: forced puzzles, weird interface, and QTE button smashes, all stemming from this being a console port.
The puzzles in the game makes ZERO sense and felt extremely "forced". For example, you find an instant camera, but the eject button doesn't work. Opening the bottom revealed that... "all the resistors had fallen out"  Huh? However, someone left enough clues on the board that I was supposed to form one complete continue line of resistors from 'start' to "finish" without violating the "number" (from 0 to 3) which is the number of resistors around each particular square. HUH? Another puzzle involving a different camera requires you to slide pieces of circuit board around to restablish the circuit among a power supply and two power destinations. Yes, the good old 15 pieces in 4x4 board sliding puzzle.
The interface doesn't help either. Most PC adventure games either use only the mouse... or only require arrow keys, space, ESC, and maybe one other key. This game requires the use of the mouse, left AND right click, space, B, V, M, AND the arrow keys. AND with the mouse you have to perform drag up / drag down / drag left / drag right actions, and it's never consistent. Many actions that could be done with arrow keys require mouse drag instead. This makes sense as this was originally designed for console controller with dual sticks AND a D-pad, plus addition buttons (4 primaries, and shoulder and trigger...)  but when it came to the PC, new keys were assigned without thought on how a PC gamer would be approaching the game.
Which brings us to the QTE... again, can never tell if you'll be doing mouse drag or actual key tap, maybe both. My first ever QTE was encountering Saul. First I hit space, then mouse drag three times (different directions) to conclude this easy test, and I flunked the first time because I wasn't gettng it.
All in all RJC's developers chose to make a barely adequate port and it shows. It's annoying to play, puzzles are forced and obtuse, which makes playing a chore rather than fun.

It's a decent little platformer, albeit a short one. Sadly, it's cluttered with a bunch of small annoyances that suck the enjoyment out of this game.
It's very visually pleasing. The levels are well constructed with the detailed pixel graphics and very nice use of colors...
But, they've decided to add a gimmick where as you die, the game changes its colors into the sepia and then the shades of gray, giving you the colors back only after beating the stage.
And since the game is rather difficult, it forces you to play the majority of it without any colors, making it not only dull looking but also more unforgiving at some parts of the game, as the projectiles blend together with the background.
They've also made a big cast of enemies (big enough for the game of this length at least,) varied in both design and attack behavior...
But, past the few initial stages, they were utilized very poorly, for the most part having them clustered together in larger amounts, making it a chore to fight with them, and therefore encouraging the player to skip entire sections of an already short levels (since they have an ability to very easily do so,) which is never a good thing.
There is also an RPG leveling-up system to the game that was tacked on as an afterthought, as it doesn't add anything substantial (just a couple of insignificant bonuses to damage, health or stamina,) and activates at seemingly random times, without any indicator on how long it will take until the next one.
The level-ups could have been easily replaced with a simple pick-ups, just as it was done with the weapons. In fact, I believe this would make the game better, by rewarding the player with tangible things for exploring the stages and beating the rows of enemies, instead of just rolling past them.
This is not a bad game, I'm sure that a platformer fan will find some enjoyment out of this. But, it's just disappointing.

Europa Universalis III is a grand strategy game and a part of one of the most renowned empire building strategy franchises of all time. EUIII gives you control over a nation of your choosing (and there is plenty material to choose from) and absolute strategic freedom to assemble your future world hegemon. This game combines a perfect balance between all areas of strategy (such as depth of war tactics, exploration, diplomacy, religion and government structure), as well as makes sure all of those stated above are realistic. Don’t expect to have an easy time defending against a Great Power with a minor. The game also introduces a lot of historical aspects into it, such as the great people of the time, geographical accuracy and random historical events, that will give you some unique experience with each new nation you play. Also, the map of the world and the amount of nations is outstanding.

+ Huge replayability potential and a lot of content for hundreds of hours

Graphics and presentation are top notch. I was floored throughout much of the game by how good it looks, it's one of the best looking games I own now in both art direction and fidelity. The UI changes are good, the menus all make sense, and the cinematography is as cool as the last game.
Gameplay is top notch but kind of weird because of the narrative. Much of the game keeps you at 50 max health and 200 armor until a point where it becomes the old 100/100. I appreciated this from a narrative context, and in a larger view of the trilogy it would make sense, but without a sequel to immediately aid the contextualizaton of the time spent here in a larger scope, the time spent at regular power didn't get as much time to breathe as I wanted (the majority, whereas now it's about half and half).
The rest of the gameplay is as good as ever. The new heavy weapons and gameplay gimmicks are welcome, while the old run and gun is as good as ever. Sound effects are great and Mick Gordon's acoustic/synth music is fire.
The narrative is what I like most about these games and I gotta say I absolutely love what's here. It keeps up the style of the first game well, imparts us with a sympathetic character arc for BJ, and exercises an interesting cast of old and new characters with surprising pathos. The length of the game was good as well, but in spite of all this I feel like it lacks the sense of closure that TNO had. It wasn't a problem when the game ended, as I felt as though it finished at an appropriate length, but it leans a bit heavily on the idea of a third game being imminent when instead it should have upped the gravity of the final level. As it stands it just sort of happens without the fanfare you would expect from an ending - some more interesting cinematography and foreboding around the final mission probably would have helped a lot.
All in all an excellent package. Well made, heartfelt, and and firing technically smooth on all cylinders. I have reccomended this to many friends and will reccomend it to whoever reads it.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing (Nth Review)
This game is better than Diablo 3. Okay, that was too easy...
This game is better than Torchlight 2. There you go!
And indeed I like it much better than TL2. The world of "Helsing" is a steampunk-ish one with a little bit of the old classic Diablo gothic horror atmosphere, combined with many throwbacks to horror classics in film and literature. The graphic style reflects that very well, being less cartoonish than D3 and TL2, while still being colorful enough to avoid monotony. The sound and voice acting are very good, just not outstanding.
The story is nothing special, but avoids being too generic via its strong characters and some interesting side quests. Especially the humor of this game is brilliant with a lot of jokes within the world, as well as on ARPGs and games in general.
In terms of gameplay this game delivers a big chunk of ARPG goodness with different playstyles, an interesting NPC partner (a ghost!) and lots of customisation for your gear and skills. The monsters require different tactics and the balance is very fair, but can be hard sometimes.
Rating: Very recommendable!

This game is as its name implies: "INCREDIBLE"!
I have played Diablo, Diablo 2, Torchlight, Torchlight 2, and not one of them was as pure fun as this.
The main characters, Van Helsing and Katharina are what makes the game great. They're incredibly funny to listen to. Great dialogue, with very nice voiceovers which seem almost impossibly good for such a small game. The references to other games, books and movies are great and fit the tone, which is always one of (mostly) lighthearted fun. The game is set in a sort of dark steampunk/clockwork setting, but it always aims to amuse and not to drag you down. It doesn't take itself too seriously and that is rare in games like this.
It is a solid ARPG, and the mechanics are simple and still have depth and it's really fun and rewarding trying out different approaches. You can play your Van Helsing as a gun-toting Monsterhunter or as a sword-fighting Slayer. You can even play him as a Mage. Each class plays very different and you can also adjust your companion similarly, which is a great idea.
As I said, I got more fun out of this than Torchlight 2, for example (the story here and the graphics fit my tastes better), so it is a definitve must buy for any ARPG fan, especially if it's on sale.

A nice looking ARPG with steampunk elements thrown in for flavour.
You battle your way through hordes of monsters that all look good and all die in satifying ways. The maps are all created as opposed to randomly generated. This mankes for a good forst time experience - and a rather bland second playthrough - can't say if the third playthrough is even more boring, I don't think anybody ever got that far.
In case you get lonely -you have your trusty sidekick with you - Katarina the ghost. I liked her, the comments from her are actually funny and you are never alone while killing monsters. She can fight for you, gather loot, buy potions etc. A really nice addition and she even comes with a full skilltree.
There are lots and lots of loot and the whole-loot end of the game is quite allright.
Aaaaand... Then theres all the annoying stuff like. Getting lost in the game and having to backtrack - I swear that some areas become unaccesable in the game so you can't go back there and finish a quest.
The game itself - the monsterkilling is done with a maximum of 6 skills (unless you want to tab between skillsets - I don't think anybody does that. I ended up with two skills - a single target and a sweep - and that's it... hour after hour...
The mobs themselves are pretty and fit the theme - but killing them gets kinda boring - especially when you end up with the ones slowing you. The only tactics that are in the game is positioning - and when a mob slows you (nothing you can do about it) positioning gets annoying.
And then there are the bugs... In my first playthrough (and the game had been out forever at that time) I had to manually skip an endlevel encounter with a code to get on and then at one point I had to wait several days because U couldn't enter the next area - bad to asy the least - it's not an early acces game...
Then there is the tower defense mode wich is horrible. Imagine a towerdefense where YOU are one of the little guys in the maze.. yop... You are running around in your maze defending. It's boring the defense quests are too long the only good thing is that after two encounters you are done. Two... why go through the whole business of making it and then only have 2 quests? Maybe because it's boring, but then remove it all together...
Did I have fun for around 14 hours? Yes would I recommend it? Yes - but it's not the new Diablo I, II or III.

The game is entirely about perfecting every jump, double jump, boost, and many more movements to be precise as possible to beat segments. This does become frusterating at times, but maybe that's myself more than others. Luckily in most places you can save whenever you want (granted you have enough energy, a resource require to save and do some other things).  Beware, if you want to achieve 100%, multiple play throughs may be required, and some places require you getting everything the first time visiting in that playthrough, as those areas become locked and the only way back is to start a new game.  And as far as story, it was very enjoyable, but nothing that will nock your socks off.  (9-12 hour playthrough)

When I first read about TransOcean Shipping, I added it to my wishlist and followed it closely for several months. The mixed reviews made me skeptical about buying it, but as I'd been starved for a good business simulation, decided to take the gamble - and I'm pleased I did!
In the game you play the founder of a shipping company, whom takes on an investor to fund his company. Starting off with one small 'Feeder' ship, you have to accept contracts and weigh decisions over speed/fuel consumption to ensure that deliveries are made on time. The campaign aspect of the game provides extra challenge, allowing you to unlock larger vessels as you progress in rank and prestige, whilst constantly trying to ensure you have enough money to provide the investor her regular payments.
Ships can be docked and cast off manually, which offers you the chance to control your ship if you'd rather avoid paying the tug fees (automatic docking/cast off) in ports. This can provide a nice little break from the 'main map' game screen, which is where you'll spend most of your time. Eventually you'll have a fleet of different sized ships, and will need to juggle factors of tight deadlines, contract penalties and the various ship sizes permitted to dock in certain ports etc.
Despite the fact that you spend so much time staring at the map screen, the challenge and reward of juggling everything around is thoroughly entertaining. It's a game that doesn't require too much thought and that you can play casually. I personally found the game addictive, but I appreciate that it won't appeal to everyone - I'm sure many would find the lack of variation a little tiresome/boring. If you're unsure whether you'd enjoy this game, do what I did and check a gameplay video online. There are many to watch, and will give you an accurate idea of how this game plays.

Red Johnson’s Chronicles is a game very similar to games like Puzzle Agent and Professor Layton, although it has a more serious tone and puzzles require a bit more effort than just pure logic. In fact, it blends together some of the better elements found in other (point-and-click) adventures games and does this successfully, but ultimately (and as expected) not without any flaws.
Red Johnson is a private investigator who’s investigating a murder at Drownedman’s Bridge. One clue leads to another and before you know it, you’re in the middle of it. The story is actually pretty cliché, and the final payoff isn’t as good as it should be. Furthermore, the game ends with a cliffhanger, one that wasn’t even necessary to begin with, in my opinion. Still, we got a part two because of it, because Chronicles is not just one game, but two. So you get two games for the price of one. Well, two chapters is more like it, but come on, that is a good deal.
But let’s not get ahead of ourselves and let’s just focus on the gameplay for a minute. You view the world from a fixed (first person) perspective and with your mouse you can click on points of interest. Some of these are useless (thankfully, there aren’t so many of these) and others are useful. The useful ones will usually zoom in on the object and let you solve a puzzle, or puzzles, next.
Puzzles range from slide puzzles and ‘detail’ puzzles (rotating an object in search of a clue, item or answer) to character confrontations where you have to pick the right answer.
Solving puzzles will earn you money and this money can later be used if you don’t know how to finish one. Hints are relatively cheap to buy so you could get through the game by just using one of the many, many hints. It clearly needed a bit of tweaking in that area.
There’s actually a good variety of puzzles here. Unfortunately, the game doesn’t always use checkpoints. Sometimes it does, but sometimes it doesn’t and when the latter happens you have to start the puzzle all over again. This is awkward game design and something that shouldn’t have happened to begin with. Some of the puzzles are tediously boring or hard to solve and if you have to quit because of a lack of time or because you don’t feel like playing it anymore you shouldn’t punish the player for this. Same goes for quitting the game while trying to solve a puzzle; the game registers it as one attempt if you quit halfway through.
Sometimes puzzles reward you with evidence and that evidence can be analyzed and compared by a device set up at your headquarters. These results can then be used to progress even further, by finding new suspects and places to go to, or interrogating suspects.
Every now and then a QTE will trigger and it’s because of the cool controls that these encounters become even remotely interesting in the first place. The mouse is used to create a motion so let’s say that you have some screws you need to get rid of then you have to rotate the mouse in a circular motion to unscrew them. During encounters the game will ask you to press the left button and move up, down, or anywhere else depending on the given situation. But, yes (there’s always a but), the controls just don’t work. I’ve failed many encounters because the game didn’t register them properly. Unnecessary and evil, because the game ranks you based on the number of tries it took you to finish an event or puzzle.
While you’re not doing any of the things mentioned above you have to search apartments and areas for clues. Unfortunately, some of the objects you have to search for are too hard to see because the graphics are either too dark or because the object isn’t instantly visible to you because it’s tucked away in a corner. So in the end it comes down to pixel hunting and that’s again something that shouldn’t be needed in this game, although it’s something we see often in the point-and-click genre.
The story is the usual ’whodunnit’ and even though it’s cliché, it’s executed pretty well. The characters all have the right motivations and the whole thing connects together nicely in the end.
The graphics consists of static backgrounds mixed with some small animations but on the PC they’re fuzzy and blurry and anything by hi-res. They’re also mostly brownish but that’s just the style of the game. Character animations are fine, but never great, and they’re also a bit unsharp. Lip syncing doesn’t seem to be there, characters just start moving their lips as soon as you enter a conversation.
Overall, the style of the game is pretty good, but it could’ve used some improvements here and there.
The voice acting is actually pretty good (which surprised me) and same goes for the jazzy music.
The game is pretty long. I think it will take anywhere between 4 or 6 hours to complete the first chapter and after that you still have chapter 2 to complete. My estimate is that it’s roughly the same length; I still have to finish it. But it’s good value for your money. You get a good amount of gameplay here.
Red Johnson’s Chronicles isn’t the game I hoped it would be. I expected another Professor Layton/Puzzle agent type of game, but got a regular point-and-click adventure instead. It mixes some fine gameplay elements found in other adventure games, and although that doesn’t make the game awesome or great it’s still become a somewhat enjoyable game in the end.

The leveling system seems random, and the weapons aren't too balanced (plus one of them hurts you when you use it but the game never actually tells you this). The controls are very slippery/floaty as others have mentioned, and there are some one block jumps in this game that end up being infuriating because of it. There's also a double jump mechanic that is difficult to master as well.
Visually, the game is great. It has its own style that's a mix of Meat Boy, Fez, and other indie classics while still doing its own thing. The more you die, the more muted the colors become until you beat a stage or use a health potion, which is a pretty unique visual trick. That's about all the game has going for it, though.
I personally cannot recommend this game as-is, however if you're a big fan of platforming games and/or the indie scene then you might get something out of Reset 1-1. There's definitelya good game somewhere in this mess.

The now classic 'Grand Strategy Game' Europa Universalis III, with its four obligatory expansions 'Napoleon's Ambition', 'In Nomine', 'Heir to the Throne' and 'Divine Wind', should perfectly well manage to both engage and challenge any avid intrepid strategy gamer out there.
The Europa Universalis strategy series (by Paradox Development Studio) is a good supplement or alternative to Sid Meier's Civilization strategy series. Playing the two franchises 'in tandem' is feasable without getting overwhelmed by "strategy fatigue". The two franchises compliment eachother and opens up for enjoyable strategy gaming experiences.
Unlike its successor Europa Universalis IV, Europa Universalis III is no longer in development and no further expansions or dlc (downloadable content) has been announced. In other words; the game is complete.
And on that note, I can higly recommend a purchase if you find the whole idea and prospect of starting Europa Universalis IV a little bit daunting.
I enjoyed Europa Universalis III to the utmost. And I still from time to time boot it up for another interesting challenge.
Highly recommended.

I got this game on a whim and I was happily surprised with what I found. It's a cover based shooter with heart and ideas. The game is quiete a looker, tho not the best for 2012, however it has aged really well. The game is well optimized and runs smooth as butter on newer hardware. The visuals are crisp and vivid with a lot of color and special effects. The animations are serviceable with some weird voice acting. The story packs a punch with a great mistery reveal and twist that you wouldn't see coming.
As far as the gameplay goes it really does mix up things with the gravity weapons (kind of like biotics from the ME series where you can lift enemies) but takes it one step further when you flip gravity up, down and to the sides so that you're working with enemies on different planes. There's also a few 0 gravity sections where you're floating from cover to cover and have to shoot enemies from all sides.
The campaign is a bit linear and has quite a few boss battles thrown in. The story takes a while to develop and the characters feel a bit unpolished. There are some nice moments and setpiecs and I found it all very entertaining. It's a solid  cover based shooters and you'll really enjoy it if you're a fan of Gears of War or third person shooters with sci-fi themes.
The game also has a MP component but I wasn't able to find anyone to play with as it's been a while since the game was released. In short it's definetly worth your while to explore the upside down world of INVERSION.

What saves this game is that the gravity weapons are a cool idea and are fun, the combat is solid, and the levels have a ton of detail and hard work put into them.
6/10. Would be 7.5 but the problems I mentioned are too big of a detractor to rate it any higher.

As far as I'm concerned, this is the best game ever - especially in this version with the first two additions to the game.
To a certain extent, it is comparable to the Total War games, if they only included the map mode, which would here be simplified to armies only being able to move from province to province and not within a province. However, you have a more complicated diplomacy and domestic policy to deal with.
Another thing that makes it different, and, for my taste, better than the Total War games, is the greater realism and historical accuracy - in this game you can't just conquer everything, and it remains challenging for the more than four centuries that its timespan covers.
The fact that the game never becomes "too easy" is what makes it so good: You know early on that you want to make the country as which you are playing as successful as possible and to that end, you have to position it so it can rise to the challenge while always remaining watchful for your rivals.
Some (minor) things which might make the game a little less enjoyable are the huge random factor in battles - one of the factors that determine a battle outcome to a sometimes massive extent is the game literally casting a dice, which might be a little frustrating sometimes, especially when your and your opponent's armies are roughly equal. Precisely this is also the next minor annoyance in the game: Armies are quite often equal, aside from their exact size, as you do not have a lot of options in structuring your military - which, while rather straightforward and easy to understand, is a bit disappointing, as the game's focus, while definitely present in diplomacy, trade, colonisation and policy, is still mainly conquest.
Also, and this has more to do with the store page than the game, I'm almost sure some of the screenshots are not from the version that is sold here, but from a version where one or both of the further DLCs (which are not included in the "complete" version) are installed.
All in all, a definite buy, as long as you are into (grand) strategy games, and don't need a game to be too action-laden.
EDIT: As I've now bought all the DLCs to this game, I am now rather certain that some of the screenshots on the store page aren't from this game at all, but rather from Europa Universalis IV, which would definitely be an avoidable mistake on Steam's side.

This review is for "Episode 1: Where the Dead Lie"  only.  Playing this game is like reading a graphic novel.  Clicking the edge of the screen is like turning the pages of a book.
You get to choose your character's reaction and depending on your reaction, other characters react diferently as well.
It is a crime adventure game where you play as a detective.  You also get to play a minor character - an ex-convict that becomes a police asset.  The game tackles a lot of mature topics from child abuse, gang violence, sexual exploitation, family relationships.  That is how deep the game is.
You can choose to be a good or a bad cop.  It's your choice.  However, there is no real consequence in the final outcome, whether or not you choose a different path. The end will still be the same.
It only affects what Steam Achievement ("SA") you can unlock.
Here lies the replay value of the game. You get to play out all the different cut scenes based on your choices at the same time unlocking the SA.  Choose one path you unlock one.  Choose the other you unlock another. There are several of them.
The visuals of the game is truely an artform.  The game is very riveting from the get go.   The very short gameplay, which is its only weakness, makes you want to play the next episodes of the game even more.  I just hope that future releases will be little bit longer.
For those who want to buy this game, a word of caution, there is NO AUDIO, only the background music.  For those who believe that "Reading is for Losers", don't even bother buying this game.  There is going to be a lot of reading here.
I give this game a 7/10.  A must have.

Episode 1:
For starters, this is a short game. I mean, I completed it in 2 hours and there are 4 more episodes left. The developers are giving a year's recess for each episode's release. I mean, 2 hours per year can be a bit of a downside for some people. But on to the game aspects. I really like the art, comic book style, but on the other hand the animations are just, and I don't mean to be rude for the developers or anything, but bad. The music (piano for the most part) really syncs up with the action moments of the game but fails in all other moments - the act talking for example. As there is no voice acting, I had to read the lines out loud so as to get myself immersed in the history a bit more, but the lack of music in these moments really was a negative aspect for me. The history is not bad but it's typical of TV shows in the crime genre like The Wire, CSI or NCIS. The board that contains the information of every character you meet and the ability of it updating itself with your choices is a nice little addition. Overall, I just hope the next episode will be longer, that it has some fixes and improvements to the game. I recommend it if you like these type of crime related stories, but otherwise, don't bother buying The Detail.

I've only played the currently available episode so a lot still remains to be seen on how the story will turn out (quality-wise). As far as the art goes, I really liked the overall design of most characters as well as the venues they visited. My personal favorite was the Lucky Dragon restaurant.
As far as pacing goes, it felt a little sluggish for the amount of content (currently) offered. It has the conventional 'skip to next area' feature when you double click to enter a new map. The annoying part about this is that there are a lot of slow walking scenes that cannot be 'sped up' (i.e. the Elevator).
Overall I can recommend it based on the visuals and the quality of the first episode's content. This can change drastically depending on how the rest of the game turns out (once released).
