I wasn't expecting much from this, seeing the low metacritic (72), but it turned out to be better than its score implied, especially considering the low price point.
The high points are solid ARPG gameplay, graphics, and atmosphere.
The atmosphere features Eastern European ("gothic-noir") influences not often seen in the genre (and steampunk elements very often seen in the genre lately).
Mechanically, it's a mix of other recent ARPG titles - most closely resembling Torchlight (with at least one overt reference to it during the game). It also has odd Tower Defense sequences thrown in at the end (think Sanctum, but with ARPG instead of FPS mechanics).
The itemization is solid, albeit relatively unimaginative. Apart from well balanced base rolls and selection of basic, magic, rare, set, and unique items, you can further enhance your gear by adding a stat (Enchant) to any item for cost, and some items can hold "essences" (a sort of socketing system, minus the sockets) for even more customization. There is also gambling and a limited form of crafting (item rerolls/recycling via Artifact Forge).
For those of you wondering - you can respec individual skill and stat points at (relatively low) cost (or all points at once for Katarina), so there is freedom to experiment and no need to grind out multiple characters to experience the entire skill tree.
Especially notable is your companion ghost, Lady Katarina, who serves as both a wose-cracking companion to make your single player adventure less lonely, and an able fighter in her own right, with her own equipment slots, inventory, skill trees, and behavior settings. She can also go shopping for you.
The most disappointing aspect is the prevalence of bugs, which have been getting fixed over time, but are still apparent as of writing. This includes some game breaking bugs that make it impossible or difficult (via a workaround) to progress with the main quest.
The low metacritic can largely be explained by the shortcomings of the original release, which have since been amended via updates and DLC. The updates include additional endgame content (high level "scenarios", Glory System (perks for completing scenarios), and a new game+ mode).
DLC adds two character classes (previously there was just one, with a melee, ranged, and magic path), a passive skill tree for Katarina, and more endgame content (high level "scenarios", and a new game+ mode). Not having played the DLC classes yet, I can't comment on whether they are worth it. Blue Blood basically makes Katarina substantially more powerful, which is certainly eyebrow raising, but that DLC could be skipped with limited gameplay consequences.
Overall, I would recommend the game as an enjoyable diversion for any fan of ARPGs, especially for anyone looking for an atmospherically unusual ARPG or fans of the source material, but keep in mind that my own experience was limited to single player.

This is a tough one to write because it is the purest possible definition of the "meh" game. The one that makes me and many others beg steam had the "thumb to the side" recommendation type.
As is... picking positive or negative is probably the hardest of the reviews I made and I'll
-> Current 9,99€ price tag or a 50% off (4,99€):
-> 2,50 - 3,something€ (66-75% off sale):
Inversion is actually quite simple to explain: It's Gears of War with a gravity control gimmick. And it is indeed a gimmick and nothing else. You have two modes, Low and High-Gravity (the latter being obtainable half-way through the game). Low creates a low gravity bubble, that not only makes enemies glide in the air (leaving them out of cover to shoot) but allows you to throw stuff at enemies within that bubble.
done in a billion other videogames.
High Gravity is a sort of projectile. Once it hits
objects, they will fall and give you some cover.
and pretty much nowhere else. You reach a sort of corridor with a turret in the end shooting at you, drop crates to create cover, reach near the turret and destroy it. Boom. Done.
It's a gimmick if not what I will dare call pretty much a damn scripted event with the illusion of freedom in the gravity control. You'll use Low Gravity for "remove this to get through the area" or "throw red barrels at the boss" sections and High Gravity for the turret dodging. That's it.
Now, the rest of the game is pretty straight forward. If you played Gears of War, you've played Inversion, I'm not joking. Even some vehicles in this game look really similar to a respective GoW vehicle. The 2 weapon system is there plus a 3rd slot for the only grenade type in the whole game.
I'd expect a grenade that created a low gravity bubble.
Maybe a sort of launcher that shot a low gravity bubble? Or even a cool High Gravity ray that made small buildings collapse because they were "heavied" up?
You get 2 assault rifles (semi vs auto), 2 shotguns (pump vs auto), 2 snipers (low vs high powered), 2 miniguns (bullets vs lava (fancy idea for just a... you know...
) and 2 plasma guns by the final 3 chapters (assault rifle and a shotgun).
Original? Nope. Not even the plasma guns or anything have cool designs. They just shoot bullets too. Not joking. Only the starting assault rifle looks different and quite interesting and the rest is generic and rather boring to look at or even use.
Audio is good as the voice acting is very solid and the overall gun sounds are also satisfying enough. Also note that the gore system is quite awesome as well. A killing headshot (I say killing headshot because enemies ♥♥♥♥ing eat ammo in their face and body like that fat cousin you never even heard of in your life that shows up at your wedding and starts eating all the crab cakes and chocolate fondue) will result in the enemy's head blowing up into a blood and brain pool and makes a distinctive sound (literally imagine what's like crushing a skull, that's it). And helps the combat feel good to the player.
Graphics are pleasing. For a 2012 game it's quite good. The gibs, the overall face textures and the such is pretty good. And even the backgrounds look quite the thing. Aesthetically it's grey 50% of the game, yellow desert-ish for 40% and the final 10% is spaceship-futuristic-style. Not that varied and considering many locations look the same (I'd even dare call some recycled), you may get a bit tired of them after a bit...
If you can handle 5 hours of the same thing over and over, that's alright, but even you know you can find better! And the fact the game has co-op and multiplayer that is DEAD and BROKEN! (Gamespy usage, which fyi, was terminated and is as dead as that cousin after eating his weight of food at that bloody wedding...)
So... TL;DR, leggo!
+ Solid audio
+ Good graphics and atmosphere
+ Nice story (the ending is the strongest part imo, really liked it) with a rather interesting twist in the middle
+ Decently made bosses at first (check cons)
+ 5 hours long (so you won't have to bore yourself to death much more)
+ Interesting premise (also check cons)
- Repetitive gameplay that makes 5 hours seem too much
- Recycled boss fights (about 5 bosses, each of them (except the final one) are repeated about 3 times each (same patterns, same everything. Not even ♥♥♥♥ing kidding. The laziness of the devs on this one is stupendous!).
-
(biggest of them all, I'd say).
- Dead Co-Op and Multiplayer (due to GameSpy shutdown, which was never patched out or added a notice about it in the steam store).
- Brutally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t difficulty spikes (including one-shot enemies).
- Overly linear (no secrets or possibility to explore this nicely thought out world).
A game with barely any redeeming qualities after 2 hours, which is when it starts feeling repetitive and it chooses to keep on repeating itself throughout the final 3 hours.

Short review: I loved Ports of Call - and i played this for 7 hours straight.
Long review: Nice modernised version of PoC. Not one single hickup in 7 hours, thats nice coding. And i have not visited the forums for any help whatsoever - the game is quite intuitive and you pick things up fast.
At first i thought "Hey, its only a map of Europe", but after you visit each port in the Free game mode, the entire world unlocks. Like with Ports of call, there aren't enough things to buy for your money. The game designers have gone with the "Euro Truck Simulator 2" moneysink - Buildings in each town that do... errm...well, they make you feel good about yourself.
Like with PoC you can command your own ships, i have done this a billion times in PoC on the Amiga and on the PC version and skipped that totally. Automatic docking fees may seem a bit high at first, but when you see how much money you make per trip it becomes small change.
I really liked the ability to upgrade and somewhat specialise your ships (Cooling unit for chemicals or Anti-shake for electronics), but it would be nice to have some sort of template thing for this so you do not have to upgrade a billion ships every time you buy em. And you can take as much cargo as the ship can hold, which makes going from port to port to pick up additional cargo more essential to maximise your profits, at least early on before you get 20 mil for shipping some antique cargo containers in your Panamax ships.
For a PoC clone, some things are missing - there are no icebergs and you do not save sailors for status points, this subracts from the whole "ship simulation" feel. The music is well done and the graphics are.. sufficient. Overall, this is a good game, even if you missed out on PoC you may end up playing this ship business simulator for days.

You liked D2:LoD? GET THIS GAME! Detailed review is below. (Sorry for English, not my native)
A short "what is it all about?" - hack'n'slash with great and complex character development, decent number of items (magic, uniques, sets, legendaries are included), great crafting system for improving gear. Good interface and interesting monsters to slay (available in great quantities). Replayable and good for multiplayer.
This is one of the best aRPG games I've ever played. And my gaming 'career' is long and glorious - started aRPG genre with original Diablo, carved my way throught D2:LoD [and kept carving it until 2012], tried my luck in Sacred series, Titan Quest and lots of other titles. Except D2:LoD, none managed to kept my attention - sure, I played them, finished them but always returned to good'ol.
What I have to say it that this game for me is second to D2:LoD only - with a chances to even surpasses it, never forget that this is only one third of full game. What made me put an unfinished game over, for instance D3 or PoE? Regarding D3 - Van Helsing is what D3 should have been. Regarding PoE - it's a close match, but i prefer graphics, interface and overall feeling to a more complex and somewhat confusing skill system. Don't get me wrong, I've played fair share of both, regretting deeply what D3 could become and seeing potential in PoE.
Game itself is fun to play, even repeatedly over and over. Price is fine, and you don't REALLY need paid DLCs (except 1.5EUR "Blue Blood") - the basic game brings more builds and customization of character than whole D3 - and I stand firmly behind this claim. Interface is excellent, any D2 veteran will find himself at home. So is the monster density and constant action (but with good measure!). Character progression is good, there is a 'respec' option (I don't like it personally, but it seems like a trend nowadays), but some choices are permanent, as it should be.
Voice casting is excellent, and dialogues between main character and ghost sidekick (which can be customized almost as much as main character, making a deadly duo in fight, and source of fun inbetween - again, clever dialogues doesn't make it boring).
I was with the game since release, and developer team knows what they are doing - many additions/changes were always for the better - I've returned to the game after few months hiatus and got surprised by amount of small, but important quality oflife improvements. And bug/exploit fixes. And new feeling and better endgame.
Pros:
- High technical quality (graphics, sound, voice-acting)
- Various builds for each character
- Complex companion development, something unseen in aRPG before
- Intriguing (and unfinished) storyline
- A unique game settings: alternate history with slavic mythology mixed with steampunk, working PERFECTLY
- Storytelling is very good
- Game lore is excellent, and so are little details who mean much - names of the people, equipment etc - all very atmospheric
- Character progression is complex, depending on several separated systems - dwarfing D3, keeping in line with PoE (on a different level, though) and succeeding D2:LoD rapidly
Cons:
- Non-random maps and moster type/positions
- Lack of random events and quest
- Scripted story - not really a problem, but little more open game with randomization and wide range of optional quests appearing randomly - would add more replayability. There is a replayability value, don't get me wrong, but more never hurts
- Bugs in multiplayer - once plagued the game, now mostly fixed - and this 'mostly' is why I mention this. Won't destroy your days of playing, but you'll maybe need to repeat quest, for instance. Big deal.
Finishing thoughts:
I understand that now there is a demo. At least try it. As of myself, I've bought several copies as a gifts to my friends. DLCs add multiplayer value - you can have dedicated melee/ranged/caster characters (and companions with different builds!) with regular game, and it's way better than parties in D3, but DLCs add more.
If you like D2:LoD, you'll probably like Van Helsing - it is true spiritual successor of a legendary game. If you think that D3 is what aRPG should be, you probably should try anyway - just to see a different side of a coin, how modern game functions with different mechanics. It's just 17% of what you paid for D3.

I really wanted to like this game. I usually enjoy these kind of adventure games, and the story seemed interesting and targeted to a grown up player. But somehow I can´t get around to giving it a thumbs up. I would say it is worth a try and that maybe you´ll like it, but all in all I wouldn´t recommend it.
The major flaw to me was that this game felt slow. I´m not speaking of troubleshooting, I´m speaking of the pace of the story itself. You have to do most things in a certain order, and if you´re thinking one step ahead you might feel like you´re being held back. The story had potential but its developement and the dialogues didn´t make it worth the being held back feeling. It just felt slow and a bit superficial (like all the coroner´s exchange).
I didn´t really like any of the characters either, as -in my opinion- they were also rather superficial and stereotyped. The story had potential, but it just followed the path of so many cop-tales before it.
The graphs were ok, nothing to write back home about, but adequate to the storyline and the mood. The backgrounds were what I found better accomplished.
I didn´t really like the soundtrack, it wasn´t noir enough, it wasn´t blue enough, it was somewhere in the middle. Same goes for the choices and the action parts: They were nothing special, the action itself was pretty lame and scarce.
Owning the game I might -might- give it another go to see if different choices make the story look better, or to see how easy it is to get all the Steam achievements. But being this a story one has to buy per episode (and since you can complete each episode in under 2 hours) I don´t think I´ll even check the future episodes.
To sum up, I didn´t really like it because I found it un-engaging and slow. But would not discourage you from giving it a go if you can find a good price or free demo so you can decide if it´s worth the investment first. I still think The Wolf Among Us was far better in all aspects.

The story? I dunno, it just felt kind of.. all over. This game can't decide if it's serious or silly. DOOM knows it's silly. Spec Ops knows its serious. This... the gunplay and all that feels DOOMy, but the story is as dark as spec ops. It's very jarring, it's hard to tell how committed to their message they were. Of course, the main message is 'Kill nazis', and it has that in spades, love it. The other message is 'screw racists', plenty of that, also love it, proud that a game's willing to be that upfront about it and not even bother with 'hmm maybe both sides are right'. It worked well for me, but I do have some complaints.
For one, the game is very short. I beat it in around 8 hours, and that was with accidentally taking one bonus mission along the way(more on that later). For something that was toted to be a megalithic 20 hour experience(and costs 6 bucks on release) it just does not hold up. The game-play was fun, but is is clear that some key designer from the first game, who's input guided that games development and fleshing out process, was no longer working on this game. The weapon variety is boring, you get an pistol that you will never use, a machine pistol that is mediocre, a decent automatic machine-gun and your laser gun and an automatic shotgun. Very near the previous-to last level you also acquire a grenade launching pistol, which I had the pleasure of shooting into one big dude I didn't like and that was it. I'm not even sure if I ever picked up more ammo for it. The other three or four types of guns are big guns dropped by big burly dudes. These involve laser, flamethrower and a minigun. All the non-heavy weapons have upgrades, you have perks too, and halfway through the game you even gain a special tool which can get some upgrades, but these all seem trivial small changes. The most innovative change was to the machine-pistol, causing its projectiles to fly slower but become heated nails. Everything else is either a scope or a magazine bonus.
Even the enemy variety is bland. Theres your basic soldier nazis, sure some of them are a bit bulkier than others but they're all just blackish blobs to kill. Then theres big burly nazis in power armor, who use either lazer, flamethrower or flak heavy weapons, and may seem intimidating at first but end up being easy pray that lets you clear the room using their dropped weapon. Then there's a few robotic Nazis, which are never really explained, that kinda zap around and shoot at you. They will evade you once and you will think that its clever but then ignore it from then on as it really makes no difference. Then there's big walking tanks of death that shoot out rockets and have a big laser. You can destroy them easily with a heavy weapon and they become a nuisance. There's occasionally a few Nazis in different costumes, like welders, scientists, hazmat-suit dudes or even a few KKK members, but they're all just dudes with a basic machine gun and the same AI as the most basic soldier. There's a few drones and some dogs, some armed with lasers(only show up on last level of the game btw)And last but not least, the nazi mechanical death panther that spews fire... The game has like 4 or 5 of them in total, and only one moment is intense. They arent as fright intimidating as in the first game either, as they just slack off and vomit fire at you periodically. That's it, that's the cast. Three flavors of nazis in various suits doing the same thing, angry dogs, and two types of mechanical monsters. And that's really it. Nothing interesting. That said the action is still fun, but it doesn't top the first game. A lot of things are made weirder. A lot of tools like cutting through fences or climbing up walls in TOB expansion are missing. You are given the cutting laser tool but  it is rarely used beyond the first level. You are given upgrades but the actual upgrade tool looks so indiscernible from the environments that I picked all mine up accidentally while running and pressing E. To make matters worse, you only really need like 4 upgrades. The rest I held onto, expecting to find better guns... which I never did.
That said the environments were rather interesting or diverse, but the level design was a notch below the previous game. The music is mostly amazing though.
And the story... wasn't bad. But I wish it was something else. The Nazis are still there, so that's good, but somewhere along the way BJ decided to pick of his worlds equivalent of the black panther movement and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥does the quality of everything drop from that point onward. The main leader, a topically sassy black woman assumes control and guides BJ and the gang into starting a revolution in The United States. And whoever wrote her dialogue should be fed to some piranha-Bill Cosby chimera, because every. other. word. that the sassy leader and her squad(technically an actual squad) says is MotherF**ker and it's infuriatingly poor. In general a lot of weird choices. BJ is haunted by his past and his atrocious racist father, BJ daydreams about his childhood, and his black bff and how his father ruined that. About his father being a soulless♥♥♥♥♥♥and just in general about how ♥♥♥♥ed up racism in the USA is. And if if sounds like I'm upset that that's the message, then I'm sorry, I'm not. That is a truly good and powerful message, and the delivery was fantastic... But it somehow manages to make the death-squad ordering, pleasure killing, mass slaughtering and infuriatingly egocentric and ignorant Nazis less bad? Like a statement saying "Yeah I know that these people are getting killed in the most brutal way possible by literal spawns of the demon lord Hans, but lets now focus on the injustice within this broken racist household." The two are not the same. The story has a lot of unanswered threads and plotholes. The doc OBSESSES over an item you give him and there's never any conclusion. Does regularly feeding the pig DO anything? Why are all my resistance members freaking Buddhists? You can almost tell exactly when the writers tried to cover for their♥♥♥♥♥When BJ asks about the garage), but the most cruel thing was this. There was no final boss. It wasnt there. You just go there, you realize you can kill Engel(this wasn't really the main goal btw) and you do it. Its satisfying to watch her in horror after all the♥♥♥♥♥♥shes done, but it's all so sudden, so unnatural. There was no buildup, it was more like bumping into someone you dislike sharing school projects with and telling them that you are totally dine with them instead of sneaking and fighting your way up to the most vile being in the world and slicing their face out and they understand the horror of what they have unleashed upon themselves(coincidentally, this is the reaction of most of my dates for some reason... no idea) The whole thing just doesn't work. They kill her, do a broadcast televising... thing... something half decent, and then it just rolls credits.
BUT WAIT THERE'S MORE
Then you are back on the sub and lieutenant sassy sassface is all like "Mhmmm you may have just beat Engels'♥♥♥♥♥but there's still some damn nazis. Gravity is the most prevelent force in the universe; but if it could be harnest as a weapon, you'd have a significant advantage on the battlefield. This game takes that very concept and introduces it in a sort of Alien invasion setting. The story is told in a very cinematic way, which gets in the way of the gameplay. Many of the scenarios don't feel all that unique to most Trench-Style third-person adventures.It's almost as if a great deal of focus went into the Multiplayer vs the Main Story, which hurts the game's appeal, since it isn't available for MP or Co-op anymore. The lack of online Co-op forces you to rely on the Ai to not die(In which you will be given an opportunity to pick them up when downed). This can make the more difficult encounters more annoying, but not so much that it's a big issue.
The game's true faults start to arise when cutscenes clutter up the gameplay. It feels almost as if you never get a full experience until you've seen 8 or 9 cutscenes. The Linear nature of this game can be kind of limiting as well; but they did hide secret ammo stashes about the areas. Sometimes you'll get lucky and grab a really great weapon from one of these stashes that will make the limitations less apparent. Bosses are another thing handled pretty decently in this game, as they're not too difficult to send more casual players away; but offer enough challenge to put up a decent fight for anyone willing to select a higher difficulty. The Ai partner that you're forced to use now isn't too bad at holding his own; However there were segments when he would disapear. I theorized that he may have been stuck behind a game barrier during these sections.
After reaching a little over the half way mark, the game's true issues start to become more of an overcumberence. The Lack of an efficient partner makes some sections more RNG based; so you're either going to have a partner capable of having your back, or you wont. The other major fault is the lack of variety in enemies, as boss fights are repeated in the later sections, and very little is done to differentiate the experience. The Gravity mechanic becomes less useful in combat; because the enemies take much more to kill than the powers you have available to you. Often you're made to take on swarms of enemies that can't be brought down easily. It also serves to note that this game will crash at random; but it's negligible since the game saves often. You wont find yourself forced to redo sections if it crashes.
Upon reaching the bitter end of the game, it ramps up the difficulty once more; but the game cleverly forces you to attune yourself to using the gravity weapons, as ammo can easily run out. Ammo that once littered the area is difficult to stockpile, as well as some sections making you drop your secondary weapon if you happened to die before the next checkpoint. The repeated encounters with bosses is drummed up to a staggering bore at this point; but the variety is shaken up a bit. Combat becomes fierce and tactical as you progress through the final sections of the game; however the issues aparent with all of these Trench-Shooters start to become apparent. Not having a life bar often forces you to cowar in fear of the unkown amount of damage an enemy can inflict. It became frustrating not knowing whether I could weather a barrage of bullets,energy blast, fire, debris used as projectiles, or remain behind a safe barricade until I could pop my head momentarily to shoot.  I find these games rather enjoyable for the fast paced action (so I die alot.) If you've enjoyed this game, and are looking for something as fun as this, I can reccomend "Binary Domain",or "Vanquish" for your next adventure.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Hellblade -- which, despite sounding like a MOBA, a phone game, and a DMC ripoff all at once -- is a terrific game. It has glaring optimization issues, it's frustrating in parts, and a lot of the puzzles leave you a little dazed and lost, but it's absolutely worth recommending if you want a story and an exploration of one character's long, long tale of hurt and pain and trauma and psychosis.
Senua is mentally ill, and that's bad enough, but it's also in Celtic times, during Vikings and the Norse mythology, which means nobody even understands what that means. Senua is abused, she's hurt, she's desperate, and she has to confront those demons in a way few can. It's a long, long road of hurt and pain, and as you learn more about Senua, she learns about herself. I am not being hyperbolic when I say this is probably as close as anyone in gaming has gotten to depicting deep, deep rooted mental disorders since Silent Hill 2. This is not Alice, where 'mentally ill' means 'haha how MESSED UP WOULD IT BE IF', this is real hurt and pain and trauma and the facial tech and the writing all convey it beautifully.
By the time it wraps up, it takes a minute to process it all, but it's a satisfying, understandable conclusion, one that feels earned by the characters and the places you've gone.
There are only two major flaws -- and I mean, MAJOR flaws, not quibbles -- is that the combat doesn't feel right for the game. Senua is a warrior but if they had made her feel really vulnerable and delicate, without awesome kickflips and slowmo-parries and flying knees, it would have fit with the horror theme that the game really wanted to be. As it is, combat is fun and violent and brutal but feels at odds, aside from the obvious "she is literally fighting her demons, but she can't conquer them with violence", with the rest of the game.
The second major flaw is that this game wants to be horror so, so badly, and is so close to realizing that, but there's not a sense of fear or terror in the air but a few moments. Senua spends much of the game gasping, shreiking, and breathing in terror, but I often plowed through the puzzle sequences without a blink. This game is so atmospheric when it takes control away, but loses all of that when you have to explore, I never felt vunlerable because combat and exploration was so clean and I had such great visibility.
There's other smaller details, like how the puzzles can suck at times or how some of the "fleeing from thing" can be frustrating, but it never took me much longer than a few moments or the occasional "Google an image of it to figure out what it is" before I got right back on track. But they're not really that critical to the part that makes me like like the game, so I give it a pass.
I really hope Ninja Theory just makes a horror game, they can do so well with the material if they just sat down and did it.

Recommended, but ONLY if, like me, you played Ports of Call on a dodgy DOS computer and couldn't get enough of expanding your fleet. As that is not likely to be the majority, I am not recommending it.
This game IS Ports of Call, there are a few additions and subtractions but the core of it is simple: Get the most out of your fleet. However, where PoC offered depth and complexity, in this it isn't difficult to achieve what you want to achieve, it is a fun(ish) time-waster for a few hours before you realise it is severely hampered by lack of depth. It is PoC but done half-hearted at points where it matters. I've just sent two ships off from New York to Algiers, loaded with medicine, to finish a contract off. Both ships for some mysterious reason left without their loads. In PoC I would turn them round and ignore the bug, here you can't: You cast-off, that is it.
In PoC part of the minigames was that you would manoeuver the ship in tricky situations, ice, reefs, castaways. Here you either damage your ship or have to wait for an unknown time. I am fine with the minigame element being gone, but now I haven't got a clue what determines how long you wait, it doesn't tell you (unlike PoC), but having a ship sail "round a reef" just of the Galician coast and it taking 12 days... It could have been in the Antarctic by that time. Some of these aspects feel like they've just been put in to slow down the player for no apparent reason.
The game is a lot easier. The upgrades to ships are a potentially nice addition, but instead are a sure-fire way to rolling in cash in no time. Once you unlock radioactive goods and weapons, you rake in the cash. I feel there is a massive missed opportunity here. They've introduced a reputation system, why not link it to that? Other goods are already linked to it, also - gaining rep should be A LOT harder, now it is linked to being on time a lot, which is the easiest thing to achieve, it should be linked to the state of your ships, quality of your crew-training, quality and quantity of subsidiaries, average cost per TEU. Reputation in turn should determine the quality of the contracts you can achieve, you begin hauling fish from Iceland to Germany for a few years, after demonstrating you can do that and keep your ship in good condition, you might get the opportunity to bid for another contract and so on.
This game COULD have been a brilliant and legit successor to the PoC throne, what it should have done was offer MORE depth, not less. The new additions really don't help and the fact that management of the fleet is now so simplified reduces its value even more. Instead of putting different goods-types central it should have gone down the route of: Container-ships/Bulk-carriers and contract-work only, you know, like the real world? It should have an AI, also bidding on contracts. Real life margins in this business are cut-throat, yet after playing a few hours in the sandbox on medium difficulty I have 15 top of the range ships and billions of dollars to instantly expand my fleet - but there is no reason to. All I do now is send ships from one radio-active port to another and rake in the cash.
Real shame as it is a huge missed opportunity. Sims become great when they have more depth, not less. Look at Paradox games for an example of how to get that right.

I love this game, though I was a bit disappointed in a few things, sadly. Lets start on the negative first.
The world variety is lacking in this one, I don't mean to say that this game should be something like Dark Legacy, but that is what compensated for the previous  game lacked. The only theme here is caves, mines, and Hell... it kinda starts to all blend in together, caves, caves, caves, lots of caves. Something that kinda baffles me is how Colosseum has ice spawners, poison spawners, yet no ice worlds or jungle levels?
The boss battles didn't feel as grand and epic though, the bosses having invuln frames felt like they're there to drag out the battle, not increase difficulty, don't get me wrong, I like a challenging monster to fight, but know the difference between challenging and tedious.
Oh also, its Gauntlet, find someone to play with cos this can be played single player, but this is a multiplayer game, always has been, always will!
The positive!
The heroes are different! Anyone who knows the previous Gauntlet games would take note of this first! Though I adore Dark Legacy with a passion <3 something that was troublesome was that all the classes were the same, they all just start with different stats though, that isn't the case in this game! The warrior is all about throwing his weight around, charging right into the hordes you fight! The elf has the enemies running in circles to catch him! The Valkyrie is able to dash into a horde and defend teammates! The wizard, oh my god the wizard! I never had any idea how to differentiate a wizard class in a game like this! They used a simplified version of Magicka's spells, but still something neat!
The enemies are something too! I love how they even got the enemies to differ from each other as well <3 I am actually very glad that ArrowHead did that! The mummies having their own mages, bloated mummies! Skeleton archers! Juggernauts, spider queens, the list goes on!
Final thoughts
I would buy this game 3 times over if it had the level variety of Dark Legacy, yet managed to have all classes different from each other! To this day, to whoever reads this maybe many years down the line, I am awaiting a game that meets that description, a game that is as grand adventure as Dark Legacy, yet provide enough variety throughout! I don't see such a game like that coming out soon, maybe not even within my lifetime. I await the day I can go on a quest to slay a fearsome yeti, enter the nightmare realm, deal with a wizard summoner who is obsessed with the desecrated temple!
The game is great, it gives plenty new but doesn't change too much, keeps the old but does something new! I want more of this!
I'll close this at this point now, a great game to play with friends if you like fighting massive hoards of enemies, I eagerly await the next installment!

This game is fantastic! It is beautiful to say the least, as each level is masterfully designed and gorgeously rendered, making this the biggest draw for the game. The gameplay is very sound, mixing together traditional platforming with physics-based puzzles to create a somewhat unique experience that falls just short of the high bar set by the game's graphics. The player can switch between the Wizard, Theif, and Warrior at will when playing in single-player mode, or play alongside up to two friends in local co-op (though why there is no online co-op is beyond me).
I would say that the only real drawback to this game is that it's pretty short. I took my time with the game and ended up completing the main story within 3 hours. Luckily, there are bonus levels, higher difficulties, collectibles, and a level-up system that helps lessen the blow of the lack of content in the main story, and provides at least a little bit of replayability.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a good platformer, and smart puzzle game, or just wants something beautiful to look at. Right now, the game only costs $0.99, so hop on this bandwagon before that sale ends! I give this game 4.5 out of 5 stars.

This is the Edition of Fallout 3 to buy.  You will get all of the additional DLC created for the game.  During Steam Sales, its not uncommon to find the GOTY Edition for $12.  I would only get the standalone edition if you are not interested in the DLC.  If you are looking for New Vegas, it is a standalone game and does not require you to have this game.
Compatability with Windows 10:
To get this game to work in Windows 10, I suggest you locate the Community Patch  created for the game.  It will solve issues that cause the game to crash.  There are some additional fixes that require you to download the old Games For Windows client.
About the Game:
You start off as a Vault Dweller and leave to search for your lost father.  Throughout the game you gather weapons, gear, clothing, and items that will aid you in surviving the Capital Wastelands.  You will meet people that can help you with your quest in exchange for completing quests for them.  Just like in real life, you will meet people who will want to help you, you will meet people who try to take advantage of you, you will meet people who want nothing to do with you, and you will meet people who want to kill you.
My advice for playing this game is to kill all hostile people and creatures you meet.  Loot every chance you get and haul it back to a place where you can store it.  Repair the equipment you have often, upgrade whenever possible, and sell off the stuff you don't need.  Make use of the fast travel whenever possible and keep your gear weight low so that you can loot and haul back.

Wolfenstein 2 is the newest in the Wolfenstein series in the "New Order" timeline where the nazis have taken over the world. You now lead a revolutionary group and kill nazis, fun! Now how is the game? The game is almost no different than the new order in terms of gunplay and stealth, only adding a couple new features such as being able to choose your own missions through a battlemap, and environmental hazards (radiation and coolant) to name a couple. So why is this game getting a thumb down? For one thing this game has (what I believe) to have several major issues with its writing.
For one, the resistance groups you recruit are southern communists and a black revolutionary front group, both of which you would not see be recruited to the main resistance group if this were a real revolution. The mere concept of you recruiting these two groups is absurd because they would not have the power or the means to survive, for example the Black revolutionary group is surviving in the nuclear fallout of Manhattan, where they all would have died from radiation poisoning by now due to them not having the protective gear, they also would have ran out of food because of this. Also, the last time I checked communism was not a popular thing in America even if we are talking about alternate history here, this group would be so small to be insignificant, they wouldnt even be on the radar of the main resistance group. The main group would be off recruiting the freedom fighting americans trying to restore their contry back to where it was, not fringe groups.
Anya is 5 months pregnant!!! Now give her a gun and have her take on a nazi airship with you! Send her with a guy who is on drugs into the slums of New Orleans!!! Wait what? Why? She is noticably pregnant. Do you see how absurd this is? No woman would be running around with an assault rifle and tossing grenades into nazi soldier groups while sliding across the floor showing no regard for her unborn children. Who wrote this nonsense?

However, the biggest disappointment is in dat ending. Oh my god did they screw that up big time. It is probably a runner up to "The worst ending award" that was taken by Mass Effect 3 back then. The final "fight" is literally won BY ONE MOUSE CLICK that triggers a cutscene from a scene that I can swear they copied and pasted straight from Homefront: The Revolution.
It is like they did not even try here and that is a real let down.
You never actually get to see any sort of revolution or warfare occur, prior to what you may believe due to this game's advertising saying stuff like "ignite the second american revolution" and "rally the resistance." There is no "resistance" of any kind once you see the ending, contrary to games like Homefront: TR and XCOM 2 which have similar revolt stories  which showed the populations rising up and overthrowing their opressors in a city-wide/global civil war, this one has absolutely none of those experiences to speak of. In the end, you feel like you accomplished literally nothing but recruit a few forgettable characters  into your "resistance".
The only thing that saves this game in my view is the gameplay itself, which is great, but can get repetitive at times. After shooting the same faceless nazi soldier 23546 times over Im gonna get bored eventually. So what about stealth? You have the same problem, you shoot or axe the same guy a bunch of times but this time you hope you dont get spotted. You will do this over and over and over again, and it doesnt get more fun, it gets boring. Stealth is also far from being quiet, you can shoot a nazi in the head with a surpressed weapon and he will fall to the floor and die, but still let out a yell that can be heard across the room but everyone is still walking in a straight line like they cant hear or something.
However, the most notable thing I remember about this game is

So now the question is, is the game worthy of $60? Put simply No. It is severely limited by the disappointing writing and repetetive gameplay that rob you of an immersion factor that the first game did much better. Game mechanics such as killing nazi top brass had an interesting concept that amounted to almost nothing. You get no sense of there being any kind of revolution occuring after you "spark" it either. The characters are mostly forgettable and a couple memorable ones get killed. It can be fun at times no doubt about it, but these flaws are simply inexcusable when the standard was Wolfenstein: The New Order which did things a lot better. Another thing people have complained about is the many bugs and glitches, although I have not experienced these, I would advise you to at least hold out on buying the game until Bethesda fixes them.

Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
11) Scuba Divers
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

I consider this game to be a classic and a gem. If you are a person who loves to play really, really, REALLY involved strategy games, then you seriously need to consider getting this game. To be honest, "Divine Wind", which is the final expansion to the game Europa Universalis III, is the only version I know because when I got this game it had all of the expansions with it. However, I am sure that this review can still apply to the base game and other expansions.
The best way I can describe this game is that it is an open-ended grand strategy game, in which you set out to achieve whatever you want - there are no victory conditions and no end game objectives. The fact that you can play as ANY kingdom, principality, republic, etc. within the game's timeframe makes it even more amazing.
The amount of depth that goes into this game is unparalleled by any other game I've ever played. There is so much fine detail involved that I learn something new about how the game works almost every time I play. And that's saying something considering how long I've played. Every aspect of the game from economy, military, politics, religion, exploration, and so on, is very detailed and it all ties together rather nicely.
What makes this game great too is that it leads to epic unwritten stories that take unexpected twists and turns throughout the game. You will be amazed at how a once-proud and mighty country that is a serious rival and threat to you in the early game can end up being completely dismantled by either you or the other computer controlled nations. And when one menace falls, there always seems to be another even bigger and more threatening one that takes its place. And sometimes, this mid/late game menace started out as a puny nation that got very lucky and quietly took advantage of opportunities...only to end up being crushed by another country, such as yours. And no two campaigns are ever the same.
Over the course of the game, you will get hit by dozens of random events that occur. These events can range from beneficial like giving you claims on wealthy neighboring lands, to disastrous like a major rebellion in your country. Many of these events give you multiple options, which can lead to difficult decisions that have to be made.
And beware of neighboring rivals who will declare war on you and effectively kick you while you're down - something the AI LOVES to do to you. You will also notice that computer controlled nations like to form deep alliances, where even declaring war on a tiny nation could possibly lead to a war with half of Europe teammed up against you.
But all of these things are what make Europa Universalis III challenging and entertaining. Trying to figure out how to defeat great alliances, trying to manage your country's economy as you build a global empire, etc., all leads to a supreme sense of achievement at the end of a campaign. Whenever I finish a full campaign, I like to sit back and admire what I achieved, and consider what I could have done differently.
Now, this game is VERY demanding in terms of time and commitment. You need to set aside plenty of time to play this game in order to fully enjoy and appreciate playing it. You also need to have a lot of patience as this is a rather slow-paced game (for good reason though). And if you've never taken on a grand strategy game before (like me, before I played this game), then you will probably find that this game has a major learning curve. But I encourage you to persevere because it is well worth it.
Overall, words cannot describe how incredible Europa Universalis III is; it has to be experienced. If you have the time, patience, and most importantly, ambition, then you should seriously consider playing this game.

Frankly speaking i am astonded.
At first, i thought that paying 10 bucks for just 150mb was a bit of a stretch, seeing as to how most games now seem to go for half a gig per dollar, but decided on buying it anyways due to the stellar reviews. I now realise that had i known beforehand exactly the type of game it was, i would have payed twice that amount.
The game is something unlike anything i have ever played. It is presented very simplisticly, with 16-bit graphics, and gameplay that is not much more than scrolling over the whole screen and clicking on the things that have a different icon over them. But the game is not about that- it is a game where the story is the only thing that truly matters. Both the graphics and the gameplay, despite being so simplistic, do a much better job of conveying the story and the feelings of the characters than almost any of the games today do- it amazed me exactlly how much emotion could be hidden behind those pixelated figures.
And finally the story- the thing that stands out head and shoulders above most of the videogame stories of today. It is neither overly complicated nor long, with the game being over in just 4 hours, but it is so heartfelt, pure and touching and jam-packed with action that not a minute of it is wasted. The chatacters all convey personality in ways that actually make the player invested in them, angry when they are angry, sad when they are sad. And the conclusion is perhaps the most satisfying conclusion that i have ever seen to any story.
All in all, even if you do not like pixelated graphics adn think that interactive stories are a waste of time, you still owe it to yourself to buy this game and play it, just for the story it tells, and how effectively it tells it. It comes to my mind that this game should especially be played by all those people that cry that videogames today are nothing but violence, and that they possess no value whatsoever in the world today- i am sure that they are gonna have to carefully rethink their points after that.

Some people's minds are so different that they are labeled as delusional or just as someone with a mental illness, but perhaps they are fighting a very personal battle that only they (or not many) can understand.
As someone with very personal, and I dare say very different, beliefs, I found it easy to relate to Senua and felt in some ways understood, albeit in a slightly creepy way. I boldly admit I also hear voices and experience hallucinations that only make sense to me, so I never speak of them and no one knows I am any different than they are.  Then again, perhaps others like me are common enough, with inner realities unimaginable by typical minds, and are able to conduct themselves in a way that makes people think they are normal. I believe It's not possible to know for sure what goes on in other people's minds, nor is it possible to know for sure whether they are right or wrong.
The graphics, animations, sounds, and voice acting are top notch in this game. I think it's worth playing just to admire the artistry.
The gameplay is good but there is nothing new about battle mechanics in this game. It's still done well enough for me to enjoy the action. All the tried-and-true are there:
- A well-timed block becomes a parry and with a potential retaliation.
- Dodging.
- A "focus" ability that appears to slow time for everything but your movements.
- Light and strong attacks that form combos that suit different situations and enemies.
All this is done with superb animation and art style.
However, I wish there weren't as many recycled enemies. So much effort was put into the rest of the game that I feel it strange for enemy variety to be so lacking. The effort just doesn't feel balanced.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone looking for an immersive experience. I would say it's a little easier than similar action titles like Dark Souls, so those hunting for a challenge might not find it here. On the flip side, it's a pretty smooth ride without any hurdles that are too frustrating.  In my opinion, the immersiveness of the game still makes it well worth the buy.

Trine is a game I can't recommend enough.  It's a physics platformer with a rather unique mechanic of 3 playable characters.  They are tied together by magic so you can switch between them at any time and use their abilities to make your way through the levels.  Puzzles are quite varied requiring a number of different strategies, especially if you want to collect all the experience orbs which can be quite difficult to reach.  All of the characters are well-balanced and necessary to proceed through the game.  The game is also very well-written and acted which is a welcome change from most platformers.
Where Trine really shines though is the graphics.  The art in this game is absolutely stunning and it's amazing how well it runs even on older hardware.  It also makes use of nVidia PhysX for high quality physics simulation (nVidia hardware not required.)  The world and levels are very well designed and quite engrossing as well.
The only thing this game is missing is coop, but that was added for the sequel which is just as awesome.  Play them both!  You won't regret it.

Graphic design is for me by far the strongest advantage of Trine. This game is simply beautiful. Gameplay is satisfying - not very challenging but smooth and really fun to play. Trine has a co-op mode so it`s definitely worth trying if you are looking for a game that you can enjoy with a friend.

This is basically a static comic book, where you get a few extra panels (at most) depending on what "choices" you make. I put "choices" in quotation marks, because none of them make any real difference. You get the same story regardless of what you choose. Even the conversations are the same, with only superficial changes before you're railroaded into the same dialogue. In fact, your character will usually end up saying the same things, regardless of what you suggest.
Moreover, given that it's a static graphical novel, the writing and grammar aren't actually that good, with grammatical errors such as comma splices and unnecessary apostrophes (e.g. "drive by's") throughout. Honestly, it might be worth playing through once for 0,99€, but only if you like interactive novels. I wouldn't pay anything near the retail price.

The writing is poor, from cliches like "Just another murder... until it's someone you know" to non sensical, such as the scene where the coroner explains that they know it was a random dog that chewed on the corpse's leg because they found the owner; implying that the police found a guy with a dog, asked him "Did your dog chew on a corpse last night?" and the guy said "yes", and the police just take his word for it and decide to drop the investigation.
Your choices don't matter (this is no Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us), the game will push you towards the same plot regardless what you do or say.
The puzzles are essentially non-existent: You're in a bathroom and you don't want people to catch you calling the police? There are only 3 things to click on: The phone, the drunk guy, and the mop. Click on the phone and your character says it's not safe yet. Click on the drunk guy and your character remarks the drunk guy's out cold. Click on the mop, and your character automatically uses it to block the door. You're at the police station trying to figure out where a photograph was developed. There are 4 possible photo labs. You could try thinking about it, or you could just click on all 4 photo labs until your character says "That's it! That's the one!". You can easily beat the game in 1.5 hours. Do a second playthrough to get all the achievements and/or (not to mention the cards you're eligible for, since 1.5 hours is too short to max that out) and you'll realize just how little your choices matter when you do the completely opposite of what you did in the first playthrough, only to yield the same results.
The game is unpolished. The animations leave a lot to be desired (contrast this with Broken Age, for example). There's a lot of inconsistency on when you're supposed to click to advance to the next frame of the animation and when you're supposed to just wait for the animation to play out. When you type in your name, the vertical bar that marks your cursor is misaligned from where the characters will actually appear. Just a general lack of attention to detail all over the place.

And now that the game has decisively been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on and lit on fire by the wise masters of game design at Arrowhead, they draw their hands back from it and call it complete. Utter waste of money buying it now that whatever enjoyment and fun the original game held has been so decisively erased. It's even a waste of money if you hadn't played it before the "Slayer" patch, as if Arrowhead reached into your game library, pulled the Gauntlet case out, smashed the game disc on the ground, and filled the case with a handful of feces before replacing it on your shelf. The worst thing about Inversion is that it's bad, but not bad enough.
When I first started playing Inversion, I quickly realized that it was a bad game - but at first, I thought it was one of those so-bad-it's-hilarious kind of games.  As I kept playing, however, I realized that this game is just your run-of-the-mill bad.
Gunplay is weak and unsatisfying as there are only 3 guns in this game - assault rifle, shotgun, and sniper - and they all sound like "pshew pshew".  Combat is simply not fun.
Voice acting is absolutely horrible!  I mean, the actors really phoned it in for this one, and it doesn't help that your best friend follows you for the whole game and won't stop saying moronic quips like "Hey, good kill, man!" or "You just shot a civilian, bro!"  Real talk, play this game on mute.
The cherry on top is the random, unexplained crashes to desktop.....like the game wants you to stop playing.
Imagine if Gears of War was really, really bad - that's what Inversion is.  Inversion is a third-person-shooter with cover mechanics where you use the D-Pad to switch between weapons, and you fight humanoid enemies that come out of the ground alongside your hispanic best friend using an assault rifle with a large melee attachment, and also everything sucks.
The tiny, tiny moments of "not crap", like the zero-G fight segments or the surprise twist (just look it up, don't bother playing this game to find out), are smothered by the fact that the rest of this game is absolute trash.
If it was just a little bit worse, at least you could have had a laugh at it.
Don't buy this.

Coming from a group of indie developers with no history of games on Steam and a name nobody knew, Depth showed that not every startup project is doomed to fail, and went beyond that by proving how polished a game can be. There are many bestselling games with huge money invested into the development, that still crash, have all kinds of glitches and bugs, lack optimization and so forth. None of this applies to Depth. In all of my nearly 200 hours I've yet to come across a visual glitch, let alone a game-breaking bug.
To add to that, for the asymmetrical kind of game it is, Depth is very balanced. Being experienced as both sides, you can't just pick one and know you're more likely to win, and none of the shark species with their own unique characteristics is superior and the go-to shark among the best players. As a result, there will always be a lot of variety in every game, with some divers choosing to go for harpoons and others choosing auto rifles, sharks going for the very different Great White and Thresher, and more.
Perhaps due to the above and lack of attempts to charge for content that affects the gameplay, the game still has a sizable playerbase. The waiting times aren't always perfect (sometimes taking up to 7-10 minutes) but there's never a time when you want to play Depth and you have to wait forever to get a match.
Bonus points to the developers for the game's perfect 21:9 support with a highly adjustable FOV slider, and good 5.1 sound for a truly immersive experience!
P.S. Don't let the game fool you into thinking that shark attacks are common. In real life, on average only about 10 attacks each year result in human deaths. So let's leave the killing of sharks to fiction, like this video game, and preserve the actual animals.

If you love map painting, then this game is for you - all the politics in Europa Universalis III is about one ultimate goal: Annihilate everyone until you are the only one left or you get bored and start all over, preferably as a different country. Some countries are better represented, other are just there to exist and perish, but overall there are enough interesting states to provide a huge amount of gameplay, especially with all the add-ons. Unfortunately, for me this game is a rather bland experience. I would vote "average" if it was possible on Steam, however, it is not. This is the worst series that comes from Paradox studio, because it doesn't provide any internal politics like Crusader Kings, nor any interesting economics and population control like Victoria. The wars are not as detailed and do not require much thinking either, this isn't anything like Hearts of Iron, where the player is challenged and has to adapt to the changing war and apply appropriate tactics. Europa Universalis III is just about attacking smaller country and overrunning it quickly with army, taking it over and repeating the same thing all the time. It has other elements of gameplay, but nothing of importance. Unlike other Paradox games EU III doesn't focus on any particular aspect of running a country, hence it is quite void of content and feels bland.
I would recommend playing Victoria II, Crusader Kings 2 or Hearts of Iron III over Europa Universalis III, depending on what exactly are you looking in such a game, because EU III has nothing special about it.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing lives up to it's title. It is pretty incredible.
The core system of the standard ARPG is there and is solid. The twists it adds (such as the combo) system are fluid and innovative. The three classes seem balanced and conform to specific role types. While the maps aren't randomized, mob placement generally is. Playing on Hard, the mob packs were huge and plentiful.
The quest line and atmosphere is wonderful. Some of the character models, when viewed up close, are kinda "meh". This doesn't matter because the environment is BEAUTIFUL. A lot of work went into creating this world, and it shows. There aren't many music tracks (they are generally recycled through different areas) but they are good and help immerse you into the world. As far as length, it took me about 20 hours to clear the campaign on Hard mode.
I won't deny, there are some bugs to be worked out (Neocore is working on a patch as of this review) but they are hardly game breaking. The fact that this game was created out of a small company is incredible. The dev team is active with the player base on their forums and you can tell they generally care.
If you have an ARPG crave, or you are trying to forget about the last few ARPG disappointments, you HAVE to play this game.

TransOcean is a pretty cool and fun game where you just run your own maritime shipping company and you can run as many ships that you can afford. The ships range from a tiny freighter to a Panamax to a UCLV (a really big ship) and you can ship goods from ore to counterfeit goods to weapons to and from countries in the world.
Gameplay wise, it's pretty simple and there is a mini game where you can dock and cast off. It does get repetitive after a while but if you play the game in bursts, it's fun. There are challenges where you can accept company contracts to ship a certain number of goods from one port to another in a certain time frame, which is rewarding in the end. There are also random events that pop up where you decide to avoid it or go through it, as well as customs checks from time to time (often on Hard difficulty). One neat feature I love about the game is there is online connectivity where players who play this game effect prices of goods if a port is visited often.
However, what I do find is that when you start expanding, the amount of ships that you have to manage gets overwhelming and I wish there was a way to easily load your freighters at multiple ports.
Overall, I do recommend this game but remember to play it in bursts or it will get repeititive. Score wise, about a 8/10.

After one playthrough of the campaign you are pretty much done with the whole game. And even within that it gets repetitive fast. There is no way to build your shipping company differntly in the next playthrough, it's always the same: load ship with goods, sell goods, fuel and repair the ship - repeat - buy more ships. No crew, port or storage management at all. You just ship goods to make money to buy more ships to transport more goods. Maybe it would be fun if there was any type of endgame like buying out the competition (there is none), buying whole ports or investing in research.
One would think it gets more interesting when your company grows bigger but it only gets more tiring because there is no automation at all. Frankly speaking i am astonded.
At first, i thought that paying 10 bucks for just 150mb was a bit of a stretch, seeing as to how most games now seem to go for half a gig per dollar, but decided on buying it anyways due to the stellar reviews. I now realise that had i known beforehand exactly the type of game it was, i would have payed twice that amount.
The game is something unlike anything i have ever played. It is presented very simplisticly, with 16-bit graphics, and gameplay that is not much more than scrolling over the whole screen and clicking on the things that have a different icon over them. But the game is not about that- it is a game where the story is the only thing that truly matters. Both the graphics and the gameplay, despite being so simplistic, do a much better job of conveying the story and the feelings of the characters than almost any of the games today do- it amazed me exactlly how much emotion could be hidden behind those pixelated figures.
And finally the story- the thing that stands out head and shoulders above most of the videogame stories of today. It is neither overly complicated nor long, with the game being over in just 4 hours, but it is so heartfelt, pure and touching and jam-packed with action that not a minute of it is wasted. The chatacters all convey personality in ways that actually make the player invested in them, angry when they are angry, sad when they are sad. And the conclusion is perhaps the most satisfying conclusion that i have ever seen to any story.
All in all, even if you do not like pixelated graphics adn think that interactive stories are a waste of time, you still owe it to yourself to buy this game and play it, just for the story it tells, and how effectively it tells it. It comes to my mind that this game should especially be played by all those people that cry that videogames today are nothing but violence, and that they possess no value whatsoever in the world today- i am sure that they are gonna have to carefully rethink their points after that.

If you liked Port of Call for DOS or Amiga as well as it was back in the day, here is a modern reincarnation.
While the 3D view perhaps still has some issues, seeing as you can't move the camera as freely as you like to do, it still breathes life into an old game from the 90s.
While it is a ship tycoon game, and not much of a Ship driving simulator (And thank god for that) it is great fun to "manage" your company.
One difference from Port of Call is that you now have to upgrade your ships to ship certain cargos, or to increase a ship's performance.
The bad side of this game is that there are some bugs in the user interface that can make you a little confused.
For an example after some time in game, when selecting cargo contracts for your ship, the checkmark to show that you have selected that contract disappears, it is still selected, so if you hit "Accept contracts" they will show up for confirmation.
Then during the campaign you will also feel like killing your second "investor" and here the devs would do the world a great favor by introducing an "Arrange accident" button for that "investor"
The investor has a tendency to pass out contracts when you least want it, and forcing you to abandon contracts you are working on and scramble to fullfill the contract or face an ONGOING penalty until fulfilled.
Mark my words when I say ONGOING, it means that you lose millions until you get it fulfilled, and this get so frustrating at times, that you really wish you could get rid of the investor, by ANY MEANS NECESSARY.
Past this, this game is worth the money it costs IF and only IF you liked Port of Call from the DOS era.
If not, I recommend you try the old DOS title first to see if a shipping tycoon game is something for you, and then consider this title.
Word of note, this game is now EOL (End Of Life) with no more patches coming, and it still has a few bugs, including one crashing bug, plus one bug that can get you stuck, and forced to either kill the process or get into the options menu to fix it.
But the worst bug that can wreck you, it is very possible to get the game stuck in fast forward mode, meaning you will have ships arriving in port, and waiting for your confirmation to unload, but time will still keep passing at a record rate, causing delayed arrivals, and thus steep penalty fees.

TransOcean is a great management game with surprisingly addictive gameplay, trying to manage each ship as it sails across the globe is fun and being able to dock manually both breaks up the monotony and serves as an interesting gameplay mechanic (free docking) the game does have it's flaws though. While each port is beautifully rendered, they are poorly designed, often forcing ships to take odd routes, without a tug or bow/stern thrusters your ships are sometimes forced to take extra long routes or to take damage while docking or undocking; they also often have inconveniently placed obstacles like islands and landmarks, which wouldn't be so bad if the ships felt right. The ships feel like they slide around far to much, it's almost like they're turning from a point far forward of the actual rudder of the ship, additionally the top speed is 10 knots, less than 20 miles per hour, but looks to be about 100 miles per hour. All in all they just feel wrong and if they were tweaked a little would feel much better.
These facts are by no means dealbreakers, and the game is fantastic even with them. If I was to suggest some changes; in addition to fixing up the ship handling (turning should be tighter, speed should feel lower and all ships should have thrusters) and the port design; I would find a way to spice up the map view a bit, it's quite dull at the moment. I would also prefer some adjustments to how the map works, clicking ports in Europe can sometimes be a challenge once the full map opens up since the game never remembers your zoom level and the ports in Europe are so close. The map outside of Europe also feels quite empty, with very limited options in North and South America.
Hopefully this review doesn't sound too negative, but I find that negative points are often more useful in deciding if I want something or not. I recommend this game fully as a solid entry into any managment game fan's library.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a game that reminds me alot of classic Metroid gameplay. That said, you can already expect an challenging Platformer. Every part of the map has its own unique challenges that need to be solved, everything is well thought and the world you play in works pretty well.
One and possibly the only downside for some people might be the challange. This game isnt easy, and it has a really steep learning curve. However I think thats exactly what this game needs to be complete.
The market is full of extreamly easy games, and most of them also have nothing I'd call a story.
Since we're at that point, the Story of Ori and the Blind Forest works. I wont spoil it, but I can say that I enjoyed the few cutscenes, it was logical and you felt like you, somehow, became part of the story - as it should be (in my opinion) in every game that does focus on story.
The gameplay itself works and extreamly challenging (And challenging means that I died > 500 times (yes there is a counter)).
The one Problem here is that many of the moves you can do will share keys, like the thing you can float around with and grabbing the wall, wich, especially in the escapes (you will know what I mean if you play the game) can become a bit problematic (yeah i like to slowly glide into water insted of grabbing that wall. In the end i think that Ori is a game that you should play. Maybe you dont like the story or spend hours in that one litte corner of the map trying to gett that pick-up - and surly its ok to take a break because of frustration.
But it has been long since i have seen such a well-working family-friendly game with such a wonderfull story.

You control a polygonal triangle which has the ability to shoot individual shots (key can be held down for repeat fire), a beam which destroys a LOT in your lane while freezing your score until you let go of the beam fire key, and a jump button so you don't run into anything along the rim of the web as you roll smoothly around (strange for a triangle which looks like kinda like a thick triangular guitar pick which rolls side to side on its edge along the side of the near edge of the playfield, but oh well).
The levels, despite rotating into view and zooming in against a starfield background, have too little variation between themselves to make a serious comparison to Jeff Minter's/Llamasoft's masterpieces or even to the versions of T2K farmed out to other studios (like the PSX and PC versions, IIRC). The baddies on the "web" are different enough flat-shaded polyhedral objects that Triblaster isn't much more than a poor copy with a bonus stage somewhat reminiscent of the final boss of the levels in the early flat-shaded arcade polygon game I-Robot.
Sound assets are lacking in a major way, but not missing, as far as I can tell. They sound pretty bad. The game has an attract mode which plays the game, which is a nice feature.
Like the robot voice says when you fail to grab enough polygons during the bonus stages for a 1up, "hah hah hah"
(You'll have that much fun when you play this game for kicks and giggles or if you have insomnia and a few minutes to waste between bedtime and sleeping supplement activation time.)
Overall, I'll recommend this game with a 4/7 (57%), but if you're a millenial or another type without a love of similar Tempest-derivatives, you probably would rate it 2-3/7.
Buy it on sale if you like the screenshots and the gameplay video.
Review will surely change if Triblaster is pulled out of the back room in its unfinished state and given some replay value.
