I think this was one of TellTale's first games, along with BTTF. As with that game, I will say that this is a very linear game, unlike their later attempts. If you're expecting the same choices and branches, you will be disappointed.
Tales of Monkey Island is... different from the older Monkey Island games, holding a very strange position in the franchise. This is, I suspect, the first game that wasn't made by LucasArts. Many of the people from the original games are involved, but there is a strangeness about the game that wasn't in the others.
The graphics aren't bad. If you've seen any other TellTale games, you'll know what they're like. The art direction is reminiscent of Curse of Monkey Island which is no bad thing. Voice acting is top-notch as always, with Alexandra Boyd, Earl Boen and Dominic Armato doing splendid work as Elaine, LeChuck and Guybrush. Music isn't bad, with some eerie voodoo music tied in with the usual Monkey Island themes.
Tales of Monkey Island, however, seems to rely very much on shock value, going to places where none of the previous games had gone to. The humour is still there, as are the quips and the fun puzzles. But it's darker, particularly the final episode, and while it did its job in shocking me when I first played the game, it's a bit jarring now that I know it's coming (and I'm in a position to compare it with Curse of Monkey Island).
Tales of Monkey Island is significantly better that the Remastered versions of the first two games (which I returned because of how uncanny valley I found the graphics), but not as good as Curse of Monkey Island. I'd rate it at about the same level as Escape from Monkey Island, which I rather enjoyed, but found a bit frustrating because of the inventory controls.
There's a pretty blatant sequel hook at the end, I wonder if anything will ever come of it. I have yet to see TellTale bring out a second season of any property.

Inversion is a trite cover shooter with one novel mechanic: ability to use gravity to your advantage. Pull enemies out of their cover, grab objects to throw when you run out of ammo or not doing enough damage, flip gravity to invert ground to ceiling and vice versa, and so on. The weapon mechanics are still the same as almost all cover shooters... move into cover, flip from cover to cover, blind fire, lean out and fire, and so on. You are always covered by your buddy. The story however, is cliche and over the top. The result is an also-ran that is worth bargain bin, but not full price.
You are Davis Russell, police in Vanguard City, and your buddy Leo Delgado were taking a lunch break and suddenly barbaric soldiers of type never before encountered, heavily armed, appeared out of nowhere and were basically killing everybody on sight. The pair fought their way into toward Russell's apartment, encountering gravitic anomalies. Upon reaching home, Russell found his wife dying and child missing. Wife died after uttering that the daughter was taken. The pair was soon knocked out by a powerful blast from an enemy lieutenant and taken prisoner, dumped into some sort of prison labor camp, where they learned the enemies are known as the Lutadores, and they have gravity manipulating technology. But where did they come from? After a chance encounter in the tunnels where the duo fought a killer robot using "gravlink", they encountered "Free Man" a resistance group member, who helped them to escape the camp into the city, where they fought their way back into the apartment looking for clues to the daughter's whereabout, then for the presence of Free Men, and perhaps they can help each other...
If I bored you with the B-movie plot... well, that's exactly what this game is. It is an also-ran, with the saving grave of the grav tech. Without it, you're basically at a rather... lame Gears of War clone. Even the weapons drew inspiration from GoW and a bit from Warhammer 40K.  There are occasion bits of brilliance, like combat in zero G zones, both positive G (make things heavy) and negative G (make things float) have tactical uses. Pull down floating crates/containers as cover, drop floating enemies to ground, flip the world upside down to get different cover, pull enemies under cover into the air, grab lava and fling it as weapon, there are uses for your grav weapon, but only occasionally. The rest of the time it's faster to shoot enemies instead, except the boss battles. Given you only have two weapons (and the grenade), combat is definitely "meh", esp. when the cover viewpoint doesn't quite shift properly, being "stuck" on over the right shoulder, even as you emerge from cover on the LEFT side.

Coming from a group of indie developers with no history of games on Steam and a name nobody knew, Depth showed that not every startup project is doomed to fail, and went beyond that by proving how polished a game can be. There are many bestselling games with huge money invested into the development, that still crash, have all kinds of glitches and bugs, lack optimization and so forth. None of this applies to Depth. In all of my nearly 200 hours I've yet to come across a visual glitch, let alone a game-breaking bug.
To add to that, for the asymmetrical kind of game it is, Depth is very balanced. Being experienced as both sides, you can't just pick one and know you're more likely to win, and none of the shark species with their own unique characteristics is superior and the go-to shark among the best players. As a result, there will always be a lot of variety in every game, with some divers choosing to go for harpoons and others choosing auto rifles, sharks going for the very different Great White and Thresher, and more.
Perhaps due to the above and lack of attempts to charge for content that affects the gameplay, the game still has a sizable playerbase. The waiting times aren't always perfect (sometimes taking up to 7-10 minutes) but there's never a time when you want to play Depth and you have to wait forever to get a match.
Bonus points to the developers for the game's perfect 21:9 support with a highly adjustable FOV slider, and good 5.1 sound for a truly immersive experience!
P.S. Don't let the game fool you into thinking that shark attacks are common. In real life, on average only about 10 attacks each year result in human deaths. So let's leave the killing of sharks to fiction, like this video game, and preserve the actual animals.

Wolfenstein 2 is the newest in the Wolfenstein series in the "New Order" timeline where the nazis have taken over the world. You now lead a revolutionary group and kill nazis, fun! Now how is the game? The game is almost no different than the new order in terms of gunplay and stealth, only adding a couple new features such as being able to choose your own missions through a battlemap, and environmental hazards (radiation and coolant) to name a couple. So why is this game getting a thumb down? For one thing this game has (what I believe) to have several major issues with its writing.
For one, the resistance groups you recruit are southern communists and a black revolutionary front group, both of which you would not see be recruited to the main resistance group if this were a real revolution. The mere concept of you recruiting these two groups is absurd because they would not have the power or the means to survive, for example the Black revolutionary group is surviving in the nuclear fallout of Manhattan, where they all would have died from radiation poisoning by now due to them not having the protective gear, they also would have ran out of food because of this. Also, the last time I checked communism was not a popular thing in America even if we are talking about alternate history here, this group would be so small to be insignificant, they wouldnt even be on the radar of the main resistance group. The main group would be off recruiting the freedom fighting americans trying to restore their contry back to where it was, not fringe groups.
Anya is 5 months pregnant!!! Now give her a gun and have her take on a nazi airship with you! Send her with a guy who is on drugs into the slums of New Orleans!!! Wait what? Why? She is noticably pregnant. Do you see how absurd this is? No woman would be running around with an assault rifle and tossing grenades into nazi soldier groups while sliding across the floor showing no regard for her unborn children. Who wrote this nonsense?

However, the biggest disappointment is in dat ending. Oh my god did they screw that up big time. It is probably a runner up to "The worst ending award" that was taken by Mass Effect 3 back then. The final "fight" is literally won BY ONE MOUSE CLICK that triggers a cutscene from a scene that I can swear they copied and pasted straight from Homefront: The Revolution.
It is like they did not even try here and that is a real let down.
You never actually get to see any sort of revolution or warfare occur, prior to what you may believe due to this game's advertising saying stuff like "ignite the second american revolution" and "rally the resistance." There is no "resistance" of any kind once you see the ending, contrary to games like Homefront: TR and XCOM 2 which have similar revolt stories  which showed the populations rising up and overthrowing their opressors in a city-wide/global civil war, this one has absolutely none of those experiences to speak of. In the end, you feel like you accomplished literally nothing but recruit a few forgettable characters  into your "resistance".
The only thing that saves this game in my view is the gameplay itself, which is great, but can get repetitive at times. After shooting the same faceless nazi soldier 23546 times over Im gonna get bored eventually. So what about stealth? You have the same problem, you shoot or axe the same guy a bunch of times but this time you hope you dont get spotted. You will do this over and over and over again, and it doesnt get more fun, it gets boring. Stealth is also far from being quiet, you can shoot a nazi in the head with a surpressed weapon and he will fall to the floor and die, but still let out a yell that can be heard across the room but everyone is still walking in a straight line like they cant hear or something.
However, the most notable thing I remember about this game is

So now the question is, is the game worthy of $60? Put simply No. It is severely limited by the disappointing writing and repetetive gameplay that rob you of an immersion factor that the first game did much better. Game mechanics such as killing nazi top brass had an interesting concept that amounted to almost nothing. You get no sense of there being any kind of revolution occuring after you "spark" it either. The characters are mostly forgettable and a couple memorable ones get killed. It can be fun at times no doubt about it, but these flaws are simply inexcusable when the standard was Wolfenstein: The New Order which did things a lot better. Another thing people have complained about is the many bugs and glitches, although I have not experienced these, I would advise you to at least hold out on buying the game until Bethesda fixes them.

After having neglected this game for a long time, I decided to give it a try. So, here are my impressions.
Visuals: This game is a real feast for the eyes. I find it redundant to describe it in detail, since it's overall beautiful.
Gameplay: The control interface is comfortable and is neither too simple, nor needlessly complicated. The interaction of the characters with their envoirment is on a highly satisfying level, be it objects or enemies. What surprised me in a pleasant way are the physics in the game, making the platforming and puzzles a fun and challenging experience. The combat is rather simple, but decently done for this type of game.
Sound: No objections, just like a cherry on top of the cake it rounds up an enjoyable game.
So far it sounds like this is a perfect game. But, it does have it flaws, mainly the sadistic difficulty of the final level. Be warned, this is one unforgiving level with literally no room for error. The reason why it is signifficantly harder than the rest of the game is that not only it punishes every big mistake with the need to restart the level, and that it is quite fast-paced compared to the other levels. Another point is the replay value. Once you've completed the game, that is all what the story can offer, it has no extra content, only higher difficulty. That hardly means the replay value is zero, on the contrary. Unless you replay it several times in rapid succession, you can always rediscover this games charms and try to complete every challenge it offers.
The verdict: 8/10

TL;DR:  Buy on sale if you've played Subnautica to death and don't need multiplayer
Okay, let me get my can opener and open this can of Worm Soup that is No Man's Lie.
First, context:  I bought it on sale after the Pathfinder update.  There's a lot of hate for this game that I mostly missed.
I almost bought it when it first came out.  I'm glad I didn't.
Second:  I've never played a crafting game before.  The closest was crafting professions in WoW like, 10 years ago.
So maybe other crafting games are better.
But the real question:  Is the game any good?  I have played quite a few hours(much more than 4) and so far, I'm really enjoying this thing.  I understand the argument that finding new planets and new creatures and such would get old after awhile, but it just hasn't happened to me yet.  Combinations are still fresh to me, at least for now.
The Good:
A lot of stuff to do(even if you factor in repetitive procedural generation, it still actually does have a lot to do)
Building a base is turning out to be very interesting.
SOME of the game's promised  epic atmosphere is here... the starship fleets make a big difference even though I've steered clear of combat so far.
The game is just complex enough that I needed to look some things up.
I do love naming things.  Just, putting that out there.
Faction rep and base-building do give the game some sense of direction.  I don't want to reach the center until it does something more than reset.
The BAD:
Lies, lies, and damned No Man's Lies.
Sometimes the game feels like Hoarding In Space Simulator 2016 V1.2
No multiplayer.  I'm dinging them for this because they said it would be there, but it still isn't.
I wish the ships had more direct controls.  I want to fly under arches and have the threat of slamming into mountains.
Physics are not there.  The planets don't rotate, the moons don't revolve... the star systems don't have suns.  Day and night are just the sky changing when you're on a planet.  A bit of a cheap hack.
This one will bring controversy:  Space is too busy and dense!  Unless the warp drive star map only shows systems that are both hospitable and too remote to be near cities, this doesn't really work for me... the planets should be further apart, and there are way too many asteroids and other ships.  This stuff won't really matter for a lot of people.  But I put a lot of time into KSP, so it leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
RECOMMENDATION:  Absolutely!  If...
1)  It's on sale or used(do not pay $60!  $35 is okay)
2)  You've played Subnautica to death or are bored between updates(Subnautica seems to be the objectively better game to most people)... I guess if you really are dead-set on outer space instead of the ocean, this is a yes as well.
3)  You don't need the multiplayer(go with Astroneer or Space Engineers for that)
So I have to recommend, because I did get it on sale, I won't be playing Subnautica(seen too many videos of it), and Space Engineers and Astroneer actually seem more limited in scope.
I would buy the game again knowing what I know now, no-brainer.  But only after the pathfinder update.
I haven't even unlocked any exocraft yet.
And I've written the same long reviews I never read when other reviewers write them.  For shame.

BUT...the story is terrible. The characters are beyond cliche (grizzled old cop that wishes things were the way they were before, the former gangbanger that has "gone clean" because he has a wife and a daughter but keeps getting dragged back in to jobs because of a police deal, etc. And are the main two partnered cops one old white guy and one old black guy? You know it!). Aside from all being cliches, the other consistency among all the characters is that they are all unlikable. In this choose-your-own-adventure style of storytelling, the whole point is that you should have SOME control over how the characters interact with others. But more often than not, regardless of your choices, all the characters are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to everyone they encounter.
Furthermore, the philosophy behind the story is painfully clear: the inner city is full of scum, and we need to give more unquestioned power and funding to cops so that they can go kill all the Bad Guys.
If that's your (simplistic) opinion, fine. If you want to make an "interactive" game that only serves to reinforce that opinion, fine. But AT LEAST add some new element to your story or characters, instead of rehashing the same old "clean up the streets" story with the same old predictably boring characters.

Set in, what I gather is an alternate world not unlike that of Judge Dredd (if you're not familiar with it, try looking for the movie with Silver Stallone), where the world is desolate and you live in a safe haven, a vibrant city in the middle.
Without spoiling too much, you are a police officer with a wife and daughter, just on your way home when the city is attacked by bandits (I gather). After some introductionary scenes explaining and training your ability with the basic controls while the storyline evolves you and your partner are captured, after which the game crashes for not apparent reason whatsoever (if the devs read this, that actually happened after the destruction of the first Unknown Robot, but I won't go into too much detail here about that)...
Anywho, what really gets this game going is the technology that enables you to shift gravity in objects you shoot at, or even yourself, allowing you to throw objects and enemies, pin them to the ground, walk on walls and ceilings, you name it. Combine that with a storyline that reminded me of Max Payne (for very apparent reasons if you have played both that game and this) and you really have something going.
The graphics look stunning closeby, but some objects did feel they were off, and some of the motion, especially on vehicles, looked really simple and something you'd expect to see in games 10 to 20 years ago... But then a building collapses in the distance with realistic smoke and debris flying everywhere, and then the building you're in does exactly the same and you forget all about that car or bus in the cut-scene.
I really don't like 3rd person shooters that much, but this one did get me captivated. I'll have another go at it later and hope the crash thing is just once in a while. The game auto-saves (more checkpoint based actually I think) so... This one is definately a keeper. Not sure what's with the multi-player, but I'm not much of a multi-player anyways.

TriBlaster is a retro-arcade style game, the type you’d envision in an arcade alley on those pay to play arcade machines. However, this game isn’t as bad or terrible as people say but I can understand where everyone is coming from.
Firstly, before I tell you what positives and negatives I found within the game and my thoughts I want you to know I played this 100% with the mouse to move and shoot, spacebar to jump and control to laser beam.
Now that you know my control scheme you can understand where I am coming from in this review, this is because I imagine playing with a joystick or controller or any other method would be vastly different.
The Positives:
♦ Arcade style retro graphics (I’ve always loved these)
♦ Awesome Game Concept (Shoot destroy survive)
♦ Shooting sound is good
♦ Good number of levels
♦ Game only Highscores
♦ Challenging
♦ Great number of arenas
♦ Random Cat Achievement (No idea how I got it, but it’s a comical addition)
The Negatives:
♦ Once you get into the game and start playing there is no ingame music (This is lame as all you can hear over and over again is you either shooting, destroying enemies, dying or collecting health/laser beam, which isn’t the best sound. Music would have spruced it up)
♦ Only way to view Highscores is when you first open the game or when you die (Really lame as you can’t scroll through them, view friends Highscores etc)
♦ Control setup aka mapping seems dodgy (Seem to be able to map way more keys than needed to play the game for some reason)
♦ Playing with a mouse sometimes seemed to lag for me when moving
♦ Using two monitors the mouse would end up on the second screen a lot (This is bad as it would pause the game and you’d have to re-open it. Also annoying when at a Rechargzorb stage as it’d cause you to miss the triangles needed)
♦ Seemed to me as though rechargzorb or whatever it was called sometimes threw the orbs off target
♦ After a while it can seemingly get really really slow and repetitive (This happens especially around the time of level 75… where after ever level there is a rechargzorb level)
♦ Level achievements don’t unlock properly even though you got there (Achievement for reaching level 25, 50, 75, 100 etc. Mine only unlocked upon verifying game files and they unlocked in the wrong order)
♦ No save menu (If you are going to play it you must do 25 levels at a time or else you have to start from the previous 25. This is okay early on but later it just gets annoying)
♦ No Quit on the main menu to get back to desktop (Must either alt+tab and right click close, put it in window mode and close or alt+f4)
Things the game could have included:
♦ Unlockable Endless Mode with choosable arena (Where you just keep playing the same level versing more and more units as time goes on until you die. This would be good soo you didn’t have to do the main levels over and over again with rechargezorb rounds after each round)
♦ Timed weapon upgrades (This would add another thing to make the game that little less repetitive)
♦ Ingame background retro music (Some really awesome retro background music would have made the world of difference!)
♦ Steam Trading Cards (Would have made for some pretty awesome cards, badges, backgrounds and emoticons)
Overall, even though I list quite a few negatives, I believe the main aim of the developers and publishers here was to recreate a look and feel as though you are actually on a retro arcade machine which I can say they have done really well. However, they need to also keep in mind this is the PC era and that they are releasing it for people with PC’s. Therefore, in my eyes the developers/publishers needed to think outside the box and think what can we do to make it have some of the qualities people love about PC gaming but still give it that Retro Arcade Machine look and feel? This I don’t think they have fully captured (No fully viewable/scrollable highscores, no ingame music, laggy controls, dodgy control mapping and no endless mode etc, to name a few things). Although, on a whole, if you ever played a retro arcade machine game like space invaders etc and want to relive one on your PC then I’d recommend this. Plus it’s a small price of $4 to pay to be able to essentially relive the retro arcade machine days. However, if you do end up buying this, don’t expect much outside of the basic retro arcade machine and be prepared for the game to get really repetitive really quick.
PS: I don’t own a joystick, so I can’t confirm if it works, but this game would best be suited to be played with joystick in my opinion.

You control a little shooty thing that sits on the rim of a surface, enemies come towards you, and you shoot them. You can also jump, should the enemies get to the rim. There's also a beam laser, which is good for shooting tougher enemies.
I started up the game... picked up my trusty 360 joypad... and started. Now, it's obvious what you do to move left and right, and there's a button that makes you jump, but the fire button? None of the buttons I tried would fire.
"Perhaps it is a Space Giraffe variant?" I thought, and allowed the enemies to get to the rim, then tried shoving them. That makes you die. So, no, that wasn't it. :P
There was a menu for mapping controls in the game launcher, so I had a look, and all buttons appeared to be mapped. I ended up looking it up on the internet - and I will write it here for you in case you are similarly stuck - you need to hold down the "A" button. Pushing it and releasing it does nothing. I don't know why there is this delay. If anything, the game may as well have constant autofire, because there is never a point that it becomes useful to take your thumb off that button.
So I went into the game again, and had a go. This game is deathly boring. The game would be considerably improved if the first 27 levels did not exist, because it seems pretty much impossible to lose, and you just sit through them thinking "ok, when does the challenge begin?". If there had been one level to introduce each type of enemy up until that point, the pace would have been much better.
Later on, it becomes a bit easier to die, but a lot of the time it is purely because there are some extremely wide levels, and the camera point for the game is a little too close to the player, so it is easy to run into an enemy on the rim just because you were not aware they were there, and you would have jumped over them if only you knew they were there.
I carried on - because I don't like to deliberately get killed off; I would carry on with my single credit - and ended up dying on level 67, still quite bored, attaining #6 on the high score boards, which is quite embarrassing, really.
Also, it appears that some of the achievements are gltched. Despite getting 9 lives quite early on, it didn't award me the achievement until about the 3rd time I'd had 9 lives, and there are locked achievements for getting to level 25, and level 50, which I suppose I should have received.
Last of all, it seems like the only way to exit the game is to press Alt+F4, which isn't ideal.
So - if you are a fan of this type of game, only get this game if you are really, really desperate. Get yourself a copy of TxK, or Tempest 2000, or some other version of Tempest. Even Pandora's Box on the C64, or Beamrider on the Atari 2600 - anything Tempest~ish you've never tried, before you resort to this.

This is my first steam review, and it probably won't be read in the sea of other comments on this title, but I felt that despite years of gaming (okay, decades) I've never felt the urge to strongly recommend a purchase until now. Sure, there are things I would have preferred to be more complex, spoilt by the combat systems of Dark souls and the Witcher, but what's so special about this game is the storytelling and the creative courage Ninja Theory bring.
This isn't just a game. This is a sincere artwork, using game design, to tell the most compelling story about psychosis I've ever experienced. They did their homework, not just with the depiction of mental illness, but also on the wonderful Norse mythology, joyously wrestled from the bubblegum claws of Marvel studios and told with all its blood and guts and grim darkness.
Senua is easily the most human heroine I've seen in any game ever, and while there have been more 'strong' female characters, there's no heroism like the heroism of the truly broken and crippled. She has to fight her demons, and it's all the more meaningful because unlike fem-Shepard who eats Reapers for breakfast, you can see in the gorgeously motion captured performance of Senua's face, that she is truly terrified as she fights.
This game is short. This game probably has awful replay value. All the same, this game is a MUST play.

SNAPSHOT
An uninspired Diablo clone that does more wrong than it does right. I wish I had more to say here.
OVERALL - 4.5 / 10
PROS
+ art is actually pretty good
CONS
- extremely clunky movement / combat
- ability point buy / upgrade system is extremely boring and lackluster
- story and dialogue are cringe-worthy
- lots of loading
- $4 DLC single talent trees
DETAILS
While I really wanted to like this game, overall it just falls flat in all regards. From the beginning, Van Helsing has been fraught with bugs and a lack of anything going right. To start, multiplayer was completely inaccessible for the first 6-7 months after release, and many quests were bugged such that they could not be completed. Releasing an extremely buggy game: strike #1.
Supposedly a lot of bugs have been fixed in the past 6 months, but this game was purchased specifically to play multiplayer at release and months went by with other (seemingly less important) bugs being fixed, and multiplayer is still not one of them. I have seen multiple instances of it being marked "fixed" in patch notes, only to find it is still as buggy as ever. Even without multiplayer, there are still a LOT of bugs that are easily found that stick out like sore thumbs. On top of this fact, DLC was apparently being worked on for the game starting after it was released, using vital manpower that should have been used to fix bugs to instead leave people that bought the game out in the cold. Focusing on future profits instead of fixing buggy products for current customers: strike #2.
Turns out that all of the DLC (at this writing) just adds single talent trees to Van Helsing or the companion, Katarina, for a "measly" price of $4. Not only that, but items in the game drop that require the DLC, WITHOUT HAVING PURCHASED THE DLC. Thinking your customers are chumps with bags of money lying around: strike #3.
Ranting aside, I can get past my personal issues with the motives of developers if the game is good, but I have to rack my brain for a while to just think of something nice to say. For a Diablo clone, it has about 1/10th of the content and customization of other games: there are no classes to choose from, the default talent trees (all 2 of them, one is a melee tree, the other is a ranged tree) are not viable to split putting points into unless you're playing on Easy difficulty, and each talent tree only has 8 abilities, of which you'll actually only use 3 or 4. There is no real diversity in any of the trees, either, especially since most of the abilities and upgrades are just terrible. The overall impression is that someone put way too much time and effort into making sure no single ability was powerful, even with upgrades, causing the entire combat experience to be extremely diluded. Given that Diablo clones are all about fun combat mechanics and getting loot, that should be enough to stay far away from this game. If that's your thing, though, feel free to keep reading.
The gameplay of fighting enemies is in itself a chore: any ability that has any real power to it has a long cooldown, meaning that you'll spend most of your time using a basic attack that has no real flair to it. Combine that with the fact that Van Helsing's movements cause him to spend way too much time standing still when actually fighting and you have a game reminiscent of the time when ATARI made consoles and not just games. What's worse is that the clunkiness could potentially be overlooked if the abilities the player used actually looked good when fighting, but for the most part combat VFX are almost non-existent. Player abilities don’t really stand out from the rest of the world, and are so short lived that the player might wonder if they cast an ability at all. There are very few noticeable VFX from enemies, as well, and if they didn't actually have physical attack animations then I wouldn't even be sure they were attacking. A lot of times the player just seems to take damage when enemies are around, but because you fight almost everything in the game you just know to expect it.
Although gameplay isn't everything, Van Helsing doesn't have much more to stand on. The dialogue between Van Helsing and his companion Katarina are terribly hokey and feels forced at all points. The art in the game is actually pretty good, but for the most part it’s all just static environments and doesn’t really engage the player at all, making it loses a lot of the potential it had at really being a “wow” moment. Because of this, some of the environments are actually very distracting and can be annoying to try and find things in, especially if there are quest-related objectives. Sound is never really my thing in games, and Van Helsing does nothing to change that. It is mostly just… there, although the constant dialogue / noises from friends and foes alike detract from whatever potential it had.
I think that covers everything, hopefully it gives people a good look at what this game is actually all about. I, for one, will hopefully not be making the same mistake twice with this company, the lackluster game and their focus on money over content has left an extremely bad taste in my mouth.

I picked this up a few weeks ago on sale and so far, have greatly enjoyed it.  It's an action rpg with surprisingly good character chemsitry and voice acting.  The interactions between the protagonist and his ghostly companion are well acted and entertaining.  The companion helps in combat, either through a ranged form, melee form, or passive form that grants you 10% damage resistance.
The skill system (for the primary Hunter character) is divided into 4 parts.  Melee, Ranged, Tricks, and Auras.  Melee and Ranged are self-explanatory.  Tricks give you spells that don't require mana but have a timer, that range from healing, to cloning your ghost, to ramming through your enemies.  Auras grant you passive improvements to your character.  One aspect I really enjoy of the skill system is the ability to upgrade your ghostly companion.  You can spec her to have skills that passively benefit you (such as increased magic find or defense) or enhance her damage and survivabilty.
Combat is a bit diferent in that you can enhance your skills with adrenaline.  Each skill offers 3 different side-grades that you can enhance your attack with all at once (e.g., +30% damage, +10% damage resistance, +10% length) or dump all of your adrenaline into one for maximum effect (e.g, +90% damage).  The combinations are interesting and even the early skills remain viable throughout the game.  Combat can be irratating because you are constantly being swarmed by gangs of monsters, so the focus tends to be more on crowd control than anything else.  As you progress through the story, some monsters are downright brutal and can kill you very quickly if you are not careful.
The story is on par for the genre and the setting, while appropriately grim, isn't anything spectacular.  There are a few bugs here and there, so be forewarned.  At times, the game will hang, which can be really annoying.  Generally it clears up but I have had to force-quit on at least one occassion.
With the vanilla pack, there is only the Hunter class.  While you can spec Van Helsing with all sorts of skills, if you want a pure magic based or technology based character, you will have to pay for them in separate DLC.
Bottom line:  If you like action RPGS, you will like The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing.  It's not perfect, but I think it has enough charm to help it stand out in the crowd.

A pretty good game, though it has it's share of problems. With an Xbox controller, a few simple things just don't function, such as the diagonal directions for the stick not working in the teleport maps or the tower-defense grid. Trying to change how low your partner's health should be before she uses a health potion shows no information. Skills and powers are in a grid, with no indication as to how they would usually progress.
When I unplugged the controller, the inventory switches from the awesome circle-dial & list view for each slot, to everything being dumped into a set of grids, which limits how much you can carry but isn't at all indicated in the controller inventory.
Attacks have power-ups: in controller mode, using Left Bumper applies one of each power-up to the next use of that attack, but only one stack of each; in keyboard mode, near as I can tell, you have to click individual power-ups to apply them, and they stack to 3, but cannot combo with other power-ups. If there are keys to apply them, it wasn't presented well and I missed it.
I'd like it more if you could choose which inventory and skill windows you got with or without a controller. Overall, Keyboard Mode has too many keys to press, but Controller Mode is still enjoyable thus far. I recommend it, but try the demo or borrow from a friend if you're both in a Steam Family Group.

Playing FNV first spoiled me a bit, particularly the superior shooting mechanics of the latter. At first, I found shooting in F3 was irritatingly random. I was going to say hit and miss but that would be one of those pun thingies.  I found assault rifles behaved in a rather un-assault like way and were generally useless. Scoped 44 mag revolver, sniper rifle and combat shotgun seemed the best set up. Absence of repair kits was both puzzling and annoying.
As the game progressed the shooting mechanics seemed to improve. Whether that was because I was increasing my skill level, or simply becoming familiar with the mechanics, is hard to say.
I wanted a player home early on. I didn't want to have to deal with being ambushed by Talon Company mercs thereafter, if I defused the bomb in Megaton. Nor did I want to blow up Megaton in order to get a pad in Tenpenny Tower. So I moved into Arlington House which was ok, if a tad dready. Eventually, I defused said bomb and got my tin shack in Megaton. The ramshackle build is wholly appropriate to the games' overall scenario. Out of curiosity, I installed a mod that allowed me to acquire the Tenpenny Tower suite. Great views and a genuine atmosphere of fetid decadence about the hotel. If this was the developers' intention, it worked. Made me think of the atmosphere of the Overlook Hotel in "The Shining".
Graphics are ok for such an old game, albeit the world space is drab and brown. Perhaps that was intentional, given the scenario of a post-apocalyptic world.
After identifying where random, Talon mercs would confront me on exiting some buildings, I would seed the area outside with mines before going inside. On exiting the mercs would appear and walk right into the minefield. Boom...bye, see ya later. Highly amusing if a little bit devious.
Despite FNV being superior in terms of graphics and gameplay, I actually liked F3. Not a great game yet still worth playing. The world space offers plenty of exploration and is actually quite interesting. But, if you have played FNV, the shooting mechanics might generate a lot of foul language, until the bullets a) hit the target and b) do what bullets do in real life.
Btw, worked perfectly well on W7, although I think I edited a line or two in the .ini file to make the game run properly.

"Great game", it's that simple. You start your adventure with a feeder, and every minutes you are planning in your mind which trade route to choose and where to stem your bunker with most economical price.
Now you are getting more and more money, and expanding your fleet with regional traders, and eventually going up to those beatiful ladies - PPMX, NPMX and Ultra-Large Container Vessel. Oh! Now you are ready for a round-the-world service. Further to ocean trading, you can always berth / unberth the vessel on your own, and I would say this is the most interesting element of this game.
The difficulties...well, I guess it's hard to name your ships. With the fleet getting ever larger, I decide to simply pick a real world Liner Operator and name all my ships as per their's.
As I said, it's a great game. But there are always ways to further enhance the gaming experience:-
1. Canal passage. It would be great if I have to pay my canal due for passage,  sail my ship through the Suez, or may be have to anchor my ship off Cristobal a day or two due to canal congestion.
2. Larger scale of map when docking/undocking my ship. It's quite often I find it difficult to expect where will I berth my lady until I see it. And if possible, it would be great to have a "longer" sailing option before berthing/after unberthing.
3. Some more "small contracts" - I find it hard to believe I am shipping some thousands TEU of Radioactive Materials to Hong Kong, or loads of weapons ex. US/Canada to Cuba...
4. More realistic color of the Equipments (i.e. containers) - The Equipments are just too sharp and colorful.
5. Players can draw the company logo in-game, and decide where to put the Operator's Color on the ship's hull.
6. More real world events - e.g.: Pay for ice-breaker when approaching Gulf of St. Lawrence, stowaways sneaked onboard at West/South African countries, economic changes that affect the global bunker price SERIOUSLY...etc.
The trading mode is realistic only if the game is for General Cargo Carriers. For Container vessels, it appears more "real world" if we are to plan and maintain service routes across the globe...well may be it's just me thinking of this only.
If you like ships, go for it. If you like trading game, go for it. If you want to sail a vessel, go for it. There's no much choice where you can sail vessels from a 480TEU feeder to a ULCV with bow/stern thrusters.

Extremely addicting! Managing the ships and company contracts can put you on the edge. Neat little random events add flavour to the journeys your ships will make. Graphics are pretty decent, sound is also good, didn't care too much for the docking/un-docking mini-game though.

I rarely post reviews of games because I just don't feel like it would contribute much to the already strong number of reviews on games.  Actually, I don't think I have done any.
For this game, I will make an exception.  While the game does have an interesting story, the voice acting and script is pretty horrible.  In addition, you don't really even like the characters.  The other promising part is the interesting concept of rotating gravity.  Unfortunately, all it provides is a promise... that it doesn't keep.
So much for the positives.  The action is completely repetitive, especially when it comes down to the boss fights.  Most of the game is casual, but then you come to boss fights later in the game where the difficulty skyrockets to levels that don't even make sense.  It would be different if the difficulty was due to requiring skill, but instead if you basically just hvae to figure out which stupid strategy is going to be required.  Is it going to be spamming lava balls?  Is it going to be running like a decapitated chicken to keep distance?  Is it reviving your somehow previously useful teammate constantly?  Either way, it is more an annoyance than some accomplishment.
Holy crap I almost forgot the cutscenes!  I have never seen so many of them in a game... ever.  And it isn't just to give the story, it is just to show you repeating the same teamwork to get over a wall sometimes.  I would say that over half the actually game was watching cutscense, with some just 30 seconds apart.  Some game designers have come up with ways to focus your attention on action/story without pulling you out of the game to watch a movie.  This game apparently wants you to watch their movie while occasionally participating in moronic boss battles and repetitive enemies.
This game is a rip off of Gears of War for the cover, HL2 for the gravity gun, and SATs for repetitive misery.  Can you find some enjoyable moments?  Yes.  Will you spend most of your time cursing the crappy controls, cover mechanics, inconsistant difficulty and insane amount of cutscenes?  Yuuuuuuup

While this game resembles Gauntlet games in a superficial way, it doesn't really play like a classic Gauntlet game.  At best, this is either a game inspired by Gauntlet, or a clone of Gauntlet, but in my opinion isn't truly worthy of the name.
I'll start by building on the clone-of-Gauntlet idea.  In my opinion, there are games older than this one that play better and look better.  Either of the Torchlight games, and by extension the second Diablo game (which is the only one of those that I played, TBH), are good examples.  Also, any of the Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale games, as well as Temple of Elemental Evil and Pool of Radiance, would work (I might add that ToEE and PoR were panned pretty badly at the time, too).  Even the older versions of Gauntlet are better and even more immersive than this.
On a related and not-so-minor note, this game is choppy even at the lowest graphic settings.  This is simply unacceptable, when so many clones of clones of games coming out these days (especally on the pay-to-win platforms like Android) seem to emphasize graphics over gameplay and content.
The keyboard controls are goofy and inconsistent among the characters.  I could probably get used to using WSAD-style controls on this game, except that there are only four directions to move.  Again, so many other games trump this by default.  If that isn't bad enough, the wizard has a completely different set of controls to get used to (except for movement), compared to the others.  Couldn't the wizard have been made to play closer to the other character types, rather than awkwardly fumbling through different spell schools?  Worse yet, the controls are not customizable at all.  I didn't try using my controller to see if the experience is better, because I lost interest in the game content and graphics too soon.

Ignore the politics.  Play the game.
The quotes and vignettes that people are calling "SJW" are largely being taken out of context, and are not relevant to the gameplay whatsoever.
Gunplay is excellent.  It feels a bit more oldschool that Doom (2016) simply because of the greater amount of hitscan enemies.  Love'em or hate'em, you are going to be seeing a lot in this game.
The new dual-wielding mechanics are nifty, but clunky.  I would have preferred the ability to create a custom weapon wheel with "loadouts" or something similar to make switching a bit more refined.
Sounds and music are satisfying.  Although Mick Gordon has also gone heavily electronic, which many people hated in Doom, the soundtrack is not as agressively present and blends with more than it dominates the gameplay.
As to bugs, I haven't had any.  That isn't to say others haven't, but they are not universal.  And so far, the majority of them are being solved by doing a DDU driver wipe and fresh driver install - something that any PC gamer should be doing regularly anyway.
There are some oddly gnarly textures though, and that doesn't seem to be a bug; rather an artistic or aesthetic choice.  A mind boggling one, but there we are.
There is more than 7 hours of content as some are claiming.  If you play on a reasonable difficulty, take time to explore for secrets, and do a few side quests, an 80% or so completion run should take you around 10-15 hours.  100% on a higher difficulty will probably take closer to 20.
Two timelines, and multiple upgrade paths may add some replayability, as the different upgrades will emphasize different playstyles.
Overall, solid 7/10.  Probably not worth it for non-fans at launch price, but a solid game.

Epistory - Typing Chronicles took me completely by surprise. After all, its premise sounds ridiculous. When I heard for the first time that there is an RPG game where you battle monsters and interact with your surroundings solely by typing seemingly random words on a keyboard, I could not help but get a chuckle on the idea. And yet this game proved me wrong - maybe it is due to its masterful execution of such concept, maybe even more because of the fact that the words are not selected that randomly at all; but I will leave all these and many other wonderful discoveries to you. Long story short: the game has an absolutely beautiful art style, its picturesque paper world unfolding around you piece by piece as you discover new access points; its music can be mesmerizing with the narrator's soothing voice never pulling you out of the moment; and last but not least, the game develops with ingenuity what seems initially to be a rather strange and simple core concept. Oh, and it also teaches you to type more proficiently as a byproduct.
TO SUM UP: This game is, in its own peculiar way, a hidden gem. If you want to try something new and learn a useful skill while doing it, try picking up this colourful, lovely-looking, well-written, expertly voice-acted one-of-a-kind experience when it is on sale.

My review of No Man's Sky so far.
So I have traveled at this point I believe to about 20 star systems. I lost count of how many worlds I've been to at this point. I think I have been to 3-5 moons too.

Today I found a black hole.
Can't wait to see what it will lead to.
With that said here is my review of this game as it exists right now.
I think this is a very interesting and good game. The idea of constant exploration which seems to be an endless Universe, despite the fact I am still only in one galaxy. The whole idea that the galaxy is named, and there are black holes heavily implies to me that very soon I will be in another galaxy.
There seems to not just be a good number of types of ships, but enough different classes of the same type of ship to fill satisfied with variety.

Plus: Being able to find other damaged ships on planets and make them your own is a very nice touch.
Variety of worlds. Though at this point some of the worlds I have visited do seem similar, each one so far does feel a bit different than the other.
Black Holes: This is very cool that they exist in this virtual universe.
Seems to be countless stars: It really does seem that there are enough stars to last even the most epic explorer a good long time.
I wish there were a few more factions, or sentient races so far, besides what seems to be the three.
However, I have already learned over 100 words. I am picking up the warrior race a-lot lately, and I can understand them better here and there.
The idea of actually having to learn different languages to even understand aliens and seemingly having to do so by learning word for word is a very nice touch.
Space Battles:
The idea of either choosing to help freighters or use pirate attacks as a decoy to attack freighters for loot is a very nice touch.
As I gradually have learned, though space pirates at the beginning of the game were really a threat to me, I have upgraded my ship and gotten now at least 2 better ships than the original one I had, so now it is starting to feel more and more of a fair fight.
The fact that there are asteroid belts where you can mine in space too is also nice.
Scenery: Though some worlds at this point are starting to seem similar, as well as some of the wildlife, each world so far does seem unique.
The last world or moon I visited was pretty close to a very hot planet, and so the moon itself was warm enough to have life as well as running water. The moon was temperate though, implying to me that the moon being a bit farther away from planet's star was a bit cooler.
The planet in question was so big that at times (especially at night) this huge planet taking up most of the skyline on it's sister moon was really nice.
Besides Space Stations, there are also Space Anomoly's like a bigger starship then your own or what could also be called a more private smaller space station.
These two guys that run it can help you out in ways that are totally cool.
Now with some critique:
Eh so I really like this game. Does that mean that this game is worth 60 bucks? At first I would have said no and 60 is a bit high.
However, there has been a-lot of work put into this game to really make it feel like a whole universe that you have free reign to explore.
On top of that the graphics are really gorgeous and not many games are made in my opinion anymore where star exploration is the key main focus.
Games in the past that might have been considered like this:
Star Control 2
Endless Space  2 (okay that just came out too) and it also has factions and abilities to take over star systems, which this game doesn't seem to have but well alright).
Oh and last and not least, I found a world for the first time for me, where I actually found geysers spewing out gas. This was also a nice touch, since real planetary scientists now are finding out more and more that so many worlds within our own solar system and exo planets are not just dead planets.
So this made me feel this universe was more real.
However with all of this said.
****    I wish there was multiplayer. Even if this means in a limited form. I wish I could meet up with 1 or 2 more people to help me explore and or explore together.
****  This type of game is serious business regarding GRINDING. I can understand then that for a-lot of players this is a game where people will get bored, because unlike a-lot of games now, progress can be slow.
Progress can be very slow, since getting improvements for your ship, exosuit and multi tool and or just getting new ships and multi tools as well as finding out a-lot more that exists in this artifical Universe  CAN TAKE A VERY LONG TIME.
I have played already 127 or so hours, and I feel now I am just getting started for example:
Some worlds I was on, part of me didn't want to leave yet, since there were areas I hadn't explored yet due to the size of just one of the worlds I was on.
So for people who hate MAJOR GRINDS, this is going to be very tough for you.
I would say this game is worth probably 40 bucks now.
I do hope for even more content as time goes on.
Bottom Line:
So with everything said, right now I give this game a B+

Summary up front: I would not recommend this game. It's a beautiful atmospheric and interesting game, but I do not want anyone to experience the rage that this game induces with certain parts in the game.
---
The creators obviously put a LOT of time and effort into creating an amazing atmosphere with the music and art they used. Which is why I don't understand why they chose to insert parts into the game you are meant to play through trial and error. A lot of trial and error. A lot of dying because you are quickly and repetitively confronted with 1 hit-game over objects being thrown at you in random sequences. To avoid those objects you are sometimes dependant on random factors outside of your control. This is what causes frustration, anger and ultimately rage. It completely destroys the well crafted atmosphere of the game.
I think they should have made an easy and hard difficulty mode. Put all the frustrating "die 100 times minimum before you understand how to respond to this sequence of events" in the hard difficulty mode.  Let us noobs enjoy the story and atmosphere! At times I felt like I was in one of Ross' Mario Maker levels. Unfairly difficult with no checkpoints in between.
Game length/replayability:
My first (and only) clear took 440 deaths and 9,5 hours, I reached 97% completion without too much trouble. It put me on the 88000-89000 rank range on the global leaderboards. I assume the remaining 3% are things I should have picked up during the rage inducing escape-sequences. I was dying enough without going the extra mile. There is no new-game+ feature. So unless you want to get 100% completion and/or compete with others on the leaderboards you are done after your first clear.
I would not recommend this game because while beautiful, atmospheric and interesting to play, I would never wish the rage that this game induces on anyone.

Playing FNV first spoiled me a bit, particularly the superior shooting mechanics of the latter. At first, I found shooting in F3 was irritatingly random. I was going to say hit and miss but that would be one of those pun thingies.  I found assault rifles behaved in a rather un-assault like way and were generally useless. Scoped 44 mag revolver, sniper rifle and combat shotgun seemed the best set up. Absence of repair kits was both puzzling and annoying.
As the game progressed the shooting mechanics seemed to improve. Whether that was because I was increasing my skill level, or simply becoming familiar with the mechanics, is hard to say.
I wanted a player home early on. I didn't want to have to deal with being ambushed by Talon Company mercs thereafter, if I defused the bomb in Megaton. Nor did I want to blow up Megaton in order to get a pad in Tenpenny Tower. So I moved into Arlington House which was ok, if a tad dready. Eventually, I defused said bomb and got my tin shack in Megaton. The ramshackle build is wholly appropriate to the games' overall scenario. Out of curiosity, I installed a mod that allowed me to acquire the Tenpenny Tower suite. Great views and a genuine atmosphere of fetid decadence about the hotel. If this was the developers' intention, it worked. Made me think of the atmosphere of the Overlook Hotel in "The Shining".
Graphics are ok for such an old game, albeit the world space is drab and brown. Perhaps that was intentional, given the scenario of a post-apocalyptic world.
After identifying where random, Talon mercs would confront me on exiting some buildings, I would seed the area outside with mines before going inside. On exiting the mercs would appear and walk right into the minefield. Boom...bye, see ya later. Highly amusing if a little bit devious.
Despite FNV being superior in terms of graphics and gameplay, I actually liked F3. Not a great game yet still worth playing. The world space offers plenty of exploration and is actually quite interesting. But, if you have played FNV, the shooting mechanics might generate a lot of foul language, until the bullets a) hit the target and b) do what bullets do in real life.
Btw, worked perfectly well on W7, although I think I edited a line or two in the .ini file to make the game run properly.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a stellar indie platformer, which is set in a beautifully stunning world. This review will rate each of the games elements, and then have an overall conclusion:
Story - 8/10 (spoiler free).
There is not a lot to say about the story in Ori, other than it is really solid. What I feel is most recognizable, is that the story is so well paced, and the world/story recognizes what you have done earlier in the game. The only bad thing I can really say about the story, is that the characters backstories are never really described ingame, but I suppose that could also be part of the charm.
Visuals and sounds - 10/10
This is hands-down the best looking game I have played in 2015. Maybe it is not a particularly taxing game, but the asthethic is the most beautiful I have seen since Trine 2. A huge pro is that the game also runs really well on my machine, and I haven't really heard of people who had problems running the game. The soundtrack and the sounds of the game are also as perfect as the visuals. The music never feels out of place, and it can go from raging and pumping, to emotional and slow, which depends on what you are doing in the game. This might not be uncommon for games, but I just feel like Ori does it so exceptionally well, that the music actually suceeds in having an impact on you. There is no real voiceacting in the game, as all of the characters speak in a sort of alien language, but for me that was one of the things which also stood out to be immersive.
Gameplay - 8/10
Ori's gameplay is solid, and I especially found the platforming enjoyable, but not so much the combat. The best thing about the combat and platforming, is probably when you acquire new moves, but the game does not forget your old moves, and you end up using all of your acquired moves in the last level. I find this to be fantastic, as it challenges the player to think fast. The platforming is extremely diverse, but the combat as pointed out earlier, can be a little dull and samey. Your main combat move is just to click close to your enemies, and then you will fire homing beams at them. But again, I don't think the developers wanted the combat to be a main part of the game, as it is sometimes blended into the platforming, and thereby making combat moves into platforming moves.
The game can be extremely punishing, especially if you don't go out of your way to find hidden pickups, which I certainly thing that you should do, as I found that to be one of the most enjoyable parts of the game. The game makes very little use of autosaves, except in some places, so you will have to save by yourself. This can both me useful, but also extremely annoying, as you can basically complete allmost the entirety of a level, die, and then be respawned close to the beginning.
Overall - 8,5/10
I really think that this game is exceptional, and I was really surprised to find such a polished product then I bought the game. This game shone through as my favorite platformer of a loooong long time almost in the 2 first hours.
I definetely recommend Ori and the Blind Forest!

It's hard to know where to begin with To the Moon, because there's just so much to say. I guess I should say right off the bat that it is well worth the money.
I played this game basically in one sitting aside from a couple breaks for food and stuff. It's like a book you just can't put down. Part of that is the pacing, which I found was an extreme positive here. But mainly, this is a tight story and a fully immersive experience that I just couldn't tear myself from. Every moment away from the game, I was thinking about it and I couldn't wait to learn more about Johnny and River through the eyes of Dr Rosalene and Dr Watts.
First off, this game is gorgeous. The pixel animation reminds me of the RPG games I'd play as a child on my Gameboy, so I'm sure nostalgia played a bit of a role when I got it. Every environment is carefully thought out and brought to life with the artwork. I love the use of colour as I went further back in time through Johnny's life.
I fell in love with the characters--each and every one of them. The cast isn't overly expansive which was appropriate for a game of its size. My favourite person was definitely River. I'm afraid to talk too much on the characters because it would be so easy to let a spoiler slip...but I'll do my best. The dynamic between Dr Rosalene and Dr Watts was amusing--Rosalene is very professional but constantly taking little shots at Watts, who is a goofball with a big heart. I very much appreciated a black female lead. It's such simple inclusion but it is so rare to see a person of colour as a primary playable character, and an interesting character at that!
Johnny's tale was incredibly interesting without being overly dramatic or too "into itself". The story was in no way self-indulgent and that kept me intrigued and immersed all the way through. Once again, there's only so much I can say about the story. There were a few twists and turns that kept things fresh. It was all incredibly emotional without being wearisome. I really need to commend the writers--those people sure know how to write a story. This easily could have been a movie, but I'm so happy it's a game because I got to be a part of it as a player. I feel like I got to know someone deeply and I think that's a huge success for a game like this.
The last half hour of the game had me a bawling mess. At times I just had to stop for a moment to compose myself. And yes, a fair number of games have made me cry, but not quite like this, I must admit...
I mustn't forget the soundtrack, but in short, it's the cherry on top of the cake. At least I think that's the saying.
The only con I can really think is that using the mouse was tricky to get used to because on my laptop the mouse lags a fair bit, specifically during dialogue. In the last quarter of the game, I figured out that I could use the arrow keys to move and enter to interact with things. A word of advice: just use the mouse to highlight objects, use the arrows and enter for everything else. Makes life much easier.
You won't regret getting this game. Every penny you spend on this game is returned to you tenfold in story and characters and beauty and tears. What an experience.

PROS:

CONS:

VERDICT?
A real gem of a detective game which does lack the polish of a telltale game but has a unique style of story telling. Only the first episode but worth a shot, im certainly looking forward to the next one.

The Detail is a beautifully executed mature crime drama that offers meaningful choices and multiple playable main characters with different perspectives. It rewards careful thought and good intuition with choices with logical paths. The characters are deep and compelling, which is amplified by the gripping story - all accomplished with brilliant writing.
The game play is point and click in the vein of Tell Tale's Walking Dead series, and you can tell they took some inspiration in how they balance the pace of the game - there are some really tense moments where you are rewarding by thinking and acting quickly. Considering how much variation there is depending on your choices within the first episode I imagine there will be really great branching in further episodes. The art style is beautiful, some of the art is really beautiful and striking - and some of it seems really amateur, along with the animation, but it all builds the atmosphere amazingly. The music is perfect, it builds the mood without being intrusive. A single playthrough is very short, will take you 1-2 hours, but there is a lot of replayability. If you like crime stories, if you liked the Tell Tale games, or if you just want to support indie devs making amazing games then buy this game!

I'm not sure why this game got so many bad reviews ... Coop not working (anymore ?) maybe, but I did not buy it for this, so not a point as far as I'm concerned.
It's a rather standard and solid TP cover shooter, with a few twists (gravity gun, fights in 0 gravity, change of gravity on specific points, destroyable cover, and so on). The story is pretty good for a shooter, except the end which is a bit disappointing. The controls are fine (if you rebind "mini zoom" to right click, as it should be), voices and sounds are ok, and graphics are decent. No performance problems (Windows 8.1, GTX 760, i5 4670k and 8 GB of RAM) and no bugs for me (except ... see next sentence).
Here are the not so good things : totally linear ... starting around the middle of the game, it has a tendancy to CTD when reloading a checkpoint ... some annoying "boss" fights, especially towards the end, enemy variety rather low, and (if you're after such things) no trading cards and no achievements.
It took me around 10 hours to finish it, without rushing too much (there's not much else to do than follow the path, anyway), but what matters to me is that I had fun playing it, and that's all I expect of a game.
No reason not recommend it then, I'd rate it at 7/10 taking into account its current price (around 10€). If you can get it on sale, all the better.

This is a rather mixed bag, so I'll throw the bad out first.
The co-op is forever broken due to gamespy shutting down, and the story and characters are so laughably bad it's almost worth checking out as a joke. Also, it's overloaded with gameplay-intruding cutscenes that could have played out better if control wasn't wrestled from the players hands and the actual quality of this console-port shows for itself on the main menu. But honestly, I've seen far-worse ports. So I should probably count my blessings they gave me keyboard prompts.
However, the gameplay itself showcases some suprisingly meaty gunplay and titillating destruction that kept me playing. While invisible walls are cumbersome and the overal design implying this was entirely meant to be played in co-op kept rearing their ugly heads, I still pressed on for the next messy firefight, even if some boss-fights repeated themselves after the 4-hour mark.
Inversion is an interesting Almagam of multiple other games (HL2 and GoW come to mind), but it does more good then bad, and for a low price, it's still fun to play on a dreary weekend or days-off from work, where you just want to hurl cars at big, muscle-bound barbarians and watch them explode into juicy lamb-chops.
Inversion is really dumb, and there are many games out there with a better story and longer running time with a lot less hectic and silly story to keep things going until the finish line, but it's still fun for what it is.
If you are still skeptical, wait for it go on sale for an even lower price :)

While the overall feel of the game was interesting, I would not recommend this game for a number of reasons; I will first go through the positive key aspects and then argue why they are not good enough to warrant the purchase (unless you buy it on offer or feel like burning that sort of cash, since it's not too expensive — consider that the first but sort-of positive note).
The animation and the audio of the game are very well done; the fluidity of the animation of the main antagonist, for one thing, is startlingly good. If you also happen to like Halloween-themed pieces, be it anime or manga or games, then you'll probably get a kick out of the campy, goofy nod at that sort of thing, reminiscent of Darkstalkers. Do note that there is an underlying motif of a big plot and what not and that this plays into what the characters look like, and we also get a glimpse at all that through their in-game interactions before and after combat in story mode.
About the story now: I don't feel like the foreshadowing used is appropriately handled, because it feels like it was meant to be an allusion that is clear enough for the more savvy players but slightly nebulous for new players; instead what we do get is an allusion that is too plainly obvious (with some simply irrelevant caveats) unless you are a very new player and a feel like the plot is underestimating the player's intelligence. It doesn't come off as funny, by the way, so I am not sure there is any value in theorizing it may have been humour on the developer's part.
Then you have the combat system. For starters, it seems clear that the team intended to make this usable only with a high-end controller. For some of us who have been used to not needing one for most games, this comes as a bit of an annoyance, especially considering that a controller with directional control and 6 buttons is really not enough to hold even the majority of functions in game (for instance, there are 6 basic attacks, so that effectively means you cannot use a 6-button controller at all). And even so, I had trouble executing even some of the more normal moves with such a controller with a D-pad, which tells me that the intention was to be used with an analog stick. That's no good, really. And even playing the game with the keyboard instead was a big deal. Wrap that up with the issue that the creature gags are somewhat off-colour, just a tad too campy, and you have to ask yourself if it should be invested on at all.

Here are a list of issues I have encountered:
When you first open the game and change your resolution the game will force your computer to reboot. When you open the game back up your menu is gone.
This can be resolved by deleting the saved files under C:\Users\%USER%\Saved Games\MachineGames\Wolfenstein II The New Colossus. You then have to go to the game properties and uncheck the box that syncs your saves to the steam cloud. It appears that syncing the game to steam breaks the menu....
One of your weapons may not appear while the other is held sideways or looks as if its been half drawn. Also, while dual wielding, one of your guns will not show the firing animation even though the ammunition count is going down.
To get Shadow Play to work you have to disable Motion Blur. I am not kidding. It has to do with the Vulcan API and enabling Motion Blur interferes with it. How they managed this we may never know.
Also Steam overlay does not work in this game.
This is a fatal bug and will happen on the same save over and over. It appears to happen at random stages in the game, but always happens in the middle of a cutscene. If you try to continue the game it will freeze it forcing you to restart it. This is the bug that has me stuck. 11 hours in and this game is preventing me from going any further.

N.B. this brief review will mainly focus on the game itself, and not the questionable behaviour of Hello Games and Sean Murray. I personally think Sean should have said something (f%$in anything!!?) after the PR sh%$ storm they received. That said, I think the hate against this game got a bit rediculous, and imagine at least 50% of negative reviews are mindless drones copying 'lies lies lies!!' cry babies. I am absolutely loving this game! The visuals are beautiful (see my screenshots!
). The progression in character abilities and enhancements is really well executed. Contrary to popular opinion, I am finding tonnes of things to do in this game. E.g. just look at steam achievements, there's a 'todo list', if you're not into a complete sandbox (i.e. objectiveless) experience. While not perfect, the random generation algorithims seem to work quite well for me, and I am constantly met with new and interesting environements and situations to explore and experience.
In short, I think the game as it stands is well worth the sale price I paid, and certainly has the potential to be worth those 60 bucks.
I am not a particularly casual gamer, so at present I have stuck to survival and permadeath. I realise this is something that the original release didn't include, and so can forgive negative reviews based on the limited casual play; personally I like a challenge. I died twice on permadeath, then decided to just stick with my survival game until I reached the center of the galaxy (getting achievement), then there's some replayability on permadeath (different achievement), when I'm more of a vet explorer.
At the very beginning the game can be very difficult, but far from unfair as I've seen some people complaining about. As long as you plan things, make use of resources and learn from your mistakes, you should be able to pull through. E.g. if you head out into a blizzard from a cave and get past 50% frost protection without turning back, you are taking a risk, and cannot complain when you end up freezing to death being whipped by wild plants and animals.
I died a few times on both survival and permadeath, before getting my bearings with the game's mechanics and vital methods required to survive. Since then, it has only gone uphill for me. I love getting a new ship, a new power tool, new game changing abilities like vehicles (exocraft) and extra inventory storage (huge driver to improve). Initially it's a bit of a grind, especially with iron, but I see that as a necessary evil in order to really appreciate the progression and upgrades towards faster grinding, including grenades that instantly mine out an area of resources for you.
So one of the biggest challenges this game faces is how to randomly generate terrain, items and biological organisms in a variety of ecosystems / environments, and make it look 'good'. I think we should acknowledge that this is a very non-trivial task. So I can excuse the odd c%$k up, and even enjoy them for the hilarious frankensteinien messes they are, big fan of
! (cracks me up every time)
In my experience, the terrain generation is working wonderfully right now. Caves, valleys and mountain ranges feel natural in most places. I actually got lost exploring a cave system so extensive my life support ran out before I could get back out (lesson learned, unplanned caving ~ risky). The planetary flora is wonderfully varied in color and style; recently found a tree that appeared to be covered in anuses, named it 'Anusesgalore'! The fauna can be hit and miss, though on average feels quite good and decently varied in the stock parts used in random generation.
Though whatever I've said here, I advise you to go look at my screenshots (maybe small spoilers, but if you're concerned, just avoid reading any text)! They say it all (I'm an sc ♥♥♥♥♥, especially in a game that includes a specialized feature to take photographs!). You may formulate your own opinion from these (and I imagine many others people have taken).
So I'm now getting lil bored writing this, and I think you get my opinion of the game as it stands. I'll list some pros and cons from my perspective, then wrap up.
There's a lot more I could say about my experience with this game, though as mentioned I'm getting bored of typing this and it's that in general I reccomend getting it on sale, or even retail price if you think it sounds like something you'll really enjoy (probably is!).
I will say that one cool feature appears to be how you can name and upload things you 'discover', and get paid based on the 'importance' of the discovery. E.g. life forms typically make you more money than rocks :P. Here is where any 'multiplayer' currently lies, as you are able to see other people's naming of discoveries, and vice versa, and it's like you're part of a community working to map out and explore this randomly generated universe. The best of the Europa Universalis games in my opinion. EUIV focuses too much on making money by releasing ridiculously small DLC and upsetting game balances.
You're in charge of a country, whether this is a historical country or a custom one, and you have to set yourself a goal. World domination will take you weeks, months, or even years to complete depending on how well you dig in and plan your battles ahead of time. Try going for something a little bit less ambitious; like wiping a neighbouring nation off the face of the planet, or being the first to circumnavigate the globe.
Balancing everything in your nation from political to economic to simply trying to figure out why that one pesky province keeps rioting against your (fair) rule is a full-time task, and while you may be forgiven for setting the clock speed to very fast to see that one project to completion, your neighbours may use that precise moment to invade your nation.
While EUIV adds some extra bits and bobs, EUIII is challenging enough in its own right to keep you busy for a long time.

The Detail is a crime noir point-and-click adventure game which manages to fascinate the player by offering a well written story, multiple playable characters and interesting choices which influence the storyline.
Episode 1 has 3 playable characters: Reggie - a veteran detective, Joe - a reformed criminal trying to protect his family and escape from his dark past, and Kate - a rookie police officer who happen to be in the wrong place in the wrong time. And it all starts with detective Reggie investigating a brutal murder...
Great graphic novel visual style, decent soundtrack, and intriguing mature story. That's what The Detail has to offer.
It takes about an hour and a half to finish the first episode, but you can also squeeze about 4 hours out of it if you plan on going for 100% achievements, at least that's how long it took me. I consider it to be priced quite fairly, 6$ for an episode is a reasonable price, however i wish there would have been an option to pre-purchase the entire season, instead of being forced to buy each episode separately.
The Detail turned out to be exactly what i expected from it, and managed to draw me into it. Now i'm waiting anxiously for the next episode.
