You know that trope in anime, where for the first episode the
OP serves as the credits?
That's exactly what Wolfenstein 2 feels like: enjoyable, yet incomplete.
First of all, the gameplay is great. Everything feels good just to do, except for climbing ladders. The gameplay loop of "stealth until you get caught, then go balls deep" might be a little stale but I still enjoy it. On the other hand, this gameplay loop doesn't get shaken up very many times, causing large swaths of the game to feel samey. It doesn't help that Death Incarnate is a TERRIBLE difficulty - almost every enemy type has a way to oneshot you no matter how much health and armor you have. This is pretty much the only reason the game took me 16 hours, and is why I resorted to save scumming half the game. I think I would've done it in 10 if I was playing on normal difficulty.
Like Mankind Divided, the game just... ends, but this time it feels a little more sour. Plot threads are laid, and addressed periodically, only to never get a payoff. Your goal is techniaclly fulfilled, but it's always framed as part of a larger plan that never gets followed up on. While I really enjoyed thew writing during the journey, the last 30-60 minutes of the game nearly undid all of that good will for me.
Oh, and after you've beaten the game,
At least the game runs well - on a 1060 I get 1080/60+ almost all the time at medium + adaptive resolution, usually 100+ fps. Wait for a sale or something I guess.

I got this game as a birthday gift from my parents in law. It takes what was already great in the previous two Wolfenstein games, and makes it even better.

First impression:
Wolfenstien is simply put a great game, but as with everything there is room for improvement… when I first got the game it crashed when I opened it (works now though). As well as I am not particularly fond of the weapon system in the game, I think it would be better if you had a bigger choice of Nazi killing tools. The difficulty is also kind of an issue I was playing on the second hardest and yes I realize that it is meant to be hard; but sometimes you’ll die out of nowhere and lose a lot of progress (if you’re like me and forget to save in between checkpoints). These are the only problems I have found in the game so far. The graphics are great, sound track is beautiful, and best of all you can kill all the fascist Nazi pigs you want.
Post Campaign Completion:
The Campaign I felt was a little short and concise almost like everything works out too perfectly for the characters (I feel this could be to leave room for the DLC’s) … however the game did do a fantastic job of making a serious campaign that shows us that Nazis are not the only villains in this world, we all have our own demons and it is our challenge to conquer them. The story also takes an intriguing approach on how government conspiracy’s like Roswell tie into the Nazi takeover of the United States, setting it aside from other similar stories such as The Man in the High Castle.    Besides the length and the fact that everything works out perfectly for the characters, I think on the face yes the story is a little meh. There are a lot of moments that left me saying WTF that doesn’t make any realistic sense. Although if you take time to read all the papers, talk to all the people, and listen to BJ’s commentary through the missions; the story becomes way, way more interesting and grasping.
Other thoughts:
I realize a lot of people are having technical issues but personally my machine was fine at running it at 1080p, no tearing or missing textures, and 60fps (I know a lot of people think that’s low but to put it in to context a regular movie even animated usually runs at 24fps).
Politically I don’t see how this game supports communism as I have seen many people say, I think it just supports everything that isn’t just being a straight up Nazi. I also don’t think the developers are playing diversity cards by have the cast majority being minorities, because that’s not even true they are plenty of white people you can find on the submarine that are fighting the Nazis, and even if it was that would make sense because if America was enslaved by Nazis minorities would be the most at risk; therefore, being the most likely to fight back.  Finally, I don’t think this game is a political statement I think it’s just a Nazi Shoot-em-up

It's Gauntlet, and Gauntlet is always best played with friends.

-really neat weapon options and unlockables for changing up/customizing gameplay
Cons:
-color system of the past is gone/no multi-classes (in other words, no RED WIZARD and BLUE WIZARD, etc., just one class per team)
-enemy variety is cool but missing classic monsters like lobbers and super sorcerers
-clicky hack-'n-slash gameplay is arcadey and can ultimately feel shallow to people who aren't expecting it, or are playing alone
All in all tho it's loads of fun with friends and definitely worth it, in my opinion. I like typing and I like games, but typing games always feel somewhat forced on their gameplay. Not this one, though. Epistory puts you a beautifully crafted world with a very unique art style, atmospheric music and an entertaining story. Even though the controls feel somewhat awkward, overall it was a lot of fun to run through the world. The combat is alright, too, though it feels like a certain type of magic is far more useful than the others. Also, playing it on higher difficulties – I suspect that is the cause, though I'm not entirely sure – rewards you with much more points than on lower difficulties, which results in unusable skill points (so you have to switch manually to the map, everytime you open the in-game menu) and enables you to unlock parts of the game it doesn't expect you to be there: I unlocked chapter 4 before chapter 3, which was kinda confusing.
Overall, it's a great game and you should play it, if not just to increase your typing abilities or your active vocabulary.

If you want to try something different, buy this game.
I'm a little ways into the story, I've unlocked three of the four powers. The story is a bit vague, and I'm intrigued to see where they are going with it, but I don't play this game for the story. There are plenty of games with amazing stories, but I have yet to encounter a game like Epistory before.
Firstly, the graphics are lovely, and the origami twist on them constantly reminds me I'm playing something different than your typical rpg/jrpg. The music and sound effects compliment the game, graphics, story and action quite well. The best part is the action, you defeat enemies, destroy barriers, etc, by typing out the name. It's amazing how much the battles can draw you in; there is nothing quite as frustrating as losing a battle right at the end to a boss because you were off by one letter!!!!
Additionally I should mention that there is also an Arena mode, along with the storyline mode, Arena mode is an endless battle, with waves of enemies where the goal is to rack up the highest score possible. It also has a high score board, so you can keep track of your highest score, and how you compare.
Definitely worth the cost, especially if you can get it on sale!

It is impossible not to be enchanted by Epistory - Typing Chronicles. The plot is not particularly elaborate, but it unravels elegantly until the end, and if you never played a game of the genre, you should consider the fact that usually the plot in this kind of games is non-existant (or, at least, the ones I tried did not have one). The art style is stunning and very original, but I believe that further descriptions would be unnecessary, for it may just spoil the surprise of seeing, well, everything. The soundtrack is quite pleasant. The gameplay is not very difficult to understand, but may require you some time to master (especially if you are not used to typing in English). I quite enjoyed it.

Overall, this game is amazing.  The visuals, character animations, acting, story, and mood are insanely good.  It is more about the experience than anything.  The fighting gameplay does feel a little disjointed since it is fairly easy and also it is such a dictated event when it happens (enemies spawn in in a very exact distance and order-- a pet peeve of mine).  However, that is a minor gripe for a game that is boldly doing something different and daring.  Hellblade is intense to play through.  It's a masterpiece.   I'm glad I bought it on launch to support this kind of risk taking in games today.

What do you get for 30 bucks? A thoroughly-explored, intriguing, damaged character, a well-realized dark Norse setting, a competent, respectful exploration of living with psychosis (at least if the devs' extensive, careful research actually got near the reality of it), combat that's easy to master and rewarding to excel at, some nice puzzles, kick♥♥♥♥♥visuals, extremely intimidating, sometimes actually terrifying enemies, great music, pretty tight controls...
And honestly, the best part? A dev team that's passionate and progressive enough to rely on more than empty hype marketing to connect with fans. Seriously, they made a ~30ish episode dev diary series that went into detail on every conceivable phase and aspect of development. They were so transparent about their process and strategy that I kind of skipped some videos just because I was afraid they might give away too much, but they didn't. And they even cared enough about the sensitive subject matter to consult several recognized Oxford and Cambridge specialists on psychosis and Norse mythology and even reached out to a psychosis help group to speak with people who suffer from it and get their take on representing their main character. I am so ridiculously happy that devs like these exist and I hope the rest of this industry takes note. I hope we can learn from them how to respect our user bases and our craft to avoid becoming another misguided stain on the game industry's history.
So yeah, you want a damn good ol fashioned linear action story by damn good devs for half the usual price? Hellblade. Do it.

TLDR: A true masterpiece and a phenomenal experience (but not really a game)
----------------------
----------------------
I absolutely loved it.
The graphics are probably the best I have ever seen in my life.
The audio quality is unbelievable (and trust me, you DO WANT to have your headphones on)
The voice acting is on divine levels.
The world is mesmerising in every moment.
The story is an unforgetable experience.
And, finally, you get to truly experience what a mental illness is.
This is what makes Hellblade absolutely outstanding: at its core it is an experience, and not so much a game - let me explain to you what I mean:
Hellblade It's a story of Senua searching for her loved one in the dark land of Hel and her struggles with her mind - and you get to experience every second of it, as the immersion levels are insane.
The voices that she hears in her head - you hear them as well all the time, sometimes cheering you up, sometimes infuriating you - just as the main character.
There is absoultely no handholding: there is no HUD, no map, no quests, no health bars, no stats, no tutorials, and you get to experience this dark and unkown world as it is - just as the main character. You wander around and figue things out and try to piece what is going on just as she would.
In that sense, Hellblade is similar to Dark Souls - but Dark Souls is a game at its core with game mechanics: fight monsters- gather loot - get stronger - fight bosses. Hellblade also has game mechanics such as combat and puzzle solving and a few others I wont spoil, but they are secondary to the story and the experience. In other words, the mechanics are adjusted to fit the story, and not the story to fit the mechanics.
So if you are looking for a mechanics-focused game, you will be disappointed, and I suggest you look elsewhere - they are good, no doubt, but they are nothing to write home about and they are really not the core of the game.
But if you are looking for an experience like no other - go for it, and you won't regret it.

I want to keep it straight and short: This is my most played beat em up in a very long Time. I played all SF4 titles, all Blazblue Titles and I own two installments of Guilty Gear (including the latest). Without any expectations i bought this game in a wintersale.
Typical feature-droppings would include: unique charakters, each with his own playstile, own story, own origin, own blablabla... etc. pp. and so on and so forth.
Here is what I think: It is way more accessible than Blazblue featuring similar but not as much depth. It is a little harder to get into then SF but is way more balanced (lesser characters) and it is way more fun to watch than SF. (I see Guilty Gear pretty similar to BlazBlue so it wont be mentioned here.)
Another plus in my opinion is the character design which is so much different from what one is used to see.
So: Great 2D-Fighter to get into the genre, really creative characters (in design as well as gameplay), nicely balanced, can be played really well with the Xbox-Controller.

The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is an ARPG. It's a very good, entertaining ARPG. I've had plenty of fun with the game, especially once the online was fixed and I picked up the Thaumaturge. The DLC classes are a bit pricey, especially since they add a bit of much-needed diversity to the game, but the base content is by no means bad. Just a bit limited in your character options, especially for more than 2-3 people.
The atmosphere and tone of the game is dark, but at the same time it's not. The dialouge is surprisingly entertaining, but not all that great. The back and forth with Katarina and the hunter is especially amusing. There are a few other humorous characters (like the priest in the village), but no one really THAT memorable.
The combat is pretty standard fare for the genre, but it's not bad, or even bland. I'm not a Diablo 2 veteran or anything, so I can't really say for sure how "done-to-death" this whole system is, but I enjoyed it.
IT"S a good game. If you like ARPGs, or want to try them, it's not a bad one to pick up. Especially if it's on sale. Like it is right now.

Note: there is a summary at the end
Many people are already aware of the hate that No Man's Sky got because it did not do what it was advertised or whatever, but I want to just clarify that I never saw the advertisement or ever heard what they promised so I cannot speak about if they did what they said and all that. However, I do like the game. No Man's Sky is a game where you can to collect mineral from rocks, plant, animals, asteroids, etcetera to later use them as fuel, to build upgrades to your equipment or to improve your base.  The game will have a relatively vague tutorial that will show you if the pace of the game will suit you or not. The game is NOT about survival, but rather exploring. I will admit that the game is a little bit too expensive, as it is an indie game (made by around 15 people), but I already bought it and played it so much that I cannot truthfully say I would return it if I could. Lastly, the game was initially made for PS4 and the controls are a little bit reminiscent of it, but you can swap the around to suit your taste.
Summary:
Some things that it does well:
1. A huge world to explore.
2. Good sense of achievement and discovery.
3. There are three races of aliens that will have individual "relationships score" (this is the closest term I could think of) that is altered by your actions.
4. You have a spaceship (for me that is always a good thing)
5. Ability to alter a planet's terrain, flora, and fauna.
6. Base construction and upgrading.
7.  Every little piece of upgrade that you can build is useful in the long term.
8. You can buy a new Multi-Tool and a new Spaceship as soon as you have the money.
Some things that I don't like:
1. The game can be repetitive and grind-y
2. The map genuinely sucks
3. Constant need for some specific materials (fortunately the latest updates made them easier to find)
4. The price is too high for an indie game
5. The Centinels can be pretty annoying at times.
6. The game is procedurally generated, so there is no telling if the next thing you find is awesome or lame.
7. The game sometimes feels rushed (That is because it was; the delay announcement got death threats. Think about this game the next time you put an aggressive comment in a delay announcement.)
Now is your turn to play it and decide if you like it or not. Otherwise, you will just be another guy saying that you don't like it because it is now cool to hate it, and that is the most self-ridiculing thing ou could ever do. Make the decision of how good the game is by yourself.

The game uses a unique narrative style, as plot and even action sequences unfold like the panels of a comic book. Since I am a huge fan of the comic book genre, I really appreciate this fresh approach. However, this feature also slows down the action and the game in general and I think that might not be every gamer's kind of thing. Another drop of bitterness are the  at times rather ugly drawings. While the black and white sequences of the game are sublime, some of the colored drawings, especially the faces of some characters, are really badly done. I think this does not do justice to the otherwise high quality of the game. Furthermore, the first episode is really, really short (about two hours) but for a price of some 5 Euros that is still somewhat acceptable. So far I'd still recommend the game due to its nice story-telling technique and I think fans of crime investigation and/or comic book style might like it, too. Nevertheless, do not expect some crazy police action, this is rather like a good novel for a quiet evening.

I dislike games made in the style of the 8 bit classics. The availability of simple game making tools has made it possible for just about anyone to hack together an "old school" title with minimal support. This has unfortunately flooded the market with so many "roguelike" and arcade style heaps of nonsense that I tend to hit "not interested" about 3 seconds into seeing one in my queue. Having the tools does not necessarily make one a craftsman.
That said, 'To the moon' does not disappoint. It has a rich and compelling story. It's full of mystery, and puzzles, and real adventure ... all without the pretenses of dragons, fairy princesses, or a single moment where anyone gets shot in the face. I should hate this game. It's simple and short and linear but the story draws you in. This is one "retro" title that actually rewards you with the kind of storytelling you don't often find in games ... indy garbage, top shelf productions, or otherwise.

You know that trope in anime, where for the first episode the
OP serves as the credits?
That's exactly what Wolfenstein 2 feels like: enjoyable, yet incomplete.
First of all, the gameplay is great. Everything feels good just to do, except for climbing ladders. The gameplay loop of "stealth until you get caught, then go balls deep" might be a little stale but I still enjoy it. On the other hand, this gameplay loop doesn't get shaken up very many times, causing large swaths of the game to feel samey. It doesn't help that Death Incarnate is a TERRIBLE difficulty - almost every enemy type has a way to oneshot you no matter how much health and armor you have. This is pretty much the only reason the game took me 16 hours, and is why I resorted to save scumming half the game. I think I would've done it in 10 if I was playing on normal difficulty.
Like Mankind Divided, the game just... ends, but this time it feels a little more sour. Plot threads are laid, and addressed periodically, only to never get a payoff. Your goal is techniaclly fulfilled, but it's always framed as part of a larger plan that never gets followed up on. While I really enjoyed thew writing during the journey, the last 30-60 minutes of the game nearly undid all of that good will for me.
Oh, and after you've beaten the game,
At least the game runs well - on a 1060 I get 1080/60+ almost all the time at medium + adaptive resolution, usually 100+ fps. Wait for a sale or something I guess.

I got this game as a birthday gift from my parents in law. It takes what was already great in the previous two Wolfenstein games, and makes it even better.

First impression:
Wolfenstien is simply put a great game, but as with everything there is room for improvement… when I first got the game it crashed when I opened it (works now though). As well as I am not particularly fond of the weapon system in the game, I think it would be better if you had a bigger choice of Nazi killing tools. The difficulty is also kind of an issue I was playing on the second hardest and yes I realize that it is meant to be hard; but sometimes you’ll die out of nowhere and lose a lot of progress (if you’re like me and forget to save in between checkpoints). These are the only problems I have found in the game so far. The graphics are great, sound track is beautiful, and best of all you can kill all the fascist Nazi pigs you want.
Post Campaign Completion:
The Campaign I felt was a little short and concise almost like everything works out too perfectly for the characters (I feel this could be to leave room for the DLC’s) … however the game did do a fantastic job of making a serious campaign that shows us that Nazis are not the only villains in this world, we all have our own demons and it is our challenge to conquer them. The story also takes an intriguing approach on how government conspiracy’s like Roswell tie into the Nazi takeover of the United States, setting it aside from other similar stories such as The Man in the High Castle.    Besides the length and the fact that everything works out perfectly for the characters, I think on the face yes the story is a little meh. There are a lot of moments that left me saying WTF that doesn’t make any realistic sense. Although if you take time to read all the papers, talk to all the people, and listen to BJ’s commentary through the missions; the story becomes way, way more interesting and grasping.
Other thoughts:

Although the name makes it sound like a cheap bargain bin brawler, the experiences within Hellblade are anything but. Games that portray mental disorders dilute it into nothing more than a gimmick, a way to make up for a character's lack of personality or relatability. Hellblade, obviously, is one of the few rare exceptions.
It's a title that is impossible to describe without spoiling the countless memorable moments that lurch out at you like some creature from a dark bog. But I will say this:
Are the puzzles unimaginative and tedious? Yes.
Is the combat simple and repetitious? Yes, but landing a devastating blow to a Norseman is never not satisfying.
These issues are rendered unimportant when you have an atmosphere so immersive, a story so engaging, and a protagonist so intriguing.
Ninja Theory, the devs behind the great DMC reboot, pegged this game as a "AAA indie title".
It damn well feels like it. Minus the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of course.
A game that raises the bar for horror. An absolute must buy.

First off, this is an awesome game. Even if you're tired of top-down games like this, it's still worth the money. Now, first ting to get out of your head is that this game has no random dungeons, so any similarities to Tourchlight and Diablo there are non-exsistant. Every area/map in the game is preset. The trade off here is that these locations are graphically beautiful and detailed as hell, and since the monsters respawn everytime you exit the game, you can just go kill them all over again if you're so inclined.
Secondly, the skills. While similar to other ARPGs with lots of skills to level up, here the skills have extra perks, things that can be added on and activated when you need them and bonuses that you can unlock once the skills reach the right level. On top of that, you're also picking the skills and stats for your ghostly companion, and many of her skills can end up helping you, like her being able to heal you when she does damage to an enemy. Yes, you heard me right; when she does damage, you can get health. Now you're not going to use every skill, and I doubt you're even able to get them all, so upgrading the skills you use the most and that benifit your play style best is key here.
Also, be prepared to die. A lot. When the enemies swarm you, it's not 5-10 like in some ARPGs, here you can get 20+ all at once, each taking a piece out of you. Respawning anywhere but town costs gold, and the more you respawn, the more it costs, so quite often you end up playing "catch me if you can" with hordes of enemies, getting a few nice hits in and then running away.
Now, a downside here is that the controller support isn't always as intuitive as you'd like (primary attack is X and not A, needing all 4 shoulder buttons to nav between menus), but the controller HUD is designed to show you what attack/skill you ahve mapped to what button, and trust me, you'll end up using all 6 of the buttons avalible on both your Melee and Ranged loadouts. Also, the camera is fixed. It doesn't rotate or zoom in/out (at least not for me) which might be a problem for some, but since most object that might get in the way tend to disapear when they get between the character and you, you'll proly not mind.

I'm not the type who post reviews but I felt the urge to do so because I had better expectations for this game. TransOcean is becoming quite old after a couple of hours. Don't get me wrong, I am the type of gamer that can grind for hours on end, but there are so few gameplay elements within this game that it started to feel quite boring after a while. Still, this does not explain my urge to post a review for this, so why then? Because there are couple of things that, in my opinion, they should have been a must!
The first and the most important missing feature is that you cannot order a custom ship. You are only able to buy pre-defined ships from the shipyard. I truly believe that it wouldn't have take that much developing time to add a couple of new menu pages + the code behind them and the result it would have definitely improve the strategy factor for the gameplay. Also the only "type" of ship is container one. Where are the oil tankers or the passenger ships? I mean, even the ore is transported in container ships? From my knowledge it is not the case. And the last major thing that bugs me is the fact that you can only take transport contracts. No possibility to purchase something that the port produces and sell it somewhere else, just transport contracts.
Other nice feature addition, would have been to have ships or cargo insurance, and having some kind of simulated stock exchange. Also, some AI competition during the campaign would have been nice.
About the game, decent graphics, and the ports have their own identity and you can zoom out to see the landmarks in the port, which is cool. Still, you will "park" your boat during the first transport missions as you really are low on cash, but after a while you will find yourself just using the auto-doc regardless of the costs, as you will have more than enough money to afford the cost. I also encountered some bugs, even though I did not made any effort in looking for them. One would be that while manually docking in England's port (can't remember the name now), the FPS drops quite badly if there is any ship in the port. Also it seems that there are some broken mechanics in the company contracts, after loading a save, you will get contracts that are 20+ mil in rewards, but after half an hour of gameplay, even bigger contracts rarely have rewards that pass the 6 mil barrier.
All in all, I completed the campaign, I doubt I'll try the free play in the near feature, considering that I experienced a better similar game, this title will probably get lost in my library. If by any chance any developer will read this, please take an hour or so and play a 1997 game called Ocean Trader. It is a DOS game, and you will then probably understand why I cannot recommend this title.

This game starts really well, and in the first few hours I was having a great time.  However VERY quickly, it completely runs out of steam and there is simply nothing to do. In free play mode, you can unlock and largest ship (at which point there's nothing else to do) and have over 1B dollars in a few hours.
The docking mini-game is interesting but gets old quickly and because it takes so long, you'll just end up skipping it.  As such it's just looking at a world map collecting money.  With no ability to automate routes etc you must endlesslessly select a cargo, refuel and cast off, urgh.
This game really needs more content because there's a lot of potential, but until there's AI players, a dynamic economy, the ability to schedule route automatically, natural and economic disasters, and diffuculty options (like cargo pays 75% less money) this is too easy and gets old too quickly.  What a pity.

Nameless is Cheritz's second otome game but is in no way similar to their first game, Dandelion. It has dark and disturbing moments with bad endings that range from "huh" to "omg what just happened that's really messed up man". The story is surprisingly interesting once you get into it and all the different choices you can make really makes it worth it to go back and try choosing differently. The voice acting is also pretty good and the art is beautiful. Not to mention the music! One thing I also really enjoyed about the game was the dark aspect of it that got more and more interesting the further you progressed. Well worth the money and time. There might be a bit too much repetition in the game, but I did not really mind. If you like interesting stories, beautiful art and decision making, then this game will not disappoint.

Good stuff
- Low-gravity powers are cool since they involve throwing objects, grabbing people from far away and smashing them into walls, etc.
- Enemies get messed up nicely. Decapitations, limbs getting severed, bodies just exploding into nothingness, etc.
- Some neat locales and cool set-pieces
- Serviceable story. There were probably plenty of holes but as an excuse for an action game, it ain't bad.
Bad stuff
- High-gravity powers are bland. One of them stops enemies from moving. Why stop when you can kill? The other creates a shield. That's nice I suppose but as soon as you get the shield enemies start doing more damage, so you're kinda forced into using it.
- Bosses get re-used so much. It's not noticeable at first but at around the 4 hour point (6 hour game) bosses are introduced and then ran into the ground.
-Difficulty needs polishing. The default setting is more than do-able, but if I could go back I would have went with something easier. That way I could focus more on using powers and not have to worry about some stray explosion wiping me out.
-The last couple weapons are energy-based. They cover the enemy in blue-white flames which kinda makes it hard to tell that you've killed them. It's just not as satisfying when you can't see their arms fly off, their head pop like a meat balloon, and so on.
-General nitpicky stuff that an extra month in QA could have fixed.
All in all Inversion is good dumb entertainment. It's basically Timeshift influenced by Gears of War. Give it a go if you can find it on the cheap.

This game is the Sharknado of the video game world. The Megashark vs Giant Octopus of the 3rd person action genre.  Its sooo bad that its good. Best to play late at night when you are teetering on the verge of laughing at any little thing, and with a friend via co-op (although if you can figure out how to do that easily in this game, then its not late enough at night)
Typical gameplay goes like this:  Combat for 30 seconds, then a 30 second cut scene. Then a movement stage of going from A to B for 20 seconds, then a 20 second cut scene. Then combat for 30 seconds... and the cycle repeats. Gameplay is interupted so much by cutscenes that it starts to get hilarious.
This is also one of those games where they put co-op type quicktime events in for no good reason. Oh look, a ledge, your buddy has to help you up, then you pull him up. Or having to hit "F" just to drop off a 4 foot ledge. Its just a speed bump in gameplay that serves no purpose, other than delaying how long it takes to see the next cut scene.
Speaking of cutscenes (and dialog), think Resident Evil 1. Its only a bit better, but every bit as funny. Some great moments: Walking down the street as a tricycle slowly comes rolling down the street towards us and my character says, "What the hell is that?" followed by the other character saying, "Where the hell did they get that?" It was just good timing, because they obviously werent talking about the tricycle, but it made for a hilarious situation. Expect laughable dialog such as "Stay tight, we've never been in this deep before" and "I guess this is where we go our seperate ways" from 2 cop buddies who have been through hell, and just gotten past a tough part. You find yourself saying, "Whaaa???" outloud a lot while playing.
One note: This game has a tendency to instant crash to desktop after any cutscene. Being that there are so many frequent cutscenes, it can be frustrating. Setting the exe to winXP compatability mode seems to help reduce it.
My son and I had more fun playing the game like we were watching a video from Birgirpall (look it up on youtube, you will understand), than if we actually tried to play it seriously. There are so many glitches and interactable objects in the world that cause just total random oddities. I know Namco tried to make a professional product, but this game really is just a bunch of laughs rolled up into something that is trying so hard to be something else.

Trine is one of those games that decided it didn't need to be mature, bloody and violent to be a successful game. While this is true, it can also hamper a game if it swings too far in the other direction and becoming childish. This is the problem I had with Trine's story. The characters and storytelling are all presented as if in a 5 year-old's bedtime story. If I were a child, I'm sure the story wouldn't have bothered me as much, but because I am not, I found the game to be much less immersive than it could have been.
However, Trine does deserve credit for it's gameplay. The level design is fantastic and challenging, regardless of what settings you play on. The characters each have unique strengths and abilities which allow creative puzzle-solving in the form of platforming through seemingly impassable areas. Each character is very balanced and the ability to switch between them is  just flat out cool. Also, the visuals of the game are unique and nicely rendered. While not necessarily the most realistic, the art style is certainly worthy of praise.
All in all, Trine is a fun, albeit short, game with a story that just feels a little to young for me. Certainly worth giving it a playthrough, but not really all that substantial of a game.

I don't usually review games on Steam, but since I bought To the Moon in part because of the glowing reviews for it, I thought it would be only fair to throw my own less positive assessment into the mix. For the record, I bought this game expecting to like it.
Maybe I'm just dead inside, but I wasn't blown away or moved by this "game," which is really a mediocre story with threadbare gameplay elements tacked on to it. The basic formula that makes up most of the game is simple and becomes tiresome quickly: dialogue, click on objects to make "memory links," complete easy "puzzle" to unlock the memory link, rinse, repeat. Although it started out promising (the opening act establishes a very mysterious and somewhat dark tone), the more the plot unfolded the less impressed I was with it.
The characters and their relationships felt one-dimensional and undeveloped, which is a shame because I feel like something much more interesting could have been done with this scenario. The story, which touches on themes of love, loss, and mental illness, just didn't present anything deep or thought provoking to me. Its presentation of mental illness felt particularly shallow and a wasted opportunity. For a game that's so story-driven, the writing is also quite bad at times, punctuated with embarassingly corny jokes. The writer has a noticeably hard time writing for child characters, and those parts (one of which is clearly intended as an emotional high point) are often jarring and unbelievable. This game feels like it's aimed at people who think Dr. Who is deep.
On the positive side of things, the soundtrack is relatively good, and I enjoy the art style.
Definitely not worth the full price, especially since there's little to no replay value here. I'd feel quite cheated if I had paid that. If you're really, really interested in To the Moon, get it 80% off on sale.

Maybe it was build up too much in my mind as the emotional rollercoaster of a life time or maybe it just didn't resonate with me. I had to make this experience my own, but how?
I walked away from the game to slobber on a cigarette trying to convince myself just to finish it and see how I felt. So I sat back down and muted the game and played a random playlist of Keaton Henson's music and my hear started to feel the game and open up to the emotional story that it had been presented with. It someone else telling you to eat their favorite food their way and you being unsure about the taste and texture but as soon as you change the sauce and you instantly sent to culinary heaven.
To cut this short if you want to experience heartbreak hearing Keaton Henson's voice break during his song sweetheart, what have you done to us during the last scenes caused me to weep like I was listening to the story be told to me personally.

After playing many indie games, I've found myself tiring of the same old games that seem to be rehased and reused. That's when I found To the Moon.
To the Moon is a breath of fresh air for me, being almost a completely narrative driven game that relies purely on its characters instead of game play. The graphics are less than detailed, but have a beautiful simplicity to them. The soundtrack is phenomenal, being one of the few I listen to almost religiously. The story is simultaneously heartwarming and heartwrenching. And the characters actually feel like PEOPLE. People who are actually real, people who you could hold a conversation with, people who you could meet.
While this game lacks astounding gameplay, I let it slide. Why? To the Moon is not trying to have astounding gameplay. Instead, it tells us a story and a message. And it does it so remarkably well, that I hold to it even after numerous replays.

I cant recommend this game enough.
I know that is said so very often in reviews, but this game really is one
of a punch in the gut, and its a punch in the gut that you will
whether you want to or not.
The story is extremely powerful, its dealing with the reality of marriage, of communication, of disability, of forgotten dreams, and of loss... not so shiny subjects that aren't often touched on with a degree of realism. None of these things ever feel forced for the drama, in fact I wouldn't even call it dramatic as much as realistic. Yet it is still the most thoroughly gripping storyline I've experienced in a very long time.
I would say it's an epecially important game for anyone on the Autism spectrum... I say this as a person with Aspergers myself, if your experience with the syndrome has been at all like mine I think you'll find some moments in the game hitting uncomfortably close to home.
Of course its not all doom and gloom, theres a fair amount of humour in the story that feels really natural, especially the pop culture references, which feel shoehorned into games far too often. They're also really easy references to get, if you're like me and sometimes feel a little out-of-it with pop culture.

There is some fourth wall humour but it is rare enough to not be a gimmick and subtle enough to avoid a Deadpool feeling, they took a moment to click and still provided a good giggle.
Really keeps you guessing, storywise, without jumping the shark at all. Don't trust your assumptions with this story... or do. It just makes the surprises all the more fun and/or painful.
If there is a downside at all I would say the gameplay, I personally quite enjoyed it, there was enough to do to keep you busy and engaged without being so challenging as to take focus off the story, everything you needed to do added to the story somewhat. But just a warning to anyone who thought this would be gameplay heavy, if you're the type that doesnt enjoy that. (In case you didn't already guess)

"The Detail" is a crime noir adventure game by a Finnish studio, Rival Games Ltd.
In "The Detail", you follow multiple characters in a dark american city. The main character is Detective Moore, and you follow him as he tries to unveal the mistery surrounding a murder. The setting is gritty and realistic, in a crime-filled city where police forces are scarce and murders and drug deals are unstoppable.
The script is really well written, giving each character multiple layers of personalities and interesting backgrounds. The game lacks sound effects and voice acting, but the music that plays perfectly fits every situation, be it an intense chase or an investigation.
The game plays like a modern point-and-click game: there are context-sensitive actions and items are instantly used without being selected. Similarly to Telltale Games' brilliant The Walking Dead, the game has a heavy focus on dialogues, and each choice might change how the story unfolds. During this first episode, there are multiple paths that you can take, and they do have different outcomes.
Most of the game is hand-drawn. That is really impressive, and there is a great attention to detail in the environments that you visit. However, the only animations that you will see is your main character moving, so all the cutscenes are comic strips.
Overall, this is a promising start to a new crime adventure. The story is engaging, the main characters are well developed and relateable. I highly recommend this game to all adventure games lovers.

The Detail is a pretty good game. Heavily focused on the story and the characters in the game, and not so much on the puzzles, at least in this first episode.

Kate - the rookie police officer, Reggie - the old and salty detective and Joe - a man with a family and a criminal past, that's catching up to him.
The story is really the strong point of the game. There is no voice acting, and if there was any, this would really look like a well made AAA title. The object of interest are easily visible, plus there is a key you can use to highlight them, with no penalty (or non that I have found out yet), so you should have no problem, figuring out your options. The choices you take, do already change the story in this episode (can't really say more about that without spoilers) and probably in future ones too, and they definitely change the achievements you get - so I would guess, you need at least 3 playthroughs to get them all.
I find the music and the strong language really fitting well with the story and the whole mood of the game and all that noir comic book style. The character animation may use some love, but then again there is not much movement around, because of the comic book style. Also, I would really like if the game doesn't have to spin up all my hard drives every time before it starts, it's REALLY getting on my nerves.
The first episode may look a bit short, but if you check my let's plays - it's as long as the episode 1 of the Wolf Among Us, so I guess it feels short because the story is good ;) Needless to say it ends up with a cliffhanger, so I can't wait for the next one to come out!

So here's my review SO FAR.
I'm an old time fan of Gauntlet Legends, having dumped some small portion of my childhood into the game...
Hours of replaying challenge levels to unlock new heroes, finding all the secrets. Owning that bloody dragon with your beasted out mage... Unlocking the wizard dude who had full stats and not beleving your eyes....
With that said every Gauntlet game since then has lacked everything that was good about Legends. Slayer Edition finally creates a decent rendition thus far of Gauntlet Legends.
Pro's
- Classic Gauntlet/Dungeon Crawl view.
- Seems to be more "mechanics" to more battles than previous gauntlet games.
- Improved combat mechanics. Takes away the "hold X" concept of the came.
- Equipment/Upgrades give it a more RPG feel rather than just level progression (like the old ones).
- Easy to play with friends, online and offline (local co-op).
- Each character is pretty diverse in their contribution to the field.
Con's
- Only 4-5 Characters
- Hard to get a random online game that is immediatly enjoyable.
- Lacking on customization for characters. Progression could be more substantial.
I feel as though a game that has made a name for itself like Gauntlets, could have taken just a little more time to add a lot more to this game. Accommodate the casual and the casual pro.

(This is from my blog - Kayas Arcade as a part of my 52 games in 52 weeks challenge)
Week 29
29/52
Epistory - Typing Chronicles
Platform: PC
Time: ~5 hours
Genre: Typing adventure
Epistory is a fantastic beautiful little game. The art style was the thing that got my interest at first, and the different play style made me buy it.
In Epistory YOU are writing the story - literally -, while removing trunks, planting flowers and defeating enemies. The pages unfold while you explore the universe you are writing.
I really love how the art and story cooperate to make this great game - and for the first time I felt like a reel keyboard warrior ;)
Its most of all a typing game - and the game are giving you great hints and tips to how to type faster. I have always been a fast typer, but I must admit. It was quite hard to type fast in English, and not danish - So for me it was a really great and fun exercise.
The constant focus on spelling every word right, unfortunately made it difficult to listen and enjoy the story at times.
Overall - A really beautiful game, and I actually felt I learned a thing or two!

Epistory - Typing Chronicles is a short, but beautiful hand-crafted action-adventure.
Its looks remind me of games like Tearaway, due to the huge amount of love, detail and effort put in design and animation it gives you the feeling that the world is alive.
The gameplay is a one-of-a kind, at least for me, as your only weapon are words.
By typing the words shown on the screen you progressively learn new abilities and open the world up.
It can be monotonous at times, but that's why I think an average playtime of 4-6 hours is perfect for Epistory - Typing Chronicles.
Something I'd like to compliment this game for is its difficulty, which felt -for me- perfectly optimized, because it scales with your Words per minute (as far as I know). That means, if you are a slow typer, the game will adjust to it, and vice versa.
The story is at its strongest during the last third of the game, as things get cleared up. Therefore, the beginning can feel boring, because you have no abilities unlocked yet and trust me - they make the gameplay a lot more fun.
I think the voice actor of the narrator did a great job at making this story interesting.
I'd like to recommend this game to everybody who's up for a story about growing up and facing difficulties in life.
And although the combat sequences can get pretty fast and chaotic, this game is mostly about storytelling and exploration,
so Epistory - Typing Chronicles is more of a slow-paced videogame.
And shoutouts for the lovely song at the end <3

The voices in my head kept arguing with the voices Senua hears. They'd get really mad when her's wouldn't address them. Other than that, the game had some performance issues. I noticed my FPS dropping as I progressed in the game, almost proportionally to the amount of progress I had made. I started off with a pretty solid 60 fps, and dropped down to 35-40 by the end. I'm not sure if that's because I played the whole thing in one sitting, or just that the environment designers were just having a little too much fun for their own good in the later levels.
The combat is pretty tight, though it is pretty easy to not realize there's a dodge button, if you only glance at the controls once before hopping in. There's a parry mechanic, that rewards blocking closer to when an attack is going to actually hit you. Dodges are pretty strong, with lots of invincibilty frames. If there's a reason you shouldn't chain dodges, I didn't notice it. The "auto" difficulty setting might take it a bit to easy, I died maybe three times over the course of my 6 hour play through, and it felt like enemies were holding back from delivering a killing blow. Enemy variety is a bit lacking, but they do toss in some gimmicks to mix things up. Thankfully, they're introduced at a good pace, and help keep things from stagnating too much, but it is pretty easy to fall into a few comfortable combat routines.
The story is a bit weird. Admittedly, I zoned out a couple of times during one of the slower sections, which probably didn't help. It feels a bit like a puzzle with a few pieces missing. I'm going to give them a little credit though, the parts that were left fairly ambiguous, where probably the ones that should have stayed that way. It feels like the ending is trying to say something big, but I don't feel like I got enough of the puzzle pieces to really understand what it was getting at. I'm not sure if that really detracts from the game overall though.

If you're looking for Ninja Theory's DmC-esque type of game, you won't find it here. This game is closer to a walking simulator with some light puzzle elements and a somewhat satisfying combat, than other action games Ninja Theory have made in the past.
The game is heavy on narrative and heavily focused on mental illness. To simulate the main protagonist's schizophrenic nature, the game would constantly barrage players with endless mad whispers straight to the earphones. Other might say it's immersive but to me, it can get pretty annoying. Which is probably the whole point of the game.
Also, note that it only took me 7 hours to beat the game. It's a short game, which can get longer to beat on higher difficulty. The puzzles themselves are clever but usually stuck to using the same formula most horror walking simulator uses such as navigating through a dark room while avoiding monsters and finding a "key" to unlock a particular door. Personally, I'm not a huge fan of these types of gameplay but others might enjoy them.
I gonna be recommending this game, solely because I want Ninja Theory to continue making games in the future. As for the Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, I'm giving it 6/10. Not a bad game but hardly GoTY material.
P.S. This game doesn't have any UI whatsoever. In other words, you have to learn the game's mechanic as you play along. I dislike it.

I made a review based on what I've managed to play during a free weekend; and what I saw was exactly what I would get later on- a well made fighting game with care for the deepest and maybe even useless details; a crowdfunded labour of love, trying to convince its player to love it back.
It's worth mentioning that the entry point to it is pretty easy thanks to the big and extremely advanced tutorial, as well as customizeable training mode.
I unfortunately suffer from not having a soft button controller, wich would make execution of more advanced moves much easier and comfortable to pull off. Knowing this I'd recommend everyone to have a pad or anything with a stick to do 360s with, several characters need them for some moves; thus you need it if you want to play online.
The game might be easy to pick up, but it's still demanding when it comes to expertise. And thanks to me being a "Tekken kid", the whole idea of 6 attack button distracts me to no end; but maybe that's just me :( .
Contents are satisfying, with 9 base characters, each with a story mode, and each with 25 color pallettes; a handful of stages and a glorious jazzy soundtrack; all for the initial price of 15$.
But if you want to get into it, everyone would advise you to pick up the character DLCs (all of wich can be played in the tutorial for free, but nowhere else), and with DLCs comes a little bit more cost- 5 characters, 5$ dollars each, all of which amounts to 25$.
So a full game becomes 40$, it all depends on how many hours you are willing to sink into it- it would feel like supporting the devs, or wasting your funds.
If you like what you see- I recemmend it without hesitations; if you're unsure- try no DLCs or during sales. Cause it's a gorgeous fighting game that would be a waste to not try out.

Overall its a simple game, but does have alot of "Depth" to it. I bought the game when it was on sale,($6) and for the price i got it, i can say its worth every penny ($20 isnt bad either though). Now I will admit that the controls can feel a bit clunky at first (especially as sharks) but once you get used to them, it comes naturally just like every other game. Ive played  only the multiplayer so far, so that mainly is what im giving this review about.
While there are only 3 game modes for now, which if im being honest, only the blood rush mode, seems to really have any games in matchmaking. However, it doesnt really stop the fun of the game, as the concept is going to always consist of surviving the rounds, which are basically team deathmatch modes...
As a diver, you get guns (expect alot of shooting at shadows), tools (useful for supporting teamates), and explosive mines! ("Smile you son of a --")  All the equipment you get during matches, has to be bought with money you earn by gathering treasure, and cracking open safes with a robot companion known as S.T.E.V.E (I wonder if he likes gummy bears?). Divers are better when they are in groups rather than alone, as they can be torn apart quite quickly so if you have a good team it makes the difference with life and (gruesome) death!
As a shark, You get teeth, fins, a hard head for bashing walls, and Evolution points, which are basically skills you can obtain through a match by eating divers. There are a few different classes of sharks that each have different stats and a unique skill, which can give you some different playstyles, but as a shark your mainly going to rely on ambushing , and swimming away bfore getting shot down..(or in my case, getting blown up). Both sides offer a different gamplay style, so there is alot of fun (and repitition) to be had in this type of game.
Graphically it looks quite good and has a total of 12 maps that offer a distinct vibe (included with lots of water!), but overall relying on tension as you descend to dark corridors inside sunken ships and ruins.
This game does have its flaws, like the combersome control as mentioned before, occasional fps drops during intense sequences, and the camera can sometimes get caught on objects. Despite its issues, it is still a worthy game of your time.
I give it 8/10!

This is a tricky game to review, and by that I do not mean to suggest anything very positive about it. I got the game when it was on sale and finished it  in 26 hours on hard difficulty. In the end it did not feel rewarding or satisfying at all.
If you've seen any trailers for Inversion then you may be excited to try out the gravity inverting gameplay that was the main selling point of the game. Indeed you can have some fun with it. But it does not last long at all. It works well in the introductory stages of the game.
The first 2 or 3 areas are actually somewhat well designed and exciting even. However the fun ends as suddenly as it starts. You will keep expecting and waiting for "something" to start, for some kind of exposition. Instead you will be treated with a lot of the same. After the areas that were paid attention to Inversion almost changes direction and feels like either different people picked up the game 1/3 in and had to quickly finish it and patch it up. If not that, then it definitely feels like a lot of the same on and on.
Some action sequences and area segments are just atrocious. But besides the level design and the misleading story you will also immediately feel like you have played this game before. It borrows so much and so liberally from other games that it is not even funny as a homage. It is visible in the enemies design, in the crouching behind cover mechanic, in the sound effects, and in the plot itself.
It is difficult to add anything substantial without spoiling the game, even though there is not much to spoil, but if you can skip it, I would skip it. If you had already decided to skip it, then take a look at the story cutscenes or reviews on YouTube to get an idea.

Among the German-style simulation game genre, this one is a gem with tons of polish. There are still minor bugs, but I haven't run into anything game-breaking or that couldn't be resolved without a quick restart.
The docking/undocking minigame is a fun diversion that lets you see the beautiful port cities. As some have mentioned the camera angle is somewhat limited denying you a full panorama, but it's not too terrible. You can zoom out further once you unlock bigger ships, but the camera is locked between about 45 degrees and straight top-down.
The rest of the game is pretty well balanced. There are some random events that provide enough risk/reward to gamble on transporting illegal goods for example, or good you don't own a license for. Sometimes you can get away with it and sometimes customs will seize your haul and hit you with a big fine.
It still remains profitable to keep your starter ships as well. Your $/ton scales depending on the size ship you have. Smaller ships have the highest $/ton while the largest have the smallest, making up for it in sheer bulk.
The campaign puts a progression track in while putting a wrench in the gears every so often to keep things interesting. You will get contracts you were forced to agree to from time to time that have a tight deadline and require a great deal of coordination to pull off.
Overall, a very polished experience in this genre, and I would highly recommend it if you're a fan of the genre already. If you are a new player, give it a try. If you don't find your zen playing this type of repetitive game, this genre may not be for you, and that's ok!

I'm a big fan of Ports of call and I think this is a highly polished revisit of that hit late 90s Amiga game. All aspects of the original wre preserved, enhanced for modern standards with a few additions here and there.
Having played the game for over 10 hours, I like it but there are a few things that I don't like.
The UI is REALLY REALLY bad:
- Even in 2560x1440, you can't fit more than 8 ships in your ship list window
- The ship list is utterly useless. It doesnt even summarize the container upgrades that were applied to each ship, which makes it a PAIN for you to know which should take care of what contracts (ie: food vs electronics)
- Ship list also doesnt tell you which are being repaired/upgraded, how long it will take, even when you expand the list items.  Designers, please take a look at how Endless space or Endless legend  manages the list of cities/planets and do the same!
- Even in large resolutions, you can't fit all your notifications in the viewport. Whetever doesnt fit goes away at the same pace and you miss out a lot of important info
- The evelope icon is a useless decoration. I wish it at least brought back recent notifications
Basic gameplay
- Whenever you go back to world map, it unpauses the game. HAAARgh
- Persistent notifications (ie: "become a tycoon", or "shipping line boss" stay on screen but they don't tell you the requirements for attaining them
- There isn't a coundtoun for when that greedy b$#&ch investor will come get her millions.
- Ports of call allowed you to take control mid-trip, to avoid a collision course, steer through a reef, etc, not only when docking in/out. Why take that out?
- There isnt a notification for "some of your ships are idle" and the funky auto pausing/unpausing system will make you lose track of which ships are bein repaired, which are just waiting for better contracts, etc etc. It's hard to keep track of 12 ships, I can hardly imagine when I have 20+
Plateau
- The early game is awesome, but I'm experiencing a painful plateau to get the post panamax ships (shipping line)
- I can only buy level two ships and yet I maxed out my reputation. I think it's a bit unrealisting and not engaging.
- No AI competitors!
- Encounters and mishaps are VERY repetitive. There should me more types, more ways to deal with them and more outcomes.
- The economy never seems to fluctuate (apart from fuel prices and loan rates).
- I'm currently stuck and can't advance to the lext level because the game says I need to build a subsidiary, yet when I try to do so (I already have one in south america) the game says I have no remaining subsidiaries.
I like the game but for this price point I expect WAY more content, ships and variety. And I won't pay 10 bucks for a DLC that includes helpful UI, features and content that should be in a 30 USD game in the 1st place.  UI and gameplay problems make you feel like you're working in a inefficient company.
But yeah, I still recommend the game because the original concept's timelessness. I think the developpers could've paid a tiny bit of praise to Rolf-Dieter Klein and Martin Ulrich on their website because it's clear that the core qualities come from the original 1986 release.  It's preetier though and the ports look great.

Trine is a side scrolling platform game in which you play three protaganists a wizard, a thief and a soldier, whose souls have somehow been gathered together by the Trine. To complete game you need to complete the levels, collecting experience to gain better weapons or skills is of use you do this be collecting bottles that are laying around or hidden, or by killing monsters and collecting the experience. Also lying around are energy bottles to top up your energy which the wizard seems to use a great deal more than the other characters (at least in the levels I have played any how.)
The idea pf three souls together  has the benefit that you can swap at anytime between the different characters if one character has a skill to solve that the others do not. This makes it interesting as you move between them to complete the different levels. So soon learn which character is best for the upcoming task. For me the Graphics make it stand out, the environment is beautifully drawn which makes it a real pleasure to play. There is a great deal of jumping about and I sometimes find it hard to control using the keyboard; especially the thief when she is trying to get onto a platform from the grappling rope. I think a game controller would  make it a bit easier, I am going to try this to see if is indeed true. The default movement controls are the standard WASD controls perhaps if you wish to use the keyboard to play, redefining the keys could also improve things.
Another positive aspect of the game is the narration which makes you feel you are creating the book as you go along. The music also adds to the atmosphere quite well.
During the hours I've played I've lost a character because they ran out of health many, many times. If you feel you wish to start over. You can choose from the menu to either start from the last checkpoint or restart the level.
Restarting from the last checkpoint doesn't reset the monsters and puzzles that you've completed whilst restarting the level does reset the puzzles and monsters. However collected experience is retained by you upon the restart so during the restart you will only see the experience you haven't collected, so far.
I thoroughly recommend Trine and I will continue with Trine2 once I've completed Trine.

I hate giving games a negative review because I don't believe in hate. Just look at all my reviews. This is the 1st and only negative review I've ever written. But I feel like I need to write this review because I don't want any other people to feel cheated after having played the game. I honestly hope people will give buying the game a 2nd thought despite the fact that it has a 97% positive review by 20k people.
As much as I've enjoyed the story and soundtrack, I can't image myself recommending this game to anyone. Not even my best friend who probably wouldn't mind if I recommended a bad game or two to him. The good stuff you can get out of playing this "game" can be easily found by watching a let's play.
I watched a let's play after finishing the game and I feel like I should had just watched a let's play and be done with it. Basically, we call this a game but there really isn't any gaming to speak of.
In fact, watching a let's play is better because its actually more enjoyable to simply watch everything unfold rather than having to "play" the game and then realise the "gameplay" is just you moving a character around which is neither fun nor require any skill, you press a button to see the next sentence of the conversation, and you solve puzzles that are laughably easy and feels more like an insult than a challenge.
I'm not even sure why this game has a 97% positive review by 20k people. I feel like I've been cheated. All I can do is move my character around, solve laughably easy puzzle and none of my decisions or responses in conversation make any difference.
The puzzle felt like a sorry excuse for people to call this a game. Its basically a square image where you decide which directions to flip the tiles in. Basically you can flip it diagonally in 2 ways, there are 3 horizontal and 3 vertical directions (for 3x3 image). You simply have to decide which of the 8 directions to flip the tiles. The 1st thing you have to do is see if you need to flip it diagonally (which is really easy since there are only 2 possibilities (yes or not) for each of the 2 diagonal directions). After that, you'll literally know the answer with one look no matter the size of the image. Even if it 10x10 its easy.
The puzzle also feels incomplete. Solving all puzzles with the least possible moves don't get you anything. Not an achievement, not even one congratulations message. I can't help but feel like the game maker and the 20k peopel who gave this game a positive review are pulling my leg. I'd rather play a telltale game where at least my response will change the game alittle and I'll get slightly different response or see different things happening. And I don't have to solve laughably easy puzzle that feels more like an insult than a challenge.

An incredible game about growth and finding yourself.
You explore a diverse and beautiful world that literally unfolds before your eyes. Much of the gameplay involves solving puzzles and fighting off hordes of monsters while getting lost in the art style and haunting music. The story is revealed to you through calming narration from both the protagonist and a narrator, giving you small snippets of what truly is happening in the main character's life. Epistory - Typing Chronicles is a rare example of a typing game, which is structured not as an educational tool. While it doesn't give the same weird satisfaction as killing zombies with words in Typing of the Dead games, it provides a pretty fun adventure with Zelda-esque elements, except where all interactions, including killing enemies, is done via typing words. It has puzzles, it has exploration, it has typing and it's all presented in a really nice looking way as well. Story also exists, but it's bland and is usually more of a background noise, full of "symbolism".
What doesn't work in the game is the fact that the action bits get frustrating and tedious after a while. Every "boss" is an arena, where you need to quickly type words, switching between magic powers (also by typing) to kill enemies until they reach you and touch you, since a single touch means death and a restart of the entire "boss" fight.  There's just way too much of this and not a lot of creativity, despite the game starting with some nice concepts and clear potential to have a bit more puzzle stuff. Also, enemies outside these "boss" fights can spawn inside you if you're unlucky enough to stand in a wrong place, so that's also not very well done. Still, it's a really good game that's totally worth checking out.

The Detail's first episode - Where the Dead Lie - strikes an interesting, if not always perfect, blend between great visual novel elements, replete with comic book stylings and a terrific sense of style, and a slightly more ho-hum game.  As a fan of the modern story-driven adventure game revolution (i.e., The Walking Dead, The Blackwell series, and Yesterday), I wound up liking Where the Dead Lie and hope it grows into the game it has the potential to become.
The first episode focuses around the intertwined stories of a weary detective investigating the suspicious murder of a prominent criminal in the middle of a gangland and that of a reformed criminal just trying to keep his nose clean for his wife and his daughter.  These aren't exactly new archetypes, but they're written well and there's lots of room for the player to play them as good, bad, or somewhere in between.
Throughout the game, the player is presented with several choices for dialogue or action, all of which have repercussions in the ways the people around you react.  My personal favorite was the necessity of playing a cop willing to bend the rules to gain access to a gang member's house.  My boneheaded moves had some real negative effects, ones that left me queasy with the results.
While this episode is mostly about laying the groundwork for the plot and characters, these moral choices lead to some excellent taut moments and a brutal showdown at the end of the episode.  If the game's creators can keep up this kind of intense action and dialogue with a pervasive sense of my actions having some real effects, I'll be absolutely delighted.  That said, some way to replay specific scenes when the player has finished with the episode to see the various outcomes without having to replay the whole game would be terrific.
When it comes to the moments when you actually have direct control of the characters, the game unfortunately loses some traction.  For example, when the player come to the crime scene of the gangland hit, the playerdo very little actual detective work, and are instead presented with very clear cut-and-dried conversation choices.  There's very little done here to actually make you feel like you're doing detective work.  This initial episode feels a little too guided.  While I'm not looking to solve puzzles or combine inventory items ala the "bad old days" of adventure gaming, some further degree of interaction would have been nice.  I want to feel like I'm doing the detective work, not having the game's characters do the detective work for me.
The game has a great sense of art style, and the music is terrific.  I'm hugely fond of the environments, which practically made me feel the grit and the grime of this terrifically crafted little universe.  The walking animations felt stiff, something I hope is addressed in future episodes.  Perhaps most head-scratching of all the game's problems is the complete lack of sound effects.  Aside from some rain, there are none.  It creates an odd little disconnect from the game.  Not having speech is fine - it works well with the comic book stylings - but some sound effects would draw me even further into the game's great setup and characters.
As it stands, while there's definitely room for improvement, The Detail looks to be a phenomenal entry into the growing world of interactive visual novels.  I'm really looking forward to seeing where the plot - and this team of developers - goes from here.

The Detail is an episodic game about a veteran detective and an ex-criminal trying to solve a murder and investigate other criminal activity. They won’t do this as a team; you’ll control both independently. The developer states that this experience was made for fans of HBO’s hit series The Wire and Telltale Games’ The Walking Dead. Obviously, these weren’t the only inspirations and the game is actually meant to be played by anyone who’s even remotely interested in it, or by anyone who’s interested in adventure games in general. Read on to see what I think of it.
In the first episode (called Where The Dead Lie) you first control a veteran detective who’s looking into a murder case. During the game you’ll eventually swap with an ex-criminal who’s forced into helping out with the investigations. I’m not going to tell you more about the story; as a story-driven adventure game it’s important that you experience as much of it by yourself.
During this first episode you’ll be clicking on several points of interest. These are all clearly shown with a yellow border around them, so there’s no pixel hunting involved like many, many other adventure games out there. Click on a border and you’ll learn more about it. Looking/reading is your primary action when investigating an object or person and sometimes it’s possible to switch between actions by scrolling the mouse. You’ll be able to easily pick things up and talk to people this way.
By playing you’ll also be able to unlock character information of people you meet and even though it’s not necessary to collect them all (or at all, really) I can see people replaying the game just to complete their ‘collection’. It’s not quite similar to The Wolf Among Us’ fairytale creatures, but in a way it is.
The puzzles are made with a casual audience in mind, meaning anyone can pick up and play this game without having too much trouble completing it. To be honest I doubt that there are people that won’t be able to finish it at all; in fact, I don’t think you can even call them puzzles. It’s all so subtle that it all feels part of the story, which is good, but if I’m going to play as an investigator I want to be challenged, even if it’s for a little bit. In this case the gameplay is very similar to The Walking Dead, which was basically non-existent. It would be nice to see future episodes have a little more depth, but I also hope they’ll keep the gameplay consistent. Otherwise it might just get messy.
So, the gameplay adds nothing new to the genre but still, what is there works as far as the story is concerned.
The graphics, unfortunately, are a bit of a mixed bag. The black and white comic book-like graphics are done extremely well. In fact, these are just excellent and if the entire game would’ve been made with this style in mind it would’ve been one pretty game. But for some reason (maybe budgetary or artistic reasons) the game uses several art styles, which gives the game an inconsistent look.
One of the things that comes to mind here are the portraits (i.e. conversations). These just aren’t very pretty (putting it a bit more mildly here), and overall they kind of distract from the game.
The environments and characters (in this case not the portraits) on the other hand get the job done, but the characters could benefit from some extra animations.
There’s no voice acting in the game, just text. Of course, there is music; this is very moody and atmospheric, and while it doesn’t make voice acting obsolete, it didn’t make me miss it either.
I agree with the choice (?)  of not using any kind of voice acting; if you have a small budget you don’t want to ruin the immersion with poor and/or cheap voice acting.
For a first episode The Detail has an average length. It took me somewhere between 60-90 minutes to finish it. Clearly it isn’t very long but you can replay the game again and make different choices that will affect the story. I suspect the consequences will be even more obvious during some of the later episodes. I thought the length was good. It was long enough to keep me interested in the story and short enough for the gameplay to become too shallow.
The Detail isn’t quite there yet when it comes to being a classic, but at this stage it’s too early to tell how the story will even unfold. There isn’t much known about the rest of the episodes, except for the fact that the entire game will consist of five of them. There aren’t any release dates so we’ll just have to wait and see. I personally expect an episode to be released every two months, but that’s just me guessing. In any case, The Detail is an interesting game that’s extremely light on the puzzles but it is its story that actually makes me want to keep playing. The first episode ends with a nice cliffhanger and I’m anxious to see and know what will happen next. Now if that isn’t a compliment, I don’t know what is.
