Without a doubt, my favorite video game of all time. I've been in love since I bought this for my Xbox 360 back in 2008.
Fallout 3 places you, the Lone Wanderer, as a ostracized vault dweller 200 years after nuclear war devistated the United States. Your story begins in the ruins of Washington D.C., now called the Capital Wasteland. Famous landmarks in the game include the Pentagon, the Washington Monument, the US Capitol Building, the Lincoln Memorial, The ruins of the White House, and even neighboring cities such as Arlington and Bethesda. There's also a pretty substantial area of the map that isn't particularly anything - there'll be little settlements every once in a while, but for the adventurous type, this will be the most enjoyable part of the Capital Wasteland. You can explore anywhere you want to, from irradiated metro stations to government buildings to raider hideouts full of people who really want to just kill you. Freedom of choice.
You can be anything you want to be in this game- if you want to be the hero of the wasteland, bringing salvation in the form of purified water, so be it. If you want to be a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥by blowing up a town with a nuclear bomb, enslaving children for profit, or just by shooting everybody, so be it. Freedom of choice is a big theme in this game. Your actions will affect the outcome of your story, as well as how people treat you in the Wasteland.
One of my favorite aspects of this game is the leveling system. In my opinion, it is superior to Fallout 4's by a long shot. While in Fallout 4 skills are non existent, in 3 the player is required to level up their skills accordingly - the first 10 levels of the game require a decent amount of strategy. For example, a player might think it's a good idea to upgrade his Lockpick and Speech ability initially, but this also means that the player won't be able to shoot a gun straight for a while. Conversly, a player with a good Small Guns skill initially won't be able to buy anything at a reasonable price for a few levels. It's all about what kind of player you want to be: you can be a smooth talker that only needs a gun when moving from settlement to settlement, or you can by a gun slinging madman that shoots his way out of everything. Freedom of choice.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. Fallout games always have a creppily hilarous vibe to them, and this game is probably the best endevour on that front from Bethesda yet. Within the Fallout universe, the culture of the United States never moved on past 1945, while technology exploded beyond our own. Everything is Art Deco influenced, and has that real 1950's cheesy optimism about the world. However, all of this technology is still based on older technology, such as vacuum tubes. It's hilarous to see giant computers that run a command line alongside plasma rifles and robots. The soundtrack is wonderful, consisting mainly of 20s-40s jazz and blues standards, and even a little do-wop; the Ink Spots are featured prominently within the game.
The add-on content to the game is superb for a couple reasons. Firstly, and most importantly, the base game is a complete game without it. You don't need to buy the DLC in order to enjoy this game. It's great on its own. That being said, the DLC is very diverse, with all five adding major, off map locations for you to explore, fight, loot, and of course... make whatever choices you want. One of them is in a computer simulation of a Chinese invasion of Alaska, one takes you to the ruins of Pittsburgh, another has you abducted by aliens, and another has you move up the coast to a swampland untouched since the nuclear war. The fifth DLC, Broken Steel, continues the main questline for another 4-6 hours.
I love this game. I've never felt so immeresed in a game as I have this one, and I don't think I ever will again. The characters, the weapons, the locations, and of course, the soundtrack, keep pulling me back 8 years later. I'll be playing this game until I die, for sure. That's kind of the catch with games like this - It's great to have them, but they have the tendency to make every other game in my library look like crap.
Buy this game, and play this game. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did, and still do.

IAVH is a fun, solid game with a few problems that keeps it from rising above a 8/10.
The Good:
Now with 3 character classes, you are no longer stuck with one guy that does everything half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Classes are still rather plain being the melee, magic and ranged stereotypes. The skills the classes feature are mostly unique, with a small selection of them being repeats of skills other classes have.
The perk system is fun and adds a unique feel to your character. Katarina the ghost WAS a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor addition. With all the patches and full dlc I feel she is actually worth putting into combat now. Having her tank damage and aggro for me has been rather effective, rather than before when she was dying in 5 hits while being built tanky. Loot drop rate is still really high, but the loot is much better and I find myself playing just to find the next drop. I've not used the glory system yet but it looks like a decent way to keep higher levels interested in their build.
The Bad:
Multiplayer community is tiny. You will rarely see more than 25 games during peak time, and as little as none during others. Rarely will the games be hosted in the US region. What this means is basically if you're in the US, you need friends to play this game with. Relying on random people from the internet is merely not enough. If you can get past the glaring lag, there's still many more issues that need to be addressed. As such, I can only recommend that if you pickup IAVH for the multiplayer, get your friends to do so as well, or don't get it at all. There are also technical problems with the graphical engine. Running IAVH on full settings produces BSOD extremely often. Although entirely capable of running the game maxed, I can't because of blue screens. Games released both before and after have no problem being maxed without technical problems. This is something that can be fixed, but there's no guarantee that it will be.
Ultimately, I enjoy the game and I think you would too. If you must have multiplayer, but do not have any PC gaming buddies to play with, I'd pass over this one, random internet denizens will just not be enough.

Before you start I want to get it out of the way. I am a fan of ARPGs. One of my first PC games (other than those free games that came on my dad's "Software of the Month club" discs was Diablo). I have played most (but somehow missed Titan Quest). I love the style and have spent far too many hours in these games over the years. So if you do not like the genre, skip the game. This is definitely not a "best in genre" type game.
That said, I found this game competent and even fun. I liked the aesthetics of the game. The loot felt fun and interesting. I admit that the combat as a caster focused character was hard at first but got better towards the end. The story was cheesy and some of the mechanics (the psuedo tower defense sections) didn't click with me. There were bugs at launch. And there have been valid complaints about DLC pricing during sales.
BUT I still think this game is worth a try. Especially when it goes on sale. Katarina is like a pet from TL2 but with a fun an interesting personality (the bickering between her and Van Helsing was sometimes my favorite part). The combat was challenging but didn't feel too much like the fantasy equivalent of being a bullet sponge. Loot was more fun than my time in Diablo 3 but not quite up to TL2 or even D2: LoD levels. The progression was simple enough and ... it has been a while... but I seem to remember a respec option.
If you are a fan of ARPGs, watch for this to go on sale. If you want to try the genre out this is not a bad first game but there may be other options (a certain popular free to play game) to see if you like the style. But keep those expectations in check. It is fun and can be enjoyable but, to me at least, is middle of the road for ARPG.

Smoothest animations in 2D fighting games history.
That alone kept me glued to the screen, to the point of not actually caring about gameplay and just enjoying beautifylly animated, and jolly ridiculous moves. I made a review based on what I've managed to play during a free weekend; and what I saw was exactly what I would get later on- a well made fighting game with care for the deepest and maybe even useless details; a crowdfunded labour of love, trying to convince its player to love it back.
It's worth mentioning that the entry point to it is pretty easy thanks to the big and extremely advanced tutorial, as well as customizeable training mode.
I unfortunately suffer from not having a soft button controller, wich would make execution of more advanced moves much easier and comfortable to pull off. Knowing this I'd recommend everyone to have a pad or anything with a stick to do 360s with, several characters need them for some moves; thus you need it if you want to play online.
The game might be easy to pick up, but it's still demanding when it comes to expertise. And thanks to me being a "Tekken kid", the whole idea of 6 attack button distracts me to no end; but maybe that's just me :( .
Contents are satisfying, with 9 base characters, each with a story mode, and each with 25 color pallettes; a handful of stages and a glorious jazzy soundtrack; all for the initial price of 15$.
But if you want to get into it, everyone would advise you to pick up the character DLCs (all of wich can be played in the tutorial for free, but nowhere else), and with DLCs comes a little bit more cost- 5 characters, 5$ dollars each, all of which amounts to 25$.
So a full game becomes 40$, it all depends on how many hours you are willing to sink into it- it would feel like supporting the devs, or wasting your funds.
If you like what you see- I recemmend it without hesitations; if you're unsure- try no DLCs or during sales. Cause it's a gorgeous fighting game that would be a waste to not try out.

This seems like a fighter for all players.

Did I really just write a whole review about what I hated about Trine, copy it to clipboard, and then accidentally lose it copying the lyrics of Supertramp's "The Logical Song" into a review for Chantelise?
Yeah. I did.
Anyway, this game starts out with the neat idea of a puzzle/adventure game - which seemed to impress a lot of people when it came out - only to stop being creative halfway through and produce a game with the audacity of a day-old gumwad. Stop playing halfway through - I guarantee you did all the enjoyable parts already, the Knight's hammer isn't even that great, and the last level is one of those pseudo-timed lava-slowly-rising dealies. The controls turn out to be too sluggish and most obstacles are better solved with methods that feel like cheating, so the whole experience sort of just falls apart and feels half lazy and half frustratingly vindictive. Sliding off♥♥♥♥♥♥into hazards that were way off screen happens way too often in the late-game.
Also the characters are idiotic tropes, the narration is predictable, cheesy, pointless, and even kind of wrong in a couple points ("and then they heard his voice" isn't really accurate if the only things he does is laugh), and the payoff at the end is just so embarassingly bad it should've been replaced with a big "YOU WON" sign. The graphical design is pretty nice in a lot of parts and only confuses you over what's actually something you can step on in a few parts, so that's, uh, positive. A big negative is that a lot of the music sounds like it belongs in a Geico commercial or a bad fantasy parody movie - or one of those off-budget CG movies that try to copy Dreamwork's titles to cash in on grandmas who want to buy their grandchildren a fun DVD but weren't paying enough attention to the ads. Although Netflix is picking up a lot of them now so I guess the irony factor is working out for them.
Anyway, if you bought this on Humble Bundle for however close to almost free you wanted to get, fine, whatever, but probably save yourself the hassle and stop after three levels.
If you bought it when it came out - thanks to your inflation of its popularity, they made a Trine 2, which I bought before actually playing through this tasteless ♥♥♥♥♥ack. So, thanks for that.

There are some really good ideas such as the gravity gun that lets you levitate objects. This should be used in several boss battles instead of the good old pull-the-trigger-until-it-dies method.
Inversion is not a bad game. It has potential but could have been given more polish. At this point it is mediocre at best and I do not really recommend it.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
The 1st time I purchased this game I got a refund due to control issues. Now that the game has joypad support, it's not a bad little game. Take on the role of a young father and husband, Davis Russell, who finds himself thrust into war when his peaceful city is invaded by an unknown enemy. With his daughter missing and conventional weapons and tactics all but useless, this ordinary cop and his partner Leo Delgado will rise up to heed the call of duty, master the fundamental forces of gravity and save the world.

Cheap Gears of War clone. Not a problem.
2 weapons limit, checkpoint save system. Not a problem.
Very common bug that oblige you to put steam friends offline, if you don't want the game to crash after the first menu. Not a problem (you can tweak it to play coop).
The problems of this game are the bad writing, bad acting, the stupid story not even explained, and an arbitrary difficulty that goes into frustration too often, since the mechanics are the only interesting thing in the game, but they are quite confusing and stiff.
The action is not bad, but it is continuously interrupted by useless cinematic.
It lasts 8 hours but it seemed an eternity to me.

snap back and had a life. Also, she didn't have amnesia
and had social awareness! But the game downplays the romances for the sake of the overarching plot, which is really not that great. It's almost like they forcibly stuck to the theme and sabotaged themselves in the process.
There's a lot of criticism in this review despite the thumbs up because ultimately I found it entertaning. I expected more, but it's a good otome to read with recognizable tropes, an overarching story and collectables.

Nameless is a step up from Dandelion ~ my opinion. There are no god forsaken stat building in Nameless like in Dandelion.
Pros:
1. Unlike Dandelion there is an in depth story rather than the majority of it being stat building like in Dandelion.
2. I guess the artwork is good. I definitely cannot draw this well, but when Yuri closes his eyes...what the heck is that?!
3. I am not sure IF it is a better story or not. There is MORE story, which is good, but I feel less silliness in dandelion...if you can believe that. I am not sure if that is really accurate though, if Dandelion had more story, would it be as silly?! Who knows? They are both pretty silly if you think about it.
4. I like how they kept up the mystery of the nameless doll the MC had forgotten about until the end.
5. Funny moments...
6. You have dialogue options...unfortunately not many as several other otome games I played. =/
Cons:
1. I often feel like this story was written by a 12-year-old (actually I felt that way about Dandelion too, but stat building hides it better). Some of the concepts are so ridiculous, but I suppose it is entertainingly funny in how some of the concepts are so ridiculous.
2. The end is abrupt I suppose it was meant that way.
3. The MC is not totally bad as far as some go for otome games (whyyyy??! do they do this???!), but so far the MC from dandelion is actually the best.
4. I hate that one character that keeps calling the MC 'master'. What kind of weird fantasies do these writers think normal people like?! Okay, okay. I get it is his character and that the MC is apparently owner of the dolls and that is where it is coming from...but gees. I dunno.
5. These dolls all have personal issues, but resolving those issues with the thing they needed (learning to trust, learning to love, being honest, etc.,) seem to fall short.  I ask myself...did they really resolve them? I think it falls short because they combined the MC earning their love at the SAME time as these characters resolving their personal issues. As a result, it sort of downplays how they actually and truly resolve their issues.  Future reference: save the acknowledgement of love for a bit later in the story instead of rushing it at the same time these characters overcome their personal issues.
6. The whole point of the story?
7. Dialogue options are few and the few choices you have can so easily lead to a terrible end or a boring bad end. The terrible ends are not so bad per say, but the boring ones end so abruptly and with little explanation. They might as well, in those ends, immediately bring up the "bad end" sign and add a "you suck" to it.
I guess I could go on, but getting tired of writing. I just hope I wrote this well enough to make an honest review. I do not hate this game, but I do not love it. I wish Steam let you have a middle ground choice instead of "do you recommend this game or not?" Since I have mixed feelings, I won't pick the recommendation.

Playing To the Moon took me about 5 hours, which was longer than I expected. I warmed up to the dialogue once the character dynamics were established and the story got rolling. Without spoiling too much, I like the story and the themes it explores, such as traveling backwards through time, exploring reconstructed memories, and alternate futures. Where do our desires really come from?
The romanticism of space travel (and time travel) reminds me of Makoto Shinkai’s first film, Voices of a Distant Star. In To the Moon, the protagonists must travel back in time so the character Johnny can travel to outer space. The concept is a lofty one for a game to tackle, and ultimately the clever writing pulls it all together. The stellar music helps it feel more like a Japanese visual novel than an RPG.
My only gripe is that sometimes finding memory links can be annoying, but that’s a minor issue. Overall, the experience was very enjoyable and thought-provoking.

The game gets very old, very fast.  It's incredibly easy to make a huge amount of money, and for a supposed business game, many things (like staff wages, stock market, competition) are absent.
The graphics are quite pretty, and it's neat that each port is "unique", but you probably won't get to see most of them. By the end of the first year, you'll most likely be auto-docking all your ships.  If not, you'd be docking HUNDREDS of times PER YEAR.
Since there are no difficulty levels in the game, there's really no reason to replay the game once you've completed the career.  Freeplay is available, but it makes an easy game even easier.  The ships basically can't lose money (example: I'll often get a single delivery contract worth $25M.  The fuel costs for this trip are less than $1M. Interesting concept, but they really needed to flesh out their game design in order to make it more fun to play.

I love aliens. My whole life I wished I could be the charles darwin of an alien planet, so I was sucked right in by the concept of No Man's Sky. I wanted it to be everything they claimed it would be, I wanted to love it! I wanted it to be the only game I'd ever play again. Unfortunately, It was very hard to like No Man's Sky. In fact, I hated it.
Never in my life have I regretted so strongly any other purchase, than No Man's Sky. Not only does the game fall short on almost all of its over-hyped promises, but it is incredibly over priced at a retail $60.00. The advertised "scale" of the immense world is only possible because the logorithmic creation of all of the planets and creatures produce cheap copies and knock offs that are boring, repetative, and uninteresting. The immensity of thier under-delivery makes Spore look like an incredible success by comparison. I sunk about 40 hours of gameplay into this, and after about 16 the patterns in the game are so blatantly recognizabgle, that any suspended disbelief comes crashing down on your head, and shatters the immersive quality.
The only joy I got out of the game was naming and categorizing the various species of the more interesting worlds (which were incredibly scarce and impossible to mark for return), and learning alien languages via an extremely grindy collection system. These are the most rewarding activities in a sea of pointlessness. This game is a sandbox, so directionlessness is to be expected, but in other sandbox games, there are unique and interesting story threads and hooks to draw you to the good bits, and you are rewarded for exploring them farther. No Man's Sky has no such story, only vague and shallow references to historic events that have no impact on the game play, or the static and stiff "characters" (if you can even call them that, as the only things you interact with in the game are dumb animals and vendor merchants).
To be fair, the engine is powerful, and the developers have broken a lot of ground with the way procedural generation can be used in games, and a lot of respect and credit is due there. The game is also beautiful. The bubbly and saturated aesthetic makes exploring very fun, and the style is detailed enough that you'll catch yourself admiring a lot of the flora and fauna. I took a lot of pretty screenshots cresting hills and looking out over crazy alien vistas, I even set my desktop backround as one for a while. It was a nice stress reliver after work to just fly around and name animals and take pictures.
Mechanically on the other hand, the game is lacking in some simple and time-tested necessary UI features. It doesn't even have a system of mapping or tracking the worlds you have visited, making it frusturating to find your way back to resource deposits or just cool sites. The game is very inventory dependent, and the tools it gives you for managing those inventories are counterintuitive and limiting, making you constantly feel like you're being punished for collection things (which i must stress is all you can really do in the game.) The gameplay is incredibly repetitive, and grindy, as you blast rocks to get resources to build things... that make you better at blasting rocks to build more things... that also blast rocks. The combat is easy to master and the enemies lack variety and challenge, not to mention they are basically a lore-less cop-out of designing a compelling antagonist. It feels entirely like an after thought.
All in all, the amount of time you have to sink into this game is immense, and the rewards are paultry and empty feeling (aside from building a ship, that was dope.) The story is weaker than hotel coffee, and the gameplay is akin to making cornmeal. A rating of 4 out of 10 would be generous, and its only because I respect the studio and what they have done here, not because I think the game experience deserves it.

Without a doubt, my favorite video game of all time. I've been in love since I bought this for my Xbox 360 back in 2008.
Fallout 3 places you, the Lone Wanderer, as a ostracized vault dweller 200 years after nuclear war devistated the United States. Your story begins in the ruins of Washington D.C., now called the Capital Wasteland. Famous landmarks in the game include the Pentagon, the Washington Monument, the US Capitol Building, the Lincoln Memorial, The ruins of the White House, and even neighboring cities such as Arlington and Bethesda. There's also a pretty substantial area of the map that isn't particularly anything - there'll be little settlements every once in a while, but for the adventurous type, this will be the most enjoyable part of the Capital Wasteland. You can explore anywhere you want to, from irradiated metro stations to government buildings to raider hideouts full of people who really want to just kill you. Freedom of choice.
You can be anything you want to be in this game- if you want to be the hero of the wasteland, bringing salvation in the form of purified water, so be it. If you want to be a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥by blowing up a town with a nuclear bomb, enslaving children for profit, or just by shooting everybody, so be it. Freedom of choice is a big theme in this game. Your actions will affect the outcome of your story, as well as how people treat you in the Wasteland.
One of my favorite aspects of this game is the leveling system. In my opinion, it is superior to Fallout 4's by a long shot. While in Fallout 4 skills are non existent, in 3 the player is required to level up their skills accordingly - the first 10 levels of the game require a decent amount of strategy. For example, a player might think it's a good idea to upgrade his Lockpick and Speech ability initially, but this also means that the player won't be able to shoot a gun straight for a while. Conversly, a player with a good Small Guns skill initially won't be able to buy anything at a reasonable price for a few levels. It's all about what kind of player you want to be: you can be a smooth talker that only needs a gun when moving from settlement to settlement, or you can by a gun slinging madman that shoots his way out of everything. Freedom of choice.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. Fallout games always have a creppily hilarous vibe to them, and this game is probably the best endevour on that front from Bethesda yet. Within the Fallout universe, the culture of the United States never moved on past 1945, while technology exploded beyond our own. Everything is Art Deco influenced, and has that real 1950's cheesy optimism about the world. However, all of this technology is still based on older technology, such as vacuum tubes. It's hilarous to see giant computers that run a command line alongside plasma rifles and robots. The soundtrack is wonderful, consisting mainly of 20s-40s jazz and blues standards, and even a little do-wop; the Ink Spots are featured prominently within the game.

For starters, let's say I didn't hate playing FO3. I've beaten it few times, did the majority of quests and even played all the DLC's. I even had fun doing that. Do I recommend playing it? Maybe. Is it a terrible game? No. There, I said it. Moving on.
Here's my main gripe: FO3 is what happens when you take a fantastically written post-apocalyptic game series and hand the rights over to a company whose writers appear to be 12-year-olds.
Imagine a world where every city, every store and every household is an entity separate from the surrounding world. Nothing has an effect on anything else. There's a town a miles down the road with a problem with Raiders? Yeah, that doesn't really affect this storekeeper couple. Heaps of radscorpions make life a living hell for a bunch of settlers living in a run-down village? Yeah, that has no bearing on this other community a stone's throw away, their only problem pertains to fixing their fertility robot. Oh, and getting their hands on a vacuum tube located 20 miles away because reasons.
When you have dozens of locations with seemingly no connection to one another or the main plot, you end up with a huge sandbox that barely resembles the intricate interconnected plots of the first two games. That's Fallout 3's setting in a nutshell. Real world doesn't work like that. If your counter-argument is "this is a game, not the real world lol" you're completely missing the point. Fallout 1 and 2 came out years before FO3 and yet they still managed to accomplish a sense of reality - albeit a very far-fetched and sometimes tongue-in-cheek one.
Take Fallout 2, where you have a complicated, interconnected political web between New Reno, Redding, Vault City and NCR. Take Fallout: New Vegas where everything rotates around the ongoing conflict between NCR and Caesar's Legion. Everyone has a say in this, everybody is affected. Your choices affect the outcome and the ongoing power structure. That's how you write a game. And that's where FO3 falls flat on its face.
The main plot is bland. I felt like I had no reason to follow the PC's dad. Instead I ran around, doing quests here and there, fetching this and killing that, getting little satisfaction from the caps and experience I accumulated. It wasn't really rewarding. None of it. Just a mindless, momentary distraction on the road to the grave.

If I had to pick an "underrated game of 2013" this is it. Beautiful animations, a compelling setting, an interesting AI companion, and an adequate story already set this game apart from its competitors in the ARPG market - and that's to say nothing of character development and the combat mechanics system.
A lot of criticisms of this game target the lack of build diversity, since the vanilla version only has one character "class" with two build paths, melee and ranged. However, these concerns are ameliorated by the DLC classes, a mage and a trap-setting ranged fighter, which are worth getting if you like the base game.
I love the setting, which is somewhere between Mary Shelley / Bram Stoker Gothic and Stephen Hunt steampunk. Katarina, the ghost companion of the player, is well-written and feels useful in combat (but not TOO useful, so van Helsing still feels like the star.)
Combat is simple enough to be accessible, but complex enough to reward careful character building. 4 primary stats - essentially Melee, Ranged, Magic, and Critical - govern around 10 secondary stats, all of which are easy to understand. The skill tree is fairly simple but has enough depth that the same class could be built effectively in a few different ways. There is a neat mechanic about managing a resource called Rage, used to enhance attacks with sub-skills called Powerups; so far these seem interesting, but not necessary to play the game if you don't want to worry about them.
I got this game on sale for $7, and at that price it's a no-brainer. At the full price ($15 + $5 DLC) it's still worthwhile, but there are better titles on Steam at that price point if you're not an action-RPG fan. In comparison to Torchlight 2, it is a bit less accessible to genre newcomers, but with a more interesting setting and a darker, more visceral tone.
TOTAL 8.5/10
+ Art style and setting
+ Animations and voice acting
+ Combat system (Power-ups/rage, balance of skills, diversity of skills and gear)
+ Endgame play modes (Scenario and Neverending Story allow players to continue after finishing the game)
- Feels limited by production cost (Short story, only a few monster models and terrain palettes)
- Some technical problems (occasional, minor bugs that do not crash the game, but get irritating)

I got this game in a humble bundle, and figured it looked like it would be at the very least somewhat entertaining, perhaps in a passive way. At the very least, to play it and see what the mystery was, I thought. But surely it was just another typing game for kids, those have been done over the years. It certainly looked pretty, but that was about all my first impression was.
I was wrong.
This game seemed pretty basic and straightforward for what I was expecting for about, oh, THREE MINUTES. It rapidly shot right past my own fairly decent vocabulary, which was highly impressive; I teamed up with a friend to send them words I didn't recognize, like sardonyx, speleothem, ettringite, etc, and they'd find and tell me the definition, which was great fun for both of us. (The ability to change screens at *any* point in the game and have everything pause, be it battle, voice over, or cutscene, by the way, is EXTREMELY handy.) I was already enjoying the advanced vocabulary, and then the first boss threw calciovolborthite at me X'D That was insane. And the game continued to surprise me with unique mechanics. I have to say, I did NOT expect an elemental aspect where you have to match them to even affect the enemies. I've never seen a typing game get so intense as the last nest battle I just fought, and I can't wait to see how much more the game throws at me. I've been raving about this game to a couple of my friends constantly as it impresses me more and more, from overall mechanics to the small details that can make or break a game. This was a surprise gem in my bundle and I feel incredibly lucky to have gotten it. If I'd somehow known in advance how amazing this would turn out to be, and had had to pay full price, or at least get it on steam sale? Worth it. Totally worth it. I love every bit of this game, and I'm not even done yet, I just felt compelled after that fight to pause and write this review.

I found Epistory: Typing Chronicles for a very low price, and I'm glad I did because I absolutely love this game. If adventure, puzzle and strategic games are your thing, but you're looking for something with a little twist: you've found it.
I'm a big fan of adventure and puzzle games, which this game does combine, and I feel like the typing mechanic is excecuted well in this game. It's what makes this game special, which does make me sad that not many other games use this as a mechanic. I'm also in love with the design: I love the way it folds out as a pop-up storybook and has the main character look like a piece of origami: it makes the game dreamy in a way and I did find myself looking in awe as the next area was revealed. Though some may argue it's relatively simple in design, I love the simplicity of the world. It's not too busy, but never too quiet. The dungeons were excecuted nicely as well, and I loved the way the powers had to be aquired and how they are used: they all have their strengths and weaknesses.
The only mechanic I wasn't a big fan of is the map: I thought it was poorly excecuted and I feel like most of the times, it wasn't much of a help at all. I couldn't find a shortcut to get to the map, so to see it I had to press Tab and then switch to it, but when I closed the map to look at where I was I'd have to do the same thing again, which was annoying when I got into an area where I wasn't sure if there would be enemies. The zoom function of the map is decent, but when zoomed in the map cannot be moved to other areas. This made navigating a little more difficult sometimes.
Plotwise, the game is pretty straightforward, though I did have to do some searching as to where the next reveal was located from time to time (as well as for the chests and safes), but it was never too hard. The fact most of the storyline is revealed in bits and pieces is something I really liked too, it kept me curious for every new area and new sentence written on the map. The voice acting is done very well too, it can really make or break a game and I'd definitely say this made the game a whole lot better. It is of good quality and really dragged me into the story as it unfolds.
In terms of enemies and boss battles, though I have been a little annoyed with bugs spawning pretty much in front of my feet (thus killing me), the enemies are very much managable, which also goes for the nests: not too difficult but not too easy either. The nests later on in the game really gave me a challenge that was fun to do, and it felt very rewarding when I finally beat them. Though the game doesn't give you much of a reward when it comes to clearing the nests (you get points to distribute though), I feel like the whole challenge of the fight is what got me excited for them. I've never enjoyed boss battles as much as in this game, especially near the end.
When it comes to the length of the game, I felt like it has much more potential and thus I wish it would have had even more areas to discover and explore, as the game takes around 7-8 hours to finish when you take a little time to backtrack for things like me (if you wouldn't, I think 4-5 would be enough to play through the whole thing) and I was a little dissappointed it was over at some point. It's not a very long game in that sense, and though I feel like the gameplay you do get in it is very rewarding, the shortness left me a bit dissappointed. However, this makes it an ideal casual game to replay every once in a while, in my opinion.
A rarely used but well-executed gameplay mechanic, good storyline, very good voice acting, great map and dungeon design, cool and creative mechanics and challenging bossfights, though a slightly dissappointing map mechanic. If you love adventure, puzzles and strategy and know your way around the keyboard, I would definitely recommend this game; although I'm not sure I would pay €15 for the game myself (I paid way less) due to the total time taken to complete the storyline. Overal, a very nice and casual game to take your mind off things, though still challenging enough to not get boring.

That doesn't mean you won't have a great time playing it alone. The gameplay flows very smoothly and has a very fluent control so you won't die by choppy, unfair deaths.
The Music in the games is fantastic and beautiful which you can listen to over and over again, so I highly recommend getting the Soundtrack And Art with the games. Speaking of the art. The Art and scenery is like the music, beautiful and will make you stop in your steps as you look over the horizon in all it's glory. The puzzles, which are quite many, can be solved in many ways, from using magic to conjure up some crates to swinging from platform to platform. The Characters are very memorable and so is the Narrator (who I really like), makes you fall in into the tale of these three so much more.
The enemies while do fell repetitive,is but a minor scratch to this game.
So I highly recommend this Side-scroller gem, for its price as it isn't that pricey and you will enjoy every waking minute of it.
So go buy this game and see what you've been missing out on.

This is a 2D platformer with puzzles designed to make use of the skills of its 3 main Heroes. It is best played as a 3 player co op game, but only supports local co op. This game can be played solo, and most of the levels have multiple ways of getting through. The level design, art and music are the games strongest points. However with the real low price tag (especially during sales), its a must have, unless you really hate platformeers. There are some balance issues with the heroes, and the controls aren't as tight as they should be, but i'm hoping they fixed that with the second one. Each of the three characters are perfect manifestations of the stereotypical types of classic fantasy. This game is an excellent romp of fantasy. The archery, magic, swinging, melee, and just about every other feature of the three characters is well thought out and impressively executed. The narrative is perfectly balanced between not actually being too imporant that it takes itself too seriously, but also adding an excellent layer of culture to the game world. The soundtrack as well is quite exceptional and really adds to the atmosphere.
Though at the end of the day it just comes to the fact the gameplay is just undeniably solid.

Playing To the Moon took me about 5 hours, which was longer than I expected. I warmed up to the dialogue once the character dynamics were established and the story got rolling. Without spoiling too much, I like the story and the themes it explores, such as traveling backwards through time, exploring reconstructed memories, and alternate futures. Where do our desires really come from?
The romanticism of space travel (and time travel) reminds me of Makoto Shinkai’s first film, Voices of a Distant Star. In To the Moon, the protagonists must travel back in time so the character Johnny can travel to outer space. The concept is a lofty one for a game to tackle, and ultimately the clever writing pulls it all together. The stellar music helps it feel more like a Japanese visual novel than an RPG.
My only gripe is that sometimes finding memory links can be annoying, but that’s a minor issue. Overall, the experience was very enjoyable and thought-provoking.

I got this game after playing hours of Mystic Messenger in the summer. People here kept saying that because both are made by Cheritz, the games are alike. Unfortunately, that's not true.
About a third of this game was genuinely good, I guess it just depends if you like the characters enough. Even on my favourite roots I found myself skipping some boring scenes. A lot of my playtime was spent skipping really. The story is naive and slow, and some of the characters are not who they seem to be, but at this stage we all know the generic otome tropes so it's hardly a surprise who is gonna be weird in what way. The "shocking" and "dark" storyline doesn't even compare to the stuff you'd see on Netflix, so I'm confused about why people think it's so intense.

To sum everything up, Nameless' story was very well written. I'm a sucker for stories that have proper progression and character development to match. Not only does your main character, Eri (who's name you can change), experience this development but all of the boys do, too. I learned a few things about myself and other people through the routes, in ways I wasn't expecting.
In terms of choices, there aren't a lot (in the grand scheme of things) and some routes have chapters where the are no choices at all. But a good portion of the choices are realistic for the situation. It's very much a story, but that was fine for me as I was captivated just reading and listening. That being said the voice acting is superb, and even for the characters that scared me pretty badly
, I enjoyed listening to them.
This game is long depending on how you read and listen, and you will have to go back quite a bit to get through all of the endings and to collect everything. This game can also get dark and/or personal, nothing about the routes is all-around lighthearted, so that should be something you think about before buying. It deals with real issues in an interesting way.
This review is kind of long, kind of ramble-y, and mostly about characters, and a little about plot, as these things impacted me the most.
~
I'm starting with Yeonho because I did his route first (after bad-ending in the prologue), although I wasn't aware of the recommended order at the time. I got attached to his character the quickest, as he was fairly innocent and sweet. This is my first game in this genre so it put me off slightly that I was supposed to love these characters, Yeonho's put me off the least and I felt more like a sister or a mom, lol.
Even after his route, and through all the others, Yeonho was kind of like a breath of fresh air when things got tense with the others.
I did Lance's route next, and I found his pretty tame in regards to Yeonho's (especially regarding the bad endings). I enjoyed his character in most aspects and was annoyed by some others, but especially as the game progressed I enjoyed seeing his care for Eri. His character progression felt very sweet and truthful.
. After his route I felt like he wasn't there enough in the game, whereas Tei was
. And that might be why I didn't feel as attached to him after his route.
Yuri's route really messed me up. It was the first one to really hit me on an emotional level. At first I was really nervous to do this one, I did not vibe with his character at all before, but it's my favorite route in the game and the first one to make me cry. Eri gets a lot of character development and Yuri does too.
Yuri's VA knocks my socks off. Also, count how many times he calls you something that makes you both recoil in the cringe but also internally scream from the attractiveness, it's fun.
Somewhere in the middle of Tei's route I took about a four month break. I, honestly, didn't like his character very much
. Every redeemable quality Tei has, didn't seem to make up for anything, and even learning his backstory I felt a twinge of understanding, but the
traits never seemed made up for, like Yeonho's did.
As a big fan of certain types of cliches, I really enjoyed Red's route but there is a big glaring turn off in it,
and I wish we got to see more of Red earlier in the game, as he only really becomes prominent in his own route, sort of like Lance, whereas everyone else, namely Tei, seems to be in it a lot more. Red's route was my second favorite, despite this. (It also doesn't help I have an affinity for the red haired characters)
Soi was a character I loved to love and loved to hate, but I think she's written to be that way.
during Tei and Red's routes. Despite some obviously glaring personality faults, she's a greatly written friend character. She is important to the plot especially as it progresses. She has a really enjoyable theme, and her voice actress fits the role quite well. Soi is a really fun character, and I'm glad Nameless also focuses on Eri's friends, and gives them a purpose and also a message like the boys do.
The last character I'm going to write about (although I would love to gush about Zion), is sharp-as-a-tack Shinbi. At one point I called her the god of this game, as she seems fairly all knowing, but she's just a very observant friend. She's not in the game as much as Soi, but when she is she usually provides some insight.
~
The OST is very pretty for the game, and the character art is really lovely.
I hope Cheritz can continue to make such moving games, because this game has become imprinted on my heart like a few forms of media have already. It's going to make you self-reflect even slightly, and teach you a bit about yourself... or, at least it did for me. It might not have an immediately replayable value, but it's that sort of game that will wiggle its way back into your brain and make you revisit some parts of it... it's an experience truly worth your time and $20.

Some of the themes of the routes hit really close to home. I cried. A lot.

This is the first game I purchased via the Steam recommendations.  I am certainly not disappointed.  So far, I have 10 hours in the game, and I feel addicted.
This is a fairly simple simulator/logistics game.  The game has a tutorial, and I'm playing through it.  However, if you played similar games, such as Cities in Motion or Railroad Tycoon, then you can probably figure this out.  You buy a ship, get a contract, and then deliver the goods.  You have investors, you can take out a loan, and your ship will need fuel and maintenance.  From that standpoint, it is very easy.  As you get more ships, you gain more capacity but lose some capability.  Eventually, you can create company specific contracts that require delivery of a certain good to a certain location; at this point the complexity starts to become apparent.  To keep it interesting, you also have to deal with storms, pirates, and fires at sea.
While the game is fun to play, it still needs some polish.  I've had a few popup notifications remain on the screen.  I can play through them and sometimes get them to disappear, but its a bug.  While there are hazards, like storms and pirates, they purely random rather location specific, thus avoidable.  For example, I had a piracy near the Canaries, and I hit a storm with one vessel while another vessel sailed through the same area at the same time without the storm.  Personally, I find these oddities to be minor imperfections and potential room for growth in the development.  Overall the game is very solid platform and is good enough for this early release.
A larger area for growth is the games focus on cargo container shipping.  I commented about this in relation to US ports on the forums.  I was happy to see the game designer respond within hours of my comments.  While my request won't go fulfilled for now, I'm satisfied knowing that they understand the issue.
I'm definitely getting my money's worth from the game.  I think the game is playable for most ages.  If you are into sims like this, you'll love it.  If you prefer FPS games, then you'll probably hate this game as it is not meant for you.  I recommend this to all the simmers out there.

LOR is a parkour running game, obviously, but it's not a good one.  The levels are all incredibly easy once you figure out the rather poor controls.  The final level, level 7, is significantly more difficult than the first 6, but none of the levels really WOW me.  I get that LOR is in early access and will likely have more content added, but that content will likely build on what is already here.  And what is already here isn't good.  At all.
LOR fails to offer anything unique.  I don't see a single mechanic that isn't already implemented in several other (more successful) parkour running games.  You jump, you have a single-use boost, and there are some obstacles to overcome.  There is no gimmick unique to this game, no special mechanic to exploit, nothing.  Top that all off with some controls that feel severely limiting and you've got the perfect recipe for a bad parkour running game.
AVOID.

I played this game shortly after it came out and I wasn't big on it at first because after they did some updating it was very playable and I enjoyed it. I was happily awaiting new content and seeing where it would go and then they went an entirely new direction.
Intially you were the hero of a village that would go out to hunt animals in order to provide meat for your village to keep them from starving to death when the next storm came, you and your dogs would travel through the tundra in search of penguins, foxes, and get chased by wolves. You could even choose one of your dogs to help you hunt at one point and the dogs overall looked different. The hunting was a major part of the game and you had afew different tools to do it, machete, crossbow, etc. You would also run into other tribes and help them and get benefits from helping them.
Now, you are a scientist trying to preserve the tundra. So, if you do anything besides fish you actually take a "penalty" as the point of the game is to get signatures by sending in data to preserve it so anytime you hunt an animal, despite needing lots of food to support your group, the ecosystem percentage drops. Which is also conflicting considering you actually get data from animal skins... Basically the whole premise of the game is going out and exploring, which would be fine if there was something to explore. Most of the game is just glaciers and mountains that look exactly the same... and then you place drills and various data collecting instruments across the landscape and have to go to those very specific places (You're only allowed to place drills and data collecting items on specific places on the map that are deemed "ideal" ) which can literally take you the full "in-game" day just to collect one or two off in the distance. Also as I'm writing this your drills won't save. So you're pretty much replacing them everytime you exit and reenter the game.
The only real improvements they've made since the game was released in EA is better graphics, your group actually helps you gather things now, and the crossbow shooting is a lot smoother. Really nothing for the overall storyline of the game. I went from becoming more and more impressed to totally bored. It's so boring now, you just travel across the landscape trying to gather data to get signatures and that's it. Nothing cool happens, wolves still chase you but they are easily out run, almost everything dies with no more than 3 crossbow bolts, and again if you kill something, you take a penalty towards the games goal... Not a lot here anymore for me. Really quite sad. :/

I have some really nice things to say about this game, but first I want to address the other bits.
First of all, the game is co-op, and I think has to potential to be the point where the game can really shine. I loved setting up the base while my friend went out and collected data mines/cameras we planted. But so far, on my end at least, it's a very clunky experience. After playing with my friend (lives in same city) after about 10 minutes, the game begins to slowly stutter over time until it becomes nearly a slideshow, until we have to reload game to fix. Which is a shame, because the game is most enjoyable I think as a smooth, limitless asthetic.
The "2nd Player" is also very limited, and cannot do much. He cannot give my dogs meat, he cannot look at our telescope for data, he cannot help manage the team, he cannot pick me up if I'm stranded with tired dogs. He can help with data and ride around in his own sled dog team, help paint, and build a bit, but his building is limited. He was a really good sport and we got to talk and hang out and explore the beauty together, but was still a noteworthy limitation.
There is also little in the way of endgame, from an objective perspective. I get that you're trying to improve your bio impact & expedition popularity, but then what? New structures might be fun, but it felt very objectiveless at some point. But...the journey to this point was lovely & really excited for what the future brings with this game.
!!!That being said!!! this game is incredible for what it is. Establishing your expedition & exploration in the Antarctic is a really wonderful part of the game, and something I found myself losing track of time with. It really, really shines on the aesthetics front. And I can see why the dev isn't pushing co-op so much, because the idea of solitude in the Antarctic and the aesthetic it brings into implemented gameplay is really something. Absolutely excellent. Very unique gameplay to what I'm used to. The music is incredible, too.
It's quite an experience, and I wouldn't knock it just because it's not going to give you Minecraft or Skyrim amounts of hours.
It's enough of a game to enjoy, become a little inspired, and forget about your world. The time I've spent on this game was not regrettable, and the $5 sale price was fair. Get this game if you want an experience.

I got this game for myself and a friend while it was on sale, and we've gotten some fun times out of it. My expectations were pretty low going in; I didn't really think that this game would be as much fun as it is. The writing and voice acting is pretty good, and I love the banter between your ghostly compainion, Lady Katarina, and Van Helsing.
From a gameplay perspective, everything seems to be well thought out and well balanced, but there are certain aspects (like the combo system) that I didn't really understand for a while (probably because I disabled the tutorial). One of my favorite things about the game is just how hard it can be sometimes. There are certain enemies that can kill you in just a few hits, so it becomes really important to use potions all the time (but don't worry... they drop off of anything and everything so you will have trouble running out).
One of the side-quests (to kill the hunter-machines) seems to be bugged for me, and I am not sure if all my skills are working the way they should (the upgrade to one of the skills should heal me each hit, but I can't really tell if it is working), but overall I love this game and think it's absolutely fantastic. The metascore clocks in at 72/100, which seems about right from a critical perspective, but the question I always ask myself is: Do I have fun playing this game, and how much fun am I having? The answer for The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing: Yes, this game is a blast and I am choosing to play it over the other games in my 181-game library on a nightly basis. Higly recommended for playing with friends (I haven't played solo).

For the three-quarters of the game, Inversion comes off as a poorly-done rip-off of Gears of War. From its story, setting and characters, to it's pop-n-shoot gameplay, you will be constantly reminded of Epic's opus in grey-and-brown. It's only in the very last 10% of the game that Inversion finally starts to develop a personality of its own.
But for all that they blatantly stole so much from Gears, the developers failed to take the one thing that really mattered; interesting gameplay. And let's face it; Gears of War barely qualifies as interesting itself, so you know Inversion has to be  scraping the barrel if they can't even match the pedantic gameplay of Gears. The game has horrible controls (not that surprising in a port but disappointing nonetheless).  Its enemies and levels are hardly notable and its gunplay is bog-standard. The hook to Inversion is its ability to play around with the gravitational field, but nothing Inversion does is new or memorable. And, oh god is this game in love with its cut-scenes; it seems almost every action you take triggers a scripted - and uninterruptible -  animation.
On the plus side, there's some nice destructibility of the environments and the graphics are passable, especially consider it is a multi-platform title. But its reliance on cliched gameplay and shoddy technical aspects result in a poorly-designed, uninteresting mess of a game

If I had noticed that Inversion was developed by Saber Interactive, the same team that TimeShift, I probably would have passed on it. When I bought it, I think I might have confused it for Hybrid, which is another cover-based third-person shooter but it's made by 5th Cell, who made Scribblenauts. I like Scribblenauts. I think TimeShift was a big letdown. Inversion is also a letdown! Here's Inversion: take Gears of War (literally all of it, the bad guys coming out of the ground, the cover system, the two weapon and grenades limit, the "find my " story, buddy of Hispanic descent, everything), and add in some goofy gravity tricks. You've got a gun that can lower gravity and raise gravity in small areas. You pass through some zero gravity areas by moving from one chunk of environment to another. Your gravity gun can also pick up and throw stuff, like cars, which only becomes useful when you're forced to do it to defeat a boss. The story is just as quickly vomited out at the end as it is in Gears of War. This game is Gears of War, except not as good-looking, and not as fun.

In short, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is a super fun game with some great writing and awesome characters. If you enjoyed 2016s Doom and The New Order, you're going to have a great time...
...if you can deal with some technical issues.
Before I go on, here are my PC specs:
AMD RX 480 4GB (Using the 17.10.2 drivers)
8GB DDR4 RAM
Intel Core i5 6500 3.2Ghz
1TB HDD
120GB SSD
The last Wolfenstein game was basically unplayable on AMD cards, so I'm glad to see that this game is using Doom's engine. I am able to get above 60fps at 1080p Ultra settings. I can even bump to Uber settings with occasional stuttering. At ultra though I need to turn on Vsync because of the screen tearing and I don't have a high refresh rate monitor.
The big technical issue with this game is the crashing. When the game runs, it runs great. However there are times where the game crashes and freezes to the point where I can't even ctr alt del and I have to shut down my PC manually to regain control of my system. I have noticed this issue only happens if there are any programs or windows that are also running. For example, having a web browser open, or streaming software, or just any window open seems to increase the risk of these crashes. If I don't have anything other than Steam in the background and maybe Discord, the game runs super smooth and I can play for as long as I want and exit the game normally with no problems. This might be different depending on your machine.
I would recommend playing the game, but at your own risk. Make sure your drivers are up to date to better your chances of a smooth experience. Hopefully, a patch is released very soon so I can play this game with a peace of mind.

Overall stealth in this game is a broken mess and definitely worse than TNO, which is a damn shame.

Great Game with Massive Flaws.
Europa Universalis 3 is an exellent game. It challenges your mind and is probably the closest you will ever come to running a country. The music is well done and while the graphics aren't great they aren't terrible either. The gameplay is expansive and the countries number over 9000. That was a joke. Sorry I couldn't resist. its actually closer to 300. The strategy is beautifully done and the historical boundries are perfectly accurite right up until you start playing.
That said, There are a lot of problems.
1.The first and most obvious is the tutorials. Namely they don't exist. They used to, but then it got buggy and now it crashes after you try to play them. I suggest learning to play with the magical cesspool that is Youtube.
2. The pirates. Coastal countries are terrible. After you get to naval tech 9, pirates spawn at your coastal cities. Lots and lots of pirates. What makes it worse is that you can't do anything about it, because after you destroy them five minutes later thier back and they brought friends. There are fixes if you get all of the expansions but these removal methods are not user friendly.
3. cost. I like this game. I really do. I understand supporting a developer so that they can continue to produce good content. But $99 is a little ridiculous for what mostly amounts to character sprites. Its sad. just buy the expansions and you'll be fine.
4. Bugs. There arent a ton but the ones that are there are almost game breaking. just warning you. Again get the Expansions and you'll be fine.
5. Eurocentrism. Playing the asian countries is still fun, but most of the action takes place in Europe. and I get it I really do. History tends to look through a Eurocentric lense but thats not really an excuse for a game no matter how historically accurate.
all in all I would give this game a 7/10 IF you are willing to spend the time to get past the learning curve. If not I would have to say 4/10. I love this game. I really do, but I would just get EU4. from what I've seen it fixes most of the problems except for the learning curve.

Everyone says don't buy it because of its poor or non-performance on newer Windows (7 and on), and this is a valid concern, but its also something you can figure out quickly and get a refund if you can't get it to run on your PC with the fan patches.
I still have yet to play New Vegas or Fallout 4 as of this review, and everyone tells me New Vegas is far superior, if this is the case I'm in for a treat, because Fallout 3 is pretty fantastic. I've sunk about 600 hours into it accross 2 characters.
I've also played through 1, 2 and Tactics completely. And while all of those had better storylines, Fallout 3 has better characters. Obviously gameplay is apples and oranges, I rather like FPS games and turn based tactics RPGs equally so I don't personally have a preference.
Pros:
Leveling and building your character is extremely fun and interesting. Trying to maximize your character strategically is pretty enjoyable with the perk system.
Exploration is this games key feature, yes, much of the areas are just wasteland, but you'll trip over something interesting fairly regularly honestly if you just wander around.
Characters are fairly memorable and interesting.
Some specific quests are really engaging and are must plays.
Neutral:
DLC with the GOTY version is a mixed bag.
Cons:
Its gunplay is probably its weakest part, you end up fighting a lot of bullet sponge enemies and unlike most modern FPS games you can't aim down your sights. Its not a significant drag or anything, its just not very fleshed out and feels kind of stiff and unsatisfying. VATS gets old.
The game is a little easy, I reccomend playing on the hardest difficulty, and focus on any perks that allow you to deal more damage, and max out repair (effects damage of all weapon types). Collecting unique named weapons is also worthwhile for their superior performance, check the wikia for fallout to find them.
The main campaign is the most fleshed out series of quests, but they are sort of meandering and there seems to be little in the way of a singular overall goal, as the goal changes many times through out the game and doesn't climax in any cohesive way like the originals. But they are fun nonetheless.
The morality of the game is pretty straight forward and binary, its rare that your moral choices are particularly hard too figure out, either be a saint or a devil.
Conclusion:
If you are looking for post apocalyptic Oblivion with guns this game is for you. If you like exploration, solid quests, and engaging leveling systems this is for you.

That being said, the game is not perfect yet. Some mechanics could be better implemented and more things could be put in to give the character more to do. There's no lore or story. There's no tutorial (not that the game is very complicated, to be fair). I'm also not sure how far you can take this game. I've not played for terribly long, but I can't help to wonder about what happens later on in the game when everything is explored, etc. The map at this stage is not procedurally generated, and as such there's probably not a whole lot of replayability. Mind you, a huge part of the point of this game is, I believe, about relaxing and zoning out, which so far, the game does well enough for me.
I don't review a lot of games, but for some reason or other I really fell in love with this one.  I'd say give it a try if it's your kind of thing, and help the dev make something really cool with his project down the road.

I don't normally post  reviews, but I felt this title worth a mention.  There have been a lot of half-hearted continental simulations released recently and this definately doesn't fall in to that category!
Ok, graphically, the "driving sim" aspect of this title could be better... It's a little 2D feeling and has a tendancy to stutter when you go for maximum speed, but it's passable most of the time.
Having said that, this is, in my option, a solid micro-management sim.  You have good control over the day-to-day running of your shipping company, but can also comfortably out-source many of the more mundane tasks (albeit at a sigificant cost).
Personally, I'm ok with that... I think it should be a significant expense in the early days to outsource any substantial portion of your management role in these kind of titles.
After 6 and a half hours (or so) of play I can tell you the following:
POSITIVES:
* Storyline is ok, driven by solid tutorials... They are progressive and detailed enough to point you in the right direction without being condecending.
* Graphics are better than anything else I have come across in this specific genre.
* Controls are pretty instictive and as expected - camera controlled from mouse and helful auto-centering.
* Sound - I've seen some negative postings, but, in general, I've been pretty impressed.  Music gets a little repetative in the world view as you spend a lot of time there, but each port is individualised and, overall, it's a pretty calming, uninvasive soundtrack.
* Overall gameplay is going to keep genre fans entertained for some time... There's certainly enough variables to grab attention, but cost and development route are inevitable and welcome challenges!
NEGATIVES:
* It seemed to take an excessive amount of time to pass the first few story objectives. I imagine this is because this is many designed to be a "sandbox" title, but I'm hoping greater structure will be added in time.
* On the subject of additions, the are many noteworthy european shipping ports which are currently missing... Let's hope this is remedied in any future updates!!!
All in all, a worthwhile spend... Enjoy!!!!!!

Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a tale of loss, torturous grief, and redemption told from the unique perspective of someone suffering from extreme psychosis. You play as Senua, a Celtic warrior woman who believes she is taking the head of her dead lover to Helheim in an effort to wrest his soul from the clutches of Hel. What ensues is a dark voyage into the psyche as Senua faces her demons as literal manifestations.
While not the first game to have a main character suffering from psychosis, it is probably the first game that has not only taken such great care to represent psychosis accurately, but also the first that brings that accurate representation  to the forefront making it an integral part of the protagonist’s journey from the very beginning.  Many games use sanity as a trick or storytelling device – here it is the story, and it allows you to experience firsthand the sort of distress these types of illnesses bring. Senua has suffered greatly in her life – both because of her mental health and the events in her life that have greatly exacerbated her condition. Sensua suffers so much you can’t help but root for her to succeed. Hellblade’s emphasis on psychosis not only works as an interesting vehicle for a story - Senua is such a sympathetic character, it helps raise awareness to the issue in the real world.
This sympathy is made possible by the great facial animations of Senua, as well as the performance of the actress that portrayed her. All of actors should be given credit, as not only is Hellblade’s story compelling, it is acted well and packaged in a beautiful, cinematic way.
Senua’s remaining tortures are in her head. She contantly hears voices that do everything from torment her to assist her, and as the player you are forced to play with these voices as well (well, unless you turn them off in the audio settings, but the narrative would suffer for it.)  Along with the graphical effects that mimic visual hallucinations, constantly being beset by voices can make for an oppressive experience. Hellblade is a relentlessly depressing game that made me feel genuinely uncomfortable at multiple points. The graphics are gorgeous with neat FMV-like effects. Real-world performances are almost projected across rocks or even darkness – memories hanging in the air like mist that interact with Senua, or drive the plot forward.
The combat is satisfying, as it feels like weapons have weight and it has a similar dodge, block and attack style as a Soulsborne game but without a stamina bar. The boss battles are also well done, with each boss being uniquely horrifying and possessing unique movesets. But spamming attacks and dodging are usually enough to bring success. You also don’t come across enemies organically; instead you are forced to face waves of them before you can proceed. This can feel as tedious as the puzzles tend to be. Most of the game’s obstacles are overcome by solving puzzles, many the puzzles consist of finding runes by making them out of shapes in the environment. Appropriate to the theme, Senua sees these shapes and patterns where there wouldn’t be to a sane person. Despite working thematically, these puzzles are rarely clever and always feel tedious.
Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a great story-driven game. The gameplay mechanics themselves feel solid enough, but there is nothing groundbreaking gameplay-wise. The story and exploration of psychosis are the attractions here, and they are presented in such a unique way that it’s definitely worth a playthrough.

Wow! Wow. I am very impressed. I'll be honest, this game sat in my library for a little while because I've played typing games in the past, and they always felt like a chore. Nothing made me want to keep playing, just tedious typing and annoying emphasis on proper finger placement.
This game has shattered all my annoyances with typing games by creating something I actually want to play.
Papercraft aesthetics are pretty overdone nowadays, but this game does the paper-craft / origami-like construction in a way that is actually plausible (for example, you can often see the folds to imagine how it's constructed), and fits the game mechanics and premise (you are typing, and the story's words appear on the paper ground around you).
You move the character using E, F, J, and I, instead of WASD, to help emphasize proper hand placement for typing to kill the monsters. At first I groaned, thinking "ugh, more emphasis on hand placement!", but you quickly get used to it and appreciate it. Typing to kill the monsters is actually entertaining, there are different types of monsters such as big, slow ones that use lots of small words (like "cat", "fog", and "big"), and small flying bugs that can be killed with just one letter ("H", "Q", "Z", etc). There are also larger "boss" bugs that take one or two very long tricky words, in-between monsters that take four or five letter words, and lots in between. The variety makes it enjoyable.
There are also powers that you unlock, such as fire and ice, that allow you to burn monsters (and skip the next word as they are burning) or freeze monsters in place (and allow more time for typing). You will also use the typing powers to destroy obstacles in your environment, or make flowers grow. I really liked how the words relate to the object, for example, rocks use words like "gypsum" and "stalagmite", brambles to burn use words like "ignite" and "tinder", and flowers to grow use flower words like "heather" and "poppy".
Probably the most entertaining is opening treasure chests, which either use treasure words (such as "money" and "award") or a fun alternation of two letters (such as "W", "O", "W", "O", "W" for a while).
Every word is subtitled by placing it directly on the landscape around you ("printed" on the paper as it is said) and the words remain on the ground forever (unless changed later, for example - your path may be blocked, and a commentary may appear about it, but later if you unblock the path, it will be replaced by something like "They broke new ground together").
Many alternate languages are present in the game to choose from using the options. This changes the displayed subtitles, words that appear over the bugs to type, and the spoken words. Additonally, different keyboard types are supported for the various languages. QWERTY is the default, but it also supports alternates for other languages such as QWERTZ, as well as alternative keyboard setups such as Dvorak, Colemak, and Workman. Interestingly, the game even distinguishes between spellings of British English and American English.
The game's difficulty will adjust depending on your typing speed. The developer has noted in the forums that it may take "several fails" initally for the speed to adjust for varying typing speeds and ability - for example, the game should adjust for a "hunt and peck" speed. The developer has also expressed that they want to ensure the game is accessible, and is willing to adjust the game settings to accomodate you - get in touch with them if you are interested. :)
I believe this game would be appropriate for younger children who can already read and are learning bigger words (the game reads all words aloud to you, and many of the words are synonyms of each other which could help improve their vocabulary). However, even adults will enjoy the game's aesthetic and the challenge. Because it adjusts to your typing speed, it will be a challenge to just about anyone, equal to or slightly above their ability. While I do think young children would enjoy the game (I'm no expert, but maybe as young as 7?), it definitely does not feel "dumbed down" or like a "children's" game.

In short, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is a super fun game with some great writing and awesome characters. If you enjoyed 2016s Doom and The New Order, you're going to have a great time...
...if you can deal with some technical issues.
Before I go on, here are my PC specs:
AMD RX 480 4GB (Using the 17.10.2 drivers)
8GB DDR4 RAM
Intel Core i5 6500 3.2Ghz
1TB HDD
120GB SSD
The last Wolfenstein game was basically unplayable on AMD cards, so I'm glad to see that this game is using Doom's engine. I am able to get above 60fps at 1080p Ultra settings. I can even bump to Uber settings with occasional stuttering. At ultra though I need to turn on Vsync because of the screen tearing and I don't have a high refresh rate monitor.
The big technical issue with this game is the crashing. When the game runs, it runs great. However there are times where the game crashes and freezes to the point where I can't even ctr alt del and I have to shut down my PC manually to regain control of my system. I have noticed this issue only happens if there are any programs or windows that are also running. For example, having a web browser open, or streaming software, or just any window open seems to increase the risk of these crashes. If I don't have anything other than Steam in the background and maybe Discord, the game runs super smooth and I can play for as long as I want and exit the game normally with no problems. This might be different depending on your machine.
I would recommend playing the game, but at your own risk. Make sure your drivers are up to date to better your chances of a smooth experience. Hopefully, a patch is released very soon so I can play this game with a peace of mind.

How to get FO3 working on Windows 10.
This worked for me (AMD FX-8350, Nvidia GTX780),  so I´ll share it with you.
1. Download Games for Windows LIVE Disabler
Just open the exe and select Disable G4WL.
2. Go to C:\users\yourname\Documents\My Games\Fallout3\FALLOUT.ini
Open the file with Notepad
Find bUseThreadedAI=0 and change it to bUseThreadedAI=1, immediately below it add a line with iNumHWThreads=2
This should be enough for most of you.

3. If the game crashes at a new game, download this modified d3d9.dll.
Go to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Fallout 3 goty\ and paste it there.
This dll makes FO3 think that you have a Nvidia 7900GS, so your graphic settings will be reset. Just adjust them to your liking again, most modern GPUs can run perfectly with the Ultra preset.
Don´t forget to enable all the data files in the launcher. For some reason, the DLCs come disabled by default.
