A LOT better than I originally thought it would be. When it was first released I was not at all interested, it looked cheap, generic, dull and just another fan fiction game with no substance. Damn, was I wrong. The base version only comes with one playable class(?) but with the DLC you can then choose from two more, the Thaumaturge which is basically your mage and the Arcane Mechanic wich is an engineer with cool gadgets.
Very different from most birds eye view RPG's I've played, different gearing and gemming mechanics and styles but it does not lack what only some can offer: a fun, changing, new, challenging, mass killing, awesome adventure.
The skill system works the same as most other games like this would, as you level up (killing monsteres, completeing quests, etc.) you gain skill poins, later on though you gain more per level but in turn your higher level abilities require more and one skill point (1, 2 and some 3). You have your main ability skills, (mostly activated and damaging abilities, some passive) Your Tricks ability page (special abilities that change or enhance game play [Thaumaturge can slow time for every thing around him, Arcane Mechanic can summon turrets, and other fun abilities]). And last are your Aura skills, you can have 2 auras on at a time that increase mana regen, critical damage boost, elemental damage increase, etc.
The game play, design, UI lay out and the game mechanics are very user friendly. One thing that most games lack is undoing skill point allocation. In this game you can remove points from skills one point at a time (for a fee, of course) so you don't totally throw you build out the window, you can instead make samll tweaks to it, which I love. You can do the same for you Ability points: Body(STR equiv) Dexterity(AGI euiv) Willpower (INT equiv) and Luck (magic item find, crit chance, dodge change modifier).
Your follower, Katarina, is a sassy spectre that helps out in battle but also adds a sense of humor to a seemingly bleak dark world. She has her own seperate Skillys and Abilities and you can change how she attacks and behave (Melee, Ranged, Passive while adding boosts to you). You can have her pick up items, and gold if you want, send her to town to do your shopping and she will back talk you the entire time. Different and weird at first, but she is a valuable asset to your goal of evil eradication.
There's a lot to say about this game, but you will just have to play it for your self to experience the fun and actually quite enjoyable graphics. There are some zones that feel laggy and I did have to tweak my video settings for it to be a little less glitchy at times (Running with two GTX 670 vid cards, i7 3.4Ghz, 16Gb RAM, 1 TB HD with a 240Gb SSD) my computer is more than capable of running any game at max graphics setting but I still experienced lag at times. Like any game, there are glitches and bugs that can some times even progression imparing, check the forums, the game has a built in repair function if a quest stops working or something similar, nothing major but it can be frustrating at times.
My over all verdict 8/10. Worth buying? Yes. Better with friends? Yes. I'ts a fun game and I have thoroughly enjoyed playing it.

A suprisingly good game. Some critics have dismissed Inversion as a Gears of War rip-off, and while it does have some obvious similarities I found that I enjoyed Inversion far more!
The story starts like a typical invasion story, but it actually has some crazy twists and becomes pretty interesting. I found myself compelled to keep playing to find out who the mysterious bad guys were and where they came from, and the answer did not disappoint. The game has colourful environments rather than being all grey or brown, and there is an impressive amount of attention to detail in the level design. The two heroes are much more likeable than the guys in GOW; they are tough guys but they are not cartoonish macho thugs, they are horrified by what is going on around them. I especially liked the player's partner Leo, who is very crass and vulgar but actually quite smart and the one who tries to figure out what is really going on. It also helps that in singleplayer your partner has excellent AI and is always a help rather than a hiderence.
The gameplay is a pretty competent cover-based third-person-shooter, but with a bunch of nice extra features. Inversion has impressive "Havok Destruction" physics that mean sustained fire will smash cover to pieces, so you have to keep moving rather than hide in one spot. There are fun bits where you are floating around in zero gravity or where walls or ceilings become the floor, which spices things up nicely.
Early in the game you aquire the Gravlink device and get special gravity powers. In the tutorial section you get to try out several abilities, but then this power is snatched away from you and you get a basic version that just lets you use Low Gravity to make objects and people float into the air.
Floating enemies take several seconds to adjust to their new situation before they resume shooting at you, and of course they are nice easy targets. The game includes typical red explosive barrels, but there are also yellow barrels that do nothing except leak when shot; however using low gravity on a yellow barrel will create a floating spherical blob of flammable liquid. You can also do a gravity shockwave attack that tears enemies to pieces, it's much better than a normal melee attack as it can kill multiple enemies, has a range of a couple of meters, and it can penetrate cover.
You gain more powers by killing bosses and taking components from their Gravlinks. You'll get the ability to grab or throw objects like Half-Life L2's gravity gun... in fact, it can even throw enemies at each other, so it is like the Super Gravity Gun that you get at the end of HL2! To prevent this from being ludicrously overpowered, so you can only grab and throw things that you have first made float using your zero gravity ability, but since you can make entire groups of enemies and objects float with just one or two low gravity blasts this is not a big inconvenience. Later you get an upgrade that allows you to throw huge objects like cars. It is especially important to remember this ability in tough fights; killing a giant boss enemy with an assault rifle takes an absurd amount of time, throwing objects at bosses is far more effective.
Later in the game you get High Gravity. You can use it on structures like guard towers and bridges to cause them to collapse, and you can cause hanging objects to fall to create cover. High Gravity pins tough enemies to the ground and make them helpless, while weaker enemies will be splatted against the floor and instantly killed. While in High Gravity mode your ability to grab and throw objects is replaced with a very effective defensive shield. The shield is essential for surviving battles in the last third of the game, and you have to get good at managing your energy so you can protect yourself and also have enough energy to do gravity attacks on enemies.
One criticism I have is that Inversion has a rather absurd number of cutscenes, like Max Payne 3 or Metal Gear Solid. You can skip them if you want to, though I recommend watching them otherwise you might miss an importatant plot point. (And in any case they were entertaining most of the time.)
This game is about messing with gravity, and I recommend that you do it constantly. If you just rely on your guns then it will seem like a pretty typical shooter, but the real fun comes from using your powers as often as possible. It is immensely satisfying causing a sniper to float out of cover, sucking him towards you and then punching his head off. Or running into the middle of a group of enemies, and just before being killed you do a ground shockwave attack and cause the entire group to explode into gory pieces. Ludicrous gibs = ludicrous fun.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful yet difficult at times, platformer with some very interesting play mechanics. It controls as good if not better than Super Meat Boy (SMB) with extra actions to overcome the many obstacles put before you such as the ability to rocket off enemies and their projectiles and the ability to pound into the ground.
You play as Ori, an orphan who was soon adopted by a forest spirit, Naru. Now, I won't say much more than this as the story is also amazing and is told though both the game play and cutscenes that utilise the game's music instead of words.
The art is very beautiful and has a strong glow for certain objects, enemies and projectiles. My first impressions of this style was 'This isn't going to work, it's going to get too confusing'. But I was dead wrong. The colours contrast really really well and are varied so much that it was hard to confuse the enemies and Ori.
To summarise, here's what I liked and under that are a couple of things I didn't quite like.
Likes:
- Controls like SMB (As a platformer, that's great! Use a controller.)
- The art (Reminds me of Fly'n, another beautiful game)
- Story (I may have cried a little during the first story bit)
- Attacks and abilities
- Ability Tree (I usually hate this mechanic in many games but this one was very simple and easy to learn)
Dislikes:
- I ran into a bug at the end where I couldn't pass a certain gate. (I was lucky enough to find a script to fix this however.)
- When the game is over, you cannot go back and get the rest of the collectables you missed

Dandelion is a very special game. But I must say, after playing Nameless, this one too became really important to me. My grasp on the English language is very limited, I’m sorry, but I’ll try my best to express how much this visual novel means to me.
This game will break your heart. It will break you in pieces, make you cry, and make you wish that things could’ve been different. But it will also make you smile, it will take all your broken pieces and put them together. This is without a doubt, one of the best visual novels I’ve ever played. The story is somewhat similar to Dandelion, but “darker” and most fitting to my personal taste. There’s a lot of touchy subjects such as fear of being abandoned/replaced, physical/mental abuse, obsession, etc. But nothing here is just thrown in the air, everything has an explanation, and you actually feel bad for the characters.
My favorite route was Tei’s. My heart really ached for him, and I cried. It’s been a long time since I’ve cried because of an otome visual novel, but his past is just too much to handle. I loved all the characters, but Tei…
He’s special.
The “true ending” blew my f*cking mind. I won’t spoil it, you’ll have to play the game. But I can tell you this: prepare your tissues because you’re going to cry
.
Cheritz is a really amazing developer team, their games have an unique style. I’m looking forward to play more of Mystic Messenger too, and I wish they can make another PC visual novel soon.
Yes, there are flaws in Nameless. But f*ck it. 10/10, totally worth every cent and if I could, I’d buy everything again.

You want some feels? You want some great art? You want some fantastic supporting female characters that aren't solely there to be love rivals? You like great voice acting?
This is the game for you.
Cheritz really pulled through with this one. Dandelion's MC is a sack of flour compared to Nameless' MC. I love going through all of the various routes, good and bad. Lance is best waifu.

This game will try your patience to a maddening degree.
I hated this game when I started playing it, made me ragequit and still annoys me to no end, but it grew on me once I learned how to work around the most frustrating aspects of it.  I understand why it does some of the things it does, so now it's more of a bittersweet flavour.
The pros:
Atmosphere and artwork.
Pacing and progression are well executed.
Stays challenging even after you've become familiar with it.
It doesn't overstay its welcome, not too long, not too short.
The characters are endearing in their simplicity.
The ability to access prior saves within the same slot is fantastic, gives you a chance to backtrack if you made a bad save.  The game doesn' t bring your attention to it though, because it is ultimately made by trolls -_-.
The cons:
The game has an obnoxious and cheap learning curve,  mostly due to abuse of spikes, instakill elements and mechanics that aren't 100% reliable.
Even maxing out the utility tree, not all items will show up on the map, and fake walls remain mostly the same even though you're supposed to be able to see through them. Feels rather useless.
You can obtain 100%  completion in areas without having collected all items, if you are a completionist this is an incredibly irritating aspect of the game, especially so in the illusionary Misty Woods.
Add to the above the fact that the game locks you out of four different areas in the game so you can't backtrack for items. Gating has never been seen positively in any videogame in history and it's just a cruel way to secure replay value.
The story feels so watered down it's bland, the ending ultimately suffers due to this, as it feels jerky and makes very little sense.
The music is gorgeous but ultimately is as generic as the story.
It's a fascinating game overall, definitely worth buying, but be warned that it must be approached with patience.

Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a tale of loss, torturous grief, and redemption told from the unique perspective of someone suffering from extreme psychosis. You play as Senua, a Celtic warrior woman who believes she is taking the head of her dead lover to Helheim in an effort to wrest his soul from the clutches of Hel. What ensues is a dark voyage into the psyche as Senua faces her demons as literal manifestations.
While not the first game to have a main character suffering from psychosis, it is probably the first game that has not only taken such great care to represent psychosis accurately, but also the first that brings that accurate representation  to the forefront making it an integral part of the protagonist’s journey from the very beginning.  Many games use sanity as a trick or storytelling device – here it is the story, and it allows you to experience firsthand the sort of distress these types of illnesses bring. Senua has suffered greatly in her life – both because of her mental health and the events in her life that have greatly exacerbated her condition. Sensua suffers so much you can’t help but root for her to succeed. Hellblade’s emphasis on psychosis not only works as an interesting vehicle for a story - Senua is such a sympathetic character, it helps raise awareness to the issue in the real world.
This sympathy is made possible by the great facial animations of Senua, as well as the performance of the actress that portrayed her. All of actors should be given credit, as not only is Hellblade’s story compelling, it is acted well and packaged in a beautiful, cinematic way.
Senua’s remaining tortures are in her head. She contantly hears voices that do everything from torment her to assist her, and as the player you are forced to play with these voices as well (well, unless you turn them off in the audio settings, but the narrative would suffer for it.)  Along with the graphical effects that mimic visual hallucinations, constantly being beset by voices can make for an oppressive experience. Hellblade is a relentlessly depressing game that made me feel genuinely uncomfortable at multiple points. The graphics are gorgeous with neat FMV-like effects. Real-world performances are almost projected across rocks or even darkness – memories hanging in the air like mist that interact with Senua, or drive the plot forward.
The combat is satisfying, as it feels like weapons have weight and it has a similar dodge, block and attack style as a Soulsborne game but without a stamina bar. The boss battles are also well done, with each boss being uniquely horrifying and possessing unique movesets. But spamming attacks and dodging are usually enough to bring success. You also don’t come across enemies organically; instead you are forced to face waves of them before you can proceed. This can feel as tedious as the puzzles tend to be. Most of the game’s obstacles are overcome by solving puzzles, many the puzzles consist of finding runes by making them out of shapes in the environment. Appropriate to the theme, Senua sees these shapes and patterns where there wouldn’t be to a sane person. Despite working thematically, these puzzles are rarely clever and always feel tedious.
Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice is a great story-driven game. The gameplay mechanics themselves feel solid enough, but there is nothing groundbreaking gameplay-wise. The story and exploration of psychosis are the attractions here, and they are presented in such a unique way that it’s definitely worth a playthrough.

As a casual gamer I choose to give this game a Positive review. However, I can see how some hardcore or no life gamers would give it a negative review.
I would say if you enjoy hyper real visual graphics, a great psychological story w/ seamless cinematic transitions that almost makes you feel like you're playing a movie then this might be worth picking up.
I can see why the devs only charged $30 for it and imo it’s worth it. However, I think I would have liked to have waited another year and paid $60 and addressed some of the issues I’ve listed below.
I hope this title generates enough revenue that the devs/publishers will make a sequel with well lets just say “more”. I heard one reviewer say it feels a lot like a tech demo and I can kinda see how they would say that but again it’s $30.
Visual Graphics 10/10:
One word “Beautiful”.
Music Score 10/10:
Very enriching, I enjoyed it very much.
Story 8/10:
I really enjoyed the story and as much as I want to give this a 10 because I relate to this story in a lot of ways; I feel the Senua’s story could have used a bit more depth as far as her history with her departed love, the history of her psychosis, etc but as my professor in college use to say, "Any story that leaves you wanting to know more is a good story." I will admit when I completed the game it had me in tears and it really left me with a feeling of still not knowing enough about Senua. Perhaps this will get addressed if there is a sequel.
Story-Telling 10/10:
Minus some of the issues about the actual story the story-telling is very well told. It feels a lot like playing a cinematic movie.
Character Acting 10/10:
One word “Amazing”.
Enemy AI ?/10:
I’m leaving this as a ? only because I played on auto setting and imo it wasn’t exactly that good or bad just kinda okay. I plan to play this on a harder difficulty to see if there is any difference.
Game Mechanics 7/10:
For the most part the game mechanics are good but lacking. Below I've listed a few issues that probably should have been addressed some were kinda deal breakers for me and some just kinda meh.
1. Character gets hijacked from player control if you choose to evade backwards to reposition. She would auto run right back to the nearest enemy.
2. No control over selecting our targets such as a tab target option to switch targets. This prevents you from having a focus target so you end up having to fight more than one target for the majority of the duration of the fights. I found this extremely annoying.
3. Puzzles were fun and somewhat innovative but they did become a bit redundant. I would have liked to have seen more variety and perhaps more puzzle combinations.
4. Senua’s run is pretty much like a slow jog. WAY TOO SLOW. Perhaps they could have implemented a sprint option.
5. For a linear game I don’t particularly enjoy backtracking. I’d rather be ported back once I have completed my task unless it’s an open world or static game play.
6. They really should have given us a 1st person mode to use while out of combat. I understand that certain areas and combat it’s necessary for 3rd person but having a 1st person option would have been nice. I would have used it.
7. This final issue really isn’t an issue more of what I would have liked to have seen or had more of physical objects that require jumping, crouching, and climbing kinda like we have in the Tomb Raider games.
Game performance 8/10:
I’m not giving this a 10 only because I found there were a few graphical game glitches when running the game at 21:9 3440x1440. 4K had no apparent visual glitches. Both resolutions ran at or above 60fps. I’m running this on a i7 6770k, 1080Ti.

Having played this game for dozens of hours via the Gameforge client, I now feel experienced enough to give you a rough overview over the game.
SKILL is a PvP online shooter though also features several PvE modes; the game covers most standard game modes like Blasting (arming/disarming a bomb), Seizure (stealing an object) and Escape as well as the standard TeamDeathMatch. For those SKILL offers several dozen maps with different layouts, from small arenas like Hangar to slightly more open ones like Russian Factory. It’s worth keeping in mind, however, that the maps in general are not too big, though usually offering multiple paths and a good mix of open and more linear parts. In addition you can participate in some so called party-modes which involve playing in arenas made of breakable glass floors or jumping over obstacles.
For everyone interested in coop-focused action there’re PvE modes against aliens and zombies as well as a moba-style mode with spawning alien bots as well as a leveling-up system.
On the technical side the game is solid, with nice sound effects and weapon models though overall slightly dated graphics; when being in a tense multiplayer match, you probably won’t notice this too much though. It has to be said, however, that the game suffers from some performance troubles due a not really perfect optimisation which seem to have gotten worse over time. You may also encounter some connection problems from time to time which seem to appear out of nowhere but usually disappear as miraculously as they appeared.
And yes, as in most F2P games you will also find hackers here in SKILL. Most of the time their numbers are rather low with the exception of some rare “hacker-waves”. While public matches are mostly fine, they seem to be a more common annoyance in clan matches.
Regarding clans and eSports in general: The game features a built-in matchmaking system for clans as well as special channels for them, while the public matches are separate. Gameforge recently announced the end of the eSports leagues due to a lack of active players there, though maintaining the so called Go4Skill cup with money prizes as well as sponsoring community-organised tournaments.
Of course you will find a lot of equipment items like hats, gloves, t-shirts etc in the ingame shop as it’s common for F2P games. The basic items are available for the normal currency SP which you can earn, more advanced ones which usually give you a money and experience boost have to be bought with Cash, the premium currency. This includes character skins which completely change your whole appearance as well as boosters, weapon camos etc.
Talking about weapon: SKILL features a large amount of non-customizable weapons for every playstyle – all available for SP. You can set-up up to three different loadouts you can switch between during a match, consisting of one main gun, sidearm and special weapon (like throwing axes, bows, …) plus 3 different grenades. There’re, however, a couple of advanced weapons with shinier camos and attachments like better scopes which can only be obtained via the so called capsule market.
Here you have to buy capsules with Cash to get a chance of winning one of those special guns. It’s pretty much a luck-based system though even if the capsule doesn’t drop the wanted weapon, you still get another item, camo or some SP.
The capsule weapons have a slight stat-boost over their normal brethren, though it’s too small to make any difference in the game. The game still is true to it’s name and very much dependant on SKILL.
It has to be said though, that there’re slightly troubling tendencies, with the last update introducing a gun with heavily improved stats for roughly three-times the price of the normal capsules. Let’s hope they don’t continue this road.
In more or less regular intervals new events are activated in the game. They usually last for only 2 or 3 weeks and aren’t really creative; the prizes are okay and can get you a temporary version of those precious capsule guns or the premium skins.
Overall the update policy currently is a little bit weird, with a large break between the last two updates. It also has to be said that most updates only contain new content like maps, weapons, skins etc and only rarely additional features. Looking at the amount of requests and suggestions by the community since the launch in 2013 it seems like the developers are not really interested in adding new features, tweaks or fixing things.
The VIP system which basically is some kind of subscription model currently offers a boost to your EXP and SP as well as access to a couple of silver or gold weapons which have the advantage of not having to be repaired. There’re some other, minor extras (special emblems, reduced quick-spawn costs, …) but overall it currently isn’t very attractive thing to invest in except right at the start of the game, where you’re more likely in money-troubles and can use the VIP-system to avoid repair-costs.
SKILL definitely isn’t the holy grail of multiplayer shooters though it’s definitely a solid game with which you can have fun for a couple of hours, even more probably in a clan. Fortunately the game so far stayed away from the dark path of P2W, though as mentioned recent changes are troubling, especially combined with the slow updates.
If you’re looking for a free, fast and simple PvP shooter or some horde-mode PvE action why not give this game a try – you most probably will spend some fun hours with it, there’re worse alternatives on the market right now ;)

This is a cool game and all but it has its negatives that quickly spoil the experience.
First, docking and undocking is tedious as hell and gets very old very quickly. Unfortunately you're essentially required to do it every time, since using a tugboat is $100K a pop -- so docking and undocking at any given port if you don't want to deal with this tedious docking mechanic is $200k. When you're starting out and your profit margins are very thin this isn't feasible.
Second, in the campaign your investor is essentially the villain. Every quarter she takes what seems like half of your cash and when you finally scrape up enough to rank up to the next size ship she saddles you with an impossible contract which requires you to ship an insane amount of goods to a specific port (including things that you can't even ship yet without ship upgrades that you can't buy) or lose $10M. Guess when this automatically kicks off? When you hit $10M in cash. Oh the best part? You have around a month to deliver everything. Twice. Twice I hit this point and this impossible burden combined with the investor taking her quarterly cut left me bankrupt. I would keep trying but the aforementioned docking mechanic saps my will to start over.
Third, the sailing mechanic isn't very deep. When your ships are sailing you'll get popups like "there's a storm a comin" and it asks you if you want to sail around it or sail through. I can't tell the difference between the two aside from the fact that sailing through practically destroys your ship. This is fine, but if a game is going to abstract this sort of thing but then require you to micromanage things like docking it seems a little schizophrenic.
Take these three things and it turns out to be a game that is profoundly unfun which is a shame because it's the first thing that really ruins it. Slashing towing fees would go a long way to making the game better.

Every route is written in-depth, and there is an excellent overarching plot tying everything together. Even if the characters aren't your cup of tea, at the end of the game, you will be able to appreciate them for who they are and who they have grown into.
Of course, like in every other game, there are also flaws - the typos, the occassional awkward CG, but that's not what is truly important. This game is able to narrate a unique, wholesome, tear-jerking story that is interesting and varied. There's a melancholic, pervasive quality to many scenes, so much so that you get emotionally invested in the characters. Most of all, through presenting the stories of a few individuals, this game made me think more about dolls, human beings, and the world at large.

Well worth the price, Nameless is undoubtedly the most well written visual novel I have ever played. Its depth and complexity took me by surprise, romance aside the plot is not at all what is expected and very well done. Emotive and full of heart, the core messages of this game are beautiful. I could go on and on and on but, the short version is simply that this game is truly beautiful.
Writing aside, the art is really nice, the voice acting adds a lot to the game (yes, even though it's in Korean) and as mentioned by many other players, there are typos, but they are sparse and don't really take away from the game. It's well scored; music, art and writing working together to create a story that will undoubtedly surprise you.
The characters all feel (ironically) quite human, and for the first time in any otome-type game I enjoyed every single character route immensely. The best part, the crowning achievement of Nameless for me, is the way the character arcs were handled. Every character had their flaws, and these flaws were not ignored or brushed over, or highlighted yet left unconfronted, or worse, glorified (EG AMNESIA). They were handled exceptionally well. Everyone deserves to be loved. Certain characters rang alarm bells for me after bad experiences with previous otome games but nothing was as it seemed. Whoops, I said I wouldn't ramble so I'll wrap it up.
This is an otome game, and thusly it is definitely directed at women but honestly, I would reccomend this game to any fan of visual novels or interactive stories, regardless of gender or sexual preference. You'll get more out of it if you like romance games, of course, but all round it's a lovingly crafted story about so much more than love. I was extremely skeptical heading into this game (just as I was before playing Dandelion - Wishes Brought To You) but once again, Cheritz took me on a surprising journey I won't forget anytime soon. I wish there were more games like this!

So. I got this game as part of a Humble Bundle and had considered picking it up before the bundle. And what I got was a very nice little surprise.
What this game is:
A fun way to sharpen your typing skills
A fox riding simulator (a major plus in my book)
A relaxing way to kill a few hours in the main story
An engrosing and well-designed method of telling the story of the life of a woman in a way that isn't really the most traditional
A beautiful work of art. The graphical style, while not the most advanced was incredibly charming and I never grew tired of seeing the world literally unfold in front of me.
What this game isn't:
An incredibly deep mechanical experience that you will rave about for ages. Seriously. This game is simple in concept and well-executed, but don't expect to spend hours picking apart how it all works.
An incredibly difficult game. This isn't Dark Souls. It will push you if you are a horrible typist, but if you are a half-decent typist who is familiar with the wonderful concept of the home row, it's going to be relatively easy, even though there are going to be some tense moments in some of the battles. It will amp up your WPM, but never your heart rate.
A fox hunting simulator. Another major plus.
All in all, it's a nifty little game, with simple mechanics that have been executed well, in a beautiful package with a very wonderfully told story that isn't actually the story you think you are getting when you start playing.

I own around 180 games on Steam and a few on the side. This is the first game I write a Steam review of, and I do it just to tell you how much you need this.
Apart from being absolutely beautiful with music you can listen to over and over, the story is unlike any I have ever come across. It is so minimalistic yet so cute and heartwarming (as well as heartbreaking). It tells it incredibly well. The game is difficult, and you will respawn over and over on certain parts just like way back when games were generally hard. In the same way, there are no annoying tips and tricks and no constant map markers; you really feel accomplished when you solve a puzzle or pass a difficult part. It's like they tried recreating what it meant to game back then, only this time the graphics are all shiny and stuff.
Of course there are some downsides to the game, like a limited options menu and (if you need this type of thing) the lack of direction I talked about earlier (sometimes I did want to know which way was right so I could explore the wrong way). First of all, I'm super grateful to Cheritz that almost all their games are available on Steam. Not a common case, right? Most otome-games are published for PS Vita, so Cheritz immediately got my loyalty.
One of the strongest points of this game is its setting. Have you ever pitied your old abandoned toys when you started to grow up? Have you ever thought that virtual persons (dolls, fiction characters, idols of all sorts) are more reliable and safe for close relationships than real people? Have you thought that those abandoned by us still remember everything? The game will give you time to think over this stuff.
'Nameless' protagonist has her precious ball-joint dolls suddenly turned into people. Every doll has its initial program, the number of features created by a puppet-maker. When turned into human every doll is doomed to strong character development. It's quite interesting to watch how the circumstances make everyone widen their horizon.
So, the obvious pros of the game are:
- Interesting setting.
- Visible character development.
- Strong protagonist. Eri is not a typical otome heroine, what a relief.
- Interesting characters. BTW, the cast has two yanderes. It's up to you if you like it or not but they are well written. Side characters are also attractive.
- Tons of various bad endings.
- Beautiful artwork. There are many CGs, rather detailed and nice. The art is much better than you find in average otome game. The backgrounds are rather poor though. The characters are animated.
- All routes are connected with a common plot. In the end you will unlock a heartrending story of a secret character.
- Gorgeous voice acting.
- The price is rather affordable.
Talking of cons...
- I'd say that the group interaction is rather poor. Well, Tei doesn't get along with Yuri and Lance dislikes Red... It could be more complicated. It could be better.
- Sometimes it's all too melodramatic but we're talking about South Korea here. Wouldn't expect less from a country that makes doramas =)
All in all, 'Nameless' is incredible. It's a high-quality otome game with interesting setting and captivating characters. Not my number one, but I'd give it the second or the third place.

Never played this game but steam say that I actually did so instead of judging the game here's a cool way to make skinny guacamoles with homemade baked tortilla chips :
Skinny Guacamole:
2 medium green sweet peppers
2 medium fresh poblano chile peppers
1 bulb garlic
1/2 teaspoon olive oil
2 roma tomatoes, seeded and chopped
1 serrano pepper, minced
2 medium ripe avocados, halved, seeded, peeled, and diced
1 teaspoon lime zest
2 tablespoons lime juice
1/2 teaspoon salt
Baked Tortilla Chips:
Corn tortillas
Olive oil spray
Salt
For the guacamole:
Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a 15 x 10 x 1-inch baking pan with foil; set aside. Quarter, stem, and seed the peppers. Place pepper quarters, cut sides down, in the prepared pan. Cut off the top half inch of the garlic bulb to expose ends of individual cloves. Leaving garlic bulb whole, remove any loose, papery outer layers. Place bulb, cut end up, on a double thickness of foil. Drizzle with the oil. Bring foil up around bulb and fold edges together to loosely enclose. Place foil packet on the pan with the peppers.
Roast peppers and garlic for 20 to 30 minutes or until pepper skins are charred and garlic cloves feel soft. Allow to cool about 15 minutes. When garlic head is cool enough to handle, squeeze garlic paste out of the individual cloves.
In a food processor combine roasted pepper quarters and the garlic paste. Cover and pulse until combined, but still slightly chunky.
In a large bowl, combine tomatoes and serrano pepper. Add roasted pepper and garlic combination and stir to combine. Add diced avocado, lime zest, lime juice, and salt. Gently toss to combine.
Serve immediately or cover the surface with plastic wrap and chill for up to 1 hour.
For the chips:
Cut corn tortillas into wedges and place on a foil-lined baking sheet. Spray lightly with olive oil spray and season with salt, to taste.
Bake in a 350° F oven for 8-10 minutes or until lightly golden brown.

I really wanted to like this game, I really truly did.
During the big sale I saw that To The Moon was only $2 and snatched it up right away because I'm cheap. For the years I've known about the game I've heard nothing but great things about it, and while my expectations weren't high, even things I didn't have standards for were disappointing.
The gaming mechanics were terrible, within the first ten minutes I had to navigate my way to the house because I kept bumping into flowers. A flower blocked my path. And this continued for most of the game, small objects blocking my way and I couldn't tell what would block me and what wouldn't. Lining up to interact was also hard as most things were off-center.
The pacing was entirely too fast, I get that it's a short game, but there was no time to take anything in. Most of the gameplay is walking around and interacting with things hoping to find orbs to break an orb to do a puzzle to get 2 minutes of "character development" (I use that VERY loosely) and you do it over again.
There's literally nothing else to do in this time.
The humor and dialogue between the doctors is extremely weak. For 2011 omnomnom and weaboo jokes were probably the norm and funny, but in 2016 I'm just cringing. Neil is extremely unlikeable and it got to the point where I started skipping most if not all of his dialogue because I couldn't stand to listen to him anymore.
The horse part with no explanation kept me trapped for a good five minutes,
The way the game treated River was also pretty terrible.
I just couldn't feel any emotion for anyone because of all these things. I'm disappointed that I didn't like the game as much I thought I would, however I'm glad I only paid $2 instead of the full $10, it's definitely NOT worth $10.
However, the pros are: The music is wonderful and River was the only character with somewhat of a personality and she was the only character I could really feel for, despite John constantly bringing her down. If I'd replay this for any reason, it'd be to study River's character more.
Update after playing the minisodes: Even more boring and a waste of time, none of the characters developed and the open ended ending
was extremely underwhelming because nothing was done with it. There's a million unanswered questions and there's never going to be answers to them. I played out of curiosity when I should've just left it alone.

This game is the reason I have bought a lot of other puzzle/platform games which didn't interest me in the past. Bought it on sale, decided to give it a crack and haven't looked back.
Stunning visuals, devious puzzles with an almost perfect learning curve make this game amazing. Essentially the game revolves around having three charactors, Thief, Warrior and Wizard who all have unique abilities. The Thief can shoot a bow, and use a grapple to swing around and over obstacles, the Warrior is your melee charactor, with sword, shield and hammer, which can be used to bash through certain obstacles, and the Wizard who can leveitate objects and create boxes and ramps. As the game progresses, some of the chests you find will equip you with loot that enhance existing abilities, and also allow you to use them in different ways. This is alongside a relatively basic levelling system, which allows you enhance your abilities also.
Some of the puzzles will have you using all three charactors to solve.
The achievements blend well with the game, and will have you playing each level over over to find all the secrets and experience. Finding some of the secrets will leave you scratching your head, until ultimately leading to the AHA! moment when you finally work out how to get there/find it.
9.5/10 for me and definately worth buying. The fact that it comes on sale for $1 relatively regularly means this game just needs to be your inventory no matter what.

LEGO Worlds is a sandbox game developed by Traveller’s Tale and published by Warner Brothers Interactive Entertainment, releasing on Steam in early access in June 2015. The game is still in Early Access and whilst the developers seem to be updating the game on a monthly basis, what they do update isn’t exactly ground breaking stuff and nothing is on the horizon for resolving the issues this game has currently.  Now, followers of my reviews will know I absolutely love LEGO games but sandbox games is probably one of my least favourite genres so I was a little sceptical going into this title but I hoped the LEGO name would carry it a little.
Gameplay wise, there actually isn’t that much to do sadly. You are parachuted into a randomly generated world using a seed system and you will encounter other Lego figures, creatures, items and vehicles. Once you encounter them, they will be “unlocked” – this will allow you to purchase said item using bolt bricks which you pick up by destroying objects in the world or by slaying enemies.  That’s it – there isn’t any crafting system, no little objectives to complete, no story, quests, nothing, just an open world with very little interaction in it. This left me very disappointed as other LEGO games are known for having exciting open worlds and little Easter eggs here and there.
The other game play element is the building mode, which is essentially the creative mode from games like Minecraft.  This was the feature I was most looking to trying out, I had craved a game where you have unlimited bricks that allowed you to just play LEGOs digitally. Minecraft was often referred to as digital LEGO when it first released, now we have just that. Let me start with the plus points of this mode; you have all the tools to build absolutely anything you want; the huge amount of different types of bricks you have at your disposal is impressive. LEGO Worlds also has a very good terrain controlling tool, much like Minecraft has but it is far better designed and you can modify your world without causing your PC to grind to a halt. Sadly these plusses are marred with the game’s biggest fault – the controls and camera.  The camera in this game is absolutely atrocious; it prevents you from having any sort of enjoyment out of the anything! Because you have such a large selection of small Lego Bricks to use when constructing your models, you obviously need to be very precise with your placement of bricks, the camera does everything and anything it can to prevent that and just ends up jumping all over the shop, not moving where you ask it to, or just plain and simply not working at all. This made the game unplayable and left me very salty.
Graphically the game is made out of Lego bricks, but there is so much visual noise on screen as literally everything is made out of bricks so all the walls and mountains are built piece by piece out of small individual bricks, which can be a little off putting when you are looking out over the world. It almost comes across as being a little pixelated which some may find distasteful.  I would have liked to see it take on the same style that the other LEGO games use, where objects are built using bricks, but the actual environment has a sort of split between bricks and normal material. The music is also fairly off putting too; it doesn’t fit the LEGO universe at all, I felt like I was marching into battle at times, it is very regimental and just not right for this type of game.
I’ve been playing LEGO Worlds for just about two hours now and I feel like I actually wanted to stop playing way before now.  This would easily be one of my favourite games if I could actually play it, I would be able to spend hours upon hours in this game just playing LEGOs – this is the sort of game that you could easily introduce small children to playing if it wasn’t so damn hard to control.
Apart from the technical problems with the camera, I also had slight performance problems too. Even on my rig I wasn’t able to get a steady 60 fps. This isn’t a rare problem either, after checking the forums people with much beefier rigs than mine were also experiencing performance problems of not even being able to breach the 30 fps mark which is absolutely absurd for the hardware being used.
This game is quite obviously in no state both technically and mechanically to be considered a worthy purchase right now. I am astounded this has been marked as “Very positive” for overall reviews because it is just unplayable. I seriously hope the devs are able to fix the problems with the camera as I really would love to play this game some more, but right now it is not worth your time or money.  It has all the potential to be a really good creative game, not so much on the “survival” side but to use it as a tool to just build LEGOs till your hearts content. I am going to rate this as a not recommended for now.
1) Stay away,
3) Purchase with caution
4) Potentially good game
5) Worthy of purchase even in current state
6) Highly recommended

Inversion is your typical "Take cover and regen" when damaged 3rd person shooter.
Weapons will start to advance as you get along, thus standard weapons turn energized etc.
The different part is gravity however, as you get a device capable of manipulating gravity. At first it's the weak (Low Gravity) only allowing you to lift small things, but also enemies to drag them out of cover. Later you can throw cars and charge up using a classic "Finger of Death" ability on enemies which instagib them. You can also throw lava...
Last upgrade being "High Gravity" allow you to make everything much more heavy. Enemies will be pushed to the ground, or groups can be insta gibbed after you "Low" lifted them from the ground and then "High" smash them into the floor turning them into a mighty puddle of goo.
Last but not least, the gravity is major in many areas allowing you to walk on walls, ceilings or fly through the air. It's like space floating just with breathable air and sound :P
The story is also quite interesting, and is a big twist compared to most games. I was sceptical with the game being released from Namco, but the game is overall a good experience.

Inversion is a solid shooter with a nice concept and an engaging storyline. There's not much variety or innovation in the gameplay, nevertheless it accomplishes what it sets out to do very well. It features fun combat with plenty of blood and gore, good level design, a decent narrative, and pretty graphics. I especially like the way the game dumps you into the middle of an invasion with no idea who your enemies are or what they want. The progression of the story is very well done even if the dialogue is a bit cheesy, and the storyline itself is surprisingly original and feeds you a little at a time, to keep you interested. There are some very nice twists which I didn't expect.
If you're in the mood for an action packed Michael Bay style third person shooter, this game is very good value for money. If you like Gears of War or Resistance Fall of Man, you will like Inversion.

So what's there to say about Inversion? A lackluster story and generic gameplay hidden behind semi-high production values. From the boring enemies that constantly remind me of God Hand but are nowhere near as interesting, to gameplay that promises to do so much and delivers so little it becomes more of a chore than a fun coop experience.
Some things it promises are destructable environments and controlling gravity. Well, most of the environment that gets destroyed is YOUR cover by enemies, not the other way around. As for the gravity powers, there's nothing very spectacular about it. It's a mix of Half Life and Psi Ops: Mindgate Conspiracy. Now this game is touted as a coop one. How does that hold up?
There are a lot of action sequences and using your powers to help each other or provide cover fire is important, but it's all marred by the soft relationship context moments where you have to 'bro' boost over a ledge or 'bro' hold a garage-ish door open so that the other guy can go through. It ends up becoming an awkward moment that really does nothing to help you feel like you're really working together to accomplish something. Instead of smart puzzles, you just get 'bro'ments.
By the end of the game, you will feel like there should and could have been so much more. It's sad because it could have been a great arcade experience, but focuses too much on its unpolished story and clunky gameplay moments to carry it across when those are its weakest points. The result is something that makes you want to finish but never provides any incentive to return. A decent 1 time play, but wait until it's super cheap before purchasing.

Everybody look at me 'cause I'm sailin' on a boat!
After two hours of play, I have to say that I'm impressed.  After just a couple tutorial missions (each and all skippable in turn), I was turned loose to make or break my company.  After a few lucrative ore contracts, I found myself smuggling contraband on the Mediterranian.  And got busted.  And my cargo seized.  And fined.  And my ship impounded for a week.  A time-based contract I still had in the hold expired, so there were penalties there.  And harbor masters didn't care to allow convicted smuggers in their ports, so harbor fees went up.  All that in two hours and not a moment that felt repeatative.
A few features that I liked:  Your home port determines what bonuses your company gets.  I picked Lisbon for +5% on ore contracts and -10% to fuel.  The trick is, the smaller the port, the larger the bonuses.  So you have a reason to keep smaller ports and the ships that can service them.
There is some ship customization.  The Feeder I started with had three levels of Hull and Engine upgrades, which increased range and speed respectively.  There was also a license upgrade that would allow me to carrry what appeared to be hazardous waste.  Unfortunately, there does not appear to be options for custom paint or appearance (other than your ship name emblazoned upon the stern and bow).
I remember reading a comment somewhere saying that the music was repeatative and annoying.  To me, it sounded like every port had it's own song.  And each port felt VERY unique.  I'm already developing favorites and least favorites.
The only meh item I encountered dealt with other ship traffic.  Large ships move fast and looked intimidating at first, but it turns out they can stop on a dime and give the player right-of-way.  I would have liked to have seen navigation lights and right-of-way implemented (and fines for failure to obey maritime traffic laws).
Anyway, back to my ship.  I'm saving up for a fleet.  And I'm naming all my vessels after internet porn sites.

Having played for just over an hour now here's what I have to say about the game. If you ever played Port of Call, Transocean - The Shipping Company is a modern version of that. Everything from the time progression to "status" or "reputation" to unlock more ships.  There are some nice features of the sim that are handy to use such as the financial statements & diagrams, also the ability to take out loans is great as well. I didn't bother playing the campaign, just went right into the free play.
After about 20-30 minutes of contracting out my small feed ship i unlocked all the ports of europe, thereafter I unlocked the entire world. I gained enough capital to purchase some bigger pre-panamax ships and began trading the lucrative routes.  Graphics wise the sim is pleasing to the eyes, beautiful colors, non-cluttered interface, lots to look at without getting bombarded with useless information.
There isn't a real challenging component to free play that I observed, eventually your larger vessels experience massive profit margins. If you complete a contract for 30 million euros, your fuel costs will only be about 5% of that, which is fine I guess, but I have a feeling that real shippers experience much more turbulent expenses. I'm not complaining, just, thinking out loud.
Anyways, this sim is shouting for tankers & drybulker vessels, stock market simulation, buyouts, further player interaction with other AI shipping companies (or even other players!) I hope Deck13 doesn't simply abandon this just yet. Oh and wait, there is more.
Many of you know the embarressing and disasterous repuation that German devs/publishing firms have for releasing unfinished products then abandoning them, i must say within the hour of playing, I didnt crash once, experience a bug or anything like that. It was flawless. Congrats!
Anyways I'll swing a 8/10 would play again. Thanks.

Van Helsing is definately not a game without flaws, but for the most part they all seem to have counterpoints.  The lack of meaningful character customization is off-set by the tightly focused story-driven nature of the game.  The static maps kill replayability a bit, but also allow for better designed set pieces.
The skill system is a shallow ocean- giving the illusion of depth but in order to be viable you really need to pick a set of a couple skills and pour all your points into them. I can't speak for the ranged tree as I primarily played melee, your choices are somewhat limited given the crazy mob density that this game throws at you- which, don't get me wrong, was definately a positive- but it means that you need abilities that will kill a lot of guys at once in order to keep from being overwhelmed or whittling guys down at a choke point one at a time for hours on end. Then, while you're doing that you realize you could just be Earthquaking all the guys in a row and be done 10 times quicker.
In short, Van Helsing is worth the price of admission, especially if you can catch it on sale.  It's a fun, short romp that does what it advertises, just don't expect a Diablo/Torchlight/Path of Exile killer.

This is basically a space survival game in one huge universe. You have the options of choosing to follow the main storyline or just go out and about just exploring the universe or settling down in a home planet of your choosing and follow the many side quests. There are 4 difficulty levels with the hardest being permadeath (everything is wiped upon death), and the easiest being unlimited amount of resources to explore and build anything to your hearts content. The game is rewarding in that they are always adding new content and the fact that the game universe is so monumentally huge with a range of planets to explore all from the frozen cold harsh snowy planets to the radioactive and extra hot and beyond. I bought this game when the Foundation expansion came out, played twenty hours and then wrote a review giving it a qualified recommendation. After that I took a long break, logging in again only to see what the Path Finder update had added. Unfortunately I managed to delete my original save (not an easy thing to do) so I had to go back right to the start with the tiny inventories and weak multitool. I played another thirty-five hours, enjoyed it, and am still playing.
NMS is the game that people seem to love to hate but if you have time, and maybe like to play while listening to music or a podcast or VOD, it's really a very solid game. The visuals are often gorgeous, it's stable, there is a sense of challenge & achievement. As my journey extends I find myself looking for a planet that would make a good base: the journey becomes more about what you want to achieve and how much you are willing to do to get it. It's not fun exactly but it's compelling, it has a gameplay loop.
I'm not arguing that the people who attack this game are wrong, but anyone coming to it now should know that Hello Games have done quite a lot to add features and that not every criticism of the game was about the game itself: a lot of it was about the pre-launch hype. Few gamers will be interested in such a lonely, grinding game but if you think you might be one of them, NMS is a pretty good experience, and it could even be seen as offering value for money at full price..

Transitioning a franchise from 3D to 2.5D can be a daunting task, as it can alienate the fanbase that's used to the traditional gameplay the franchise has established on.  Fortunately, Assassin's Creed Chronicles: China is  a game that successfully pulled it off.  Despite the limitations of 2.5D the game still manages to be enjoyable.  It helps that the smooth controls, the beautiful graphics, and challenging gameplay are here.
The story is a bit lackluster with cutscenes limited to paintings, but it shows the character development of Shao Jun, who was once a fledgling waif seeking help from Ezio way back in Embers.  It's a shame that her voice actress wasn't retained although the new one is fitting once she hits the elder status.
I can't help but compare this to Arkham Origins: Blackgate, being both games that transitioned from 3D to 2.5D.  I felt that Assassin's Creed is way more fun compared to the Batman game, which felt like a chore while playing it.  The only thing that this AC game comes up short against Blackgate is the crappy combat mechanics, although it can be justified for encouraging the use of stealth.
Overall, this game is a good experience.  I might get India and Russia sometime in the future if I have spare cash to spend.

So far it's the only Early Access game i seriously regret i bough. For more then a year the game has been sitting in my inventory, it has gone through at least 3 major concept changes, and now it's only a shade of what i've been buying.
First it was lonely gathering survival experience in some realistic, vast, long abandoned area. Not unlike TLD, but with interesting, even if simplistic design, and a little twist of having 4 dogs with diffirent possible stats and needs, about which you should've care, and you could've untie one dog and take it for a hunt with you.
Then the map transformed into abomination: it was islands connected to each other by some narrow bridges of ice, floating in iced waters. It still was somewhat realistic, with some shipwrecks and such, and core mechanics were mostly untouched.
Then it turned into alienated-i-don't-know-what with some weird buildings scattered around the map, weird looking structures player can build, and some placeholder for the something-to-be-finished-later that looked like an energy rifle of sorts. Looting was almost completely eliminated, and gameplay become somewhat hollow. Map has changed yet again, and was close to the current version, i think.
Somewhere inbetween those two paragraphs villagers were added, and their functions has been slowly evolving into what we have now. Player were now required to gather resources for the village to survive incoming storm. Another interesting idea, by the way.
Then ability to untie one dog for a hunt, as well as stats for these dogs has been eliminated. There was sled inventory at some point as well, not anymore. It's now merely a mean of transportation rather then mobile defence and inventory for few more items.
There were also numerous HUD and icons redesigns, and i'm sure alot more i've missed.
Now buildings and villagers took yet another regesign, yet another mechanics changes are coming, and everything looks quite nice. For now. But for how long, it remains to be seen.
I may be mistaking about which feature has been added or cut when, but i hope my main point is clear: Since the day i've bought it, it is now 3 times not the game i bought.

I really wanted to like this game, I really truly did.
During the big sale I saw that To The Moon was only $2 and snatched it up right away because I'm cheap. For the years I've known about the game I've heard nothing but great things about it, and while my expectations weren't high, even things I didn't have standards for were disappointing.
The gaming mechanics were terrible, within the first ten minutes I had to navigate my way to the house because I kept bumping into flowers. A flower blocked my path. And this continued for most of the game, small objects blocking my way and I couldn't tell what would block me and what wouldn't. Lining up to interact was also hard as most things were off-center.
The pacing was entirely too fast, I get that it's a short game, but there was no time to take anything in. Most of the gameplay is walking around and interacting with things hoping to find orbs to break an orb to do a puzzle to get 2 minutes of "character development" (I use that VERY loosely) and you do it over again.
There's literally nothing else to do in this time.
The humor and dialogue between the doctors is extremely weak. For 2011 omnomnom and weaboo jokes were probably the norm and funny, but in 2016 I'm just cringing. Neil is extremely unlikeable and it got to the point where I started skipping most if not all of his dialogue because I couldn't stand to listen to him anymore.
The horse part with no explanation kept me trapped for a good five minutes,
The way the game treated River was also pretty terrible.
I just couldn't feel any emotion for anyone because of all these things. I'm disappointed that I didn't like the game as much I thought I would, however I'm glad I only paid $2 instead of the full $10, it's definitely NOT worth $10.
However, the pros are: The music is wonderful and River was the only character with somewhat of a personality and she was the only character I could really feel for, despite John constantly bringing her down. If I'd replay this for any reason, it'd be to study River's character more.
Update after playing the minisodes: Even more boring and a waste of time, none of the characters developed and the open ended ending
was extremely underwhelming because nothing was done with it. There's a million unanswered questions and there's never going to be answers to them. I played out of curiosity when I should've just left it alone.

Wow. Just wow. This game is a cut above. If there is one RPG to top all RPGs, this would be it.
If you haven't played the game, stop reading now. Devote 4 hours to play this all in one go, you will not regret it. The best way to play a Freebird game is completely blind. With that said, this review contains spoilers.
Graphics:
Beautifully crafted 16-Bit styled spritework. Everything looks defined, this is one of the few retro styled games to get pixel art right. It is perfect, exquisite in every aspect.
Music:
Stunning. Just amazing. Beautiful piano music, expertly made to suit the gameplay. I highly recommend purchasing the soundtrack yourself, to keep anyone from listening to it would be criminal.
Story:
If "To The Moon" has a defining feature, this is it. The story is probably the most effective and most powerful you'll see.  After 30 minutes, you are opened to a deep, rich storyline. It will make you cry. It'll make you smile. It'll make you feel alot of things. You will be invested in the characters, this is one of few RPGs to nail this point.
And thats it. I literally have no other words to describe how good this game is. You truly do have to play it in order to fully appreciate it. And that ending. My god.

FJong is a short, but fun little physics puzzle game.
Your objective is to make the "Pelicans" get to the delicious magical "Flying Candy" by triggering switches or just doing some tricky platforming.
The difficulty comes from gauging your power and distance with the "arrow" indicator...basically if you've played Worms or Angry Birds you'll be familiar with how this game works at a base level.
Trial and error will be the name of the game as you try to aim for 3 (and later, 4) star completion scores.
=================================
The game is clearly meant (or was on) Mobile Devices, but it isn't a huge detriment and the devs appeared to transition the game rather well to PC format.
Music is calming but very limited. You'll hear the same sexy saxophone solo pretty frequently...but it's not mind numbing so that's a plus.
There are some frustrating spots (namely 4 Star, level 7) that seem to be at the whims of the RNG gods in terms of getting your Pelican where you want it to be. Rest assured, it CAN be done but it's extremely frustrating after about 20 restarts or so.
A couple puzzles make use of the Heavy Pelican quite interestingly for achieving 3 and 4 stars. It's satisfying to figure out those little tricks.
=============================================
If you like Physics Platforming puzzle type games like Angry Birds, this will give you something to do for an hour to several hours depending on skill and ability to learn.

Diablo-style isometric games seem to be enjoying a rennaissance since Torchlight and in spite (or maybe because) of how abysmally shallow Diablo 3 was. The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing is another entrant in this category, but one that smartly does a few things differently than its contemporaries. I won't go as far as to say that it's necessarily better than my current fave, Torchlight 2, but it's DIFFERENT. And it does it well. If you've never played one of these, Torchlight (1 or 2) might be a better introduction, but for the money they're asking Van Helsing will do fine.
Since I already made the Torchlight 2 comparison, I should stick with it. Gameplay is largely similar, but Van Helsing amps the utility of the companion character. This is a sharp-tongued ghost whose banter with Van Helsing brings in a smattering of levity in sometimes not so appropriate circumstances. While she has a bit less depth than the player character she brings her own skill trees, stats and gear to taylor her to your needs. Which is to say, for my heavy hitting ranged attacker I've specced her to be a 'tank', but she can set up for added damage or support as well. On top of that, Van Helsing has a set of aura skills which further refine the relationship between the two characters. This alone allows for a number of gameplay variety. Add to this a tower defense style subgame for even more fun and two DLC character classes for even more variety and you have a game that seldomly feels boring.
But the real star to me is the setting of Van Helsing. Taking cues from the Hugh Jackman movie of the same name and not being afraid to reach deeply into a cliché vault, the game presents a turn of the century world full of fairy tale monsters, mythical beasts and mad scientists replete with clockwork soldiers and mutant troopers. As hinted at above the game often doesn't take itself too seriously and that is ultimately what makes the mixture work. While not as thought through as the backdrop of, say, Dishonored, it's a nice departure from the generic fantasy tropes you get in most any form of RPG to this day.
The game is far from perfect, still plagued by bugs and balance issues and the way scenery fades out so as to not obstruct your view (or pops back in) can be pretty jarring. But for the price it's being sold at I find that perfectly acceptable. It's not like it's the 3rd part in an acclaimed series from a purported top studio that is a dumbed down version of its predecessor, it doesn't force you to be always online, has no attached con artistry like a cash auction house... you probably get the idea. For what it is, it's a rocking game.

Story: Like Dandelion (same creator), the premise is fantastical but carries a lot of dark and mature themes. The bachelors are your set of (ball-jointed) dolls come to life, who all have their own personalities based on the ones given to them by their manufacturers. It seems ideal for a while, but as you travel down their respective paths, you begin to understand the existential difficulties these guys have and how it affects their relationship with you, themselves and each other. Yes, there's angst.
Like Dandelion and Amnesia, the 'multi romances' are a factor built-in to the central plot and you'll need to go through all the routes to unlock the mysterious 'true plot', which reveals itself increasingly throughout.
Bachelors: I generally enjoy Cheritz's bachelors - they aren't safe from tropes, but they do their tropes well and add a few surprises to keep players on their toes. There are two characters with yandere-like tendencies hiding amongst a cute 'little brother', a caring 'big brother', an aloof ice prince, a playful 'best friend', and a careless playboy.
Romances: The priority is on the emotional connection you build. This is interesting because as your dolls they already "like" you, but this is more or less a shallow reflection of what they think you want to see. Once you get more involved, its fascinating the layers that are revealed - replaying a new route after developing a previous one will help you see how distant the characters really are at the beginning.
Art: The art remains consistent in quality, with a good amount of CGs that you can collect and review in your album.

Mystery and romance. That pretty much sums the game up without revealing too much. It also has fantasy elements to it, but the game is much more than that. The plot is interesting enough with just the mystery, fantasy and romance itself. However, the story is much deeper than that. It deals with issues that anyone of us could have, has had or might be having right now. That is what makes things game impactful. It might make you think. It might make you laugh. It might make you uncomfortable. And it might make you cry. But it's all worth it, when you finally finish that last ending.
Others have noted the same thing that I'm about to say now; even if one of them wasn't your type, most likely you'll like them all at the end. They're a nice set of characters fit for different tastes. All of them grow so much mentally and yet they still can keep that one thing that first drew me to them. They all have issues and they overcome them, not just the romanceable characters but also the heroine herself. The side characters were awesome too, so even if your chosen bishie isn't on the screen, you're most likely to enjoy your time anyway.
While I do like the art, it's not the prettiest one I've seen. Game graphics and art are what first draw me to a game. This game's art is indeed really nice, but CGs looked a bit... awkward at some points. But I'm picky when it comes to game art, so don't let it push you away from this game. It still looks really nice.
Voice acting was great. Really great. I don't understand Korean, so when one word ends and another begins put me off a bit at first. Especially if I'm trying to hear whether the voice ended or just pausing for an effect. But for me, who always keeps voices on (even the annoying ones), it's part of the appeal.
Now, that one minus part. This game has quite a few typos. It's not noticeable all the time, but you might laugh at a bit inappropriate time. But consindering it's only a one minus part, I learned to ignore it.
With only that one minus part, I can definitely recommend the game. The story is deep on the long run, the characters (hopefully) can stir your heart and it leaves an impression on you. The price might be a bit high, but there's always a game that costs even more. I got in on a sale but I saved only a few euros, so it doesn't make much difference. The game is worth the money. All of it.

Nameless is an incredibly context-rich otome visual novel by Cheritz, the same company who created Mystic Messenger and Dandelion, an otome mobile app and Steam game, respectivly. I first became interested in Nameless after playing Mystic Messenger and experiencing how much care, detail, and extensive work Chertiz put into a free mobile app. I thought, surely since they put this much content and love into an app, their Steam games are worth looking into.
Though the $30 price tag may deter many from bothering to pick this game up, I can assure you it's worth every penny and urge you to reconsider.
Overall, I 100% recommend Namless ~The one thing you must recall~ to anyone looking for a high quality and doki doki inducing otome game with a deep and intriguing plot most dating sims don't bother with. In addition, I recommend Cheritz's other two games if you're looking for the same quality, writing, and experience.

Coming in from playing Mystic Messenger, I am not disappointed in the least. I thought this game would be worse than MM, actually, since MM is their newest project, but this is at least just as good. (It's hard for me to say better because MM is close to my heart, but Nameless is just as close at this point.)  Using a traditional visual novel format gives Cheritz a lot of room to work, and they make the absolute best use of it.
A lot of people are saying "this is not your average visual novel, there's an overarching plot," and I just want to emphasize this 100%. I've been playing VNs for years, and I've never played one like this. While each individual route is fantastic, the air of mystery behind all of them really motivates you to play, and this game is magnificently creepy at times. I don't want to spoil anything, but the way this story is done is such a creative and effective use of the visual novel format that I was completely blown away. The overarching story here is a lot deeper than in MM, and it is fantastically executed.
On the whole ball-jointed doll concept: I honestly thought it was the most ridiculous fantasy in the world, but the story is
for it. Like, it's not a weird thing you overlook because the game is so good; it
the game good. A lot of the things that are utterly unique about the characterizations and the overall story would simply not be possible if not for the fact that they're ball-jointed dolls.
Characters and individual routes are amazing. Of course, as with all games, some are better than others (I personally found Yuri's to be the blandest, though I did enjoy his), but even the ones where you're not interested because you want to marry the character or something are still page-turners. The characters are all subversions of standard character types: the kuudere, the shota, the ladykiller, the gentle mom-type, the silly boyish type (I recognize the last one isn't a standard type, but please work with me), and as you delve deeper into their true characters, you start needing to realize why they are the way they are. It's really well-executed; only once does their reasoning behind characterization seem to fall flat, but you let it go because the characterization is just that interesting.
Speaking of individual routes, by the way, I heavily advise you stick to the order the game wants you play the routes in: Lance > Yuri or Yeonho > Tei > Red. Lance is honestly one of my favorite routes and I don't really like to tell you to play it first, but in terms of mystery, Lance's route really reveals nothing. It's just a very good route. Also, make sure to play with the Steam Guide and get every bad end. They're super creepy and super enjoyable, and they also reveal stuff about the overarching plot.
On the technical aspect: amazing voice acting and you can look at the character art for yourself. As well as that, the main character is really sweet and not a pushover. Even if she's a little slow at times, she's cute and nice so it's okay. The rest of the side characters also have really strong personalities, and the minigames are pretty easy.
I know the price is pretty steep, but I assure you that if you can pay it, it's worth it. I'm in Nameless hell. Please play this game.
